en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Section on Virtue in the Dīgha Nikāya.
Commentary on the Introduction to the Work:
At the commencement of the commentary, the homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of announcing the origin, the support, and the purity of the Dhamma to be commented upon;
furthermore, that is for the purpose of generating great respect among the wise toward the commentaries on the Dhamma, so that they may properly attain the virtues such as learning and retention.

It is for the purpose of accomplishing all benefit and happiness through right practice. Alternatively, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem in this commentary is performed because it is auspicious, because it is the preliminary duty for all undertakings, because it is the conduct rightly practiced by the wise, and because others in the future will follow one's example upon seeing it.
Alternatively, the making of this homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of generating a specific merit consisting in the worship of those worthy of worship.
This is for the purpose of generating the power of the karma that has its sign in the success he himself has attained;
for the purpose of preventing its contraction in the interim; and for the purpose of completing the commentary on both of these without obstacle.
And this alone is the purpose intended by the Teacher here. For he will say: "Thus, with a mind clear in faith... [etc.]..."
“By its power. For the worship of the Three Jewels is a preeminent field of merit; it is a superlative merit of immeasurable potency.

Thus, even amidst the manifold obstacles of worldly existence, it is capable of destroying all defilements that constitute those obstacles, and it wards off calamities such as fear and the like. As it has been said:
“‘When one worships those worthy of worship, whether they be Buddhas or their disciples’—and likewise:
‘Monks, those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost. For those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
And: ‘The rapture that arises in the body for one who extols the Buddha...’”
“Indeed, that joy would be better than even the entire Jambudīpa continent.
‘The Dhamma’ … [as before] … ‘The Saṅgha’ … [as before] … ‘The Island.
Likewise—
“Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred... nor by delusion,” and so forth;
“In the forest or at the foot of a tree...
fear or trepidation...”
“Lomahaṃsa shall not exist.

In this context, he spoke these three verses beginning with “whose heart is cooled by compassion,” in order to demonstrate the possession of extraordinary qualities in the Triple Gem which he wished to worship.
For it is through the possession of such extraordinary qualities that one becomes worthy of veneration.
And the homage paid to one worthy of homage accomplishes the intended purpose.

In this regard, the teaching for which he intends to provide a commentary is neither dominated by compassion like the teaching on the Vinaya, nor is it dominated by wisdom like the teaching on the Abhidhamma;
rather, it is dominated by both compassion and wisdom. First, concerning that very dominance of both in the Perfectly Enlightened One:
Because it is the root of all other jewels, it is described as "the heart cooled by compassion" (*karuṇāsītalahadaya*), and so forth.
In this context, *kirati* means "it scatters"; the meaning is that it scatters away or removes the suffering of others. Alternatively, *kiṇāti* means "it afflicts";
the meaning is that when there is suffering in others, it afflicts or troubles the compassionate one. When there is suffering in others, for the virtuous—

Or, it is *karuṇā* because it causes trembling (*kampana*) and heart-weariness (*hadayakheda*). Alternatively, *ka* means happiness (*sukha*); it obstructs that, thus it is *karuṇā*. For this [compassion] has the characteristic of the desire to remove the suffering of others;
by its disregard for one's own happiness, it obstructs—that is, hinders—the happiness of those who are compassionate.
"Cool with compassion" means cool through compassion (*karuṇāsītala*); he whose heart is such is "one whose heart is cool with compassion."

One whose heart is cooled by compassion, that "one whose heart is cooled by compassion. In this regard, although it is observed that both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) are causes for the state of mental coolness—
due to their nature of desiring not to abandon the welfare, happiness, and so forth of others, and due to being the direct opposites of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and aversion (*arati*),
thereby functioning in the mode of cutting off the burning within the continuum of sentient beings— nevertheless, [compassion is distinguished] because it functions in the mode of removing suffering.

Compassion (*karuṇā*), which has as its essence the inability to endure the suffering of others and which is non-violent toward beings, is specifically said to be the cause of the state of coolness for the Blessed One’s mind, just like the tranquility of the mind (*cittapassaddhi*);

thus it is said: "one whose heart is cooled by compassion. Alternatively, it should be understood that through the medium of compassion, the causes for the cooling of the heart of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) are also stated.

Alternatively, because it is the basis for a unique distinction of knowledge—possessing a pervasiveness toward its objects that is both preeminent and exhaustive like the knowledge of omniscience—and has attained the state of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), it is compassion alone that is the cause for the Blessed One’s heart being exceptionally cooled;

thus he says, "one whose heart is cooled by compassion. Alternatively, even though loving-kindness (*mettā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) are also causes for the heart’s cooling in a preeminent way...
Because it is the cause of all the specific qualities of a Buddha, compassion is also called the cause of the Blessed One’s state of coolness in his heart.
Indeed, all the qualities of a Buddha have compassion as their source.

For the Blessed One, whose heat of suffering in saṃsāra was extinguished by the power of compassion, through his desire to remove the suffering of others, even for many incalculable eons, he remained as if untiring.
For one who was certain of accumulating the requisites for all the qualities of a Buddha without exception and who had attained mastery over the Dhamma,
there was not even the slightest alteration in the coolness of his mind, despite the presence of signs that cause the heart to burn when confronted with the conditioned formations of sentient beings.
And in this interpretation of the meaning, it should be understood that the Blessed One’s compassion is encompassed throughout all three stages.
It understands, thus it is wisdom (*paññā*); the meaning is that it penetrates by way of modes according to the true nature of things.
Wisdom itself is a "lamp of wisdom" (*paññā-pajjota*) in the sense of illuminating the specific nature of phenomena through its various modes by means of abandoning the veil of the knowable.

That which is specifically destroyed, eradicated, and dispelled by the abandonment of even the latent tendencies (*savāsanā*) is "dispelled by the lamp of wisdom" (*paññā-pajjota-vihata*). They are deluded...
Because of that, one is either deluded oneself, or the mere state of being deluded is the "delusion" (*moha*);

it is "ignorance" (*avijjā*). Because it conceals the true nature of objects, it is like darkness; thus it is "darkness" (*tamo*). One for whom the darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom is "one for whom the darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom" (*paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo*);
such is the meaning of *paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ*. For indeed, although all those whose taints are exhausted possess the lamp of wisdom...
Since there exists a distinction in the abandonment of defilements among the disciples who have attained vision— just as among those resolved through faith— and among the Paccekabuddhas,
due to the destruction of the darkness of ignorance through the total eradication of even the latent tendencies (*savāsanā*),
he spoke in praise of the Blessed One with reference to his preeminent abandonment of ignorance, saying: "The darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom."
Alternatively, because he has produced within his own continuum the complete disappearance of the darkness of ignorance without depending on the instruction of others,

and because he has attained omniscience therein as well as mastery over the [ten] powers, and because he has correctly set that [knowledge] in motion within the continua of others through the power of his preeminent teaching of the Dhamma—
it is the Blessed One alone who should be especially praised for the removal of the darkness of delusion; thus he said.

“‘The darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom’ (paññāpajjotavihatamohatama). In this interpretation of the meaning, it should be understood that by the phrase “the lamp of wisdom,” both the Blessed One’s wisdom of penetration (*paṭivedha-paññā*) and his wisdom of teaching (*desanā-paññā*) are included through a general designation, either by way of a collective term (*sāmañña-niddesa*) or by the method of mentioning one of two similar things (*ekasesa-naya*).

Alternatively, because the Blessed One’s knowledge extends to the very limits of all that is knowable, it is capable of awakening to the true nature of every dhamma within the entire range of the knowable.

Because the darkness of delusion (*moha-andhakāra*), which obscures the true nature of all knowable phenomena, has been dispelled by the lamp of wisdom (*paññā-pajjota*) known as unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa*),
it is said that "the darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom," making this the destruction of the darkness of delusion unique to the Blessed One.

And herein, because the destruction of the darkness of delusion has been attained, unobstructed knowledge— by way of metaphorical attribution to its cause— is [said to be present] within one's own continuum.

The dispelling of the darkness of delusion is what must be seen. For the abandonment of the defilements together with their latent tendencies through the perfection of the formal resolution is indeed called the "abandonment of the cognitive obstruction" (ñeyyāvaraṇappahāna).

However, because it serves as the cause for the dispelling of the darkness of delusion in the mental continuums of others, unobstructed knowledge is called the "dispelling of the darkness of delusion."

But what is the reason that only the destruction of ignorance (*avijjā-vighāta*) is taken as the basis for praising the Blessed One by way of his perfection in abandonment, rather than the abandonment of all defilements (*kilesa*) with their specific excesses?

It is because, by the very mention of its abandonment, the eradication of the entire mass of defilements is manifested due to their being associated with it; for there is no such defilement that remains when ignorance has been abandoned without remainder.

"It is not abandoned. Alternatively, just as with true knowledge (*vijjā*), ignorance (*avijjā*) is the primary cause for the arising of all unwholesome states without exception, for the production of all unwholesome phenomena, and for the continuation of *saṃsāra*.
Therefore, by stating that which destroys it, the total eradication of the entire mass of defilements is indeed expressed;
thus it is said: "The darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom."
Humans and immortals (gods) are *narāmarā*; together with humans and immortals is *sanarāmara*. That which is both *sanarāmara* and the world (*loka*) is *sanarāmaraloka*;
his respect for that is *sanarāmaralokagaru*; [the Blessed One] is one who has such respect for the world of humans and gods.
By this, he shows the Blessed One’s quality of being a benefactor even to those remaining beings—just as he is to gods and humans—by bestowing appropriate distinctions of virtue upon them.

And here, one should not raise the objection regarding the status of what is primary (padhāna) and what is secondary (apadhāna). For the order of words (saddakkama) is one thing, while the order of meaning (atthakkama) is another.
In such compound expressions, even that which is primary is presented as if it were secondary, as in the phrase "the assembly together with the king" (*sarājikāya parisāya*).

Granted, in this context, the world is threefold—by way of sentient beings (*satta*), formations (*saṅkhāra*), and the vessel-world (*bhājana*)—but because the state of being weighty (*garubhāva*) is intended here, [the former is placed first].
The meaning should be understood by way of the world of beings (*sattaloka*), for it is only that which is capable of showing respect that is appropriate [here].

Indeed, that is called "the world" (*loka*) because merit and demerit, as well as their ripening, are experienced (*lokyanti*) therein. And here, by the mention of "immortals," the deities of rebirth (*upapattideva*) are intended.
Alternatively, the word *loka* has the sense of a collection; it is so called because, as a totality, it is perceived (*lokīyati*) or made known. "Together with men" (*saha narehi*).

"Sanarā" means together with humans; "sanarāmarā" means together with humans and those immortals (*amarā*). It should be construed in the same manner as before: "the world of those [beings]" is the "world of humans and immortals.
Furthermore, by the term "immortal" (*amara*), the purified deities (*visuddhideva*) are also included therein, for they are in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) immortal due to the absence of death.
And the mention of only humans and immortals is by way of an inclusive designation (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*), just as in the case of: "The Teacher..."

“Of gods and humans. For indeed, by means of his unsurpassed perfection of application—which is preceded by the avoidance of all that is harmful and intent solely upon the provision of welfare and happiness without exception—the Blessed One is the supreme among all beings, owing to his state of being the ultimate benefactor to the generation consisting of gods and humans, and because he possesses immeasurable and incomparable distinctions of power and virtue;
thus, in infinite world-systems, he is the highest for infinite beings.
It is a ground for reverence; therefore it is said: "He who is revered by the world of men and gods.
He whose going (gati) is beautiful (sobhana) is the Sugata. For the Blessed One’s approach to those who are to be trained is beautiful because it invariably accomplishes their welfare and happiness;
likewise, his physical body is adorned with the primary marks and secondary characteristics, and his gait is neither hurried nor sluggish.
Free from defects such as stumbling, dragging, pressing down, hunching, crookedness, and confusion, his bodily movement and the movement of his knowledge—
resembling the gait of a graceful royal swan, a bull, an elephant, and the king of beasts— accompanied by the distinguished qualities of vast, stainless compassion, mindfulness, energy, and so forth,
was indeed beautiful in its faultlessness from the initial resolution until the attainment of Great Enlightenment.

Alternatively, he is the Sugata because, through his self-existent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), he has rightly gone to and understood the entire world by means of the realization of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*).

Likewise, he is the Sugata because, through the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*), he has rightly gone beyond and transcended the origin of the world (*lokasamudaya*) by abandoning it and bringing about its state of non-arising (*anuppattidhammata*).
[He is the Sugata] through the realization of direct experience (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*) regarding the cessation of the world, which is Nibbāna.

He has gone rightly and has attained [the goal], thus he is the Sugata. He has gone rightly and has practiced the path leading to the cessation of the world by means of development and clear realization, thus he is the Sugata.

This meaning should be elucidated in such a manner as: "He does not go back to, does not return to, and does not come back again to those defilements which were abandoned by the stream-entry path; therefore he is the Sugata," and so forth. Now...
He is the Sugata because he has gone to or attained a beautiful state—namely, perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) or even Nibbāna itself.
Alternatively, he is the Sugata because he speaks the Dhamma that is real, true, beneficial, and appropriate for those to be trained, at the right time;

thus, having changed the letter *da* to *ta*, he "speaks well" (*sammā gadati*), hence he is the Sugata. Thus, he is the Sugata by virtue of his beautiful gait and other such qualities; [the text refers to] that Sugata.
The "destinies" (*gati*) are the specific states of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), so called because they are to be gone to by way of arising through meritorious and evil kamma.
These are fivefold, categorized as hell and so forth.

Because all kamma leading to existence has been turned back by the attainment of the Noble Path—rendering it incapable of ripening—the Blessed One is well-liberated and dissociated from even these five destinies.

He said: “Liberated from the realms of existence. By this, he shows that the Blessed One is not included within any realm whatsoever, which is why the Blessed One is called the “God beyond gods. For this very reason it is said:
“By whom one would be reborn as a god, or as a gandhabba, or as a bird;”
“Those taints by which one might go to the state of a *yakkha* or fall back into the human state—
those taints of mine are exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless. For,
at the very foot of the Bodhi tree, those defilements of action (*kamma-kilesa*) that lead to various states of existence were completely abandoned by means of the supreme path.

"There is no inclusion of the Blessed One within any state of existence" means that the Blessed One is absolutely and completely liberated from all states of being, wombs, destinies, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and classes of beings;
thus, "liberated from destiny" (gativimutta) means "I worship," "I bow down to," or "I praise him.
Alternatively, "liberated from destiny" praises the Blessed One by virtue of his attainment of the element of Nirvana without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Herein—
Indeed, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in two ways: by way of the attainment of his own welfare and by way of his practice for the welfare of others.

Among these, the attainment of his own welfare is to be understood through the acquisition of unobstructed knowledge, the absolute abandonment of all defilements together with their latent tendencies, and the realization of *nibbāna* without residue.
The practice for the welfare of others is [to be understood] through the mind that is indifferent to gain, honor, and the like.

This is because he teaches the Dhamma that leads out of all suffering; because his intention is always for the welfare of others, even toward those who oppose him; and because the time has arrived for the ripening of his knowledge.

Furthermore, herein, his practice for the benefit of others is shown to be twofold—by way of disposition (*āsaya*) and by way of application (*payoga*)—and his attainment of his own welfare is shown to be threefold.
How so? By the phrase "whose heart is cooled by compassion," his practice for the benefit of others by way of disposition is indicated. By the word "rightly" (*sammā*),...
By the word *sugata* in the sense of "gone well" (*gadanattha*), there is the practice for the benefit of others through its application;

and by the word *sugata* in the sense of the penetration of the Four Truths—through the phrases "whose darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom" and "released from rebirth"—there is the threefold attainment of one's own welfare.

By the remainder, namely the phrase "whose darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom," both the attainment of one's own welfare and the practice for the benefit of others are fully revealed.
Alternatively, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood through three aspects: by way of cause, by way of fruit, and by way of benefit.

Therein, the cause is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which is indicated by the first phrase. The fruit is fourfold: perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*), perfection of abandonment (*pahānasampadā*), perfection of power (*ānubhāvasampadā*), and perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāyasampadā*).
Among these, the perfections of knowledge and abandonment are indicated by the second phrase, in the sense of the penetration of the truths.

And they are manifested by the word *sugata*. The perfection of power is indicated by the third term; the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is indicated by the word *sugata* in the sense of the beauty of the body and its gait as previously described, since that [beauty] cannot exist without the fulfillment of the primary marks (*lakkhaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*).
The benefit consists in teaching the Dhamma of liberation through the three vehicles, making no distinction between internal and external;
this is indicated by the word *sugata* in the sense of "one who has gone rightly" (*sammā gadana*).
It should be understood that this has been explained.
In this context, by the phrase "whose heart is cooled by compassion," he shows the root of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).

For the Blessed One, his mind impelled by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), made a formal resolve to uplift sentient beings from the mire of *saṃsāra*, and [cultivated] the perfections (*pāramitā*) in successive stages.
Having fulfilled [the perfections], he attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; thus, compassion is the root of perfect enlightenment.

By the phrase “The darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom,” he demonstrates perfect enlightenment. For path-knowledge has unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause, and unobstructed knowledge has path-knowledge as its proximate cause;
this is what is called “perfect enlightenment. By the word *sugata*, in the sense of having gone rightly (*sammā gadana*), [he indicates] perfect enlightenment.
The word *sugata* indicates the practice (*paṭipatti*), because it reveals the Middle Way (*majjhimā paṭipadā*)—

which is embraced by compassion and wisdom and is free from the two extremes such as attachment to the pleasure of sensual indulgence and self-mortification, or the adherence to eternalism and annihilationism,

which serve as the basis for and the accumulation of dullness and agitation. By the other [words], the purpose is shown through the distinction between the primary and secondary efforts toward Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
He shows this. Herein, the primary purpose is the crossing over of sentient beings from the great flood of saṃsāra; any other purpose is secondary.
Among these, by means of the primary purpose he shows the practice for the benefit of others, and by the other he shows the attainment of one's own benefit.
By both together, he shows that among the four types of persons—those practicing for their own benefit and so forth—the Blessed One is the fourth type of person.
And by this, he demonstrates the Blessed One’s state of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*anuttara-dakkhiṇeyya*), his state of being the supreme object of veneration,
and his own status as having entered the field (*khetta*) for the act of paying homage.

Furthermore, here, by the inclusion of "compassion" (*karuṇā*), there is the illumination of the Blessed One’s extraordinary qualities that have attained the state of loftiness (*mahaggata*) among worldly beings.

The attainment of all mundane qualities is shown; by the mention of "wisdom" (paññā), the attainment of all supramundane qualities is indicated, because it illuminates the knowledge of the path which has the knowledge of omniscience as its proximate cause.
For the meaning established by the inclusion of both these [qualities] is elaborated upon in such passages as "the one revered by the world of men and gods.
Furthermore, by the mention of "compassion" (karuṇā), he shows that his approach is free from defilement; by the mention of "wisdom,"...

...the departure. Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), he shows the Blessed One’s activity in accordance with worldly convention, because compassion is within the domain of worldly discourse; by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), he shows not overstepping that convention.

For it is through the failure to understand the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena that one oversteps convention and clings to [notions] such as "a being. Likewise, by the mention of compassion...

He demonstrates the dwelling in the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti-vihāra*). By the mention of "wisdom" (*paññā*), there is included knowledge unimpeded regarding the three times, the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths, the knowledge of the four analytical insights (*catu-paṭisambhidā*), and the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vessārajja*).

By the mention of "compassion" (*karuṇā*), since the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is already included, there are included the remaining unique knowledges, the six direct knowledges (*cha-abhiññā*), the knowledges of being unshakable among the eight assemblies, and the ten [powers].

He demonstrates the range of his knowledge by way of many such classifications of wisdom (*paññā*), such as the powers (*balāni*), the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha (*buddhañāṇāni*), the sixteen modes of conduct of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*), the eighteen qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadhammā*), the forty-four bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthūni*), and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthūni*).

Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), he shows the perfection of his conduct (*caraṇasampatti*); by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), he shows the perfection of his true knowledge (*vijjāsampatti*). By the mention of compassion...

By the inclusion of compassion (*karuṇā*), there is the state of being the lord of beings; by the inclusion of wisdom (*paññā*), there is the state of having the Dhamma as one's lord. By the inclusion of compassion, there is the status of being a protector of the world;
by the inclusion of wisdom, there is the status of being one's own protector. Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion, there is the quality of being a pioneer;

by the inclusion of wisdom, there is gratitude. Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion, there is non-affliction of others; by the inclusion of wisdom, there is non-affliction of oneself. Or else, by the inclusion of compassion, there is the accomplishment of the qualities that constitute a Buddha.
By the inclusion of wisdom (paññā), the attainment of Buddhahood is established. Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion (karuṇā), the rescuing of others is shown;
by the inclusion of wisdom, one's own rescue is shown. Similarly, by the inclusion of compassion, a mind of benevolence toward all beings is indicated;
by the inclusion of wisdom, a mind detached from all phenomena is indicated. Furthermore, compassion is the beginning of all the qualities of a Buddha, because it is their primary cause.
Wisdom is the culmination, because there is nothing further to be done beyond it. Thus, by showing both the beginning and the culmination, all the qualities of a Buddha are demonstrated.
Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion, the aggregate of concentration—preceded by the aggregate of virtue—is shown.
For virtue has its source in compassion, since it proceeds from the abstention from killing living beings and so forth; and that compassion is associated with the three jhānas.

By the term "wisdom" (paññā), the aggregate of wisdom (paññā-khandha) is meant. Virtue (sīla) is the beginning of all the Buddha-qualities, concentration (samādhi) is the middle, and wisdom is the end.
Thus, by this method of exposition, all the Buddha-qualities are shown to be beautiful in their beginning, middle, and end, because they are presented through a systematic principle (naya).
For this indeed is the means for demonstrating the Buddha-qualities without exception: namely, grasping them by way of their underlying principle.
Otherwise, who indeed would be capable of showing the virtues of the Blessed One in their entirety, even word by word?
For this very reason it was said: "Even a Buddha, speaking the praise of a Buddha for an eon, without uttering anything else..."
“The eon might pass away in its long duration, yet the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.

And for this very reason, even the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, when questioned regarding the delimitation of the Buddha’s qualities, rejected [the attempt to define them] by saying, “Certainly not, Bhante,” and added, “But rather, Bhante, the sequence of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya) has been understood by me.”
Having thus praised the Blessed One in brief by means of all his qualities of omniscience, he now spoke the words beginning with "Buddho pi" in order to extol the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*).
Therein, "Buddho" is a designation of the agent; "buddhabhāvaṃ" is a designation of the object; "bhāvetvā" and "sacchikatvā" are designations of prior actions;
"yaṃ" is an indefinite designation of the object; and "upagato" [is the designation of the subject].
The exposition of the act of paying homage at a later time. "Vandeti" (he pays homage) is the exposition of the action; "tanti" (the [text]) is the restriction.
"Dhammaṃ" (the Dhamma) is the exposition of the object of the act of paying homage. "Gatamalaṃ" (whose stains are gone) and "anuttaraṃ" (unexcelled) are its qualifiers.
In that regard, first concerning the word *buddha*: "He is a Buddha because he has awakened to the truths; he is a Buddha because he awakens the generation," and so forth.
The meaning should be understood according to the method of exposition (*niddesa*).

Alternatively, he is "Awakened" (*buddha*) because of the absolute departure of the sleep of ignorance along with its latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), or because of the state of blossoming of his intelligence; thus, he is *buddha* in the sense of waking up and blossoming.

Alternatively, it is because there is no knowable phenomenon (*ñeyyadhamma*) whatsoever that has not been awakened to, and because no specific object of knowledge is left ungrasped as an object of action.
Since there is no intention to perform an action (*kammavacanicchā*), the designation of the agent is obtained solely in the sense of understanding;
thus, "he has awakened" (*buddhavā*) is "the Awakened One" (*buddho*), just as in the expression, "one who has been ordained does not give.

In terms of meaning, however, he is one whose defilements have been entirely destroyed and shattered by self-born knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*) together with its latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), being thoroughly refined by the perfections (*pāramitā*), and possessing immeasurable qualities such as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
The Buddha is the continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna) which is the locus of a multitude of virtues. As it is said:

"Buddha means that Blessed One who is self-become (sayambhū), teacherless, who by himself awakened to the truths regarding phenomena unheard of before, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers.
The word *api* is used in the sense of esteem; by it, one intends: "Even that Blessed One, endowed with such distinguished qualities... [referring to] the qualities about to be described.
He demonstrates esteem for the Dhamma. "Buddha-nature" means perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). "Having developed" means having produced and increased it.
"Having realized" means having made it manifest to direct experience. "Attained" means reached or achieved;
this is the meaning, and it is connected with the term "Buddha-nature. "Gata-mala" means free from stain; the meaning is "faultless. "I venerate" means I bow down and praise.
"Anuttara" means devoid of anything superior; the meaning is "supramundane.
"Dhamma" is so called because it holds (dhāreti) those who practice according to its instructions, preventing them from falling into the states of misery or into the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
This is the summary of the meaning here: even the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is thus endowed with manifold qualities, [proclaimed] that which is designated as the Noble [Path].
Having developed the Dhamma and having realized that which is termed the fruit and Nibbāna, he attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;

I pay homage to that very True Dhamma of penetration, which is the cause of even the Buddhas’ Buddhahood, which is free from all stains of defilement, and which is unsurpassed because there is nothing superior to it.
Since it also elucidates the True Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti), [it is included] here.

The inclusion [of the Dhamma] should be understood. Alternatively, since it is stated in the Commentary that "having developed the ocean of the Abhidhamma method, he attained it, and he comprehended the three Piṭakas," the term "realization" (*sacchikiriyā*) and "comprehension" (*sammasana*) also apply to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*);
therefore, it should be understood that this too is indeed mentioned here. Likewise, regarding the phrase "having developed and realized which Dhamma... [the same principle applies].

And because it has been so stated, it should be understood that here, by the term *dhamma*, the trainings in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and the rest during the preliminary stage are also included along with the perfections (*pāramitā*), which constitute the qualities that make one a Buddha.
For these too are "stainless" (*vigata-mala*) due to being free from opposites, and "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) due to not being shared by others.
Thus, for the sake of the liberation of beings from the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*),...
What is this great resolve? It is the mastery attained over deeds and other factors through the thorough cultivation, without omission, continuously and with reverence,
for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons, of the supreme qualities— such as generosity, self-control, tranquility, and restraint—
which are purified by the excellence of wisdom and characterized by a noble disposition imbued with great compassion.

The Blessed One, possessing marvelous and inconceivable great power, having reached the supreme pinnacle of higher virtue (*adhisīla*) and higher mind (*adhicitta*), dispatched the Great Vajra-knowledge through twenty-four million four hundred thousand modes regarding the nature of conditions (*paccayākāra*), and thus awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara sammāsambodhi*).

And herein, by the word "having developed" (*bhāvetvā*), he praises the Dhamma through the perfection of true knowledge (*vijjā*); by the word "having realized" (*sacchikatvā*), [he praises it through the perfection of liberation].
[The first is] by way of the perfection of liberation; likewise, the first is by way of the perfection of jhāna, and the second is by way of the perfection of liberation.
Or, the first is by way of the perfection of concentration, and the second is by way of the perfection of attainment.

Alternatively, the first is by way of the state of the knowledge of destruction, and the second is by way of the state of the knowledge of non-arising. Or, the former is by way of its resemblance to lightning, and the latter is by way of its resemblance to a thunderbolt.

Or, by the first [term] there is the attainment of dispassion (*virāga*), and by the second, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*). Likewise, by the first there is the state of escape (*niyyāna*), and by the second, the state of renunciation (*nissaraṇa*).
Or, by the first there is the state of cause (*hetu*), and by the second, the state of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).
Or, by the first there is the state of vision (*dassana*), and by the second, the state of seclusion (*viveka*). Or, by the first there is the state of predominance (*adhipati*), and by the second...

He praises the Dhamma by way of its being the Deathless (*amata*). Alternatively, he praises the Dhamma for its being well-expounded by the phrase, "having developed that Dhamma, he attained the state of a Buddha";
he praises it for its being directly visible (*sanditthika*) by the phrase, "having realized it.

Likewise, he praises it for its being timeless (*akālika*) by the former [phrase], and for its being inviting one to come and see (*ehipassika*) by the latter. Or alternatively, he praises it for its leading onward (*opanayika*) by the former, and by the latter...
He praises the Dhamma because it is to be personally realized.
By the phrase "with stains gone," he shows the purity of the Dhamma through the indication of the absence of defilement;
by the word "unsurpassed," he shows its vast perfection through the indication of the non-existence of anything else superior to it. Or, by the first [phrase], he shows the perfection of abandonment.

By the first [phrase], he shows the nature of the Dhamma; by the second, its perfection of radiance. Alternatively, the state of being free from impurity (*gatamala*) should be applied to the Dhamma because it is to be developed (*bhāvetabba*);

for through the quality of development, it becomes the eradicator of defilements. Its unsurpassed nature (*anuttara*) should be applied by way of its being that which is to be realized (*sacchikātabba*);
for once the realization is produced, there is nothing further to be done, and thus it is not shared with others.

"Unsurpassed" (anuttara). Likewise, by the term "having developed" (bhāvetvā), the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom pertaining to those in training (sekkha) are shown along with the preliminary virtues and so forth;

by the term "having realized" (sacchikatvā), the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom pertaining to those beyond training (asekkha) are shown along with the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu).
Thus, having praised the True Dharma (saddhamma) in brief by means of all its qualities, [the text now praises] the Noble Saṅgha.
To offer praise, he spoke the words beginning with "of the Sugata. Therein, "of the Sugata" is a genitive expression of relationship; its connection is with the word "sons.
"Orasānaṃ" (of the legitimate) is a qualification of "sons. "Mārasenamathanānaṃ" (of those who crush the army of Māra) is a statement of the reason for their status as legitimate sons;
by this, he acknowledges that the very abandonment of the defilements is the cause for the Blessed One’s status as having them as his legitimate sons.

It shows [this]. "Of eight" is a description delimiting the number; by this, it shows that although they possess the status of distinct beings and thus number in the hundreds of thousands, they do not exceed this numerical limit, because they do not transcend the state of being established in the path or the fruit.
"Community" is a description of a collection. "Noble Saṅgha" is a description of the state of being a community distinguished by its virtues; by this—
This shows that even in the absence of physical harmony among noble persons, they possess the status of the Noble Saṅgha because they are united by the commonality of their view and virtue.
In this context, "urasā" means those who exist in, are born from, or have grown in the breast (the heart).
Just as the legitimate sons of beings—by virtue of being born from them—are especially entitled to the inheritance belonging to their father, so too are these noble persons.
They are "legitimate sons" (*orasa*) because they are born from the Noble Birth at the ear of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
and thus are the absolute partakers of the bliss of liberation belonging to the Blessed One and of the jewel of the Noble Dhamma; or else,

because the Noble Disciples— both those entering and those who have entered the plane of the Noble Ones— have been produced by the exertion of the Blessed One’s breast through the power of his teaching of the Dhamma.

In the primary sense (*nippariyāya*), they are worthy of being called "sons from the breast" (*orasaputta*). For even when the teaching of the Dhamma is being carried out by disciples, it is still called the "Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma" because it has its source in him and because it lacks any distinction in terms of its characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth.

Even though, at the time of the noble disciples’ attainment of the Noble Path, there may be those who act to create obstacles for them—just as there were for the Blessed One—[the teaching remains his].
Neither Māra the Son of the Gods nor the host of Māra rejects [the Buddhas] absolutely;
however, when the grounds for their rejection have been undermined by them, they too are indeed said to be "overthrown. Thus it is said:

"of those who crush Māra’s army. In this sense, although one should say "of those who crush Māra and Māra’s army," the term "of those who crush Māra’s army" is formed by a single-remainder compound (*ekadesasarūpeka-sesa*) based on a partial similarity.

It should be understood thus. Alternatively, just as with the Māras of the aggregates and the formations, the host of the power of the defilements is called an "army" because it enters into the state of being an ally in the slaying of the Devaputta-Māra. As it is said: "Sensual pleasures are your first army," and so forth.

And that river of defilements, consisting of one thousand five hundred divisions or indeed infinite divisions, [is to be overcome] by the weapons of such qualities as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, and serenity.
They have crushed, shattered, and scattered Māra’s army; thus, noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) are "crushers of Māra’s army.
By this, he shows that they are sons born after the Blessed One.

They are called "noble" (ariya) by way of etymology because they are far removed from defilements, because they do not proceed in what is not the right way, and because they proceed in the right way. Now...

Or, it is the "Ariya-saṅgha" because it is worthy of being approached (*araṇīya*) as a refuge (*saraṇa*) by the world including the devas, and because for those who have approached it, their purpose is accomplished;
thus it is the Saṅgha of the Ariyas. Alternatively, it is the Ariya-saṅgha because it is both noble (*ariya*) and a community (*saṅgha*). That is the Ariya-saṅgha.
After the Blessed One, the attainment of even the jewels of the Buddha and the Dhamma is dependent upon the jewel of the Saṅgha.
It should be understood that the words "I worship with my head" were spoken right here in order to demonstrate the great helpfulness of that Noble Saṅgha.
And herein, by the phrase "the legitimate sons of the Sugata," he demonstrates the perfection of origin of the Noble Saṅgha;
by the phrase "the destroyers of Māra’s army," he demonstrates the perfection of abandonment, because this indicates the abandonment of all defilements. Of the eight [types of noble persons]...
By the term "assembly" (*samūha*), he indicates the perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*), because it illustrates the state of being established on the path and the fruit.
By the term "Noble Saṅgha" (*ariyasaṅgha*), he shows the perfection of origin (*pabhavasampadā*), because it illustrates the preeminence of all assemblies.
Alternatively, "the legitimate sons of the Sugata" illustrates the Noble Saṅgha’s state of having a pure basis (*visuddhanissaya*), while "the destroyers of Māra’s army" [illustrates their power].

The phrase "those who have entered upon the right way, the straight way, the proper way" illustrates their state of practicing correctly; "the assembly of eight" illustrates their status as those worthy of offerings (*āhuneyya*) and so forth;

and "the Noble Saṅgha" illustrates their status as the unsurpassed field of merit (*puññakkhetta*). Likewise, by the phrase "the legitimate sons of the Sugata," he demonstrates that the Noble Saṅgha possesses the quality of having gone for refuge to the supramundane. Through this going for refuge to the supramundane—
For they were born as the legitimate sons of the Blessed One.

By the phrase "crushers of Māra’s army," he shows the practice in the prior stage accomplished through the perfection of the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*). For those who have made the resolve and have practiced rightly conquer Māra or Māra’s retinue.
By the phrase "the host of even the eight," he refers to the qualities of those in training (*sekkha*) and those beyond training (*asekkha*), whose adversaries have been shattered.

It shows [the excellence of the Saṅgha] because the qualities of the path and its fruits are proclaimed by way of reference to individuals. By the term “Noble Saṅgha,” it shows their state as the most worthy recipients of offerings.

Furthermore, for disciples, going for refuge is the beginning of all virtues; the virtuous aggregates (sīlakkhandha) and so forth of those in training, together with their preliminary practice, constitute the middle;
and the virtuous aggregates of those beyond training constitute the end. Thus, it is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
In brief, all the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha are thus revealed.

Having thus paid homage to the Triple Gem by way of a concise summary of its entire range of virtues through these three verses, he now says "Thus to me," etc., dedicating that prostration toward his intended purpose. Therein:

It is a treasure (*ratana*) in the sense of producing delight; [this refers to] the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. For when one reflects upon their qualities as they truly are, beginning with "Thus indeed is the Blessed One," a no small measure of rapture and joy arises, which serves as the cause for attaining the Deathless. As it is said:
"Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time he does not..."
The mind is not obsessed by lust, the mind is not obsessed by hatred, and the mind is not obsessed by delusion;
rather, at that time, his mind is directed straight toward the Tathāgata.
And when, Mahānāma, a noble disciple has a mind directed straightly, he gains inspiration from the meaning, he gains inspiration from the Dhamma, and he gains...
“Delight connected with the Dhamma arises; in one who is delighted, rapture is born,” and so forth.
Alternatively, the meaning of “jewel” (ratana) is its state of being esteemed and so on. For this has been said:
“It is esteemed and of great value, incomparable, and rare to behold;”
“Because it is enjoyed by beings who are peerless, it is therefore called a ‘jewel’ (ratana).
Furthermore, qualities such as being held in high esteem are found only in the Buddhas and others, and not shared with anyone else.

“Consisting of worship” (vandanāmaya) means simply worship (vandanā), just as there are expressions like “consisting of giving” (dānamaya) or “consisting of virtue” (sīlamaya). And here, worship is the inclination toward the virtues of the Three Jewels through body, speech, and mind.
Or it is "praise" (*thomanā*). It is "merit" (*puñña*) because it produces the fruit of becoming worthy of honor, or because it purifies one's own continuum (*santāna*).
"With obstacles well-destroyed" means with obstacles thoroughly destroyed;

by this, he shows that through the excellence of his own faith and the excellence of the Triple Gem as a field, that merit is capable of destroying those calamities that obstruct the exposition of the meaning.
"Having offered" (*hutvā*) is an action in the prior time; it is connected with the phrase "I shall explain its meaning.
"Of that" (*tassa*) refers to that merit consisting of homage to the Triple Gem. "By the power" (*ānubhāvena*) means by the strength.
Having thus shown the purpose for performing service toward the Triple Gem, [the author now proceeds] to that teaching of the Dhamma...
Desiring to praise the meaning, the words beginning with "of the long" (*dīghassā*) were spoken for the purpose of introducing it by way of extolling its virtues.
Therein, "of that which is marked by a long thread" (*dīghasuttaṅkitassa*) means of that which is characterized by a thread of long measure;

by this, he shows that the designation "long" (*dīgho*) is a conventional name (*samaññā*) of this Āgama that conforms to its meaning. But is it not the case that the sūtras themselves are the Āgama? To whom [does the name apply]?
"But is it marked by the suttas? This is true from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*); however, the "tradition" (*āgama*) is designated based upon the suttas.

For just as the conventional term "sutta" is used for a collection of meaning and phrasing, so too the term "āgama" is used for a collection of suttas. It is "precise" (*nipuṇa*) because of the presence of subtle meanings such as dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
[The word *āgama* is derived thus: they come (*āgamissanti*) to this, by means of this, or from this.

Or, it is an *āgama* because it concerns one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth; it is an *āgamavara* because it is both an *āgama* and excellent (*vara*), or because it is excellent among those recognized as *āgamas*.
Of that [work]. Those who have awakened after the Buddhas are the "Buddha-anubuddhas" (those awakened after the Buddhas);

these are the noble ones, such as the chief disciples, who have penetrated the Truths by following the Buddhas’ penetration of the Truths. By means of them, through the exposition of the meaning and through the exposition of their qualities...
And [it refers to] that which has been praised. Alternatively, it should be construed as "the Buddhas and those awakened after the Buddha" (*buddhānubuddhā*).

For the sequence for commenting on the meaning of all three Piṭakas was indeed spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself; this is what is called the "Miscellaneous Teaching" (*pakiṇṇakadesanā*).
From that, [the commentary was established] by the disciples through means such as the communal recitation (*saṅgāyana*), so say the teachers.
"Of the quality that brings forth faith" means of that which possesses the excellence of inspiring confidence in the Buddha and others.

For this scripture [the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*] does so by way of the exhaustive description of virtue, view, and so forth in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* and others; by way of the description of the qualities of previous Buddhas as well in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta* and others;
by way of the roaring of the irreversible lion’s roar after crushing the heretics in the *Pāṭika Sutta* and others; and in the *Anuttariya Sutta* and others...
Moreover, it specifically brings about an exceptional degree of serene confidence (*pasāda*) toward the Triple Gem by means of the manifestation of the Buddha’s qualities.
This is the custom of the Master in his commentaries:

that at the beginning of each respective commentary, there is a praise consisting of a proclamation of the specific virtues of the particular doctrine (*dhamma*) to be commented upon. For instance, this is seen in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, and the *Manorathapūraṇī*.
And in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* and other works, praise is offered for it in successive order as follows: "Of that Abhidhamma, which crushes the arguments of opponents,
generates the differentiation of knowledge, produces diverse eloquence for the preeminent teachers of the Dhamma,
is plunged into by profound insights, and is constantly variegated by manifold methods."

It is called *atthakathā* because meaning (*attha*) is explained by it; that itself is the *Aṭṭhakathā*, having changed the letter *ttha* to *ṭṭha*, as in the expression "the meaning of the oppression of suffering" (*dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho*).
"From the beginning" means in the first council (*paṭhamasaṅgīti*) at the beginning [of the text].

[He is so called] because he was endowed with supreme mastery over the mind through the possession of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and because of the presence of the fivefold mastery in the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and other states.
The masters are the elders Mahākassapa and others. By five hundred of them. "Yā" refers to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

It is called "recited" (*saṅgītā*) because it was spoken by collecting [the explanations] in appropriate places for clarifying the meaning, saying, "This is the meaning of this; this is the meaning of that.
And it was "recited subsequently" (*anusaṅgītā*) later on by the elder Yasa and others during the second and third councils. By this, [he shows] his own...
By means of this commentary, he demonstrates the purity of its lineage.
One who is taken from or seized by a lion (*sīha*) is a *Sīhaḷa*; thus [is] Prince Sīha.

Because they were born of his lineage, the khattiyas in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, and because it was their dwelling place, the state of being *Sīhaḷa* should be understood to apply both to them and to the island of Tambapaṇṇi. "Brought" means brought from Jambudīpa.
It was brought [to Ceylon]. Then, later on, for the sake of non-confusion, the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) was established in the Sinhalese language.
Therefore, he shows that since the original commentary (*mūlaṭṭhakathā*) was not common to all, this exposition of the meaning must be performed unconditionally;
thus he says, "for the benefit of those dwelling on the island. In that context, "those dwelling on the island" means those dwelling on Jambudīpa.
The construction is as follows: "For the sake of the inhabitants of the island" (*dīpavāsīnaṃ*) means for the sake of those dwelling on the island of Siṃhala;

it was established in the Siṃhalese language. "Having removed" (*apanetvāna*) means having removed the Siṃhalese language, which is like a covering (*kañcuka*). "From that" (*tato*) means from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "I" (*ahaṃ*) refers to himself.
"The delightful language" (*manoramaṃ bhāsaṃ*) means the Māgadhī language; for that is the natural mode of expression (*sabhāvanirutti*) for the wise.

"It delights the mind. For this very reason, he says: "Conforming to the method of the threads" (*tantinayānucchavikaṃ*), which means it is in accordance with the course of the Pāḷi and conforms to the Pāḷi language.
"Free from faults" (*vigatadosaṃ*) means devoid of unrefined expressions and other languages.

"Not violating the system" (*samayaṃ avilomento*) means not contradicting the established doctrine (*siddhanta*); by this, he states the absence of defects in meaning. Because it is non-contradictory...
For it is indeed the Theravāda that will be elucidated here. Regarding the phrase "of the lamps of the Theravamsa":

they are called *theras* because they are endowed with the stable aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth; these are Mahākassapa and the others. The lineage transmitted by them is the *theravamsa*.
Being included within that lineage, they are "lamps of the Theravamsa" because, being perfected in scripture and realization, they cause it to blaze forth with the light of wisdom (*paññā*).
The elders who dwell in the Mahāvihāra; [the word] *tesaṃ* refers to them. It is called a *vinicchaya* (decision) because it is determined in various ways;

it is a discourse that cuts off doubt, proceeding in the manner of removing a splinter from knotted places. Those for whom the decision (*vinicchaya*) is very subtle and refined are "those of very subtle decisions" (*sunipuṇavinicchayā*).
Alternatively, it is a *vinicchaya* because it decides (*vinicchinoti*); it is the knowledge regarding the aforementioned objects. Very...
"Those whose determinations (*vinicchaya*) are skillful and clever are 'those of most skillful determination' (*sunipuṇavinicchayā*).

By this, he shows that [this work] is derived from the succession of the elders beginning with the Elder Mahākassapa, and for that very reason, it is the unerring, subtle, and refined determination of those who dwell in the Great Monastery (*Mahāvihāra*), thereby demonstrating its status as an authoritative standard.

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and for the sake of the virtuous person" (*sujanassa ca*) has the sense of inclusion; by it, he indicates that it is not only for the sake of those dwelling in Jambudīpa.

This shows that it was for the purpose of pleasing virtuous people; by this, the meaning that it was also for the benefit of those dwelling on the island of Tambapaṇṇi is established, because it is of great assistance to them as well, since it makes learning and so forth easy.

"For the sake of long endurance" means for the purpose of its long-lasting persistence; the meaning is: for its stability over a long period of time. For this exposition of the meaning [is based] upon the correct arrangement of the syllables without error.
And because it serves as a means for correctly interpreting the meaning, it conduces to the long endurance of the True Dhamma. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, these two things conduce to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the True Dhamma. Which two? Well-expounded words and phrases, and well-interpreted meaning.
Since he wished to compose a commentary on the meaning, he stated “The Discourse on Virtue,” and so forth, in order to avoid the charge of excessive prolixity.

For this very reason he said: "I shall not investigate that here. Alternatively, pointing out the instruction for those who would speak, [he says] that the *Visuddhimagga* should be taken as representing a portion of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) that one intends to compose;
thus, by way of enumeration, he shows the doctrines already investigated therein with the words beginning "The Discourse on Virtue" (*sīlakathā*).
Therein, "the discourse on virtue" is a detailed discussion of virtue by way of what is to be practiced and what is to be avoided, and so forth.
The *dhuta-dhammas* are the thirteen qualities that shake off the defilements, beginning with the practice of eating only almsfood.

"All meditation subjects" refers to the thirty-eight mentioned in the Canon and the two mentioned in the Commentary; these are, without exception, the bases for the practice of the development of yoga.
"Accompanied by the exposition of temperaments" means accompanied by the exposition of the nature and other characteristics of those of lustful temperament (*rāga-carita*) and so forth.
The jhānas are the four fine-material-sphere jhānas; the attainments are the four immaterial-sphere attainments.
Alternatively, the eight jhānas are those merely acquired, while they become "attainments" when mastery over entering them has been achieved.
Or, the jhānas are the fine-material and immaterial-sphere jhānas, while the attainments are the attainment of fruition and the attainment of cessation.

All six superknowledges (*abhiññā*), distinguished as mundane and supramundane, are "all superknowledges. The "determination by way of the compendium of wisdom" is the determination reached by classifying and grouping wisdom according to the method found in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* and other texts, beginning with the singlefold division.
The "conditioning mode" (*paccayākāra*) is the state of being a condition—such as the root-cause (*hetu*) and so forth—of those phenomena that arise by way of conditions;

the "teaching on the conditioning mode" is the teaching concerning that, meaning the discourse on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). Furthermore, that [teaching] serves for the resolution of the compact mass...

Because they are extremely difficult to master, subtle and delicate, free from the confusion of the tenets of other schools, and accompanied by the principle of unity (ekattanaya) and so forth, they are investigated therein;

thus it is said: "possessing very pure and skillful principles. Because they are investigated without abandoning the principles as they appear in the *Paṭisambhidā* and other texts, they are called "unreleased paths" (*avimuttamaggā*).

In the phrase *iti pana sabbaṃ*, the word *iti* indicates completion, and the word *pana* is a rhetorical ornament; thus, the meaning is "all this. *Idha* means "in this commentary. "I shall not analyze it" is said because it would involve redundant repetition—this is the intention.
Now, in order to determine the sole reason for that very non-analysis, he says: "The *Visuddhimagga* stands in the middle," and so forth.
Therein, by the expression "standing in the middle," which illustrates its central position, it is shown to be specifically the common commentary (*sādhāraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) for the four Āgamas.
This shows that it is the *Visuddhimagga*, and not like the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* and other such works, which are non-common commentaries (*asādhāraṇaṭṭhakathā*).

The phrase "specifically" (*visesato*) is stated with the understanding that the *Visuddhimagga* also serves as a commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, each according to its proper place.
"Thus indeed" (*icceva*) means "just so. "That too" (*tampi*) refers to the *Visuddhimagga*. "By this" (*etāya*) refers to the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*. And here:
By the words “brought to the island of Siṃhala,” etc., he shows the cause (*nimitta*) for the exposition of the meaning;
by the words “for the sake of the inhabitants of the island, for the satisfaction of virtuous people, and for the long endurance of the Dhamma,” he shows the purpose (*payojana*);
and by the remainder, he shows the manner of composition (*karaṇappakāra*). For even the non-investigation of the discourse on virtue and so forth constitutes the manner of composition here.
The commentary on the introduction to the book is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the introductory narrative (*nidānakathā*):

since the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of those possessing divisions occurs precisely by way of showing their divisions, first, by way of the suttas of the chapters (*vagga*), [it is explained as follows].
In order to show the division [of the text], he said: “Therein, ‘the long augment’ (dīghāgama), etc. Therein, “therein” (tattha) refers to that statement which was uttered:
“I shall explain the meaning of the excellent long augment. The meaning is this:
that which was promised as “I shall explain its meaning” is called the long augment, and its division is thus according to the chapters (vagga) and suttas. Alternatively, “therein” (tattha) means:

Regarding the statement, “The meaning is dependent on the long vowel (*dīghāgamanissitam-atthan*”), the sense is that the long vowel which was mentioned is of such a kind by way of its class (*vagga*) and so forth.

He said, “In its own commentary... the introduction (*nidāna*) and so forth are stated,” in order to show that it proceeds according to the very sequence established during the First Great Council (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti*). But why is the long vowel [mentioned] among the four Āgamas?
Was it recited first, and was the Sīlakkhandhavagga placed at the beginning of that [recitation], and within it the Brahmajāla?
This inquiry does not fail to apply anywhere; nevertheless, the Dīghanikāya was recited first because of its quality of inspiring faith.
For faith is the seed of wholesome states (kusala-dhamma). As it is said: "Faith is the seed, austerity is the rain."
Furthermore, its quality of inspiring faith has already been demonstrated.

Moreover, it is because it comprises a collection of several suttas, and because it is easy to grasp and retain due to its limited size. For it consists of a collection of thirty-four suttas and measures sixty-four bhāṇavāras.
However, the Sīlakkhandha-vagga was placed first because of the abundance of discourse on virtue; for virtue is the foundation of the Dispensation.
"Beginning," because virtue is the foundation of all qualities. For this very reason it was said: "Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first purify the beginning among wholesome states.
And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is perfectly purified," and so forth.
By this, the fact that this chapter has a name corresponding to its content is stated. Furthermore, because it contains a discourse on the unraveling of views...
It should be understood that the *Brahmajāla Sutta* was placed first as the exhaustive analysis of views within the Sutta Piṭaka.
For within the Word of the Buddha contained in the Tipiṭaka, there is no discourse like the *Brahmajāla* that analyzes various speculative views by making them free from thicket and free from tangle.
The Commentary on the Account of the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā):

Desiring to provide a commentary following the sequence established in that First Great Council, and showing the reason for mentioning it here as it has been included in the Canon (Tanti), he says: "The First Great Council... should be understood."

He said: "In that regard, *saṅgīti* is the chanting or recitation [of the Dhamma and Vinaya] by collecting together those teachings and disciplines which were taught and established here and there according to circumstances and were thus scattered.

By this, the words of the compilers (*saṅgītikāra*)—which are placed at the beginning and end of various training rules (*sikkhāpada*) and discourses (*sutta*), as well as in between them for the sake of connection—are included. Because its scope is vast..."
Because it is greatly worthy of worship, it is a "great recitation" (saṅgīti), that is, a "great council" (mahāsaṅgīti). The first great council is the "first great council" (paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti);
the time of its occurrence is the "time of the first great council," and [it is said] "at that time of the first great council. Regarding the term *nidāna*:
it is called *nidāna* because it points out (*nidasseti*) the teaching by making known what was previously unknown through such factors as the place and time of the teaching. Of beings...
Although other activities of the Blessed One exist that serve as causes for obtaining the unsurpassed vision, refuge, and so forth, he stated,
"beginning with the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma," because the activity that— by way of the promise "the Buddha shall awaken"—
is the cause for those to be trained (veneyya) attaining the paths and fruits in accordance with that promise, is the primary function of a Buddha (buddhakicca) in its literal sense.

In this context, the very phenomena such as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) and so forth are called the "Wheel" (*cakra*) in the sense of proceeding; thus it is the "Dhamma-Wheel" (*dhammacakka*).

Alternatively, *cakra* means command; because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, it is both the Dhamma and the Wheel, hence the "Dhamma-Wheel. It is also the "Dhamma-Wheel" in the sense of being a wheel by way of the Dhamma, that is, by way of the proper method (*ñāya*). As it has been said:

“*Dhammacakkaṃ* means ‘he sets in motion the Dhamma and the wheel,’ or ‘he sets in motion the wheel and the Dhamma,’ or ‘he sets it in motion by means of the Dhamma,’ or ‘he sets it in motion through the practice of the Dhamma’—and so forth.
By the phrase “having performed the duties of a Buddha,” he shows that there remains nothing whatsoever yet to be done by a Buddha.
But is it not the case that even those disciples who were trained by the disciples were in fact trained by the Blessed One alone; for this reason, a discourse spoken by a disciple...

“It is called ‘the word of the Buddha,’ yet the disciples are not yet disciplined? This is not a fault, because the means for their discipline has been established among the disciples. For this very reason it was said:
“I shall not pass into final nibbāna, O Evil One, until my bhikkhu-disciples have become accomplished...”

“Disciplined, confident, learned, and upholders of the Dhamma... having thoroughly refuted with the Dhamma any arisen opposing doctrines, I shall teach the Dhamma accompanied by miracles,” and so forth.
The passage beginning with “In Kusinārā” is a demonstration of the specific place and time of the Blessed One’s final passing; it is said [in contrast] that “the Blessed One has not yet passed away.”
This is for the purpose of showing the wrong view regarding the household life, and for the purpose of showing that [the Bodhisattvas] were born and raised in the world.
For indeed, in order to make their human state fully manifest, Great Bodhisattvas even undertake the taking of wives and so forth in their final existence.
It is called *upādi* because it is grasped by karma and defilements; it consists of the aggregates of result and the matter produced by past action (*kaṭattā-rūpa*). Furthermore, that...

The element of nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) is that which is unrelaxed in the attainment of nibbāna through the crushing of the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra) and the Māra of volitional formations (abhisankhāra-māra), but is relaxed and exhausted here through the crushing of the Māra of the aggregates (khandha-māra) and the Māra of death (maccu-māra).
Furthermore, by "the element of nibbāna" (nibbānadhātu), mere extinction (nibbuti) is intended;

and this use of the instrumental case is in the sense of a characteristic of a state already attained (itthambhūtalakkhaṇe). As for the phrase "on the day of the distribution of the relics" (dhātubhājanadivase):
This is not a qualification of the word "assembled" (*sannipatitānaṃ*), but rather a qualification of the act of generating enthusiasm;

that is, "he generated enthusiasm among the bhikkhus on the day of the distribution of the relics. For the bhikkhus had already gathered on the days preceding the day of the distribution of the relics.
Alternatively, it means "of those assembled on the day of the distribution of the relics," being together by way of physical concord (*kāyasāmaggī*).
The meaning is as follows. "An elder of the Saṅgha" means a senior of the Saṅgha (*saṅghatthero*). To the question, "What is the extent of that Saṅgha? he says: "Of seven hundred thousand bhikkhus.
For in such cases, a compound is indeed formed due to the constant requirement [of the genitive], just as in the expression "Devadatta’s family of teachers" (*devadattassa garukulaṃ*).
The connection is that the Venerable Mahākassapa, considering them again to be difficult to find, generated enthusiasm among the bhikkhus.

The phrase “of those assembled on the day of the distribution of the relics” (*dhātubhājanadivase sannipatitānaṃ*) should also be connected with the word “of the bhikkhus” (*bhikkhūnaṃ*) in the passage “he inspired the bhikkhus.
The connection is: “recalling the words spoken by Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age.
In that context, the intended meaning is “recalling them by way of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma. [He thought: “They might cause the true Dhamma to disappear...”
The connection of these words—“I would recite together... [etc. ...what other debt-free state will there be for him so that his teaching may endure long?”—is with the phrase “thinking thus.
Likewise, the connection of “and what I” is with “favored and praised.
In the expression “whatever wicked monks,” the word *yaṃ* is merely a particle, or it is a designation of the cause (*kāraṇaniddeso*), by which—
"By a cause they would cause it to disappear"—the meaning is that such a cause exists. "Fit for the journey" (*addhaniya*) means going along a long road;
the meaning is "enduring the journey.
Regarding the phrase *yañcāhaṃ*: here *yaṃ* [is used] because of which (*yasmā*), meaning "by which reason"; or else, this is a reference to the action (*kiriyāparāmasana*).
In the phrase "favored and praised," it is "favoring" and "praising" that are being referred to.

Regarding the expression "by sharing the use of robes," one should bring forward the word *attano* (of oneself) from the phrase "by placing [the robes] on an equal footing with oneself," and connect it thus:
"by sharing the use of robes with oneself. For wherever there is a connection between two things, even if they are far apart, they are to be construed together.

And its *tanti* (textual tradition) is as follows; or alternatively, it should be construed thus: "He was favored by the Blessed One through the shared use of robes," for this instrumental case ending (*karaṇaniddesa*) can also signify the sense of an accompanying agent (*sahayogakattū*).

"As long as" (*yāvadeti*) means "for as long as," whether referring to a certain duration of time or to a certain period of dwelling in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) or super-knowledge (*abhiññā*), as he so desires.

The meaning is: "I both dwell [in meditative attainments] and engage in worldly discourse; so too did Kassapa. This should be understood as a mere expression of praise based on the commonality of possessing the nine successive dwellings and the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).

For the Venerable Mahākassapa does not, like the Blessed One, enter meditative attainments numbering twenty-four hundred thousand million times every day, nor does he perform such things as the twin miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*).
Or he employs the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). For this very reason it was said: "in the nine successive dwellings and the sixfold higher knowledges.
What other debtlessness could there be for him, apart from the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya? This is the intended meaning.
By the passage beginning with "Did not the Blessed One [say] to me," etc., he clarifies the aforementioned point by means of a simile.
"From then on" means after that time when the monks' enthusiasm was generated. "Unrighteousness shines forth first" means it indeed begins to shine;
the meaning is that it does so even before unrighteousness becomes capable of obstructing righteousness.

For this word *pure* (first) is used here in reference to something imminent. And "shines forth" (*dippati*) refers to what will shine forth (*dippissati*). This is due to its connection with the word *pure*.
For this is a present-tense usage referring to a future state, just as in the expression: "It will rain before long.

By the phrase, "He gathered together four hundred and ninety-nine [disciples] who maintained the study of the Teacher’s entire dispensation consisting of the nine branches," it is indicated that although those aforementioned individuals—ranging from dry-insight practitioners to those whose taints were destroyed—possessed both scripture and realization, [they were not yet fully perfected].

However, by means of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), it demonstrates the great utility of the communal recitation (*saṅgīti*) because it has reached the highest excellence through the perfection of scripture and realization in those endowed with qualities such as the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*).
This is stated in the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka*: "There is nothing called 'not witnessed' (*apaccakkha*) because of its state of being well-mastered and active";
yet in the *Samantapāsādikā*, it says: "'Received not in the presence [of the Teacher]' (*asammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ*)..."
When it was said, "There are none," that was stated with the understanding that even what was said—"two thousand from among the bhikkhus"—had indeed been received in the presence of the Blessed One.
"Eighty-four thousand" refers to the divisions of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*). "Recited" means mastered.
Because the assembly of nine lay followers had departed due to the Elder Ānanda, the Elder Mahākassapa spoke thus: "No..."
“Or this young man thought he was intoxicated. In this context, *matta* means measure (*pamāṇa*). The analysis of the compound is: *chanda-āgamana-viya*.
As for the phrase “even though he is one in training” (*sekkha*), it should be understood that this is not stated because those in training are capable of going on the wrong path;
rather, it is said because only those beyond training (*asekkha*) were selected [for comparison]. For indeed, the four ways of going on the wrong path are abandoned by the first path alone.

“Unable to follow a wrong course through desire... and so forth; this is a statement of existing qualities by demonstrating his fitness for the Dhamma-recitation (Dhammasaṅgīti). “Pariyatta” means studied. “Gocara”:
that wherein cattle graze is a *gocara*; like a pasture, it is a place for wandering for alms. A person of dissimilar nature.
"Like Subhadda. "The cage of spears" refers to the protection of the Blessed One’s relics by the Malla chiefs through men holding spears, swords, and other weapons in their hands.
"Having severed that obstacle, let him perform what is to be done" means that the attendant should sever whatever must be severed so that he may perform his sole duty.
"The great multitude" means many people. "The Fragrant Chamber."

The intention is that [he did so] because it was a *paribhoga-cetiya* (an object of use worthy of veneration). "As the tradition" (*yathā tanti*) means "just as another [person] of the aforementioned nature," such is the sense.
"He caused [him] to be moved" (*saṃvejesi*) means he generated a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) by saying, "Has it not been declared by the Blessed One beforehand:
'There is indeed separation and parting from all that is dear and beloved'? and so forth. "With aggravated humors" (*ussannadhātukaṃ*) means with accumulated defilements (*upacitadosa*).

“Medicine-measure” (*bhesajjamattā*) means a small amount of medicine; for this word *mattā* has the sense of "little," as in such expressions as “the relinquishing of even a measure of pleasure” (*mattāsukhapariccāgo*).

“On the second day” means on the second day from the day he was stirred by the deity, or from the day he entered the Jetavana monastery. “The wheel of command” (*āṇācakkaṃ*) is the wheel of authority (*āṇā*).

“Etadaggaṃ” means this is the foremost. This designation is made by a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa). As for “yadidaṃ,” it should be construed as “yo ayaṃ” (this which) or “yadidaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ” (namely, the five aggregates).
Why was it said, “Friend Upāli, where was the first *pārājika* offense laid down?
Is it not the case that its status as “first” is inappropriate prior to the time of the Council? It is not inappropriate.
This is because the first existence [of the teaching] was established through the sequence laid down by the Blessed One and the sequence for the recitation of the Pātimokkha.

For it should be understood that, for the most part, the three Piṭakas were chanted during the Blessed One’s lifetime according to the very order in which they existed—specifically the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas.
The phrase “He asked about the subject matter,” etc., refers to the inquiry beginning with “Where was it laid down? and so forth.
