This is stated by way of inclusion, encompassing both what has been shown and what remains. "In the first *pārājika*" means in the text of the first *pārājika*;
for this very reason it is said: "The Tathāgatas do not utter even a single syllable in vain.
In the *Jātaka* and other works included within the *Khuddaka Nikāya*, as well as in the corresponding *Abhidhamma Piṭaka*, which for the most part consists of expositions of the Dhamma.

The Dīgha-bhāṇakas state that the *Jātaka* and other such works are included within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, as they are suitable for inclusion there and not in the Sutta Piṭaka—such as the various Nikāyas beginning with the Dīgha-nikāya—nor in the Vinaya Piṭaka, which consists of the Paññatti and Niddesa.

However, the Cariyāpiṭaka and Buddhavaṃsa are not included here because they fall under the same category as the *Jātaka*. The Majjhima-bhāṇakas, however, [hold that] the *Jātaka* and others taught by way of occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*)...
They state that because it contains teachings given in accordance with [the listeners' capacities], the Jātaka and other such texts are appropriately included in the Suttanta Piṭaka,
but not in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which is the teaching of the Dhamma according to its true nature (*sabhāva*) and consists of a systematic exposition of phenomena.
One should accept this after investigating whether it is logical in that regard.
Having thus shown the first council by way of its cause, purpose, time, place, agent, instrument, and manner, he now says "Thus indeed...
and so forth, in order to show the various classifications—such as the singlefold and others—for the sake of proficiency in the various aspects of the Dhamma and Vinaya established therein.
In that context, "the flavor of liberation" (*vimuttirasa*) refers to the quality of liberation (*vimuttiguṇa*), which consists in the attainment of liberation (*vimuttisampatti*).
Or it is the "function of liberation" because it brings about the supreme fruit; or it is the "taste of liberation" because it effects the absolute liberation from the defilements.
Some, however, say it is the "taste of liberation.
Although, without distinction, the entire word of the Buddha is the Vinaya by virtue of its subduing of the defilements according to the instruction, [it is so called here specifically].

It is called *dhamma* because it sustains one from falling into the states of misery (*apāya*) and so forth when one practices accordingly. However, in order to distinguish what is intended here within this *Dhamma-vinaya*, he said:

"Therein, the *Vinaya Piṭaka*... and so on. The remainder of the Buddha’s word is *dhamma*, because it consists predominantly of teachings on phenomena (*dhamma*) that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.
Alternatively, although the *vinaya* is indeed *dhamma* as well—since it exists as the *pariyatti* (the teaching) and so on—yet, in the presence of the word *vinaya*, [it is distinguished].

The word *dhamma*, when used with a sense of different grammatical loci (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*), indicates a textual tradition that is inconsistent with the Vinaya canon, as in the expressions "the equipment of merit and knowledge" (*puññañāṇasambhārā*) and "the cow and the ox" (*gobalibaddha*).

This verse, "Through many a round of births... (*anekajātisaṃsāraṃ*), was spoken by the Blessed One to indicate the attainment of Arahantship, which is the foundation for his own omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
This was spoken by him while reviewing it immediately after the nineteenth reviewing-knowledge.
Therefore he said, "This is the first word of the Buddha. Indeed, this is the *udāna* (inspired utterance) never abandoned by any Buddha.
Its summary meaning is as follows: "While seeking the builder of this house of selfhood, the carpenter of craving, by whom..."

That [state] can be seen through knowledge; for the sake of that knowledge of enlightenment (bodhiñāṇa), having made my aspiration at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, I have wandered and transmigrated through this cycle of existence for so long—through many births, numbering many hundreds of thousands of births—failing to obtain and failing to find that knowledge.
Because it is mixed with old age, sickness, and death, [I wandered].
This thing called birth is painful because it must be undergone again and again, and it does not cease as long as that [truth] has not been seen;
therefore, the meaning is that they will run on, searching for it. "You have been seen" means: now you have been seen by me while penetrating the knowledge of omniscience.
"Again to the house" means: again to this house of mine, which is designated as this personal existence (*attabhāva*). "You shall not do" means: you will not do.
All the remaining rafters of your defilements have been broken by me.
The pinnacle of this house of a personal existence built by you—the central dome known as ignorance—has been dismantled and destroyed.
My mind has now entered and reached Nibbāna, the unconditioned, by taking it as its object; and I have [reached] that which is known as the destruction of craving.
“I have attained, reached, and acquired the path of Arahatship. This is the beginning of those phenomena that proceed by way of the mind.
However, they say that the verse, “When indeed phenomena become manifest,” is the beginning of those phenomena that proceed by way of speech.

It is said that the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with “Through many births in saṃsāra” by way of internal muttering. As for the phrase “on the day of the first lunar day (pāṭipada),” this refers to [the time] when he had attained omniscience.
It should not be connected with that [phrase]; rather, it should be connected with the words, “arisen for one who is reviewing.
For it was on the full moon day of the month of Visākha, at the time of dawn, that the Blessed One attained omniscience.

By the phrase “subject to vanishing,” he reveals the characteristics of suffering and non-self through the gateway of the characteristic of impermanence, according to the principle: “Whatever is impermanent...”
"Whatever is suffering is non-self"—from this statement.

Furthermore, it should be understood that by demonstrating insight (vipassanā) which takes those [three characteristics] as its object through the very method of analyzing the three characteristics, he reveals the unerring path leading to Nibbāna, which has the four noble truths as its meditation subject;
a path unique to the Buddhas and beyond the reach of all other sectarians. Now, regarding the correct practice therein:

He enjoins them, saying, "Accomplish [your task] with diligence. Alternatively, having stirred their sense of urgency by means of the brief formula, "All conditioned phenomena are subject to decay," he shows the complete and exhaustive right practice by means of that same brief formula:
"Accomplish [your task] with diligence. For the term "diligence" stands encompassing the entire, perfect teaching contained within the three trainings.
The Saṅgītikkhandhaka, the Kathāvatthu, the Pakaraṇa, and so forth, were not recited at the First Council.
Some, however, claim that even the Subha Sutta was not recited at the First Council;
but that is incorrect, for it was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda while residing in Jetavana, prior even to the First Council.

The purpose of making firm and loosening is, respectively, with regard to training rules that are inherently blameworthy (*pakatisāvajja*) and those that are blameworthy by convention (*paṇṇattisāvajja*). "By that" means by way of various methods and so forth. "This" refers to the verse statement beginning with "by way of various specific methods.

"Of this" refers to the Vinaya. Regarding the classification into one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so on: for one who recites, hears, causes to be recited, reflects upon, or teaches that Sutta, the welfare consisting of virtue and so forth included within that Sutta belongs to them as well; because it is to be accomplished for another by means of that [teaching], it also belongs to another.

The word "hoti" (is) indicates and illuminates both of those [qualities] in that sutta. Likewise, by means of the word "ādi" (etc.), it includes meanings such as "pertaining to this life and the next life," "mundane and supramundane," and other such divisions.
Furthermore, this word "attha" (meaning/benefit) is a term for welfare (*hita*), not a term for the literal meaning of what was spoken;
for if it were the latter, the sutta would indicate its own literal meaning as well as that of another.
This meaning might be stated thus: "The meaning revealed by a sutta belongs to that [sutta] alone;
it does not indicate another's purpose (parattha), because there is no other purpose to be indicated or to be set aside by it, and therefore the mention of 'meaning' (attha) need not be made.
Furthermore, since there is no meaning of speech that is distinct from one's own purpose or another's purpose, the mention of 'beginning' (ādi) is also unnecessary."

This must be done. Therefore, since the meaning of the aforementioned "synonym for welfare" (hitapariyāya) cannot exist within the Sutta itself, the benefit for oneself and the benefit for others are stated by way of the person who upholds the Sutta.

Alternatively, disregarding the Sutta, those classifications of meaning such as "benefit for oneself" and so forth were stated [in the commentary] in the passage: "Not killing, not taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and praise for gain."
In the exposition of this term, the following sutta passage is cited: “The welfare of oneself, the welfare of others, the welfare of both, the benefit pertaining to the present life,
the benefit pertaining to future lives, the manifest meaning, the profound meaning, the hidden meaning, the concealed meaning,
the meaning that requires further guidance, the meaning already drawn out, the blameless meaning, the meaning free from defilement, the purified meaning, and the ultimate meaning.”
The meaning is "it is well-spoken. In this interpretation of the meaning, the word *attha* (meaning) also functions as a synonym for that which has been spoken (*bhāsita*).
For here, the first five divisions of meaning are synonyms for benefit (*hita*); those following them are six divisions of what has been spoken; but the final ones possess the nature of both.
Among these, it is "profound" (*gambhīra*) because its depth cannot be reached when its manifestation is difficult to discern. It is "not disclosed" (*na vivaṭa*).
*Gūḷha* (hidden): concealed or covered by something like soil, such as the arrangement of syllables and so forth, like a root or water.
*Neyya* (to be inferred): that which must be understood by extracting [the meaning]. *Nīta* (definitive): that which is to be known according to the literal sense. *Pariyāya* (figurative):

spoken by way of a method for the purpose of blamelessness, the absence of defilements, and purification; or by way of wholesome states, results, and functional states (*kiriya-dhamma*). *Paramattha* (ultimate): Nibbāna, the non-perverted intrinsic nature of phenomena.

Or rather: the phrase "he himself is of few desires" indicates his own welfare (*attattha*), while "he is one who speaks to others about being of few desires" indicates the welfare of others (*parattha*).
In this same way, discourses such as "he himself abstains from taking life" and so forth should be applied.
Furthermore, having distinguished it from the *Vinaya* and *Abhidhamma*, the meaning of the word *sutta* should be stated.

Therefore, it is through the teaching proceeding according to the disposition of those to be trained (*veneyya*) that self-benefit, benefit for others, and so forth, are most eminently manifested, because that is its primary purpose;

it is not so through the teaching proceeding by way of the nature of the command or the nature of the Dhamma itself. And it is precisely for this reason that it is said: "A *sutta* is so called because it indicates meanings.
Furthermore, in a *sutta*, both the nature of the command and the nature of the Dhamma conform to the disposition of those to be trained, whereas this is not the case in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma.
The disposition of those to be trained [is considered] in relation to the nature of the teaching and the Dhamma.

Therefore, it is said, "And herein they are well-spoken," etc., because the teaching of the Suttanta leads to the attainment of absolute welfare for those to be trained. "Pasavati" means it bears fruit.
To clarify the meaning of the term "suttāṇā," it is said, "It protects them well. And regarding the various arrangements of one's own welfare and so forth, of the Sutta...

The status of being an authoritative standard (*pamāṇabhāva*) and the quality of encompassing one’s own welfare and so forth should be applied, because the Sutta has as its primary purpose the elucidation of that meaning.
Furthermore, the distinction from the Vinaya and Abhidhamma should be applied. "This" refers to the definition of the term *sutta*, beginning with the words "because it indicates meanings.
"Of this" refers to the Sutta.
Regarding the word *abhikkamanti*: here, the prefix *abhi-* indicates the state of increase or excess (*atirekatā*) of the action of going.
In the phrase *abhiññātā abhilakkhitā* ("well-known, distinguished"), it indicates the specific quality of the clarity of the actions of knowledge and discernment.

In the phrase *abhikkantena*, it is appropriate that it signifies the superiority or excellence of beauty (*kantī*), because the prefix functions as a qualifier of the action. [The same applies to] *abhirājā* and *abhivinaye*.
But how could it be appropriate to say that the prefix *abhi-* occurs in the terms *abhirāja* and *abhivinaya*, which denote "honored" and "delimited"?
It is appropriate because it illuminates the actions of honoring and delimiting, and because those actions are connected with kings and discipline (*vinaya*).
For here, just as the prefix *ati-* in words such as *atimāla* expresses an action together with its instrument, so too do the terms *abhirāja* and *abhivinaya*.
It should be understood that in this way, in the term *abhidhamma*, the prefix *abhi-* indicates an action such as increase (*vuḍḍhi*) together with its accomplishment;
thus, this meaning has been shown.

Furthermore, phenomena (*dhammā*) possessing increase have been described by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), pervasion (*pharaṇa*), and growth (*vuḍḍhi*). By "by way of object and so forth" is meant by way of object, association, karma, door, path, and so on.
“Not distinguished” (*avisissa*) means not distinguished—that is, identical—with the Vinaya suttas and the Abhidhamma, which are distinguished from one another;
the meaning is that it is the word *piṭaka*. “In the manner already described” refers to the way stated in the passage beginning with “in this twofold sense.

Teaching (*desanā*) is the imparting or awakening [of understanding] of the meanings to be told, by means of the method of instruction such as commands, etc., depending on the teacher and the audience.
*Śāsana* (the teaching) is the instruction and discipline consisting in the act of instructing individuals who are to be trained, according to their respective offenses and other circumstances.
*Kathā* (discourse) is the speaking of the meaning—such as restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)—which is to be spoken, or the making of that [meaning] dependent upon words;

alternatively, it is called *kathā* because it is spoken therein. Thus, "discourse on restraint and non-restraint" (*saṃvarāsaṃvarakathā*) is the discourse concerning restraint and non-restraint. This same method applies [to the following terms].

"In the others as well": the word *bheda* (division) should be joined individually [to each term], as in: "one should clearly illustrate the division of the teaching (*desanā-bheda*), the division of the dispensation (*sāsana-bheda*), and the division of the discourse (*kathā-bheda*), as appropriate.

Furthermore, *bheda* means diversity (*nānatta*). "The training (*sikkhā*), the abandonments (*pahāna*), and the profound nature (*gambhīrabhāva*)"—that is, the profundity of the training and the abandonments—one should also clearly illustrate that.
Here, "as appropriate" (*yathā*) refers to the mastery of the causes for censuring, escaping, and protecting the treasury of the Dhamma.
"By these modes" means by way of right practice and wrong practice. "Worthy of command" (*āṇāraho*) means he is worthy of giving commands because he is a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*).

He says "because of the abundance of his commands" because both conventional and ultimate meanings exist [in his teaching]. This same method applies to what follows as well. "Those of many offenses" refers to Seyyasaka and others.
"Intention" (*ajjhāsaya*) is, in its actual sense, both view and knowledge. And this has been said:
“Eternalism and annihilationism, as well as conformable acceptance,
and that knowledge which is in accordance with reality— this is what is termed ‘disposition’ (āsaya).
The underlying tendencies (anusaya) are seven future defilements, consisting of sensual lust, lust for existence, views, aversion, doubt, conceit, and ignorance.
Those of the past and the present are likewise so described; for there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena due to a difference in time.
As for "conduct" (*cariyā*), there are six root types of conduct, which become manifold through internal subdivisions, and by way of association, they amount to sixty-three.
These have been shown by us in detail in the commentary to the *Asammohantaradhānasutta*; those who desire them should take them from there.

Alternatively, *cariyā* means conduct (*carita*); that is twofold, by way of good conduct and bad conduct. *Adhimutti* (inclination) refers to the preference of beings based on their previous associations;
it is twofold, distinguished as inferior and superior. Due to the absence of analysis of the compact [aggregates], they possess the perception of "I" and "mine" by way of views, conceit, and craving.
Great restraint is non-restraint. The meaning is intelligence (*buddhi*).
For this letter *a* is [used] as in the expression “the qualities beyond training” (*asekkhā dhammā*).

Furthermore, regarding these three—the Dhamma, the meaning, the teaching, and the penetration—it is here that the meaning of the thread, the teaching of the thread, and the penetration of the meaning of the thread have the thread as their object;
thus, it is logical that the Piṭakas possess the status of being the basis for the meaning, the teaching, and the penetration of the Vinaya Piṭaka and so forth. The Piṭakas...
But how could the state of being the support (*ādhāra*) for those [factors] be logical, given that they are themselves the *tantras*?
It is because the individual *tantra* is the support for the collection (*samudāya*) of *tantras*. For a whole is spoken of as the support of its part, just as one says, "the branch is in the tree.

And since the factors (*dhamma*) and so forth are difficult to fathom, the Vinaya and other [Pitakas] are profound by virtue of them; furthermore, there are four kinds of [profundity] regarding the Vinaya and the rest.

The state of profundity has been stated. Therefore, one should not object that only the Dhamma and so forth are profound because they are difficult to fathom due to suffering, while the Vinaya and so forth are not;
for this has been stated both directly and by way of the relationship between the object and the subject, as it is precisely the Vinaya and the rest that possess profundity.
For the Dhamma consists of the Vinaya and the others; their object is the meaning (attha), and both teaching and penetration have the meaning of the Dhamma as their object.
In this context, because penetration is difficult to achieve, the state of the phenomena and their meanings should be understood as difficult to fathom;

and because the knowledge of teaching is difficult to achieve, the teaching itself should be understood as difficult to penetrate. Furthermore, because penetration cannot be brought about [by others], and because the arising of knowledge regarding its object is difficult to achieve, it should be understood as difficult to fathom.
Regarding the statement, “Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā),” how is the causal nature of phenomena to be understood by this expression?
It is because, when explaining the meaning of the constituent members of the compound term “analytical knowledge of phenomena,” it is stated as “knowledge regarding the cause.
For in the phrase “analytical knowledge regarding phenomena,” the meaning of the word “regarding phenomena” is shown by [the following].
It was stated, "In the cause," and by showing the meaning of the term "analytical knowledge" (paṭisambhidā), it is said to be "knowledge" (ñāṇa).

Therefore, by stating that the words *dhamma* and *hetu* have the same meaning, as do the words *ñāṇa* and *paṭisambhidā*, the fact that the *dhamma* is the cause and the *attha* is the fruit of that cause is established; this is how it should be understood.

And here, the word *dhamma* in the phrase *yathādhammaṃ* includes both cause and all effects of causes. For this term denotes intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), not merely the state of being a teaching or a cause;
therefore, *yathādhammaṃ* means "in each respective case," referring to whatever phenomenon there may be, such as ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth.
Alternatively, *yathādhammaṃ* means "in accordance with the phenomena. For the teaching is indeed like the penetration [of reality].
Because it manifests its object without error, it proceeds in accordance with the phenomenon (dhamma); hence it is called "unerring expression" (*aviparitābhilāpa*).
"Expression of phenomena" (*dhammābhilāpa*) refers to an unerring expression that reveals both the meaning and the phrasing;

by this, he demonstrates the "linguistic expression of phenomena" (*sabhāvadhammanirutti*) mentioned in the passage: "In that linguistic expression of phenomena, knowledge is the analytical power of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*)," since [this expression] has the nature of sound.
...regarding the teaching. For indeed, the fact that the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*) has limited objects and so forth is stated in the *Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga-pāḷi*.
And in the Commentary, its having sound as its object is shown by such passages as: "Having made that sound, which is natural language, the object," and so on.
Having determined the relationship between the expression and the expressed—thinking, "This sound is the designator of this meaning"—one [discerns] each respective expressed meaning...
For "teaching" (*desanā*) is speech that proceeds by way of analytical exposition (*vibhāvanā*).

By the phrase "or speaking by way of conformity (*anuloma*) and so forth," he shows that "speaking" refers to the utterance of that linguistic expression of the Dhamma (*dhammanirutti*), which is the occurrence of that speech.

By the word "intention" (*adhippāya*), he indicates that the statement "teaching is a designation" (*paññatti*) was spoken with reference to the utterance of the linguistic expression of the Dhamma, and not [to the underlying reality].
He shows that this refers to a designation (*paññatti*) that is conceptually constructed (*tabbinimutta*).

But would it not be the case that, on this view where "Dhamma" means "string," there could be no distinction between the Dhamma itself and the teachings of the Dhamma, since the Dhamma has the nature of sound?
No; for [the Dhamma] is known as the means of making known various meanings, by way of learning and so forth.

Furthermore, the "dharma" is the continuity of sounds previously established; the "teaching" (*desanā*) is the sound subsequently set in motion for the purpose of making it understood by others, which illuminates that meaning.

Alternatively, the "teaching" is the mental state (*cittuppāda*) that gives rise to the aforementioned sounds, just as [the intention] does for false speech (*musāvāda*) and so forth. And the phrase "the setting in motion of speech" refers to the aforementioned mental state.
It is appropriate. For he sets forth the word, and that [word] is set forth and taught by him.

In order to make clear—by way of the manner in which one realizes, that which is realized, and the intrinsic nature of that realization—the "realization" (abhisamaya) thus described as being both mundane and supramundane, he said:
"By way of the object and by way of non-delusion, according to the meaning among the phenomena," and so forth. Therein:

For indeed, mundane clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*) is the understanding of phenomena and so forth according to their meaning and so on in terms of their objects; it has as its object the designation of the meaning of both the formations such as ignorance and so forth, and the phenomena themselves.
Supramundane clear comprehension, however, is the understanding of phenomena and so forth according to their meaning and so on through non-delusion;
it has Nibbāna as its object, is associated with the Path, and destroys delusion regarding the aforementioned designations of phenomena and meanings.
In order to show another meaning of penetration (*paṭivedha*) distinct from "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*), he said, "of this or that," and so forth.
For by the verbal definition "penetration is the act of penetrating," clear realization is called "penetration";
and by the definition "it is penetrated," the unerring intrinsic nature of each respective phenomenon—such as form and so on—is also called "penetration."
In order to show the profundity of the Piṭakas by means of the phenomena (dhamma) and so forth already mentioned, he said: "Now, because in these Piṭakas...
and so on. Regarding the phrase "whatever penetration there is here," it should be construed as follows:

whatever penetration there is into the respective phenomena and so forth contained within those various Piṭakas, and whatever unerring intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of those respective phenomena exists within these Piṭakas. Furthermore, [the profundity consists in] the difficulty of fathoming ignorance, volitional formations, and the rest.
It should be understood that this is because the state of phenomena (*dhammatthāna*) is difficult to penetrate, because it is hard to establish them for others,
because it is impossible to produce or make the object of penetration— that which is termed "penetration" (*paṭivedha*)— and because penetration,
which consists of the non-perverted intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), is itself difficult to discern.
This was said with reference to a wrong grasp of the scriptures (*pariyatti*). "The meaning" (*attha*) refers to both the meaning of what was spoken and the purposeful meaning.
"They do not examine" means they do not investigate. "They do not accept after reflection" means they do not tolerate the wisdom of reflection;
the intention is that these [teachings] are not to be accepted after having reflected upon them, seen them with wisdom, and found them pleasing. "Thus" (*iti*) means in this way, by means of this...

Regarding "through study": they master the Dhamma for the purpose of escaping from debate—that is, for the sake of liberation from the censure imposed by others upon themselves—or rather, for escaping debate or escaping blame.

"For whatever purpose" means that they master the Dhamma according to the proper method for the sake of fulfilling virtue and so forth, or for the sake of the liberation through non-clinging. Thus, they master it by way of the right principle.
This is the intended meaning. "Of this" means of this Dhamma. "They do not enjoy" means they do not find [the benefit].
Because those teachings have been wrongly grasped by them, they lead to their harm and suffering for a long time, by way of being causes for criticism, pride, deceit, slander, and so forth.
One appointed to a storehouse is a "storekeeper"; like a storekeeper is a "storekeeper"—one who guards the treasure of the Dhamma.
“Learning for the sake of the storekeeper alone,” not with regard to anything else, is “storekeeper-learning.

The restriction “of those very [three knowledges]” is stated with reference to the absence of detailed explanations in the Vinaya regarding the six direct knowledges, the four analytical insights, and so forth, which are to be attained.
For in the Verañjā Chapter, only the three true knowledges (*tisso vijjā*) are analyzed. In the second [chapter...].
However, the restriction "of those very [knowledges]" is made with reference to the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), not the three true knowledges (vijjā).
For those [three] are indeed explained in the Sutta as being included within the six direct knowledges (abhiññā).
He grasps what is wrongly grasped, thinking: "I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: 'That very thing is this.'"
“Consciousness runs on and wanders about, not another,” and so forth. “Reflection on the Dhamma” (dhammacintā) means investigating the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva), such as:

“A gift is complete by the mere arising of the thought [to give], consciousness itself becomes its own object, and every consciousness has as its object a phenomenon that lacks intrinsic nature,” and so on.
“Of them” (tesaṃ) means of those Piṭakas.
This much is the word of the Buddha. It is "conformable" because it conforms to the meaning. To clarify its very conformability, the passage beginning with "But why...
was stated. "Even a single nikāya" means even a single collection. The Poṇikas and Cikkhallikas were Kṣatriyas;
their residence was the Poṇika-nikāya and the Cikkhallika-nikāya.
Regarding the phrase "ninefold division": how is it ninefold here? For the *sutta* that contains verses is *geyya*, while the *sutta* that is devoid of verses is *veyyākaraṇa*.
Apart from these two, there is no *sutta* component free from them that lacks a specific designation such as *udāna* and so forth, which could constitute a separate *sutta* factor;

furthermore, *maṅgalasutta* and other such discourses would not be included within the *sutta* factor because they lack the status of being [standard] verses, unlike the *Dhammapada* and similar works.

Or could it be that [the *Sutta Nipāta*] is included as a *geyya* because it contains verses, just like the *Sagāthavagga*, and likewise for the sections containing verses within the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and so forth?
It is said in reply: "The term 'sutta' is a general designation;
the others are specific designations."
“With a sign, because it is established, together with another, not from another.
For indeed, *sutta* is the general designation for the entire word of the Buddha. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāna said in the *Nettippakaraṇa*:
“The investigation of the ninefold *suttanta*. “So much is that which has come down as *sutta* and is included within *sutta* of that Blessed One.”
And such passages as “five hundred suttas in our own school” are proof for this meaning.

Regarding the specific categories: the others, along with their defining characteristics (*nimitta*), are the specific categories; the Geyya and the rest are established by their respective characteristics.
For instance, the possession of verses (*sagāthakatta*) is the characteristic that establishes the status of Geyya. Even in the world, [something is called] *sasiloka*...

They say that prose mixed with verses is "Geyya. However, when there is an absence of verses, the state of posing a question and providing an answer constitutes "Veyyākaraṇa," on account of that very nature.
For the answering of a question is called "byākaraṇa" (explanation), and "byākaraṇa" itself is "veyyākaraṇa" (exposition).
This being so, even for those works containing verses and the like, [the status of Veyyākaraṇa applies] by way of posing a question and providing an answer.
Does it follow that for those [texts] in circulation, the status of being a *veyyākaraṇa* (exegesis) is attained?

It does not so follow, because there is no occasion for the designations such as *geyya* and so forth, and because of the specific qualification: "provided there is an absence of verses. For instance, this applies to the *Dhammapada* and similar works, which consist solely of verse compositions;

even to those containing verses (*sagāthaka*), provided they are joined with verses consisting of joy and knowledge; and to those connected with statements such as "For this was said" (*vuttañhetaṃ*).
In specific discourses connected with marvelous phenomena (*abbhutadhamma*), the designations *gāthā*, *udāna*, *itivuttaka*, and *abbhutadhamma* were established according to their respective order;
likewise, even though they consist of verse composition, those [discourses] that reveal the power of the Blessed One’s conduct in past births are designated as *jātaka*;
and even though they consist of answers to questions and some of these discourses contain verses, they are designated as *veda*.

Because it causes one to obtain [the goal], the designation "vedalla" is established; thus, by means of various characteristics such as being accompanied by verses (*sagāthaka*), the designations "geyya" and so forth are established for those specific types of discourses (*sutta*). Therefore, the "geyya" and other categories following the "sutta" division are specific modes.
However, that which is devoid of the characteristics of the "geyya" division and so on belongs to the "sutta" division, being designated by its general name through the exclusion of specific names.

Regarding "by way of occurrence": might it not be objected that the *sutta* division is untenable, since a discourse with verses (*sagāthaka*) is *geyya*, while a discourse without verses (*niggāthaka*) is *veyyākaraṇa*?
That objection does not hold, because it has already been established.
For it was previously established that when there is an absence of verses, the nature of question and answer constitutes *veyyākaraṇa*, and that this is its defining characteristic.

As for what was said—that "because they consist of verses, the *Maṅgalasutta* and other such texts would not be included within the category of *sutta*"—that is not so, because the term is conventional.

For the status of being a *sutta* is conventionally established for the *Maṅgalasutta* and others. Indeed, these are not renowned as being "verses" (*gāthā*) like the *Dhammapada*, the *Buddhavaṃsa*, and so forth;
rather, they are renowned as being *suttas*. It is for this very reason that it is called "named a *sutta*" in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

The naming [of the Nikāyas] has been completed. Furthermore, as for what was said—that "because it contains verses, it might be included in the Geyya division"—that too is not the case, because it is accompanied by something else. For "with verses" (sagāthaka) means "together with verses.

Indeed, co-existence (sahabhāva) exists in fact only in relation to something else; and in the Maṅgala-sutta and other such texts, there is no portion of a sutta that is devoid of discourse, which could be called "together with verses."
If one were to say this, it would follow that there is no such thing as a "collection" (samudāya).

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that "portions containing verses from the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and so forth might be included within the *geyya* factor"—that too is not the case, because they are otherwise. For those verses are indeed different, being comprised within the *Jātaka* and other categories.

Therefore, by means of them, the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and so forth do not possess the status of the *geyya* factor. In this way, the absence of mutual confusion among the factors, such as the *sutta* and the rest, should be understood.

"‘This is the Dhamma... [and so on] ...this is the Vinaya; these are the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma’"—having thus defined the word of the Buddha according to its divisions such as the Dhamma and the Vinaya, the community of elders headed by Mahākassapa, while reciting it at the Council adorned with the manifestation of many wonders, established this *Dīgha Āgama* as being among the first of the Buddha’s words, namely the Majjhima and other collections.
He shows that it has been "established" by the words, "Thus this is [to be understood] without distinction," and so forth.
The commentary on the Nidānakathā is finished.
1. Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Wanderers:
Having thus shown the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti), for the purpose of which it was presented here, he now says "of this" and so forth in order to show it by way of conclusion.
1. Having thus far shown the common external introduction (*bāhiranidāna*) to the Brahmajāla Sutta, he now [shows] the internal introduction (*abbhantaranidāna*).
To provide a commentary, the words beginning with "therein, thus" (*tattha evam*) were spoken. Alternatively, the commentary should be composed in six ways:

by way of connection (*sambandha*), by way of the word (*pada*), by way of the analysis of the word (*padavibhāga*), by way of the meaning of the word (*padattha*), by way of the inquiry (*anuyoga*), and by way of the resolution (*parihāra*).

Therein, "connection" refers to the connection of the teaching (*desanāsambandha*), which worldly people call "the extraction" (*ummugghāta*). That, moreover, is according to the introductory narrative of the text (*nidānapāḷi*).

Furthermore, since the connection of the Nidāna-pāḷi was demonstrated by showing the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti) as the means for its recitation, [the commentator], providing a commentary by way of the words and so forth, said: "‘Evaṃ’ is a particle-word," and so on.
Regarding the phrase "‘Me,’ ‘ti,’ etc.," it must be stated whether the words *antara* and *ca* possess the status of particle-words (*nipātapada*), or whether they do not.
Because they are included by grasping the method (*naya*) for those [words], and because the remaining words beginning with *āpaṭi* are subsumed under the word *ādi*.
"Analysis of words" (*padavibhāga*) refers to the distinction between words, not the grammatical compounding of words (*padaviggaha*).

Alternatively, "analysis of words" may refer to both the words themselves and their analysis (*padāni ca padavibhāgo ca*), or it may refer to both the compounding of words and the analysis of words through the principle of "retention of one" (*ekasesa*).

It should be understood that [the meaning] is expressed by way of the division of words (*padavibhāga*). In this context, "word-formation" (*padaviggaha*) is to be seen in word-units such as "the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

"By way of meaning" (*atthato*) means by way of the meaning of the words (*padatthato*). Now, showing the meaning of the word *evaṃ* first according to the sequence for extracting meanings, he says: "First, the word *evaṃ*... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "certainty and so forth" (*avadhāraṇādi*), here the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes meanings such as "this," "questioning," "measure," and others.

The inclusion [of the word *evaṃ*] should be understood. For instance, in such expressions as “gone thus,” “of such a kind,” or “of such a form,” the word *evaṃ* has the same meaning as the word *idaṃ*.
Indeed, the word *gata* is a synonym for “manner” (*pakāra*), as are the words *vidha* and *ākāra*.
For people in the world say that the word *gata*, when joined with *vidha*, signifies the sense of “manner. Thus: “Is it thus? Is it not thus? What indeed?”

“How indeed?”; “Is it thus that you, well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, wearing garlands and ornaments, clothed in white garments, endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, enjoy yourself, just as you do now together with your teachers?”—in such cases, this refers to a question. “Thus is its rapid transformation.”
In such passages as “*evaṃ āyupariyanto*,” it has the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*).

But is it not the case that in the passage “*Evaṃ nu kho, evaṃ su te, evaṃ āyupariyanto*,” because the word *evaṃ* expresses both the mode of questioning and the mode of measure, the word *evaṃ* must have the sense of mode (*ākāra*) alone? No, because there is a distinction [between them].
Here, what is intended by the sense of mode is that which expresses mere mode, as in “*evaṃ*... [and so forth].

Regarding the terms *byākhā* and so forth, however, they do not denote a specific mode [of expression]. And by taking it thus, examples such as “By a mortal born in this way,” etc., become appropriate within the context of similes and the like.

For instance, in the passage beginning “Just as... much,” the term refers to the collection of causes for the performance of merit—such as giving, the attainment of wealth, hearing the true Dhamma, proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), reliance upon noble persons (*sappurisa-upanissaya*), and rebirth as a human being—which stand in the place of a heap of flowers.
Because they possess qualities such as beauty and fragrance, they are like garlands;
and because abundant meritorious deeds are to be performed by a mortal being whose nature is subject to death, they are illustrated as being like heaps of flowers and garlands.

Since the manner of this comparison is stated non-specifically by the word "yathā" (just as), it is appropriate to say that the word "evaṃ" (thus) serves the purpose of concluding the manner of the comparison.
However, when the mode of comparison (*upamākāra*) is being defined, it is in substance simply a comparison; thus he said, "it has come down as a comparison.

Likewise, when the perfection of deportment (*ākappasampatti*) appropriate for a recluse is being pointed out in this manner—by way of such expressions as "one should advance" and so forth—the mode of pointing it out therein is in substance simply an instruction (*upadesa*); thus it was said: "In this way, for you... [etc.]"

"In the instruction. Likewise, regarding the phrase "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sublime One," here "encouragement" (*sampahaṃsana*) should be construed as the act of gladdening and uplifting—by means of various modes—the qualities found therein by those who understand the matter exactly as spoken by the Blessed One without error;
that is, the manner of encouragement present therein. Furthermore, they explain it in this way here:

It should be construed as "the mode of reproach. And it is understood that this mode of reproach—such as the disparaging words beginning with "outcaste" (*vasalī*)—is indicated here by the word *evaṃ* (thus) because of its proximity to those words of disparagement.

Just as it is here, so too should it be seen that the "mode of comparison" and others are [indicated] by the word *evaṃ* due to their proximity to words such as "heap of flowers," which are spoken by way of comparison and so forth. And thus, when one says, "Speak in such a way as I... [it is understood].
The manner of speaking—“I say, Ānanda, speak thus to the ascetic”—is what must now be stated; since it is indicated by the word *evaṃ* (thus), it is called the sense of indication (*nidassanattha*).

Regarding the phrase *evaṃ nu kho* (is it thus?), here too, for the purpose of generating certainty regarding the fact that those aforementioned phenomena bring about harm and suffering, it is used in the sense of seeking consent, as in:
“Do they lead [to such results], or not? Or how is it in this regard?”
When the question "Is it so? was asked, because the reply "It is so for us here" was given, it is understood that the determination of that specific mode is revealed by the word *evaṃ*.
Furthermore, since that mode—which leads to harm and suffering for those phenomena—is being delimited, it serves the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*);
thus he said: "In such cases as 'It is so for us here,' [the word *evaṃ*] has the sense of restriction. "So it is, venerable sir."
However, because it was spoken by the bhikkhus who had been diligently engaged in listening to and attending to the Dhamma,
by way of their own admission of being established therein, the word *evaṃ* here is used in the sense of accepting what has been said;
thus, it means "So be it, venerable sir," "Excellent, venerable sir," or "Well said, venerable sir."

"Skilled in various methods" (*nānānayanipuṇaṃ*): "Various methods" (*nānānayā*) refers to the various kinds of methods categorized as unity, diversity, non-exertion, and suchness; or those known as the "Joyous Turn" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa*), the "Triple-Pointed" (*tipukkhalā*), the "Lion's Play" (*sīhavikkīḷita*), and "Direct Vision" (*aṅkusadisālocana*), according to the distinctions of the basis (*ādhāra*) and so forth.

Alternatively, "methods" (*nayā*) refers to the ways of the textual tradition (*pāḷigatiyo*). These are further classified by way of the primary rule (*paññatti*) and its supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*), by way of the side of defilement (*saṃkilebhāgiya*) and so forth, the mundane (*lokiya*) and so forth, their mixture, and so forth, by way of the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth, and by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.

"Various methods" (*nānānaya*) refers to the various ways [of teaching], such as by way of the means of integration (*saṅgaha*), etc.; by way of those liberated by occasion (*samayavimutta*), etc.; by way of setting aside (*ṭhapanā*), etc.;

by way of the roots of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*), etc.; and by way of the *Tikapaṭṭhāna*, etc. "Refined through these various methods" (*nānānayanipuṇa*) means that it is subtle and delicate (*saṇhasukhuma*) by means of them.

"Inclination" (*ajjhāsaya*) is the same as "disposition" (*āsaya*); and these are manifold due to the distinctions of eternalism (*sassata*), etc., and therein [due to] the state of having little dust in one's eyes (*apparajakkhatā*), etc., as well as self-inclination (*attajjhāsaya*), and so forth.
"Arising from many inclinations" (*anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ*) means that its cause of origin (*uppattihetu*) is such [an inclination].
"Endowed with meaning and phrasing" (*atthabyañjanasampannaṃ*) means complete in meaning and phrasing because there is nothing further to be added;

it is so by way of the six terms for meaning—namely, making known, manifesting, explaining, analyzing, clarifying, and describing—and by way of the six terms for phrasing—namely, phonemes, words, phrases, syntax, etymology, and demonstration.
Or rather, the meaning should be understood as "endowed with.

Regarding the phrase "various miracles" (*vividha-pāṭihāriya*), they explain the meaning of the word *pāṭihāriya* here as follows: "It is called a miracle (*pāṭihāriya*) because it removes adversaries, that is, because it eliminates defilements such as lust.
However, in the case of the Blessed One, there are no adversaries such as lust that need to be removed.

The various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) also occur in the minds of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) when those minds are free from defilements, endowed with the eight qualities, and have destroyed their opposites;
therefore, it cannot be called a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*) here based on the conventional usage that applies to that [former] case.
However, if the defilements residing in those to be converted are the opposites for the Blessed One, who is Greatly Compassionate, then because of his removal of them—
It is called “pāṭihāriya”; this is appropriate in that sense. Alternatively, the heretics are the adversaries of both the Blessed One and his Teaching;

it is called “pāṭihāriya” because of their removal (*haraṇa*). For they are removed and expelled by means of the miracles of supernormal power, mind-reading, and instruction, through the overturning of their views and because they are rendered incapable of manifesting those views. Or else, this word *paṭi* means “afterwards.”
It makes its meaning understood, as in such passages as, "When I had entered therein, another brahmin arrived.

Therefore, it is called *paṭihāriya* because, once the mind has become concentrated and free from defilements, and the task has been accomplished, one must subsequently carry [the result] away or put it into practice;
or else, it is the subsequent carrying away [of the mind] once its own defilements have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the path.

The miracle (*paṭihāriya*). The miracles of supernormal power (*iddhi*), mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsani*) should be performed again for the benefit of beings by one who is free from defilements and has completed his task.
Furthermore, because they remove the defilements of other beings when one’s own defilements have been removed, they are called "miracles" (*paṭihāriya*).
A miracle itself is a "wonderful miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*). Or, it refers to the collection of supernormal power, mind-reading, and instruction which constitutes the miracle.
Each one of these is called a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*). Alternatively, the fourth jhāna and the Path are "wonderful" (*paṭihāriya*) because they remove opposing factors;
that which is born therein, or that which has that as its sign, or that which comes from that, is thus a "miracle.
Since many kinds of miracles—such as those of psychic power and so forth—are found within the Blessed One’s teaching, he says "various miracles."
“Not otherwise” means not otherwise than the manner in which it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One;
it does not mean otherwise than the manner in which it was taught by the Blessed One. For the teaching of the Blessed One possesses inconceivable power.
By taking it in this way, the statement, “Who is capable of understanding it in every aspect? is justified, and the demonstration of the power of retention is not contradicted.

Because what is intended is the non-separation from the form of the sutta. For here, there is no need to avoid the charge of [the two meanings] being different, since both meanings have the same objective;
otherwise, one would fall into the position that the Elder was both capable and incapable of receiving the Blessed One’s teaching in its entirety.

This is because [the term *ajjhatta*] is applied to one's own continuum (*sasantati*), which is designated as "one's own internal" (*niyakajjhatta*) in the statement: "That which is not another is the self."

Although the word *me* appears with only a single meaning, it is said that "the word *me* is seen in three meanings" with reference to its existing distinctions as a designation for the instrument (*karaṇa*), the recipient (*sampadāna*), and the possessor (*sāmin*).
Although a prefix (*upasagga*) qualifies an action, nevertheless, because it is merely an indicator (*jotaka*), even when it is present, it is the word *suta* itself [that conveys the meaning].

He says, "both with a prefix and without a prefix," showing that when the meaning of the word *suta* (heard) without a prefix is being extracted, it is not contradictory to include the form with a prefix, because it "expresses that very same meaning. The word "its" (*assa*) refers to the word *suta*.

Since the instrumental (*kamma*), nominative (*bhāva*), and passive (*sādhanāni*) constructions are possible here for the word *suta*, he says: "either as 'that which is held' (*upadhārita*) or as 'the holding' (*upadhāraṇa*)."
"Or else, it means 'there is'. Regarding "when *mayā* has the sense of 'there is'": this means when the word *me* is used as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of its agent (*kartr*).
Regarding "when *mamā* has the sense of 'there is'": this is when it is used as a possessor (*sāmin*) by way of a relationship (*sambandha*).
It is stated that in the presence of the word *suta*, the word *evaṃ* employed [with it] must be one that illuminates the act of hearing (*savana-kiriyā*).
“Thus, this is a demonstration of the function of consciousness such as ear-consciousness and so forth.

By the word “and so forth” (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of the five-door consciousnesses beginning with receiving (sampaṭicchana) and those mind-door consciousnesses brought forward by them.

Since all sentences are accompanied by the sense of the particle “only” (eva), the meaning “heard only” is obtained for the word “heard” (suta); thus he said, “by way of the negation of its being unheard.”

By this restriction, he shows what has been excluded. And since it must be determined that "what is heard is indeed heard," he says, "the demonstration of grasping [the object] without deficiency, excess, or inversion," meaning that it becomes properly heard.

Alternatively, because "a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meanings of other words," the word *suta* (heard) does not mean "not heard"; thus its meaning is stated as "by way of negating the state of not being heard."
By this, he effects the turning away from [claiming] "seen" and so forth. This is what is meant:
"This was not seen by me, nor realized through independent knowledge (sayambhuñāṇa); rather, it was heard, and that too correctly. For this very reason, he said:

"It is a demonstration of grasping that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor perverted. Alternatively, when the word *evaṃ* is used in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), this application of meaning is made; thus, for the word *suta*, which depends upon that [emphasis], [the following applies]:
This meaning was stated as "by way of the negation of the state of not hearing. For that very reason, he said: "a demonstration of grasping [the teaching] without deficiency, excess, or error.
And here, the word *savana* (hearing) should be understood in the sense of the object (*kamma*), as in "that which is heard" (*suyyati*).
Thus, the application of the meaning of the three terms has been shown in one manner, by way of the cause of hearing, the person who hears, and the specific act of hearing.
Having shown this, he now says "in the same way" and so forth in order to demonstrate it by other modes as well.
Therein, "of that" refers to that cognitive process of the mind-door (*manodvāra-vīthi*) which occurred in the presence of the Blessed One in the manner of hearing the Dhamma;
for that [process] is capable of proceeding toward objects of various kinds. And thus it was said: "by following the ear-door."
“By way of various modes” means by way of the various modes of grasping the phrasing and meaning of the many kinds that will be explained;

by this, he indicates that in this construction the word *evaṃ* (thus) is taken in the sense of mode (*ākāra*). “The manifestation of the state of occurrence” means the manifestation of the existence of the occurrence.
Regarding the statement, “‘It was heard’ is the manifestation of the Dhamma,” it refers to the cognitive process (*viññāṇavīthi*) of the aforementioned type with respect to the object.

It occurs in various modes; it is stated because of its nature as a phenomenon (*dhamma*), not because the word "heard" (*suta*) has the nature of a phenomenon. The clarification of the very meaning already stated begins with "For here... and so forth.
In that context, the term *viññāṇavīthiyā* is used in the sense of an instrument (the ablative case). *Mayā* is used in the sense of location (the locative case).
Having taken the word *evaṃ* for the purpose of illustration—since it is said that "‘Thus’ is the manifestation of that which is to be demonstrated"—it refers to that which is to be pointed out.
Because there is no state of being that must be demonstrated [as such], he shows by means of that word *evaṃ* (thus) that the entire sutta is referred back [to it].

Since the word *suta* (heard) is an action-word (*kiriyāsadda*), and because the act of hearing is connected to a common continuum of consciousness (*viññāṇappabandha*), and because the designation "person" (*puggalavohāra*) applies therein, it is said: “‘Suta’ is the manifestation of the function of a person. For [the term] is not devoid of the designation "person."
The activity of hearing is obtained regarding a continuity of phenomena (*dhammappabandha*).

The phrase beginning with “of which mental continuum” (*yassa cittasantānassa*) was stated in order to show an alternative application of the meaning by taking the word *evaṃ* in the sense of manner (*ākāra*), rather than its previous application.
In that context, “conceptualization of manner” (*ākārapaññatti*) is precisely a derivative conceptualization (*upādāpaññatti*) of phenomena.
It is spoken of in that way by way of the mode of occurrence and the grasping [of the object]. Regarding the statement, “‘Hearing’ (suta) is a designation for the object”:
it is said because the dhamma, which has become the object of hearing, is the locus of occurrence for the person who is the agent of the act of hearing, by way of that act of hearing.

Although there is no agent whatsoever in the ultimate sense apart from the continuum of consciousness, [the term is used] through conventional linguistic usage, according to the desire for words expressing a distinction imagined by the intellect.

It is stated as if that [consciousness] were something other than the mental continuum, making it the possessor of that [continuum], in the phrase "by means of the mental continuum, for the possessor thereof.

Furthermore, although the dharma to be heard is the object of the act of hearing, it is here [designated as the agent] because the mental continuum proceeding by way of the act of hearing constitutes the agent in the ultimate sense;
or else, because the occurrence of consciousness itself by way of hearing constitutes the state of the act of hearing.
It is stated, "within the range of the agent possessing that [state]," because it is the domain of the agent who performs that action.
And because the Elder, whose manner of hearing was such, had reached a correct conclusion, he said, "the finality of grasping";
or rather, it should be understood that this construction of the meaning was made by taking the word *evaṃ* (thus) for the purpose of restriction.

The word *evaṃ* has the nature of manifesting the form, the indication, the demonstration, or the determination of the meaning and the phrasing of various previously heard discourses (*sutta*) that are so designated;

thus it is said, "‘Evaṃ’ is a designation for the function of a person," because the act of determining such forms and so forth is the operation of the continuum of phenomena (*dhamma-pabandha*) which serves as the basis for the conceptual designation of a person (*puggala-paññatti*).
Furthermore, since even for the Puggalavādins there is no act of hearing that is independent of consciousness, it is specifically the operation of consciousness [that is meant]; thus he says:

"‘Hearing’ is a designation for the function of consciousness. Because the term ‘me’ (I) refers exclusively to a sentient being through the occurrence of speech, and because the function of consciousness must be subsumed under that very [sentient being], he says:
"‘Me’ is a designation for the person endowed with both functions."

It has been stated. Since the meanings of the words *evaṃ* and *suta* respectively consist in the nature of a designation for what does not exist and a designation for what exists, he said—showing them as having the function of being the basis for such designations:
"‘Evaṃ’ is a designation for the function of the person; ‘suta’ is a designation for the function of consciousness.
And here, it is by way of clarifying the distinctions of instrument, action, agent, and object that [the meaning is established].

It should be understood that the four applications of meaning beginning with the accusative case are shown by way of: (1) the person, the object of the person's activity, and the demonstration of that person's activity; (2) the mode of grasping, the grasper, and the specification of the particular object grasped;

and (3) the agent, the instrument, the activity, and the agent of the activity. This is because every meaning attainable through language must be approached solely by means of its designation (*paññatti*), and because all designations...
Because it is included among the six types of designations by way of "existing" and so forth,
he says, "‘Thus’ and ‘mine,’ etc.," while determining the specific nature of the designations such as "thus" within those [six]. Therein, because the meaning expressed as "thus" and "mine"—
namely, the aspect (ākāra) and so on— and the phenomena themselves cannot be observed, he states that they are "designations of the non-existent."

“Designation of what does not exist by way of the true, ultimate meaning. In this context, “by way of the true, ultimate meaning” means by way of the meaning that is real and the meaning that is supreme.
This is what is meant: that which is not unreal like an illusion or a mirage, nor is it a non-supreme meaning like something to be grasped through hearsay and the like;
rather, it is the intrinsic nature of form, sound, and so forth, characterized by being subject to change, experiencing, and so on.
Or, the meaning [of the term] is called "the actual state" (*saccikaṭṭha*) and "the ultimate state" (*paramattha*); it is not the meaning of the words "thus for me" (*evam me*).

To make this very point clearer, it was said: "What is there in this? and so forth. Furthermore, the word "heard" (*suta*) is spoken with reference to the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*), as in:
"that which is here apprehended by the ear," which is a "designation of what exists" (*vijjamāna-paññatti*). For that very reason, it is said: "yañhi tamettha sotena upaladdhaṃ."
It has been said: "When it is stated, 'apprehended by way of the ear-door,' everything—including both the meaning (attha) and the phrasing (byañjana)—is thereby included.

Because it can be expressed in relation to this or that [object]: in relation to those phenomena that have entered the path of hearing, one says "thus" (evaṃ) by way of referring back to their determined mode and so forth;
and in relation to the aggregates included within one's own continuity, one says "mine" (me).

The meaning is as follows: Although the conventional usage of the term "heard" (*suta*) occurs with respect to the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*), which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of being seen and so forth—just as the expressions "second," "third," and so on occur in relation to "first" and the rest—it is said, "because it must be spoken of in reference to what has been seen, etc.
For that object which is indicated by the word "heard" is not actually something heard [in the primary sense].
The specific modes of the discourse as personally realized by the Elder are summarized by him with the word “thus”; thus he says, “it illuminates non-delusion.
By the phrase “one becomes capable of various modes of penetration,” he shows both the manifold nature and the difficulty of penetrating the discourse that is about to be spoken.
By the phrase “it illuminates the non-forgetfulness of what has been heard,” it is because the mode of what was heard is being shown exactly as it is.

It has been stated. "By non-delusion" means by the absence of delusion; or rather, through the very wisdom (*paññā*) that arose at the time of hearing, there is the accomplishment of wisdom at a subsequent time—this same principle should also be stated here regarding "by non-forgetting.
The aspect of the phrasing (*byañjana*) to be penetrated is not exceedingly profound;
since what is to be done therein is simply the retention of what was heard, the function of mindfulness (*sati*) is predominant, while wisdom is subordinate in that context.

It is said, “preceded by wisdom,” and so forth, because it has wisdom as its precursor (*paññāya pubbaṅgamā*). Here, being a precursor means having the status of the primary factor, as in such expressions as “the mind is the precursor.
Alternatively, since the eye-consciousness and the rest are subordinate to the preliminary mental application (*āvajjana*) and so forth due to that precursory state, this meaning is also appropriate:
“wisdom is the precursor of this [action]. Thus, [it is also said] “preceded by mindfulness.”
Here too, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated, as far as applicable.
"Endowed with both meaning and phrasing" means being complete in both meaning and phrasing:

through the six factors of meaning—namely, revealing, manifesting, explaining, analyzing, clarifying, and defining—and through the six factors of phrasing—namely, letters, words, phrases, syntax, etymological interpretation, and exposition.
Or rather, the meaning should be understood as "endowed with.

"It illustrates proper attention" means that the intention is that the modes, indications, and determinations expressed by the word "thus" have as their object the true nature of phenomena (dhamma) without inversion.
"It illustrates non-distraction"—where [is] the *Brahmajāla*?

The phrase beginning with "spoken" (*bhāsita*) is stated because the hearing of the sutta—which is about to be explained after having reached its formal presentation by way of a question—is not possible without prior concentration (*samādhi*).
The passage beginning with "of one whose mind is distracted" (*vikkhittacittassa*) is stated as a supporting argument for that very same point.

"All perfections" (*sabbasampatti*) refers to the perfection of meaning, phrasing, teacher, purpose, and so forth. By means of [the teachings] whose objects are the true Dhamma (*saddhamma*) without error...

Just as the accomplishment of right disposition toward oneself (*attasammāpaṇidhi*) and previously performed merit (*pubbekatapuññatā*) is stated by means of wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*)—which functions through the senses of resemblance, illustration, and determination—as being inseparable from it; and just as [the accomplishment of] non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) is stated by means of hearing the true Dhamma (*saddhammassavana*);
so too, by means of non-distraction as the fruit, the causes consisting of hearing the true Dhamma and reliance upon a good person (*sappurisūpanissaya*) are established.
Success (*siddhi*) ought to be demonstrated for the person who has not heard [the Dhamma] and for one who lacks reliance upon true persons (*sappurisa*), because such success is absent in them.

However, by the statement beginning with “For one whose mind is distracted,” which establishes the capacity [for hearing], the attainment of the hearing of the True Dhamma—which is the fruit—is shown through non-distraction as the cause and through reliance upon true persons as the supporting condition. This is the appropriate intended meaning here.
Hearing the true Dhamma and relying upon virtuous friends are not exclusively causes for non-distraction because they are external conditions;
however, non-distraction is an exclusive cause for hearing the true Dhamma, just as reliance upon virtuous friends is for non-distraction.
Even so, this demonstration of the accomplishment of reliance upon virtuous friends through non-distraction is indeed capable, and not incapable, for those whose minds are distracted.
This is because the purpose is accomplished through the absence of attending upon true persons (*sappurisa*).
Here, the first [example] should be seen as a demonstration of the establishment of a cause by means of its fruit—like the presence of rain upstream indicated by the swelling of a river;
the second is a demonstration of the establishment of a fruit by means of its cause—like the occurrence of rain resulting from the unerring rising of a cloud.

It is said, "Such is the auspicious manner," because it is the cause for fulfilling the welfare of others without exception, by way of penetrating the entirety of the excellence of the Dispensation through the distinctions and divisions of the meaning and phrasing of the Blessed One’s word. This is connected with the phrase "because it does not exist.
"The perfection of the latter two wheels" refers to what is comprised of one's own right aspiration and previously performed merit.

There are two qualities. Here, they are called "wheels" (*cakka*) because of their function of moving from one state to another; or else, because beings move by means of them through states of prosperity.
It is with reference to these that it was said: "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels; possessed of which, for gods and humans, the fourfold wheel revolves," and so forth.
Furthermore, the sequence of first and last here should be understood according to the order of the teaching.
“By the accomplishment of the two final wheels” means by the presence of the two final wheels.
Because his mind is rightly directed and he has previously performed merit, he possesses a pure intention (*āsaya*) due to the distancing of the defilements that are the causes of its impurity;
thus it is said, “the purity of intention is accomplished. For it has been said: “A mind rightly directed makes one better than before.”
“You have performed merit, Ānanda; apply yourself to striving, and you will soon be one free from taints. For this very reason it was said:

“The accomplishment of proficiency in realization [comes] through purity of disposition. Regarding “purity of application”: this refers to the clarity of the application of hearing the Dhamma, which is preceded by wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
Accordingly, it was said: “The accomplishment of proficiency in the scriptures. Of all...

Or [it is] because of the faultless nature of his bodily and vocal application. For one whose bodily and vocal application is pure, being free from remorse, has an undistracted mind and is confident in the scriptures.

By the phrase "by that which demonstrates various kinds of penetration," etc., [the author shows] the Elder’s [mastery] regarding both the meaning and the phrasing through the words *evaṃ* (thus) and *sutaṃ* (heard).
By way of the four analytical knowledges (*catu-paṭisambhidā*), he demonstrates the application of the meaning through the illumination of non-delusion and non-confusion.

Therein, by the phrase "by the illumination of the penetration into the various kinds of what is to be heard," he shows that this word *suta* (heard), due to its proximity to the word *evaṃ* (thus) or by virtue of its reference to what is about to be stated, touches upon the specific category of the Dhamma that is to be heard in a general sense.
[This occurs] specifically through the thorough examination and excellent penetration of the mental objects, views, and the Dhamma of the scriptures.
Having connected the word *evaṃ*— which illustrates proper attention (*yonisomanasikāra*)— with the phrase "bound to attention" according to the method already stated,
and having connected the word *suta*— which illustrates non-distraction— with the phrase "bound to the application of the ear through the excellence of hearing, retaining,
and verbal mastery of the Dhamma of the scriptures," he demonstrates his zeal for hearing the Dhamma as a perfection of the Dispensation.
It generates [insight]. Therein, "the Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*).
"Examined with the mind" means examined by the mind in such a manner as: "Here the virtue is taught, here the concentration, here the wisdom; there are so many connections here," and so forth.

"Well-penetrated by view" means [penetrated] by the view that has become patient through reflection (*nijjhāna-kkhanti*), or by the view known as full understanding through knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*).
Having thoroughly determined the material and immaterial phenomena mentioned here and there as "this is form" and "so much is form," they have been penetrated.
The phrase "by means of the entire expression" is stated because [the meaning] was previously applied separately by means of three distinct phrases.
"The plane of the bad person" refers to ingratitude; for instance, "here, a certain evil bhikkhu, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata..."
This refers to the state of ignoble speech (anariyavohārāvatthā) mentioned [in the text]. That very state of ignoble speech is the "non-Dhamma" (asaddhamma).

But is it not the case that the statement regarding the transcendence of the plane of the unworthy (asappurisabhūmi), and so forth, is purposeless? For surely there was no overweening pride (adhimāna) on the part of the Elder Ānanda thinking, "This is my word," nor was there any such suspicion on the part of the Elder Mahākassapa and others. This is not so.
Thus, by saying "Thus have I heard," this meaning is also shown to be clarified. However, some say:
"Such an objection—that those words were spoken with regard to the reflections of deities—is without foundation.
For it is said that at that moment, a reflection arose in the minds of certain deities: "The Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna..."

"This venerable one is skilled in teaching; he is now preaching the Dhamma. Born of the Sakyan clan, the Tathāgata’s brother and son of his younger paternal uncle, does he perhaps teach the Dhamma that he has realized for himself, or is it merely the word of the Blessed One as he has heard it?
Thus, by way of such doubts and by way of having entered the plane of a person of no integrity, there is the overcoming [of those states].
"Vibhāvitaṃ" means: "Attano adahanto" means not placing [the object] within oneself by thinking "this is mine.

"Appeti" indicates that he leads beings appropriately toward the goals pertaining to this life, the future life, and the ultimate goal; thus it is a "netti" (guide). The Dhamma itself is the guide, hence "dhammanetti.
"Vicikicchā" is doubt firmly established [in the mind]. "Vimati" is a mere state of mental division, lacking the tendency to move excessively [toward an object]. "Assaddhiyaṃ" is lack of faith.

It is destroyed because it was taught by the Blessed One, because it was received in his presence, and because there is an absence of faults such as the grasping of slips of the tongue or harsh speech.
Herein, the first three applications of meaning are shown by taking the word *evaṃ* in the sense of "thus" (*ākāra*) and so forth, without including any specific distinction;
the three following [applications] are elucidated by taking the word *evaṃ* in the sense of "manner" (*ākāra*) alone. The last...

However, it should be understood that the three [instances of] the word *eva* have been employed in sequence for the purpose of indicating manner (*ākārattha*), for the purpose of illustration (*nidassanattha*), and for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇattha*).
The word *eka* is seen in the senses of "other," "best," "without companion," and "number. For instance, it is used in such passages as: "The self and the world are eternal..."
In such passages as "This alone is true, all else is vain," it is seen in the sense of "other";
in "one-pointedness of mind" (*cetaso ekodibhāva*), in the sense of "preeminent"; in "alone, withdrawn," in the sense of "without companion";
and in "Monks, there is indeed one single moment and occasion for living the holy life," in the sense of "number. Showing that here too it is in the sense of number:
He said: “It is a single exposition defining enumeration. “Time and occasion” means both the appropriate time and the completeness of conditions.
“Moment” (khaṇa) means opportunity. For the arising of a Tathāgata and so forth is the opportunity for the holy life of the Path, because it is the cause for obtaining its requisite conditions.
And the moment itself is the occasion. The meaning is that what is called both “moment” and “occasion” is one and the same.
“Mahāsamaya” means a great assembly. “Samayopi kho” means even the cause for fulfilling the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). “Samayappavādake” means those who proclaim their own doctrines (*diṭṭhi*).
For it is there that the non-Buddhist teachers (*titthiya*), sitting together, proclaim their respective doctrines.

“Atthābhisamaya” means the attainment of welfare. “Abhisamayo” is that which is to be fully realized; thus, “abhisamayaṭṭho” means the purpose of full realization. This is the [meaning of the] pressure (*pīḷana*).

These [terms] are stated as having a unified nature by way of being what is to be fully understood (*abhisametabba*). Alternatively, the meaning of "full understanding" (*abhisamaya*) is the state of being the object of penetration (*paṭivedha*);
