In this context, *samaya* means a coming together or a meeting; it is a conjunction (*samavāya*) because the cooperative causes (*sahakārīkāraṇa*) meet and assemble there.
It is a "moment" (*khaṇa*) because the noble life-quest (*brahmacariya*) meets and comes together with the individuals who are its support.

It is "time" (*kāla*) because a sentient being, a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), or [a process] such as arising, meets and coincides with [other factors] such as co-nascent conditions (*sahajātādi*) or [phases] such as origination (*uppāda*). This is because it is merely the occurrence of phenomena (*dhammappavattimattatā*).
For although time does not exist in an ultimate sense (*atthato*), it serves as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the occurrence of phenomena;

and like an instrument (*karaṇa*), it is conventionally expressed through a form established by mere conceptual construction (*kappanāmatta*). *Samaya* means the simultaneous or common movement, proceeding, or persistence of parts;
thus it is a collection (*samūha*), just as in the term "aggregate" (*samudāya*). For a collection is indeed the simultaneous persistence of parts. [This refers to] the remaining conditions...
It is called *samaya* because it comes together (*samāgame*) as a fruit; from this, it arises and proceeds. It is a cause (*hetu*), just as [the term] "origination" (*samudaya*).
Alternatively, it is *samaya* because it comes together (*sameti*) through the state of being a fetter (*saṃyojana-bhāva*) and thus connects (*eti*) to its own object, proceeding therein;

or because beings come together (*ayanti*) and proceed according to their adherence through the state of firm grasping. Thus, it is *samaya*, which is view (*diṭṭhi*). By means of the fetter of view...
For beings are indeed bound exceedingly [by it]. *Samaya* means meeting, conjunction, or coming together; it is acquisition (*paṭilābha*).

The going toward what is right, or the right going away, is *samaya*; it is abandonment (*pahāna*). That which is to be approached face-to-face by means of knowledge, that which is to be fully realized (*abhisametabba*), is *abhisamaya*;
it is the non-erroneous intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena. It is so called because one goes toward, proceeds toward, or awakens to [reality] by way of facing it directly.
*Abhisamaya* is the realization of the true nature of phenomena (*dhammā*) as they actually are. In this way, the application of the term *samaya* to various meanings should be understood.

Regarding the extraction of the meanings of the word *samaya*, the example of the word *abhisamaya* is to be understood according to the method already stated. The word "of" (*assa*) refers to the word *samaya*.
Its meaning here is "time," because other meanings such as "conjunction" (*samavāya*) and so forth are impossible in this context.
And because time must be referred to as the introductory cause (*nidāna*) of the discourse, just as it is for the assemblies of the noble ones and the countryside.

The connection is: "the description is made by means of the instrumental case (*karaṇavacanena*) as 'how' (*yathā*). "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the Abhidhamma and Vinaya. "Thus" (*tathā*) refers to the locative and instrumental cases.

The sense of "locus" (*adhikaraṇattha*) is the sense of "substratum" (*ādhārattha*). "State" (*bhāva*) is indeed action (*kiriyā*); the definition of one state by another state through action is "the characterization of a state by a state" (*bhāvena-bhāvalakkhaṇaṃ*).

thus he says, "diversity of resolve" (*nānādhimuttikatā*). Furthermore, that resolve is the constituent element of inclination (*ajjhāsayadhātu*), which consists of seeing, accepting, and delighting in things in various ways; thus he says, "diversity of inclination... [and] delight" (*nānājjhāsayatā... rucitā*). By means of the knowledge of diversity of resolve...
And here, it is omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) that is intended, not the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabalañāṇa*); therefore he said, "by omniscient knowledge.

Regarding the phrase *iti ha me*: the word *iti* has the meaning of the word *evaṃ*; the syllable *ha* is merely a particle, and it is stated "thus these" (*evaṃ ime*) to show that the vowel *a* has been elided.
4. By means of the path of arahantship, eradication has been accomplished; hence it is said regarding the Buddha’s qualities: “There is no mind that is not engaged.

Having spent the time in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), and having dressed himself by way of changing his dwelling-robe for the robe used while in the monastery, [the Blessed One] approached [the assembly].
The passage beginning with “Sometimes alone,” etc., shows the Blessed One’s approach in accordance with the training of various disciples.
The attainment of evenness upon the ground at the moment of setting down the foot is the natural result (*nissandaphala*) of having well-placed feet;
it is not a feat of supernormal power (*iddhinimmāna*). The phrase "as soon as the right foot was set down" is stated because Buddhas are preeminent in all respects.
The connection is: "they were established in Arhatship."

"Attainments are hard to obtain" means that even when one has acquired human birth, qualities such as dwelling in a suitable locality, the integrity of the sense faculties, and the acquisition of faith are difficult to find.
"The abode of the Four Great Kings" means that they go to the empty palaces within the deva-world of the Four Great Kings.
This same method applies to the abodes of the Thirty-three Gods and so forth. "Appropriate to the time" means [appropriate] for this particular occasion.

"Thus it should be spoken" means according to the requirements of each particular time. "Appropriate to the occasion" (*samayayutta*) is a synonym for that same thing, or else it means appropriate to the specific context (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
Alternatively, "appropriate to the occasion" means accompanied by reasons and examples; for the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma with its supporting evidence at the proper time.
The intention is that he takes account of the season, but does not wash away the impurity [of the listener's mind]. For there is no impurity on the body of the Blessed One.
“He smears himself with dust and dirt.
*Kilāsa-bhāva* means weariness. It should be understood that he adopts the lion’s posture for the purpose of releasing the body from weariness.
As for the statement, “He surveys the world with the Buddha-eye,” this refers to what was frequently practiced by the Blessed One during the final watch of the night.
It has been said: "Sometimes the Blessed One establishes that matter by means of the remaining powers of knowledge and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).

The teaching beginning with "These are the bases of views" is the lion's roar. Having synthesized the mode of conditions for them through such statements as "With feeling as condition, craving arises," [the Buddha spoke] "As if lifting up Sineru, as if striking the sky"—this refers to the *Brahmajāla Sutta* teaching.
This was said for the purpose of showing that it is extremely difficult to perform because it is not shared by others. "Etam" refers to these two words, "yena" and "tena.
Alternatively, "yena" is used in the instrumental case to express cause; the meaning is: "by whatever reason that maṇḍalamāḷa was to be approached, by that same reason he approached it.
As for the reason, it has already been stated in the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) beginning with, "These bhikkhus... and so forth.
“Wood” (kaṭṭha) means a log of timber suitable for making a seat.
“The former” (purima) refers to the meaning expressed as “What is your name? The word *ca* in the phrase “And what, moreover” (*kā ca pana vo*) indicates contrast;
it illuminates the fact that the conversation, as it was asked, will be interrupted by what is about to be said. The word *pana*...
This is an ornament of speech (*vacanālaṅkāra*). For that very conversation by which those bhikkhus were seated together became an intermediate discussion (*antarākathā*) that was left unfinished;

thus it is specifically asked again. He states the meaning of the word *antarā* as "other" (*añña*), for this word *antarā* is used in the sense of "other," as in expressions such as "another place" (*bhūmantara*) or "another time" (*samayantara*).
Alternatively, the meaning of *antarā* is "in the middle" (*vemajjhe*). But [one might object]: "Was it not by them..."
Was that conversation brought to its conclusion by the monks according to their original intent through the words beginning with "Thus indeed to me"?
It was not brought to its conclusion, because it was interrupted by the Blessed One’s arrival.
For had the Blessed One not arrived at that moment, the conversation—still further bound to that very subject—would have continued; but due to the Blessed One’s arrival, it did not proceed.
For this very reason it was said: “This indeed... [omission] ...has arrived. But why, when compiling the Dhamma and Vinaya, is the introductory statement (nidāna) included?
Is it not the word of the Blessed One alone that should be compiled? It is said: for the purpose of ensuring the stability, non-confusion, and credibility of the teaching.
For a teaching connected with its time, place, teacher, subject matter, doctrine, and recipient remains stable for a long time and possesses the quality of being free from confusion.
And it is to be believed. The determination of the conventional expression is like a binding by way of place, time, agent, hearer, and cause;

for this very reason, when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked questions regarding the place and so forth—beginning with, "Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla spoken?"—the Dhamma-keeper (Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika), providing the answers to those questions, spoke the Nidāna. Thus he said this.
“[The words] ‘the time... [and so on]... ‘the introduction was spoken.

Furthermore, the statement of the introduction is for the purpose of establishing the Teacher. For the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, is established as the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) due to the absence of prior composition, inference, scripture, and reasoning.
Indeed, it is by virtue of his state as a Perfectly Enlightened One that there is an absence of prior composition and the like in all respects.”

Because of the unimpeded range of his knowledge and because all knowable phenomena are of a single measure; likewise, because he lacks the "teacher’s fist" (holding back teachings), stinginess regarding the Dhamma, and any favoritism toward disciples, his status as one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is established.
For it is through the destruction of the taints that there is an absence of the teacher’s fist and such traits, and that his activity for the benefit of others is purified.
Thus, ignorance and craving—which are defects in the teacher and which corrupt the perfection of view and conduct—[are absent].

By means of the states of purity of the Perfectly Enlightened One indicated by the absence [of faults] and characterized by the perfection of knowledge and abandonment, the first two grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*) are established; and from that very fact,
because the absence of delusion regarding obstructive and emancipating phenomena is established, the latter two grounds of self-confidence are established—

thus the Blessed One’s possession of the four grounds of self-confidence is demonstrated, and his practice for his own welfare and the welfare of others is likewise revealed by the introductory statement (*nidānavacana*).

Because he illuminates the teaching of the Dhamma through spontaneous eloquence appropriate to the inclinations of the assembled audience, and because of such statements as "by one who knows and sees," it is said: "The introductory statement [is made] for the sake of establishing the Teacher.
Likewise, the introductory statement is for the sake of establishing the Teacher; for the Blessed One’s every action is encompassed by wisdom and compassion.
There is no activity that is purposeless, nor is there any for one’s own benefit alone;

therefore, every deed—whether of body, speech, or mind—of the Perfectly Enlightened One, who acts solely for the sake of others, is the Teacher himself. It is not merely the composition of poetry or similar works that constitutes the Teaching.
Hence it is said: “The introductory statement [is made] for the sake of establishing the Teacher. Furthermore, by means of this, the Teacher’s status as an authoritative standard is elucidated.
This is the introductory statement for establishing the authoritative status of the Teaching (*sāsana*).

For by the phrase "by the Blessed One," through the illumination of the Tathāgata’s state as a being distinguished by supreme qualities and so forth, and by the phrase "knowing" and so on, through the illumination of the application of the knowledge of underlying tendencies (*āsayānusaya-ñāṇa*) and so forth, this meaning is established.
This is merely a brief indication of the purpose of the introductory statement here.
For who indeed is capable of fully elucidating the purposes of the introduction spoken by the Steward of the Dhamma,
who awakened after the Buddha?
The commentary on the Introduction is finished.

5. "Of what has been laid down" means of what has been taught. For even the teaching itself is called a "laying down" (*nikkhepa*) because it lays down the meaning—such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth—to be taught within the mental continuums of those to be trained.

In this regard, just as the discourses (*suttanta*), though divided into many hundreds and thousands of types, do not exceed sixteenfoldness according to the method of the exposition of the Dispensation beginning with the "partaking of defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), so too [the teachings] are categorized by way of the laying down of discourses such as those expressing one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*).
He said, "The fourfold manner of being" means "the four ways of introducing a discourse.

Although here a distinction in combination is possible between the speaker's own intention (*attajjhāsaya*) and the arising of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*) on one hand, and questions based on another's intention (*parajjhāsaya-pucchā*) on the other—since there exists a connection through the sequence of intention and questioning—there is nevertheless no mutual combination between the speaker's own intention and the arising of a specific occasion;
therefore, the method of detailed exposition is not presented here in its entirety.
It is possible; therefore, it is said, “there are four ways of laying down a sutta.

Alternatively, although there might be a distinction in the case of the occasion-arising (aṭṭhuppatti) and the underlying intention (ajjhāsaya), it should be understood that because the remaining ways of laying down are included within them, only four are shown by way of the fundamental laying down (mūlanikkhepa).
Furthermore, this laying down of a sutta comes first because of its general nature.
It should be investigated; once that has been investigated, then, by way of analyzing the specific occasion for the arising (*aṭṭhuppatti*) upon which this discourse was set forth,
the commentary on the discourses and passages of the discourses occurring in the sections beginning with "Or to me, monks," "But this is indeed trifling," and "There is,
monks," will be stated for the sake of making it easy to see the respective connections between them.
"It is easy to understand" means that "when spoken after having investigated the placement of the discourse (suttanikkhepa), it becomes clear.

Regarding the phrase "placement of the discourse" (*suttanikkhepa*) and so forth: placing is *nikkhepa*; the placing of a discourse, the speaking of a discourse, is "the placement of the discourse," meaning the teaching of the discourse.
Alternatively, it is called *nikkhepa* because it is placed down; thus, the discourse itself is the *nikkhepa*.

The laying down of a discourse (*suttanikkhepa*). "One's own inclination" (*attajjhāsaya*): it is one's own inclination; because that [inclination] exists as the cause for the teaching of the discourse, it is called "one's own inclination.
Or, that which has one's own inclination is "one's own inclination. The same method applies here to the term "another's inclination" (*parajjhāsaya*).

"Under the influence of a question" (*pucchāvasika*): the power of a question is "question-power"; because that exists in this [discourse], it is "under the influence of a question. "Meaning" (*attha*) is so called because it is desirable (*araṇīya*).

The basis for the teaching of the Sutta is the *vatthu*. The arising of the meaning is *atthuppatti*; *atthuppatti* itself is *aṭṭhuppatti*, and because it possesses this, it is called *aṭṭhuppattika*.
Alternatively, that by which the Sutta is set forth is *suttanikkhepa*, namely one’s own intention (*attajjhāsaya*) and so forth.
In this interpretation, however, one’s own intention is *attajjhāsaya*, [and] that of others...
*Adhyāśaya* (inclination) and *parādhyāśaya* (the inclination of others). That which is asked is an "inquiry" (*pucchā*); it is the matter that ought to be asked.

The speech of those who receive the Dhamma, proceeding from the necessity of hearing it, is "dependent on inquiry" (*pucchāvasika*). That very term is expressed in the masculine gender in accordance with the word used in its formal placement (*nikkhepa-sadda*), as "pucchāvasiko.
Likewise, "dependent on occasion" (*aṭṭhuppattiko*) means simply "an occasion" (*aṭṭhuppatti*); in this way, the meaning here should be understood.
And here, it is appropriate that the independence from causes such as the ripening of the faculties of others constitutes the separate inclusion of one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*).
For this very reason, it is said: "He speaks solely by his own inclination.

However, regarding those discourses delivered when there arises the occurrence of questions reflecting the inclinations of others—which serve as the occasion for the teaching—how [is this to be understood]?
There is no restriction regarding the "occasion for a discourse" (*aṭṭhuppatti*). Nor should it be objected:

"How can there be no restriction regarding another's inclination (*parajjhāsaya*)?"—for this is because teachings delivered in response to questions or on an occasion for a discourse proceed in accordance with the inclinations of others.

For the state of being an "occasion for a discourse" consists precisely in the arising of a cause for teaching a sutta that is free from [the need for] a formal resolution (*abhinīhāra*) or a detailed inquiry (*paripucchā*) by others.

Because they have already been included [in the previous categories], those [teachings] given on account of another’s disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) or on account of a question (*pucchāvasika*) are mentioned separately.
For instance, in the *Dhammadāyāda-sutta* and others, the teaching of the acquisition of material goods and so forth is called "occasion for discourse" (*aṭṭhuppatti*).

It is clear that what is taught by making another’s disposition alone the motive, without a question from others, is "on account of another’s disposition," while that taught by means of a question is "on account of a question. This is the meaning.
It should be understood that he spoke solely out of his own inclination for the purpose of establishing the lineage of the Dhamma.

"A bearer of discourses on the right efforts" refers to the collection (*āvaḷi*) of discourses connected with the right efforts found in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* as they are presented in successive order;

likewise for the bearers of discourses on the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), and so forth. The "qualities that ripen liberation" are the faculties of faith and the rest. "Directing" (*abhinīhāra*) means aspiration (*paṇidhāna*).
Regarding the phrase "praise and dispraise" (*vaṇṇāvaṇṇa*): here, the praise uttered by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus beginning with "It is wonderful, friends! is also included.
Having made that the occasion for the teaching, he will begin the subsequent instruction with the words, "There are, bhikkhus, other qualities as well," and so forth.
As for the statement, "Or others might speak in praise of me, bhikkhus," this was said by Brahmadatta in reference to this teaching.
It is said, "The complexion was mentioned," making it an *aṭṭhuppatti* (an occasion for a teaching); thus it is stated, "Having made this praise and dispraise an *aṭṭhuppatti*.
The word *vā* is seen in many senses, such as comparison, conjunction, doubt, release, filling out a line of verse, and alternative.
For instance, it is seen in the sense of comparison in passages such as, "He is wise, as it were (*vāpi*). In this case, it means "in a similar state."

The word *vā* [has the following meanings]: in such passages as “The wise sages also perceive that,” it signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*); in such passages as “Who are these, or whose [are they]? it signifies doubt (*saṃsaya*);
in such passages as “Of these ascetics and brahmins, this one is the most foolish and the most deluded,” it signifies exclusion (*vavassagga*, i.e., emphasis or specification);

in such passages as “This boy did not know his measure,” it serves to complete the meter (*padapūraṇa*); and in such passages as “Whatever ascetics there may be, monks... [it functions as a particle of generalization].
In such passages as "or brahmins," it is used in the sense of an alternative; here, showing that this [particle] is indeed used in the sense of an alternative, he says:
"The word *vā* has the meaning of an alternative. The word *para* occurs in the sense of "another" in such passages as "If I were to teach the Dhamma, others would not understand me";

it occurs in the sense of "additional" in such passages as "the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa*"); and it occurs in the sense of "subsequent" in such passages as "he will come from elsewhere (*parato*)."
It occurs in the sense of being an opponent, as in such passages as: “Having thoroughly refuted with the Dhamma the arisen doctrine of others.
Here too, showing that it means “in the sense of being an opponent,” he says: “‘Pare’ means those who are opposed.

In the phrase “even in such cases as these,” the particle *pi* (even) expresses possibility; by this, it is indicated that even the arising of unwholesome states of mind directed toward the Triple Gem [is included].
It shows that [anger] should not be produced, let alone by means of worldly gain, material gain, or signs.

To indicate the absence of an agent other than the phenomenon of intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), it uses the word *āhanati* (strikes); thus, it shows the word *āghāta* in the sense of an agent. In that context, "he strikes" (*āhanati*) means he harms, oppresses, and afflicts.
Furthermore, the meanings of instrument and state are also possible: "one strikes by means of this" (*āhanati etena*), or "mere striking" (*āhananamattaṃ*) is *āghāta*.
Having thus explained the meaning of the word *āghāta* by analyzing its components, he now states, "This is a designation for anger," while showing its meaning there also by way of a synonym.
This same method should be applied, as appropriate, to such terms as *appaccayo* (displeasure) and *anabhiraddhi* (lack of satisfaction).
As for the word *appaccaya*, it is [explained] by way of a common synonym as that by which one becomes dissatisfied (*appatītā*).
It is the manifestation of the object; however, it should be understood as "without condition" (*appaccaya*) because one does not believe [in its existence] by way of that [manifestation].

"Abhirādhayati" means to accomplish. "By two" refers to the terms *āghāta* (malice) and *anabhiraddhi* (discontent). "By one" refers to the term *appaccaya*. "Of the rest" refers to the aggregates of perception (*saññā*) and consciousness (*viññāṇa*), or to those comprised within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) remaining after perception and consciousness.
"Karaṇa" means production. For [it is the production] of malice and so forth.
Here, the convergence of conditions for the occurrence [of a state] is called "making" (*karaṇa*); yet in actual fact, this is simply "arising.
For it was with reference to non-arising that the Blessed One said, "it is not to be made.

This is because [the mind] is indeed excluded from having a single arising, a single basis, a single object, or a single cessation. "Therein" means in that mental corruption (*manopadosa*). "Yours" (*tumha*) is a word identical in meaning to "your" (*tumhāka*); just as...
The word "amha" has the same meaning as "amhākaṃ. As it is said: "Therefore, our youths do not die.
"Obstacle" (antarāyo) is a statement of the reason why mental malice (manopadosa) should not be committed;
for if that anger and so forth were to arise, it would constitute an obstacle to the first jhāna and the others for you yourselves. Therefore, by way of such anger and so forth...
The meaning is that anger and the like have been declared as things not to be done.
By this he shows: "I do not forbid you from [calling me] 'Omniscient' by virtue of my lordship; rather, it is for this specific reason.
Since that statement of reason serves to reveal the danger (*ādīnava*), he says, "showing the danger. With the words beginning "Would you then... he refers to mental corruption (*manopadosa*).
It is not only an obstacle to benefit and happiness that arises at a later time; rather, it is also an obstacle to benefit and happiness occurring even at that very moment.
Thus, having made the danger in mental corruption more emphatic, he demonstrates it.
The meaning is not restricted solely to those who are not in opposition, as in the case of the word "others" (*pare*) and so forth. For this very reason, he says "one who is angry," and so on.
"Blinding darkness" (*andhatamaṃ*) means that which produces blindness. "Where" (*yanti*) refers to where; this is the nominative case used in the sense of the locative. The connection is:
"At whatever time anger overcomes a man, at that time there is blinding darkness. Alternatively, "where" (*yaṃ*) is a word expressing cause:
"Because anger, as it arises, overcomes a man, therefore at that time there is blinding darkness—at the time when there is anger."
The word *yaṃ* has the sense of "that," because it stands in an exclusively correlative relationship with the word *taṃ*.
Alternatively, *yaṃ* refers to the action [of bearing]. "Anger bears him" means that this endurance or overcoming of anger is the state of being in blinding darkness;
such is the meaning. Alternatively, for that man whom anger bears—that is, overcomes—there is then blinding darkness; from that...
"One who is angry does not know the goal; one who is angry does not see the Dhamma. "From within" means from the inside, or from the mind.
By the phrase "this and that reason," he shows this meaning: our Teacher alone is omniscient because he teaches the Dhamma without error;
the Dhamma is well-expounded because it leads exclusively to liberation; and the Saṅgha has practiced rightly because it is free from defilement.
[The Blessed One] shows this. By the phrase "this and that reason," the statement beginning with "he is not omniscient" is refuted as being unreal and untrue.
The second word is the word "untrue" (*ataccha*). "Of the first" refers to the word "unreal" (*abhūta*).
And "the fourth" refers to the phrase "but this is not found among us. "Of the third" refers to [the phrase] "and this does not exist..."
Regarding the word "among us" (*amhesu*): "only in blame" (*avaṇṇeyeva*) means only in censuring by way of establishing faults after having stated a semblance of a reason.
"Not in all cases" (*na sabbattha*) means that in instances such as mere reviling, scolding, or disparaging, one should not invariably offer an excuse.
He demonstrates this very point clearly with the words beginning "If indeed" (*yadi hi*).
6. By stating that "beings who possess this state rejoice and delight by means of this dhamma," it shows that the word *ānanda* has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
[Objection: One who possesses a beautiful mind (*mano*) is *sumana*; or, a beautiful mind is *sumana*. Its state is *somanassa*.

[If this were the case], would it not follow that even other associated states (dhammas) would possess the nature of joy (*somanassabhāva*)? [Reply: It does not so follow, because it is a conventional term (*ruḷhīsadda*).
Just as one might show that the term "mud-born" (*paṅkaja*) is a designation for mental pleasure (*cetasika-sukha*), so it is said here.
It is called *ubbila* because it causes one to swell; the meaning is that it breaks through its previous state and attains a distinction. That which is *ubbila* itself is *ubbilāvita*;
the state of being so is *ubbilāvitatta*. When this [feeling] has arisen, the body and mind reach a state of inflation, like a leather bag filled with air.
This is a designation for that worldly rapture (*odaggiyapīti*) which has become excited; for this very reason, he said, "leading to agitation," and so forth.

Here too, [the meaning is]: "Although there was no actual frivolity on the part of those monks, nevertheless, by prohibiting the arising of unwholesome states in sons of good family in such situations in the future, he establishes the guide to the Dhamma. This is expressed by two phrases.

Regarding the passage, "The aggregate of formations [is mentioned]; by that one, the aggregate of feeling is stated," the meaning should be understood here according to the method explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—namely, "By means of those [two], the performance [of the function] of the remaining associated states is also excluded"—and according to the method stated here as well, such as "the word *pi* (also) is used in the sense of inclusion (*sambhāvane*"), as applicable. Regarding the phrase, "That obstacle belongs to you alone": [the same applies].
The meaning of the phrase beginning with “‘Obstacles,’ this... should be understood according to the method explained previously in the section on dispraise.
As for the question “But why is this so?,” he raises an objection while keeping in mind the very meaning that is about to be stated.

The Teacher, acknowledging that point by saying “It is true it was praised,” then addresses the objection with the words “But that [praise] was based on renunciation,” and so forth. In that context, the word “this” (etaṃ) refers to...
This is the statement regarding the non-performance [of the practice] by Ānanda and others. The connection is: "Was it not indeed praised by the Blessed One?
"By means of the *kasiṇa*" means by way of its being a *kasiṇa*, that is, by its totality. Some, however, say: "'Of Jambudīpa' is a genitive used in the sense of the instrumental";

according to their view, the coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇabhāva*) of the words *kasiṇa* and *Jambudīpa* should be understood. "Therefore" means because of the joy and gladness based on the household life.
Because it creates an obstacle for the jhānas and so forth; for this was said by the Blessed One:
“O Devānaminda, I declare that joy is twofold: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.

The passage beginning with “For this” is stated in order to show that specific [type of] joy associated with which [the state] becomes an obstacle. In that context, “for this is joy and gladness accompanied by greed.”
It might be argued that by the inclusion of "joy" (*pīti*), "mental happiness" (*somanassa*) is also already included, because there is no joy devoid of mental happiness;

therefore, it should be understood that only "joy" is taken here. Alternatively, since the distinction between what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated is stated, the obstructive nature of mental happiness is well known, whereas that of joy is not so evident; thus, it is specifically "joy" that is taken here due to its association with greed.

These have been stated by way of distinction. The meaning of the verses beginning with “If one is greedy for wealth,” etc., should be understood in the same way as the verses beginning with “If one is angry for wealth,” etc.
“Bhikkhus, if others were to speak in praise of me, or speak in praise of the Dhamma, or speak in praise of the Saṅgha, and you were there—elated, joyful, and exultant—would you [be so]?”
"May you understand the well-spoken and the ill-spoken of others. "Certainly not, Bhante. This is the third section;

it should be understood that although this was not included in the teaching because no person [to whom it would apply] was present at the time of the discourse, it is nonetheless included in terms of its meaning (*atthato*), since the possibility of such a case exists—just as in the *Kathāvatthu-pakarana* when treated in detail. This is the intended sense.

By the phrase “It has indeed come down [in the text] by way of meaning,” he shows that at the time of the commentary, that section should be brought forward and stated according to those beings who would understand it in that manner.
By the words “Just as indeed,” etc., he clarifies the very occurrence of that meaning.
“In the manner already stated” refers to such passages as “In that context, by you means by you in that praise,” and so forth, and “The second word [is the explanation] of the first word.”
And according to the method stated in such passages as, "The fourth is a synonym for the third," and so forth.
The *Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā* concludes:

[The question] is withdrawn because, due to its lack of a basis, there is no need to provide an answer; yet it continues [to follow] because of its relevance to the subject matter of what ought to be answered.

He will show the connection by means of the passage beginning with, “There are, monks... The word *ora* may mean the subsequent part, as in such expressions as “wealth from this side” (*oraṃ bhogaṃ*) or “this shore” (*oraṃ pāraṃ*).
Alternatively, the word *ora* has the sense of “below,” as in such passages as “Those conditions for returning [to this world] are the fetters pertaining to the lower” (*orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni*).
For morality is the subsequent part when compared with concentration and wisdom.
"And it is a lower state. Regarding the phrase "mere virtue" (*sīlamattaka*): here the word *matta* either has the sense of "little," as in "a mere dose of medicine" (*bhesajjamattā*) and so forth;

or it has the sense of "excluding a distinction," as in "states consisting of applied thought and mere sustained thought" (*avitakkavicāramattā dhammā*), and "the element consisting of mind alone is the mind-element" (*manomattā dhātu manodhātū*).
Indeed, the same meaning is expressed in a general way by the two terms "insignificant" (*appamattaka*) and "trifling" (*oramattaka*).

The term "mere virtue" (*sīlamattaka*) is used in the sense of a specific distinction. Alternatively, the word *matta* is employed here in the sense of denoting a small portion for the purpose of including only a part of that [virtue] through virtue, or else it serves to exclude other qualifications.
For indeed, the virtues consisting of restraint of the sense faculties and those dependent on requisites have not been included in the teaching here; for they are not [the subject of this discourse].
The precepts of the Pātimokkha and the purity of livelihood are evident among all ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*).
By the phrase "having made an effort," he shows that in the word "speaking" (*vadamāno*), the term *māna* has the sense of exertion (*satti*).
Adornment (*alaṅkāra*) is decoration or embellishment, such as earrings and other ornaments; beautification (*maṇḍana*) is the filling of deficiencies.
*Maṇḍana* means the cause of adornment. Alternatively, one who adorns is *maṇḍana*, referring to a person of an ornamental nature.
This singular form is used here in the sense of the plural; thus, the meaning is "among those of an ornamental character.

In the phrase *paripūrakārī*, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" or "manner," by which he indicates the entire Sutta on the Exhortation to Sīla. *Candana* is so called because of its association with sandalwood.

There is the fragrance of sandalwood, and likewise that of tagara and other [scents]. Regarding the phrase "the fragrance of the virtuous," here "fragrance" is used in the sense of being like a fragrance;
it is a sound of praise bound to virtue. For virtue is the cause of renown. As it is said: "In one who is virtuous, endowed with virtue, a beautiful report of their fame spreads abroad.
"Pavāyati" means it shines forth. "Gandhā" refers to those things that possess the nature of fragrance.
“‘The small and the great’—this is said in relation to each other, like this shore and the far shore; thus he says, ‘in comparison with the higher qualities.
As for the word *hi* in the phrase ‘for virtue indeed,’ it has the sense of a reason (*hetu*); by this he shows:
‘Because although virtue is of great benefit to concentration by way of being its foundation, yet when compared with the specific qualities of its power and so forth...’”
“It does not even approach a fraction [of it], so too with concentration and wisdom. For this very reason, he says “therefore,” and so forth.
Now, having asked “how,” he elucidates in detail the majesty of concentration. The phrase “At the foot of the Bodhi tree...
is intended to show that the Twin Miracle was perfectly manifest, and to distinguish it from other miracles performed at the root of the Bodhi tree, during family gatherings, and on other occasions.
It has been said. For when the intention arose in the Blessed One’s mind to perform the Twin Miracle, it was necessary to have a location suitable for that purpose;

thus, they say that the jeweled pavilion and other structures were fashioned by Vissakamma at the command of Sakka, the king of the gods, while others maintain they were created by the Blessed One himself.
"Is there anyone capable of performing such a miracle? [he asked].

Because it is similar to an exhortation such as "let him come," it is called "the indication of taking up oneself" (*attādānaparidīpana*). In that context, "taking up oneself" (*attādāna*) refers to the undertaking;

and because the heterodox teachers (*titthiya*) were unable to do so, and because they had previously risen [to challenge] with the thought "we shall do it," it is the "crushing of the heterodox teachers" (*titthiyaparimaddana*).
The passage beginning with "from the upper part of the body" and so forth is found in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
In this regard, the canonical text is as follows:

“From the lower part of his body a mass of fire issues forth, and from the upper part of his body a stream of water issues forth. From the front part of his body fire issues forth, and from the back part of his body water issues forth.
From the back part of his body fire issues forth, and from the front part of his body water issues forth. From the right eye...”
Fire is on the left eye, water on the right eye. Fire is on the left eye, water on the right eye.
Fire from the opening of the right ear, water from the opening of the left ear. Fire from the opening of the left ear, water from the opening of the right ear.
Fire from the opening of the right nostril, water from the opening of the left nostril. Fire from the opening of the left nostril, water from the opening of the right nostril.
From the right shoulder-peak fire [issued], from the left shoulder-peak water. From the left shoulder-peak fire, from the right shoulder-peak water.
From the right hand fire, from the left hand water. From the left hand fire, from the right hand water.
From the right side fire, from the left side water. From the left side fire, from the right side [water].
Water. From the right foot comes fire, from the left foot comes water. From the left foot comes fire, from the right foot comes water.
From each finger comes fire, from the spaces between the fingers comes water. From the spaces between the fingers comes fire, from each finger comes water.
From each individual pore comes fire, from each individual pore comes water. From every single hair-pore, a mass of fire issues forth.
“Streams of water flow from every single pore.
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated as “from each individual pore.
Regarding the phrase “of the six colors,” etc., which occurs according to that method, there too [are mentioned] the blue, yellow, red, and white [colors].
“Of the mañjiṭṭha [flowers], radiant”—this is the textual reading (*pāḷiseso*). “Beams of golden color”—this is stated because they are for the most part so.

Regarding the phrase “it should be expanded”: here too, based on each of the four postures—such as “the Teacher stands, while the emanation walks, sits, or lies down”—there are four [descriptions] according to the Teacher.
"By way of the created [person], there are four"—thus it should be expanded in all eight instances.

"Honeyed milk-rice" means milk-rice sprinkled with honey. Regarding "the self, the friend, the neutral person, and the enemy," this is the meditation subject of loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*) endowed with four factors by way of the breaking down of the four boundaries.
Furthermore, this phrase "endowed with four factors" refers to the "foundation of energy."
This should also be applied here. In that context, the possession of the four factors is to be understood by way of the canonical passage beginning, “Willingly, let skin and sinews [remain].

Having introduced knowledge regarding the mode of conditions through the gateway of aging and death with the words, “Alas, this world has fallen into hardship,” etc., one enters the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*).
Here too, the phrase “the practice of all Buddhas” is to be understood with a change of grammatical case.
Having done so, it should be applied. For they say that this too is indeed the established practice of all Buddhas.
Having increased insight by taking up the womb of the Great Vajira-knowledge through three million six hundred thousand openings;
a *kuṇḍa* is a reservoir measuring thirty-two *doṇas*. A *daribhāga* is a mountain cleft. The great ocean at the base of the world-system is the *cakkavāḷa-mahāsamudda*.

The passage beginning with “Two types of worldlings” (duve puthujjanā) is stated for the purpose of showing the divisions found among worldlings, not for the purpose of singling out specific types of worldlings as in the *Mūlapariyāya-vannanā* and other such works.
For indeed, no worldling whatsoever is able to manifest the qualities superior to those of the Blessed One;
let alone the worldling, the qualities of a Buddha are beyond the scope even of disciples and paccekabuddhas.
For it will be said: “Stream-enterers,” and so forth. *Uggaha* (learning) is the act of bringing [the words] to the lips. *Paripucchā* (inquiry) is the questioning of the meaning.

*Savana* (hearing) is the hearing of the meaning by way of the commentaries. *Dhāraṇā* (retention) is the upholding of the Dhamma through the excellent arrangement and clear exposition of both the phrasing and the meaning.
*Paccavekkhaṇā* (reviewing) is the mental examination of those things thus heard, retained, and mastered.

They are called *puthujjana* because they have not destroyed (*avihatattā*) the many various kinds of defilements and the view of a personal entity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), and thus they generate them, or they are generated by them.
Alternatively, the word *jana* expresses the sense of "not having destroyed" (*avighāta*). Regarding the phrase "they look toward the faces of various teachers," the etymological meaning is:
those for whom there are many people recognized as teachers are *puthujjana*. [The compound] *puthu...pe...avuṭṭhita* [is analyzed as follows].

In this context, *jana* refers to those who are to be born, or those who are born here; thus, it means the destinies (*gati*). Those for whom there are many such *jana*s are *puthujjana*s (worldlings).

Alternatively, *jana* refers to those from whom others are subsequently born, namely the formative volitions (*abhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth. Since these exist manifoldly for them, they are called *puthujjana*s.
Or, the word *jana* should be understood as having the meaning of "formative volition" and so on. [The factors involved are] sensual lust, lust for existence, views, and ignorance.

The floods (*ogha*). The torments (*santāpa*) are the fires of lust and so forth. Those very same things, or all defilements (*kilesa*), are the fevers (*pariḷāha*). "Attached to the various five strands of sensual pleasure" (*puthu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu ratto*):
here, one who is born [in this state] is a "person" (*jana*); such as lust, greed, and so forth. They have various persons [as their objects], thus they are "worldlings" (*puthujjana*);
or alternatively, the word *jana* should be understood in the sense of lust and so forth, meaning "persons born attached to various [objects]. "Hindered" (*palibuddha*)...
“Perfectly enlightened ones,” or “those who are afflicted. By the phrase beginning with “of the many, beyond the path of counting,” he shows that “puthujjana” means “many people.
To demonstrate those specific qualities which serve as the basis for applying the term “Tathāgata” to the Blessed One, he says:
“The Blessed One is a Tathāgata for eight reasons,” and so forth. For all the names of the Blessed One are based solely upon his qualities. As it has been said:
“Countless are the names of the Great Sage according to his qualities;
even from a thousand names, a name should be selected on account of his virtue.
Regarding the phrase “thus come” (*tathāgata*), here the word *tathā* serves the purpose of providing a simile by way of determining the mode [of coming]. This is because it is a general designation.

The word *āgata* has the sense of "coming by way of the path" because of its specific establishment [in this context], not the sense of "coming by way of knowledge" as in such phrases as "come to the characteristic of suchness" (*tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato*), nor the sense of physical movement and so forth as in such phrases as "the Great Ascetic has indeed arrived at Giribbaja of the Magadhans.
In that regard, the word *tathā* has the purpose of providing a simile by way of determining a particular mode; and because that [mode] is dominated by compassion—
By way of the gateway of great compassion, showing in general the path traversed by previous Buddhas through the use of examples, he said:
"Just as [all the world...pe... have come]," because the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* possess an absolute state of mutual connection.
Furthermore, that path is well-known from the detailed descriptions found in such discourses as the Mahāpadāna Sutta, concerning Vipassī and the other Buddhas who were numerous and proximate.
Pointing to the examples of the six Perfectly Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas), he said, "Just as the Blessed One Vipassī," and so forth.
Therein, "by that aspiration" refers to the great aspiration consisting of the bodily resolve endowed with eight factors, namely:

the attainment of human birth, the perfection of the male gender, the meeting with a Teacher, the going forth into homelessness, the perfection of qualities such as the higher knowledges (abhiññā), and the zeal for the specific purpose. For all Buddhas, indeed...

"The aspiration for the body is fulfilled by this very resolve. Having thus shown the meaning of the term "Tathāgata" by way of the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*), he now spoke the passage beginning with "Just as the Blessed One Vipassī... [and so on]...
the Blessed One Kassapa, having fulfilled the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*)" in order to show it by way of the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramī*).
And here, for the purpose of generating proficiency in the Great Vehicle of Enlightenment according to the Discourses, this is the detailed exposition on the perfections (*pāramīs*):

What are these perfections? In what sense are they "perfections"? How many kinds are there? What is their sequence? What are their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), functions (*rasa*), manifestations (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*)?
What is their condition? What is their defilement? What is their purification? What is their opposite? What is their practice? What is their classification? What...
What is the gathering [of beings]? What is the means of accomplishment? In what length of time is accomplishment achieved? What is the benefit? And what is their fruit?

Herein is the answer: What are these perfections (*pāramī*)? The virtues of giving and so forth, when uncorrupted by craving, conceit, and the like, and embraced by compassion and skillful means, are the perfections.

In what sense are they called "perfections"? Because, through their association with the distinguished qualities of giving, virtue, and the rest, Great Beings (*mahāsatta*) are supreme (*parama*) due to their being the highest among beings.
*Bodhisatta* refers to the being or the activity of those [beings]; *pāramī* is the practice of giving and so forth. Alternatively, *paramo* means "one who goes beyond" (*paratīti*);
thus, the Bodhisatta is one who fulfills and protects the qualities such as giving. *Pāramī* is that which belongs to such a person (*paramassa*), or the state or activity of such a person;
it is indeed the practice of giving and so forth. Alternatively, one "binds" (*mavati*) another being to oneself through the possession of distinguished qualities.
Alternatively, it sinks deeply and is purified from the stains of defilement; or it especially reaches (mayati) the supreme (paraṃ), the most excellent (seṭṭhaṃ), Nibbāna;
or it measures (munāti) and delimits the further world (paraṃ lokaṃ) by means of a specific knowledge that has become a standard, just as it does this world;
or it measures (minoti) and places within its own continuum an exceedingly great multitude of qualities such as virtue (sīla).

He measures (mināti) or harms (hiṃsati)—that is, overcomes—the other, which is distinct from his own self-nature as the Dhamma-body, or the opposing host of defilement-thieves that works for his harm;
thus he is *paramo*, the Great Being. The phrase "This belongs to the Supreme One" (*paramassa ayan*) and so forth should be construed according to the method already stated.

Alternatively, he rejoices (*majjati*) and purifies himself in the further shore (*pāre*), namely Nibbāna, and cleanses sentient beings there; or else, he causes sentient beings to rejoice and be bound therein.

It is called *pāramī* because it joins [beings] to the further shore (*pāra*), or it goes to that [shore] and causes others to go; or it measures (*munāti*) things as they truly are, or it measures (measures out) and places beings therein;
or it measures (harms) and destroys the enemy of the defilements (*kilesāri*) of beings therein—thus it is *pāramī*. It is the Great Being (*mahāpurisa*).
Its state or its activity is *pāramitā*, which is simply the practice of giving and so forth. In this manner, the etymological meaning of the *pāramīs* should be understood.
As for how many kinds there are: in brief, they are tenfold, and these are indeed set forth in their specific forms in the Pāḷi itself. As it is said:
“Searching at that time, I saw first the perfection of giving,” and so forth.
And as it is also said:
“How many, venerable sir, are the qualities that make a Buddha? “There are ten, Sāriputta, qualities that make a Buddha.

Which ten? Generosity, Sāriputta, is a quality that makes a Buddha; virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity are qualities that make a Buddha. These, Sāriputta, are the ten...”
"The qualities that make one a Buddha. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
"Generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, and energy as the fifth;
patience, truthfulness, resolve, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these are the ten."
Some, however, say they are "sixfold," which is stated by way of their grouping; that grouping will be made clear later. As for the question "What is their order?":
here, "order" means the order of teaching, and that is based on the order of undertaking [the precepts]; the undertaking is based on investigation.
Thus, they were taught in the same manner as they were investigated and undertaken at the beginning. And therein—
Giving is of great assistance to virtue and is easy to practice; thus it was mentioned first. Virtue, when embraced by giving, becomes of great fruit and great benefit;
thus virtue was mentioned immediately after giving.
Virtue is embraced by renunciation, renunciation is embraced by wisdom, wisdom is embraced by energy, energy is embraced by patience, and patience is embraced by truthfulness.
Truth is embraced by resolution; resolution is embraced by loving-kindness;
and loving-kindness, when embraced by equanimity, becomes of great fruit and great benefit—thus, equanimity is mentioned immediately after loving-kindness.

Furthermore, it should be understood that equanimity is embraced by compassion, and compassion is embraced by equanimity. But how is it that the Bodhisattvas, who possess great compassion, [behave] toward sentient beings?
"Are they equanimous? Some say: "They are equanimous for a time toward those things associated with equanimity, but not in all places and at all times.
Others, however, say: "They are not equanimous toward sentient beings, but they are equanimous toward the misfortunes caused by sentient beings.
Another method: because it occurs even among ordinary people, because it is common to all beings, because its fruit is small, and because it is easy to perform.

And generosity was mentioned at the beginning. Morality is mentioned immediately after generosity because it purifies both the giver and the recipient; because, having spoken of benefiting others, it speaks of refraining from harming others;

because, having spoken of active phenomena (*kriyādharma*), it speaks of non-active phenomena (*akriyādharma*); and because, having spoken of the cause for the attainment of wealth, it speaks of the cause for the attainment of existence (*bhava*).
Through renunciation (*nekkhamma*), the perfection of morality is accomplished; [this refers to] good conduct of body and speech.
Having spoken thus, because it is stated that mental good conduct leads to purity; because for one of purified virtue, meditative absorption (jhāna) is achieved with ease;
because after stating the purity of application through the abandoning of faults in action, the purity of disposition is stated through the abandoning of faults in defilement;

and because the abandoning of the obsessions of the mind is stated through the abandoning of transgressions—renunciation (nekkhamma) is mentioned immediately after virtue. [This is] by means of wisdom (paññā).
Because of the accomplishment and purification of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), and because it is stated that in the absence of meditation (*jhāna*) there is an absence of wisdom (*paññā*).

For wisdom has concentration (*samādhi*) as its proximate cause, and concentration has wisdom as its manifestation. Furthermore, after mentioning the sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*), the sign of equanimity (*upekkhā-nimitta*) is mentioned;
and because of the mention of skill in means for accomplishing the welfare of others through meditation for the benefit of others, wisdom follows immediately after renunciation.
It is stated thus: because the function of wisdom is accomplished through the arousal of energy;

because, after speaking of the patient contemplation of the dharma of the emptiness of beings, it speaks of the wonderful nature of the exertion undertaken for the benefit of beings; because, after speaking of the sign of equanimity, it speaks of the sign of exertion;
and because, after speaking of acting with circumspection, it speaks of energetic striving. For the striving of one who acts with circumspection brings about a distinction in the fruit.
Energy is stated immediately after wisdom.

This is because endurance is accomplished through energy. For one who possesses energy, by virtue of having initiated energy, dwells having overcome the suffering brought about by the conditioned formations of beings; this is because energy serves as an ornament for endurance. Indeed, for one who possesses energy, there is endurance.
It is fitting. This is because, after stating the sign of exertion (*paggahanimitta*), it speaks of the sign of calm (*samathanimitta*);

and because, through excessive application, it speaks of the abandoning of the fault of restlessness (*uddhaccadosa*). For the fault of restlessness is abandoned by the acceptance of the contemplation of the Dhamma (*dhammanijjhānakkhanti*). Because it speaks of the persistent practice of one possessed of energy;

for one who abounds in patience is unperturbed and acts with persistence. Because it speaks of the absence of craving for reward in one possessed of diligence when undertaking the work of benefiting others.
For when there is contemplation of phenomena as they truly are (*yāthāvato dhammanijjhāna*), craving does not arise.

Furthermore, because it is said that one endures the suffering caused by others even while engaged in the supreme undertaking for the welfare of others, patience (*khanti*) is mentioned immediately after energy (*vīriya*). Because truthfulness (*sacca*) is firmly established through patience;

and because, having spoken of enduring the harm done by those who cause harm, one speaks of non-deception in returning benefit to them; and because of the unshakability of slanderous speech through patience.

Truth (*sacca*) is mentioned immediately after patience (*khanti*), because it consists in speaking the truth without abandoning the quality of speaking what is real, and because it consists in speaking the truth through knowledge that has been further developed by reflecting on the Dhamma of the emptiness of beings.

This is because truth is established through resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*); for when one’s resolution is unshakable, abstinence (*virati*) is accomplished. It is mentioned next because, having spoken non-deceptively, one speaks of being immovable therein; for one who is true to their word (*saccasandha*)...

One proceeds unshakably in generosity and the other perfections in accordance with one’s promise. This is because, having spoken of the truth of knowledge (*ñāṇasacca*), there is the statement regarding the completion of the practice within the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).

For one who possesses knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*) is firmly established in the requisites for enlightenment and brings them to completion, being unshakable by opposing factors;

thus, determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is mentioned immediately after the truth. Furthermore, this is because through loving-kindness (*mettā*), the establishment of the commitment to accomplish the welfare of others is achieved.

It is stated [that loving-kindness follows] after the resolution because it consists in speech that brings about welfare. For one who resolves upon the requisites for enlightenment dwells in loving-kindness.
Loving-kindness is mentioned immediately after the resolution because the resolution is unshakable and because it arises from undertaking [the practice].
Equanimity follows because it is the purification of loving-kindness; having spoken of the bringing about of welfare toward beings, [it follows] regarding their transgressions.

Equanimity is taught immediately after loving-kindness because of the statement regarding neutrality, because of the statement that it is a meditation on the outflow of that [loving-kindness], and because of the statement regarding its marvelous quality:
"He is equanimous even toward beings who desire his welfare. Thus should their sequence be understood.
What are their characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes? Herein, first of all, without distinction, all the perfections (pāramīs) are...
It has the characteristic of assisting others; its function is to perform a service for others, or its function is non-shakability;
it is manifested as the desire for their welfare, or it is manifested as Buddhahood; its proximate cause is great compassion, or its proximate cause is compassion and skill in means.
In particular, however, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is the volition of relinquishing one’s own person and requisites when embraced by compassion and skill in means.

The perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramitā*) consists, in substance, of good conduct of body and speech embraced by compassion and skillful means, as well as the volition to refrain from what should not be done and to perform what should be done.

The perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramitā*) is the arising of a mind intent on emerging from sensual existence and becoming, preceded by the vision of its dangers, and embraced by compassion and skillful means.
The perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramitā*) is the comprehension of the general and specific characteristics of phenomena, embraced by compassion and skillful means.
The perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramitā*). The perfection of energy (*vīriyapāramitā*) is the undertaking of the welfare of others through body and mind, embraced by compassion and skillful means.

The perfection of patience (*khantipāramitā*) is the arising of a state of consciousness characterized primarily by non-hatred, which endures the offenses of sentient beings and conditioned phenomena, being embraced by compassion and skillful means.
Non-deception, consisting of various types such as the volition of abstinence, is embraced by compassion and skillful means.

The perfection of truth (*saccapāramitā*). The perfection of determination (*adhiṭṭhānapāramitā*) is the arising of a state of consciousness proceeding in that mode, characterized by an unwavering commitment and resolve, and embraced by compassion and skillful means (*upāyakosalla*).

The perfection of loving-kindness (*mettāpāramitā*) is, in its essential meaning, non-malevolence (*abyāpāda*), consisting of the promotion of the welfare of the world, and embraced by compassion and skillful means. [The perfection of equanimity] is embraced by compassion and skillful means, and destroys both attachment and aversion.
The perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramitā*) is the state of even-mindedness toward agreeable and disagreeable conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
Therefore, giving (*dāna*) has the characteristic of relinquishing; its function is the destruction of greed regarding the object to be given;

it is manifested as non-attachment, or alternatively, as the attainment of prosperity in both existence and non-existence; and its proximate cause is the thing to be relinquished. Morality (*sīla*) has the characteristic of composing.
It is said that virtue (sīla) has the characteristic of concentration and the characteristic of being a foundation. Its function is the destruction of immorality, or its function is blamelessness;
its manifestation is purity; and its proximate cause is moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa). Renunciation (nekkhamma) has the characteristic of emerging from sense-desire and from existence;
its function is the discernment of the danger therein; and its manifestation is the state of turning away from them.

It has the state of spiritual urgency as its proximate cause. Wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating things according to their true nature, or the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer;
it has the function of illuminating the object, like a lamp; it is manifested as non-delusion, like a guide in the forest;
it has concentration as its proximate cause, or the Four Noble Truths as its proximate cause. It has the characteristic of exertion.

Energy has the characteristic of exertion; its function is to support; it is manifested as non-collapse; its proximate cause is the basis for the arousal of energy, or it has spiritual urgency as its proximate cause.
Patience has the characteristic of forbearance; its function is to endure the desirable and the undesirable; it is manifested as endurance, or it is manifested as non-opposition;
its proximate cause is seeing things as they truly are. Truthfulness has the characteristic of non-deception.
[The faculty of wisdom] has the characteristic of discerning things as they truly are (yāthāvavibhāvana); its function is the manifestation of goodness; its proximate cause is gentleness.
Resolve has the characteristic of determination regarding the requisites for enlightenment;

its function is the overcoming of their opposites; its manifestation is immovability therein; its proximate cause is the requisites for enlightenment. Benevolence has the characteristic of proceeding with a mode of helpfulness.
Loving-kindness has the function of promoting welfare or the function of subduing ill will; it is manifested as a state of gentleness, and its proximate cause is the perception of beings as dear.
Equanimity is characterized by proceeding with an attitude of neutrality;

it has the function of seeing things with impartiality, is manifested as the subsiding of aversion and attraction, and its proximate cause is the reflection on the fact that beings are owners of their own kamma. And herein:

The fact that generosity and the other perfections are embraced by compassion and skillful means (*karuṇā-upāyakosalla*) must be stated as a qualification of their characteristics—such as relinquishment—because it is through this that they receive the designation of "perfections" (*pāramī*).

What is the condition? The initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*) is the condition; for it is this which is accomplished by the convergence of the eight factors beginning with "human birth" and "possession of the male gender."

The aspiration expressed as, “Having crossed over, may I help others cross; being liberated, may I liberate others; being awakened, may I awaken others; being purified, may I purify others; being tamed, may I tame others;

being at peace, may I bring others to peace; having attained consolation, may I console others; having attained final Nibbāna, may I lead others to final Nibbāna,” and so forth, is the condition for all the perfections (pāramīs) without distinction. For through its occurrence, the perfections [arise] hereafter.
The discernment, establishment, undertaking, resolution, and accomplishment of Great Beings come into being.
And just as with the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*), so too are great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and skill in means (*upāyakosalla*).

In this context, "skill in means" refers to the wisdom that serves as the cause for the factors of enlightenment, such as giving and the rest; it is by means of these qualities—great compassion and skill in means—that Great Beings [attain their goal].

Indifference toward one's own happiness, constant devotion to performing the welfare of others, the absence of despondency even through the extremely difficult deeds of a Great Bodhisattva, and the state of being a cause for sentient beings to obtain welfare and happiness even during the occasions of seeing, hearing, recollecting, or gaining faith in [the Buddha]—all these come to pass.
For thus, by means of wisdom (*paññā*), the state of Buddhahood is accomplished; by means of compassion (*karuṇā*), the Buddha-activities are accomplished. By means of wisdom...

One crosses over by oneself and carries others across through compassion. Through wisdom one fully understands the suffering of others; through compassion one undertakes the remedy for that suffering.
Through wisdom one becomes disenchanted with suffering; through compassion one accepts suffering.
Likewise, through wisdom one is oriented toward final Nibbāna, yet through compassion one does not reach it. Likewise, through compassion one is oriented toward the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Through wisdom, he does not take delight therein; and through wisdom, he becomes dispassionate toward everything.
Yet, because it is accompanied by compassion, it does not fail to proceed for the sake of assisting all beings;

through compassion, he feels sympathy for everyone, and because it is accompanied by wisdom, his mind does not fail to be dispassionate toward everything. Through wisdom, there is an absence of the notions of "I" and "mine," and through compassion, there is an absence of indolence and dejection.

Likewise, through wisdom and compassion, there arise respectively: the state of being one's own master and the master of others; the nature of the steadfast and the heroic; the state of not tormenting oneself or others;
the accomplishment of one's own welfare and the welfare of others; the state of being fearless and free from terror; the state of being a lord of the Dhamma and a lord of the world;

the state of being grateful and a doer of good in the past; the removal of delusion and craving; the perfection of true knowledge and conduct; and the accomplishment of the powers and intrepidities—this constitutes the fruit of all the perfections.

In particular, wisdom and compassion are conditions for the perfections (*pāramī*) by way of being their means. Furthermore, these two are conditions not only for the perfections but also for the aspiration (*paṇidhāna*).

Likewise, it should be understood that energy (*ussāha*), ingenuity (*ummagga*), steadfastness (*avatthāna*), and conduct for the welfare of others (*hitacariyā*) are conditions for the perfections; they are called "Buddha-grounds" (*buddhabhūmi*) because they are the basis for the arising of Buddhahood. As it has been said:
“But how many, venerable sir, are the stages of a Buddha? “There are four stages of a Buddha, Sāriputta. Which four? There is exertion and energy;
there is ingenuity and the cultivation of wisdom; there is steadfastness and resolution;
and there is the cultivation of loving-kindness and conduct for the welfare of others. These, Sāriputta, are the four stages of a Buddha.”
Likewise, there are six inclinations, which are distinguished as: renunciation, seclusion, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, and escape. For this has been said:
"Bodhisattvas have an inclination toward renunciation, seeing the fault in sensual pleasures; [an inclination toward] seclusion... [and so on]... [seeing the fault] in socializing;

[an inclination toward] non-greed... [and so on]... [seeing the fault] in greed; [an inclination toward] non-hatred... [and so on]... [seeing the fault] in hatred; [an inclination toward] non-delusion... [and so on]... [seeing the fault] in delusion; and Bodhisattvas have an inclination toward escape, seeing the fault in all states of existence."
Therefore, it should be understood that these six inclinations of Bodhisattvas are the conditions for giving and the other perfections.
For indeed, the perfections such as giving do not arise without the vision of the danger in greed and the rest, and without the predominance of non-greed and the rest.

For when there is a predominance of non-greed and the rest, the state of a mind inclined toward relinquishment and so forth is what constitutes the inclination of non-greed and the rest. Just as these [inclinations] are, so too are the inclinations toward giving and the rest. As it has been said:
“But, Bhante, how many aspirations do Bodhisattvas who are practicing for awakening have?
“Sāriputta, there are ten aspirations of Bodhisattvas who are practicing for awakening. Which ten?

Sāriputta, Bodhisattvas have an aspiration for giving, seeing the fault in stinginess; [an aspiration for] virtue... [and so on] ...Sāriputta, Bodhisattvas have an aspiration for equanimity, seeing the fault in pleasure and pain.”
For among these— namely, stinginess, lack of restraint, sensual desire, doubt, laziness,

intolerance, deception, lack of resolve, ill-will, and pleasure and pain— it is the inclination toward giving and so forth, characterized by a mind bent on generosity and the like preceded by the vision of their disadvantages,

that constitutes the cause for the production of the perfections (pāramīs) such as giving. Likewise, there is the reflection upon the disadvantages and advantages, respectively, regarding non-renunciation and renunciation.
This is the condition for the perfections such as giving.

Herein, this is the method of reflection: because for beings whose minds are obsessed with possessions such as fields, lands, gold, silver, cattle, buffaloes, slaves, servants, sons, and wives, these fields and so forth are highly desirable as objects of sensual desire (*vatthu-kāma*), and because they are common property shared with kings, thieves, and others; [therefore, one reflects on the need to give them away].
Because they are the basis for disputes, because they cause enmity, because they are devoid of substance, because they lead to harming others in both acquiring and protecting them,

because they are a cause for destruction and bring about various calamities such as sorrow, and because attachment to them leads— through the defilement of the stain of stinginess— to rebirth in the states of misery;
thus these things called "wealth" bring about manifold and vast misfortunes, and their renunciation alone is the remedy.
Regarding "the state of safety": one must exercise heedfulness in renunciation.
Furthermore, [one should think]: "This beggar, by asking for what he needs, reveals my secret; thus he is trustworthy to me";
and "By taking what belongs to me—which must eventually be left behind—and departing for the next world, he is an instructor to me"; and "When [the house] is on fire..."

"Like a house set ablaze by the fire of death in this world, he is my companion who carries away what belongs to me," and "He is the place where what has been carried away is deposited for contemplation.
This is because he acts as a companion in the performance of wholesome deeds known as giving,
and because he is the cause for attaining the state of Buddhahood— the most difficult to reach and the pinnacle of all attainments.
And one should reflect: "He is my supreme spiritual friend. Likewise:
"I have been honored by him with sublime tasks; therefore, that honor must be made not false. And:
"Since life is destined for certain dissolution, I should give even when unasked, much more so when asked. And: "By those of sublime aspirations..."

“Even if one must search for them, they should be given; he has come of his own accord through my merit,” and “Under the pretext of giving to a petitioner, this is actually a favor to me alone,” and “Just as I am, this entire world should be favored by me,” and “If there were no petitioners, how could I fulfill the perfection of generosity?
and “For the sake of petitioners alone, everything should be acquired by me,” and “Without being asked...”
"How might beggars take what belongs to me of their own accord? and "How might I be dear and pleasing to beggars?

and "Or how might they be dear and pleasing to me? and "How might I be joyful, glad, and filled with rapture and happiness while giving, and even after having given? and "How might I have beggars [at my disposal]?"
One should reflect: "My inclination toward generosity is sublime"; "How might I give to supplicants even without being asked, simply by understanding their hearts?";
"If I possess wealth and there are supplicants, yet I do not relinquish them, it would be a great deception on my part";
and "How might I relinquish even my own limbs or my very life to supplicants?"

Furthermore, one should generate a state of mind that is indifferent toward material things, thinking: "This thing called 'wealth' follows its owner regardless of his wishes, just as a termite follows a woodpecker regardless of his wishes.
However, if the person who is begging is a loved one, one should generate joy, thinking: "A dear person is asking me for something. But if it is a neutral person... [the text continues: "this..."
One should arouse joy, thinking: "Surely by this act of relinquishment, he who asks me becomes a friend.

For even while giving, one becomes dear to those who beg. Furthermore, if an enemy person asks, one should feel especially joyful, thinking: "An adversary asks me; surely by this act of relinquishment, even this enemy, because of his request, becomes dear as a friend."

It should be generated. Thus, even toward neutral persons and hostile persons, one should give only after establishing compassion preceded by loving-kindness (mettā), just as one would toward a beloved person.
However, if, due to the long-term cultivation of greed, greedy states regarding the object of the gift should arise in him, [he must counteract them].

Therefore, one who professes to be a bodhisatta should reflect thus: "O noble person, when you made the aspiration for full enlightenment, did you not relinquish this body for the sake of benefiting all beings, as well as the merit arising from that renunciation?
In that case, this excessive attachment even toward external objects is like a bath for an elephant."
Therefore, you should not give rise to attachment toward anything. Just as, for example, when a great medicinal tree stands there, those who need its roots take the roots;
those who need the bark, the rind, the trunk, the branches, the heartwood, the twigs, the leaves, the flowers, or the fruit take the fruit—yet that tree does not think, "This belongs to me."

"these carry it away"—such is the manifestation of discursive thought. In the same way, when I am exerting myself for the welfare of the whole world and dedicating this body—which is subject to great suffering, ungrateful, and eternally impure—to the service of others, not even the slightest wrong thought should be allowed to arise.
For what difference is there here between the internal and external primary elements (mahābhūta), all of which are by nature subject to breaking, scattering, and destruction?
But this clinging—namely, "This is mine, this I am, this is my self"—is merely a manifestation of delusion.

Therefore, one should become indifferent toward the internal parts, such as the hands, feet, eyes, and flesh, just as one is toward external things, and should remain with a mind that has relinquished them, thinking, "Let those who need them take them. Thus...
As he reflects in this way, being resolute for awakening and indifferent toward body and life, his bodily, verbal,
and mental actions become thoroughly purified with little difficulty. With his bodily, verbal, and mental actions thus purified,
possessing purity of livelihood, and established in the practice of the True Way, he— through his possession of skill in means regarding gain and loss— furthermore gives away gifts to be given.

And by means of the gift of fearlessness and the gift of the true Dhamma, he is capable of assisting all beings. This, first of all, is the method of reflection regarding the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
