As for the perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramitā*), it should be reflected upon in this way: "This so-called virtue is the water that washes away the stain of defilement which cannot be cleansed by the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers;
it is the remedy that subdues the fever of lust and other passions which cannot be removed by yellow sandalwood and other such things."

It is an extraordinary ornament for the virtuous, surpassing the common ornaments of necklaces, crowns, earrings, and the like; it is an unconditioned fragrance that wafts in all directions and is appropriate for all seasons;
it is the supreme incantation for subjugation, bringing about a state of being worthy of veneration by noble householders, great landowners, and deities;
it is a flight of stairs for ascending to the celestial realms of the Four Great Kings and others; and it is the foundation for the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).

It is the means for realization, the path leading to the great city of Nibbāna, and the foundation for the enlightenment of disciples, the enlightenment of paccekabuddhas, and perfect supreme enlightenment.
Because it is the means for accomplishing whatever is desired or sought after, it surpasses even the wish-fulfilling gem, the tree of plenty, and other such things.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, it succeeds for one who is virtuous..."

“Because of the purity of the mental aspiration. Furthermore, it is said: “Monks, if a monk should wish, ‘May I be dear, pleasing, respected, and esteemed by my fellow celibates,’ he should be one who fulfills the precepts,” and so forth;
likewise: “Ānanda, wholesome virtues have non-remorse as their purpose,” and: “Householders, there are these five benefits...”

The virtues of virtue should be reflected upon by means of such suttas as, "For one who is virtuous, through the perfection of virtue," and likewise the dangers in the absence of virtue by means of such suttas as the *Agniskandhopama-sutta* (The Simile of the Mass of Fire). [Virtue should be cultivated] because it is a cause of rapture and gladness;
because it is free from the fear of self-reproach, reproach by others, punishment, and an unhappy rebirth; and because it is a state praised by the wise.

Virtue should be reviewed by way of its cause of non-remorse, its state of security, and its surpassing of the excellence of noble birth, wealth, sovereignty, long life, beauty, relatives, and friends.
For one who possesses virtue, great joy and gladness arise on account of his own perfection of virtue, thinking:
"Indeed, I have done what is wholesome; I have done what is beautiful; I have provided a refuge for those who fear."
Likewise, for one who is virtuous, his own self does not reproach him, nor do wise others; there is simply no possibility of punishment or fear of an evil rebirth.
Furthermore, he is praised by the wise as "a virtuous person of beautiful character.
Likewise, for one who is immoral, there is that remorse which says, "Alas, I have done evil! I have done cruel deeds! I have done wicked things!"—but for the virtuous, such remorse does not exist.

That which arises does not exist [as a permanent entity]. Furthermore, this virtue (sīla) is the supreme state of security because it is based on heedfulness (appamāda), because it accomplishes great benefit by way of warding off the ruin of wealth and other misfortunes, and because it possesses the nature of an auspicious sign (maṅgala).

Even one of low birth who is virtuous becomes worthy of honor by kṣatriyas, great householders, and others; thus, the perfection of virtue surpasses the excellence of lineage. "That... [the rest of the passage follows].
"What do you think, Great King? Suppose there were a man here who was your slave and laborer," and so forth—this statement serves as proof in this context.

Because it is not shared with thieves and others, because it follows one to the next world, because it yields great fruit, and because it is the foundation for qualities such as serenity (samatha), virtue (sīla) surpasses external wealth;
furthermore, because it is the basis for the supreme sovereignty of the mind, [virtue] [surpasses] the [status of] kshatriyas and others.
Virtue surpasses sovereignty. For the sovereignty of beings within their respective classes of beings is surpassed by virtue as the cause for it;

this is because it is said that even a single day of life for one possessed of virtue is superior to a lifespan of a hundred years, and because, while life exists, it is said that the casting aside of the training constitutes death—thus virtue is more distinguished than life.
Furthermore, it brings a state of endearment even to enemies, [and protects from] old age, disease, and misfortune.

Virtue surpasses physical beauty because it cannot be overcome by it. Virtue surpasses specific positions—such as palaces, halls, and the like, or specific ranks such as kings, crown princes, and generals—because it is the foundation for the attainment of superior happiness.

Virtue surpasses even one's own kinsmen and friends, who are naturally affectionate and stay close by, because it brings about absolute welfare and follows one into the next world. "Neither mother nor father..."

The statement beginning with “One should act... is the proof for this point. Likewise, compared to elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth, as well as the employment of mantras, medicinal herbs, and wealth, virtue alone is far superior as a protection for oneself;
for it is dependent on oneself, not dependent on others, and its scope is vast.
Therefore it is said: “Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by Dhamma,” and so forth. Thus, [virtue] is endowed with manifold qualities.
When he reviews his virtue (*sīla*), his incomplete accomplishment of virtue reaches fulfillment, and its impurity attains purity.
However, if through long-standing habituation opposing states such as hatred should arise from time to time, that one who professes to be a bodhisattva should reflect thus:
"Did you not make the aspiration for full enlightenment?"
It has been said that one deficient in virtue cannot attain even mundane success, let alone supramundane;
moreover, for the sake of Perfect Enlightenment—the pinnacle of all successes—one must reach the highest excellence through virtue, which serves as its foundation.
Therefore, by guarding virtue properly according to the method stated in the verse beginning with "As a hen guards her eggs,"...
You must be very gentle. Furthermore, through your teaching of the Dhamma, you must effect the introduction and maturation of beings in the Three Vehicles.
Moreover, the word of one deficient in virtue is not to be accepted, just as the treatment of a physician who consumes unwholesome food and conduct is not to be trusted;
therefore, how can I become trustworthy so as to effect the introduction and maturation of beings?
"One should act"—thus one must possess a virtue that is pure by its very nature. Furthermore, one should purify virtue correctly, thinking:
"Through my connection with the specific qualities of the jhānas and so forth, I shall be capable of benefiting sentient beings and fulfilling the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī) and the others;
and these qualities, such as the jhānas, do not arise without the purity of virtue."
Likewise, by means of such passages as “Household life is crowded and dusty,” regarding the household life;
“Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton,” and “Even a mother disputes with her son,” regarding sensual pleasures;

and “Just as if a man, having taken a loan, were to engage in work,” etc., regarding sensual desire and the other [hindrances]—preceded by the vision of their dangers—one should, by the reverse of what was stated, [regard] the open air [of the renunciant life].

The reflection on the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramitā*) should be understood as the contemplation of the benefits found in going forth (*pabbajjā*), etc., by means of such passages as "going forth...

This is the summary of the meaning here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood through such suttas as the *Dukkhakkhandha Sutta* and the *Vīmaṃsa Sutta*, as well as the *Dukkhakkhandha Sutta* and the *Āsivisa-upama Sutta*.
Likewise, one should attend to the qualities of wisdom, reflecting: "Without wisdom, the virtues such as giving are not purified, nor are they capable of performing their respective functions.
For just as the body does not shine without life and is incapable of engaging in its own activities, and just as the sense faculties such as the eye [are useless] without consciousness...
Just as [the other faculties] are unable to perform their respective functions without [wisdom], so too the faculties such as faith are incapable of fulfilling their own functions without wisdom;
thus, wisdom is the primary cause for the practice of relinquishment and the rest.
For the Great Beings, having opened the eye of wisdom, do not exalt themselves even when giving away their own limbs and members.
Furthermore, they do not disparage others; like medicinal trees, they are free from conceptual contrivance and are filled with joy throughout the three periods of time.
Through the application of skillful means by way of wisdom, their relinquishment attains the status of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) as it proceeds for the benefit of others.
For giving for one’s own sake is merely like an increase in wealth.
Likewise, in the absence of wisdom, because one cannot be separated from the defilements such as craving, even the purification of virtue itself is not possible;

how much less, then, can there be the state of being the foundation for the qualities of omniscience? Only one possessed of wisdom, clearly perceiving the danger in household life, in the strands of sensual pleasure, and in saṃsāra, as well as the benefit in renunciation, in meditative attainments, and in Nibbāna, goes forth into homelessness.
Having produced the meditative attainments (*jhāna-samāpatti*), one inclines toward *nibbāna* and establishes others there as well.
Furthermore, energy devoid of wisdom does not accomplish the desired goal because it is difficult to undertake; indeed, it is better not to undertake it at all than to undertake it poorly.
However, with energy accompanied by wisdom, nothing is difficult to achieve due to the application of skillful means (*upāya*).
Likewise, it is only the wise person who is by nature able to endure injuries inflicted by others and so forth, not the one of poor wisdom.
For one devoid of wisdom, injuries brought upon him by others only nourish the very opposite of patience;
but for the wise person, those same injuries lead to the strengthening of his perfection of patience, resulting in its firmness. It is only the wise person who [possesses] the three...
Having understood the truths, their causes, and their opposites as they truly are, he does not deceive others.

Likewise, having fortified himself with the power of wisdom (*paññābala*), through the perfection of steadfastness (*dhitisampadā*), he possesses an unwavering resolve and commitment to all the perfections (*pāramīs*).
And being wise, he does not differentiate between those who are dear, neutral, or hostile, but is skillful in promoting the welfare of all.
Likewise, by way of wisdom, one remains neutral amidst the gathering of worldly conditions such as gain and loss due to being free from agitation.
Thus, since wisdom alone is the cause for the purification of all the perfections, the qualities of wisdom should be reflected upon.
Furthermore, without wisdom there is no excellence of vision, and without the perfection of view there is no perfection of virtue.
For one devoid of perfection in virtue and view there is no perfection in concentration;
and by one who is not concentrated, it is impossible to accomplish even one's own welfare, let alone the supreme welfare of others.
Therefore, one practicing for the sake of the welfare of others should admonish oneself thus: "Must you not indeed apply yourself with diligence to the purification of wisdom? By the power of wisdom—
For indeed, the Great Being, established in the four foundations and favoring the world with the four bases of sympathy,

leads sentient beings onto the path leading to liberation and brings their faculties to maturity. Likewise, through the power of wisdom, being preoccupied with the investigation of the aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth,
and understanding the processes of occurrence and cessation as they truly are, he causes the virtues such as giving to possess the quality of being conducive to penetration.

Having established the qualities of wisdom in their many aspects through such passages as, "Leading [others], a bodhisattva becomes one who fulfills the training," the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī) should be cultivated.
Likewise, even those worldly tasks that appear to have reached the further shore are impossible for one of inferior energy to attain.
But for one who has initiated energy without regard for weariness, there is nothing indeed that is difficult to attain.

For one of inferior energy is not even able to begin with the thought, "I shall ferry all beings across the great flood of saṃsāra. One of middling energy, having begun, reaches an intermediate cessation.
But one of superior energy, being indifferent to his own happiness, reaches the further shore of the undertaking; such is the perfection of energy.

These should be reflected upon. Furthermore, even for one whose undertaking is solely for the sake of pulling oneself out from the mire of *saṃsāra*, it cannot be expected that their aspirations will reach their ultimate fulfillment through laxity of energy;
how much less so for one who has made the resolve to pull out the world together with its devas from the mass of defects such as lust and the rest? And: "Of the groups of faults such as lust..."
Because they are as difficult to restrain as intoxicated great elephants; because the undertaking of kamma resulting from them is like that of an executioner with sword raised;
because the miserable destinies caused by them always have their mouths wide open;
because evil friends who incite one to them are always present; and because it is possible for an ignorant worldling to act upon such advice.
In this manner, one should reflect upon the virtues of energy (vīriya) by such lines as:

"It is fitting for me to escape from the suffering of saṃsāra by my own effort," "Wrong thoughts are driven far away by the power of energy," and "If enlightenment can be attained through energy that is under one's own control, what is difficult about it?
Thus should the qualities of energy be reflected upon.
Likewise: "Patience is indeed the unimpeded weapon of the virtuous for the accomplishment of good qualities, owing to its dispelling of anger—the adversary of all virtues without exception;
it is the ornament of those capable of overcoming others; it is the perfection of strength for ascetics and brahmins;
it is a stream of water that subdues the serpent of anger; it is the birthplace of the fame and reputation of the noble; [it is the destroyer] of evil persons..."
One should attend to it thus: "It is a mantra-remedy that pacifies the poison of speech; for those established in restraint, it is the supreme nature of the wise;

by its profound depth, it is like the ocean; it is the shoreline for the great ocean of hatred; it is the closing door-leaf for the gate of the states of misery; it is the staircase for ascending to the worlds of the devas and brahmās;
it is the ground for the abiding of all virtues; it is the supreme purity of body, speech, and mind. Furthermore—
And: "These beings burn both here and in the next world because they lack the perfection of patience, and because they are devoted to things that cause burning";

and: "Even though suffering arises on account of harm done by others, it is my own personal existence that serves as the field for that suffering, and my own karma that serves as its seed"; and: "This is the means for becoming free from debt regarding that suffering."
And: "If there were no one who causes me harm, how could my perfection of patience arise?
and "Even though this person is currently harmful, such was the help he once rendered to me in the past"; or, "Indeed, harm itself is a benefit by virtue of being the occasion for patience";
and "All these beings are like my own children; and who would be angry at the offenses committed by their own children?"
And [he reflects]: "That possession by the spirit of anger by which this person has offended me—that possession by the spirit of anger must be subdued by me";
and "I too am the cause of this harm through which this suffering has arisen for me";
and "All those factors by which the offense was committed and the place where it was committed have all ceased at that very moment; to whom, then, [is this now directed]?"
“By whom should anger be directed? and “Since all phenomena are non-self, who can offend whom?”—contemplating thus, one should cultivate the perfection of patience.
However, if through long-standing habituation, anger triggered by the thought of another’s harm should seize and persist in the mind, [one must apply the appropriate remedy].
Thus one should reflect: "This patience is indeed the means of responding to the hostility of others by performing a counter-service";
and "And this hostility is a condition for my faith, which has suffering as its proximate cause, and for the perception of non-delight in the entire world";
and "This is the nature of the sense-faculties, namely, the encounter with desirable and undesirable objects; therein, the encounter with undesirable objects..."
"How could it be possible for me not to have [anger]? and "A being under the sway of anger is maddened and distracted in mind;
what is the use of retaliating there? and "All these beings are protected by the Perfectly Enlightened One like his own biological sons;
therefore, I should not harbor even a thought of anger toward them," and "When there is a fault, there is also a virtue..."

"One should not give way to anger toward one who possesses virtues," "one who lacks virtues should be treated with special compassion," "through anger my virtues and fame are diminished," "by being angry,
undesirable states such as ugliness and painful sleep come upon me,
which are dear to my enemies," and "this thing called anger is a powerful adversary that brings about all that is harmful and destroys all that is beneficial."

And: "When there is patience, there is no adversary whatsoever"; and: "Whatever suffering would be experienced by an offender in the future on account of his offense, through patience there is the absence of that for me"; and:
"By thinking [malice] and by becoming angry, I have merely followed after my adversary"; and: "When anger has been overcome by me through patience, [the adversary...]"

“An adversary who has become a slave is truly overcome,” and “It is not fitting for me to abandon the virtue of patience for the sake of anger,” and “If anger—which is contrary to virtue (the conduct opposed to virtue;
see *Aṭṭhasālinī*, *Pakiṇṇakakathā*)—is present, how could my qualities such as moral discipline reach fulfillment? And if they are absent...”
"How shall I, being of great benefit to beings, attain the supreme success in accordance with my promise?

And: "When there is patience, because of the absence of outward distraction, one who is concentrated contemplates all conditioned phenomena as impermanent and suffering, all phenomena as non-self, and Nibbāna as unconditioned, deathless, sublime, and so forth; thus they become objects of his reflective acceptance."
"‘The Buddha-qualities possess inconceivable and immeasurable power,’ and furthermore, ‘Established in conformable patience, one realizes:
“These phenomena alone, devoid of a self or anything belonging to a self, arise and pass away according to their respective conditions;
they do not come from anywhere, they do not go anywhere, and they are not established anywhere.”’"

In this regard, the reflection on the perfection of patience (*khantipāramitā*) should be understood through such passages as: "When there is no interference from anyone toward anyone else, the patient acceptance (*nijjhāna*) that does not insist upon the notions of 'I' and 'mine' is pleasing;
by means of this, the Bodhisatta becomes fixed for enlightenment and subject to non-retrogression.

Likewise, [the reflection on the perfection of truthfulness is understood] because virtue and the other perfections cannot exist without truth, and because there is no practice in accordance with one's promise.
Because when one transgresses the dharma of truth, all evil qualities converge therein; because one who is untruthful in his word lacks reliability;
and because it brings about the state of having speech that is not to be accepted in the future; because for one endowed with truth, truth serves as the foundation for all virtues;
because through the resolve of truth, all the requisites for enlightenment are accompanied by purity and fulfillment; and because of non-deception regarding the nature of phenomena.

The perfections of the truth-pāramī should be reflected upon in such ways as: "Because it performs the function of providing all the requisites for enlightenment, and because it brings to full completion the practice of a bodhisatta.
Likewise: "Firm commitment to giving and the other perfections, and their unshakable maintenance even when confronted by their opposites; therein..."

Furthermore, one should reflect upon the virtues of resolute determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) by considering such statements as: "Without a state of firmness, the accumulations of giving and the other perfections cannot arise as causes for perfect enlightenment.
Likewise: "Even for one who remains intent solely on their own welfare, it is impossible to achieve success in this world and the next without a mind of benevolence toward all beings."
“...how much more so for one who wishes to establish all beings in the attainment of Nibbāna”;
and “for one who desires the supramundane success of all beings hereafter, it is now appropriate to desire mundane success”;
and “at present, being unable to provide for the welfare and happiness of others through mere intention alone, when will I [be able to do so] through actual application?”
“I shall accomplish that,” he thought; and, “Now, having been raised by me through the provision of welfare and happiness, they will later become my companions in the sharing of the Dhamma”;
and, “Without these, the requisites for enlightenment cannot arise for me;

therefore, because they are the cause for the production of the manifestation of all the Buddha-qualities, they are for me the supreme field of merit, the unsurpassed sphere of the wholesome, and the highest object of veneration.”

Furthermore, one should establish a specific inclination toward the welfare of all beings; moreover, through the foundation of compassion, loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be cultivated toward all beings.

For when one delights in bestowing benefit and happiness upon beings with a mind free from barriers, a powerful and firmly rooted desire arises to remove their harm and suffering, and [this] is compassion for all.

The qualities of loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be reflected upon by means of such passages as: "Loving-kindness is the beginning, the footing, the foundation, the root, the mouth, and the foremost of the qualities that make one a Buddha.
Likewise, [one should reflect]:
"In the absence of equanimity (*upekkhā*), the various provocations caused by sentient beings would produce agitation in the mind; but when [equanimity] is present..."
Furthermore, it is said: "When the mind is subject to mental distortion, the very possibility of the requisites for giving and so forth does not exist";
and, "When the mind is moistened by the affection of loving-kindness (*mettā*), there can be no purification of the requisites without equanimity (*upekkhā*");
and, "One who lacks equanimity is unable to dedicate the accumulation of merit and its result for the welfare of sentient beings among the requisites"; and, "By means of equanimity..."
And because one cannot renounce without making a distinction among those to whom gifts are to be given and those who receive them;
and because one cannot purify one's restraint without equanimity, by disregarding obstacles to life and the requisites for living;
and because the power of renunciation is established through the very fact that one endures both aversion and delight by means of equanimity, as well as through rebirth.
Because all the duties of the requisites are accomplished through equanimity alone; because if energy were over-exerted, the duty of striving would not be performed due to a lack of equanimity;
because endurance and meditative absorption arise only from equanimity; because through equanimity there is no deception regarding beings and formations;
and because by means of equanimity toward the worldly conditions (lokadhamma), one achieves an unshakable resolve in the qualities one has undertaken.

"Because the dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettāvihāra*) is accomplished through the very absence of effort regarding the harming of others and so forth, the undertaking, the commitment, the fulfillment, and the accomplishment of all the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) are achieved through the power of equanimity (*upekkhā*).
In this manner, and by such a method, the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhāpāramī*) should be reflected upon.

Likewise, the reflection on the disadvantages and advantages (*ādīnavānisamsa*) regarding non-renunciation and renunciation, etc., in their respective order, [should be understood] as applying to the perfections of giving (*dāna*), and so forth.
These should be understood as conditions.
Likewise, there are fifteen factors of conduct together with their requisites, and the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). Among these, the "factors of conduct" (*caraṇadhamma*) are:
restraint by virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, and the seven...

The true teachings (*saddhamma*) and the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). Among these, for the four beginning with virtue (*sīla*), the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutadhamma*) as well as fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and so forth are the requisites (*parikkhāra*).
Regarding the true teachings, faith consists of the recollections (*anussati*) of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, and the deities;

of tranquility (*upasama*); of avoiding persons who are coarse, and associating with persons who are gentle; of reflecting upon the qualities that inspire confidence (*pasādanīya-dhamma*); and of being intent upon those [qualities].
The requisite [for shame and fear of wrongdoing] consists of: reflecting on the unwholesome dangers; reflecting on the dangers of the states of deprivation;

reflecting on the supportiveness of wholesome qualities; reflecting on the nature of shame and fear of wrongdoing; avoiding persons devoid of shame and fear of wrongdoing; associating with persons endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing; being intent upon those qualities; for erudition: previous application; the state of being an inquirer; devotion to the true Dhamma;

cultivation of blameless fields of knowledge and so forth; maturity of the faculties; distancing from the defilements; avoiding those of little learning; associating with those of great learning; and being intent upon those qualities.

For energy: reflecting on the fear of the states of loss, reflecting on the path of progress, reflecting on the greatness of the Dhamma, dispelling sloth and torpor, avoiding persons who are indolent, associating with persons who have aroused energy, reflecting on the right exertions, and being intent upon that;
for mindfulness: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and being intent upon that.

The requisites for wisdom are: being inquisitive; purifying the objective field; bringing the faculties to evenness; avoiding persons of deficient wisdom; associating with persons possessed of wisdom; reviewing the course of profound knowledge; being intent upon that;
the preliminary development of the fourfold set beginning with virtue in relation to the thirty-eight objects of meditation;
and gaining mastery over the processes of adverting and so forth. Among these, by means of virtue and the other factors, there is purity of application.

One should determine, as appropriate, how conduct (*caraṇa*) and other factors serve as conditions for the requisites of giving (*dāna*) and so forth—such as by stating that one is capable of the gift of fearlessness to beings, the gift of material things through purity of intention, and the gift of the Dhamma through purity of both; however, we have not determined them here for fear of excessive prolixity.
In this way, the wheels of prosperity (*sampatticakka*) and others should also be understood as conditions for giving and the rest.
What is defilement? In general, being affected by craving and the like is the defilement of the perfections.
Specifically, conceptualizing a giver and a recipient is the defilement of the perfection of giving; conceptualizing beings and time is the defilement of the perfection of virtue;

conceptualizing delight or non-delight in sense pleasures and existence, as well as their pacification, is the defilement of the perfection of renunciation; and conceptualizing "I" and "mine" is the defilement of the perfection of wisdom.
The conceptualization of dullness and agitation is the defilement of the perfection of energy; the conceptualization of self and others is that of the perfection of patience;

the conceptualization of "seen" and so forth regarding the "unseen" and so forth is that of the perfection of truth; the conceptualization of faults and virtues regarding the requisites for enlightenment and their opposites is that of the perfection of determination; the conceptualization of the beneficial and the harmful is that of the perfection of loving-kindness;
and the conceptualization of the desirable and the undesirable is that of the perfection of equanimity—thus it should be understood.

What is their purification? It should be understood that their purification consists in being unafflicted by craving and the other defilements, as well as the absence of the aforementioned conceptualizations regarding them.

For when the perfections such as giving are unimpaired by the defilements—namely craving, conceit, views, anger, resentment, denigration, insolence, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, impetuosity, arrogance, and negligence—and are free from conceptualizations concerning the giver, the recipient, and so forth, they are utterly pure.
"They become radiant.
As for what their opposite is: in general, all defilements (*kilesa*) and all unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*) are their opposites;
specifically, however, it should be understood as the stinginess and so forth mentioned previously. Furthermore, regarding the object to be given, the recipient, and the fruit of giving...
Generosity is the antidote to greed, hatred, and delusion by virtue of its association with the qualities of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion;
virtue is the antidote to greed and the rest because it removes the crookedness of bodily misconduct and so forth;

renunciation is the antidote to the three types of aversion because it avoids sensual pleasure, harming others, and self-mortification; and wisdom is the antidote to greed and the rest because greed and the like cause blindness, whereas wisdom does not.
Wisdom (*paññā*); energy (*vīriya*) as the antidote to greed and the rest by way of initiating the method that is neither sluggish nor agitated;
patience (*khanti*) as the antidote to greed and the rest through the endurance of the desirable, the undesirable, and emptiness;

truth (*sacca*) as the antidote to greed and the rest through proceeding in accordance with reality regardless of the benefit or harm caused by others; and [steadfastness] through remaining unshakable in the requisites as they were undertaken, having overcome the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).

The foundation is the antidote to greed and the other [defilements]. Loving-kindness (*mettā*) is the antidote to greed and the rest because it is secluded from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and because it destroys attraction and aversion toward the desirable and undesirable, as well as because it proceeds with equanimity.
Equanimity (*upekkhā*) is to be understood as the antidote to greed and the rest because it functions with evenness.
What is the practice? It is by means of the relinquishing of pleasant requisites, body, and life; by the removal of fear; and by the instruction in the Dhamma.
And the practice of giving consists in providing manifold assistance to sentient beings. Herein, this is the detailed method:

one gives a gift of food with the thought, "By means of this gift, may I bring about for sentient beings the excellence of long life, beauty, happiness, strength, eloquence, and so forth, as well as the delightful excellence of the supreme fruit.
Likewise, one gives a drink for the purpose of allaying the thirst of sentient beings' karma and defilements.
Likewise, he gives garments for the sake of attaining a golden complexion and for the production of the ornaments of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*);
he gives a vehicle for the sake of producing the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) and the bliss of Nibbāna; he gives perfume for the sake of producing the fragrance of virtue (*sīla*);
he gives garlands and ointments for the sake of producing the splendor of the Buddha-qualities; and he gives a seat for the sake of producing the seat at the terrace of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
He gives a bed for the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s reclining; a dwelling for the accomplishment of the state of being a refuge; and a lamp for the attainment of the five eyes.

He gives a gift of form for the accomplishment of the fathom-wide radiance; a gift of sound for the accomplishment of the Brahma-voice; a gift of flavor for the sake of being dear to the entire world;
a gift of touch for the state of the Buddha’s exquisite delicacy; and [he gives] for the state of being free from aging and death.

The gift of medicine; the gift of freedom to slaves for the sake of liberating them from the servitude of the defilements (*kilesa*); the gift of blameless play and delight as a cause for taking pleasure in the True Dharma (*saddhamma*);
the gift of children by bringing all beings into the state of being one’s own children through noble birth (*ariyā jāti*);
the gift of wives for the sake of becoming the counterpart of the entire world; and [the gift] for the attainment of the marks of beauty.
The gift of gold, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth; the gift of various kinds of ornaments for the sake of the perfection of the secondary marks (*anubyañjana*);

the gift of a treasury of wealth for the attainment of the treasury of the True Dharma (*saddhamma*); the gift of a kingdom for the state of being a Dharma-King; the gift of groves such as monasteries and parks for the perfection of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and other qualities;
the gift of feet for approaching the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) with feet marked by the wheel (*cakka*); [and] for the crossing over of sentient beings from the four floods (*oghā*).
The gift of hands is for the purpose of bestowing the hand of the true Dhamma; the gift of ears, nose, and so forth is for the sake of attaining the faculty of faith and the rest;
the gift of eyes is for the sake of attaining the universal eye (samantacakkhu); and the gift of flesh, blood, and so forth is with the thought:
"May my body bring benefit and happiness to all beings at all times through seeing, hearing, recollecting, serving, and the like, and may it be a source of sustenance for the entire world."
Thinking, “May I become supreme over the entire world,” one gives the gift of the head.
And giving in this way, one does not give through improper search, nor by harming others, nor out of fear, nor out of shame, nor because of anger toward those worthy of offerings,
nor when something excellent is available, give what is coarse, nor through self-exaltation, nor through disparaging others, nor with a longing for the fruits [of merit].
He does not give out of loathing for the beggar, nor does he give with a lack of respect;
rather, he gives respectfully, with his own hand, at the proper time, with a sense of esteem, without making distinctions, and with joy in the three moments [of preparation, giving, and aftermath].
Having given for these very reasons, he has no regret afterwards, nor does he treat the recipients with pride or contempt. Regarding the recipients...
He is of pleasant conduct, generous, open-handed, and gives with a retinue. And he dedicates that success in giving for the welfare and happiness of the entire world,
and for his own unshakable liberation, for the inexhaustibility of zeal, the inexhaustibility of energy,
the inexhaustibility of concentration, the inexhaustibility of knowledge, and for the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment.

He dedicates it. And by the Great Being practicing this perfection of giving, the perception of impermanence regarding life and wealth must be established, as well as great compassion toward all beings.

For in this way, grasping the essence that is to be taken from wealth—just as one who carries out all one's property from a burning house and casts oneself outside leaves nothing behind—one leaves nothing remaining, without exception.
He indeed relinquishes it. This, then, is the sequence of practice for the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

As for the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*), since one who desires to adorn sentient beings with the ornaments of the virtues of the Omniscient One must first purify one's own virtue, one should therefore possess a mind of such compassion toward sentient beings that even in a dream—
No resentment should arise. Because he is devoted to the welfare of others, he should not grasp at the property of others as if it were a venomous snake.
He conducts himself far from unchastity, abstaining from the seven forms of sexual union, let alone from going to another’s wife.
He speaks at the proper time a discourse on the Dhamma that is true, beneficial, pleasant, and measured. He is free from covetousness.
Being free from malice, possessing unerring vision, and being firmly established in faith and affection toward the Perfectly Enlightened One—

one who has desisted from the paths of unwholesome action that lead to the suffering of the cycle of the four miserable states, and who is established on the paths to heaven and liberation through the paths of wholesome action—
will, by virtue of the purity of their intention and application, have their heart’s desires fulfilled, bringing about welfare and happiness for sentient beings.
They are quickly accomplished.
For therein, by desisting from harming, one gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings, accomplishes the development of loving-kindness with little difficulty,
attains the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, and becomes free from affliction, free from illness, and long-lived.
Abounding in happiness, one attains distinguished marks and eradicates the latent tendency toward hatred.
Likewise, by abstaining from taking what is not given, one acquires vast wealth not shared with thieves and the like; one becomes unassailable, dear, agreeable, and trustworthy;
with a mind unattached to the attainment of riches, one is disposed toward renunciation and eradicates the latent tendency toward greed. By abstaining from unchastity...
He becomes free from greed, with a tranquil body and mind; he is dear and pleasing to sentient beings and beyond suspicion;
a fine reputation for his goodness spreads abroad; his mind is unattached to women and his disposition is not covetous;
he abounds in renunciation, attains distinguished characteristics, and utterly eradicates the latent tendency toward greed.
By abstaining from false speech, one becomes an authority for beings, trustworthy, reliable, and one whose words are accepted;

one is dear and pleasing even to the deities, possesses a mouth with fragrant breath, guards the conduct of body and speech, attains specific marks of excellence, and eradicates the latent tendencies of the defilements.
By abstaining from malicious speech, one becomes a person whose body cannot be split by the machinations of others, and whose retinue is not divided.
One possesses faith that penetrates the true Dhamma; one becomes a firm friend, uniquely beloved even by beings known from previous lives, and is largely free from defilement.
By refraining from harsh speech, one becomes dear and pleasing to beings, virtuous in character, sweet-spoken, and worthy of esteem;
moreover, a voice endowed with eight qualities arises for such a person. And by refraining from idle chatter—
He becomes dear and pleasing to beings, worthy of honor and respect, and his words are authoritative;
he speaks in moderation, possesses great influence and majesty, and is skilled in answering questions with spontaneous eloquence.
Furthermore, on the level of a Buddha, he is capable of answering the manifold questions of beings who speak many languages using only a single utterance.
Through freedom from covetousness, one obtains what is desired, gains a taste for magnificent wealth, becomes esteemed by wealthy kṣatriyas and others,
remains unconquerable by adversaries, does not suffer from deficiencies of the sense faculties, and becomes a person without rival. Through non-ill will,
one becomes pleasant to behold and respected by beings, owing to one’s delight in the welfare of others.
He gladdens beings with little effort, possesses a gentle nature, dwells in loving-kindness, and becomes influential and majestic.
Through the absence of wrong view, he gains virtuous friends; even when facing execution, he does not commit an evil deed;
and because he perceives that one is the owner of one's own karma, he does not seek omens or superstitious charms.
And his faith is established and rooted in the true Dhamma; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgatas;
like a royal swan in a place of refuse, he finds no delight in other systems; he is skilled in fully understanding the three characteristics;
and at the end, he attains unobstructed knowledge. Until he reaches enlightenment, throughout each respective class of beings—
One becomes increasingly superior and attains sublime and magnificent success.
Thus, having generated great reverence for virtue— thinking, "Virtue indeed is the foundation of all success,

the source-ground of all the qualities of a Buddha, the beginning, the footstep, the entrance, and the foremost of all the factors that make one a Buddha"— one should practice restraint of body and speech.

In the taming of the sense faculties, in the perfection of livelihood, and in the use of requisites, one should—by means of the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension—be heedful and regard gain, honor, and fame as enemies with friendly faces;

thus, according to the method stated in the passage beginning "Like a hen guarding her eggs," one should carefully fulfill virtuous conduct (*sīla*). This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, is in the *Visuddhimagga*.

This should be understood according to the method already stated. Furthermore, this virtue is not for the sake of liberation from the defilements of one’s own miserable rebirths, nor even for the sake of a happy rebirth;
it is not for the attainment of sovereignty, nor for the status of a wheel-turning monarch, a god, Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā;

nor is it for the sake of one’s own possession of the threefold knowledge and so forth, nor for the sake of private enlightenment (paccekabodhi); rather, it is for the sake of omniscience for the benefit of all beings.
It should be dedicated solely for the purpose of accomplishing the adornment of unsurpassed virtue (*anuttara-sīlālaṅkāra*).

Likewise, one should reflect on how the life of a householder provides no room for the happiness of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and so forth— due to its being a dwelling place for all defilements, its great overcrowding with wife, children, and the like,
and its preoccupation with various occupations such as farming and trade— and how sensual pleasures are like "a drop of honey clinging to the edge of a sword."
“Like something that must be seized before it slips away, they provide little satisfaction and lead to vast calamity”;
and “like a dance to be caught by the flash of lightning, they are perceived for only a brief moment; like the ornaments of a madman, they are experienced through perverted perception;
like the pleasure of covering oneself with dung, they serve as a mere remedy; like drinking the water from a well while one’s fingers are submerged in it...”
They are never-satisfying; like food that fills one's hunger, they are accompanied by affliction; like bait on a hook, they are the cause for the convergence of calamities;
like the heat of a fire, they are the source of the arising of suffering throughout the three periods of time; like monkey-glue, they are the cause of bondage;
like the slough of a venomous snake, they conceal harm; and like dwelling in a village of enemies, they are places of fear.
They are like the nourishment of one's enemies, being the bait for the Māras of the defilements and so forth; they are like the pleasures of a festival, consisting of the suffering of change;
they are like a fire in the hollow of a tree, burning from within; they are like honeycombs on the grass hanging over an old well, possessing manifold dangers;

they are like drinking salt water, being the cause of thirst; they are like liquor and wine, being frequented by base people; and because they offer little gratification, they are comparable to a skeleton, and so forth.
And by observing the danger through this method, and seeing the advantage in renunciation as its opposite,
one should fulfill the perfection of renunciation with a mind that is inclined, leaning, and bent toward the bliss of renunciation,
seclusion, and tranquility. Likewise, because wisdom— like light— does not coexist with darkness, namely delusion, therefore the causes of delusion [must be abandoned].
These should be avoided by the Bodhisatta. In this regard, these are the causes of delusion:

discontent, lethargy, yawning, laziness, delighting in socializing with crowds, a habit of sleeping, a habit of indecisiveness, lack of interest in knowledge, false conceit, failure to inquire, lack of proper care for the body, an unconcentrated mind, and association with persons of poor wisdom.
Associating with those possessed of wisdom, failing to pay them honor, self-contempt, wrong reflection,
perverse adherence, excessive physical rigidity, a lack of sense of urgency, and the five hindrances. In brief,
whatever states one cultivates such that unarisen wisdom does not arise or arisen wisdom declines— avoiding these causes of delusion, one should practice.
One should apply oneself to erudition and to the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and so forth.

Herein, this is the classification of the objects of erudition: the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the twelvefold dependent origination, and likewise the foundations of mindfulness and the rest.

And [it includes] the various classifications of wholesome and other phenomena; those blameless fields of knowledge in the world; and those specialized branches of grammar capable of providing for the welfare and happiness of sentient beings.

Thus, one should thoroughly master this entire range of the subject matter of the scriptures—preceded by skill in means and supported by mindfulness and energy—through diligent learning, hearing, memorizing, practicing, and inquiry.
Having entered therein, wisdom consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayā paññā*) should be produced by establishing others [in that same knowledge];

likewise, wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayā*) should be produced by contemplating the modes of the constituent phenomena (*khandhādi*) such as their intrinsic natures through the process of thorough investigation;

and mundane full understanding (*pariññā*) should be produced by means of discerning the specific and general characteristics of those very constituents, which constitutes the preliminary-stage wisdom of cultivation (*pubbabhāgabhāvanāpaññā*).

They should be accomplished. For in this way, one who thoroughly understands internal and external phenomena without distinction—realizing that "this is merely name-and-form which arises and ceases according to its respective conditions;

herein there is no agent or instigator; it is impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having been, suffering in the sense of being oppressed by rise and fall, and non-self in the sense of lack of mastery"—[should accomplish them].
Having abandoned attachment therein, and having caused others to abandon it as well,
he established beings in the three vehicles through their introduction and maturation solely by means of compassion;
and while bringing the attainments of meditation, liberation, concentration, and meditative absorption to mastery, he was exceedingly proficient in wisdom.
"It reaches the summit.
Likewise, by the Great Being who had made the aspiration for perfect enlightenment, reflecting day after day, "What store of merit and knowledge has been accumulated today?
And what benefit for others have I performed? there arose an effort for the sake of the welfare of beings.
One should perform what is to be done for the benefit of all beings by relinquishing one’s own body and life;
all beings should be pervaded with boundless loving-kindness and compassion; whatever suffering arises for any beings, all of that should be expected to fall upon oneself;
and the merit of all beings should be rejoiced in—this is the greatness of the Buddha.
One must constantly reflect upon this: whatever action one performs, whether by body or speech, it all must be preceded by a mind inclined toward enlightenment (*bodhininnacitta*).
For by this means, the immeasurable portion of merit of the Bodhisattvas is accumulated.
Furthermore, for the sake of the enjoyment and protection of sentient beings, one’s own body and life [should be dedicated].

Having renounced [worldly things], one must seek the remedy for the sufferings of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, sun, and so forth. Furthermore, one experiences the happiness that arises from the remedy for those aforementioned sufferings which one attains for oneself;

likewise, one finds happiness in delightful parks, gardens, palaces, and upper chambers, as well as in forest retreats, because of the state of being thoroughly calmed (*abhinibbuta*) through the absence of physical and mental torment.
And one hears [of the happiness] of the Buddhas, the Buddhas who followed them, the Paccekabuddhas, and the Bodhisattvas.
He bestows upon all beings, without exception, the bliss of meditative attainment (*jhānasamāpatti*), which constitutes a dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).
This, first of all, is the method regarding the stage of non-concentration (*asamāhitabhūmi*).
But one who is concentrated bestows upon all beings the joy, tranquility, and bliss produced by the attainment of specific distinctions as experienced by himself.
He resolves thus: seeing the multitude of beings submerged in the great suffering of *saṃsāra* and in the suffering of defilements and volitional formations which are its cause—
beings who, in the hells, experience for a long duration and without interruption intense,
harsh, and bitter feelings of pain produced by cutting, splitting, cleaving, piercing, and the heat of fire, while [also] [experiencing] one another...
Animals experience suffering through anger, torment, harassment, injury, lack of independence, and so forth; and hungry ghosts (petas),

whose bodies are wreathed in flames, who cry out with arms upraised, who are scorched by fire-spitting mouths and tormented by hunger, thirst, and the like, and who subsist on vomit, spittle, and other such food,
undergo great suffering and fall into immense ruin and calamity rooted in their constant searching for sustenance.
Because they are subject to the severing of hands and other such punishments; because they exist in states of ugliness, deformity, and poverty;
because they are beset by hunger, thirst, and the like; because they are to be overcome by the powerful, are carried about by others, and are dependent on others;

and because they experience suffering no different from that in the woeful states—whether as hell-beings, ghosts, or animals, or as humans—their minds are distracted by the consumption of the poison of sense-objects.
Even though they are burning with the obsession of lust and other defilements—like a mass of fire consisting of dry wood gathered together and ablaze with flames fanned by the force of the wind;

and even though their feverish heat is unappeased and they remain subject to others without having overcome them—just as birds that have plunged far into the sky with great effort, or like arrows shot by strong men, [the devas of the sense-sphere]... even so, "although... [they are].
"Because they have existed for a long time and are not eternal, they end in a fall; they have indeed not transcended birth, aging, and death.
Seeing even the gods of the fine-material and immaterial realms in this way, one should pervade all beings with loving-kindness and compassion without exception.
Thus, by continuously accumulating the requisites for enlightenment through body, speech, and mind, one should exert effort.

Furthermore, the energy that is worthy of exertion and encouragement for the sake of Buddhahood—which is the source of an accumulation of qualities that are inconceivable, immeasurable, vast, sublime, stainless, incomparable, and free from defilement—is indeed of inconceivable power.
It is such that ordinary people cannot even hear of it, let alone practice it. For instance, there are three ways in which the thought of the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra-cittuppatti*) arises:
The four stages of Buddhahood; the four bases of sympathy; the state of being disposed toward compassion; patient reflection upon the qualities of a Buddha; non-attachment to all phenomena;
the perception of all beings as one's own children; tirelessness regarding the sufferings of saṃsāra; the relinquishing of all things worthy of giving; and the absence of pride because of that;
the commitment to the training in higher virtue and so forth; and steadfastness therein in the performance of wholesome deeds.
Joy and gladness; a mind inclined toward seclusion; devotion to meditative absorption (jhāna); insatiability in hearing what is blameless;
teaching the Dhamma as it has been heard with the intention of benefiting others; establishing beings in the true method (ñāya); firmness in exertion; the state of being steadfast and heroic;
the absence of mental disturbance in the face of others' slander or harm; resolve upon truth; and [mastery] in the meditative attainments (samāpatti).
Mastery, the attainment of power in the higher knowledges (abhiññā), the realization of the three characteristics,
the accumulation of the requisites for the supramundane path through application to the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth, and the entry into the nine supramundane states—

all such practice for the requisites of enlightenment is accomplished solely through the power of energy; thus, one should practice with care, never relaxing from the initial resolution until the attainment of great enlightenment.

Vigor must be cultivated without interruption. When vigor is perfected, all the requisites for enlightenment—such as patience and so forth, as well as generosity and so forth—become perfected as well, because they exist in dependence upon it.
In the case of patience and the others too, the practice should be understood by this same method.
Thus, practicing through giving consists in manifoldly assisting beings by relinquishing the requisites for their happiness;
through virtue, it consists in protecting their lives, property, and wives, as well as refraining from divisive speech, unkind words, harmful talk, and violence;

through renunciation, it consists in various modes of beneficial conduct toward them, such as accepting material gifts and bestowing the gift of the Dhamma; and through wisdom, it consists in skillfulness regarding the means for accomplishing their welfare.
Through energy, there is enthusiasm, undertaking, and steadfastness in that regard; through patience, the endurance of their offenses;

through truthfulness, non-deception, the undertaking of actions for their benefit, and freedom from falsehood; through determination, the unwavering persistence in performing what is beneficial even when faced with obstacles;
through loving-kindness, the constant reflection on their welfare and happiness; and through equanimity, the absence of mental disturbance whether they provide help or cause harm.

Thus, it should be understood that "practice" here refers to the immeasurable accumulation of the equipment of merit and knowledge, which is not shared with ordinary worldlings, belonging to the Bodhisatta who has compassion for all immeasurable beings;
and it also refers to the diligent fulfillment of whatever conditions for these have been stated.
What is the classification? There are thirty perfections (pāramī): ten perfections, ten secondary perfections (upapāramī), and ten ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramī).

In that regard, for a Bodhisatta who has made the resolution and whose intention and application are inclined toward the welfare of others, the bright qualities mixed with dark qualities are the perfections; those bright qualities unmixed with them are the secondary perfections.
Some say that the ultimate perfections (*paramattha-pāramī*) are neither black nor white. The perfections being fulfilled at the time of their full attainment are the perfections;
those fulfilled on the stage of a bodhisattva are the secondary perfections (*upapāramī*); and those fulfilled in every aspect on the stage of a Buddha are the ultimate perfections.

Alternatively, on the stage of a bodhisattva, they are called perfections because they bring about the welfare of others, and secondary perfections because they bring about one's own welfare; on the stage of a Buddha—

Others say that their classification is according to the beginning, middle, and end— that is, the aspiration, the undertaking, and the completion— since they fulfill both kinds of welfare through the attainment of power and self-confidence,

and thus constitute the perfections in the ultimate sense. Still others say that their classification is according to the different ways of accumulating merit for those whose nature is compassion and the pacification of hatred, and who have attained the bliss of existence, the bliss of liberation, and the supreme bliss.

Some say that the classification as previously stated—namely, *pāramī*, *upapāramī*, and *paramatthapāramī*—is based on the attainment of the three types of enlightenment (bodhi) by those who have shame (*lajjā*), mindfulness (*sati*), and self-respect (*māna*) as their refuge;

who take supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*) as their sovereign; who revere virtue, concentration, and wisdom (*sīla-samādhi-paññā*); and who are themselves crossed over, have caused others to cross over, and are causing others to cross over;

[referring to] the *anubuddha*, *paccekabuddha*, and *sammāsambuddha*. Furthermore, the requisites (*sambhāra*) are those that proceed from the mental aspiration (*citta-panidhi*) up to the verbal aspiration (*vacī-panidhi*).

Others say that from the aspiration of speech up to the aspiration of body, they are called *upapāramīs* (secondary perfections); from the aspiration of body onwards, they are the *paramatthapāramīs* (ultimate perfections).
Still others, however, maintain that the requisites (*sambhāra*) practiced by rejoicing in the merit of others are *pāramīs*;
those practiced by causing others to perform them are *upapāramīs*; and those practiced by performing them oneself—
Some say they are "the ultimate perfections" (*paramattha-pāramiyo*). Likewise, some maintain that the equipment of merit and knowledge which brings about the happiness of existence is a *pāramī*;
that which brings about one's own happiness of Nibbāna is an *upapāramī*; and that which brings about both kinds of happiness for others is the *paramattha-pāramī*.

Furthermore, the relinquishing of requisites such as children, wife, and wealth is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramī*); the relinquishing of one's own limbs is the near-perfection of giving (*dāna-upapāramī*).
The perfection of giving in its ultimate sense is the relinquishing of one’s own life.

Likewise, there are three perfections of virtue (*sīla-pāramī*) by way of not transgressing for the sake of the three kinds of things, such as children and wife; and there are three perfections of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) by way of departing after severing attachment to those same three kinds of objects;
and [there are three perfections of wisdom] by way of uprooting craving for requisites, limbs, and life among sentient beings.
There are three perfections of wisdom by way of making the determination between what is beneficial and what is harmful;

three perfections of energy by way of striving in the aforementioned types of relinquishment and so forth; three perfections of patience by way of enduring those things that create obstacles to requisites, limbs, or life;
and three perfections of truth by way of not abandoning the truth for the sake of requisites, limbs, or life.

The perfections of giving and so forth are accomplished precisely through the power of unshakable resolve; thus, there are three perfections of resolve by way of an unshakable resolve even when one's requisites and such are destroyed.
There are three perfections of loving-kindness by way of not abandoning loving-kindness toward beings who harm one’s requisites and such.

And [there are] [the perfection of equanimity] by way of attaining a state of neutrality toward beings and formations—whether they act as benefactors or malefactors—with respect to the three aforementioned bases.
The classification of these perfections should be understood through such passages as "the three perfections of equanimity" (*upekkhā-pāramī*).

As for their synthesis: just as these thirtyfold perfections are tenfold by way of being the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramī*) and so forth, they are likewise sixfold by way of being the perfections of giving, virtue, patience, energy, meditation, and wisdom. For among these, the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*)...

The perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*) is included within that [perfection of renunciation] in its aspect of going forth (*pabbajjā*), and within the perfection of meditation (*jhānapāramī*) in its aspect of seclusion from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*);

however, in its aspect of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), it is included within all six perfections. The perfection of truth (*saccapāramī*) is merely a portion of the perfection of virtue, belonging to the side of verbal truth and the truth of abstention;

but in its aspect of the truth of knowledge (*ñāṇasacca*), it is included within the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*). The perfection of loving-kindness (*mettāpāramī*) is included within the perfection of meditation alone; as for the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhāpāramī*)...
The perfection of determination (*adhiṭṭhānapāramī*) is included within all the perfections of meditation (*jhāna*) and wisdom (*paññā*).
Furthermore, among these six virtues beginning with giving (*dāna*), there are fifteen pairs and so forth that establish fifteen pairs and so forth through their mutual connection—namely:

by the pair of giving and virtue (*dānasīla*), the pair of performing what is beneficial for others and refraining from what is harmful is accomplished; by the pair of giving and patience (*khanti*),...

The accomplishment of the pair of non-greed and non-hatred; the accomplishment of the pair of generosity and wisdom through the pair of generosity and energy; the accomplishment of the pair of abandoning sensual desire and hatred through the pair of generosity and meditative absorption;

the accomplishment of the pair of the burden of the Noble Vehicle through the pair of generosity and discernment; the accomplishment of the pair of purification of application and intention through the pair of virtue and patience;
the accomplishment of the two types of development through the pair of virtue and energy; and [the accomplishment] of the pair of virtue and meditative absorption.
The accomplishment of the twofold abandonment of the obsession with immorality; by means of the pair of virtue and wisdom, the accomplishment of the twofold giving;

by means of the pair of patience and energy, the accomplishment of the twofold power of forbearance and ardor; by means of the pair of patience and jhāna, the accomplishment of the twofold abandonment of opposition and compliance;

by means of the pair of patience and wisdom, the accomplishment of the dyad of the penetration of emptiness and patience; by means of the pair of energy and jhāna, the accomplishment of the dyad of exertion and non-distraction; and by means of the pair of energy and wisdom...

The accomplishment of the dyads of the refuges is through the dyad of jhāna and wisdom; the accomplishment of the dyads of the vehicles is through the same. The accomplishment of the triads for the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion is through the triad of generosity, virtue, and patience;

the accomplishment of the triad for the acquisition of the essence of wealth, life, and the body is through the triad of generosity, virtue, and energy; the accomplishment of the triad of bases for meritorious action is through the triad of generosity, virtue, and jhāna;

and the accomplishment of the triad of the giving of material things, fearlessness, and the Dhamma is through the triad of generosity, virtue, and wisdom. In this way, [the accomplishment occurs] through the other triads, as well as through the tetrad-groups and so forth.
And the triads, tetrads, and so forth should be combined as appropriate.
Furthermore, the inclusion of these sixfold perfections (pāramīs) should be understood by means of four foundations (adhiṭṭhānas).
For there are four foundations that include the entire collection of all perfections. They are as follows: the foundation of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna),...
The foundation of relinquishment, the foundation of tranquility, and the foundation of wisdom.
In this context, it is called a "foundation" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) because one stands firm by means of it, or because one stands firm upon it, or simply because it is a foundation itself.

It is a "truth-foundation" (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) because it is both truth and a foundation, or because it is a foundation for truth, or because truth is its foundation. The same applies to the remaining [foundations].

Therein, first of all, in general: for the Great Being who has directed his resolve toward supramundane qualities and who has compassion for all beings, there is the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) because he encompasses all perfections in accordance with full understanding;
the foundation of generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*) because he relinquishes their opposites;

the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*) because he attains tranquility through the qualities of all the perfections; and [the foundation of wisdom] because of his skill in means for the welfare of others by means of those very same qualities.
The foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*). Specifically, however, it consists in: making a promise with the thought, "I shall give without deceiving those who need";
giving without deceiving one's promise; expressing appreciation without deceiving the act of giving; the relinquishment of the opposites of stinginess and so forth;
the pacification of greed, hatred, delusion, and fear regarding the object to be given, the recipient, the act of giving, and the exhaustion of the gift to be given; and [acting] as is appropriate.
Generosity is the foundation for the four foundations of wholesome states through giving at the proper time and according to the prescribed method, and through wisdom being supreme.

Likewise, virtue is the foundation for the four foundations through the non-transgression of undertaken restraints, the relinquishing of immorality, the pacification of misconduct, and through wisdom being supreme.
It is also the foundation through enduring according to one’s promise and through the relinquishing of conceptualizing the faults of others.
Patience has the four foundations as its proximate cause because it pacifies the obsession of anger and because it is headed by wisdom.

Energy has the four foundations as its proximate cause because it accomplishes the welfare of others in accordance with one's promise, because it abandons despondency, because it pacifies unwholesome states, and because it is headed by wisdom.
Mindfulness has the four foundations as its proximate cause because it reflects upon the welfare of the world in accordance with one's promise and because it abandons the hindrances.
Jhāna has the four foundations as its proximate cause by way of the settling of the mind and by way of having wisdom as its culmination.

Wisdom has the four foundations as its proximate cause by way of skill in the means for the welfare of others according to one’s promise, by way of abandoning unskillful action, by way of the settling of the fever born of delusion, and by way of the attainment of omniscience.

In this context, the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) is established through conformity with what is known and what is acknowledged; the foundation of relinquishment (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*) through the abandoning of sensual objects as things and sensual objects as defilements;
the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*) through the subsiding of hatred and suffering; and the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*) through full understanding and penetration.

The foundation of truth is embraced by the threefold truth and opposes the threefold corruption; the foundation of relinquishment is embraced by the threefold relinquishment and opposes the threefold corruption.
The foundation of serenity, which is opposed to the three types of corruption and is embraced by the threefold pacification;
and the foundation of wisdom, which is opposed to the three types of corruption and is embraced by the threefold knowledge.

Furthermore, the foundations of generosity, serenity, and wisdom are embraced by the foundation of truth, because they do not deceive and because they conform to what has been promised. And the foundations of truth, serenity, and wisdom are embraced by the foundation of generosity.
[They are so called] because of the relinquishing of opposites and because they have the relinquishing of everything as their fruit.

The foundations of truth, relinquishment, and wisdom are embraced by the foundation of peace because of the subsiding of the fever of defilements, the subsiding of sensual desires, and the subsiding of the fever of sensual desires.

The foundations of truth, relinquishment, and peace are embraced by the foundation of wisdom because they are preceded by knowledge and because they revolve in accordance with knowledge. Thus, all [of them...]
The perfections are manifested by truth, embellished by generosity, augmented by tranquility, and purified by wisdom.
For truth is their cause of birth, generosity is their cause of acquisition, tranquility is their cause of growth, and wisdom is their cause of purification.
Likewise, at the beginning there is the foundation of truth because of the declaration of truth; in the middle, there is the foundation of generosity for one who has made the vow.
The foundation of serenity at the end, because it is the culmination of all forms of peace, arising from the sacrifice of oneself for the sake of others;

and the foundation of wisdom at the beginning, middle, and end, because when that [wisdom] exists, [the other foundations] come to be, and when it is absent, they do not exist, and because they exist in accordance with what was promised.

In this regard, Great Beings possess the foundations of truth and relinquishment, which bring about their own welfare and the welfare of others, and which produce the state of being venerable and dear.
Having become householders, they assist others by means of the gift of material goods (*āmisa-dāna*).

Likewise, having become renunciants, they assist others by means of the gift of the Dhamma (*dhamma-dāna*) through the bases of serenity, wisdom, and the two foundations that bring about one's own welfare and the welfare of others, as well as the state of being respected and beloved.
In this context, the Bodhisatta fulfills the four foundations in his final existence. For one who has fulfilled the four foundations—

For some say it was during his final birth. For there, at the descent into the womb, the stay therein, and the emergence, through the realization of the foundation of wisdom, he was mindful and clearly comprehending;

and through the fulfillment of the foundation of truth, having been born, he walked seven steps facing north, surveyed all directions, and with speech revolving around the truth, [declared]: "I am the foremost in the world, the eldest... [and so forth]."
"I am the best in the world"—thus he uttered the lion’s roar three times.

Through the realization of the foundation of tranquility, he who was skilled in the four sections of the Dhamma—having seen those who are aged, afflicted by disease, dead, and gone forth—was free from the intoxication of youth, health, and life;
and through the realization of the foundation of relinquishment, he [renounced] his vast circle of kinsmen and the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch that had come into his hands.
"Relinquishment without expectation.
Regarding the second stage, the full awakening (*abhisambodhi*), some say that the four foundations are perfected.

For therein, through the realization of the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) in accordance with one's promise, there is the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four noble truths; therefore, it is the foundation of truth.

It is fulfilled. Through the accomplishment of the foundation of generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*), there is the relinquishing of all defilements and secondary stains; thus, the foundation of generosity is fulfilled.
Through the accomplishment of the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*), there is the attainment of supreme peace; thus, the foundation of peace is fulfilled.
Through the accomplishment of the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*), there is the acquisition of unobstructed knowledge; thus, the foundation of wisdom...
"Complete": this is not established, because even at the moment of full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), it exists only in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
Others say that in the third stage, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakkappavattana*), the "foundation of the fourfold determination" (*caturadhiṭṭhāna*) is complete.
For therein, through the teaching of the Noble Truths in twelve aspects by one who has mastered the foundation of the Truths (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*), the foundation of the Truths is fulfilled.
The foundation of generosity is fulfilled by performing the great sacrifice of the True Dharma for one who has brought forth the foundation of generosity.
The foundation of tranquility is fulfilled by bringing others to peace for one who has brought forth the foundation of tranquility and is himself peaceful.
The foundation of wisdom is fulfilled by thoroughly understanding the inclinations and so forth of those to be trained for one who has brought forth the foundation of wisdom.
"Complete" is also unestablished because the Buddha’s duty is not yet finished.
Regarding the fourth point, others say that at the time of final *parinibbāna*, there is the fulfillment of the four foundations (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

For therein, through the attainment of the ultimate truth by virtue of having attained final *parinibbāna*, there is the fulfillment of the foundation of truth; and through the relinquishing of all acquisitions (*upadhi*), there is the fulfillment of the foundation of generosity (*cāga*).

The fulfillment of the foundation of tranquility occurs through the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena; the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom occurs through the final consummation of the application of wisdom.
In this regard, for the Great Being, the fulfillment of the foundation of truth is particularly manifest at birth in the field of loving-kindness, having emerged from the foundation of truth;
and [the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom] is particularly manifest at the moment of full enlightenment in the field of compassion, having emerged from the foundation of wisdom.
It should be understood that the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom is especially manifest in the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, which is the field of sympathetic joy;
the fulfillment of the foundation of generosity is especially manifest in one who has attained the foundation of generosity;
and the fulfillment of the foundation of peace is especially manifest in the final Nibbāna, which is the field of equanimity.
There too, the virtue of one who has accomplished the foundation of truth is to be known through living together with them;

the purity of one who has accomplished the foundation of generosity is to be known through their dealings; the fortitude of one who has accomplished the foundation of peace is to be known in times of adversity;
and the wisdom of one who has accomplished the foundation of wisdom is to be known through discussion. In this way, the purifications of virtue, livelihood, mind, and view are to be understood.
Likewise, through the accomplishment of the foundation of truth, one does not go astray due to hatred, because of being non-deceptive;

through the accomplishment of the foundation of generosity, one does not go astray due to greed, because of being free from attachment; through the accomplishment of the foundation of tranquility, one does not go astray due to fear, because of being blameless;
and through the accomplishment of the foundation of wisdom, one does not go astray due to delusion, because of awakening to things as they truly are.
Likewise, by the first [foundation of mindfulness], one who is not corrupted endures; by the second, one who is not greedy partakes;
