by the third, one who is not afraid avoids; and by the fourth, one who is not deluded dispels.

It should be understood that through the first there is the attainment of the bliss of renunciation, while through the others there are the attainments of the bliss of seclusion, the bliss of tranquility, the bliss of enlightenment, and the bliss of purity of mindfulness. Likewise, there are the attainments of the joy and bliss born of seclusion, the joy and bliss born of concentration, the bodily bliss born of the absence of joy, and the bliss of equanimity born of the purity of mindfulness.

"These four [foundations] occur respectively in this manner. Thus, the inclusion of the entire collection of all perfections (pāramīs) should be understood as being comprised by these four foundations (adhiṭṭhānas), which are followed by manifold virtues.
And just as the inclusion of all perfections is achieved through the four foundations, it should likewise be seen that they are also included through compassion (karuṇā) and wisdom (paññā).
For the entire equipment for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) is comprised within compassion and wisdom; indeed, it is embraced by compassion and wisdom.
For the qualities such as giving are the accumulations for great enlightenment, which culminate in the attainment of Buddhahood; thus should their inclusion be understood.

What is the means of accomplishment? It is the complete gathering of the entire accumulation of merit and so forth, directed toward perfect enlightenment, by way of practicing without deficiency, by way of practicing with thoroughness through devotion and great respect, and by way of practicing with constancy.

The practice of the four factors—the uninterrupted application, the application over a long period of time, and the absence of cessation in the interim—is the means for accomplishing these [perfections].

Moreover, in brief, the means for accomplishing them is the exhaustion of attachment to oneself and the increase of affection for others on the part of one who has made the great aspiration for the attainment of perfect enlightenment. For... [of one who has made the great aspiration for the attainment of perfect enlightenment]...
Through the thorough comprehension of things as they truly are, the Great Being becomes unstained by all phenomena, and his attachment to himself comes to exhaustion and total disappearance;
yet, by virtue of his union with great compassion, as he regards all beings as if they were his own beloved children, his affectionate love for them increases.
Consequently, in accordance with those respective states, within his own continuum and that of others—
The Great Being— who has distanced himself from the opposites of the requisites for enlightenment, such as stinginess, through the disappearance of greed, hatred, and delusion—
brings about the entry into and the full maturation of people in the higher Three Vehicles by means of the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu)—
namely, generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality— which are accompanied by the four foundations. For the great wisdom and great compassion of the Great Beings [are such].
Generosity is adorned by pleasant speech; pleasant speech is adorned by beneficial conduct; and beneficial conduct is adorned and embraced by impartiality.
For a Bodhisattva, who has become the self of all beings, the accomplishment of impartiality arises from the state of having equal pleasure and pain in all circumstances.
But when he has become a Buddha, through those very bases of social integration, which have reached perfection by fulfilling the four foundations, [he attains supreme enlightenment].

By means of performing thorough integration through absolute intimacy with people, he effects their complete discipline. For among the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, generosity is fully realized through the foundation of selflessness;
kind speech through the foundation of truth; beneficial conduct through the foundation of wisdom;
and impartiality is fully realized through the foundation of peace. Indeed, among all the disciples and paccekabuddhas, [these qualities are supreme] for the Tathāgatas.
There is equality in final Nibbāna; for therein they are indistinguishably one. Therefore it was said: "There is no diversity in liberation.
And on this point there are these verses:
"He who is truthful, generous, peaceful, wise, and compassionate..."
Having gathered all necessary provisions, what purpose would he not accomplish?
The Teacher is possessed of great compassion, seeking the welfare [of beings] yet impartial;
indifferent toward everything—oh, how marvelous is the Victor!
Detached from all phenomena and equanimous toward all beings,
always intent on the welfare of beings— oh, how marvelous is the Victor!
For the sake of the benefit and happiness of all beings at all times.
“Exerted and untiring—oh, how wonderful is the Victor!
Regarding the duration required for its accomplishment: according to the minimum limit, it is four *asaṅkhyeyya* kalpas and one hundred thousand *kalpas*;
according to the middle limit, eight *asaṅkhyeyya* kalpas and one hundred thousand *kalpas*; and according to the maximum limit...

Sixteen incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons—these divisions should be understood respectively according to those who are predominant in wisdom, predominant in faith, and predominant in energy.
For those predominant in wisdom, faith is dull and wisdom is sharp; for those predominant in faith, wisdom is middling;
and for those predominant in energy, wisdom is dull. And it is by the power of wisdom that full enlightenment is to be attained.

This is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. However, they say that these three types of distinctions are also appropriate for the factors conducive to liberation (*vimuttiparipācanīya-dhamma*) according to their sharp, middling, or dull nature.

For there are three kinds of Bodhisattvas at the moment of making the aspiration (*abhinīhāra*), distinguished as those who understand by a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*), those who understand through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*), and those who are to be guided (*neyya*).
Among them, one who understands by a brief indication hears a four-line verse in the presence of a Perfectly Enlightened One and [comprehends it] at the third line.

The first possesses the necessary support (upanissaya) capable of attaining Arahatship together with the six direct knowledges (cha-abhiññā) and the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) even before the [teaching] is finished;

the second, while hearing a four-line verse in the presence of the Teacher, possesses the necessary support capable of attaining Arahatship through the six direct knowledges even before the fourth line is finished; the other, in the presence of the Blessed One...
Upon hearing a four-line stanza, one possesses the necessary potential to attain Arahantship once that stanza is completed.

These three [Bodhisattas], having received their prophecies through the resolution made at the time of the [respective] difference in eras while fulfilling the perfections, reach Perfect Enlightenment in due order according to the aforementioned distinctions of time. However, regarding those various differences in eras...

It is not the case that those Great Beings (*mahāsattas*), even if they were to give gifts day after day like the gift of Vessantara and accumulate all the qualities of the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as virtue (*sīla*) accordingly, would become Buddhas in the interim. Why?
Because their knowledge (*ñāṇa*) has not yet reached maturity. For it is like a crop produced within a limited time; [only at the end of that] limited time...

Perfect enlightenment has been fully accomplished. However, it should be understood that even by one striving with every effort, it is impossible to reach it without the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramīs) during the specific period of time already mentioned.
What is the benefit? For those Bodhisattas who have made their resolution—
“Thus, men endowed with all these factors are certain of enlightenment;
even after wandering through the long course of existence for hundreds of millions of eons,
they are not reborn in the Avīci hell, nor likewise in the Lokantara hells,” and so forth.
The benefits consisting in the manner of not falling into the eighteen states of incapacity have been described.

Furthermore, there are the sixteen types of wonderful and marvelous qualities, beginning with: "Mindful and clearly comprehending, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta descended from the Tusita realm into his mother’s womb";
and those beginning with: "The cold was dispelled and the heat became tranquil"; and [those beginning with]: "When he was being born, Sāriputta..."
Furthermore, there are thirty-two kinds of prior signs, such as "when the Bodhisatta [is present], this ten-thousandfold world-system trembles, quakes,

and shakes," as well as others such as "the fulfillment of the Bodhisattas' intentions" and "mastery over karma and so forth," which are shown in various places in the Jātakas, Buddhavaṃsa, and other texts.
The benefits: all of these are their benefits; likewise, they should be understood as the pairs of qualities such as non-greed and non-hatred, according to the distinctions already shown.
What is their fruit? In brief, the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddhatā) is their fruit.

In detail, however, it is the splendor of the multitude of numerous qualities—such as the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, and so forth—which constitute the excellence of the physical body; and [the attainment of] the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the six unique Buddha-knowledges, and the eighteen special attributes of a Buddha.
The splendor of the Dhamma-body is adorned by the accumulation of many hundreds of thousands of such qualities;
however, as for the Buddha-qualities which even a Perfectly Enlightened One could not finish describing with words throughout many eons—this is the fruit of those [virtues].
This is the summary here; the detailed account, however, should be understood from the *Buddhavamsa*, the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, the *Jātaka*, the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*, and so forth.
He says, "having fulfilled the thirty perfections," with reference to the state of having completed the perfections as they were previously defined and divided according to the aforementioned method.

Although the great renunciations are indeed instances of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), they are mentioned separately as "the five great renunciations" both to show their specific nature as exceptional forms of renunciation and to demonstrate their extreme difficulty; for this very reason, [they are distinguished] from the renunciation of limbs.

The separate mention of the sacrifice of one’s eyes is made because, although there is a commonality in the nature of sacrifice regarding both possessions and acquisitions, the sacrifice of children and wife is mentioned separately from the sacrifice of wealth and kingdom.

The "prior application" (*pubbayoga*) consists of the accomplishment of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) together with the preliminary practice known as the "conduct of going and returning. It also includes the accomplishment of an especially distinguished practice within the very same acts of giving and so forth.

"Former conduct" (*pubbacariyā*) refers to that conduct which is included within the *Cariyāpiṭaka*. Some say that "former conduct" means the former application (*pubbayoga*), the practice of giving and so forth, or living alone by way of physical seclusion.
[It consists] in the manifestation of giving and so forth, as well as fewness of wishes and so forth, and the defects and benefits of saṃsāra and nibbāna;
and in the establishing and maturing of beings for the three types of enlightenment.

The discourse that proceeds is the proclamation of the Dhamma. Conduct for the benefit of relatives is "conduct for the welfare of relatives" (*ñātatthacariyā*), and that too occurs solely through the mode of compassion.
By the word "etcetera," conduct for the welfare of the world and so forth are included. The range of knowledge (*ñāṇacāra*)—which is the practice of wisdom (*buddhicariyā*)—consists in:

the knowledge of one's own karma as one's own property; proficiency in blameless bases of action and fields of learning; proficiency in the aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth; and the investigation of the three characteristics.
In terms of its essential meaning, however, that is simply the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*); it is mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the equipment of knowledge (*ñāṇasambhāra*).
"The limit" (*koṭi*) means the boundary or the highest point. The connection is: "having developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness.

In this context, "having developed" (*bhāvetvā*) means having produced; "having cultivated" (*brūhetvā*) means having increased. By the mention of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, the path of arrival is indicated.
It shows [the goal] having reached the summit; or rather, the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, accompanied by insight, are to be seen.

Herein, it should be understood that the beginning of the path of approach is shown by the passage beginning with "by which resolution," the middle by "the perfection of giving" and so forth, and the conclusion by "the four foundations of mindfulness" and so forth.
"Immediately born" means having been released from the hand [of the gods], he was born for a moment; it does not mean merely having emerged from the mother's womb.
For as soon as the Great Being had emerged, first the Brahmās received him with a golden net;
from their hands, the Four Great Kings received him with an antelope-skin mat; and from their hands, humans received him with a *dukūla* cloth swaddling-cloth.
"Having been released from the hands of men, he stood firm upon the earth," as the Blessed One said in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*.
"In the white parasol" means in the divine white silk parasol. "While being carried" means while being held up.

And here, it should be understood that by the mention of the parasol alone, the five insignia of royalty—the sword and so forth—are also implied. [These include] the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather fan, the yak-tail fan, and the turban-cloth.
For at that time, they stood waiting with the parasol and other items. Only the parasols and such were visible then, not those who held them.
"All directions" means the ten directions. This surveying of all directions is not to be understood as occurring after the seven steps had been taken.
For the Great Being, having been released from the hands of men, looked toward the eastern direction; there—
Devas and humans, worshipping him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, said: "Great Being, there is no one here even equal to you; how much less anyone superior?

Thus, having surveyed all directions—the four cardinal points, the four intermediate points, below, and above—and seeing no one anywhere who was his equal, [he thought], "This is the northern direction," and there, with a stride of seven steps...
He arrived. "Foremost" (*āsabhi*) means supreme. "The best" (*agga*) means the very first. "The eldest" (*jeṭṭha*) and "the most excellent" (*seṭṭha*) are synonyms for that same term.
"This is the final birth; there is now no further becoming"—with these words, he prophesied the attainment of Arahantship to be reached in this present existence.

He demonstrates in detail, starting with "For indeed," the meaning that was stated briefly as "by way of being a precursor to many distinguished attainments. In that context, "therein" (*ettha*)— [End of excerpt]
The gods held aloft in the sky a parasol with many branches and a thousand circles;
golden-handled yak-tail fans fluttered about.
“Nor are the holders of the yak-tail fans and the parasol seen.
Regarding this verse: because the knowledge of omniscience itself functions everywhere without obstruction, it is called “unobstructed knowledge”;
thus he said, “of the attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience. “In the same way, this Blessed One also went... [as before] ...by way of being a preliminary sign.”
By this, he shows that the specific modes of arising by way of natural law (*dhammatā*) pertaining to noble birth are common to all Bodhisattvas;
for these are the outflow (*nissanda*) of the perfections (*pāramitā*).
"He strode" means he went. "Marūs" refers to the gods. "Equal" means they were equal and similar by virtue of the equality of their surveying. The Great Being (*mahāpurisa*).
For just as he looked toward one direction, so too did he look toward the remaining directions; there was no obstruction whatsoever to his looking.
Alternatively, "samā" means "fit to look at. For at that time, no forms—whether deformed, hideous, or repulsive—appeared in the directions that were unfit for the Bodhisatta to look upon.

Having thus explained the word *tathāgata* by means of the word *gata* in the sense of physical movement, he now says “Or alternatively,” etc., in order to show it in the sense of the movement of knowledge.
Therein, “by renunciation” (*nekkhammena*) means by an arising of wholesome consciousness dominated by non-greed;
for here, wholesome states are what is meant by “renunciation,” not the act of going forth (*pabbajjā*) and so on. “By the first jhāna”...
And they say: "Having abandoned" (*pahāya*) means having relinquished. "Gone" (*gata*) means attained; the meaning is that one has entered upon the path for further distinction.
Alternatively, "having abandoned" refers to the cause of abandoning or the characteristic of abandoning. For this word *pahāya* carries the sense of both cause and characteristic.

Here, in the phrase "gone by way of the cause of abandoning sensual desire and so forth," "going" (*gamana*) means either realization or the very practice itself. By the abandoning of sensual desire and so forth...
And that is indicated by it. This same method applies to the terms "having split open" and so forth. "By non-ill will" means by loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"By perception of light" means by the manifestation of the perception of light through mental attention that has made [the object] clear. "By non-distraction" means by concentration (*samādhi*).

"By the definition of phenomena" means by the discernment of phenomena such as the wholesome according to their true nature; some also say it means "by the definition of name-and-form together with its conditions."

Having thus shown the Blessed One’s state of being a Tathāgata through the preliminary practice for the first jhāna— described by the words “having abandoned covetousness for the world,” etc., which consists in the abandoning of the hindrances such as sensual desire—
he now says “by knowledge,” etc., in order to show that same state together with the means,
namely, the eight attainments and the eighteen great insights. For [the purpose of] the discernment of name-and-form and the overcoming of doubt...

By removing delusion, which acts as an obstruction, for one established in the full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*), the perception of impermanence and the other [perceptions] are accomplished;

likewise, through gladness (*pāmojja*)—the sign of delight in the meditative attainments (*jhāna-samāpatti*)—and with the removal of lack of delight therein, the attainment of the *jhānas* and so forth occurs.
Thus, the means for both meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and insight (*vipassanā*) consists in the dispelling of discontent and the shattering of ignorance.

However, the presentation in reverse order should be understood as being for the purpose of showing that ignorance—which has the nature of an obscuration—is included even among the obscurations mentioned below.
Because they obstruct entry into the dwelling of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-vihāra*), the obscurations are like door-bolts; thus it was said, "having thrown open the bolt of the obscurations.
Regarding the passage, "Having thought and deliberated at night, one applies oneself to work by day," [it is explained as follows:]
Since initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra) are intended here as being like smoke, he says "the smoke of initial application and sustained application.

Although suffering is abandoned precisely in the access to the first jhāna and pleasure is abandoned precisely in the access to the fourth jhāna, he says "having abandoned pleasure and pain by means of the fourth jhāna" with reference to their complete abandonment.

“Contemplation of the impermanent as impermanent” (*aniccānupassanā*) is the name for insight (*vipassanā*) that proceeds by grasping the impermanence of phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.
“Perception of permanence” (*niccasaññā*) refers to the false perception that occurs in regard to conditioned phenomena, thinking, “They are permanent, they are eternal.
By way of the term “perception,” one should understand that views and consciousness are also included. This same method applies hereafter.
"In others too. "Contemplation of disenchantment" means contemplation occurring in the mode of becoming disenchanted with formations (*saṅkhāra*).
"Delight" (*nandi*) refers to craving accompanied by rapture. Likewise, "contemplation of fading away" means contemplation occurring in the mode of fading away.
"Contemplation of cessation" means contemplation of the cessation of formations. "Those formations simply cease..."
Or, contemplation in this way—"they do not arise in the future by way of origination"—is the contemplation of cessation.

For this reason it was said: "By means of the contemplation of cessation, one causes cessation; one does not cause origination. For this is the state of wishing for deliverance that has reached its full strength.
Contemplation occurring in the mode of relinquishing is the contemplation of relinquishment. It is reflective discernment and stabilization.

This is indeed so. "Grasping" (ādāna) is the apprehension [of things] by way of permanence and so forth. "The perception of compactness" (ghanasaññā) is the grasping of unity by way of continuity, collection, function, and object.

"Accumulation" (āyūhana) is the formative activity (abhisaṅkharaṇa). "Transformation" (vipariṇāma) is the attainment of a specific state. "The perception of stability" (dhuvasaññā) is the grasping of a solid nature.
"The sign" (nimitta) refers to the formations (saṅkhārā) by way of their compactness as a collection and so forth, and by way of their delimitation of their own respective functions.

The inclusion of the term "with a basis" (*saviggahaggahaṇaṃ*). "Aspiration" (*paṇidhi*) refers to the aspiration of lust and so forth; in its actual meaning, however, it is the inclination toward volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) by way of craving (*taṇhā*).

"Adherence" (*abhinivesa*) refers to the view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*). "Insight into phenomena through higher wisdom" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) is the investigation of all phenomena by way of their impermanence, suffering, and so forth.

"Adherence to grasping at the essential" (*sārādānābhinivesa*) is the perversion (*vipallāsa*) of perceiving essence in what is essenceless. [The phrase] "The world has arisen through the creation of Īśvara and so forth... refers to the adherence to a creator.
Adherence (*abhinivesa*) is adherence through delusion (*sammoha*). Some, however, say that adherence through delusion is the falling into doubt that occurs in such ways as, "Did I exist in the past?
and so forth. The grasping at volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) as a shelter or protection is adherence through attachment (*ālaya*).

Because of the statement, "Delighting in attachment, arisen from attachment," attachment is craving (*taṇhā*); it is precisely this [craving] that functions by way of adhering to the eye and so forth, and to visible forms and so forth.

Some say that "clinging and adherence" refers to the process of existence (*pavatti*). The knowledge that occurs as "such formations are to be relinquished" is the contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*).
Nibbāna is "turning away" (*vivaṭṭa*) because it is removed from the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*);

the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) is the "contemplation of turning away" (*vivaṭṭānupassanā*) because it occurs through the act of taking that [Nibbāna] as its object. "Adherence by way of conjunction" refers to the state of being conjoined.
Adherence to volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). "Associated with views" (*diṭṭhekaṭṭha*) means associated with views by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of abandonment (*pahāna*).

"Gross" (*oḷārika*) is said in relation to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths; otherwise, even those to be abandoned by seeing would be gross in comparison to those to be abandoned by the second path.
"Subtle" (*aṇusahagata*) means minute; this is said in relation to what is to be abandoned by the lower paths.
It has been stated. "All defilements" refers to all remaining defilements; for those defilements abandoned by the first and subsequent paths are not abandoned again.
Hardness is the state of being solid. Oozing is the state of being fluid.

That by which a particular group [of atoms] becomes inflated like a bellows by worldly air, or possesses rigidity, is *vitthambhana* (distension). Even though [other qualities] exist within the same group...

Regarding the state of non-contact with other groups of primary elements (*kalāpa*), space is the limit of form (*rūpapariyanto*) in the sense that it is the distinctness from each respective element.

It is precisely not in contact with those things which constitute its own delimitation; otherwise, the nature of the delimitation of the primary elements would not exist, because they would then attain a state of being all-pervasive (*byāpī*).
For non-pervasiveness is indeed non-contact. In whichever group of elements there is a delimitation, [space is that very delimitation].
The state of not being touched by those [other elements] is the characteristic of non-contact. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the description of the space element:
"It is not touched by the four great elements.

Impingement (*ruppana*) is the production of something dissimilar when there is a concurrence of opposing conditions. Because volition (*cetanā*) is predominant among the phenomena of the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), [it is so designated].
This was stated by way of volition (cetanā): “The characteristic of formations is their forming.

For in the *Suttantabhājanīya* of the *Vibhaṅga* on the aggregate of formations, it is volition alone that is analyzed, beginning with “volition born of eye-contact,” and so forth; and volition indeed has the characteristic of forming.
As it is said: “In this context, what is the meritorious formation? It is wholesome volition pertaining to the sense sphere,” and so on.
Pervasion (*pharaṇa*) is the state of being expansive. In the phrase "in lack of faith" (*assaddhiye*), it means "due to lack of faith"; the locative case is used in the sense of a cause.

The same method applies to the phrases "in laziness" (*kosajje*) and so forth. The characteristic of tranquility (*vūpasama-lakkhaṇa*) is the characteristic of the subsiding of the feverish distress of body and mind.

When the higher mind (*adhicitta*) proceeds free from lethargy and agitation, equanimity (*ajjhupekkhanā*) is the reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) resulting from the absence of engagement in exertion, restraint, or encouragement.
Because it cuts off partiality;
because right speech—which is embracing by nature—is the opposite of harsh and non-embracing speech such as lying, which has the function of deceiving;
and because it is affectionate toward the associated mental states and toward the listeners of well-spoken words that serve as conditions for right speech.
"Grasping at a person" is the characteristic of right speech as grasping (*pariggaha*). Physical action (*kāyikakiriyā*) arouses whatever is to be done;
and since it itself is the arising and the effort (*ghaṭana*), the abstention known as right action (*sammākammanta*) should be understood as having the characteristic of arousing (*samuṭṭhāna*).
Alternatively, "arousing" (*samuṭṭhāpana*) is the lifting up of the associated mental states by means of physical action.

It is like the lifting of a burden. It is the purification or cleansing of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*)—or of the associated mental states—of a living being, or it is the purity of one’s livelihood itself.
It is the right exertion (*paggaha*) that prevents the mind, together with its associated states, from falling into the side of defilement.
“Volitional formations” (*saṅkhārā*) here is intended to mean volition (*cetanā*); thus it is said: “The characteristic of volitional formations is volition.

Inclining (*namana*) is the state of being directed toward an object. Proceeding (*āyatana*) is the act of proceeding. For it is by way of the bases (*āyatana*) that the occurrence of mind and mental factors—which are termed “the self” (*āya*)—takes place.
“The characteristic of craving as cause” refers to its status as the cause that generates the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), whereas for the Path, it refers to its quality of leading to Nibbāna.

This is precisely their distinction. The characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*) is the non-perverted intrinsic nature (*aviparītasabhāva*). Their single flavor (*ekarasa*) is the state of not overstepping one another and being neither deficient nor excessive. Tranquillity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*) are indeed yoked together; some also say they are "faith and wisdom, exertion and non-distraction.

"Exhausted" (*khīṇa*) means the defilements are exhausted; thus it is the Path (*magga*). Because its culmination is non-arising, it is "non-arising" (*anuppāda*); this is the Fruit (*phala*). "Tranquillity" (*passaddhi*) is the subsiding of the defilements.
"Of desire" (*chandassa*) means of the desire characterized by the wish to act. Its characteristic as a root is its state of being a foundation.

Its characteristic as an originator is its being the cause for the arising of associated states by way of presenting them with an object. "Conjunction" (*samodhāna*) is the mode in which they are to be grasped through the coming together of the sense-object and so forth;
it is what is called "conjunction" (*saṅgati*). It is so called because "associated states are joined together" (*samaṃ saha odahanti*) by means of this.
Or, it is contact (*phassa*) because of its convergence. It is called a "convergence" (*samosaraṇa*) because things come together and meet therein.
It is said thus because associated states, which do not function in the absence of feeling, become as if converged for the purpose of experiencing feeling.
The characteristic of being foremost is the state of leadership among the associated states, like the ridge-pole of rafters. From that...
"Superior to those associated states" means *taduttari* (superior to that). For wholesome states have wisdom as their superior (*paññuttarā*).
"Of liberation" refers to the fruit (*phala*), for that is the essence by virtue of being the ultimate excellence of the essence consisting of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).

And this analysis of characteristics is according to various Sutta passages—such as the six elements and the five jhāna factors—and in accordance with the method transmitted in the ancient commentaries.
And it should be understood as "and what [is it]? For even though some state has already been mentioned, it is shown again for the purpose of explaining it by way of another method;
and for that very reason, it is said: "Wholesome states have desire as their root, are originated by attention, converge upon contact, and culminate in feeling";
"wholesome states have wisdom as their supreme"; and "this holy life has liberation as its essence."

Based on such Sutta passages as, “For the holy life, friends, has Nibbāna as its goal and Nibbāna as its consummation,” it was stated that “desire has the characteristic of being the root,” and so forth.

The “suchness of phenomena” refers to the Four Noble Truths because their intrinsic nature is non-erroneous. They are “such” (*tathā*) because they possess that nature; “not otherwise” (*avitathā*) because they do not have a different nature; and “not otherwise than that” (*anaññathā*) because they are devoid of any other mode of appearance.
"Jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho" means the state of having arisen and come together through birth as a condition;
that is to say, the state of having come successively upward for that which has arisen by way of the condition of birth and is joined with its own corresponding conditions.
Alternatively, "sambhūtaṭṭho ca samudāgataṭṭho ca" is "sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho. Aging-and-death does not exist apart from birth, nor...
The sense of being produced with birth as a condition (*jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭha*) means that it exists from something other than birth.

And the sense of having arisen with birth as a condition (*jātipaccayasamudāgataṭṭha*) means that it emerges from birth in this way. The meaning is that whatever kind of birth serves as a condition in whatever manner, there is a manifestation corresponding to that.

Regarding the phrase "the sense of conditions for volitional formations (*saṅkhārānaṃ*) by way of ignorance (*avijjā*)," here too, it is not that ignorance is not a condition for volitional formations; rather—

Ignorance exists, and without ignorance, volitional formations do not arise. In whatever way ignorance serves as a condition for whichever volitional formations, this is the meaning of "the conditionality" of ignorance with respect to volitional formations; the sense is "the state of being a condition.
The connection is: "The Blessed One knows and sees that. "By him" means by the Blessed One. This should be construed with "analyzing that."

That is the base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). By the word "etc. in the phrase "desirable, undesirable, etc.," it includes the neutral; likewise, it includes the divisions of past, future, and present; limited, internal, external, both, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by way of the terms actually occurring":
because of the statement, "The base of visible form is seen, the base of sound is heard, the base of odor, the base of flavor, and the base of tangible are touched;
all form is cognized by the mind," there are both the term "seen" and the term "cognized."
It is obtained with respect to a visible-form object (*rūpārammaṇa*). It is [designated] by many names such as: "visible-form object; desirable, undesirable, or neutral;
limited; past, future, or present; internal or external; seen or cognized; form, the base of form, the element of form;
appearance of color; visible and impinging; blue, yellow," and so forth. Or, it is [explained] "by thirteen sections."
He says this with reference to the thirteen sections of exposition (*niddesa-vāra*) found in the *Rūpa-khaṇḍa*.

And in each section, by way of four methods of defining (*vavatthāpana-naya*) each [category], he says, "by fifty-two methods. This is because of his seeing things exactly as they are, without error, and because of his teaching that is beyond refutation.
By saying, "I know, I have fully understood," he demonstrates the occurrence of knowledge in both the present and the past tenses.

It should be understood that the occurrence of knowledge regarding the future has indeed been stated. The word *vidita* (known) should be understood as not specifying a particular time, just as in such expressions as "seen, heard, sensed" (*diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ*).
"It did not appear" means it did not approach [the mind] by way of being a self or belonging to a self.
One sees, knows, and goes toward those phenomena—such as visible objects and so forth—exactly as they are in their own nature and in their specific modes.
The derivation of the term *tathāgata* should be understood in this way. However, some explain it as follows:

"By means of etymological rules (*niruttinaya*), either through the elision of the word *dassī* according to the *pisodarādi* class of compounds, or by the addition [of a letter] to the word *āgata*, one arrives at *tathāgato*.
It is faultless because it is beyond reproach. It is not deficient because there is nothing to be added. It is not redundant because there is nothing to be removed.
"Perfect in every aspect through the excellence of its meaning, phrasing, and so forth. "Not otherwise" completes, by way of contrast, the very meaning already stated as "just so.

By this, he shows the quality of unerring teaching: that because it accomplishes its purpose exactly for which it was spoken, it is "just so," in the very manner in which it was spoken by the Blessed One. By the phrase "the meaning of what was said," [he indicates] the truth (*tatham*).
He shows that the letter *da* has been changed to *ta* in the word *tathāgata* according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*) by the rule "he goes, thus he is a *tathāgata*.
Furthermore, "one who has gone thus" (*tathāgata*) means one whose going (*gata*)—that is, the activity of body or speech—is such (*tathā*).
And when "thus" (*tathā*) is stated, because of the inseparable connection between the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ*, the meaning "as" (*yathā*) is indeed present.

There is. And in order to show this meaning—that bodily and vocal actions stand in mutual conformity, such that the body stands in relation to speech and speech to the body by way of being connected—he said, "For the Blessed One," and so forth.
Furthermore, in this sense, the meaning of "Tathāgata" as "one who speaks thus" (tathāvādī) is also established. Moreover, previously...
He said, "Thus he is a Tathāgata by virtue of acting accordingly," because he has been shown through another grammatical derivation (*pakārantara*).
By the phrase "horizontally in immeasurable world-systems," he refutes what some say, namely, that "there are world-systems above and below just as there are horizontally.
Just as the splendor of the teaching itself consists of the splendor of the teaching, so too...

In such passages as "consisting of merit" (*puññamaya*) and "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*), because prefixes and particles function by indicating the meaning of a word when placed in proximity to it, the word *gata* itself expresses the sense of "understood" (*avagata*) and the sense of "past" (*atīta*).
Thus he said: "Gata means understood and past. Alternatively, from the perspective of the formal resolution (*abhinīhāra*):

From his initial setting out until his full enlightenment, because there was no decline, standing still, defilement, or turning back during this interval in his practice of the Great Vehicle of Enlightenment, he went "thus" (*tathā*) according to his aspiration;
thus, having practiced in accordance with his resolve, he is the Tathāgata.

Alternatively, because of his great psychic power, his attainment of the excellence of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and his lack of obstruction due to the absence of any resistance anywhere, [he is the Tathāgata].
He is the Tathāgata because his bodily, verbal, and mental movements, goings, and activities proceed in such a way (tathā).

Furthermore, since in the world the words *vidha*, *yutta*, *gata*, and *pakāra* are seen to have synonymous meanings, this Blessed One is also a Tathāgata because he is of such a kind (*vidha*) as the Blessed Ones Vipassī and the others.
And just as those Blessed Ones were endowed (*yutta*)...

This Blessed One is also a Tathāgata because he has gone in that same way. Alternatively, since "truth," "reality," and "suchness" (tatha) are designations for knowledge, he is therefore a Tathāgata because he has come by means of such knowledge. Thus also is the meaning of the word *Tathāgata* to be understood:
"Having abandoned the stains of sensual desire and the rest, just as they have gone..."
Vipassī and the other Great Seers, the Sage of the Sakyas, and Jutindhara are considered Tathāgatas because of their knowledge of meditative concentration.
Thus, one is regarded as a Tathāgata for that reason.
And likewise, the Victor, through his self-arisen knowledge,
has fully realized the characteristics of the elements, bases, and so forth,
according to their distinctions in individual essence, commonality, and classification.
The Bull of the Sakyas is called the Tathāgata because he has,
with his all-seeing eye, seen things as they truly are,
and likewise the principle of specific conditionality in its entirety.
Because he has clearly manifested [the truth] through his own realization,
not by relying on others, he is therefore the Victor, the Tathāgata,
who knows things as they truly are— even throughout world-systems of manifold divisions.
Regarding the Victorious One’s range of perception,
such as the sense-sphere of visible forms, his vision is indeed manifold and diverse, yet it is precisely according to reality;
therefore, the Tathāgata is one whose vision is all-pervading.
But when one speaks of the Dhamma exactly as it is,
and acts in accordance with one's own words,
one dwells having surpassed the world by means of one's virtues.
The Tathāgata, the Leader of the World,
likewise [manifests] according to his original aspiration and according to his inclination, through the manifestation of speech, body, and mind.
“In whatever manner and by whomsoever the Great Seers were formerly [described], in that same manner and by that same person is the Victor, the Tathāgata.

This is merely the opening of the summary verses (*saṅgahagāthā*). Why? Because, like the term "heedfulness" (*appamāda*), it encompasses all the qualities of a Buddha through the practice of the entire Dhamma. For this very reason, he said: “In every aspect,” and so forth.
By the phrase “‘What is that? he asks,” the general nature of the question in the statement beginning with “And what, monks, is that?

is shown. For, in order to make known the specific nature of that question without distinction, [the author] shows all the questions found in the *Mahāniddesa* by way of extracting their meaning, starting with “In this context, ‘question’ means... and so forth. Therein, the word “therein” (tattha) means...
Regarding the phrase “‘What is that? he asks,” it refers to that general interrogative statement.

A “characteristic” (*lakkhaṇa*) is any essential nature (*sabhāva*) that one wishes to know. By saying “unknown” (*aññāta*), he expresses the state of being unknown by any kind of knowledge whatsoever;

by saying “unseen” (*adiṭṭha*), he expresses the state of not having been seen as if before the eyes by means of knowledge consisting of vision. By saying “unmeasured” (*atulita*), he means “this is only this much.”

"Untrodden" means not having been traversed by that which serves as a means of comparison; "crossed over" means not having reached the completion of the activity of knowledge by means of that which serves as a means of crossing over;
"unmanifest" means the state of knowledge being unapparent; "unclarified" means the state of not having been made apparent by knowledge.
That by which what was not seen is illuminated is "the illumination of the unseen. That by which what was seen is brought into harmony is "the harmonization of the seen," by way of discussion.

The making of a decision (*vinicchayakaraṇa*). It is called "the cutting off of doubt" (*vimaticchedanā*) because by means of it, uncertainty (*vimati*) is severed. A question regarding consent is an "inquiry for consent" (*anumatipucchā*).
For in a question such as, "What do you think, monks? and so forth, consent is being asked by way of [the implicit question], "What is your consent?
"Desire to speak" (*kathetukamyatā*) means [the state] of desiring to speak.
8. *Atipāta* (excessive killing) means falling excessively, that is, falling even before the natural time of falling—as in the case of a *sarasena* (a bird or creature);

the meaning is that it causes one to fall quickly, not allowing it to fall slowly. Alternatively, *atipāta* is the causing of death by surpassing [the life-force] or by overcoming it with weapons and the like.

"A being" (*satta*) refers to the continuum of the aggregates (*khandha-santāna*), for it is there that the designation "being" is applied. "Life-faculty" (*jīvitindriya*) refers to both the material and immaterial life-faculties.
For when the material body and the life-faculty are destroyed, the other [faculties] also perish because they are connected to them.
But why, in this context, is the singular number used in the expressions “the taking of life” (*pāṇassa atipāto*) and “a living being” (*pāṇo*), as in the conventional usage “a being”?
Is it not the case that here what is intended is abstention from the taking of life of *all* living beings? For he will say later: “compassionate toward the welfare of all breathing beings.”
Is it by way of a plural designation, as in “all beings that have breath,” and so forth? This is true;
however, here a singular designation is made by way of the commonality of the state of being a living being (*pāṇabhāva-sāmañña*).

Since multiplicity is already understood through the proximity of the word “all” (*sabba*), the plural designation is made not by omitting the general designation, but rather by the desire for a term expressing differentiation. Furthermore, from the standpoint of generality...

This distinction in phrasing should be understood as being made for the purpose of making known this specific difference: namely, that while there is the undertaking of restraint (*saṃvara-samādāna*), there is also the breaking of that very restraint (*saṃvara-bheda*).

That volition (*cetanā*) by which, while one is acting, because of the performance of an injury toward the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the support for the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), those great elements arising with those [supporting] great elements as their condition will not arise—[that volition is what is meant].
The volition that initiates such an application is the taking of life (*pāṇātipāta*).
For beings whose faculties have already developed are not as sensitive as other beings; thus, they do not serve as the cause for those of the same species.
By the phrase "of the doors of body and speech," he rejects the status of taking life for the murderous volition that occurs at the mental door (*manodvāra*).

The gravity of the offense (*mahāsāvajjatā*) should be understood through the magnitude of the preliminary effort (*payoga*), the object (*vatthu*), and so forth, because of the powerful nature of the volition (*cetanā*) arising by means of those conditions. For the magnitude of the effort is to be understood by way of the concluding volition (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*),
which accomplishes the task by swiftly bringing the intended effort to completion and which has acquired proficiency through repeated occurrence in the impulsion moments (*javana*).
Furthermore, even when the living beings—both small and large—are equal in terms of the effort required, a stronger volition (*cetanā*) arises in one who kills a large being;
this is due to the greatness of the object (*vatthu*). Thus, both of these factors occur precisely through the strength of the volition itself.

For instance, just as a volition directed toward providing benefit arises there because of the great virtue of the one to be killed, so too [is it] by way of the production of a specific field (*khetta*).
The volition of doing harm also arises powerfully and more intensely; thus its great blameworthiness should be understood.

Therefore, even when the conditions such as the preliminary effort and the object are not great, the state of being greatly blameworthy is to be understood by way of the power and other qualities of the volition itself, due to conditions such as its great efficacy.

They are called *saṃbhārā* (requisites) because one prepares (*sambharīyanti*) by means of them; they are the constituent factors (*aṅgāni*). Among these, the perception of a living being and the murderous mind are present even in the preliminary stage.
The "application" (*upakkama*) is that which is instigated by the volition (*cetanā*) to kill. The volition of killing a living being possesses five requisites;

therefore, it should be understood as being distinct from those five requisites. That which consists of science (*vijjāmayo*) refers to the practice of reciting mantras, such as that of the *āthabbaṇika* (sorcerers) and others.
"Consisting of psychic power" means consisting of the psychic power born of kamma-vipāka, such as that of the Daṭhākoṭaka and others. "Excessive prolixity" means an overly extensive elaboration.
Here it may be asked: among conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), whose nature is to cease moment by moment, who is the killer and who is killed?
If it is the continuum of mind and mental factors, then because it is formless, it is incapable of being disturbed by means of cutting, breaking, and so forth; nor...
Furthermore, the continuity of form (*rūpa-santāna*) is subject to disturbance;
because it is insentient, like a piece of wood or a wooden peg, the taking of life through cutting and so forth is not applicable there, as it is in the case of a dead body.

Moreover, the application (*payoga*) for the taking of life—such as the manner of striking—might occur in relation to past, future, or present formations (*saṅkhāra*); however, among these, it does not first apply to the past or the future.

Because of their non-existence, [the application of force] would be impossible; and because present formations (*saṅkhāra*) are momentary, having by their very nature the quality of ceasing through their own essence, any application [of force] would be useless toward those already facing destruction.

Furthermore, since destruction is devoid of a cause, death is not caused by such applications as striking with weapons and the like. Moreover, since formations are inactive (*nirīhaka*), to whom would that application belong?
For one who perishes at the very same moment as the intention to kill arises, due to their momentariness, there can be no agent.
Because it does not persist until the conclusion of the action, to whom does the bond of the kamma of killing belong?
It is said: the "slayer" is a collection of formations termed a "being," accompanied by the aforementioned volition of the killer;
on account of the murderous effort initiated by him, the life-faculty and consciousness have departed, which is the basis for the application of the conventional designation "dead."

When the aforementioned application of killing is not performed, the aggregate of material and immaterial phenomena that is liable to arise is destroyed, or else the entire continuum of mind and mental factors is destroyed.
Even though that [continuum] is not the direct object of the application of killing, because its existence in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokārabhava*) is dependent upon the material continuum,

through the application employed by another to sever the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) within the material continuum, there occurs the arising of dissimilar matter that obstructs the production of that [continuum].
When there is destruction, there is a severance; thus, it is not the case that killing is impossible, nor is killing without a cause.

Furthermore, the preliminary effort (payoga) is not purposeless, because due to the effort exerted regarding present formations, the complex of formations that ought to arise immediately thereafter does not so arise.
This is because for momentary formations, there is "momentary death" in this context.
Because death in its essential nature is not intended [here], and because the death of the continuity (santati-maraṇa) possesses causes according to the method already stated,
there is no such thing as causeless death; nor is the act of taking life devoid of an agent,

since the designation "agent" is established even for passive formations (saṅkhāra) when they function as contributing factors by their mere presence, being determined to produce a result corresponding to themselves.

Just as it is said, "The lamp illuminates, and the moon, the maker of night," and because killing is not intended for the mere aggregate of mind and mental factors that coexist with the intention to kill—
since it is only that which persists by way of a continuum (*santāna*) that is admitted [as the agent]—
and because the accomplishment of purposeful action is seen in the case of lamps and so forth as they proceed by way of a continuum, there is indeed such a thing as killing.
“Bound by karma. This analysis should also be applied, as far as possible, to the cases of taking what is not given and so forth.
By the phrase “or abstaining from the time of its abandonment,” he shows that it is the “abstention by eradication” (samuccheda-virati), which has abandonment as its cause, that is intended here.
For, because the unwholesome conduct of killing living beings has been abandoned through the knowledge of the destruction of karma, the Blessed One is absolutely...
"Therefore, one is said to abstain from it" is stated because what is intended here is the abandonment and the abstinence [from evil] by way of complete eradication (*samuccheda*).
Although there is no temporal sequence— neither prior nor posterior— between the act of abandoning and the state of abstinence,

when the relationship of cause and effect is considered between the path-factors such as right view and so forth, and right speech and so forth, they exist as cause and effect even when they are co-nascent (*sahajāta*).

Since the apprehension occurs precisely as a prior and subsequent state, the designation of "prior time" refers to the act of abandoning with respect to the conditions—the factors such as right view—that constitute the abandoner, by way of the mode of the arising of that apprehension;
and the designation of "subsequent time" refers to the act of abstaining with respect to the abstinences that have arisen from those conditions.
This is how the meaning should be understood here. Alternatively, "abandoning" (pahāna) is used in the sense of total eradication (samuccheda).

Abstention should be applied by way of subsiding. Alternatively, "killing" (*pāṇātipāta*) is that by which a living being (*pāṇa*) is killed; it is the collection of factors that serve as the cause for the destruction of life.
What, then, is this? It consists of the defilements such as shamelessness, lack of moral dread, hatred, delusion, and cruelty.
For the Blessed One, having abandoned and eradicated these by means of the Noble Path, [is completely free] from the misconduct of killing living beings.

"One who abstains" is said because, when the defilements have been abandoned, the karma that has those defilements as its cause no longer arises. This same principle applies to such passages as "having abandoned taking what is not given.
By the restrictive particle *vā*, he shows that this abstinence is unlimited in terms of time and other factors;
for while others, though having undertaken the abstinence, may—due to an unstable mind or for the sake of gain, livelihood, and so forth—[violate it].
They break their formal undertaking, but the Blessed One does not. For the Blessed One, having entirely abandoned the taking of life, is absolutely abstinent.
"I shall transgress" refers to weak unwholesome states that arise intermittently, mixed with blameless states.
Furthermore, because the wise are able to know, upon perceiving the application of body and speech, "Defilements have arisen in this person," [these states are so designated].

Therefore, it should be understood that these [objects] are spoken of by this method as "to be cognized by eye and ear. The term "bodily" (*kāyika*) is said with reference to powerful unwholesome states that produce [actions] such as the taking of life.
The connection is: "a designation obtained by way of lineage (*gotta*). It is appropriate to illustrate this with the description spoken by Brahmadatta.
Because this teaching was undertaken by way of showing the connection [between the two]. Herein, this is the clarification:

"Having abandoned the taking of life, the Saṅgha of disciples of the ascetic Gotama abstains from the taking of life; they have laid aside the rod, they have laid aside the weapon"—this should be expanded in detail.
But is it not the case that the praise of the Dhamma was also spoken by Brahmadatta? True, it was spoken.

However, because the Dhamma originates from the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) and because the Noble Saṅgha is its support, and because the power of the Dhamma is established through them both, it is illuminated by the very illustration of those two; thus, it is not mentioned separately.

Indeed, it was solely through the power of the True Dhamma that the Blessed One and the community of monks became capable of abandoning killing and other evils; as for the teaching, it begins from the start...
"starting from this point, it has come down thus.

Herein, this is the intended meaning: wishing to extend the teaching further by taking as his theme the Buddha-qualities that are not shared with others, beginning with the words "There are, monks, other qualities," the Blessed One, starting from the outset, [spoke] while speaking the praise of the Tathāgata.
With the words "He would speak," etc., he began the teaching by way of the Buddha's qualities alone, and not by way of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
For this is the nature of the Blessed One’s teaching: that in order to show the teaching as having a single flavor, there is the non-inclusion of anything else even if it were applicable.
Thus, in the Rūpakanda, in the sections on the aggregates (duka) and their respective expositions, the heart-base (hadayavatthu) was not included among the other bases.
The difference in teaching arises because they do not share the same mode of occurrence.

For while visual consciousness and the others have exclusively the eye and so forth as their supports, mental consciousness does not have the heart-basis as its support in such an absolute sense. And it is on the basis of this support that the teaching concerning the number of bases and so forth proceeds, [stating]:
"There is matter that is the basis for visual consciousness; there is matter that is not the basis for visual consciousness," and so on.

Furthermore, since [the heart-base] is exclusively dependent upon the physical heart-basis, even when pairs and so forth are stated—such as "There is matter that is the basis for mind-consciousness" and so on—it is not possible to find corresponding pairs of objects (ārammaṇa-duka) and so forth.
For it is impossible to say: "There is matter that is the object of mind-consciousness; there is matter that is not the object of mind-consciousness."
If the pairs of bases and objects were of different destinies, the teaching would not be of a single flavor.

Likewise, because they are not mentioned in the *Nikkhepakanda* through the classification of thought-arising (*cittuppāda*), one could not say "and vicāra" in the response to the term "without initial application and sustained application" (*avitakka-avicāra*).

Therefore, although initial application (*vitakka*) is present in the response to the term "without initial application but with sustained application" (*avitakka-vicāramatta*), it was not explicitly mentioned; otherwise...
“‘And applied thought’ should have been stated.

He said, “for the purpose of harming others,” and so forth, in order to indicate the laying down of weapons and staves—that is, the avoidance of staves in the form of violence consisting of the harming of others. “From the state of harming” means from the state of injuring.
Since it was said, "It is also appropriate to illustrate this by way of the community of bhikkhus," he spoke the passage beginning with "But as for those bhikkhus," illustrating that point in part.
Regarding the term *lajjī* (conscientious), it should be understood that by the sense of shame (*lajjā*) mentioned here, moral dread (*ottappa*) is also implied;
for there is no loathing of evil devoid of fear of evil, nor is there fear of evil that is not accompanied by shame. Or rather, [it refers to] the reverence for the Dhamma of the Buddhas.

Because the Dhamma is dependent upon oneself, it is said that shame (*lajjā*) has oneself as its sovereign; however, dread of blame (*ottappa*), which has the world as its sovereign, is not so described.

Why is it said, "He has attained compassion and a mind of loving-kindness"? For is it not the case that the word *dayā* occurs in such phrases as "one who has attained compassion" (*dayāpanna*) to signify pity (*karuṇā*)?
This is true; however, this word *dayā* here includes within its scope the sense of protection (*anurakkhaṇa*).

When it occurs, it occurs as loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*); here, it is stated as occurring through loving-kindness. It is called *mettā* because one is softened (*midati*) and moistened (*siniyhati*).
That which possesses this loving-kindness is *mettaṃ*. One who has a mind of loving-kindness is *mettacitto*;
the state of being such is *mettacittatā*, which simply means loving-kindness. By the phrase "compassionate and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings,"...
He shows the boundlessness of that abstinence by way of its sevenfold nature. "Toward living beings" means toward those born as living beings.
"Compassionate" means one who feels compassion. Since loving-kindness (*mettā*) is a specific condition for compassion (*karuṇā*), it is therefore said:
"by that very state of being moved by pity. Thus, by those factors through which the abstinence from taking life is accomplished—namely, shame (*lajjā*), loving-kindness, and compassion—

The state of being endowed [with these qualities] has been shown. "He dwells" (viharatī) means that, having become thus, he carries on and maintains his existence by interrupting the suffering arisen in one posture with another posture;
or, the meaning is that he sustains his personal existence (attabhāva). For this very reason it is said:
"He moves about (iriyati), he maintains (yapeti), he sustains (yāpeti), he protects (pāleti)."
"Merely the virtue of conduct" means merely the virtue consisting in the conduct of virtuous people;

by this, he shows that even through qualities such as restraint of the sense faculties, an ordinary worldling is unable to speak in praise of the Tathāgata. For it is the case that restraint of the sense faculties, the virtue regarding the use of requisites, and so forth, are not analyzed here in this discourse on virtue.
"Taking away from another" means seizing what belongs to another. A "thief" (theno) is called a robber; the state of being such is "theft" (theyya).
Here too, it is less blameworthy when the property belonging to another is small, and more blameworthy when it is large. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort involved.
However, when the qualities of the object are equal, it is less blameworthy due to the mildness of the defilements and the methods employed.
This method should also be applied to the phrase "extremely blameworthy for a woman.

Regarding the terms "by means of one's own hand" and so forth: here, taking what belongs to another by means of reciting mantras is the "magical" (*vijjāmaya*) application; drawing away what belongs to another through physical or verbal effort without mantras, by means of such a power of accomplishment, is the "supernormal" (*iddhimaya*) application.
The remainder refers to passages such as "having abandoned, he abstains," and so on, for that follows the method already explained previously. Although this is not [explicitly] mentioned here...
By the conventional usage of the term *sikkhāpada*, abstention (*virati*) is expressed;

however, in other scriptural passages, as well as in the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, both abstention and volition (*cetanā*) are referred to by the conventional usage of the term *sikkhāpada*. This is because they serve as the basis for the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and so forth, and because they constitute one of its constituent parts.
Therefore, he says "in the first *sikkhāpada*. In this context, [the word] "one who has a sense of shame" (*lajjī*)— [...]*
It is not explicitly stated that he was "filled with compassion," yet it should be understood that this is already implied by the sense of the context.
For just as shame and the other [virtues] are specific conditions for the abandoning of killing, so too are they for the abandoning of taking what is not given;
therefore, that passage from the Canon should also be cited. This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. Alternatively, [the phrase] "by one who has become pure" [is used].

By this it should be understood that since the possession of moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*), as well as the abandonment of shamelessness (*ahirika*) and so forth, have already been stated, the terms "the conscientious" (*lajjī*) and so on were not mentioned separately.
"Base conduct" (*aseṭṭhacariya*) refers to the conduct of those who are base or inferior, or to conduct that is base, wretched, and lowly; namely, sexual intercourse (*methuna*).
The meaning is as follows: by the phrase "the supreme brahmin conduct," he refers to abstention from sexual intercourse.
By the statement, "One who lives far from sexual intercourse," it is meant that here, O Brahmin, a certain person... [omitted] ...does not indeed engage in the union of the two organs with a woman;
nevertheless, he consents to the woman's being rubbed, massaged, bathed, and kneaded, and he relishes that.
It should be understood that by the passage beginning, “he desires it, and finds satisfaction through it,” the abstention from the seven forms of sexual union is also shown.

Here too, unchastity (*abrahmacariya*) should be construed as the volition arising from the engagement of the body door with the intent to practice unrighteous conduct (*asaddhamma*), which gives rise to the practice of the path with what is not the path;
whereas in the case of sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*), it is the volition that transgresses against places that should not be approached.

In this context, "unapproachable women" refers to twenty types of women: ten protected by their mothers and so forth, and ten who have been purchased with wealth and so forth. Regarding men, there are twelve types other than those [twenty]: the ten [protected women] such as those purchased with wealth, and the two who are protected and subject to punishment.
Misconduct with one devoid of virtues is of slight blame; with one of great virtue, it is of great blame.

Furthermore, it should be understood that even when [the partner] lacks virtues, the occurrence [of the act] after having overcome her is a great offense; whereas, even if both have the same desire, it is a minor offense due to the mildness of the defilements and the effort involved, but a great offense due to their intensity.
Its two constituent factors are the mind desiring to engage in sexual intercourse and the practice of the path where there is no path.
In the case of sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*), however, it consists in approaching a place that is not to be approached.
There are four [factors]: the mind of service, sexual intercourse with one who is not one’s own wife, consenting, and so forth.

They say: "In the case of transgression after having overcome [the woman's resistance], because there is no prior intention or effort for service, there is no wrong conduct on the part of the one being overcome.
However, when the mind of service is present, the absence of effort is not a valid criterion, given that there is effort for service toward a woman.

Because [such a case] generally does not exist, it follows that even for a woman who has previously aroused the intention to engage in sexual intercourse, there would be no sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*), due to the absence of the actual effort (*payoga*).
Therefore, it should be understood that at most four [offenses] are stated by way of the man;
otherwise, when a woman performs the function of a man, there would likewise be no sexual misconduct for the man, because of the absence of his own effort to engage in intercourse.

"Some say it would not be [an offense]. However, the definitive conclusion here is this: there are three cases for what is done by one's own preference, three for what is done by force, and four when including all instances without exception. One modality is that which is performed by one's own hand alone.
To show that it has reached the level of a full course of action (*kammappatha*), it is stated as "one who destroys welfare. This refers to either vocal modality or bodily modality.
This demonstrates that the word *musā* (falsehood) has action as its primary referent. It refers to the intention to deceive both at the preceding moment and at the actual moment [of speaking].
For it is said: "First he thinks, 'I will speak falsely,' and while speaking, he thinks, 'I am speaking falsely. These two [thoughts] constitute the essential factors (*aṅga*);
as for the other [the actual utterance], whether it occurs or not is irrelevant—it is no cause [for the offense]. *Assa* means "of the one who deceives."
False speech (*musāvāda*) is the volition (*cetanā*) by which one speaks, makes known, or brings forth that which is false as previously described in its application.

In the previous method, because the definition was not all-encompassing and because the word *musa* could possibly denote something other than what is to be contradicted, the definition of false speech is shown in its full form by the passage beginning: "‘Musa’ means an unreal, untrue matter."
The second method is commenced. And in this method, it is said that lying is spoken by means of this; thus, volition is lying.
By the phrase "that which destroys the purpose," he explains the slight blameworthiness and great blameworthiness of lying by way of the object.
It is slightly blameworthy when the person whose purpose is destroyed has few virtues, and greatly blameworthy when they have great virtues. [This same principle applies] to taking what is not given.
It should also be applied by way of its qualities (*guṇa*). Lightness and heaviness of offense are indeed found even by way of the mildness or intensity of the defilements (*kilesa*).
False speech (*musāvāda*) consists precisely in the intention to deceive, whether through unwillingness to give what belongs to oneself or through the method of Pūraṇa’s discourse;
however, because the volition (*cetanā*) therein is not powerful, it is described as being of light offense. [This applies to] a deficient matter due to its smallness...
“Pūraṇakathā” means a discourse proceeding by way of filling out;
it is so called because it is of that nature, meaning it conforms to deception. By the term “effort” (vāyāma), he refers to the preparatory application (payoga) under the heading of effort.
For even if an application is made with the intention of deceiving, deception is not accomplished if the other person does not understand that meaning.

The other's comprehension of that meaning is stated to be one constituent. However, some say there are three constituents: "a false statement, a mind intent on deception, and the other's comprehension of that meaning.
One is bound by the kamma of lying at the very moment of the volition that originates the action, because it is produced by the decisive volition; even if, due to slowness, one deliberates [further].
The intention is that another person knows that meaning.
In expressions such as “saccato thetato,” the word *theta* is a synonym for firmness; and since this state of firmness is predicated upon truthful speech, it should be understood by way of discourse.
Thus he says: “the meaning is ‘one of firm discourse. One who does not have firm discourse is—as follows:”
Yellow dye and the like are not stable because their intrinsic nature is unstable; likewise, one whose discourse is not stable is called "one of unstable discourse.
Just as yellow dye and the like serve as a simile for discourse, it should be applied in this way.
This same method applies to the expressions "like a line on stone" and so forth.
"Saddhāyo" means that which comes (āyati) and proceeds (pavattati) therein; thus they are "saddhāyo. "Saddhāyiko" is simply "saddhāyo," just as in the term "venayiko.

Alternatively, "saddhāyiko" means that which is to be approached (āyitabbo) by means of faith (saddhāya); the meaning is "one who is to be believed. The intention is that he incurs the state of being blameworthy due to his deceptive nature.
"Suññabhāvaṃ" refers to emptiness (rittataṃ) because of the absence of joy (pīti). "That is malicious speech" (sā pisuṇavācā) refers to this aforementioned nature of sound.

By the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), it explains the meaning as "malicious speech" (*pisuṇavācā*) because it creates a void of affection through speech. Alternatively, it is "malicious" (*pisuṇā*) because it splits;
the meaning is that it causes beings who are in harmony to become divided into separate factions.
It is "harsh" (*pharusa*) because of its lack of affection; it is also harsh by its very nature, since it originates from mental distress (*domanassa*).

Harsh. And here, the application of the term "harsh" (*pharusa*) to speech should be understood through the metaphorical transfer of the quality to the action—namely, "it makes harsh" (*pharusaṃ karoti*)—or by way of the verbal root *pharusayati*.

Furthermore, the application of the term "harsh" to speech should be seen as referring to its intrinsic nature of being absolutely cruel due to its cutting into the vital points of others, and also by way of the figurative expression for its cause, namely, that it itself is harsh. For this very reason:
It is neither pleasant to the ear; because it is devoid of meaning, it does not reach the heart.

"By which one prattles nonsense" (*samphaṃ palapati*): by means of that useless speech known as "palāpa," which bears no fruit of pleasure or welfare, but rather scatters, destroys, and ruins—therefore given the name *sampha*—one prattles whatever is of no benefit to oneself or others.
"Of one with a defiled mind" means one whose mind is afflicted by greed or hatred, or whose mind is tormented;
the sense is that it is a mind that has been corrupted. "Cetanā pisuṇavācā" means that by means of this, they speak divisively. Regarding the gravity of the offense:

when one causes a division between those who were not yet divided, the offense is slight; when they are already divided, the offense is grave. The same applies according to the specific degree of mildness or intensity of the underlying defilements.

Whether the one to whom he conveys the slander breaks apart or not, the mere communication of that matter is the criterion; thus it is said, "the understanding of its meaning. However, the actual transgression of the course of action (*kamma-patha*) occurs only when [the relationship] has been broken.
"Anuppadātā" means a provider of support, or one who provides by way of following along. To what does this following and providing refer?
Since it is stated, "of those who are united," it is understood to mean "of the reconciliation. For this very reason, it says, "one who does not provide for the reconciliation."
However, because the placing down or the protection—that is, the strengthening—of the steps occurs by way of following along, it is said:
"the meaning is 'to perform the act of strengthening'. It is called an *ārāma* because they delight (*āramanti*) therein; it is a place for taking pleasure.
Since this same meaning is obtained even without the prefix *ā*, it is therefore said: "The Pāḷi reading is also *samaggarāmo*."
“This is precisely the meaning here.
“Vital points (mamma) like vital points”: when even those parts of the body that are merely touched by harsh speech—as if struck by a poisoned arrow—the mind experiences excessive suffering.
What, then, are they? They are the bases for abuse, such as birth and so forth. These...
That bodily or vocal application by which things are cut or broken is "marmacchedaka" (wound-cutting).
It is called *pharusavācā* (harsh speech) because one speaks harshly through an exclusively harsh volition (*ekantena pharusacetanā*). But how does it become an exclusively harsh volition?

Through a corrupt state of mind (*duṭṭhacittatā*). "Of that" refers to the very existence of harsh speech through an exclusively harsh volition. It is "wound-cutting" due to the harshness of its sound when heard.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Due to gentleness of mind, harsh speech does not exist because it has not reached the state of a path of action (*kamma-patha*);

however, its status as a *kamma* cannot be denied. Having thus established harsh speech through the method of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of the harshness of volition (*cetanā*), he now says "by gentleness of speech" and so forth, in order to establish that same point by way of its opposite (*paṭipakkha-naya*). That is harsh speech. As for "which":
Regarding the person: here too, when the action has not yet reached the status of a full course of kamma (*kammappatha*), it is less blameworthy;
otherwise, it is more blameworthy. The same applies to the mildness or intensity of the underlying defilements (*kilesa*). Some, however, say:

"The head [of the offense] falls upon the person in whose presence harsh speech is employed"; others say: "Harsh speech remains blameworthy even when spoken in the absence of the person. In this regard, the intended meaning is as follows:

It may be appropriate [to say this]: because those who speak without respect when face-to-face possess a powerful state of mind, their volition (*cetanā*) is strong, as is the other person’s awareness of that intent; it is not so when they are not face-to-face.
However, just as an apology made at the funeral pyre for one who has been insulted and is dead prevents the obstacle of further reproach, so too can it be said:
"Even harsh speech employed in the absence of another is indeed [harsh speech]."
"Having understood": "An angry mind" means a mind that is angry specifically with the intention of reviling, not with the intention of killing;
for when the mind is agitated with the intention of killing, it is simply ill will (*vyāpāda*). "In this case"—[referring to the verse]:
"The chariot with faultless parts, white canopy, and single wheel rolls on."
"Behold him coming, free from distress, with the stream cut off and unbound"—this refers to this verse.
Herein, "faultless-limbed" (*nelaṅga*) is said to mean virtue (*sīla*). For this very reason, the householder Citta said:
"Venerable sir, 'faultless-limbed' is a designation for virtues. "Delicate" means soft due to lack of harshness. "From before" (*purassa*)...
