Here, the word *pura* (city) should be understood as denoting the inhabitants of that city, just as in expressions such as "the village has arrived. For this very reason, he says "of the city-dwellers.
That which nourishes and increases the mind (*mano*) is *manāpā*. Therefore it is said: "causing the increase of the mind. *Āsevanā* means cultivation and frequent practice. Regarding the offense:
it is a minor offense when committed toward one who has not been made to accept [the teaching], and a major offense when committed toward one who has been made to accept it.
Here too, the degree of slight or grave offense is indeed obtained according to the mildness or intensity of the defilements.
The phrase beginning with "speaking at the proper time" (*kālavādī*) demonstrates the practice of one who abstains from idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*).

For just as the phrase "abstaining from taking life" (*pāṇātipātā paṭivirato*) demonstrates the practice of abandoning the taking of life, so too [the former phrase] shows the practice of one who, having abandoned the taking of life, dwells [therein].
When this has been said, [one asks]: "How does the abandoning of the destruction of life come about? Because of the absence of longing, it is said:
"He abstains from the destruction of life. But how is that abstinence? He says: "One who has laid aside the rod, one who has laid aside the weapon.
And how is that laying aside of the rod and the weapon? It is said: "One who is possessed of shame," and so forth. Thus, there is a demonstration of each subsequent means for each preceding one.
In the same way, this should be applied to taking what is not given and so forth, as appropriate. Therefore it was said:

“‘Speaking at the proper time,’ etc., shows the practice of one who abstains from idle chatter. For even speech endowed with meaning may fail to bring about that benefit if employed at an inappropriate time;
thus, it conforms to speech that conveys what is disadvantageous. Consequently, by one who abandons idle chatter, speaking at the wrong time must be avoided.
"It should be avoided" refers to what was stated as "speaking at the proper time. Even when speaking at the proper time, one must avoid what is untrue because it accomplishes both kinds of harm;

thus he said, "speaking what is true. And to show that even when speaking what is true, one should speak only that which brings about welfare in this world and the next, he said, "speaking what is beneficial.
Furthermore, even when speaking what is beneficial, one should not speak only that which is dependent on worldly matters.
It should be said; however, in order to show the rapture (*pīti*) based on the supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttaradhamma*), it is stated, "one who speaks the Dhamma" (*dhammavādī*).
And in order to show how that meaning is based on the supramundane Dhamma, it is stated, "one who speaks the Vinaya" (*vinayavādī*).
For [the Vinaya] consists of the fivefold restraint: restraint by the *Pātimokkha*, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy.
When its meaning is explained by way of the five types of discipline— namely, discipline as restraint,

discipline as removal by means of its factors, discipline as suppression, discipline as eradication, and discipline as tranquilization— it is based on supramundane states because it serves as the cause for the attainment of Nibbāna.
To show that a subject endowed with such specific qualities shines when being taught, provided there is skill in teaching, and that it becomes effective for its purpose and not otherwise, it is said:
"He spoke words that were well-founded. Now, in order to clarify that skill in teaching, he says "At the proper time," and so forth.

[This refers to] when the scope of the teaching has been entered upon by way of the listener's disposition (*ajjhāsaya*), the occasion for the arising [of the discourse] (*ṭhuppatti*), and the question (*pucchā*).
Having discerned the distinctions between categorical and other types of answers, one who— through a teaching that is limited and well-defined in form, yet which encompasses a vast, profound, noble,

and abundant expansion of meaning— clarifies the setting aside (*ṭhapanā*), the reasons (*hetu*), the examples (*dāharaṇa*), and the connections (*saṃsandanā*) according to the requirements of each occasion,
establishes others in the attainment of the ultimate truth (*paramattha-siddhi*) according to their respective inclinations, is called "skilled in teaching" (*desanā-kusala*).
In this way, the application of the meaning here should be understood.
Having thus analyzed the seven fundamental training rules (mūla-sikkhāpada) in their proper sequence,

although the abandonment of covetousness and so forth is included within the training of the virtue of restraint (saṃvara-sīla), [the subsequent section] is taught as a "higher teaching" (uttara-desanā) because it comprises further qualities and because it lies beyond the sphere of ordinary worldlings (puthujjana).

Setting aside that [view] for the sake of gathering [the disciples], and analyzing only the conduct and virtue well-known among the common people, the Blessed One said: "From the destruction of seeds and the destruction of living plants," and so forth.
In this context, *gāma* means a collection (*samūha*). Now, are not trees and such things not living beings (*jīva*) because they lack consciousness?

And are they not devoid of consciousness because they lack movement, because they grow back when cut, because they belong to a different species, and because they are not included within the four modes of birth (*yoni*)?
Furthermore, growth is found even in coral, stones, and salt; therefore, these are not reasons for their being considered living beings.
And the apprehension of objects is merely a mental construction, like the dreaming of *ciñcā* trees and the like; the same applies to pregnancy-longings (*dohala*) and so forth.

Why, then, is it desired that one abstain from injuring seed-life and the community of living beings? Because it is befitting for a recluse (*samaṇa*), and because it protects the sentient beings dependent upon them.
For this very reason, he said: “For people, O foolish men, perceive a living being in a tree,” and so forth.
“Of blue grass, trees, and so on” means of fresh grass as well as fresh trees and the like. By the word “and so on” (ādi), medicinal herbs, shrubs, creepers, and so forth are to be understood.
“One meal” is *ekabhatta*; one who has that is an *ekabhattika*—one who eats only once in a single day.
"One who eats. Since this might include eating at night, he said "one who abstains from the night" (*rattūparato*) in order to exclude that.

Furthermore, since one who eats after midday might also be considered "one who eats but once," he stated "one who refrains from eating at the improper time" (*virato vikālabhojanā*) in order to dispel that suspicion.
From the rising of the dawn until midday—this is the practice consistently observed by the Buddhas.

The "proper time for eating" (bhojana-kāla) is that [time]; any other time is "the wrong time" (vikāla). However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), because eating at night is prohibited by the second phrase, the afternoon is called "the wrong time.
In brief, the Blessed One’s teaching, which proceeds according to the method beginning with "the non-doing of all evil," [is so called] because it proceeds from absolute desire and passion.
He said, "Because it is not in conformity with the Teaching," meaning that watching dancing and so forth does not accord with the Sāsana.
Dancing performed by oneself and dancing caused to be performed by others are both included under the single term *nacca* in the Canon due to their commonality as dancing;
likewise for the terms *gīta* (song) and *vādita* (instrumental music). Thus he said, "by way of dancing, causing to dance, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...
It includes singing, causing others to sing, playing instruments, and causing others to play instruments.

Here, hearing is also included under "seeing" by way of the grammatical principle of "residual unity despite diversity. Alternatively, because the five types of consciousness have the nature of looking (ālocana), even the act of hearing is subsumed under the category of "seeing";
thus, it is simply called "seeing. He says "unpleasant" (*visūkabhūtā*) because the hearing of music that has become unpleasant is sometimes permitted.
"...for the sake of seeing. For thus it is said in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*:
"In this context, singing that is connected with the Dhamma is permissible, but the Dhamma that is connected with singing is not permissible.
*Uccā* is another word having the same meaning as the word *ucca*. *Sayanaṃ* means "that wherein one lies. *Uccāsayanaṃ* [means] a high bed.
And since a "great bed" (mahāsayana) is intended here as that which is devoid of suitability for a recluse, it is said: "exceeding the proper measure, with an unsuitable covering.
Furthermore, in this context, chairs and other such seats should be understood as being included under the term "bed" (sayana).

However, because when the physical basis (the seat) is prohibited, the action supported by that basis is already prohibited, it is therefore stated simply as "high beds and great beds" (uccāsayanamahāsayanā); [this is] in terms of the actual meaning.
However, it should be understood that the abstention from sitting and lying down—which constitute the enjoyment of those [luxuries]—is also shown here.

Alternatively, this expression "high beds and large beds" (uccāsayana-mahāsayana) is formed by the method of single-remainder (ekasesa-naya) for the sake of this meaning, just as in the formula "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases.
Since the act of lying down precedes the act of sitting, it should be understood that the seat is included by the mention of the bed itself.

He said, "He does not cause [it] to be taken up, nor does he accept what has been set aside," because the meaning of "acceptance" (paṭiggahaṇa) is found in both causing others to take it up and in accepting what has been placed near.
Alternatively, acceptance is threefold: by body, by speech, and by mind.
Among these, acceptance by body is taking up; acceptance by speech is causing to be taken up; and acceptance by mind is...

Regarding the phrase "accepting" (*sādiyananti*), it is stated as "acceptance" (*paṭiggahaṇā*) by taking all three types of acceptance through a general designation or by the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*).
Thus he says, "he does not accept it," and so forth. This same method applies to the phrases "acceptance of raw grain" (*āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇā*) and the rest.
Because secondary grains such as *nīvāra* are included within the primary grains such as *sāli*, it is said, "of the sevenfold [grain]. "I allow..."

Because it was said, "Monks, there are five kinds of fat as medicine: the fat of a catfish, the fat of a fish, the fat of a crocodile, the fat of a pig, and the fat of a donkey," this is called what is specifically permitted (*odissa-anuññāta*).
However, since it was further stated that "it must be accepted at the proper time," receiving it is allowable; thus he said, "except for what is specifically permitted."
"Akkamati" means to press down. The connection is with "presses down in the prior stage. "Hṛdaya" refers to the interior of measuring vessels such as the *nāḷi* and so forth.
At the time of measuring sesame seeds and other substances with the *nāḷi* and so forth, the peak that has been raised up is itself the "peak"; its "breaking" is its reduction.
"Some" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa* and those residing at Uttaravihāra.
"Killing" (*vadha*) means harming by means of blows with the fist, striking with the palm, and so forth; the meaning is "afflicting.
Indeed, the word *vadha* is seen to have the sense of "afflicting" in such passages as "having killed oneself again and again.

Just as, although there is a commonality in the state of not being accepted [as gifts], [the Buddha] specified certain items that must not be accepted by those who have gone forth—such as women, boys, female slaves, male slaves, and so on—in order to demonstrate those specific objects.

They are stated separately because, although they share the common nature of taking what is not given due to the fact that another's property is being taken, weights and measures are stated separately for the purpose of showing them as specific instances of taking what is not given.

However, there is no such purpose in restating killing—which is already included in the category of the destruction of life—by saying, "In that case it was done by oneself; here it is done by another. Nor is it the case that...
It could be argued that "volition which originates bodily and vocal application is the sixfold application," because this has been stated;

therefore, the meaning as previously explained is indeed more excellent. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said, "killing (*vadha*) means slaying (*māraṇa*)," and this too can be understood as referring specifically to striking (*pothana*), since the word "slaying" is seen to be used even for the sense of harming (*vihiṃsana*).
“By this much” means by the extent of the text beginning with “having abandoned the taking of life,” and so on, up to “abstaining from cutting... [and] from violence.

It is called the *Cūḷasīla* (Minor Code of Conduct) because it comprises twenty-six training rules (*sikkhāpada*) without including the intermediate divisions, as most of the training rules are not analyzed in the manner they appear in the Canon. For here, the status of being “minor,” “middling,” and so forth, is determined according to the method of teaching.
This is intended by way of the persons [concerned], not by way of the rules themselves.

For here, the teaching on the intermediate morality proceeds by way of analyzing the training rules that were briefly listed and not yet analyzed. Therefore he said, "expounding the intermediate morality.
The commentary on the Minor Morality is concluded.
The Explanation of the Middle Virtues (Majjhimasīlavaṇṇanā) 11.
In this context, *yathā* is a particle used in the sense of a simile. *Vā* is used in the sense of an alternative. *Panā* is a poetic embellishment (*vacanālaṅkāra*). *Eke* means "others.
*Bhonto* is a respectful address used by virtuous people; for the virtuous address others as "venerable ones" (*bhonto*) or "those dear to the gods" (*devānaṃ piyā*).
Or they address them as "Venerable Sirs. This refers to anyone who has entered the homeless life as a recluse (*śramaṇa*).

They are called "Brahmins" merely by virtue of their birth. This is what is meant: even an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), while speaking in praise of me with enthusiasm, might do so either by way of instruction to others—saying, for example, "Having abandoned the taking of life, he abstains from the taking of life"—or in the manner of some venerable recluses and Brahmins who [claim] the state of being a recluse or a Brahmin.
While they claim [to be such], others perceive them as such; yet because they do not know the practice corresponding to that [claim] and lack the capacity for it, they fail to achieve it.

Thinking, "This one is not so, but this ascetic Gotama fulfills the practice appropriate to an ascetic in every respect," they would thus describe him by way of a specific distinction, saying he possesses only conduct and virtue in every respect, and nothing beyond that.

In the phrase "the undertaking of the seed-creatures and the creatures of the soil," although the seed-creatures and the creatures of the soil are subordinate according to the sequence of the words (*saddakkama*), they attain a state of prominence because they are what must be demonstrated.
For the sequence of words is one thing, and the sequence of meaning (*atthakkama*) is another; thus he asks, "What is that seed-creatures and creatures of the soil?
For when that [seed-creatures and creatures of the soil] is analyzed, the undertaking, by virtue of having them as its object, is also thereby analyzed. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Root-seed,” and so forth. A root that is itself the seed is a “root-seed” (*mūlabīja*); or, that of which the root is the seed is also a “root-seed.
The same method applies to the others as well. “Fibre-seed” (*phaḷubīja*) means a bark-seed.

The word “seed” (*bīja*), being conventionally established for a hard fruit capable of sprouting due to its specific causal efficacy in producing a similar fruit when combined with other conditions, is used here by extension for certain roots and so forth because it fulfills that same purpose.

It is stated as "seed-seed" (*bījabīja*) by qualifying it with one word "seed" (*bīja*) for the purpose of excluding [the seed] from that which grows from a root and so forth, just as in the cases of "form-form" (*rūparūpa*) and "suffering-suffering" (*dukkhadukkha*).
But why, after asking about both the seed-aggregate and the aggregate of living beings, is only the seed-aggregate analyzed here?
It should not be viewed in this way. Have we not already said: "The root itself..."?
“Seed” (*bīja*) means “root-seed” (*mūlabīja*); it is also called “root-seed” because its root is the seed. Herein, by the first [explanation], the category of seeds (*bījagāma*) is indicated;

by the second, the category of living beings (*bhūtagāma*). This twofold division should be understood as indicated in the Canon through a general designation (*sāmaññaniddesa*), or by the method of single remainder (*ekasesanaya*), as in “root-seed and root-seed” being termed simply “root-seed. Therefore, he said: “All this,” and so forth.

12. Regarding the phrase “of what has been stored up” (*sannidhikatassa*), this demonstrates that in the expression “enjoyment of what has been stored up” (*sannidhikāraparibhoga*), the word *kāra* carries the sense of the object (*kamma*).

Alternatively, just as when one ought to say “leading to accumulation” (*ācayaṃgamino*), the designation “leading to accumulation” (*ācayagāmino*) is made by eliding the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*), so too, when one ought to say “enjoyment of what has been stored up” (*sannidhikāraṃ paribhogaṃ*), it is called “enjoyment of what has been stored up” (*sannidhikāraparibhogaṃ*) by eliding the nasal vowel.
It is said; the meaning is "enjoyment after having made a store.

It is *sallekha* because it scrapes away (*likhati*) defilements thoroughly; this is practice according to the method of the Suttas. It is *pariyāya* because it is traversed (*pariyāyati*) or fashioned (*kappīyati*);
this is practice according to the sequence of allowable speech (*kappiya-vācā*). It is *āmisa* because it can be touched by defilements; whatever...

An object worthy of enjoyment. For this very reason, it says: "‘Material goods’ refers to what remains after [the aforementioned]. This is a demonstration of the method regarding the objects of hoarding.
"In water and mud" means in both water and mud. "Sit down" means sit. "Stretching the neck" means having stretched the neck;
the meaning is that it is just as one's neck must be stretched due to overeating after a meal. "The measure of a fourth part" means...
"A measure of a *kuḍuba*. The phrase "in a kitchen" (*kappiyakuṭiyam*) and so forth is stated according to the Vinaya.
13. "Even this much" refers even to the description of the basis for investigating the analysis [of the text]. "Merely the purpose" means merely the application of the meaning of the words.
However, in the case of a word whose meaning cannot be understood without an extensive commentary, there is also an extensive commentary.

It is included under the heading of "footings" (*padattha*). It is called *pekkhā* because it is to be viewed out of curiosity; it is the performance of actors according to the rules of the dramatic arts (*naṭasattha*).
However, it is termed "actor’s festival" (*naṭasamajja*) by way of instrumentality, referring to the assembly of people [gathered] by means of the assembly of actors.
In the *Sārasamāsa*, it is called "the great spectacle" (*pekkhamaha*). What is known as a "solid drum" (*ghanatāḷa*) is a drum made of wood, or a drum made of stone or bamboo.
"Or: 'Some' refers to the masters of the Sārasamāsa and those who dwell in the Uttaravihāra. And as it is here, so it is in all subsequent places where 'some' occurs.

A 'four-cornered tambourine' (*caturassa-ambaṇaka-tāḷa*) is a musical instrument made by fashioning a four-cornered frame from any kind of heartwood such as a staff, and then binding it with leather on all four sides. *Abbhokkiraṇa* (strewing)."

“Coloring the strength” (*raṅgabalīkaraṇaṃ*) refers to that which is called “delight” (*nandī*). “Making beautiful” (*sobhanakaraṇaṃ*) means the act of beautifying; it is stated in the *Sārasamāsa* as “the house of beauty” (*sobhanagharakaṃ*).
“This belongs to the Caṇḍālas” (*caṇḍālānamidaṃ*) means it is for the Caṇḍālas. “Washing the hemp” (*sāṇadhovanaṃ*) is the sport of wetting hemp with water and beating it against one another.
“By means of the Indra-net” (*indajālena*) means having recited the bone-washing charm (*aṭṭhidhovanamantaṃ*), so that others [perceive] only bones.

They see it thus through the illusion of making the nails and so forth disappear. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the wagon-array and so forth," one includes the wheel-array, the lotus-array, the stalk-array, and others.
14. "Footprints" (*padāni*) refers to the places where the pieces (*sārī*) are established. What is called "ten-footed" (*dasapada*) is a game played with twenty pieces arranged in two rows.
A "die" (*pāsaka*) is said to be a game made by showing one to six spots on each of its six sides.

Having increased that [number], they play by removing and replacing the *sāris* (counters) according to what has been obtained, starting from one and so forth. Some say that "playing with a jar" (*ghaṭikā*) refers to this.
Others say that "the hand of sticks" (*salākahattha*) refers to taking a single stick that lacks distinction among many sticks, inserting it back among them, and then drawing it out again.
A tube made of leaves in the shape of a bamboo is called a *nāḷikā*. For this very reason, he said:
“‘Blowing that’: some say that *akkharikā* is a game for knowing gain and loss, etc., by taking the syllables that come from the mouth of one who asks while his breath is lost.
Others say it is dancing or singing in accordance with the musical instrument, according to the fault.
[It is so called] because of performing the practice while placing victory or defeat before oneself, thinking, ‘If it is done thus, there will be victory; otherwise, there will be defeat.’”

It should be understood that even the paths of retreat and so forth constitute grounds for gambling and negligence. It should also be seen that the application of bamboo and other materials—such as those used for making *paṅgacīra* (dice)—is said to bring about the accomplishment or failure of tasks, as well as victory or defeat.

Furthermore, the phrase "according to the fault" (*yathāvajja*) refers to the state of playing dice by way of victory or defeat through the display of similarities in form, such as being one-eyed and so on.
15. "Fur-bearing forms" (*vāḷarūpāni*) refers to these very fur-bearing forms. "A *pallaṅka* is indeed an improper bed," according to the *Sārasamāsa*.

"Variegated by weaving" (*vānavicitraṃ*) means variegated by weaving in the manner of wall-coverings and so forth. Regarding the three types of cotton: [there are] cotton from trees, cotton from creepers, and cotton from silkworms.
"Some say it is *uddalomi*" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa* and the residents of the Uttaravihāra. Likewise for *ekantalomi*.
“Made of silk and *kaṭṭissa* cloth” means made of silk and *kaṭṭissa* cloth. “Pure silk” means devoid of any stitching with jewels.
By the phrase “except for a mattress,” it is indicated that even a mattress devoid of stitching with jewels is not permitted.
By the phrase “stitched with jewels,” those which are stitched with jewels [are prohibited] by way of being floor coverings.
It is indicated that it is appropriate to place [the items] on beds, stools, and so forth, according to their suitability. "With antelope skins" means with the skins of the ajina deer.
It is said that those skins are fine; therefore, they are sewn together after making them into double or triple layers. Hence it is called "an antelope-skin rug.
"In the manner stated" means in the manner stated in the Vinaya.
16. It is merely an ornament and ointment, not a medicine, because it is intended for the pursuit of adornment. The word *mālā* is established in the Teaching as referring even to simple flowers;
thus he says, “or a woven garland. *Mṛttikākalka* refers to a medicinal paste (*yoga-mṛttikākalka*) prepared with medicinal herbs.
*Calita* means agitated or provoked. *Lohite sannisinne* means when the vitiated blood has subsided.
17. It is called *niyyāna* because one goes forth from it, namely from misfortune and from *saṃsāra*; thus it is the path to heaven and the path to liberation.
That which is worthy of that *niyyāna*, or that which is devoted to the *niyyāna*, or that which possesses the *niyyāna* as its fruit, is *niyyānika*.
Alternatively, it is *niyyātika*, meaning "it goes forth from the defilement of verbal misconduct"; here the long vowel *ī* is shortened, and the letter *y* is changed to *k*.
Having made [it so], it is leading-out; the abstention from frivolous chatter together with volition. By contrast, that which is not leading-out is its opposite;
the state of being that is "non-leading-out-ness" (*aniyyānikatta*); therefore, because of that non-leading-out-ness. "Become horizontal" means become a screen.
"In the cultivation of the meditation subject" means in the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Truths associated with impermanence. "Together with the goal" (*saha atthena*).
“Meaningful” means connected with welfare. “Street” refers to a residential area;
by the mention of the street, its inhabitants are included, just as in expressions such as “the village has arrived. For this very reason, he says, “brave and capable,” and “faithful and confident.
By way of referring to the water-jars, the female water-carriers are meant; thus he says, “or the talk about the female water-carriers.”
It is called "an exposition of the world" (*lokakkhāyikā*) because it explains the world by way of its arising, its persistence, its requisites, and so forth.
18. "Connected" (*sahita*) means not contradictory in its preceding and succeeding parts. 19.
"Duty of an envoy" (*dūteyya*) is the work of a messenger; the discourse concerning that is "discourse on the duty of an envoy" (*dūteyyakathā*).

20. "In three ways" means by way of the three types: whispering in the presence of others (*sāmantajappana*), depending on deportment (*iriyāpatha*), and making use of requisites (*paccayapaṭisevana*).
"Causing wonder" means producing in others the thought regarding oneself, "Oh, what a marvelous person!
"Flattering" means speaking by exalting oneself or the donor in such a way that one incites them to give something, having thus made a request. By means of a sign (*nimitta*).
They move about, or they give signs, thus they are "sign-givers" (*nemittika*); "sign" (*nimitta*) refers to bodily and verbal action that causes others to perceive it as an offering of requisites.
They squeeze out, thus they are "squeezers" (*nippesa*); those who are precisely squeezers are "squeezers-by-trickery" (*nippesika*).
"Squeeze" (*nippesa*) refers to such things as reviling, censuring, mocking, and backbiting, like a rogue man, for the sake of gain and honor.
The commentary on the medium virtue is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the great virtue:
because it proceeds by way of the factors (*aṅga*), the teaching associated with those factors is called "factors" (*aṅga*). As for the "sign" (*nimitta*):

The same principle applies here as well. Some, however, say that "a limb" means a "deformation of a limb," for even by seeing a deformation of another's limbs, one knows gain, loss, and so forth. "Paṇḍu-rāja" refers to the sovereign of Dakkhiṇāpatha.
By the word "great," he shows that a small sign is a "sign," whereas a great sign is an "omen" (*uppāda*). "He sees such-and-such" refers to one who [sees] a bull or an elephant.
"One sees oneself in a dream as having ascended a palace or a mountain; such is the fruit for him"—this is what is meant by "dream" (*supinaka*), namely the science of dreams (*supinasattha*).
By the term "limbs" (*aṅga*), the indication [of fortune] is stated merely through the observation of the presence or absence of bodily parts;
however, by the term "characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa*), it is stated through the demonstration of specific bodily characteristics that produce great majesty.

"This is their distinction. "New" (*ahata*) means fresh. "From this point on" refers to the fact that when various portions of cloth—distinguished by being from gods, *rakkhasas*, humans, and so forth—are torn here or there, such specific results as enjoyment and the like arise.
The *dabbi-homa* and others are presented by way of showing the distinction in fruits resulting from specific implements and other factors of the sacrifice.
*Aggi-homa* is the sacrifice performed by way of the remaining means already mentioned.
*Aṅgalaṭṭhi* means the body. *Abbhinaṃ satthaṃ* means the weapon of thunderbolts. *Māsurakkha* refers to a treatise composed by Māsurakkha;

according to the *Sārasamāsa*, it is the science (*vijjā*) for causing the increase of crops. Regarding "those with wings" (*sapakkhaka*)... up to "four-footed creatures" (*catuppada*): this refers to winged insects such as *piṅgala* flies, wingless creatures such as house-lizards, two-legged beings such as gods, humans, and herons, and four-legged animals such as thorny lizards and jackals.

23. “On such-and-such a day” means stated by way of the lunar date (*tithi*), such as “the second or third of the fortnight. “Under such-and-such a constellation” means by way of conjunction with a constellation such as Rohiṇī.
24. “The falling of meteors” means the falling of meteoric lights. For when masses of wind strike one another with great force, a light arises like the glow of a lamp and falls from the sky;
this is the conventional expression “falling of a meteor” (*ukkāpāta*). “Impurity” refers to [the sky being obscured] by clouds, mist, and so forth.
25. *Dhārānupavecchanaṃ* is raining. A hand-gesture (*hatthamuddā*) is the making known of what is intended by the hand; however, that is indeed counting by means of the contraction of the fingers.
Counting by means of seeds (*navanta*), as practiced by the Persians, the Mlecchas, and others, is "counting with seeds" (*acchiddakagaṇanā*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "producing [the sound] *saṭṭu*, etc.," it includes vocalization, division, calculation, and so on. "By way of reflection" (*cintāvasena*) refers to the object (*vatthuṃ*).
A "thought-poet" (cintākavi) is to be understood as one who, having personally reflected for a long time on a connection (anusandhi), composes [a work] by way of that reflection;
a "heard-poet" (sutakavi) is one who, having heard something, connects what was not previously heard with it and composes [a work] by way of that hearing;

an "meaning-poet" (atthakavi) is one who, having considered some meaning, composes [a work] by way of its condensation, expansion, and so forth; or [one who composes] whatever poem or drama has been created by another.
Having seen that [the other] is indeed similar [to himself], one should be understood as a *paṭibhānakavi* (an improvising poet) by way of acting through spontaneous wit appropriate to the occasion.
26. *Āvāhana* is the taking of a girl in marriage by way of formal acceptance; likewise, *vivāhana* is the giving her away in marriage.
*Payoga* (application) is the employment of goods by way of purchasing them at double or triple the price in another region. Whether there or elsewhere, it is according to the time-limitation.
“Uddhāra” (interest) refers to the purpose consisting in the taking of an increase.

Some say: “The ‘payoga’ (loan) is the giving of wealth with the instruction, ‘Having carried out trade free from the cost of goods, give back the principal together with this much profit’; the ‘uddhāra’ is the lending on a temporary basis.
Regarding the phrase “by three causes”: here, when the embryo perishes due to wind or microorganisms, it is not the case that space was created by previous karma.

Because of that [condition], karma ripens. However, since space is created by karma itself, it should be understood that the statement regarding karma as a distinct cause implies that wind or insects do not necessarily need to be taken into account. "Extinguishing" means making for pacification.
"Counter-measure" means acting in such a way that they do not eat [the crops]. "For the purpose of turning away" means by means of weapons and so forth.
It is for the purpose of turning [the object] by means of lifting up the hand that has already been lifted.
*Kaṇṇajappana* (whispering in the ear) is the muttering of the desired object into the ear of a deity.

*Ādiccapāricariyā* (service to the sun) is the attendance upon the sun by performing worship with *karavīra* garlands and standing facing the sun throughout the entire day. "Calling out 'Sir! (*siravhāyana*).
Some read [the text] as follows: "Having recited the mantra of its meaning, it is the invocation of the desired object with the head.

27. *Samiddhikāla* means at the time of the accomplishment of the requested object. *Santipaṭissavakamma* means the performance of the act of promising—that peace which is to be undertaken through the petitioning of a deity; it is the application of the petition for peace.
Meaning: In that [act], which is the fruit of the promise (*paṭissava*)—namely, the action performed according to one's aspiration, as it was said:
"If this specific thing of mine should succeed"—of that peaceful promise, which is also called "aspiration" (*paṇidhi*).

For when an offering is made in accordance with the promise, the aspiration and the entreaty are fulfilled and delivered. [The phrase] "merely the state of being without desire" (*acchandikabhāvamattaṃ*)...
It refers merely to the state of a woman’s lack of desire. "Sexual organ" (*liṅga*) means the male sexual organ.

"Performing propitiatory rites" is for the purpose of warding off calamities as well as for the purpose of bringing about prosperity. "Of the humors" (*dosānaṃ*) refers to bile and the other humors. And here, "emesis" (*vamana*) is intended in the sense of purging.
"Upper purgative" (*uddhaṃvirecana*) is emesis, because it is described as "the removal of humors from above. Likewise, "purgative" (*virecana*)—

"Purgation" refers specifically to downward purgation (*adhovirecana*). However, because it is stated that "it is the removal of humors from below," the term also includes cleansing procedures such as those using *suddhivatthi*, *sāvatthi*, and so forth.
Head-purgation (*sīsavirecana*) consists of the removal of phlegm (*semha*) and similar treatments. "Films" (*paṭala*) refers to the membranes of the eye.
"The work of the probe-surgeon" (*salākavejjakamma*) refers to ophthalmic surgery; this is mentioned here for the purpose of including all remaining types of surgical treatment (*sālākiya*).
"Should be seen. For even cupping and so forth are indeed part of surgery (*sālākiya*).
"Root medicines" (*mūlabhesajja*) are primary medicines capable of pacifying diseases; or alternatively, they are medicines for root-diseases (*mūla-vyādhi*), thus "root medicines.

Disease is indeed twofold according to its connection with the root. And when the root disease is treated, the other [secondary symptoms] are for the most part pacified. "The treatment of the body..."

The phrase "he shows" is stated by way of elimination (*pārisesavasena*), because specific types of medical practice—such as pediatrics (*komārabhacca*), surgery (*salla-katta*), and osteopathy (*sālākīya*)—have been mentioned here and there; therefore, the inclusion of the remaining types of medical practice should also be understood here.
And all these are intended here solely as being caused by livelihood (*ājīvahetuka*): "by wrong livelihood, one makes a living..."
Because it is stated [in the text], "they fashion. Furthermore, regarding the expression "iti vā" (or thus) that occurs here and there in the Pāḷi:
therein, *iti* is a particle in the sense of manner, and *vā* is in the sense of an alternative. This is what is meant: "in this manner, and not otherwise than this.
By this, those crafts, fields of knowledge, branches of science, and so forth—which are means of livelihood belonging to those who have gone forth outside of this [teaching]—are excluded.
They live off their own livelihoods; thus it should be understood that their possession has been established.
The commentary on the Great Virtue (Mahāsīla) is finished.
The commentary on the eternalist views of those who speculate about the past.
28. "The praise spoken by the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus" refers to the praise expressed beginning with the words, "To such an extent indeed [has this been done] by that Blessed One," and so forth.
Herein, the connection is as follows: "Monks, these alone are not all the qualities of a Buddha that are manifest to you;

however, those that are not manifest have been stated in detail thus: 'There are, monks, other states,' and so on. In that context, it is said: "'These bases of views were grasped in such a way,'" and so forth.
Because it demonstrates the state of emptiness regarding the modes in which the bases for views such as eternalism are grasped;

because it reveals the absence of a permanent essence and so forth by showing that the understanding of those [bases] does not involve misapprehension, and by illustrating how virtue and the other [factors] lead to liberation through non-misapprehension;
and because these fluctuations of views arise in outsiders due to their lack of dispassion toward those feelings in which they remain unliberated.

And because this teaching is primarily intended to reveal emptiness—by way of demonstrating that all phenomena are devoid of selfhood or what belongs to a self through the demonstration that the conditions such as delusion lack the intrinsic nature of an experiencer or an agent, and by way of revealing final Nibbāna without clinging—it is said:
“He undertook the elucidation of emptiness. “Pariyatti” refers to the tradition (tanti) divided into the categories of Vinaya and so forth. “Desanā” [refers to the teaching].

When that lineage has been established by the mind, its "elucidation" (*vibhāvanā*) consists either in the manifestation of phenomena through verbal expression in accordance with their true nature, or in their exposition by way of the "conformable" (*anuloma*) and so forth;
since the distinction between the "scripture" (*pariyatti*) and the "teaching" (*desanā*) was already established previously, he says:

"in the teaching and the scripture. Regarding the phrase "and so forth," the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes such categories as the truths, intrinsic nature, concentration, wisdom, the aggregates, merit, offenses, and the knowable.
They are grouped together. For this word *dhamma* occurs in the sense of truth in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, through not awakening to four things...

(A I 286); in the sense of intrinsic nature in such passages as, "Wholesome states, unwholesome states... (D I 137); in the sense of meditative concentration in such passages as, "Those Blessed Ones were of such a nature" (M II 140);
and in such passages as, "Truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity—he indeed does not grieve after passing away" (Dhp 165).
In such passages as, "Monks, in beings subject to birth, this desire arises," it refers to *pakati* (nature);
in such passages as, "Dharma well-practiced brings happiness," it refers to *puñña* (merit); in such passages as, "The four *pārājika* dharmas," it refers to *āpatti* (offense);
and in such passages as, "All phenomena in all their aspects come within the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One," it refers to... [the term *dhamma*].
It is appropriate to understand it thus: "They are phenomena" means they are empty, being mere phenomena.
By the word "hard to see," the profound depth of those phenomena is revealed.
However, if someone who does not know their own limits should make an effort to plunge into those phenomena with wisdom, that wisdom of theirs will find no foothold at all.
He said, "Like the Makasa-tuṇḍa-needle in the great ocean, it is 'without a foothold to be found.
The analysis of the compound should be understood as: "that wherein no foothold can be found" is *alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā*.
Because it is impossible to plunge into that which has no foothold to be found, it is stated, "Because of its very depth, one cannot see [it], saying, 'These are so many and such-like.'"
"Difficult to see. As for those things which cannot even be seen, there is no talk of entering into them and awakening to them;

therefore he said, "Because it is difficult to see, it is difficult to awaken to. Because it arises at the conclusion of the subsiding of all feverish distress (*pariḷāha*), and because it is permeated by the attainment in which all feverish distress has been extinguished, it is "one in whom all feverish distress has been extinguished. Its objects are peaceful.
The path, fruits, and Nibbāna possess a state of peace because of the absence of defilements and formations, which by nature are not peaceful.

Alternatively, the state of peace of the phenomena that are their objects should be understood through the power of attention that is constantly concentrated due to the eradication of distraction—just as the infinity of consciousness is understood through its objective range of space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa. This is the penetration of the sign without wavering.

He said, "in the sense of being insatiable," because the awakening to the true nature of phenomena (dhamma) as they actually are—unlike the arrows of archers which miss their mark—is both sweet-tasting and of great flavor.

He said, "because it is the object of supreme knowledge," and so forth, because for those who have attained penetration—and especially for the Buddhas alone—it has become an object in every respect, and thus it is not within the range of speculative intellect (*takka-buddhi*). "Subtle" (*nipuṇā*)...

They are "skilled" because their activity regarding objects of knowledge is sharp and keen. Furthermore, since that state of skillfulness is made manifest by its unimpeded operation toward the object and its capacity to grasp subtle objects of knowledge, it is said: "because of its subtle and delicate nature.

According to another method: they are "profound" because they reveal profound objects of knowledge such as the Vinaya-paññatti (the formal rules of discipline). At times, for incalculable great eons...
Even when transcended, it is difficult to see because its appearance is rare; and here, "seeing" should be understood solely by way of the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*).
It is difficult to awaken to because awakening—consisting of the discernment of the sequence of phenomena (*dhamma-anvaya*)—is possible only for some.
It is peaceful because of its true nature and because it is the ultimate consummation of the perfections of those to be trained (*veneyya*). And it is preeminent through its own conditions.

It is sublime because it is definitive. It is beyond the sphere of mere reasoning because it has realized the characteristics of truth, or because it must be understood by a knowledge that is not based on conjecture.
It is subtle because it reveals, in a refined manner, the meaning through the factors of the truths, conditions, modes, and so forth.
It is to be known by the wise because it is realized and proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme sage in the world. This is due to the attainment of unobstructed knowledge.
For the Blessed One proclaims his own qualities, such as omniscience, by saying, "I am all-knowing; monks, the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers," and so forth.
For this very reason, he says, "Having realized it through direct higher knowledge, he makes it known.
In this regard, although the knowledge of omniscience does not have the nature of something to be realized in the same way as the fruits and Nibbāna do, [it is nevertheless so described].

But when the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa) has been attained, it is indeed already attained; thus, its "realization" (sacchikiriyā) is the making it directly evident to oneself.

Therefore he said, "having made it directly evident by means of distinguished knowledge. The instrumental case in the phrase "by means of distinguished knowledge" (abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena) is used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is: "on account of the attainment of distinguished knowledge. Alternatively, "distinguished knowledge" refers to the knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa).

The instrumental case is indeed appropriate here as well. In this context, "proclaiming" (*pavedana*) should be understood as the accomplishment of the task of teaching the Truths and so forth, which are objects of higher knowledge, and as the act of professing, "I alone am the Fully Enlightened One," and so on. Regarding the word *vadamānā*, the suffix *-māna* has the sense of existence;
thus, the meaning is "one who makes an effort to speak. And since those who are thus disposed are called "desirous of speaking," he said [the following].
Regarding the phrase “desiring to speak praise”: even one who speaks with something remaining [unsaid] cannot be said to “speak correctly,” as if they were speaking erroneously;
therefore, he says “without omitting. By this, he shows that the word *sammā* here has the sense of “without remainder.
With the words “they would be able to speak,” he indicates that the verb “vadeyyuṃ” expresses the same meaning as the noun “vattuṃ. And here, although the Blessed One’s...
The knowledges of the ten powers and so forth are also not shared with others;
however, because those knowledges have limited scope, the Buddha-qualities are not said to be fully grasped by them.
But because the knowledge of omniscience has unlimited scope, when that is grasped, all the Buddha-qualities are indeed grasped. It is this meaning that he shows [with the words]: "By which... pe..."
"‘They would say’—that which has manifold objects (*puthu-ārammaṇa*) is ‘manifold-objected’; the intention is that its object is everything.

Alternatively, in the sense of ‘having manifold-objected objects,’ it is stated as ‘from the manifold-objected’ (*puthu-ārammaṇato*), having elided one of the two words *ārammaṇa*, just as in the case of ‘lip-mouthed’ (*oṭṭha-mukha*) or ‘sense-sphere-bound’ (*kāmāvacara*). By this, its accomplishment of the function of manifold knowledge is shown."
It demonstrates this: for indeed, it is the unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times; the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth; the knowledge that delimits the five destinations;
the remaining uncommon knowledges among the six uncommon knowledges; the knowledge that distinguishes the seven noble persons; the unshakable knowledge in all eight assemblies;
the knowledge of full comprehension of the nine abodes of beings; the knowledge of the ten powers; and so forth.
It accomplishes the function of the many hundreds of thousands of kinds of knowledge as they arise.
By the phrase "by way of repeated arising," he shows that omniscient knowledge proceeds in succession.
For it operates upon its objects in sequence, not all at once, contrary to what the outsiders claim: "The Omniscient One knows everything all at once, not in succession."

If it is asked: "How can there be a complete penetration (*paṭivedha*) by means of a single knowledge that possesses limits, regarding the knowable (*ñeyya*) which has such inconceivable and immeasurable divisions?"—who indeed says that "the Buddha-knowledge possesses limits"?
For that knowledge is infinite, just like the knowable. Indeed, this has been said: "As far as the knowable extends, so far extends the knowledge; as far as the knowledge extends..."

"Only that much is to be known. Even if one were to grasp the knowable—which is divided into many categories such as birth, plane, nature, and so forth, as well as direction, place, time, and so on—progressively, it would still be impossible to achieve a complete penetration without remainder. This is not so. Why?
Because whatever the Blessed One desired to know, whether in its entirety or in part, [his knowledge] possesses unimpeded range therein.
Knowledge proceeds by way of direct perception; and because there is no distraction, it should be understood that the Blessed One is always in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
It is impossible to deny the direct perceptual nature of what he desires to know, according to such statements as: "The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is dependent upon his wish.
Nor is this like those who look at a cloth from a distance with their minds; for [the Blessed One perceives] all phenomena...

And it should be understood that, like those practicing insight (vipassanā) on "non-self," the Blessed One’s knowledge proceeds at the time of awakening to manifold phenomena in an unascertained form, due to the inconceivable power of a Buddha’s knowledge. For this very reason, it is said: "The domain of a Buddha is inconceivable.
This, however, is the conclusion here: for one who is capable of awakening to all phenomena in every aspect...

By the attainment of unobstructed knowledge, which functions independently of desire, the Blessed One became capable of penetrating all phenomena through his mental continuum due to the abandonment of all veils that obscure what is to be known;
therefore, he is "omniscient" (*sabbaññū*), not merely because of a single simultaneous awakening to all phenomena,
just as fire is called "all-consuming" (*sabbabhū*) because of its capacity to burn all fuel through its continuity.
“Vavatthāpanavacanaṃ” means a word of determination; the meaning is a word of restriction.
In the phrase “aññe vā,” he shows what is excluded by that restriction: “not the abstention from taking life and so forth.
Furthermore, this word *eva*—like the word *ca*—when used in a location of indefinite scope, stands for other places as well, according to the speaker’s intention.
He said, "Or 'profound,'" and so forth. "By all the terms" means by all the terms up to the phrase "to be experienced by the wise.

"Disciple's knowledge of the perfections" (sāvakapāramiñāṇa) refers to the knowledge consisting of the threefold science, the six direct knowledges, the four analytical insights, and so on, which is accomplished through disciples' fulfillment of the perfections such as giving. "Than that" (tato) means than the disciple's knowledge of the perfections. "Therein" (tattha) means in the disciple's knowledge of the perfections. "Even than that" (tatopi) means than what was just mentioned.

The intention is that this applies even compared to the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, let alone the knowledge of a disciple’s perfections (sāvakapāramiñāṇa). Herein, this is the application of the meaning:

although the knowledge of a disciple’s perfections is profound when compared to the knowledge of those still in training (sekkha) and the knowledge of worldlings (puthujjana), it cannot be called "profound indeed" when compared to the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, as it is not so profound in relation to that.
Similarly, the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha cannot be defined in relation to the knowledge of omniscience;

however, the phenomena of omniscient knowledge are profound because they lack any shallowness in comparison to the knowledge of the disciples' perfections and so forth, just as [the former] is defined in relation to the latter.
And just as this definition has been shown here, so too is the knowledge of the disciples' perfections difficult to see.

But the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha is even more difficult to see than that; therefore, one should understand the presence of discernment (*vavatthāna*) through such statements as "there is no discernment therein.
For this very reason he said: "In the same way, it is indeed difficult to see... [and so on]... it should be understood.
But why was this undertaken in this manner? Herein, this is the intention: let it be granted for now that [this section] serves as the means for elucidating the Buddha’s qualities in their entirety.
Although the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is a single unity, it was taught with the plural form "there are, monks, other states" (*atthi bhikkhave aññe dhammā*) and so forth,
because its function is established through various bases and objects. However, instead of beginning its exposition by means of a method of analysis unique to itself—
such as the specific distinctions of the truths, conditions, and modes— it was undertaken by way of analyzing the views together with their respective bases.

Why was this begun? Herein, just as the analysis of the modes of the conditions for the Truths and so forth is not shared by others but is the domain of the Omniscient One’s knowledge alone, so too is the exhaustive analysis of the various speculative views; it is to show this that the passage beginning with “For the Buddhas... was begun.
In this context, “grounds” (*ṭhānāni*) means causes (*kāraṇāni*). “The thundering is great” means...
Because the meaning to be taught is of many kinds and difficult to comprehend, the thundering roar of the teaching proceeds by way of various methods;

thus it becomes great, vast, and manifold in its divisions. "It enters into knowledge" means that, for this very reason, the knowledge of the teaching enters into the phenomena to be taught as it analyzes them into their constituent parts;
the sense is that, having entered into them, it stands as if it were one with them.

"The greatness of the Buddha’s knowledge is made manifest"—thus, the sublime nature of the Buddhas' knowledge of teaching and their knowledge of penetration becomes evident regarding one who teaches and realizes such a Dhamma as this. And here, although it is said:
"All verbal action of the Blessed Buddha is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge," [the following applies].

It should be understood that there is no teaching of the Blessed One whatsoever that is devoid of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Because his conduct is like that of a lion, his exertion proceeds with equal intensity in all cases;
however, depending on the specific dhamma to be taught, the teaching becomes particularly distinguished by knowledge and more profound.
But how is it that, upon reaching the formulation of the Vinaya (*vinayapaṇṇatti*), the teaching is struck by the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*) and connected with emptiness (*suññatā*)?

Does it happen so? Even there, the teaching proceeding in accordance with the inclinations of the assembled assembly reveals the impermanence and other characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and demonstrates the absence of self or what belongs to a self in all phenomena.
For this very reason, he said: "Having given a discourse on the Dhamma in many ways," and so forth.
"Bhūmantara" (difference of planes) refers to both the difference in the state (*avatthā*) and the difference in the location (*ṭhāna*) of phenomena.

Therein, the difference in state is the classification of phenomena such as mindfulness (*sati*) into the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), path-factors (*maggaṅga*), and so forth. The difference in location is the classification into the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) and so on.
The meaning of the term "paccayākāra" (conditionality) has already been explained above. "Samayantara" (difference of time) refers to differences in views; the meaning is variously formulated views.

Or at another time. "When the matter has thus descended" means: when the matter has thus descended according to its corresponding lightness, heaviness, and so forth, there is the promulgation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

Although the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth are analyzed in the Sutta Piṭaka by way of the contemplation of the body and so forth, [they are also treated] by way of the *Suttantabhājanīya* and so forth.
However, since these are analyzed in detail specifically in the Abhidhamma, he says: "These four foundations of mindfulness... having analyzed the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
In that context, "seven contacts" is stated by way of their association with the seven consciousness-elements; likewise for "seven feelings," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "supramundane states," here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" or the sense of "manner."
Or rather, it comprises the remaining modes of analysis of phenomena (*dhamma*) taught therein that appear in the Abhidhamma.
It is called the *Caturviṃśatisamantapaṭṭhāna* because the twenty-four *samantapaṭṭhānas* (comprehensive foundations) are found herein; that is, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
Here, the twenty-fourfold nature of the *samantapaṭṭhāna* is stated by way of the phenomena themselves, without taking the method of conditions (*paccayanaya*) into account. As it has been said:
“The excellent and most supreme *tika-paṭṭhāna*,
the *duka-tika* and the *tika-duka*;
the *tika-tika* and the *duka-duka*.”
Six methods in the forward order are very profound.
Likewise—[the] triad... [and so on] ...six methods in the reverse order are very profound.
“The triads... [and so on] ...the six methods of the positive-negative sequence are very profound;
the triads... [and so on] ...the methods of the negative-positive sequence are very profound.

Thus, among the twenty-four divisions according to the phenomena (dhamma), such as the *Paṭṭhāna* of Triads and so forth, each one is [treated] by way of the method of conditions (*paccayanaya*) through the positive sequence and so forth.
"It is fourfold" refers to the ninety-six *samantapaṭṭhānas*.

Among these, in the *Dhammānuloma* section of the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, within the *Kusala-ttika* under the "Dependent" chapter (*paṭicca-vāra*), in the "Positive Condition" (*paccayānuloma*) and "Root Condition" (*hetu-mūlaka*) sections, there are forty-nine modes of questioning and seven modes of answering, and so forth.
Thus, because the methods (*nayas*) shown therein possess infinite divisions, it is called "the infinite method. And on this point, there is this [verse]:

“*Paṭṭhāna* is the sevenfold method, distinguished by its roots of conditions, which proceeds in four ways through the triplets, dyads, and so forth, among the individual phenomena, beginning with their positive concomitance (*anuloma*).
By “in nine modes” is meant by the nine modes of conditionality, beginning with arising (*uppāda*). In this context, *uppāda* (arising) is that from which the fruit arises;
it is the state of being the cause for origination. And when ignorance (*avijjā*) exists, volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) arise, not when it does not exist; therefore...
Ignorance (avijjā), having become the arising of volitional formations (saṅkhārā), serves as their condition. Likewise, when ignorance exists, volitional formations proceed, persist, and settle;

being present through ignorance, they cast their fruit into existence (bhava) and so forth, they strive, they exert themselves for the production of that fruit, they conjoin with their own fruit, and they fetter that continuum (santāna) in which they themselves have arisen.

In the convergence of other conditions, they arise and emerge; they "go" (hinoti) in the sense that they become the cause of the formations (saṅkhārā), and "depending on ignorance, formations go," meaning they proceed.
Thus, the specific characteristics such as arising and so forth should be understood as the ways in which ignorance attains the state of being the cause of formations.
The same applies to formations and the rest in relation to consciousness and the subsequent links.

Regarding the terms "arising and presence" (*uppādaṭṭhiti*) and so forth: that by which something stands is "presence" (*ṭhiti*), meaning a cause. Arising itself is the presence; thus it is "arising and presence.

The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Since improper attention is a condition for ignorance—according to the statement, "With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance"—it is said:
"Both these states are dependently arisen. [This concludes the section on] the discernment of conditions.
“Wisdom” (paññā) is wisdom that functions by discerning and grasping the mode of conditions, such as the arising and so forth of formations and ignorance.

“Knowledge of the stability of phenomena” (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) is knowledge regarding dependent origination, which is termed the “stability of phenomena” because it consists in the state of being a condition for those phenomena that have arisen from conditions.
For the conditioning phenomena in dependent origination are referred to as “the twelve dependent originations.”
According to the wording, there are twelve conditions. Furthermore, this method applies not only to the present, but also to the past and future;
nor does it apply only of ignorance with respect to volitional formations, but also of volitional formations and the rest with respect to consciousness and the rest.
Thus, in order to show the analyzed nature of the mode of conditionality by making it complete, the text begins with the words, "In the past time as well," and so forth.
The conditions such as the root-cause (hetu) and others shown in the *Paṭṭhāna* are indeed included here by way of the modes of conditionality such as "arising" (uppāda).
Having extracted them according to their respective possibilities, they should be applied; however, for fear of excessive prolixity, we have not applied them here.
"Of that and that phenomenon" means of that and that phenomenon arisen from conditions such as formations (saṅkhāra). "In such and such a way..."
"By way of being a condition" means by way of being conditions such as arising, causes, and so forth.

"Three periods" (*tiyaddha*) refers to that which has three time-periods (*addhā-kālā*) consisting of the past, present, and future. "Three connections" (*tisandhi*) refers to that which has three junctions (*sandhi*) consisting of cause and fruit, fruit and cause, and cause and fruit.
"Concise" (*saṅkhepa*) refers to that wherein ignorance and the rest, as well as consciousness and the rest, are condensed; [it consists of] karma and its result.
Alternatively, *saṅkhepa* means that which is condensed (*saṅkhippanti ettha*); [in this sense] it refers to ignorance and so forth, as well as consciousness and so forth.
Or, the word *saṅkhepa* has the sense of a "division" or "section. It is called *catusaṅkhepa* because it possesses four condensations—namely, the condensations of karma and so forth—in the past.

Although not explicitly stated in their own form, they are "scattered" (*ākiriyyanti*) within those respective condensations; that is, they are made manifest by the inclusion of ignorance, formations, and the rest.
"Modes" (ākārā) refers to the modes of the past causes and so forth; these, being fivefold each when condensed, constitute twenty modes for this [view], hence it is called "twentyfold" (vīsatākāraṃ).

Although divided into many categories such as Kṣatriyas and others, the eternalists—due to the cause of their dogmatic adherence to things like the recollection of hundreds of thousands of births—[hold this view].
By way of this [classification], there are exactly four, and not more than that;

thus, in order to show that the definitions and limits of the eternalist views (*sassatavāda*) and so forth do not have any other object, he said, "four persons," and so on. Therein, "four persons" means four groups of people.
"Depending on this" refers to this incorrect grasping of specific conditionality (*idappaccayatā*); and even therein, by way of the relationship between cause and fruit...

Because the continuity of related things is undifferentiated, there arises—based on the grasping of unity, which is apprehended without reflecting upon the principle of diversity that exists as a basis for differentiation even from the perspective of ultimate reality—the adherence to this [grasping].

"Grasping this" means they adhere to and express themselves through this eternalist grasping; in this manner, the doctrines of partial eternalism and so forth should also be applied here as appropriate.

It should be stated thus: "Having broken open" means having analyzed by means of the passage beginning with "exerting himself with ardor," and having pounded it out by means of the passage beginning with "This, monks, the Tathāgata understands," thereby making it free from tangles and free from knots through the disentangling of the tangle of views and the opening up of the thicket of views.
By the words "Therefore," etc., having pointed out the knowledge of omniscience because the teaching was originated concerning the qualities of the Buddha.
It shows that the Blessed One, skilled in teaching, responds solely with his omniscient knowledge by way of grasping the distinctions between the various systems.
By the word "exist" (*santi*), the King of Dhamma illuminates the uninterrupted continuity of those proponents of views due to their actual existence;
furthermore, he demonstrates the fulfillment of the function of his own teaching through the loosening and the removal of their false graspings, as well as its unerring nature.
29. *Atthi* is a single indeclinable (*nipāta*) whose scope is plural and which has the same meaning as "exists" (*saṃvijjanti*), as in such passages as "In this body there are head-hairs.
They are called "speculators about the past" (*pubbantakappikā*) because they speculate about the past in terms of eternalism and so forth.
Furthermore, because they speculate about that past by means of previously established conceptualizations of craving and views, and due to the strength of their habitual practice...

And because of their state of being mentally constructed, having first conceptualized and then subsequently grasped through the seizing of craving and views—which have become objects of adherence—they grasp, adhere to, and misapprehend them;
therefore it is said, "having conceptualized and constructed the past, they grasp it.
Alternatively, the acts of conceptualizing and grasping should be understood by way of craving and clinging, for clinging has craving as its condition. Regarding the phrase "in the parts":
Here, the meaning should be understood as "in sections and so forth. For the word *anta* is seen even in the senses of "filling out a line," "proximity," and "wrong path.
Thus, in such instances as, "Come now, you should master the discourses (*suttanta*), the verses (*gāthā*), or the Abhidhamma;
having made space for the discourses," the word *anta* functions in the sense of filling out a line. [And it is used in] "he should descend to the village boundary (*gāmanta*)."

In such passages as "a lodging within a village," the word *anto* means "in the vicinity"; in such passages as "Devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure is one extreme; 'it exists,' Kaccāna, this is another extreme," it means "an inclination.

The term *kappa* applies to the duration of a great aeon (*mahākappa*), the state of being bounded by [defilements], the defilements (*kilesa*), sensual desire (*kāma*), discursive thought (*vitakka*), time (*kāla*), and conventional designation (*paññatti*), among others.
He said: "It applies to many meanings. For instance, it applies to a *mahākappa* (great aeon) in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, there are these four incalculable periods of a *kappa*";
to the sense of "all around" in such passages as, "having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana grove";

to *kilesakāma* (defilement-desire) in such passages as, "intention is desire, lust is desire, intention-and-lust is desire"; and to [the mental factor of] thinking in such passages as, "reasoning, applied thought, and intention (*saṅkappa*)."
In such passages as “by which indeed I always dwell,” *kappa* occurs in the sense of time; in such passages as “thus said the venerable Kappa,” it occurs in the sense of a designation (*paññatti*);
and in such passages as “Alas, we did not realize that we were conversing with a disciple who is like the Teacher himself,” it occurs in the sense of similarity.
And when it is said, “It is also stated,” he says this with reference to the *Mahāniddesa*. “By way of craving and views” means:
It is by way of craving— which serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for views and is co-nascent (*sahajāta*) with them— and by way of wrong grasping,

which consists in adhering to [the self] through modes such as eternalism; for here the word "prior" (*pubba*) denotes the past time because it is intended as a conceptualization (*kappanā*) whose object is phenomena previously experienced,
since there is no basis for conceptualization existing apart from the aggregates of form and so forth.
And since the word *anta* signifies a "portion," he says: "a portion of the past aggregates.
"Having postulated" (*kappetvā*) refers to the establishing and finalizing of craving and dogmatic adherence regarding that past limit. "Abiding" (*ṭhitā*) means not abandoning that tenet.
"Taking as a basis" (*ārabbha*) means having made it an object; for the past limit is the objective domain (*visaya*) of that view, because it exists as its object.
For it is indeed by way of that [condition] being its place of arrival and its object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) that it is said, "having come to" (āgamma) and "depending on" (paṭicca).

"Designation-terms" (adhivacanapadāni) means conceptualization-terms (paññattipadāni). Just as the words "Sirivaḍḍhaka" and so forth are applied to slaves and others merely by making them the subject of discourse, so too a designation (adhivacana) is a conceptualization (paññatti) because it occurs by taking something as its primary focus (adhikāra).
Alternatively, the prefix *adhi* denotes "superiority" or "above," and it is said (*vuccati*)—
"Vacana" means a statement; "adhivacana" means a designation. The meaning is that it is a "derived designation" (*upādāpaññatti*) because it is designated based upon derived matter and so forth.
Therefore, the sense should be understood as "words that illuminate a designation. For this which is called "self" and "world" is said to be a mere designation (*paññattimatta*);
it is not an ultimate reality (*paramattha*) like form, feeling, and the rest. Or, [it is so called] because of its figurative usage (*adhikavutti*).

“Adhivuttis” refers to views (*diṭṭhiyo*). For views proceed by superimposing upon phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) such as permanence (*sassata*), primordial matter (*pakati*), substance (*dabba*), the soul (*jīva*), or the body (*kāya*), which are non-existent objects. 30.
“They assert” means they speak after having adhered [to their position], saying: “This alone is the truth; all else is false,” and “This is the Dhamma.”
They dispute [with the words] beginning, "This is not the Dhamma. The use of the present tense is for the purpose of showing that the act of salutation remains uninterrupted even to this day.
"Diṭṭhigata" means simply "view" (diṭṭhi), just as in expressions such as "muttagata" (the state of urine) or "saṅkhāragata" (the state of formations).
Alternatively, because there is nothing further to be gone toward, it is merely the "gone" of the view; the meaning is "merely the grasping of the view. It is a manifestation of the view.
Or it is a speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*). For worldly people accept that the words *vidha*, *yutta*, *gata*, and *pakāra* have the same meaning.
And because there is a designation based on the specific apprehension of each [object] as "self" (*attā*) and "world" (*loka*), he said:
"having apprehended one or another among form and so forth as both self and world. "Immortal," "permanent," and "stable" are synonyms for eternalism (*sassata*). Because of the absence of death...
Or it is "immortal" (*amara*); it is "permanent" (*nicca*) because of its existence in every way due to the absence of arising;

it is "steadfast" (*dhruva*) in the sense of being stable and the absence of change. With the words "As it has been said," etc., he elucidates the aforementioned meaning by means of the *Niddesa* and *Paṭisambhidāmagga* texts. And this meaning is [expressed in the Sutta]:
"One regards form as self, one regards feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness as self."

This is stated by way of these fivefold views of identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*). However, by way of the fifteenfold views of identity beginning with “the self possesses form,” there is also this meaning to be understood:
having grasped four aggregates each as “self,” they designate the one remaining aggregate as “the world. Likewise, [they grasp] one aggregate as “self.”

Having grasped those [aggregates] as their own sphere of enjoyment, they designate other things as "the world"; or, having grasped the aggregates included within their own continuity as "self," they designate other things as "the world"—this is how the meaning here should be understood. Here it is asked:
why is it said that "their doctrine is eternal"? Is it not the case that for them, it is the self and the world that are intended to be eternal, and not the doctrine?
Is this true? This is indeed true; however, because it is associated with eternalism, it is called "the doctrine of eternalism" (*sassatavāda*), just as one says "the spears are walking.
Alternatively, the word *iti* should be understood as having been elided, such that it means "those for whom the doctrine is 'eternal'.

Or else, they are "eternalists" (*sassatavādā*) because, being obsessed by the view of eternalism, they speak and express themselves, saying "this alone is the truth"; thus the meaning here should be understood.
31. *Ātāpana* is the tormenting, the suppression, and the abandoning of the defilements. *Padahana* is the exertion of the mind, not allowing it to fall into the side of indolence.
*Anuyoga* is the repeated practice of energy in such a way that concentration reaches the stage of distinction.
Here, because the energies for taming the access and absorption minds are intended, he says: "threefold."
“Energy” (*vīriya*). It is called “heedfulness” (*appamāda*) because one does not neglect by means of it; it is non-forgetfulness.

It is called “right attention” (*sammāmanasikāra*) because one attends to the meditation subject by means of it with the correct method; it is knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Thus he said, “energy, mindfulness, and knowledge.
“In this” refers to this passage: “With ardor... [and] following upon right attention. Together with purification of virtue, of the four...
The method for attaining the fine-material-sphere jhānas should be stated; however, since that has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*, he says, "the meaning in brief.
By the phrase "of such a kind," he refers to the state of being tamed by means of the fourteen modes of taming the mind.
These [powers] are the manifestations of concentration belonging to a yogi who possesses the four factors beginning with composure, pertaining to the fourth fine-material-sphere jhāna.
Worldly direct knowledge (*lokiyābhiññā*) is the power of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).

Regarding the phrase “of absorption and so forth,” this was said with reference to the fact that for one who has attained absorption, the states of absorption specifically come into the range of the cognitive door, and through that gateway, all other states [also do so].

It rejects the status of being a producer. For if there were a status of being a producer, then—just as in the case of material form and other phenomena, or pleasure and other mental states—[the same would apply here].

Because it exists in dependence on conditions, its state of being subject to arising is understood; and since there must necessarily be cessation when there is arising, permanence would have no room to exist.
Alternatively, the word *kūṭaṭṭha* (immovable) should be seen as established in common usage for that which is absolutely permanent.
By the phrase "standing firm like a pillar," it is shown that just as a pillar does not waver due to the impact of wind and so forth, so too [this state] is not moved by anything.
“Undergoes change” (vikāraṃ āpajjati) expresses the absence of change; by the term “immovable” (kūṭaṭṭha), however, he expresses the absence of impermanence.
Since change is indeed destruction, he says: “By both [terms], he illuminates the world’s lack of destruction.

By the phrase “only as it exists” (vijjamānameva), he illustrates the theory of manifestation (abhibyaktivāda) through the demonstration that the effect exists within the cause. And by “emerges,” he refers to manifestation.
The meaning is "it goes. But how is it that something which already exists, though previously unmanifest, comes to manifestation?
It is like a jar hidden by darkness coming to manifestation through light.
This must be investigated here: what does the light do when it is said that it "reveals" the jar? If [the light] has the jar as its object...

If one were to say that [the jar] produces consciousness, then because this would imply the arising of a consciousness that had not previously arisen, the theory of manifestation (*abhivyaktivāda*) would be undermined.
Alternatively, if one says it dispels the darkness that acts as an obstruction to the consciousness of the jar, even so, the theory of manifestation is likewise undermined.
For if the consciousness of the jar already exists, how could darkness be an obstruction to it? [Otherwise, it would be an obstruction] just as [darkness is an obstruction] to the jar itself.
It is not tenable, and the same applies to the self as well.

For even in that case, if the arising of cognition were due to the conjunction of the sense faculties, objects, and so forth, then by the very mention of its "arising," the theory of manifestation (*abhivyaktivāda*) would be abandoned, as would the doctrine of eternalism (*sassatavāda*).

Alternatively, [if it is argued that cognition arises] through the dispelling of delusion—which stands in the place of darkness and acts as an obstruction to the functioning of cognition—then cognition exists [prior to that].
How is delusion an obscuration? Because it is possible for there to be a distinction [between them].

For when there is a distinction among the manifestors—such as the moon, the sun, gems, or lamps—there is no distinction among the objects manifested, such as jars and the like. Yet, since there is a distinction in cognition according to the distinction in the object, manifestation itself is even more untenable.
