Furthermore, the postulation of a "function" (vutti) here is not logical, because [the function] is not distinct from that which possesses the function (the entity).

And [it is said] "because of not admitting that there is no other way. And those beings "run on" means that those who are established here in human form go elsewhere from this state by attaining the state of a deity and so forth;
for otherwise, the destruction of karma already performed and the arrival of karma not yet performed would follow—this is the intended meaning.

"From one to another" means from a subsequent existence to another existence. "They go by this reckoning" means that because they possess an eternal intrinsic nature (*niccasabhāva*), there are no actual deaths and rebirths;

nor, because of their all-pervasiveness, are there any running about or wandering through saṃsāra. Rather, it is through the specific modes of activity of phenomena alone that they go by this reckoning and are so designated—this is the intended meaning. By this, [it is shown] that for that which has a fixed intrinsic nature...

This demonstrates the doctrine of transformation (*vipariṇāmavāda*), which holds that for oneself and for things possessing a nature (*dhammino*), there arises and perishes merely a phenomenon (*dhammamatta*). What ought to be said regarding this matter, we shall explain later.

"He breaks his own doctrine" means that he breaks the eternalist doctrine previously asserted, which was established by such statements as "running about" and so forth; the sense is that he destroys it. "Equal to eternity" (*sassatisamaṃ*)...
The meaning should be understood as: "this [self and world] is eternal, stable, and for all time.
"Showing the reason" means showing the reason for those who, holding this particular view, proclaim the self and the world to be "eternal.
For one does not [establish] an object directly perceived by oneself through one's own view alone.
It establishes [the point]; moreover, by means of a matter directly experienced by oneself, it establishes even a matter that is not directly experienced by oneself.
For one makes others understand exactly what one has desired, and not what one has not desired. Regarding the phrase "showing the cause," this is the demonstration of the cause:
among these many hundreds of thousands of births, this self of mine is but one, because of the existence of recollection regarding the world.
For whoever experiences a particular object, only that person remembers it, and no one else.
Indeed, one person cannot remember an object experienced by another, just as Dhammarakkhita cannot remember what was experienced by Buddharakkhita.
And just as it is with these [present] births, so it was with those even more remote than these. Why? "My self and the world are eternal. Just as...
And does he [hold] for himself, as well as for other beings, that "the self and the world are eternal"?

One who has fallen into the thicket of views through the mode of eternalism, being a proponent of such views, establishes others therein as well. However, because of the statement in the Pāḷi, "They assert various kinds of designations;
he speaks thus," it is intended here that the demonstration of the reason is by way of inference from another's perspective.
It is understood. "Cause" (*kāraṇa*) is threefold: the cause that brings about (*sampāpaka*), the cause that produces (*nibbattaka*), and the cause that makes known (*ñāpaka*).

Among these, the Noble Path is the cause that brings about Nibbāna; the seed is the cause that produces the sprout; and such things as the state of being dependently arisen are the causes that make known impermanence and so forth.
Here too, only the cause that makes known is intended. For the cause that makes known [is so called] because it makes known the object that is to be made known.
It is called a "cause" (*kāraṇa*) because it is the causal basis for knowledge. Because knowledge exists in dependence upon it, it is called a "ground" (*ṭhāna*) since knowledge stands there;

and it is called a "basis" (*vatthu*) because knowledge dwells there and functions there. For indeed, although the Blessed One indicated them by means of the word "basis," he explained them by means of the word "ground."
32–33. There is no difference between the second and third doctrines other than the difference in time;
thus he says, "The same method applies to the two subsequent doctrines as well. If this is so, why is the eternalist doctrine divided fourfold?
Should it not be divided into only two types, like the fortuitous origination doctrine? To this he replies, "For the heretic is of dull wisdom," and so forth.
34. "Takkayati" means to speculate; the meaning is that one directs the mind toward various objects in modes such as eternalism and so forth.
"Takkā" (speculation) is a form of initial application of thought (*vitakka*) characterized by striking or by deciding, and it serves as a basis for views. "Vīmaṃsā" (investigation) means pondering;
in this context, however, it refers in substance to an arising of consciousness accompanied by greed, which is a counterfeit of wisdom and constitutes a wrong adherence.
Or it should be understood as improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), or as the fluctuation of views (*diṭṭhi-vipphandita*) in the prior stage.
For this very reason, he said: "weighing, approving, and tolerating. "Striking" (*pariyāhanana*) is simply the striking at the object of thought; thus he said: "having thought in various ways.
"Discoursed upon" (*anuvicarita*) means set in motion by investigation (*vīmaṃsā*), or accompanied by investigation.

It is that which has been reflected upon by investigation. It is called *paṭibhāna* because it shines forth repeatedly (*paṭi-paṭi bhāti*); it is a mental state that discerns the specific aspects of the form as it was intended.
That which is born from such shining forth is *paṭibhāna*; "one's own shining forth" means one's own *paṭibhāna*.
For this very reason, he said: "arisen merely from one's own *paṭibhāna*. By the word *matta* ("merely"), he excludes the attainment of special qualities and so forth.

The statement, “In the future too it will be thus,” should be understood as not being spoken solely by way of the reasoning of one who reasons here [in the present], but rather as being spoken by way of showing the possibility, since such reasoning is also possible for one who possesses gain (*lābhī*).

Here, “gain” (*lābha*) refers to whatever form, feeling, and so forth, or pleasure and so forth, that one has personally acquired; it does not refer to specific distinctions such as meditative absorption (*jhāna*). “When this exists, that comes to be.”

He shows the manner in which the rationalist seeks logical consistency: [he argues that] if things were impermanent (*anicca*), one would commit an error by asserting that "one person acts and another experiences [the result]," for if that were the case, there would be the destruction of what was done and the arrival of what was not done.
However, if things were permanent (*nicca*), then there would be no fault in asserting that "whoever acts is the same one who experiences [the result].
Thus he demonstrates the way the rationalist investigates logic.
"By mere reasoning alone" means by pure reasoning itself, due to the absence of scriptural authority, personal realization, oral tradition, and so forth.

But is it not the case that even those eternalists who have attained distinction— on account of their own attainment of distinction— recall their own continuum as it was experienced over many hundreds of thousands of births,
across ten cycles of cosmic contraction and expansion, or forty such cycles?

And having recollected that which is bound up with them as "self" and "the world," they became adherents of eternalism by means of reflecting on the existence of such a self in previous and even earlier births,

and by means of reflecting on the state of being thus for all beings. And this being so, every proponent of eternalism— whether through tradition, recollection of past lives, or reasoning— is likewise bound by the basis of what has been personally apprehended.
Because his discourse proceeds by means of reasoning, he would remain on the side of the rationalists (*takkīpakka*), and such reasoning as has been described must necessarily be accepted;
otherwise, the eternalist who attains specific distinctions might fall into the faction of partial-eternalists or the faction of those who maintain spontaneous origination (*adhiccasamuppannika*).
However, this is not to be viewed in that way, because for those who attain specific distinctions, [the distinction pertains] to the continuum of the aggregates (*khandhasantāna*).
Recollection over long, longer, and longest periods of time is the specific cause for the adherence to eternalism (*sassataggāha*).
For instance, in the passage, "I recollect my manifold past lives; by this I know this," it is the act of recollection itself that is shown to be the primary cause.
However, the conjecture that occurs therein—"By this I know this"—is not what is intended here.
Recollection is subordinate to the exertion because it is not itself the primary effort. If it is argued that, in this case, even hearsay and the like would follow as being primary, the answer is no;
for these lack direct realization and are primarily based on mere conjecture.
Furthermore, a designation is established by way of its principal cause both in the Teaching and in the world, as in the cases of "eye-consciousness" and "a barley sprout."
Alternatively, in order to demonstrate that reasoning devoid of the basis for specific attainment functions as an independent cause for the adherence to eternalism,
the specific attainment itself must be stated as a separate cause for the adherence to eternalism; and since that [attainment] is threefold according to dull,
medium, and sharp wisdom, the Blessed One, having taken all such reasoners together under the commonality of their state as "reasoners," has established them as fourfold.

The doctrine of eternalism (*sassatavāda*). Although a manifold division exists even among those of dull wisdom and the like—just as it does for logicians—due to the presence of numerous sub-classifications such as "inferior" and so forth, all those who have attained distinction are nonetheless grouped into three classes according to their dullness of wisdom and other factors.

Among these, according to the superior class, [the recollection] occurs by remembering many hundreds of thousands of births, ten cosmic cycles of dissolution and evolution, or forty cosmic cycles of dissolution and evolution.
This classification has been stated. Among the three groups, those whose wisdom is inferior or middling recollect only less than the stated limit.
However, those among them whose wisdom is superior do not fail to recollect beyond the stated limit;
such is this teaching. Therefore, the Blessed One [taught] four points by way of including one particular division.
"Divided" means established as the fourfold nature of the eternalists (*sassatavādī*). For here, the King of Dhamma does not teach the Dhamma in an incomplete manner.
To show the meaning of "by one or another," it is said "by one. To show that the word *vā* has the sense of indefiniteness, it is said "or by two or by three.
By this, in the four places, according to what is appropriate, one part [is shown] for another.
This shows that they are the cooperative causes for establishing [the view]. But are these bases the cause of the misapprehension itself, or rather of its establishment?
In this regard, if they were the cause of the misapprehension, why are only recollection and reasoning mentioned, and not the perversions of perception and so forth?
For indeed, perverted perception, improper attention, reliance on bad persons, listening to false doctrine, and so on [are also factors].

Regarding the points where wrong view arises: if, like the logical reasons for establishing [a thesis], scripture (*āgama*) must also be stated as a basis (*vatthu*), then in both cases the statement "there is nothing outside of this" would be untenable—is that not so? No. Why?
First, regarding the side of dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*): this person of wrong view, through reliance upon unworthy persons and hearing of false doctrine, [enters into such views].

Having immersed himself in an improper manner, his perception being distorted because he failed to understand that phenomena such as form possess a nature of breaking up moment by moment, he overreached the logical consistency of things.

Grasping the principle of unity incorrectly, through the aforementioned recollections and conjectures, he produced the dogmatic adherence toward the aggregates that "the self and the world are eternal. Thus, because it was the proximate cause and the predominant cause—
And since the others are included by the very mention of "grasping" (taggahaṇa), only recollection and reasoning are taken here.
However, on the side of establishing [the view], even scripture is included within the side of reasoning—especially because outsiders are characterized by their grasping at reasoning;
thus, only recollection and reasoning are taken as the basis for the view. Furthermore, the characteristic of ultimate phenomena is twofold:

[There are] the characteristic of individual essence (*sabhāvalakkhaṇa*) and the characteristic of commonality (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*). Therein, the realization of the characteristic of individual essence is direct knowledge (*paccakkha-ñāṇa*);

the realization of the characteristic of commonality is inferential knowledge (*anumāna-ñāṇa*). Furthermore, since scripture (*āgama*) is a means for accomplishing wisdom born of hearing (*sutamayā paññā*), it brings about precisely inferential knowledge;
however, by reflecting on the modes of the teachings one has heard, one who stands in "acceptance through contemplation" (*nijjhānakkhanti*) develops wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmaya*).
Having generated wisdom, one gradually attains direct knowledge through meditation;

thus, even scripture does not transcend the domain of reasoning, and it should be understood that this is included by the mention of that [reasoning]. This is appropriate because it is elucidated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* by the inclusion of "what is heard" (*anussuti*) and "reasoning" (*takka*).
Indeed, this is evident from the statement: "There is nothing outside of this," and "The various kinds of designations."
One should understand that what is intended here are the bases for establishing [views], because of the statement: "They praise [them], proclaiming a self and the world to be eternal.
(36) A view itself is a "basis for views" (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*), because it serves as the cause for manifold kinds of misfortune due to its being the ultimate reproach.

By the phrase “As it was said: ‘Bhikkhus, I declare that wrong view is the foremost fault’,” and so forth, he demonstrates the classification of the bases for views according to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
Therein, even the aggregates (*khandhā*) are a basis for views in the sense of being an object (*ārammaṇa*), as stated in such passages as “one regards form as self.
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is also a basis for views because it functions as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) and so forth.
As it is said: "Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling, not seeing the Noble Ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones," and so forth.
Contact (*phassa*) is also a basis for views; as it is said: "That too is conditioned by contact; experiencing it again and again," and so on.
Perception (*saññā*) is also a basis for views; and this has been stated: "For conceptual proliferation (*papañca-saṅkhā*) has its source in perception; having perceived earth from the earth..."
And so forth. Applied thought (*vitakka*) is also a basis for views. For this has been said:
"Having fashioned reasoning among views, they speak of the two-fold dharma as 'truth' and 'falsehood,'" and "He is a reasoner, an investigator," and so on.
Unwise attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) is also a basis for views. Therefore the Blessed One said: "For one who attends unwisely in this way, of the six views..."
“A certain view arises: ‘I have a self’—thus a view arises for him as true and firm,” and so forth.
It is called a *samuṭṭhāna* because it originates by means of this; the state of being an origin is the meaning of *samuṭṭhāna*. “Caused to proceed” means produced in the mental continuums of others.
“Fully established” means brought to the conclusion, to the summit of the dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*). “By way of the object” (*ārammaṇavasena*).
He spoke with reference to the aggregates within the eight bases of views (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*). "By way of occurrence" refers to ignorance and the rest. "By way of habituation":

even the cultivation of bad friends, the hearing of others' voices, and so forth, is indeed included as "cultivation. Alternatively, "having such a destination" (*evaṃgatika*) means "having such a course," that is to say, "having such a conclusion.
This is what is meant: these bases of views, which are termed "views," are thus [characterized] in the ultimate sense.
These foolish prattle, having superimposed a non-existent self and its state of eternity, are grasped and adhered to;
they continue and proceed only so long as the wise do not investigate them.
However, when investigated by the wise, their basis being unstable and unable to withstand scrutiny, they vanish like drops of dew at sunrise or like fireflies.
And they break up and perish like that.

Herein, this is the brief explanation for one who investigates: For if the self or the world imagined by another were eternal, then because it would be devoid of change and would not abandon its prior form, it would be impossible to effect any improvement whatsoever.
For the eternalist (*sassatavādin*), instruction would be purposeless, both for the sake of turning away from what is unbeneficial and for the sake of practicing what is beneficial;

or else, how could such instruction proceed, given the absence of any modification? And thus, for him, actions such as giving and so forth, as well as actions such as violence and so forth, are impossible, like that of the sky which is inherently free from impurity.
Likewise, for the eternalist, the very basis for the experience of pleasure and pain [would be untenable].
It is not tenable because there would be an absence of bondage by karma and because birth and the other [stages of existence] would be impossible; how then could there be liberation?

If, on the other hand, you were to say that it is merely a phenomenon (dhammamatta) which arises and perishes, and on account of which this conventional expression of "action" and so forth occurs—even so, since it is established without abandoning its prior form, it is impossible for it to be a "mere phenomenon" of a self (attano).
To conceive [of these states], those factors of his must either be identical to the state itself or different from it.
If they are different, there is no distinction whatsoever in him even when those [states] have arisen—those very states by which he is intended to act, experience, pass away, and be reborn;
therefore, the aforementioned fault remains exactly as it was. Furthermore, the conceptualization of "factors" (dhamma) is also pointless.

If [it is argued that] the self is non-different from the states which possess arising and passing away, then since the self would likewise possess arising and passing away just as those states do, what opportunity is there for its permanence?
Or else, if those states were permanent just like the self, then bondage and liberation would be impossible;
thus, the eternalist doctrine is indeed untenable. Furthermore, no proponent here has presented a pure [argument] regarding the eternality of phenomena.
One who is capable of speaking with reason, for a statement devoid of reason does not please the minds of the wise. Therefore it was said:
"As long as the wise do not subject one to examination, so long do they go on and proceed.
Because one passes away facing toward this by means of kamma, it is called *abhisamparāya*, which is the world beyond (*paraloka*).
The phrase “and omniscient knowledge” is stated here because omniscient knowledge is being analyzed;

or, since that [knowledge] has been mentioned, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) is included by virtue of its being based upon it, and all of the Blessed One’s ten powers and other knowledges are likewise understood as being inseparable from it—this is how it should be taken.
As for the word “even” (*pi*) in the expression “even while knowing,” it expresses a high degree of esteem (*sambhāvane*). By means of it—
He states the meaning of the word *ca* (and) as used here in the phrase “*tañcā*” (and that). This is what is meant:

the Tathāgata does not adhere even to those distinguished qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), which are more excellent than and more essential than those [mere] views; how much less, then, to the bait of the round of existence (*vaṭṭāmisā*)!
In the phrase “*aham*,” he expresses the manner of misapprehending by way of a view. In the phrase “*pajānāmīti*,” the word *iti* has the sense of a mode.
By this, he shows the mode of misapprehension through the influence of craving (*taṇhā*) as "mine.

Misapprehension (*parāmāsa*) is the grasping of something as being other than it actually is, by overstepping the true nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena. For among the aggregates (*khandha*), there is nothing that could be grasped as "I" or "mine.

Furthermore, such misapprehension consists of craving and the like, and these were abandoned by the Blessed One at the very foot of the Bodhi tree; thus he says, "of the defilements of misapprehension," and so forth.
Alternatively, "not grasping" (*aparāmasato*) is a statement regarding the cause of the feeling of Nibbāna; with reference to the word "known" (*viditā*), it is a genitive case used for the agent.

Or rather, the meaning here should be understood as follows: by means of a practice free from grasping—the very cause of non-grasping—the Tathāgata himself has realized the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).
“*In whichever feelings...*” and so forth, [the author] demonstrates the Blessed One’s elegance of teaching.
For indeed, although there exist many kinds of teachings on the Four Truths by way of the aggregates, bases, and so on, this is the method of teaching of the Tathāgatas:
it is intended to show that those who follow wrong views plunge into the thicket of views through their wrong practice, and thus [the Buddha] speaks specifically of feeling (*vedanā*).
These have been extracted for the purpose of showing the stages of full understanding (*pariññā*). "Meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna*) refers here to the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths.

"Having known it as it really is" means having understood—by means of the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) through the penetration of the object regarding the origin and so forth of feeling, and by means of the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*) through the penetration of non-delusion; the meaning is "having penetrated it. "In the sense of the arising of conditions": "In this..."
By means of the arising of conditions such as ignorance, and by the non-eradication [of them] through the Path—according to the characteristic stated thus: "When this exists, that comes to be;
with the arising of this, that arises"—there is the characteristic of production (*nibbatti-lakkhaṇa*), which is the characteristic of arising;
the meaning is "birth. Regarding the phrase "of the five characteristics," here one should understand that even for the four conditions, it is precisely the characteristic of arising that is taken.
"It is said" (vuttaṃ) should be understood as that which is stated, because the characteristic of condition (paccayalakkhaṇa) is indeed obtained [here], and it has been explained accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the cessation of conditions" (paccayanirodhaṭṭhena), the meaning should be understood here too by following the method already stated. "Yam" means "because";

or alternatively, "yam" refers to the pleasure (sukha) and mental joy (somanassa). "Paṭicca" means having obtained feeling (vedanā) as its object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) and so forth. "Ayaṃ" means...
The state of being a condition for pleasure and joy, or pleasure and joy themselves—this is expressed in the masculine gender because it refers back to the word "assāda" (gratification).

This is the summary of the meaning here: when joy arises in dependence upon a previously arisen feeling, that aspect of the previous feeling which is to be gratified—the aspect of the gratification of joy—is what is called "assāda. But how [is this so]?
Is it that pleasure arises based on feeling? There is no fault here, because mental pleasure (*cetasika-sukha*) is intended.
Here, the inclusion of “mental joy” (*somanassa*) serves as a qualification, just as one says “the tree is a *siṃsapā*.

By the term “impermanent,” he states the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) of equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*) by way of the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-dukkhatā*), or indeed the disadvantage of all feelings.
The other two terms should be applied respectively according to the state of suffering and pleasure of the feelings, or alternatively, all three terms should be applied generally to all feelings.
"This" refers to the impermanent nature of feeling in the sense of its non-existence after having existed; its painful nature in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away;
and [its nature as not-self] in two ways: through aging and through death.
The state of being subject to change is the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) of feeling, from which arises supreme compassion or distress.
Regarding the phrase "the escape from feeling" (*vedanāya nissaraṇaṃ*): here, "from feeling" (*vedanāya*) is an ablative expression.
As long as one does not abandon the desire and lust bound up with feeling, this person remains clinging to feeling. But when that desire and lust...
When he abandons it, then this person is escaped from and dissociated from feeling; thus, the abandoning of desire and lust is stated to be the escape from feeling.
And here, by the mention of "feeling," the material and immaterial phenomena that are co-nascent, supported by, and objects of feeling are certainly included;
therefore, this should be understood as the inclusion of all five aggregates of clinging.

However, the teaching has been presented by way of feeling (*vedanā*). The reason for this has already been stated; or else, this meaning should be clarified by means of the method of the "conveying of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*).
In that context, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) included under the mention of feeling constitute the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*);

the ignorance (*avijjā*) and other factors included under the mention of the origin of feelings constitute the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*); and [the truths of cessation and the path are shown] by way of the terms "passing away" (*atthaṅgama*) and "escape" (*nissaraṇa*).
The truth of cessation, and by the phrase "having known as it really is," the truth of the path; thus, in this context, the four truths are to be understood.

Because the remaining types of clinging have their root in clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), and because when clinging to sensual pleasures has been abandoned there is no remainder of clinging, it is said:
"through the absence of desire and lust, he is without clinging. "Liberated through non-clinging" refers to his own attainment of the fruit of the path.
The Blessed One shows this by means of the passage beginning with “of feelings.

For the King of Dhamma points out the ground for the arising of that omniscient knowledge— along with its preliminary practice— by virtue of which, through having thoroughly penetrated the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu), he was able to analyze this speculative view in detail, together with its causes and its destinations.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Theory of Partial Eternity (Ekaccasassatavāda): 38.
One who holds that some among beings and formations are eternal is a "partial-eternalist" (ekaccasassata); this refers to the theory of partial eternity.

Thus, because they hold that "these [beings] exist," they are called "partial-eternalists" (*ekaccasassatikā*). Furthermore, since the doctrine of partial eternity belongs to them—that is, it is their view—they are known as "proponents of partial eternity" (*ekaccasassatavādā*);
therefore, in order to show this meaning, he said, "proponents of partial eternity.
In this same manner, the meaning of "partial-non-eternalists" (*ekacca-asassatikā*) should also be understood. Now, one might ask: regarding the term "partial-eternalists"...
When this was said, does the conclusion that some [beings] are non-eternal become established for others?
Truly, it is established in meaning, but not in terms of the literal expression. Therefore, in order to make it perfectly clear, it is stated: "some who hold to non-eternalism.
For here, the Lord of Dhamma does not teach the Dhamma by leaving anything remaining; thus, it is said: "some who hold to eternalism."
"In this phrase": they are said to be "grasped," and the meaning is shown accordingly. Or, "here" refers to this teaching;
for thus the first three doctrines are analyzed by way of beings (*satta*), while the fourth is analyzed by way of formations (*saṅkhāra*).
The statement, "those who hold to partial eternalism regarding formations," is spoken by way of showing the actual nature of those phenomena which are grasped as being eternal by them.
But this is not by way of viewing the mind as being partly eternal. For his view is that what is considered eternal is indeed the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).

Therefore he said: "Or it is called 'mind'... [it] will endure. Indeed, it is impossible for one who is not insane to assert that a state which he himself admits has been conditioned by causes is also permanent and stable. By this, [the argument] that "because it possesses the nature of arising, passing away, and stability... [is refuted].

By such statements as "it may be permanent, it may be impermanent, it may be indescribable," the irrationality of the theory of the sevenfold predication (*sattabhaṅgavāda*) is demonstrated. Herein, this demonstration of its irrationality is as follows:

if it were said that "by the very same nature by which a phenomenon is said to exist, by that same nature that phenomenon does not exist," and so forth, then there would be the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekantavāda*). But if [it were said] by another [nature], then [it would be rational].

It is not the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekantavāda). Nor is it reasonable to assert here the existence of a connection with another place and so forth, because that is established for all the world and there is no dispute regarding it.

However, as for those who say: "Just as when a golden jar is fashioned into a crown, the state of being a jar perishes, the state of being a crown arises, yet the state of being gold remains; in the same way, some property of all phenomena [remains]."
"Something perishes, something arises, but the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) remains. They should be asked: "What is that gold which persists in both the jar and the crown?
If it is the form and so forth (rūpādi), then like sound, it is impermanent. If it is the collection of form and so forth, a 'collection' is merely a conventional designation (sammutimatta).
Neither its existence, its non-existence, nor its permanence can be established. Thus, this is the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekantavāda).

It could not be so. Furthermore, the fault in the alteration or non-alteration of phenomena (dhamma) and the possessor of phenomena (dhammin) has already been stated during the investigation of eternalism (sassatavāda).

Therefore, that [fault] should be understood according to the method explained therein. Moreover, since the self (attā) and the world (loka)—whether considered permanent, impermanent, or indescribable—are admitted to exist in the ultimate sense (paramatthato), they must possess one of the forms such as permanence, or else—

[This refers to] lamps and so forth. For it is impossible to discern in lamps and such things—which possess the nature of arising and passing away—that they have a nature that is permanent, impermanent, or inexpressible, in the same way that one might [discern] any one of the [alternatives] such as permanence for a soul (*jīva*). Thus, just as with the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅga*), the other predications are likewise impossible;
therefore, the doctrine of the sevenfold predication should be understood as untenable.
And herein, those who maintain the doctrine that "the Lord is eternal, but other beings are impermanent" are eternalists regarding some beings, such as the proponents of the Lord (Īśvara).

Those who maintain the doctrine that "ultimate atoms are eternal and stable, while dyads and so forth are impermanent" are eternalists regarding some conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), such as the followers of Kaṇāda.
Is it not the case that they hold: "some phenomena are eternal, and some are non-eternal"?
In this doctrine, the determination that the eye and so forth are impermanent is simply the realization of their true nature;
how, then, could this be a wrong view? Or who says that "the determination that the eye and so forth are impermanent is a wrong view"?
Rather, it is the adherence to the permanence of certain phenomena that are actually impermanent which constitutes wrong view here.
However, by that [view] occurring even once, the realization of the non-eternality of the eye and so forth is corrupted;

because it is mixed with [the view of] association, like clarified butter mixed with poison, it is incapable of performing its own function and thus does not deserve to be placed on the side of right vision.
Or rather, although the eye and so forth are determined to be non-eternal, they are still regarded by those holding wrong views as having the very nature of a soul (*jīva*) superimposed upon them.
When they are grasped, the state of wrong view regarding their realization cannot be prevented. For this very reason, it was said: “‘The eye, indeed...

... ‘the body, indeed—this is my self,’ and so forth. And having done so, even the doctrine of analysis (*vibhajjavāda*), which proceeds by way of the unconditioned and conditioned elements respectively, stating that “some phenomena are eternal, some are non-eternal,” [is thus accounted for].
The objection that "one falls into the doctrine of partial-eternalism" has no basis, because this involves a correct apprehension of the true nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.

While it is certainly a false view (*micchā-dassana*)—specifically so in the former case—to grasp impermanent phenomena as "eternal," the apprehension of what is actually eternal as "eternal" is not a false view, because it is an apprehension in accordance with their true nature. [This applies] only to those things that are actually impermanent.

However, the statement that this doctrine is a "different view" (vādantara) is made because it functions by making a distinction among the phenomena to be grasped— namely, that "some phenomena are eternal,
while others are non-eternal. And in this case, it cannot be said that "because a part is included within the whole,
the apprehension of partial eternity merges with the apprehension of absolute eternity," for the proponent [speaks] according to the specific distinctions within his own domain.
Because two types of doctrines prevail. For one group of theorists is attached to the view that "all phenomena are eternal," while another group holds that "some are eternal.
The total exhaustion of conditioned formations (*saṅkhārā*) without remainder and the grasping of only a single portion are indeed well-known as these two doctrines.
Furthermore, regarding the continuity of the aggregates (*khandha-pabandha*), which consists of many kinds of physical bases (*samussaya*) as well as a single kind of physical basis:
Because of the nature of their dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*).

For even the fourfold type of eternalist has become one who adheres dogmatically to the eternity of the mass of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*)—which are dependent upon a physical body (*rūpakāya*) of various kinds according to the distinction of birth—due to grasping the dissolution of the physical body through direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), tradition (*anussava*), and so forth.
And thus it is said: "Having passed away from there, he arose elsewhere," and "They pass away and reappear," etc. [He is] one who attains distinction.

The partial-eternalist (ekaccasassatika) produced an adherence by grasping at the aspect of eternity within the continuity of phenomena (*dhammapabandha*), without having discerned the distinction [between them], because that adherence has as its object the continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) comprised within a single existence.
And thus, in all three doctrines, it is stated only this much: "He recollects that past life, but does not recollect beyond that."

It has been stated that for the logicians—the proponents of eternalism (*sassatavāda*) and partial-eternalism (*ekaccasassatavāda*)—the specific adherence to eternalism is indeed clearly evident because its object consists of both material and immaterial phenomena.
39. "With the passing of a long period of time" means by the removal of those who abide in the cycles of evolution and devolution (*vivaṭṭa*).
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *vaṭṭa* (cycle) when joined with the prefix *saṃ-* signifies destruction; thus he says "it perishes" (*vinassati*), in the sense of dissolution.

The meaning is "it revolves. For it is said that the world contracts (*saṃvaṭṭati*) from the moment the great cloud that causes dissolution arises until not even a subtle formation (*saṅkhāra*) remains. And here, by "world" (*loka*), the receptacle-world consisting of earth and so forth is intended.
"In the upper Brahma-worlds" refers to the form-sphere Brahma-worlds beginning with the Parittasubha. For the eon's emergence [from dissolution] occurs by means of fire.
What is intended here is [the rebirth] that occurs frequently. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "They become conducive to the Ābhassara realm.

Regarding the phrase "or in the formless realms," the word "or" (vā) should be understood as an alternative meaning: "or in other world-systems than those world-systems currently undergoing contraction.
For it cannot be known that "all beings in the states of deprivation (apāya) arise at that time in the form or formless realms," since [they remain] in the states of deprivation.
Because it is impossible for those with the longest lifespan to be reborn in the human world.

Although all beings are produced by the mind of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra-manas*), the beings of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) are called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because they are produced by the mind alone, without external conditions.

If this were so, would it not follow that beings of the sense-sphere (*kāmabhava*) who are of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) would also be mind-made? It does not follow, because [the term applies] to that which consists of higher consciousness (*adhicitta*).
Showing that the term "mind-made" (*manomaya*) is used for beings produced by an extraordinary mind, he says: "They are mind-made because they are produced by means of jhāna.
If it is argued that this would imply that even beings of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*) are mind-made, the answer is no;

for in that case, there is no possibility of suspecting that they must be produced by external conditions, nor is it possible to apply the restrictive definition that they are "produced by mind alone."
This conventional expression "mind-made" (*manomaya*) is well-established in the world regarding beings belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
For thus do the proponents of the Vedas describe the self in five ways: "consisting of food, consisting of drink, consisting of mind, consisting of bliss, and consisting of consciousness.

Even in the doctrine of annihilationism, it will be said: "divine, material, mind-made. They are called *subhā* because a beautiful radiance (*sobhanā pabhā*) exists within them. "In the highest sense" (*ukkamsena*)—
This is said with reference to the Ābhassara devas; however, the Parittābha and Appamāṇābha devas remain for two and four eons respectively.
"Eight eons" means eight great eons (mahākappa). 40.
"It forms" refers to the earth, the supporting water, the sustaining wind, the great earth, and so forth, beginning from the arising of the great rain-cloud that brings about prosperity.
It stands by way of simultaneous arising; or rather, the meaning is "it originates," since verbal roots have multiple meanings.
"By nature" means by its own essence (*sabhāva*); this is connected with the word "empty" (*suñña*). He states the reason for that:

"because of the non-existence of beings born there"—the meaning is "because they have not arisen. By this, it is shown how certain celestial palaces (*vimānas*) [are empty] because of the beings born therein...
It shows that because they have been cut off, they are empty, and not in this way [as one might otherwise think].
The Brahma-pārisajja, Brahma-purohita, and Mahābrahmā deities, as well as those belonging to the Brahma-kāyika realm, and even the ground which is their dwelling place, are called "Brahma-kāyika.
That which has kamma as its condition by way of decisive support (upanissaya) is "kamma-paccayā. Alternatively, it refers to the kamma of the beings born there that is undergoing ripening.

Because it exists as a cooperative condition (*sahakārī-paccaya*), it is a condition for karma; thus, it is a "kamma-condition" (*kammapaccaya*). That which has temperature (*utu*) as its origin is "temperature-originated" (*utusamuṭṭhānā*).

Alternatively, the reading is *kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānā*: a condition accompanied by karma, or a condition that has become an auxiliary to karma, is a "kamma-condition"; that very temperature is the "kamma-condition-temperature," and that is its origin.
It should be joined [to the context]. "Therein" means in the plane of the Brahmakāyika devas, which is described as the "Brahmavimāna.
To the question, "How can there be rebirth for those established in the superior plane of the second jhāna in the inferior plane of the first jhāna?
he says, "Then, of beings," and so forth. "Descending" means they go to a lower plane by way of rebirth.
"Short-lived" means that although a sublime meritorious deed has been performed, one is short-lived because the continuity of the result due to arise from it is of limited measure.
"By the measure of the lifespan itself" means by the maximum measure of the lifespan. But what is this so-called "maximum lifespan," and how is its measure delimited? It is said:

it is that which, for various beings in their respective specific states of existence, arises through the influence of the decisive support (*upanissaya*) of a previously established aspiration for that state of existence.

Just as there are specific distinctions regarding the color, shape, and size of the limbs of the body, so too, for beings in the various realms of existence (gati) and classes of beings (nikāya)—namely, those born from a womb, those of the sense-sphere gods (kāmāvacara-deva), and those of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara)—there is generally a fixed determination of limits.
This is the fixed duration of the continuity of kamma-result (vipāka), which is supported by conditions arising from such factors as semen, blood, temperature, and food.
This [duration] persists for its own respective momentary existence, even for those [mental states] that endure only for a single moment.

Because the material and immaterial life-faculties (rūpa- and arūpa-jīvitindriya) function by maintaining the state of established existence for material and immaterial phenomena, they are not merely protectors by being the cause of their momentary stability;
rather, they are also the cause for the non-interruption of the continuous succession [of those phenomena] until the cutting off of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Therefore, because they have life as their cause, they are called "life" (āyu) through a metaphorical application of the cause to the effect, according to the limit of their maximum duration.
And it is also called "the supreme limit" (*paramāyūti*). That [limit], however, is fixed for the gods, the denizens of hell, and the inhabitants of Uttarakuru;
for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, it is exclusively and absolutely fixed.
But for the remaining humans, ghosts, and animals, when there is an abundance of karma conducive to long life, it arises from the semen and blood produced by a continuum accompanied by that karma.

And by way of the conditions— such as food and climate— produced by the regular and irregular revolutions of the moon and sun which are rooted in that [kamma], there is an indefinite delimitation in terms of long and short durations;

and just as the determination of specific qualities such as color and shape within various destinies and classes was established for that [being] through the force of previously established aspirations for existence, as proven by observation and tradition, so too...

First, regarding the establishment of the grasp: thus, for beings born in various states of existence, having generally obtained the duration of their stay through seeing and hearing, one should understand that the determination of the initial limit occurs by way of the aspiration for existence that proceeds from clinging to that supreme state.
For it is because karma, in those various states of existence, brings about the production of the specific color and other characteristics determined for each particular rebirth...
It is capable [of producing rebirth], yet it is not capable of producing a result by exceeding the limits of those rebirths where the lifespan is fixed;
therefore it is said, "they pass away precisely at the measure of their lifespan.

For the mode of occurrence of the acquired aggregates (*upādinnaka-khandha*), supported by the sustaining auxiliary conditions that act as protectors, is in fact the supreme lifespan (*paramāyu*). Of that—
Because there is no possibility of remaining even when a residue of karma exists, since one cannot exceed the previously stated limit, it is said:
"He is not able to remain by the power of his own merit alone.
The word "vā" (or) has the sense of an alternative, meaning either for an *asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*, or for half of that, or for less or more than half a *kappa*.
41. "Discontent" (anabhirati) means discontent with dwelling alone. Since that [discontent] is a desire for association with others, it is said: "the longing for the arrival of another being.
Mental distress caused by separation from a beloved object or by failure to obtain a beloved object is "longing" (ukkaṇṭhitā);
in its actual meaning, this is simply an arising of a state of mind associated with displeasure (domanassa), hence it is said: "associated with aversion" (paṭighasampayuttā).

For one who has long delighted in the joy of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), the "fear" (*paritassanā*) mentioned here consists of craving and views which serve as the cause for the grasping at "I" and "mine," arising from the aforementioned grounds for dissatisfaction. These, moreover, are the wavering and trembling of the mind from its prior state;
thus it is said: "trembling and quivering. For this very reason, he says: "the thirsting of craving..."

“Even the longing for views is appropriate. However, as for what was stated in the *Atthuddhāra*—“‘Oh, may other beings too come to this state!’, this is called the longing for craving”—that was said by extracting only the longing for craving from that [passage], in order to show a separate example for the longing for views;
it was not because the longing for views was present there.
It should be understood as "due to non-existence. *Tāsa* is the mind’s trepidation. *Bhayānaka* is a terrifying object or sign that produces intense fear.
By means of that, there is rigidity of the body, which is *chambhitatta*. Regarding the terms *bhaya* (fear) and *saṃvega* (agitation):

here, *bhaya* refers to the knowledge of fear (*bhaya-ñāṇa*) that arises from the state of fearing all conditioned phenomena while one is practicing the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*). *Saṃvega* refers to...

It is knowledge accompanied by moral dread (*ottappa*), or moral dread itself. It is the knowledge of being terrified of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) through the contemplations of fear, danger, disadvantage, and disenchantment.
It "goes forth" or "proceeds" together with [something], or it "covers over" faults; thus it is *sahabyo*, meaning a companion.
The state of that is *sahabyatā*. (42) The intention is: "He stands having overcome these beings. For he, by virtue of being praiseworthy and by virtue of his excellence...
And because he thinks of himself, "I stand having overcome those beings," it is therefore said, "I am the eldest.

By the statement "I am the tenfold one" (*aññadatthu daso*), which expresses the absence of any obstruction to seeing and the quality of grasping the specific objects of knowledge, he claims for himself unobstructed vision;
thus he says, "the meaning is 'I see everything'. Regarding the phrase "of the past and the future" (*bhūtabhavyānaṃ*):
They have been (*ahesuṃ*) thus they are "beings" (*bhūtā*); they are, and they will be, thus they are "capable" (*bhavyā*).

In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, the meaning of the word *bhavya* is shown solely by way of the present tense. "At the first moment of consciousness" means at the moment of rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).

Although that Brahmā, due to his unstable vision, [lacked] the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakatāñāṇa*) even though it had been familiarized in previous births by an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).

Having relinquished [the view], one who is perverted by the manifestation of beings— which depends merely upon the arising of consciousness through the power of supernormal transformation (vikubbaniddhi)—
and who leaps into the vision of a creator-god (issarakutta) with such thoughts as "I am the Lord, the maker, the fashioner," is established solely by way of adherence (abhinivesa),
not by way of establishing [another], because it is said, "it occurs to him thus"; rather, it is precisely by way of the sequence of establishment.
However, in order to show that such a dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*) had arisen in him, it was said: "desiring to establish [his view] by means of a reason" and "having made a formal declaration.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "For what reason? and so forth. In this context, "mental aspiration" (*manopaṇidhi*) means an aspiration by the mind alone;
the meaning is that it is merely a movement of the mind. "Such a state of being" (*itthabhāva*) refers to this particular mode of existence.
However, since "ittham" here refers to the state of being a Brahmā, it is said that "the meaning is 'the state of a Brahmā'.

But is it not the case that immediately upon rebirth, the gods possess a reflective awareness such as, "Having passed away from such-and-such a destination, we have been reborn here by means of such-and-such karma"?
True, they do; however, that [awareness] pertains to the knowledge of the ownership of one's own actions (*kammassakataññāṇa*) regarding previous births.

[This refers to] those whose underlying tendencies (*ajjhāsaya*) were correctly established. However, it should be understood that these beings, even in previous births, had fixed attachments due to the perception of a creator god (*issara*). Therefore, it was said: "By this, we... and so forth. 43.
*Īsa* means one who rules; the meaning is "the overcomer. A great ruler is a *maheśa*. Furthermore, because of his well-established greatness as a ruler, he is [called] by others...

“Maheso” (the Great Lord) means one who possesses great authority (*mahesakkha*) by virtue of being worthy of such a designation; the etymological meaning should be understood as “one who is exceedingly authoritative, a greater authority” (*mahesakkhatara*).

Since that state of possessing great authority is recognized through the perfection of lordship and a retinue, it is therefore said: “one who is even more renowned on account of his sovereignty and retinue.”

"Comes right here" means that one comes by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) precisely in this human world. Regarding the phrase "a certain being" (*yaṃ aññataro satto*), *yaṃ* is merely a particle;
or else, it is a designation of the personal pronoun in the instrumental case, meaning "by which state," or it refers back to the action itself.
"Comes to this state of being" (*itthattaṃ āgacchati*): herein, that which is this coming to the state of being—this [is what is meant].
The meaning is: "it is possible. This same method applies to these phrases as well: "he goes forth," "he attains concentration of mind," and "he recollects past lives.
For this phrase, "But it is possible, monks, that a certain being...
should be joined individually with each of the phrases beginning with "he goes forth."

45. "Corrupters by sport" (*khiḍḍāpadosika*) means those who corrupt through sport; they are called "corrupters by sport" because they are indeed corrupters by sport, or because corruption by sport exists within them.
"Beyond the proper time" (*atikkantavelaṃ*) means excessively, that is, having transgressed the time for the enjoyment of food.
"The pleasure arising from sexual union" (*methunasampayogena uppajjanaka-sukhaṃ*) is the pleasure of play and laughter, the nature of delight, the essence of sensual gratification.
Regarding this, what is the food of the gods, and when does the time for eating come? For all the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), ambrosia (sudhā) is the food;
it is most exquisite for those in the higher realms compared to those below, and they consume it day by day according to their respective days.
Some, however, say that they consume an amount of ambrosia the size of a cat's footprint, which [enters] through the tongue.

They say that as soon as it is placed [in the mouth], it pervades the body from the tips of the hair to the tips of the nails, and it becomes capable of sustaining them for seven days according to those very days.
The statement "eating and drinking continuously" is said by way of supposition.
The strength of the kamma-born heat is due to its being produced by sublime merit, and because of the digestion of the sublime, heavy, and unctuous food of *sudhā*.
And: the feebleness of the body born of karma (*karajakāya*) is due to its being soft and delicate.
For it was for this very reason that the Blessed One said to Sakka, the king of the gods, who was unable to stand upon the natural ground in the Indasāla Cave, "Resolve [to make] your body gross.
"Of them" refers to human beings. "Basis" refers to the body born of karma. "Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri.
47. *Manena* means by a mind corrupted by envy (*issā*). *Manopadoso* (corruption of mind) is the corruption of the mind itself through the influence of envy;
or alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: "those who possess this [corruption], which has become the cause of their destruction, are thus called *manopadosika*.

Regarding the phrase "one who is not angry protects": for one who is angry, that anger—because the other person does not retaliate in kind—is abandoned without further grasping (*anupādāna*) after arising only once.
If it is not cultivated, it cannot cause one to fall away; rather, like a fire that reaches the edge of water, it is extinguished.

Therefore, when it is not provoked, anger protects one from falling away. But when both [the object and the subject] are provoked, anger arises with an increasingly intensified manifestation toward one another, having the function of burning its support.
As it arises, striking at the heart-base, it consumes the extremely delicate royal body.
It destroys them, and consequently the entire personal existence (*attabhāva*) vanishes. Therefore he said, “But in both cases,” and so forth.
And thus the Blessed One said: “With minds corrupted toward one another, their bodies exhausted... [they] pass away. “Dhammatā” means the fixed order of things (*dhammaniyāma*).
This occurs because of the weakness of their body born of karma (*karajakāya*) and the intensity of the anger arising at that moment.
The intention is that "falling away" (*cavana*) is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of those material and immaterial phenomena. 49.

"He sees the breaking up of the eye and so forth": because he sees the occurrence of change upon the meeting of opposing conditions, and because they reach a state of non-appearance at the end, he sees their destruction; this is due to the grossness of the breaking up of material phenomena. "Having provided the condition..."
"Having become a condition by way of the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya) and others. The term "more powerful" is stated with reference to the more rapid dissolution of consciousness;
for while a single material form persists, sixteen moments of consciousness dissolve.
"He does not perceive the dissolution" means that although consciousness dissolves moment by moment, it dissolves precisely by way of being the proximity-condition for the subsequent [moment].

Because the arising of the subsequent consciousness occurs as if concealing the non-existence of the preceding consciousness, the aspect of existence is more powerful and manifest, whereas the aspect of non-existence is not; thus, one does not perceive the destruction of the consciousness.

Furthermore, this meaning is clearly understood through the illustration of the firebrand circle (*alātacakra*). For the proponent of reasoning (*takkīvādī*), however, because of the method of diversity...
Because even the single principle of oneness is grasped incorrectly due to its extreme remoteness, it gives rise to the dogmatic adherence [abhinivesa] such as:
"This very consciousness, which proceeds in a uniform manner at all times, is this very self (attā), eternal," and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Not seeing that... and so on.
[Commentary on the Doctrine of Finitude and Infinite] (Antānantavādavaṇṇanā)
53. Regarding the term *antānantikā*: here, *anta* (end) refers to that which is measured (*amati*) or traversed (*gacchati*), namely the limit (*osāna*) or boundary (*mariyādā*) of one's own nature.

By its negation is meant *ananta* (infinite). The terms *antānanta* (both finite and infinite), *nevantānānanta* (neither finite nor infinite), and *antānantā* (the finites and infinites) are used through a general designation (*sāmañña-niddesa*) or by the principle of "one-remainder" (*ekasesa*), as in such expressions as "the six sense bases have name-and-form as their condition.
But of what is there an end or infinity? Of the world (*loka*). It is so called because it is viewed (*lokīyati*).
For those who hold views and seek escape from saṃsāra, it is called "the world" (loka) because merit and demerit, as well as their result, are experienced (*lokīyanti*) therein;
thus, it is the self that has come to be designated by that term. Therefore the Blessed One said: "They proclaim the finitude and infinity of the world. But what is this self?
It is the sign of the kasiṇa which has become the object of jhāna. For herein, this holder of views perceives the world.

And so it has been said: "Having grasped that as 'the world'. Some, however, say: "In this context, both jhāna and the states associated with it are grasped as 'self' and 'the world'. The term *antānanta* refers to a doctrine associated with the finite and the infinite;

for example, "spears are moving" [where the word for spear implies those carrying the spears], or "beds are crying out" [where the word for bed implies those on the beds]. Since these [views] possess that [association], they are called *antānantikā*.

The Finitists and Infinitists. Now, because they hold views—according to the method already stated—regarding the finite, the infinite, or both the finite and the infinite, they are called "Proponents of the Finite and Infinite" (*antānantavādā*).
Therefore, having stated "Proponents of the Finite and Infinite" in the Commentary, the meaning is analyzed by the words "or the finite," and so forth.
Here it is asked: It is indeed appropriate for the first three proponents [to be characterized] by finitude, infinitude, and both finitude and infinitude.
Because it occurs as a doctrine concerning [the world] as having an end, it is "end-and-non-end-ism" (*antānantikatta*);
but as for the latter, why is it "end-and-non-end-ism" since it occurs by way of negating both of those? Precisely because it is a doctrine occurring by way of negating both of them.
For even a doctrine that negates both the end and the non-end has the end and the non-end as its object, since it occurs with reference to them. It is for this very purpose [that it is so called].
For it is with this intention that it is stated in the Commentary: “They are proponents who speak by taking [a specific position] as their starting point.

Alternatively, just as in the third argument both finitude and infinitude can occur for the very same person due to the difference in location, so too in the argument of the logicians (takkī), because both are possible through the difference in time, both are indeed stated by way of mutual negation. How so? By the negation of finitude...
For "endlessness" (anantatā) is what is spoken of, and by the negation of endlessness, "finiteness" (antavantatā) [is implied].
Furthermore, there is no third position regarding both the finite and the infinite, because it is the distinction of time that is intended here. This is what is meant:

since it is traditionally reported that this self—designated as the "world"—was at some time directly perceived as infinite by great seers who had attained special distinctions, therefore it is not "finite. However, since it was [perceived] by those very same [seers]...
"Perhaps he has seen that it is finite," so he hears; therefore, he does not conclude that it is infinite.

And just as this is the case by way of reasoning based on hearsay (*anussuti-takkī*), so too should it be applied, as appropriate, to those who reason based on recollection of past births (*jātissara-takkī*) and others.

For this reasoner, because the increase of the counterpart signs (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) is preceded by their non-increase, due to the lack of direct perception regarding the time of their increase, he remains at the mere level of hearsay and the like.
Having stood [in that position], he rejects it by saying, "Neither finite. But by way of the non-extension of time, he says, "Nor infinite";
for there is an absolute absence of both finitude and infinitude, just as in the case of "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.
And this rejection of the preceding three positions must necessarily be understood in this way, because they lack the specific characteristics intended by him.
Otherwise, the fourth position would merely fall into the side of distraction (*vikkhepa*).

For there is no mode of self that is distinct from being finite, infinite, or both; and the proponent of reasoning (*takkīvādī*) follows the path of logic. Furthermore, those two—being finite and infinite—are not incompatible even in a single entity when considered according to the distinction of time.
However, some [hold that] if this self were finite, the accomplishment of functions such as remembering rebirths in distant locations would be impossible.
It could not be so. If, on the other hand, it were infinite, then for one standing here, there would also be the experience of pleasure and pain in the heavenly worlds, the hells, and so forth.
But if it were both finite and infinite, there would be a conjunction of both those faults.
Therefore, they explain the occurrence of the fourth view by way of such reasoning: "The self is finite" and "the self is infinite" are undeclared. Even in this way, it is logical.

First, as for the two latter proponents, their status as "proponents of the finite and infinite" (antānantika) is due to the fact that their doctrine has both [the finite and the infinite] as its objects, by way of the finite and the infinite.
But how is it that the two former proponents are individually "proponents of the finite and infinite"?

It is through figurative application (upacāra). For the term *antānantika*, which applies to the proponents of the finite and infinite when they are taken together, is established there [in each individual case] even separately.

It occurs among those who propound views on the finite and the infinite, just as there is a separate application of the eight liberations for each of the formless jhānas, and as in the world one speaks of "a hundred creatures.
Alternatively, this conventional expression was used there by way of its prior occurrence before the time of dogmatic adherence;
for prior to the attainment of such mental concentration (*cetosamādhi*) by those proponents of views, [it was so designated].

The state of being an "extremist" (*antānantika*)—a designation established by way of a reflection that clings to both modes [of thought], namely, "Is this world finite, or is it infinite?"—is still expressed using the conventional terminology of the previously established usage, even when a one-sided adherence has arisen therein due to the attainment of a specific conclusion. 54–60.

"In the manner stated" refers to [the definition] from the perspective of etymology, such as "one who reasons is a *takkī*," and from the perspective of classification, such as "there are four kinds of *takkīs*."

In terms of meaning, it is according to the method stated under the doctrine of eternalism (*sassatavāda*). "By way of following what was previously seen" means by the recollection of what was previously apprehended—such as having limits and so forth—by means of consciousness functioning as seeing.
By taking it this way, the inclusion here of those who rely on hearsay (*anussuti*) and those with pure reasoning (*suddhatakkī*) is established.
Alternatively, by the very mention of "view" (*diṭṭhi*), [the inclusion of] such things as "watching dancing, singing, music, and theatrical performances" is also implied.
It should be understood that the inclusion of the views beginning with "like a palm fruit" is likewise intended to include the [views] beginning with "the soul is like a palm fruit.

Because these doctrines proceed by way of misapprehending the soul as existing at all times—through such expressions as "it is finite"—they must be seen as being comprised within the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). For he will say later: "The remaining ones are eternalist views.
Commentary on the Eel-Wriggling Doctrine (*amarāvikkhepavāda*):

61. "It does not die" means it is not annihilated. "Vividha" (various) refers to the manifold ways of evasion; "nānappakāra" (of different kinds) refers to the casting aside by another, that is, the throwing back of the arguments of opposing disputants.
Alternatively, they are called *amarāvikkhepino* because they evade through the view and speech of the "immortal" (*amara*).
They are *amarāvikkhepikā* precisely because they are those who practice such evasion. They run hither and thither because they do not abide in any single nature.
Alternatively, the meaning of the word should be understood according to the previous method as "those who scatter like immortals.

(62) Since those who advocate distraction lack the power of knowledge to understand even unwholesome states among the superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) except by way of their specific intrinsic natures (*sabhāvabheda*), the meaning of the terms "wholesome" and "unwholesome" is [to be understood] solely by way of the wholesome and unwholesome courses of action (*kusalākusalakammapatha*). This is according to the first method.
In order to clarify the "endless equivocation" (*amarāvikkhepa*) by way of its boundless wavering, it is said: "‘It is not so for me’ is an unrestricted equivocation.
In this context, "unrestricted equivocation" means causing wavering without settling upon any single mode among eternalism and so forth;
the meaning is that it is a denial of whatever mode is questioned by the opponent. By way of the second method...
In order to demonstrate the "Eternalist-Eel-Wriggler" (amarāvikkhepika) mode of evasion regarding the immortal realm, he said, "When asked, 'Is this wholesome?

and so forth. Alternatively, because they reject each respective doctrine by means of a non-committal negation—such as "I do not say even thus"—through the denial of eternalism, partial-eternalism, annihilationism, and agnosticism, they are called "Eternalist-Eel-Wrigglers" due to their practice of endless wriggling. But as for themselves...
Because he does not stand firm in any position due to his unstable speech, it is said: "But he himself... [etc. ...answers.
Now, by not answering regarding what is wholesome and so forth, he clarifies that very instability with the words: "When asked, 'Is this wholesome?
and so on. For this very reason, he says: "He does not stand even in one position."
63. Even for one who does not understand wholesome and unwholesome states as they really are, if there were to arise in me desire or lust when people—
on account of my making such declarations as "this is wholesome" regarding what is indeed wholesome, and "this is unwholesome" regarding what is indeed unwholesome—
pay honor and respect, thinking, "Oh, what a wise man he is!"— it is in this sense that the meaning here is possible.
“Hatred or aversion” should be applied here by way of the reverse of what was stated [in the previous section].

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, the application is made by way of lust and the other [defilements] that have one’s own state of being wise as their object. “The dyad of desire and lust is clinging” is stated according to the method of the Abhidhamma;
for in the Abhidhamma, it is only craving and views that are presented as “clinging,” whereas in the Suttanta—
Furthermore, hatred (*dosa*) is also called "clinging" (*upādāna*) in such passages as, "Those bound by the clinging of anger fall into distress.
Therefore it is said: "Or both [greed and hatred] are 'clinging' by way of firm grasping. Firm grasping means non-relinquishing.
For even aversion (*paṭigha*), when it proceeds by way of resentment (*upanāha*) and so forth, does not relinquish its object. "Vihananam" means harming or obstructing.
For even lust, by way of its burning nature and its state of agitation, afflicts its support;
thus, the connection is that it grasps the object with the desire to destroy it.
64. "By wisdom" means by *paññā*. For that quality (*dhamma*) endowed with which one is called "wise" is "wisdom" (*paṇḍicca*).
By this, he shows wisdom consisting of what has been heard and reflected upon (*sutacintāmaya-paññā*), not innate wisdom (*sābhāvikapaññā*) produced by natural karma.
Because the word *kata* expresses the general sense of action—as in such terms as *katavijjo* (“one who has mastered the sciences”)—the word *kata* here denotes being devoted to knowledge;

thus he says, “those who have understood the doctrines of others. One who can pierce with the tip of a hair’s strand a hair that has been split sevenfold is intended by the term *vālavedhī* (“hair-piercer”).

65–6. And here, although the first three [types of persons] are indeed dull because they lack comprehension of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of wholesome and other phenomena, they still possess a specific degree of comprehension regarding their own lack of comprehension of those wholesome and other phenomena.

Because that [specific degree] is absent, only the last one is described as being dull and utterly bewildered (*momūha*). Is it not the case that even for the last one, [there is the thought]: "There is a world beyond"?

"Even though there is indeed an awareness of his own non-comprehension of the Dhamma— based on such statements as, 'If it were so for me that "there is a world beyond," I would declare it to you as such;

yet it is not so for me'— nevertheless, he lacks the same degree of dread and loathing for falsehood and other evils that arises from declaring a Dhamma one has not fully understood, as was the case with those who preceded him."

But he was indeed utterly deluded. Alternatively, by means of the evasion of the question through such statements as “Even thus it is not so for me,” he merely displays the posing of a counter-question—“If you ask me whether there is a world beyond”—rather than his own lack of comprehension of the Dhamma;
for this very reason, he is specifically called “both dull-witted and utterly deluded. For it is precisely because of that [evasion] that [the Buddha spoke of] one who speaks in such a manner...
Concerning Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, it was said: "He is the most dull and the most deluded among these recluses and brahmins.
In that context, the question "Is there a world beyond? is asked from the standpoint of the view of eternalism (*sassatadassana*) or from the standpoint of right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).

The question "Is there no world beyond? is asked from the standpoint of the view of nihilism (*natthikadassana*) or from the standpoint of right view. "There both is and... [is the next part of the inquiry].
The question, "There is no world beyond," is asked either by way of the view of annihilationism or by way of right view.

When there is a negation of the three aforementioned modes—namely, "There both is and is not a world beyond"—since no other mode is possible, the world beyond is of an indefinable nature in terms of existence and non-existence;
this is [the answer] by way of right view, having prioritized the evasion known as "eel-wriggling" (vikkhepa).
Or [this is] a question. The meaning in the remaining three tetrads should also be understood according to the method already stated.
For, just as with the triad of meritorious formations (*puññasaṅkhārattika*), the meaning included in the first tetrad by means of the triad of bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhārattika*) is the same.
By the remaining three tetrads, it is included according to the method of the exhortation regarding the fruit of self-identification, merit, and so forth.
The Evasive (Amarāvikkhepika), because he finds none of the views such as eternalism to his own liking, employs evasion everywhere, saying, "It is not thus for me," and so forth.
In this context, the phrase "It is not thus for me" and so on demonstrates the manner of evading by way of negating each specific form in which he is questioned.
But is it not the case that for one who propounds evasion, the admission of the side of evasion [itself] constitutes a position?
Is persistence (avaṭṭhāna) appropriate? No; because even there he was confused, and because the doctrine of evasion proceeds precisely by way of denial.

For instance, when Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta was questioned by King Ajātasattu regarding the visible fruit of recluseship, he gave an evasive answer by means of denying the threefold questions concerning the next world and so forth.

Here it may be asked: Surely this Eel-Wriggler, not understanding as they truly are the states such as the wholesome and so forth, nor the triad of the next world and so on, merely resorts to evasion whenever he is questioned on various points;
how then can he be considered one who holds a speculative view? For he is not like one who refuses to speak because he does not know the matter asked about.
Is it logical that one becomes a holder of wrong views merely by resorting to evasion? It is said: No, indeed;
it is not by mere evasion that one becomes a holder of wrong views, but rather through false adherence (*micchābhinivesa*).

For it is precisely the person who has adhered falsely through the adherence to eternalism (*sassatābhinivesa*), and who—due to dullness of intellect—fails to comprehend as they truly are such things as wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) and the triad of the other world (*paraloka-attika*), etc., who [becomes a holder of wrong views].
He falls into equivocation because he is unable to make another understand a matter that he himself does not understand, and out of fear of lying and other such faults.
For he will say: "Of those views, seven are annihilationist views; the rest are eternalist views.
Alternatively, it is due to his lack of comprehension and lack of conviction regarding merit, demerit, and their respective results, concerning the question about their object.

It should be understood that this view, which arises in one who produces a liking and preference for it, thinking that "only the causing of distraction is beautiful," and who then adheres to it, is a distinct view in its own right, just like the sevenfold view (sattabhaṅgadiṭṭhi). And so it has been said:
"The view and the speech of one who follows a course of views are without limit. But how is this included within the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi)? By way of annihilationism (uccheda).
Because there is no non-adherence [to views]. There is no one who truly knows the nature of phenomena (*dhamma*) because the world is full of dispute.

However, by means of the word "just so" (*evameva*), through the mode of grasping that "the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammanijjhānā*) in the world is beginningless," the stain of eternalism (*sassatalesa*) is indeed found here.
The commentary on the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannavāda*).

67. Whatever cause occurs by chance or at will—whether preceded by growth or not—the view that takes as its object the mode of spontaneous arising of the aggregates known as the self and the world is called "fortuitous origination" (*adhiccasamuppanna*).
This is because it proceeds by relying on that mode [of spontaneity] and because it is concomitant with that mode, just as [the word] "beds" [is used for those on the beds].
Showing this meaning in the passage, "They cry out, the spears wander about," he said:
"The view that 'the self and the world are arisen by chance' is the 'chance-originated' [view].
(68–73) "The heading of the teaching" means grasping it by way of its preeminence within the teaching; therefore, having made perception itself the primary focus—
The Blessed One gave this teaching, but he did not do so to show that other immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) exist therein;

for that very reason, he said, "without the arising of consciousness," and so forth.
