For just as the Blessed One makes concentration or wisdom the primary focus when teaching supramundane (lokuttara) states, so too does he make consciousness or perception the primary focus when teaching mundane (lokiya) states.

In that regard: "At whatever time one develops supramundane jhāna—right concentration consisting of five factors, right concentration consisting of five knowledges—and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed";
likewise: "At whatever time a wholesome mind pertaining to the sense sphere..."

Suttas such as "A thought arises," "What is your state of mind, monk? "Mind is the forerunner of all states," "There are beings, monks, who are diverse in body and diverse in perception," and "The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," should be seen as establishing this meaning.

Regarding the phrase "in the sphere of the sectarians" (*titthāyatane*), it refers to the doctrine of other sectarians (*aññatitthiya-samaye*). For the sectarians [assert] a specific excellence of rebirth...

Perceiving [this state] as liberation, or having seen the danger and the benefit in the fading away and non-fading away of perception, they produce the attainment of non-perception and arise in the plane of no-opportunity;
they are not followers of the Dispensation. "Having performed the preliminary work on the air-kasina" means:
having produced the first three jhānas on the air-kasina, and having mastered the third jhāna therein, from that...
Having emerged from the fourth jhāna and performed the preliminary work for its attainment, he says: "Having produced the fourth jhāna.
Why, however, is the preliminary work described here specifically with the air-kasina? It is said:

Just as a specific distinction of formless attainment—consisting in the cultivation of dispassion toward form through the elimination of form—is realized by means of certain kasinas that are counterparts to form; so too...

Thus, by means of the contemplation of the formless—which is the cultivation of dispassion toward form—accomplished through the discernment of the formless within a specific *kasiṇa* that serves as a counterpart to the formless due to its lack of distinct physical structure, a specific attainment of form (*rūpa-samāpatti*) is reached.

In this regard, one should proceed by seeing the danger in the occurrence of the formless through such methods as, "Perception is a disease, perception is a boil," and "Fie on the mind! Fie on that mind! and so forth, and by [contemplating] its absence.
The preparation for the form-sphere attainment is by means of the final determination regarding the state of being heated;
however, the development of dispassion toward form consists of the formless attainments along with their access, and among those, specifically the first formless jhāna.
If this is so, should it not be said that "this applies even to the limited-space kasiṇa"? For even that possesses a resemblance to the formless.
This is indeed what some would wish, yet it has not been accepted here by the ancient teachers because it was not included among their teachings.

For just as the development of dispassion toward the form realm (*rūpa-virāga-bhāvanā*) is fully established merely by the existence of phenomena subject to dispassion, and manifests in specific objects that are counterparts to those phenomena subject to dispassion, so too is it with the development of dispassion toward the formless realm (*arūpa-virāga-bhāvanā*);
thus, there is no contradiction in saying this.

However, it should be understood that because this attainment must be practiced by the *titthiyas* (heretics), and because that *jhāna* is practiced only by binding its object within their own sphere of experience,

the former teachers who held such views stated that the preliminary work for the development of dispassion toward the formless (*arūpa-virāga-bhāvanā*) pertains only to the fourth true-kasiṇa (*bhūta-kasiṇa*).
Furthermore, just as in the case of the color-kasiṇas (*vaṇṇa-kasiṇa*), there is indeed a concealment of color even in the first three true-kasiṇas.
The designation (paṇṇatti) as the object of jhāna proceeds solely in accordance with worldly convention.
By doing so, the comparison of the earth-kasiṇa to a mirror or the orb of the moon in the *Visuddhimagga* is justified;
however, the fourth primary-element kasiṇa becomes the objective range of jhāna only as the reflection of the actual element, and thus it alone possesses the character of an immaterial counterpart.
It should be understood that "suitable" refers to the preparatory work (parikamma) mentioned specifically for the air-kasiṇa.
"Right here" means in the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) itself. "Therein" means in the non-percipient existence (asañña-bhava).

If only the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) manifests in the non-percipient existence, how does form proceed there without dependence on the immaterial (arūpa), and how, moreover, [does it proceed] without dependence on the material (rūpa)?
In the formless realm, the formless occurs without [physical] form; this too is of the same nature as that. Why?
Because it is not seen here [in the sense-sphere]. If that is so, then in the fine-material realm, material form should not occur without physical nutriment;
what is the reason? Because it is not seen here. Furthermore, just as for whatever continuum of consciousness there is a cause for its production...
For one who has not abandoned craving for form, [consciousness] proceeds dependent on form because it arises together with form;
but for one whose cause for production has abandoned craving for form, it proceeds without form due to the cause being independent of form.
Likewise, for one whose cause for the production of a continuity of form has abandoned craving for the formless, it proceeds without the formless.
Regarding the phrase "there is a process": in the non-percipient realm (*asaññabhava*), only the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) arises. Now, one might raise the objection:
"How is it to be understood that there, a mere continuity of form proceeds for a long time, devoid of present conditions?
Or for how long does it proceed? Bearing this in mind, he says: "Just as an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring," and so forth.
By this, he shows that it is not merely scripture (*āgama*) but also reasoning (*yutti*) that establishes this point here.

"For just so long" means that, at most, non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*) remain for five hundred great eons (*mahākappa*). "The momentum of jhāna" refers to the momentum of kamma conditioned by the attainment of non-perception (*asaññasamāpatti*).
"It disappears" means it ceases and no longer proceeds due to the cessation of its conditions.
"Here" means in the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*). But how does consciousness arise here from a consciousness that has long since ceased, having transcended many hundreds of eons?
For is it not seen that when the eye has ceased, visual consciousness does not arise? This should not be viewed as an absolute rule.
For even though a mind has long since ceased, because there is no arising of another [mind] of the same class in the interval, [it can give rise to its successor].
It is merely an immediately preceding condition (*anantarapaccaya*), not a seed; rather, karma is the seed.

Therefore, for those who have passed away from the non-percipient realm (*asaññabhava*) due to conditions such as the object (*ārammaṇa*) based on that seed-like karma, rebirth-consciousness (*upapattiviññāṇa*) certainly arises in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Thus he said: "Here, the perception of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhisaññā*) arises. And here, just as in the case of the taking up of flowers according to the law of the seasons,
Just as when a fixed period has been set for trees, the certainty of their flowering is no longer guaranteed once that period of flowering has passed,
even so, when the period for the cultivation of dispassion toward form and formless phenomena— which exist inseparably within the five-aggregate existence—
has expired, then, in accordance with the power of that attainment-period, [the certainty of rebirth] in the formless realm and the non-percipient realm is lost, respectively.
It should be understood that the occurrence of the aggregates takes place both with form and without form. One might ask:

"Is it not the case here that, based on the occurrence of the non-percipient realm—which occurs either at the end of or within the periods of a hundred thousand births and ten aeons of dissolution—an Adhiccasamuppannika (fortuitous-originist) doctrine of many varieties could arise, just like the Sassatavāda (eternalist) doctrine?
True, such a thing is possible; however, because [the non-percipient realm] follows immediately upon [the fine-material realm],...

It should be understood that, by way of rebirth in the non-percipient realm (*asañña-upapatti*), the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhicca-samuppattika-vāda*) is shown as only one from the perspective of its underlying method.

Alternatively, because it is included within the eternalist view (*sassata-diṭṭhi*), the entire method of teaching found in the eternalist doctrine should be applied to the doctrine of fortuitous origination as far as possible; this is the meaning of the following [passage].
For the sake of showing the distinction, the Blessed One taught the doctrine of fortuitous origination without analysis for those who hold it.

Furthermore, the doctrine of fortuitous origination must necessarily be included within the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), because the inclinations of beings on the side of defilement are of two kinds.
Thus it is said in the Commentary: "The views of eternalism and annihilationism..."
And so he will say: "Of those views, seven are annihilationist views; the rest are eternalist views.
But is it not the case that the inclusion of the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannikavāda*) within eternalist views is inappropriate?

For it proceeds by way of such statements as "I indeed did not exist before," and because it grasps at the manifestation of a previously non-existent being, whereas an eternalist view grasps at the perpetual existence of the self and the world.
Is it because [the view] proceeds by asserting, "There is indeed an eternal existence"? No, that is not tenable, because it fails to see the limit in the future.

For even though this doctrine proceeds by way of misapprehending the past limit of oneself and the world—thinking, "I was not previously existing, but have now become transformed into a state of continuity"—nevertheless, from the present time onward, it does not perceive any boundary for them in the future.
And specifically, the eternalist view (sassatavāda) is produced by the failure to see limits regarding the present and future times, as it is said:

"It will remain exactly thus for all eternity. If this is so, is it not inappropriate to include this doctrine and the other eternalist views among those who speculate about the past, since they function by way of misapprehending the future time?
No; because their actual manifestation (samudāgama) belongs to the past portion [of existence].

For their origin is comprised within the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of past existences (*atītasat-pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*), as well as by reasoning (*takka*) produced by hearsay and the like that resemble them;

and it has been described accordingly. Alternatively, the Lord of Dhamma, the foremost of speakers, having himself directly known through unimpeded knowledge everywhere both the non-path and the path as they truly are, and having realized them through direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), [taught them].

These views have been proclaimed; therefore, whatever views have been taught by the Blessed One, and in whatever manner they were taught, they should be accepted with firm conviction exactly as they are.
No investigation through reasoning should be applied here, because this is the domain of the Buddha.
For the domain of the Buddha is inconceivable.
The commentary on the second recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the doctrine of those who speculate about the future:
In such passages as “knowledge regarding the future, those with views regarding the future,” the word *apara* here denotes the future time.

He said: "It is reckoned as the section concerning the future. In such passages as "having speculated about the future limit" (*aparantaṃ kappetvā*), the meaning should be understood according to the method already explained in the case of "having speculated about the past limit" (*pubbantaṃ kappetvā*).
We shall state only the specific distinction. This concludes the commentary on the doctrine of those who maintain that consciousness persists after death (*saññīvāda*).
75. *Uddhamāghātanikā*: the doctrine that proceeds beyond the cemetery (*uddhamāghātana*) is called *uddhamāghātanika*; those who possess this are *uddhamāghātanikā*.
Since those proponents of views (*diṭṭhigatika*) assert that "the self is unchanging after death," it is said:
"They are called *uddhamāghātanikā* because they declare the self to exist beyond the cemetery. Those who possess the doctrine of perception (*saññivāda*) are *saññīvādā*.

“Buddha” is [derived] as in the expression “he has awakened, thus he is a Buddha. Alternatively, the term *saññīvāda* refers to those whose doctrine proceeds by way of a conscious being (*saññī*), according to the method of association;
that is, those for whom the doctrine is one of a conscious being are *saññīvādins*.
76–77. Regarding the phrase “the self possesses form” (*rūpī attā*): here, surely the self must be something distinct from form, just as it is with perception (*saññā*). As for form, too...
Because it is not self-possessed. For in the phrase "the self is percipient," perception here is not the self.
Precisely for that reason it is said: "having grasped the perception occurring therein as 'self'. If this is so, why is the kasiṇa-form spoken of as having been grasped as "self"?
This should not be viewed in the sense of "one who has form because form belongs to him"; rather, it is in the sense of "one whose nature is to be affected (ruppanasīla)."
"Material" (*rūpī*). Here, "materiality" (*ruppaṇa*) refers to the attainment of specific qualities by the kasiṇa-form—whether it has increased or not—in accordance with its similarity to form;
and it cannot be said that this is non-existent, because distinctions such as limitedness or vastness do indeed exist.
If this is so, does it not follow that this doctrine is included within the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*)? No, it is not incorrect, because of the distinction of the body's dissolution.
Because it is intended by him [the Blessed One] as being free from agitation regarding his own future state; for thus it is said: "He is healthy beyond death.

Alternatively, there is no fault even if it is stated that "one who has form is 'possessed of form' (rūpī)"—for we see that even when a distinction is established through conceptual designation, it may be used to express non-distinction, as in the expression "the body of a stone statue" (silāputtakassa sarīraṃ). Or else, "form" (rūpa) is the very nature of being subject to transformation (ruppana).
Form (*rūpa*); that which possesses this is "possessed of form" (*rūpī*), as in [the expressions] "the self" (*attā*) or "form-possessing phenomena" (*rūpino dhammā*).

Having established it thus, the statement "the self is possessed of form" is indeed logically consistent because the self has the nature of form; therefore it was said: "having taken the kasiṇa-form as 'self'.
Because they deny the fruit of action due to their dogmatic assertions, there is no attainment of meditative absorption (*jhāna-samāpatti*) among the Ājīvakas; thus he said.

“Or, like the Ājīvakas and others, [they hold] that the self (attā) is merely material (rūpī). For indeed, among the six classes of beings (chaḷābhijāti) such as the dark class (kaṇhābhijāti), some Ājīvakas profess a certain self.
The word *aroga* should be understood as a synonym for permanence (*nicca*), in the sense that there is no disease or destruction for it;
or rather, its permanence is due to its state of being undisturbed, by way of its freedom from disease.
He asserts that the proponent of such a view is a "speculator" (diṭṭhigatika), and thus says:

"It is healthy and eternal. The space resulting from the removal of the kasiṇa, the first immaterial attainment, consciousness, the state of non-existence, and the base of nothingness—these are the signs of the immaterial attainments.
Just as the bitter taste exists in the neem leaf, so too the formless self, having the size of the body, abides therein; thus they are called Nigaṇṭhas.

He said, "Like the Nigaṇṭhas and others. "By way of grasping a mixture" means by way of grasping the signs of both the form and formless attainments together as "a single self," and by way of grasping the perception that occurs therein as "perception.
For this one who holds such a view, because he has attained the form and formless attainments, the self stands established through those signs as having both a form-nature and a formless-nature.

Therefore, like those who maintain the doctrine of an internal self (*ajjhattavādino*), one generates the misconception that "it is both material and immaterial," or else, by means of mere reasoning alone through the apprehension of material and immaterial phenomena as a mixture,
one holds that "the self is both material and immaterial. By means of this conceptual grasp—
just as with phenomena that have reached a subtle state due to the remainder of formations— it is because they have reached an ultimate subtlety [that this occurs].

By means of a conceptual apprehension (*takka-gāha*) such as this: "Because it is incapable of performing its own function, it is neither material (*rūpī*), like a collection of pillars, walls, hands, feet, and so forth;

yet it is not immaterial (*arūpī*), because it does not transcend the intrinsic nature of matter. Alternatively, the meaning should be understood by way of mutual negation, as in the fourfold doctrine of the finitists and infinitists (*antānantika-catuṣka-vāda*).
However, in that context, the third and fourth doctrines were presented specifically according to the distinctions of place and time.
In this context, the distinction lies precisely in the difference regarding the basis (*vatthu*) and time (*kāla*).
Here, the third position proceeds by way of the difference in time, because the signs of the material and immaterial [realms] do not appear simultaneously.

The fourth position, however, proceeds by way of the difference in basis, through the act of conjecturing that "there is a single self" based on the collection of material and immaterial phenomena; this should be understood according to the method explained therein.

Regarding what should be said concerning the second tetrad, it is to be understood by the method explained in the discussion on the "finite and infinite" views (antānantikavāda), beginning with: "The state that goes there is the conclusion.

Although this doctrine—that "the self possesses diverse perceptions"—is also applicable from the perspective of one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), since a differentiation of perception occurs through the differentiation of those attainments, nevertheless, within the attainment itself...
Because it appears to perception as a single form, he says "perceiving unity" with reference to one who has attained [jhāna].
For this very reason, the mention of "one who has attained" is made here. Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as referring specifically to one who has obtained a single attainment.

Although a differentiation of perceptions may arise through the differentiation of attainments, the state of "perceiving diversity" is defined by the coarse diversity of perception regarding external, manifold objects.
To show this, it is said: "one who perceives diversity by way of one not in meditative attainment.

By the phrase "one who perceives the limited by way of a limited kasiṇa," it is demonstrated that even though there are phenomena dissociated from perception, he asserts that "perception alone is the self.
Here, the mention of the *kasiṇa* is intended to show the object of perception; the same meaning should be understood for the expression "by way of an expansive *kasiṇa*" as well. And thus...

Having established [the views] regarding the doctrines of finitude and infinity, here, within this tetrad on finitude and infinity (*antānantika-catuṣka*), the distinction between these two doctrines is established by means of the first and second positions;

otherwise, among the types of doctrines mentioned, even if there is some distinction due to the difference in the conceptualization of the past and future limits (*pubbantāparanta-kappa*), for others there would be none at all. Alternatively: "The self is the size of a thumb, the size of a barley grain..."
The meaning here should be understood as follows: one who perceives a limited self, such as by the view that "the self is minute" and so forth, is "one with limited perception" (*parittasaññī*);
and one who perceives an immeasurable self, such as by Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others, who profess that the self is omnipresent, is "one with immeasurable perception" (*appamāṇasaññī*).

By means of the knowledge of the destination according to kamma—which is an adjunct to the divine eye—one [knows] through the knowledge of the destination according to kamma produced by the power of the divine eye.
Even though the possession of pleasure and so forth by beings is not visible [to the physical eye], it is seen only by the divine eye; therefore, he said, "by the divine eye," and so on.

But is it not the case that since doctrines such as "the self is exclusively happy" constitute views regarding the future limit (*aparantaditthi*), the statement "seeing them being reborn" is inappropriate?
It is not inappropriate, for it refers to the mental construction (*pakappana*) of a state of exclusive happiness and so forth that has not yet come to pass.
It is intended by way of seeing the production of the present. For this very reason it was said: "Having seen [beings] being produced, one grasps them as 'exclusively happy'.

And here, the grasping of them as "exclusively happy" should be understood as resulting from seeing the frequent occurrence of phenomena accompanied by happiness and so forth within those respective planes.
Alternatively, the proponents of views are like the blind men who saw the elephant.
Whatever they see, they adhere to that very thing and express it; no logical justification need be sought here.
[This concludes] the commentary on the views of "non-percipient" and "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.
(78–83) Regarding the doctrine of non-perception, the first statement refers to a being reborn in a non-percipient existence, who regards perception as self. ("He regards perception as self.")

The second thesis proceeds by taking perception itself as the "self" according to the method stated here, and because there is no other perception existing as its possession, it is called "non-percipient.

Likewise, the third thesis proceeds by taking material phenomena together with perception—or indeed all material and immaterial phenomena—as the "self. The fourth thesis proceeds solely by way of speculative grasping.
It has proceeded. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

In the second tetrad as well, because the universal form (kasiṇarūpa) lacks the nature of being perceived, it is termed "non-percipient" (asaññī); thus, all four should be understood in the same manner as explained in the discussion on the doctrine of the finite and infinite (antānantikavāda).

Likewise, in the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda), [it applies] specifically to the passing away and rebirth-linking of a being born in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Alternatively, the first position proceeds by way of asserting the existence of a subtle perception that is incapable of performing the function of clear perception in all instances;

and the second position and those following it proceed, according to the method stated for the doctrine of non-perception (*asaññīvāda*), by way of a subtle perception and by asserting the nature of cognizing.
Thus, in this one manner, even though the search for a cause is possible.

It should be understood that the statement, "In this matter, one should not seek a definitive reason," was said for the purpose of showing that the doctrines of those who hold views are not to be respected.

Furthermore, since these proponents of the views of being percipient, non-percipient, and neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient state that "after death there is no illness," their inclusion within the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) is indeed evident.
Commentary on Annihilationism (Ucchedavādavaṇṇanā): 84.
Since destruction is impossible for that which is non-existent, it is said "of what exists" (*sato*) because annihilation is dependent upon the state of existence.
Just as in the case of intrinsic phenomena (*sabhāvadhamma*) proceeding by way of cause and effect, even though they are included within a single continuum (*ekasantāna*),...

Because causes and effects possess distinct intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) in the ultimate sense, there is a false apprehension of diversity (*nānattanaya*) through the conclusion of absolute difference—as if they belonged to separate continua—among those [factors] that fall within a single continuum.
This is a cause for the dogmatic adherence to annihilationism (*ucchedābhinivesa*).
Thus, even though there exists a distinction in the intrinsic nature of phenomena that function as cause and effect, because they are included within a single continuum...
In order to show that even the perception of absolute non-difference is a cause [of the view of self], it is stated in the Pāḷi:
"of a being" (*sattassa*). For when the aggregates are occurring by way of continuity, there arises a grasping for a "being" due to the absence of a clear discernment of their composite nature;
and based on the grasping for the existence of a being, there arises the grasping for annihilation, thinking: "As long as this self is not annihilated, so long..."
"It exists indeed" refers to its apprehension; or rather, "annihilation" (uccheda) here is intended as cessation without arising, hence he says "cutting off" (upaccheda).
Destruction (vināsa) is specific destruction, which is non-existence. That, moreover, is simply the passing beyond the range of vision of both the fleshly eye and the eye of wisdom;

thus he says "non-appearance" (adassana), for the word "destruction" is conventionally established in the world in the sense of non-appearance. "Departure from being" (bhāvavigama) means the removal of intrinsic nature (sabhāva).
For that which is cut off by way of non-arising and non-destruction does not persist by its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

"One who has attained" means one who has attained the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*). "Merely passing away" means that even for those in training (*sekkha*) or worldlings (*puthujjana*), there is merely the act of passing away.

"Not [seeing] rebirth" means that due to a lack of prior application (*pubbayoga*) or because he has not performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*), he is unable to see rebirth. "And who is one who has not attained..."
“He does not know the other world” is said either by way of nihilism (*natthikavāda*) or through sheer great delusion, meaning he has no realization that “there is another world beyond this one.
“The range is only this much, which is the domain of the sense faculties” refers to the sphere of the senses.
Or it is due to greed for sensual pleasure, like a king who takes his own daughter’s hand in marriage. “They do not grow back again” refers to fallen leaves.

By the word *vaṇṭena* (by the stalk), he expresses the state of being without rebirth (*appaṭisandhika*). "In the same way, all beings" means that just as a withered leaf, once detached from its bond, does not reconnect, so too all beings undergo death without rebirth; for his tenet is that "beings are like bubbles on water.
"In that manner" means in the way already described. This is because even those who have attained [meditative states] are no longer seen after their passing away.
He said, "or having conceptualized," because these views arise in this manner. Here it is asked:

Just as the doctrines of the Eel-Wrigglers (*amarāvikkhepika*) were shown solely by way of those who are absolutely unsuccessful, and just as the tetrad of the doctrine of conscious existence after death (*uddhamāghātanika-saññīvāda*) was shown solely by way of those who are absolutely successful, this [present case] is not like that.
Rather, this is like the doctrines of eternalism (*sassata*) and partial-eternalism (*ekacca-sassata*), etc., which are shown by way of both the successful and the unsuccessful.
It has proceeded thus; for it is said: "In that regard, there are two kinds of persons," and so forth.

If this is so, why is the teaching here presented in a different manner from the teachings on eternalism and the rest? It is said: because it has reached a state of pedagogical elegance (*desanā-vilāsa*).
For the Blessed Buddhas have attained such pedagogical elegance; they teach the Dhamma in manifold ways according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
Otherwise, here too the Blessed One would have taught thus: "In this case, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor...

[as before] ...having directed his mind toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings with a concentrated mind, sees with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the death-moment consciousness of an Arahant, and [the death-moment consciousness] of ordinary persons."
Or [regarding] other beings, it is not merely their rebirth beyond that [life] which is meant; rather,

having distinguished those who have attained specific distinctions from those who rely on reasoning, one should understand that this teaching proceeds differently from the teachings on eternalism and so forth,
by means of a skillful mode of instruction in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained (*vineyya*).

Alternatively, unlike in the case of certain eternalist views and the like, the doctrine here regarding the attainment of distinction is not a distinct form from the doctrine of the rationalists (*takkīvāda*);
rather, because the classification is the same, it is of an identical form.

To clarify this specific point, the Blessed One taught this doctrine of annihilationism as having a form distinguished from the preceding doctrines. For even among rationalists, [the attainment of distinction] can occur by way of oral tradition and so forth.

In this context, there is an adherence as if one possessed direct realization (*adhigama*). Alternatively, these views were not taught by the Blessed One with reference to future occurrences, nor were they taught by way of mere conceptualization;

rather, in whatever manner those who hold to views have formulated them—saying, "This alone is the truth, all else is vain"—the Blessed One, having delimited each accordingly through his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), [taught them] exactly as they truly are.
They have been proclaimed. By means of these [qualities], the Buddha-dhammas—which are profound and of various kinds, and which are not within the domain of ordinary persons—are made manifest;
and by the description of these qualities, the Tathāgatas are rightly praised.

Furthermore, by way of refuting the doctrines of those who hold views of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*)—who see only subsequent existences as opposed to those who see future existences—their respective doctrines [are likewise refuted].

Since this teaching proceeds in the same manner as those previously established, one should not raise an objection regarding the difference in the way this teaching proceeds compared to the earlier ones.

And having done so, the doctrine of annihilationism (ucchedavāda) should be understood by analyzing it according to the divisions of the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava) and the fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava), just as it was analyzed according to the divisions of the immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava).
Alternatively, it may be viewed as being analyzed individually according to the divisions of both the sense-sphere and fine-material existences.

Nor can it be stated [as a cause] by way of existence in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*). And if that were the case, the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) would result in having either more or fewer divisions than the sevenfold classification taught by the Blessed One; thus, even such an objection finds no footing.

Here it is said: It is indeed appropriate that in the first three doctrines the phrase "with the breakup of the body" (*kāyassa bhedā*) was used, as it pertains to existence included within the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokārabhava*).

Because those doctrines proceed by taking the individual existence (*attabhāva*) as their basis, why is it said in the four views beginning with the fourth—which proceed in dependence on an individual existence included within the fourfold existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*)—“with the breakup of the body” (*kāyassa bhedā*)? For indeed, no body exists for those who are formless (*arūpin*).

This is true; however, the proponent of the view (*diṭṭhigatika*) [uses this expression] solely by way of the conventional designation (*vohāra*) that applies to a material individual existence (*rūpa-attabhāva*).
Even though it is a formless existence, he uses the conventional expression "body" and says, "with the breakup of the body.
Just as those who hold wrong views proclaim their views, so too does the Blessed One demonstrate them;

or rather, because it is a formless state consisting of a collection of phenomena such as contact and so forth, the designation "body" should be understood as referring to that formless existence. And here, [it refers to] those who establish the complete dissolution of the existence of sense-sphere deities and so forth.
The status of being speculators regarding the future life (*aparantakappika*) applies to the second and subsequent views because those views have the future time as their object;

however, it does not apply to the first view, which has the present time as its object and establishes the annihilation of the human existence that is directly perceived by the proponents of wrong views.
For, in the case of the second and subsequent views, [the proponent] is one who, having been included within each preceding view, is reborn in a progressively higher state of existence.
The view of the future life as annihilation is logically consistent with total eradication; and thus it was said:

"But, sir, this self is not completely annihilated by that much," and so forth. As for what was stated there—"There is, sir, another self"—that was said with reference to a specific distinction within the human body, and not because it exists as something entirely different in nature. Is this not the case? It is not incorrect, even though it is included within this world.

And since it is precisely that future time which is the object of the first proponent's statement that is intended here, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that even the first proponent is one who speculates about the future limit (*aparantakappika*).
**Commentary on the Doctrine of Nibbāna in the Present Life (Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda)** 93.

"The present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) means a phenomenon (*dhamma*) apprehended by knowledge that functions as seeing. Among those [phenomena], that which is not within the range of the sense faculties...

Because that [object] also becomes as clearly manifest as a sense-object (*indriyavisaya*), it is said: "The 'seen dhamma' (*diṭṭhadhamma*) is called the directly perceived dhamma (*paccakkhadhamma*).
For this very reason, it is stated: "This is a designation for the state of existence obtained here and there.
95. "Characterized by inward brooding" means: when the mind is struck by calamities concerning relatives, wealth, illness, virtue, or views, [it broods] within.
*Antonijjhāyana* means internal brooding and grieving; that which has this as its characteristic is "characterized by internal brooding" (*antonijjhāyanalakkhaṇo*).

Regarding "characterized by intense lamentation based on that" (*tannissitalālappanalakkhaṇo*): *tannissita* means dependent upon that grief, which is the cause of its origination; *lālappana* means excessive wailing.
That which is both dependent on that and is lamentation is "lamentation based on that" (*tannissitalālappana*); that is its characteristic.
"Of this" refers to that which has the characteristic of lamenting based upon it.

*Upāyāsa* (despair) is the intense distress arising from internal grief when one is unable to do anything by means of lamentation after being struck by the loss of relatives and so forth. Since that, moreover, is a state of mental dejection, it is described as "having the characteristic of despondency."

96. Regarding "the act of thinking" (*vitakkanaṃ*) and "that which has been thought" (*vitakkitaṃ*): since *vitakka* itself has the nature of directing the mind toward an object, it is said, "directing...
*vitakka*. This same principle applies here to the term "investigating" (*vicāritaṃ*).
Because *vitakka* and *vicāra* have the nature of causing agitation, the *jhāna* accompanied by them becomes as if "throbbing," which is why it is said, "it appears as if with thorns."
97. That rapture (*pīti*) by which, when it has arisen, the mind is said to be "exhilarated" (*ubbilāvita*) is called "the state of being exhilarated.
Since the mind's state of exhilaration exists only when that rapture is present and not when it is absent, it is therefore described as "the cause of the state of exhilaration.
98. Alternatively, "involvement" (*ābhoga*) means the mind’s state of being uplifted, or its state of being inclined toward the object. For by means of pleasure (*sukha*), the mind...
It is bent toward the object; it is not bent away as if by pain, nor is it neither-bent-nor-averse as if by neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

In this regard, for one who is being separated from sensual pleasures—such as agreeable food and so forth—by one overcome by hunger, thirst, and the like, the longing for the object of clinging increases especially.
However, for one who has eaten their fill of excellent, delicious food with a sublime flavor...

"Just as one who has already eaten and is satiated has no desire to eat more, so too there is no craving for sensual pleasures; through lack of greed for sense objects, one releases oneself from even those objects difficult to leave, just as a leech does.
Thus the first proponent, having emerged from improper reflection, declared the subsiding of the suffering of *saṃsāra* to result from being satisfied by the strands of sensual pleasure.
[This was said] because of his vision of the danger in sensual desires and the like, and because of the bliss of the first *jhāna*.

And because they see the state of peace and are satiated with the bliss of the first jhāna and so forth, those who maintain the second and subsequent views prophesied the cutting off of the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
Here too, the analysis regarding the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) described above should be applied as far as possible.
However, this is the distinction here: for five doctrines are found within a single individual existence (*attabhāva*). For this very reason, it is said in the Pāḷi:
The term "another self" (*añño attā*) was not used [in the sutta].

But how, in this context, is the doctrine of one who teaches ultimate Nibbāna—the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life (*diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna-vāda*)—included within the eternalist view (*sassata-diṭṭhi*) and not the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*)?
Because it demonstrates that the pure self remains in its own essential nature, having attained liberation from bondage through the possession of various specific types of happiness.

"‘The rest’ refers to the remaining fifty-five views. Among those, the fact that the doctrines of the finitists (*antānantika-vāda*) and others constitute the eternalist view (*sassata-diṭṭhi*) has already been explained in various places. 101–3.

But what is the reason that only the past limit (*pubbanta*) and the future limit (*aparanta*) are shown as the objects of dogmatic adherence to views (*diṭṭhābhinivesa*), and not both of them combined into one?
Because it is impossible. For [a combination] distinct from both the past and the future limits does not exist."
The conceptualization of views (*diṭṭhikappanā*) is possible in the middle because it is limited in duration; however, the present existence (*paccuppannabhava*) lies between those two.
This being so, since its nature—which is capable of being conceptualized as a view—is included within the very limits of the past and the future, how could it be said not to be shown?
Alternatively, the "middle" is called "the limit of the past and the future" because it possesses both a past and a future limit.

And this [term] should be understood as having been stated separately from "speculators about the past and the future" (*pubbantāparantakappika*) by one who says "those who hold views regarding the past and the future" (*pubbantāparantānudiṭṭhi*); for even in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, they are included under the general designation "all those speculators about the future" (*aparantakappika*)— which is to say, "speculators about the past and the future"—
either by the method of "omitting the rest" (*ekasesa*) or otherwise by way of a collective summary.

[The question] arises: "How could one incur the fault of making what has been said meaningless? Who, then, are those theorists of the past and future (*pubbantāparantakappika*)? They are to be understood as those of such a kind who, having been proponents of the finite and infinite [world], are proponents of Nibbāna in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*).
And herein, "all of them [are included] by means of these sixty-two bases, or by one or another of them; there is nothing beyond this... [is the meaning].
Because of the statement "externally," and because there is no proponent of views whatsoever who is not included within the three types of speculators concerning the past,
those various forms of views— such as the doctrines of non-action, causelessness, and nihilism mentioned in other discourses like the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*,
as well as the diverse categories of views such as those concerning God, Pajāpati, the Primordial Man, Time, Essential Nature, Fate, and Chance— are [all subsumed].
Even those views appearing externally are to be understood as included within these very categories and as being subsumed therein. How so?

First, the doctrine of non-action (*akiriyavāda*) is included within eternalism (*sassatavāda*), because it demonstrates the absence of action through such statements as "barren" and "fixed like a peak.

Likewise, the doctrine of Pakudha, which proceeds by the method of "these seven bodies," and [the doctrine of Makkhali Gosāla] which states, "There is no cause, there is no condition for the existence of beings... [are also included].
Because of such statements as "for the sake of defilement," the doctrine of causelessness (ahetukavāda) is included within the doctrine of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppannikavāda).
Because of such statements as "there is no other world," the doctrine of non-existence (natthikavāda) is included within the doctrine of annihilationism (ucchedavāda);
for it is said therein, "with the breakup of the body, one is annihilated," and so forth. By the first word "etc. (ādi), the doctrines of the Nigaṇṭhas and others are comprised.

Although the fourfold restraint (*cātuyāmasaṃvara*) appears in the Canon as the doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, nevertheless, because it involves a denial of the seven bases (*sattavatātikkama*) and is characterized by equivocation,
the doctrine of Nātaputta is included among the doctrines of "Eternal Indeterminacy" (*amarāvikkhepa*), just like the doctrine of "Accumulation" (*sañcaya*).
Doctrines such as "the soul is the same as the body" or "the soul is one thing and the body another" [are included under] "the self possesses form" (*rūpī attā*).

These fall under the category of eternalist views (*sassatavāda*), such as the statements: “The Tathāgata exists after death,” and “There are beings of spontaneous birth. Those of the form: “The Tathāgata does not exist after death;
there are no beings of spontaneous birth,” are included under annihilationist views (*ucchedavāda*). [Those of the form: “He both exists and does not exist...”
“The Tathāgata exists after death; there both exist and do not exist beings of spontaneous birth”—such types as these are included within the doctrine of partial eternalism.
“The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death;

there neither exist nor do not exist beings of spontaneous birth”—such types as these are included within the doctrine of the Eel-Wriggler (amarāvikkhepa). [Likewise are included] the doctrines of God (Issara), Pajāpati, Primordial Matter (purisa), and Time (kāla).

The doctrine of partial eternalism is included within [the first two views], as is the doctrine of Kaṇāda. The doctrines of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), destiny (*niyati*), and chance (*yadicchā*) are subsumed under the doctrine of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppannika*).
By this method, it should be understood that the various speculative views found in other discourses and outside [this text] are included within these sixty-two views.

“Intention” (ajjhāsaya) here refers to the intention regarding views (diṭṭhijjhāsaya). For, on the side of defilement, the intention of beings is twofold by way of the views of eternalism and annihilationism.

And the Blessed One [knows] that very intention—even though it is divided into many types because it arises in relation to immeasurable specific objects of knowledge for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems—by means of such statements as, “There are four kinds of proponents of eternalism,” and so forth.

Having delimited [the world] by means of omniscient knowledge through its sixty-twofold classification and showing it as such, he is like one holding it with a standard scale; thus he said, "as if weighing it with a scale.
For he will say later, "enclosed within a net," and so forth. By the phrase, "as if drawing up sand from the foot of Mount Sineru,"...
This shows that it is impossible for anyone other than the Omniscient One (sabbaññutaññāṇa) to deliver this teaching.

*Anusandhi* means connection; a connection made by way of a question is a "question-connection" (*pucchānusandhi*). Alternatively, it is a "connection" (*anusandhi*) because it connects (*anusandhayati*);
or it is a "question-connection" because the question is the connection for this [teaching]. Or else, it is a "question-connection" because it is connected by way of a question.
The connection by way of question (*pucchānusandhi*). The same method applies to the connection by way of underlying intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*).

Regarding the term *yathānusandhi*: here, it is called *anusandhi* because it is connected (*anusandhīyati*). Whatever the connection may be, that is *yathānusandhi*; or, the lexical meaning should be understood as "in accordance with the connection" (*anusandhianurūpaṃ*).
That [connection] is "by means of whatever dhamma the teaching was initiated at the beginning, according to a dhamma corresponding to that dhamma."

Alternatively, it should be understood according to the sequence of connection (*yathānusandhi*) by way of those suttas in which the subsequent teaching occurs, whether by way of a contrast or otherwise.
As it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "For example, in the *Ākaṅkheyya-sutta*, the teaching arose below with virtue (*sīla*), while the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) appear above...
In the *Kakacūpama-sutta*, [the teaching] arose below with impatience (*akkhanti*), while the simile of the saw (*kakacūpamā*) appears above," and so forth.
"Thus they say" is an indication of the Blessed One’s own lack of approval for the self-emptiness (attasuññatā) as it was taught.
"Sir" is an address to the Dhamma. "Done by one who is not-self" means either not done by a self, or done by aggregates that are not-self.
"What self will they touch? means: since there is no self and because the aggregates are momentary, what self will the kamma touch with its own fruit?

"They will experience [it]": the meaning is, "who experiences the fruit of karma? "The ignorant" (*avidvā*): one who is not wise due to a lack of proficiency in the noble Dhamma because of being devoid of learning and so forth.
"Enveloped in ignorance" (*avijjāgata*): one who has approached ignorance; the meaning is, one whose ignorance is not abandoned due to a lack of discipline regarding the noble Dhamma.
"With a mind dominated by craving": [the thought], "If there is no such thing as 'I,' then for the karma performed by me..."

"Who experiences the fruit? But if that [self] exists, there might be the enjoyment of the fruit"—this refers to one who is dominated by craving (*taṇhādhipateyya*), meaning one for whom craving is predominant.
"With a mind accompanied by the clinging to a self-doctrine" (*attavādupādānasahagata-cetasā*).

"It should not be overstepped" means that even though conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are momentary, because the fruit arises in the very same continuum where the karma was performed, it belongs merely to a heap of phenomena (*dhammapuñjamatta*).
And when the connection between action and its fruit is established, one might wrongly grasp at the principle of identity, thinking that there must be a single agent who is also the experiencer;

otherwise, "the connection between actions and their fruits would not exist"—thus, one might think it necessary to overstep the Teacher’s instruction which clarifies the emptiness of self and what belongs to a self. This is the meaning.
The phrase “the six higher knowledges have been presented above” shows the sequence of connection (*yathānusandhi*) by way of corresponding states; the others [are shown] by way of their opposites.
By the word “defilement” (*kilesa*), it refers to the defilements in such passages as “greed is a corruption of the mind.

By the particle *pi* (“also”) in the phrase “in this too,” he shows that just as there was a sequence of connection by way of opposites in the previously mentioned suttas and so forth, so too is there one in this sutta.

For this teaching, which arose by way of the various speculative views that posit such things as a permanent core, is brought to its conclusion by the elucidation of the emptiness of those very things—such as a permanent core.
[This concludes] the commentary on the section on agitation and vacillation (105–117).
"For the purpose of showing the delimitation" means for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of confusion between the presentation of views such as eternalism and right view.
The connection is: "that too is felt. "Not knowing, not seeing" means:

for those who do not know and do not see according to reality that "the self and the world are eternal"—this being a standpoint of views (diṭṭhiṭṭhāna) thus grasped, thus adhered to, thus seized, and thus leading to such a future state—and likewise, because of the lack of freedom from craving for that feeling, such a course of views [arises].
They cling to that feeling because they do not know and do not see it as it truly is from the perspective of its arising and so forth.

By this, he shows that while the Tathāgatas possess knowledge and vision here exactly as it is through unobstructed knowledge and the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*), such is not the case for those who follow wrong views;
rather, for them, there is only the misapprehension of craving and views. And for this very reason, this teaching [is given].

They arose for the purpose of showing the distinction between the limits [of the two truths]. In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated without qualification: "for those who do not know and do not see the individual essence (*sabhāva*) of phenomena as it really is. For it is not the case that people adhere erroneously merely by not knowing the individual essence of conditioned phenomena.
This specific application has been made on the principle that "a general statement rests upon a particular instance."
“Feeling” (*vedayita*) refers to the experience undergone by view, which occurs by way of establishing the view that “the self and the world are eternal.
“Of those gone into craving” (*taṇhāgatānaṃ*) means of those who have gone into, approached, or proceeded along with craving.

Furthermore, the phrase “and that very same” (*tañca kho panetaṃ*) refers back to the aforementioned feeling; for that [feeling] consists of the bait of the round of existence (*vaṭṭāmisabhūta*), because it is pierced by the thorns of views and craving.
Because of its nature as worldly happiness, it is fickle; it does not remain in a single mode like the bliss of the paths and fruits.
For this very reason, he said, "by agitation," and so forth.
Alternatively, having thus analyzed the sixty-two types of views by way of their specific causes, [he now analyzes them] by way of their non-specific cause.
In order to demonstrate those [views], the teaching beginning with “In this regard, monks,” was commenced.
For for all those who follow wrong views, feeling, ignorance, and craving function in an undifferentiated manner.

Therein, “that too” refers to that very act of proclaiming—“the self and the world are eternal”—found in the phrase “they proclaim the self and the world to be eternal. This [proclamation] is distinguished by pleasure and so forth.

For those who do not know and do not see the threefold feeling—respectively as suffering, a dart, and impermanence—either in its undifferentiated sense or by way of its origin, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape;
and for that very reason, because the longing for pleasure and so forth arises, they have entered into craving (*taṇhāgatānaṃ*).
Thus, through the agitation of craving (*taṇhāparitassitena*), there is merely the flickering of views (*diṭṭhivipphanditaṃ*), which is simply the movement of views (*diṭṭhicālanaṃ*).
The question, "In the absence of a self, who experiences feeling? refers merely to the occurrence of a view through the doors of body and speech;
it does not mean that there exists any eternal phenomenon to be established by such a view. The same principle applies to the various theories of partial eternalism and so forth.
Commentary on the Section on Contact as Condition.

118. "For the sake of showing the succession of conditions" means that the teaching—that feeling (*vedayita*) is the condition for those views which proceed through the agitation of craving (*taṇhā-paritassita*), and contact (*phassa*) is the condition for feeling—is an analysis of the chain of conditions for view.
Therefore, just as view is the phenomenon that establishes [the position], so too are its conditions phenomena.

It should be understood that this point is demonstrated as follows: just as [mental states] arise solely by way of their respective conditions and not without conditions, so too should phenomena such as form and feeling be made known;
herein there is no self or world that is eternal. This concludes the commentary on the section "This state does not exist."
"Of that condition" means of the condition of contact (*phassapaccaya*). "In feeling associated with views" (*diṭṭhivedayite*) means in feelings that serve as conditions for views;
the meaning is that [views] must be produced by their own conditions, of which contact is the primary factor.

Feeling arises even without the bases such as the eye, and without some of the associated mental states (*sampayuttadhamma*), but it never arises without contact; therefore, contact is [the primary condition].
He said, "The cause for the strength of feeling," meaning "for the purpose of showing its state of being strong.

For even if an object is present, if the arising of consciousness lacks the mode of contact (*phusanākāra*), it does not serve as a condition for that [consciousness] by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
Thus, contact alone is the specific condition for associated states. Indeed, when the Blessed One was analyzing the arising of consciousness, he [stated] contact alone...
The first [term] has been extracted; however, it is precisely the "adhiṭṭhāna" (basis) in relation to feeling.
144. Commentary on the Discussion of the Cycle of Bases for Those Holding Wrong Views:
Because it was added in the three preceding sections and because it will be stated above as "they experience," [the term is included].
"Experiencing (vedayita) is the foremost here," he said; thus, "he collects all experiences of views" means that he brings them together.
And by the word "also" (*pi*) occurring here and there in the phrase "those which also," he shows the meaning of that term.
The inclusion of experiencing within contact is simply the demonstration of its being conditioned by contact: "the experiencing of the six objects through the six internal bases."
“Exclusively caused by the six types of contact. Regarding the word *sañjāti*, since it means “that wherein they are born,” it has the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*);

thus he says, “in the place of birth. The word *samosaraṇa* (convergence) should also be understood in this same way. It is called an *āyatana* because the fruit extends (*āyatati*) therein, owing to its dependence upon that;
or, it is an *āyatana* because it stretches out (*tanoti*) and brings into operation its own fruit, which is its source (*āya*), that is, its cause. [This refers to] a collection of trees and shrubs.
Regarding the expression "forest terminology," it is said that "in the mere designation" means that the forest itself is the "forest base.

In the phrase "also in the three meanings," the word *pi* (also) should be understood as including meanings not explicitly stated; by this, it encompasses the senses of source (*ākara*), dwelling (*nivāsa*), and foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

In such cases as "source of gold" (*hiraññāyatana*), "source of silver" (*suvaṇṇāyatana*), "abode of Vāsudeva" (*vāsudevāyatana*), and "source of action" (*kammāyatana*), the term *āyatana* refers to a source, a dwelling, or a foundation.

In the eye and the other [sense bases], contact and the rest are crowded together; they are its dwelling place, and it is their foundation because of its status as a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*).
Contact is called "conjunction" (*saṅgati*) because it is to be grasped through the coming-together of the three—object, faculty, and consciousness.
For that reason, it is said to have "assembling" (*sannipāta*) as its manifestation. By this method, even though others exist...

Just as in that sutta, “The eye... contact,” the teaching was given under the heading of contact in order to show that contact is the primary cause for feeling among the associated states, so too here in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, beginning with contact in the phrase “with contact as condition, feeling arises,” etc., the succession of conditions is shown by illustrating dependent origination from the future perspective, starting with: “From the sense-bases of contact...”
"By touching, by touching"—this is stated by way of contact (*phassa*).
Although contact is an immaterial phenomenon (*arūpadhamma*) and does not adhere to the object in its entirety, it occurs in the mode of touching;
thus, as if it were actually touching, it is said: "Contact itself touches each respective object. By this, it is characterized as having the characteristic of touching (*phusanalakkhaṇa*).

It is said, “the essence of which is impact. Is it the case that there are four kinds of conditions, and that the painful [condition] is twofold by way of being a mere object and a natural decisive support? This is true;

But how is it for the mere-object (ārammaṇamatta) and the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati)? Because these too share the commonality of being objects.

"Of the fourfold" refers to the fourfold [clinging], from sense-desire clinging (*kāmupādāna*) up to self-theory clinging (*attavādupādāna*). But is it not craving (*taṇhā*) itself?
What is clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*)? This is true. In this context, weak craving is simply craving (*taṇhā*), while powerful craving is clinging to sense-pleasures.

Alternatively, craving is the longing for an object not yet attained, like thieves stretching out their hands in the dark; clinging is the grasping of an object already attained, like the seizing of wealth by the thieves when it has reached their hands.
Craving is the opposite of fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*); it is the opposite of contentment (*santosa*).
Grasping (*upādāna*). Craving is the root of the suffering of seeking; grasping is the root of the suffering of guarding—this is the distinction between them.

Regarding the phrase "of grasping," it should be understood that for non-conascent grasping, it is by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), while for the other [conascent], it is by way of conascence (*sahajāta*). Therein, for the immediately preceding [grasping], it is by way of the conditions of immediacy (*anantara*), contiguity (*samanantara*), immediacy-decisive-support (*anantarūpanissaya*), absence (*natthi*), disappearance (*vigata*), and repetition (*āsevana*).

That which is not immediate is [related] by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*); however, that which has become an object is related by way of object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), object-decisive support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), or simply by way of being an object.
Having included all of this under "decisive support" alone, it is stated as "by the pinnacle of decisive support.

The decisive support (*upanissaya*). Likewise, one who is confused regarding the distinctions of form and so forth adopts wrong view, such as "there is no giving," and so on;

one who desires to be liberated from *saṃsāra* clings to the grasping after a path of purity in what is not a pure path; and one adopts the view of self-existence (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), which consists in the apprehension of a self or what belongs to a self within the aggregates.
Therefore, craving should be understood as the decisive support for these others as well. Regarding the co-nascent...
However, craving is a condition by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root-cause.
With reference to all of that, it is said: "by way of the limit of co-nascence.
"Likewise" means both by way of the limit of decisive support and by way of the limit of co-nascence. "Of existence" refers to kamma-existence (*kammabhava*).

And [it is the cause] of both rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) and [existence-in-general]. In this context, all that is comprised by volition and the rest is "kamma-existence" (*kammabhava*), which leads to existence;
while the ninefold [existences], beginning with sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), are "rebirth-existence.

For rebirth-existence, the fourfold clinging (*upādāna*) is a cause by way of being the primary decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*), because it serves as the cause for kamma-existence—which is itself the cause of rebirth-existence—and because it functions as its auxiliary condition.

It serves as a condition. However, at the time of performing an action that becomes the object [of rebirth], the *kāmupādāna* (clinging to sensual pleasures) co-arising with that karma serves as a condition for the *upapattibhava* (existence at rebirth) by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).

But for the co-arising *kammabhava* (existence as karma), the co-arising *upādāna* serves as a condition in numerous ways—by way of the conditions of co-arising, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance, as well as by way of the root-cause and the path.
It is a condition for that which is not co-nascent by way of proximity, contiguity, immediate-proximity, decisive-support, absence, disappearance, and repetition;
for the other [type], it is a condition by way of natural decisive-support; and at times such as during the act of comprehension, it is a condition by way of object.
In this context, it is stated by including proximity and the others within the decisive-support condition, and co-nascence and the others within the co-nascence condition.
“Both by way of decisive support (upanissaya) and by way of co-nascence (sahajāta).

Regarding the statement “existence [is the condition] for birth,” here “existence” (bhava) refers to kamma-existence (kammabhava), for that is the condition for birth, not rebirth-existence (upapattibhava).
For rebirth-existence consists of the aggregates (khandhas) first produced at conception, which is itself birth. Therefore it was said: “In this context, ‘birth’...”
“The five aggregates with their modifications (savikāra) are to be seen. Regarding the phrase “with their modifications,” they are “with modifications” by way of the modification of arising;
and in actual fact, these are simply the rebirth-existence (upapattibhava). For it is not logical that the very same thing should be its own cause.
And since kamma-existence (kammabhava) serves as a condition for rebirth-existence by way of both the kamma-condition and the decisive-support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), he said [this].
“Becoming is a condition for birth by way of decisive support.

And because aging-and-death occurs when there is birth, and sorrow and so forth arise for the fool who is touched by aging-and-death and the rest, but do not occur when they are absent, it is therefore said: “Birth...
[is] a condition. This is an investigation of conditions under the heading of co-nascent decisive support.

even though it exists, no boundary or starting point for ignorance is discerned— such as that ignorance arose at the time of a certain Sammasambuddha or a Cakkavatti, but not before that— precisely because it is non-existent.

The meaning is as follows: this condition is *idappaccaya* (this-condition); therefore, from this condition (*idappaccayā*), meaning "from this cause, there is the condition for the taints" (*āsavapaccaya*).

Sinking downwards by way of rebirth in the states of deprivation (*apāya*), and rising upwards by way of the existence of success (*sampattibhava*). Likewise, by way of the limited plane (*parittabhūmi*) and the sublime plane (*mahaggatabhūmi*).

Furthermore, it is so called because right view is clarified through the discernment of views and the manifestation of emptiness.

The "net of views. Because it is the means for crushing the doctrines of the sectarians (tīrthikas), it is called "the unsurpassed victory in battle"—this is how the construction of the meaning should be understood here.

"For this is called an analytical exposition because it is without verses.
In the phrase "in others too," the word "too" (*pi*) includes the cultivation of the perfections (*pāramiparicaya*). For it is said in the *Buddhavaṃsa*:
“As he comprehended these phenomena— those characterized by their own intrinsic nature,
essence, and defining marks— the earth of the ten thousandfold world-system trembled through the power of that Dhamma.
By the power of energy means by the radiance of the energy that served as the cause for renouncing the glory of a wheel-turning monarch at the Great Renunciation.

“Struck by the force of wonder” means impelled by the impact of the power of his marvelous deeds. Regarding the washing of the rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*), some say it was “by the splendor of merit”;

It is said to have "trembled at an improper time" because it shook many times.

This, then, is the explanation of the hidden meaning (*līnatthavaṇṇanā*) according to the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The Explanation of the System of the Treatise (Pakaraṇanaya): This is the commentary on the meaning of the text according to the system of the treatise.
Now, this commentary on the meaning is easy to perform and easy to understand once the origin, the purpose, the recipients, and the summarized meanings of the teaching have been determined.
Therefore, we shall first determine the origin and other factors of the Sutta teaching. Regarding that, the origin has been stated as "speaking praise or dispraise.
Furthermore, there is no offense in cases of blame or praise when the state of aversion, joy, and so forth, has been removed from the listener;
in such a case, the vision of danger [in those emotions] is the origin. Likewise, it is the sequence of how one should proceed regarding blame and praise.

The origin [of this misconception] is the lack of understanding regarding the Tathāgata’s unimpeded range of activity—both within the spheres of eternalism and other views, and beyond them—with respect to his virtue, which is manifold (such as the minor precepts and so forth) and constitutes the object of praise; and with respect to his omniscience and his state of being unconditioned by anything whatsoever.

The purpose should be understood as the opposite of what was stated above: namely, the attainment of a state free from resentment, joy, and the like toward those to be trained. For this [misconception] is the first...
"He applies the teaching" means: its purposes are the destruction of various forms of wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy and flattery;

the unraveling of the sixty-two-fold net of views; the elucidation of the mode of conditions by way of views; the instruction on the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths by way of the six bases of contact;
the exhaustive elimination of all types of speculative views; and the demonstration of one's own parinibbāna through non-clinging.
Those whose minds are possessed of attachment and aversion for the sake of praise or blame, who delight in various wrong livelihoods such as hypocrisy,

who are submerged in the mire of views such as eternalism, and who— due to their failure to fulfill the aggregate of virtue and the rest— lack the knowledge to discern the excellence of the qualities [of the Buddha],
are the vessels for this teaching of the Dhamma.

As for the summary meaning: by means of the statement regarding the non-performance of malice and so forth, there is the directing of one toward the perception of a recluse in accordance with one's vow;

the practice of patience and gentleness; application to the development of the divine abodes; the conjunction of faith and wisdom; the foundation of mindfulness and clear comprehension; the accomplishment of the power of reflection and development;
the abandoning of active obsessions and underlying tendencies; the practice for the welfare of both [self and others]; and [freedom] from the worldly conditions...
And non-staining is demonstrated. Likewise, by the statement of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*) is demonstrated;

and through that, the perfection of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*), the possession of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*), the abandoning of transgression, the abandoning [of defilements] by way of their specific factors (*tadaṅga-pahāna*), the abandoning of the corruption of misconduct, the accomplishment of the threefold abstinence, and the achievement of being dear, pleasing, and worthy of respect are demonstrated.
The attainment of gain, honor, and renown; the state of being the foundation for serenity and insight; the thinning of the roots of unwholesomeness;
the planting of the roots of wholesomeness; the distancing of both kinds of harm; confidence in assemblies; dwelling in heedfulness; being difficult for others to overcome;
and the possession of freedom from remorse and other such qualities are demonstrated.
By such statements as “profound,” there is the elucidation of the profound Dhamma; its state of being without a foothold;
the difficulty of its manifestation even in an incalculable number of eons; the impossibility of penetrating it through direct perception even with subtle knowledge;
the difficulty of attaining it even by inferential knowledge known as *dhammanvaya*; and the state of all disturbances having been stilled.

The manifestation of the true nature of reality, the excellence of the final conclusion, the state of being insatiable, the attainment of the state of exertion, the domain of knowledge as it truly is, the subtle intrinsic nature, and the manifestation of great wisdom are thus shown. In brief, by means of the words illustrating views, the views of eternalism and annihilationism are revealed;
this constitutes the manifestation of the avoidance of sinking and over-exertion, and the description of being unbound by means.
The proclamation of wrong adherence; the manifestation of practice on a false path; the presentation of perverted grasping; the embracing of misapprehension;
the establishment of views regarding the past and the future; the differentiation of views concerning existence and non-existence; the occurrence of craving and ignorance;

the description of views that the world is finite or infinite; the leading into the two extremes; and the detailed classification of the distinctions between the taints, floods, yokes, defilements, knots, fetters, and clingings.
Thus, by such statements as "the origin of feelings," the realization and penetration of the Four Noble Truths are established;

there is the abandonment through suppression and eradication, the removal of craving and ignorance, the grasping of the signs for the endurance of the True Dhamma, the perfection of scriptural knowledge and realization,
the practice for the welfare of both [self and others], the embracing of the threefold wisdom, and the application of mindfulness and clear comprehension.

The conjunction of faith and wisdom, the application of right effort and serenity, and the accomplishment of serenity and insight are shown. By the phrase “of those who do not know and do not see,” the establishment of ignorance (*avijjā*) is demonstrated;
by the phrase “the agitation and vacillation of those gone under the sway of craving,” the establishment of craving (*taṇhā*) is demonstrated.

Through both of these, the establishment of the two fetters—hindrances and fetters—is shown, as well as the non-cessation of the cycle of existence in saṃsāra which has no discernible beginning, and the drawing back from the past and the linking on to the future.
The classification of causes by way of past and present time, the mutual assistance of ignorance and craving in the sense of their not transcending one another,
and the indication of the opposites of wisdom-liberation and mind-liberation are thus shown.

By stating that even "that [feeling] has contact as its condition," and by explaining that the manifestation of eternalism and so forth depends upon conditions, the dependency of phenomena on conditions is demonstrated.
The negation of permanence, the establishment of impermanence, the rejection of an agent and so forth from the perspective of ultimate reality,
the description of suchness and similar principles, the illumination of emptiness, and the manifestation of the characteristics of the uniformity of conditions are thus demonstrated.
By the phrase “one whose conduit to existence is cut,” the Blessed One’s perfection in abandonment, his inclination toward true knowledge, and his mastery are shown.
The accomplishment of the three trainings, the distinction between the two elements of Nibbāna, the fulfillment of the four foundations, and non-inclusion within the realms of existence,

modes of birth, and so forth, are demonstrated. Furthermore, by means of the entire passage of the sutta, the Blessed One’s state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*) toward both the desirable and the undesirable,
his establishing of others therein, and the two primary states that are the source of wholesome qualities [are shown].
The exposition [of the Dhamma] should be determined as including: the instruction on the three trainings; the establishment of the four types of persons beginning with the "tormentor of self";

the classification of the fourfold set of kamma beginning with the dark-with-dark-result; the exposition of the objects of the four immeasurables; the realization of the fivefold set beginning with origination as it really is;
the manifestation of the six qualities conducive to harmony; and the foundation in the ten qualities that provide protection, and so forth.

Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Investigation (*vicayahāra-vaṇṇanā*):

Even in the absence of actual conceptualization (*kappanā*), the term "mine" (*mama*) is used by way of conventional expression (*vohāra*) and by way of censure (*anuvāda*); it is used for the purpose of alternative designation (*vikappana*) because there is no fixed restriction (*niyama*).
The term "speech" (*vāc*) is employed for the sake of indicating possession of qualities and for the purpose of addressing [the audience] as "monks.

The word "others" (*pare*) is used because of their distinctness and because of their opposition; the word "disparagement" (*avaṇṇa*) is used because it is the opposite of praise and because it is not to be praised.
The phrase "they would speak" (*bhāseyyuṃ*) is used in the sense of proficiency and in the sense of elaboration; it is used because of the state of retaining [the words].
It is called "of the Dhamma" because it is the opposite of what is non-Dhamma;
it is called "of the Saṅgha" because of its state of being bound together by right view and virtue, and because it brings about the destruction of the defilements.

It is called "therein" (*tattha*) because of the reference to what was previously stated and because of the introduction of the statement; it is called "by you" (*tumhehi*) because of presence before one's eyes and because of plurality. Because of the slaying of the mind...

It is called "resentment" (*āghāta*) because it strikes at the object; it is called "displeasure" (*appaccaya*) because its activity is contracted toward the object and because it takes the form of dissatisfaction;
it is called "mental" (*cetaso*) because it reflects upon the object and because it has the mind as its support;

it is called "discontent" (*anabhiraddhi*) because it fails to accomplish what is beneficial and repeatedly accomplishes what is harmful; and it is so designated because it is unworthy of the cause [of peace] within the Teacher’s dispensation.
And because it is impossible for those who are established [in the path] to perform it, it is said that "it is not to be done. In this manner, the analysis should be applied to all the passages.
