Thus, for fear of excessive prolixity, I have not elaborated upon the Mode of Conveying Investigation (*vicayahāra*) through the method of investigating each word;
however, a wise person can clarify this meaning by following the *Aṭṭhakathā* and its commentary on the hidden sense (*līnatthavaṇṇanā*).
The Explanation of the Application of Reasoning:

It is logical that the total non-performance of malice and so forth leads to the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*), because of the presence of even-mindedness toward the desirable and the undesirable.
In whatever mental continuum malice and so forth have arisen, an obstacle caused by those [states] occurs.
It is logical that this leads to an obstruction of success for that very person. Why? Because it does not transfer to other mental continua (*santāna*).
It is logical that ill-will (*āghāta*) and so forth, which arise having overwhelmed the mind, lead to an incapacity even for discerning well-spoken words and the like;
for this is because those possessed of anger and greed are enveloped in blinding darkness. Abstinence from unwholesome conduct such as the taking of life [is beneficial] for all beings.
It is appropriate to say that this leads to a state of praise for joy. For through the perfection of virtue, there arises a great outpouring of renown.

It is also appropriate that a description of the Tathāgata’s qualities—though it may be only a partial account—leads to the grasping of the entirety of his omniscient qualities, because those qualities are not shared by others.
These [qualities] are conditioned by the corresponding appropriate and thorough attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
It is logical that speculative reasonings lead to dogmatic adherence to eternalism and other views, because the net of conceptual construction has not been eradicated.
It is logical that craving for feeling increases through a lack of understanding of the danger in feeling, because there is the presence of contemplation on gratification.
And it is logical that when there is passion for the feeler, the grasping at self and what belongs to self, as well as the grasping at eternalism and so forth, quivers there.

Because the cause is present. For those who propound the doctrines of eternalism and so forth, it is logical that contact (*phassa*) is the cause for grasping (*upādāna*) conditioned by craving (*taṇhā*), or for those experiencing the feeling corresponding thereto; this is because such [grasping] cannot exist without the conjunction of object, faculty, and consciousness.
It is also logical that there is no cessation of the cycle caused by the six bases of contact (*cha-phassāyatana*), because ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving have not been abandoned therein.

It is logical that the thorough understanding of the origin and so forth of the six bases of contact stands transcending all speculative views, because it constitutes the penetration of the Four Noble Truths.

It is also logical that all speculative views are encompassed within the net of these sixty-two views, since the doctrines of non-action (akiriyavāda) and the doctrines of a Supreme Lord (issaravāda), and so on, are included therein. Likewise...

And it has been thus praised. It is fitting to say that "the Tathāgata’s body has cut off the conduit to existence," because through the perfection of his initial resolve, the Blessed One established his mind in the four foundations of mindfulness and developed the seven factors of enlightenment exactly as they are.
It is fitting to say that "they shall not see him who has attained final nibbāna after the breaking up of the body" in reference to the attainment of nibbāna without residue.
"Without remainder in respect of form and so forth for anyone whatsoever"—this is the Mode of Conveying Reason (yuttihāra).

Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Footings (padaṭṭhānahāra): The footings for such failures as being unworthy of praise, lacking praise, failing to attain what is appropriate, and having speech that is not to be accepted; and the footings for such successes as being worthy of praise, attaining praise in accordance with one's worth, and having speech that is trustworthy.

The proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). Likewise, malice and so forth are the proximate cause for the suffering of hell and other realms. The non-committal of malice and so forth is the proximate cause for all forms of excellence, such as the attainment of heaven.
Abstinence from killing living beings and so forth is the proximate cause for the Noble One’s aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).
The Noble One’s aggregate of virtue is the proximate cause for the Noble One’s aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*).
The Noble Aggregate of Concentration is the proximate cause for the Noble Aggregate of Wisdom.
The Blessed One’s knowledge of the mode of penetration, endowed with distinctions such as profundity, is the proximate cause for his knowledge of teaching.

The knowledge of teaching is the proximate cause for the escape from the entire suffering of the round for those to be trained. All views constitute the clinging to views; accordingly, [it is abandoned].
It is the proximate cause for all nine kinds of existence (*bhava*). Existence is the proximate cause for birth; birth is the proximate cause for aging-and-death and for sorrow and the rest.
The realization and penetration of the four noble truths through the correct perception of the arising and so forth of feelings is [the goal].
Therein, realization is the proximate cause for penetration; penetration is [the cause] for the fourfold fruit of recluseship.

The proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). In the phrase "of those who do not know and do not see," ignorance (*avijjā*) is mentioned; therein, ignorance is the proximate cause of volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*), and this should be applied accordingly down to feeling (*vedanā*) as the proximate cause of craving (*taṇhā*).

In the phrase "the agitation and vacillation of those possessed by craving," here craving is the proximate cause of clinging (*upādāna*). In the phrase "that too is conditioned by contact (*phassa*)," [it refers to] the postulation of eternalism and so forth.

It is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the wrong adherence of others; wrong adherence, in turn, is the state of being turned away from hearing the true Dhamma, relying on spiritual friends, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma, while it is the proximate cause for hearing what is not the true Dhamma and so forth.
In such passages as "apart from contact," contact is the proximate cause for feeling;
the six bases of contact are the proximate cause for contact, and they are also the proximate cause for the entire suffering of the round of existence.
The thorough understanding, as it really is, of the origin and so forth of the six bases of contact is the proximate cause for disenchantment;

disenchantment is the proximate cause for dispassion—and this should be traced all the way up to final Nibbāna through non-clinging. The severing of the conduit to existence by the Blessed One is the proximate cause for omniscience;
likewise, it is the proximate cause for final Nibbāna through non-clinging. This is the Mode of Conveying the Proximate Cause.

Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*Lakkhaṇahāravannanā*): By the inclusion of "animosity" (*āghāta*) and so forth, there is a grouping of anger, enmity, slander, spite, envy, avarice, agitation, and disparagement of others;

for these share a single characteristic by virtue of being comprised within the category of hostile mental states (*paṭighacittuppāda*). By the inclusion of "delight" (*ānanda*) and so forth, [there is a grouping] of covetousness, improper greed, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, and so forth.

“Grasping” (*saṅgaha*) is included because it shares the same characteristic with the arising of a covetous mind. Likewise, by the mention of “malice,” the remaining fetters (*gantha*) and hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are included, because they share the same characteristic as the bodily fetter and hindrance.
By the mention of “delight” (*ānanda*), contact and the other [mental factors] are included, because they share the same characteristic as the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
By the mention of “virtue” (*sīla*), the trainings in higher mind and higher wisdom are also [included].

There is inclusion because they share a single characteristic by virtue of the characteristic of training (*sikkhā*). Here, however, it should be understood as referring specifically to virtue (*sīla*), such as the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) and so forth.
By the mention of "views" (*diṭṭhi*), there is also inclusion of the remaining types of clinging (*upādāna*), because they share a single characteristic by virtue of the characteristic of clinging.

In the phrase "of feelings" (*vedanānaṃ*), by the mention of "feelings," there is also inclusion of the remaining aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), because they share a single characteristic by virtue of the characteristic of an aggregate (*khandha*).

Because they possess a single characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇattā*). Likewise, because feeling is included within the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), there is an inclusion of all bases and elements that come under investigation by means of the characteristic of a base and the characteristic of an element, due to their having a single characteristic.

In the phrase "of those who do not know and do not see," by the mention of ignorance (*avijjā*), there is an inclusion of the taints of cause (*hetu-āsava*), the floods (*ogha*), the yokes (*yoga*), the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and so forth, due to their having the characteristic of being causes and so on.
Because ignorance has a single characteristic, it is likewise included by the mention of "craving" in the phrase, "the agitation and vacillation of those possessed by craving.

And in the statement, "that too is conditioned by contact," perception, mental formations, and consciousness are included by the mention of "contact" because they share the same characteristic as the aggregates through their status as causes for perversion, and because they possess the same characteristic as the aggregates.
By the mention of the "six bases of contact," the aggregates, faculties, elements, and so forth [are included].

“Comprehension” [is so called] because of having the same characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇa*) by virtue of being the cause for the arising of contact and by virtue of having the nature of full comprehension.

By the inclusion of the “guide to existence” (*bhavanetti*), there is also the inclusion of the defilements such as ignorance, etc., because they have the same characteristic by virtue of being the causes of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). This is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāra*). Commentary on the Mode of Conveying the Fourfold Array (*catubyūhahāra-vaṇṇanā*)
The introduction to this teaching concerns those to be trained who— having minds shaken by blame and praise, being unrepelled by wrong livelihood,

adhering to false views such as eternalism, and lacking a firm footing in the aggregates of virtue and other qualities— are averse to relishing the flavor of the virtues of the Perfectly Enlightened One. How, then,
might they be freed from the aforementioned defects and [established] in right practice?
"May they be intent on the welfare of both"—this is the Blessed One’s intended meaning here. The analysis of words (*padanibbacana*) is etymology (*nirutti*).

Because that [analysis] of the introductory phrases beginning with "Thus" and the scriptural phrases beginning with "my" is easily understood through the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), we have not elaborated upon it here for fear of excessive prolixity.
[The structure of the discourse] is according to the categories of word, word-meaning, indication, arrangement, discourse-teaching, and connection.
There are six kinds of connection (*saṇḍhi*). Among these, the connection of one word with another word is "word-connection" (*pada-saṇḍhi*).

Likewise, the connection of one word-meaning with another word-meaning is "meaning-connection" (*padattha-saṇḍhi*). The connection of a sutta containing various transitions with those respective transitions, as well as the connection between what precedes and what follows in a sutta containing a single transition, is "explanatory connection" (*niddesa-saṇḍhi*), which is [described] in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

It is analyzed as threefold by way of the connection of questions (*pucchānusandhi*), the connection of underlying intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*), and the connection of the sequence of the discourse (*yathānusandhi*).

These three connections have indeed already been examined in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Furthermore, the "connection of the sūtra" (*suttasandhi*) was previously shown by us according to its initial presentation.
The "connection of the teaching" (*desanāsandhi*) is the correlation of one teaching with another teaching.
That [passage] should be understood as follows: “Monks, whether it be me...
[as in the Sutta] ...you should not harbor mental dissatisfaction”—this teaching accords with the teaching:

“Monks, even if bandits with saws having teeth on both sides were to hack away at your limbs and members one by one, whoever should let their mind become corrupted thereby would not be following my instruction.”
“‘The obstacle will be yours alone by that act’—this accords with the teaching: ‘Māṇava, beings are owners of their karma… they will be heirs to their own actions.
‘But will you… know this?’—this accords with the teaching: ‘An angry man does not achieve his purpose… for he overcomes himself.’”
“Monks, when others praise me... [as before] ...you should not allow a state of mental elation to arise.
This accords with this teaching: “Monks, even phenomena (*dhammā*) are to be abandoned, let alone non-phenomena (*adhammā*).
Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma as similar to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping. “In that regard, if by you... [as before]...”
This accords with these teachings: "Exulting, that very thing will be an obstacle for you"; "The greedy man... [endures] the aim...";
and "Blinded by desire, shrouded in a net, covered by the veil of craving. Also: "A mere trifle...
[endures] a mere bit of virtue," and "He enters and dwells in the first *jhāna*. This indeed..."
This accords with the teaching beginning, “Brahmin, this sacrifice is more excellent and less troublesome than previous sacrifices,
and it is more fruitful and more beneficial,” because by stating that the first jhāna is more fruitful and more beneficial than virtue,
it demonstrates that virtue is inferior to jhāna.
“Having abandoned the taking of life,” and so forth, accords with such teachings as: “The ascetic Gotama, indeed, is virtuous... endowed with wholesome virtue.

“Other phenomena are profound,” and so forth, accords with the canonical text: “This Dhamma realized by me is profound,” and so on. For it is through the penetration of phenomena endowed with specific qualities such as profundity that the depth and other characteristics of knowledge are understood.
“There are, monks, some ascetics and brahmins,” and so forth, [accords with] “There are, monks, some ascetics and brahmins who are speculators about the past... and so on.
They assert: "The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. Some assert:
"They are non-eternal," or "both eternal and non-eternal," or "neither eternal nor non-eternal";
"they are finite," or "infinite," or "both finite and infinite," or "neither finite nor infinite"—asserting that "the self and the world are thus, and this alone is true, all else is false."
This accords with the teachings beginning with, “In this regard, some [recluses and brahmins] assert thus,” and so forth.

Also, the passage beginning, “There are, bhikkhus, some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the future” (santi bhikkhave eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā aparantakappikā), and so on, up to: “There are, bhikkhus, some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the future...
they assert: ‘The self is percipient and unimpaired after death. In this regard, some assert thus.’”
This accords with such teachings as: "The self is non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, and healthy after death";
or "Some proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being"; or "Some proclaim Nibbāna in the present life. And:
"The Tathāgata [is not defined] by feelings... this is conditioned. Thus it is said: "This is conditioned."

This accords with such teachings as: "It is gross; however, there is indeed a cessation of formations, and it exists"—having understood this, the Tathāgata, seeing the escape from it, has transcended it.
As for the statement, "That too is merely the vacillation of those...," this refers to [the views] of those venerable ones, apart from their own desire and apart from...
"Without personal realization— apart from hearsay, apart from logical reasoning, and apart from reflective acceptance of a view—

that there will be a knowledge that is purified and cleansed, this is impossible. But, monks, when there is no personal realization that is purified and cleansed, then as for those venerable recluses and brahmins..."
This accords with such teachings as: “Therein they merely purify the portion consisting of knowledge;
yet even that is declared to be clinging on the part of those venerable recluses and brahmins.
And this phrase, “That too is conditioned by contact,” [is explained by: “Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises...”
This accords with such teachings as: "The meeting of the three is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging," and:
"Friends, these states have desire as their root, are produced by attention, converge upon contact, and meet in feeling."
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu [regards] the six bases of contact,” and so forth;
“Ānanda, when a bhikkhu does not regard feeling as self, nor perception, nor volitional formations, nor consciousness as self—and not regarding them thus, he does not cling to anything in the world;
not clinging, he is not agitated; being unagitated, ...”
This accords with such teachings as: “One attains final nibbāna within oneself.
And the statement: “All those are encompassed within these sixty-two bases,” accords with such passages as: “Bhikkhus, whoever...
[they all] assert either these five aggregates or one or another of them.”
It is consistent with the teachings: “With the breakup of the body...
gods and humans”—“Just as a flame cast by the force of the wind, Upasīva, goes out and no longer enters into reckoning,” said the Blessed One.
"Thus the Sage, liberated from the group of names, reaches the goal and does not enter into reckoning.
This [verse] accords with the initial teachings; thus it is the "Fourfold Array" method of interpretation (*cātubyūho hāro*).
The commentary on the removal of the cycle (*āvattahāra*):

By the statement that malice and so forth are not to be committed, there is the practice of patience (*khanti*) and gentleness (*soracca*). Therein, patience includes faith (*saddhā*), wisdom (*paññā*), and the endurance of harm and suffering caused by others;

gentleness includes virtue (*sīla*). And by the mention of faith and the rest, all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*), beginning with the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), are included.

They are included. By the mention of "virtue" (sīla), all the qualities that are benefits of virtue, such as freedom from remorse and so forth, are included. By the expression "abstention from killing living beings and so forth," the dwelling in heedfulness is included;

by that, the entire holy life of the Dispensation (sāsana-brahmacariya) is included. By the mention of the Dhamma endowed with distinctions such as profundity, the Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi) is indicated.

For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) has unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints has [the knowledge of the path] as its proximate cause.
Unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) is Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*); through it, all the qualities of a Buddha, such as the Ten Powers (*dasabala*), converge.

By the inclusion of views such as eternalism (*sassata*), craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) are subsumed; through these two, the cycle of existence (*saṃsāravaṭṭa*) without beginning or end revolves.

Through the knowledge of the arising and so forth of feelings exactly as they are, there is the Blessed One’s purification via the threefold full understanding (*pariññāttaya*); through that, all the perfections (*pāramī*) converge by way of the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpārami*).

By the mention of ignorance in the phrase “of those who do not know and do not see,” there is the inclusion of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), and by that, the states rooted in improper attention are included.
By the mention of craving in the phrase “the agitation and vacillation of those gone under the sway of craving,” the nine states rooted in craving are included.
The passage beginning with “that too is conditioned by contact” demonstrates that the proclamation of eternalism and so forth exists in dependence upon conditions.

By this, the three characteristics beginning with impermanence are included. The description of the attainment of liberation through the thorough understanding of the six bases of contact includes the seven purifications.
The statement, “The Tathāgata’s body has severed the conduit to existence,” refers to the abandonment of craving;
by this, the Blessed One’s abandonment of all defilements is included. This is the Mode of Conveying the Inclusion (Āvatta-hāra).
Commentary on the Analysis:
Unwholesome states such as malice and delight have unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and so forth as their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).

Those wholesome states such as non-malice (*abyāpāda*), by means of which there is the non-doing and non-occurrence of malice, delight, and the rest, [have wise attention as their proximate cause]. Their...

Proper attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and so forth are the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). Among those, malice and the like belong only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while non-malice and the like belong to all four planes.

Likewise, abstinence from killing and so forth is either wholesome (*kusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*); for its proximate causes are the factors such as moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*).
In that regard, the wholesome [abstinences] may be either sense-sphere or supramundane (*lokuttara*), whereas the indeterminate ones are exclusively supramundane.
Regarding the statement, “There are, monks, other states that are profound,” those states may be either wholesome (*kusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*).

Among them, for the wholesome states, insight leading to emergence is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*). For the indeterminate states, the path-phenomena, insight, or adverting consciousness (*āvajjanā*) are the proximate causes.
Of these, the wholesome states are supramundane (*lokuttara*), while the indeterminate states may be either sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) or supramundane.
All views are indeed unwholesome and belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). In general, improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) through false adherence is their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).

Specifically, however, the false grasp of the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*), due to the absence of the analytical resolution of the compactness of continuity, accompanied by the recollection of past births and speculative reasoning, is the proximate cause for the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). [This occurs] regarding the state of connection existing as the relation between cause and fruit.

From the non-apprehension of the principle of diversity, a wrong grasp arises; when accompanied by the corresponding attention, it is the proximate cause for the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*).
In the same way, this should be stated for the remaining views as applicable. Regarding the phrase "of feelings" (*vedanānaṃ*):
here, feeling may be wholesome, may be indeterminate, may belong to the sense sphere, may belong to the fine-material sphere, or may belong to the immaterial sphere; contact is their proximate cause.
The knowledge of the path is the knowledge of feelings as they truly are in their arising and so forth; the fruit is liberation through non-clinging.
Regarding these, the classification of phenomena and so on should be understood according to the method stated in the passage: "Other phenomena are profound.

In such passages as "of those who do not know, who do not see," ignorance and craving are unwholesome states belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*); among these, the underlying tendencies (*āsava*) of ignorance, or improper attention itself, are the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).

The footing for craving is the perception of gratification in things that fetter. Regarding the statement, “That too is conditioned by contact,” the classification of contact into mental objects (*dhamma*) and so forth should be understood in the same way as that of feeling.

Following this method, the classification of mental objects and so forth should be applied accordingly to the bases of contact (*phassāyatana*) and the rest; this is the Mode of Analysis (vibhattihāra).
Commentary on the Reversal:

By cultivating patience and gentleness so as not to harbor resentment and the like, one achieves the power of reflective contemplation and meditative development, which brings about practice for the welfare of both oneself and others.
However, when resentment and the like do arise, they lead to ugliness and a painful sleep.
Bringing about the loss of enjoyments, ill-repute, and being difficult for others to approach, they produce great suffering in the hells and other realms.
Abstinence from killing living beings and so forth brings about, in succession, the excellence of freedom from remorse and the like.

Killing living beings and so forth, however, bring about, in succession, the unwholesomeness of remorse and the like. [This leads to] knowledge endowed with distinctions such as profundity for those to be trained.
Just as [wisdom] brings about specific qualities such as direct knowledge and supernormal powers by means of awakening to all that is knowable according to its true nature,
so too, knowledge devoid of distinctions such as profundity does not bring about those aforementioned specific qualities because it is obstructed regarding the objects of knowledge.

Furthermore, all these views constitute the two extremes— namely, eternalism and annihilationism— according to their respective natures, and thus they reach the shore of *sakkāya* (personality-belief).

They do not transcend [the world] because their intrinsic nature is non-emancipatory. However, right view, together with its requisites, being the middle way by virtue of its emancipatory nature, transcends the shore of identity-view and arrives at the further shore.

Because it constitutes the path, it brings about liberation through non-clinging, which is the realization of the arising and so forth of feelings as they truly are. The failure to penetrate the arising and so forth of feelings results in confinement within the prison of saṃsāra.
It brings about [the result] by way of being a condition for the formative forces (*saṅkhāra*). Delusion, which conceals the nature of what is felt, brings about delight in that [feeling].
However, the realization of things as they truly are brings about disenchantment and dispassion toward it.
Craving, accompanied by improper attention, spreads out the manifold web of views regarding wrong adherence. The complete cutting off of the aforementioned craving—

The first path contracts that web of views. Contact (*phassa*) is the condition for the establishing of doctrines such as eternalism (*sassatavāda*), because in the absence of contact, those [views] do not exist.

Since there is no cessation of contact and so forth through the non-cessation of the bases of contact (*phassāyatana*) and other factors bound by the fetters of views, there is simply no turning back from the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
The thorough knowledge (*pariññā*) of the bases of contact and so forth, according to reality, [is what brings about] the vision that transcends all views.
One does not transcend [the cycle]; as long as there is non-comprehension of the spheres of contact and so forth, one does not transcend that thicket of views.

The cutting off of the conduit to existence leads to the non-production of a personal identity in the future; for as long as the conduit to existence is not cut off, the continuity of existence will simply revolve in the future.
This is the Mode of Conveying the Reversal.
The Explanation of Synonyms:
“My,” “mine,” and “me” are synonyms. “Monks,” “ascetics,” and “those who practice austerities” are synonyms.
“Others,” “another,” and “adversaries” are synonyms. “Disparagement,” “infamy,” and “censure” are synonyms.
“Would speak,” “would say,” and “would do” are synonymous expressions. “Of the Dhamma,” “of the Vinaya,” and “of the Teacher’s instruction” are synonymous expressions.
“Of the Saṅgha,” “of the assembly,” and “of the group” are synonymous expressions. “There, there, among them” are synonymous expressions.
“By you,” “by your honors” are synonymous expressions. “Ill will,” “hatred,” and “malice” are synonymous expressions.
It is a synonymous expression. “The absence of pleasure, mental grief, and mental suffering” is a synonymous expression.
“Discontent of mind, corruption of consciousness, and malice of mind” is a synonymous expression.

“Not to be done, not to be produced, not to be set in motion” is a synonymous expression. Thus, in this manner, synonyms should be stated for all the terms; this is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacanahāra).
Commentary on the Exposition of Designations:

Ill-will (*āghāta*) is designated in ten ways or nineteen ways according to its objective basis (*vatthu*). The absence of conflict (*appaccaya*) is designated in six ways according to the modes of mental access (*upavicāra*).
Joy (*ānanda*) is designated in nine ways according to joy, rapture (*pīti*), and so forth. Rapture (*pīti*) is designated generally, and specifically as "slight" (*khuddikā*) and so forth.

It is classified in five ways. Mental joy (*somanassa*) is classified in six ways by way of its mental applications (*upavicāra*). Virtue (*sīla*) is classified in many ways by way of abstinence, observance, and so forth.

Knowledge (*ñāṇa*) associated with distinctions such as profundity is classified in four ways or twelvefold by way of the arising of consciousness, and in many ways according to the differentiation of its objects.
It is also classified by way of the sixty-two divisions, such as views regarding eternalism and so forth.
It is described in many ways through its internal divisions. Feeling is described in six ways, one hundred and eight ways, and in many other ways.
Its origin is described in five ways, and likewise its passing away. Its gratification is described in two ways. Its danger is described in three ways.
Its escape is described in one way and in four ways... [and so on] ...non-clinging liberation is described in two ways.
Ignorance (*avijjā*), expressed as “not knowing and not seeing,” is designated in four ways and eight ways according to the distinction of its objects.

Craving (*taṇhā*), expressed by the phrase “of those gone with craving” and so forth, is designated in six ways, one hundred and eight ways, and in many ways. Contact (*phassa*) is designated in six ways by way of its support.
Clinging (*upādāna*) is designated in four ways. Becoming (*bhava*) is designated in two ways and in many ways. Birth (*jāti*) [is designated] by way of its synonyms.
Old age is described in seven ways. Death is described in eight and nine ways.
Sorrow is described in five ways. Lamentation is described in six ways. Pain is described in four ways, as is mental grief.
Despair is described in four ways. “There is an origin” is a description of its source; [it is to be understood] as it truly is.

“...he understands”: this is the designation for the full understanding of suffering, the designation for the abandoning of its origin, the designation for the realization of its cessation, and the designation for the development of the path.
“Entangled within a net,” etc., is the designation for the inclusion of all views. “One whose tether to existence is severed,” etc., is [the designation] in two ways.

The designation of final Nibbāna (*parinibbāna-paññatti*). Thus, by way of designations such as the "designation according to source" for unwholesome and wholesome states like resentment (*āghāta*) and so forth, the various types of designation should be analyzed according to this method—for instance, "resentment" being a designation as a synonym for ill will (*byāpāda*), and "displeasure" (*appaccaya*) being a designation as a synonym for grief (*domanassa*).
This is the Mode of Conveying Designation (*paññatti-hāra*).
Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Descent:

By the inclusion of resentment (*āghāta*), there is the inclusion of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*); likewise by the inclusion of dissatisfaction (*anabhiraddhi*). By the inclusion of the absence of conditions (*appaccaya*), there is the inclusion of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).
This is the descent by way of the aggregates. Likewise, by the inclusion of resentment and so forth, there is the sphere of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*).

When the *dhammadhātu* is taken as either the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) or the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*), this constitutes an entry by way of the bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the truths (*sacca*).

Likewise, ignorance (*avijjā*) co-arising with malice (*āghāta*) and so forth is a condition by way of the conditions of root, co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance;
whereas that which does not co-arise [with them] is a condition by way of the conditions of proximity, contiguity, decisive-support, absence, disappearance, and repetition.
It is a condition; it is a condition by way of proximity and decisive support (*upanissaya*) alone.
The manner in which craving, clinging, and so forth, as well as contact and the rest—whether co-nascent or non-co-nascent—act as conditions for those [states] should be stated according to the case.

Furthermore, in some instances here, it is by way of predominance (*adhipati*); in some, by way of kamma (*kamma*); in some, by way of nutriment (*āhāra*); in some, by way of faculty (*indriya*); and in some, by way of jhāna (*jhāna*).
"Sometimes there is also a condition by way of the path. This distinction should also be understood; this is the entryway by means of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
In the same manner, the entryway for Ānanda and others by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth should be clarified through this very method.

Likewise, virtue (*sīla*) is the volition of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, as well as mental factors such as non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*); [while] killing living beings and so forth...

The inclusion of volition and those factors conducive to it—such as moral shame (*lajjā*) and compassion (*anuddaya*)—within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), and so forth, as well as the method of entry by way of the aggregates and other categories, should be explained in the same manner as previously described. This same method applies to the inclusion of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), views (*diṭṭhi*), feeling (*vedanā*), ignorance (*avijjā*), craving (*taṇhā*), and the rest.

Furthermore, in the case of the inclusion of escape (*nissaraṇa*), non-clinging (*anupādā*), and liberation (*vimutti*), the method of entry by way of the elements (*dhātu*) should be explained by way of the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhatadhātu*).

Likewise, by the statement, “...of feelings... [and so on]... liberated through non-clinging,” the Blessed One’s five aggregates of Dhamma beginning with virtue, as well as the factors conducive to enlightenment beginning with the foundations of mindfulness, are revealed;
thus, that should be understood as an entry-point by way of the door of the Dhamma.

Furthermore, by the statement, “That too is conditioned by contact,” the fact that even the manifestation of right view depends upon conditions is illustrated; thus, it is an entry-point by way of impermanence.

The method of entry (*otaraṇa*) is as follows: entry by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) through suchness and the nature of phenomena; and entry by way of the signless (*appaṇihita*) and emptiness (*suññatā*) due to the state of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
This same method applies to the remaining terms as well; this is the "Method of Entry" (*otaraṇa-hāra*).
Commentary on the "Method of Purification" (*sodhana-hāra*):

“‘They might speak against me...’—this is the introduction (ārambha). ‘[They might speak against] the Dhamma... or ‘the Saṅgha...’—this is purity of the words (padasuddhi), but not purity of the introduction.
‘In this matter, you should...’—this is both purity of the words and purity of the introduction.
The same method applies to the second method and those that follow. Likewise, ‘But this is indeed a trifling matter,’ etc., is the introduction. ‘Which one? and so forth...”
The question: “Having abandoned the taking of life,” and so forth, is purity of phrasing (*padasuddhi*), not purity of undertaking (*ārambhasuddhi*), nor is it purity of questioning (*pucchāsuddhi*).
“This indeed,” and so forth, is both purity of questioning and purity of phrasing, as well as purity of undertaking.
Likewise, “There are, monks,” and so forth, is the undertaking. “And which are they? and so forth, is the question. “There are, monks,” and so forth...

The commencement (*ārambha*). The passage beginning with "What" (*kiṃ*) and so forth is the inquiry regarding the commencement. The passage beginning with "As concentrated" (*yathāsamāhita*) and so forth is purity of words, but neither purity of commencement nor purity of inquiry.
The passage beginning with "These indeed are those" (*ime kho te*) and so forth is both purity of words, purity of inquiry, and purity of commencement.
In this manner, the commencement and the other factors are to be understood in all instances. This is the Mode of Conveying Purification (*sodhana-hāra*).
Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Resolutions (*adhiṭṭhāna-hāra*):

“Dispraise” (*avaṇṇa*) is a resolution in a general sense; without specifying that, it is a particular expression such as “of me,” “of the Dhamma,” or “of the Saṅgha. The same method applies to the bright side (*sukkapakkha*) as well.
Likewise, “virtue” (*sīla*) is a resolution in a general sense; without specifying that, it is a particular expression such as “abstaining from taking life,” and so forth.

“‘Other phenomena (aññe dhammā),’ etc., is a general determination; without specifying that, the particular statement is ‘This, monks, the Tathāgata understands,’ etc. Likewise, ‘Speculators regarding the past (pubbantakappikā),’ etc., is a general determination;

without specifying that, the particular statement is ‘Eternalists (sassatavādā),’ etc. Following this method, the general and the particular must be distinguished in all instances; this is the Mode of Conveying Determination (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra). Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Requisites (parikkhāra-hāra):
The cause for hatred and the like, as well as the nineteen grounds for resentment such as "He has done me harm," is [resentment].
The cause for joy and the like is attachment to the object. The causes for virtue are moral shame (*hiri*), moral dread (*ottappa*), fewness of desires, and so forth.

For the qualities described by the words "profound" and so on, all the perfections (*pāramitā*) are the cause, and specifically the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*). The cause for views is association with unworthy persons.
Hearing false doctrine and improper attention through wrong adherence are the causes in general;
specifically, however, the causes for doctrines such as eternalism are the recollection of past births and so forth. For feelings, ignorance, craving, kamma, and contact are the causes.
For liberation without clinging, the Noble Path is the cause. For the manifestation [of views], improper attention is the cause. For craving...
Contemplation of gratification in things that fetter is the cause. The six sense bases are the cause of contact; name-and-form is the cause of the six sense bases.
The development of purification is the cause for the total cutting off of the conduit to existence—this is the Mode of Conveying Requisites.
Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Coordination:

By the statement regarding the non-performance of malice and so forth, the perfection of patience (*khantisampadā*) is shown. By the passage beginning with "But this is only a trifle," the perfection of gentleness (*soraccasampadā*) is shown.
By the passage beginning with "There are, monks," the perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*) is shown.

And by the passages "For one who does not cling, Nibbāna is personally realized" and "Having understood feelings... as they really are, he is liberated through non-clinging," the perfection of concentration (*samādhisampadā*) is shown.

Together with this, the perfection of mastery over clear vision and deliverance is demonstrated. In this context, the perfection of patience is the proximate cause for the perfection of gentleness, because it is established through the power of reflective discernment.

Furthermore, the perfection of gentleness is in meaning simply virtue (*sīla*); likewise, the mention of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth is for the purpose of showing a figurative classification of virtue.
In that regard, virtue is the proximate cause for concentration (*samādhi*).
Concentration is the proximate cause for wisdom. Among these, through virtue, the abandoning of transgression and the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct are accomplished;
through concentration, the abandoning of the obsessions, the abandoning by suppression, and the abandoning of the defilement of craving are accomplished;
and through wisdom, the abandoning of the defilement of views, the abandoning by eradication, and the abandoning of the underlying tendencies are accomplished.

"It succeeds" (*sijjhati*) refers to the fulfillment of the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) through the three aggregates of the Dhamma—virtue (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*)—and the accomplishment of the three abandonments (*pahāna*).
This is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (*samāropana-hāra*).
The commentary on the sixteen modes of conveying is concluded.
Commentary on the Fivefold Method;
Commentary on the Method of the Swinging of the Balance.

By the statement regarding the non-committal of malice and so forth, the contraction of craving and ignorance is shown. For when there is mindfulness regarding the bases of self and what belongs to self...

In the case of affection (*sineha*) and delusion (*sammoha*), resentment arises through such thoughts as, "He has done me harm," and so forth. Likewise, by statements such as "abstaining from the destruction of life," and by such statements as, "Nibbāna is realized within oneself;
he is liberated through non-clinging; he understands the six bases of contact...
as they truly are," the absolute abandonment of craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) is demonstrated. Of these, however—

The objective basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for craving and ignorance—which are shown by their own nature through such terms as "speculators on the past" (*pubbantakappika*) and so forth, and through such phrases as "not knowing, not seeing" (*ajānataṃ apassantaṃ*)—are material phenomena and immaterial phenomena respectively.
Their respective remedies (*paṭipakkha*) are serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
Their fruits (*phala*) are liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) and liberation by wisdom (*paññāvimutti*). Among these, craving, or craving-and-ignorance, is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*).
The material and immaterial phenomena that serve as the basis for that [craving] are the truth of suffering; their non-occurrence is the truth of cessation;
and the understanding of cessation—namely, serenity and insight—is the truth of the path. In this way, the application of the Four Noble Truths should be understood.

Furthermore, by the inclusion of "craving" (*taṇhā*) here, all [defilements] by way of deceit, fraud, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, maliciousness, association with evil friends, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, and so forth, are included.

The unwholesome side is to be understood accordingly. Likewise, by the inclusion of ignorance (*avijjā*), the unwholesome side is to be understood by way of distorted attention, anger, resentment, denigration, spite, envy, avarice, hostility, harshness of speech, the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*), the view of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*), and so forth.
By the reverse of what was stated, [the wholesome side] is to be understood by way of non-deceit, non-craftiness, and so forth, as well as non-distorted attention and so forth;

likewise, by way of the factors conducive to serenity (*samatha*) such as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), and the factors conducive to insight (*vipassanā*) such as the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).
The side of the wholesome is to be led [to conclusion] by way of this. This is the ground for the method of the "Turning of Joy" (nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya).

Regarding the commentary on the method of the "Threefold Basket" (tipukkhalanaya): through the statement regarding the non-commissioning of malice and so forth, the absence of hatred is established; likewise, through the statements regarding abstention from killing living beings and harsh speech.

The accomplishment of non-greed (*alobha*) is established by the statement regarding the non-doing [of harm] toward Ānanda and others, as well as by the statement regarding abstaining from unchastity (*abrahmacariya*).

However, the accomplishment of both [non-greed and non-hatred] is established by the statement regarding abstaining from taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and so forth. The accomplishment of non-delusion (*amoha*) is established by the passage beginning, “This, monks, the Tathāgata understands,” and so on.
Thus, when the three roots of unwholesomeness are grasped, their opposites are implied by the statements regarding the non-doing of malice (*āghāta*) and the like.

And thus the three roots of the wholesome are established. Therein, by means of the three unwholesome roots, the entire unwholesome side should be expanded upon by way of the threefold misconduct, defilement, impurity, unevenness, unwholesome perception, thought, false dhammas, and so forth.

Likewise, by means of the three roots of the wholesome, the entire wholesome side should be clarified by way of the threefold good conduct, purification, evenness, wholesome perception, thought, wisdom, true dhammas, concentration, the doors of liberation, the liberations, and so forth. And here too, there is a conjunction with the Truths.
It should be understood. How? Greed—or indeed all wholesome and unwholesome roots—is the truth of origination;
the aggregates of clinging, produced by them and serving as their basis and domain, are the truth of suffering. In this manner, the application of the truths is to be understood.
This is the ground for the Tipukkhalo method.
Commentary on the Lion’s Play Method:

By the statement regarding the non-performance of malice, joy, and so forth, mindfulness (*sati*) is established. For it is through mindfulness that one discerns the blameworthy and the blameless, as well as their respective dangers and benefits;
having thus observed them, one abandons the blameworthy and undertakes the blameless. Likewise, [it applies] to wrong livelihood.
Through the mention of abstaining [from unwholesome deeds], energy (*vīriya*) is established. For it is by means of energy that one dispels thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty;

and the virtue of purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhisīla*) is accomplished through energy. Through the mention of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, mindfulness (*sati*) is established.
For it is by means of mindfulness that, having discerned the blameworthy and the blameless, as well as the dangers and benefits therein, one abandons the blameworthy and [cultivates] the blameless.
It proceeds by undertaking [the practice]. For it is said that this [faith] "has the state of being directed toward the object as its manifestation.

Through the passage beginning, "Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands this," there is the accomplishment of concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā). For through wisdom there is understanding of things as they truly are (yathābhūtāvabodha), and one who is concentrated understands things as they truly are.
Likewise, through the passage beginning, "Permanent, eternal," regarding what is impermanent, [one perceives it] as "permanent."

Perverted view (*vipallāsa*) consists of: the perversion of perceiving what is not happiness as "happiness" through such statements as, "After death, the self is free from disease and possesses absolute happiness, having attained Nibbāna in this very life";
the perversion of perceiving what is not beautiful as "beautiful" through such statements as, "Endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure";
and the perversion of perceiving what is not-self as "self" by means of all words that indicate [false] views.
In this way, the four perversions (vipallāsā) are established here; by way of their opposites, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānāni) are likewise established.
In that regard, four types of persons are to be demonstrated by means of the four faculties (indriyāni).

How so? For those who are temperamentally dominated by craving (taṇhācarita) are of two kinds: those with dull faculties (mudindriya) and those with sharp faculties (tikkhindriya); likewise for those temperamentally dominated by views (diṭṭhicarita).
Among these, the first— possessing the perverted view that sees the foul as beautiful—

enters the fixed course of rightness after discerning the true nature of the body as it really is through the power of mindfulness. The second— possessing the perverted view that sees the unpleasant as pleasant—
[does so] by means of the power of energy, known as the restraint of energy, as described in the passage beginning, "He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire."

He dispels that perversion. The third [type of person], who grasps at what is impermanent as "permanent" through a lack of accordance with reality, penetrates the momentary nature of formations as it truly is by means of the power of serenity (*samatha*) due to their state of being concentrated.

The fourth [type of person], who falsely adheres to a non-self as "self" because of the dense and variegated mass of the continuity, the collection, the function, and the object—namely, the mere heap of phenomena such as contact and so forth—[does so] by means of mental attention to the emptiness of the fourfold limit.

He shatters that false adherence. Furthermore, in this context, the entire unwholesome side should be traced back by way of the four perversions, the four taints, the four floods, the four yokes, the four bodily ties, the four ways of going, the arising of craving, the four kinds of clinging, the seven stations of consciousness, and the lack of full understanding.

Likewise, the entire side of purification should be traced back by way of the four foundations of mindfulness, the fourfold abiding in jhāna, the qualities conducive to happiness, the immeasurables, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, and so forth.
This is the ground for the "Lion’s Play" method (*sīhavikkīḷita-naya*). Here too, by means of the perception of beauty and the perception of pleasure—
Alternatively, the truth of origination should be understood through the four perversions, while the five aggregates of clinging—which serve as their basis and object—are the truth of suffering;
in this way, the application of the truths is to be known.
This concludes the commentary on the two methods of the "Goading Hook" for determining direction.

Thus, with the establishment of these three methods of meaning (*atthanaya*), the two methods of conventional expression (*vohāranaya*) are also established. For indeed, the "surveying of directions" (*disālocana*) is the examination of the phenomena that constitute the directions of the methods of meaning; the "hook" (*aṅkusa*) is the bringing together of those [phenomena]. These are the five methods as they have been defined.
The commentary on the fivefold method is concluded.
The commentary on the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna* [follows].

This discourse belongs to the sixteenfold *suttanta-paṭṭhāna* as that which pertains to defilement, to the latent tendencies, and to the state of one beyond training—or specifically, as that which pertains to both defilement and penetration, and to the state of one beyond training.
In the twenty-eightfold *suttanta-paṭṭhāna*, however, it is mundane and supramundane, based on seven categories of phenomena, consisting of knowledge, the knowable, vision, and cultivation;
it belongs to our own tradition and to the traditions of others, is answerable or unanswerable, and is wholesome or unwholesome.
It should be understood that there are things both permitted and prohibited.
The commentary on the method of the treatise is finished.
The commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*: Commentary on the Discourse to the King’s Minister. 150. Regarding the word "Rājagaha":
it is so called because it is preeminent due to its possession of excellence in terms of its difficult terrain, its location, and other such factors, and because it is frequented by kings.

"Taken" means "Rājagaha," as it was said: "Of Mandhātu... so it is called. In that context, since it was already taken possession of by King Reṇu and others after being taken possession of by the Great Being, the Great Steward (Mahāgovinda), the mention of Mahāgovinda is made.
Some say that "Mahāgovinda" refers to a certain ancient king of great power. "Because of being taken possession of" means because of being taken possession of as the capital city.
It is called Rājagaha because it was made by a king who had entered the city; it is also called Rājagaha because it resembles a house surrounded by kings, such as Gijjhakūṭa and others;
it is also called Rājagaha because it is a royal dwelling (*rājamāna-geha*) due to its excellent mansions;
and [it is so called] because of the security provided for those approaching it, which prevents harm from rival kings.
It is called Rājagaha because it is the "home" (*gaha*) or abode of kings; it is called Rājagaha because it is the home established by kings after they had seen it and settled there properly.

It is called Rājagaha because it "shines" (*rājate*) with its delightful groves and parks, and because it is "grasped" (*gahati*) or "seized" (*pariggayhati*) by beings through the sense of ownership due to the comfort of dwelling there.
In such a manner, that region is a distinguished place enjoyed by exalted beings.
He said: “But as for that,” and so forth. “Of them” means of the *yakkhas*. “Residence-grove” (*vasanavana*) refers to a pleasure grove that serves as a place of recreation.
“Without distinction” refers to such passages as: “he dwells restrained by the restraint of the *Pātimokkha*”; “having attained the first *jhāna*, he dwells therein”;
“he dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*mettā*); and “by not attending to any signs (*nimitta*).”
It is [the term] without the qualification of another word, as in such passages as “having entered and dwelt in the signless concentration of mind.
It is called the *iriyāpatha* (posture) because it is the means for the occurrence of bodily activity (*kāyikakiriyā*).
For standing and the other postures cannot bring about any bodily activity without their respective states, such as the cessation of movement and so forth.

One dwells by means of this and it is itself dwelling; thus it is "vihāra. A vihāra that brings about a divine state is a "divine vihāra" (dibbavihāra), which refers to the sublime meditative absorptions (mahaggata-jhānāni).
However, in the *Nettippakaraṇa*, it is stated: "The four formless attainments are imperturbable dwellings" (āneñjā vihārā).

That statement was made with reference to their specific nature as a particular mode of cultivation, just as the meditations on loving-kindness and so forth are designated as "divine abodes" (brahmavihāra).
In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, these too are called "divine abidings" (*dibbavihāra*) because they generally bring about a divine state.

They are "divine abidings" (*brahmavihāra*) because they are abidings that have become sublime (*brahma*) or excellent (*seṭṭha*) through their occurrence by way of promoting welfare and so forth; [they refer to] the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the rest.

They are "noble abidings" (*ariyavihāra*) because they are the abidings of the noble ones (*ariya*), being not shared with others; [they refer to] all four attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). "Illustrating the state of possession" means illustrating the condition of being possessed.

The explanation of the combination of postures (*iriyāpatha*) is [included] because there is no distinct statement explaining the combination of other modes of dwelling (*vihāra*), and because the purpose of explaining the combination of postures has already been accomplished. Regarding the term "dwells" (*viharati*):

here, the prefix *vi-* indicates the sense of separation, while *harati* means "to lead" or "to carry out"; thus, the meaning is "to practice. In this context, what is separated from what, and how is what practiced?
Having in mind the exhortation contained within [the phrase] *antolīnaṃ*, he said, “So hi,” and so forth.

He said, “*Idam assā*,” and so forth, because he stated “at Rājagaha” for the purpose of showing the village that served as the Buddha’s range of activity, and stated “in the mango grove” for the purpose of showing the dwelling place appropriate for Buddhas. “*Etan*” refers to this locative expression, “at Rājagaha.”

In the sense of proximity, it is as in the examples: "The cows graze by the Ganges" and "The Gagga family lives at the well. "Brought up by a prince" (*kumārabhata*) means one who was nurtured by a prince;
that very person is a *komārabhacca*, just as the best of medicines is simply called "medicine" (*bhesajja*).
"Overwhelmed by humors" (*dosābhisanna*) means having humors aggravated by wind, bile, and so forth. "Having purged" (*virecetvā*) means having separated [the humors] from their provocation.

"Aḍḍhateḷasahi" means with thirteen hundred and fifty bhikkhus—that is, with thirteen hundred less fifty. Since that amounts to twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus, he said "with a half-hundred," and so forth.

"Rājatī" means it shines; the meaning is that it is beautiful. "Rañjeti" means it delights. "Rañño" refers to his father, King Bimbisāra. An enemy (sattu) is so called in the sense of opposing the teaching and in the sense of harming.
"Bhāriye" means heavy or difficult for others to accomplish. "Suvaṇṇasatthakena" means with a golden knife.
He says that it is improper to bring an iron [implement] near the king’s body. "With a golden lancet" means having had the arm slit with a lancet encrusted with gold;
having thus slit the arm by piercing the veins and mixing it with water, he made her drink it because blood alone is difficult for a pregnant woman to digest.
"The leaders" (dhurā) means those who have become the leaders of the group.
The meaning is “I carry. “I take up the burden” means I perform the duties of a leader and the responsibilities of a group head.
The passage beginning with “Formerly indeed... is the Khandhaka text itself. *Potthaniya* means a knife, which is also called *nakhara*;
[it is also said that *potthaniya* is a knife, and *khara* is also a knife]. *Divā divassa* means even during the day of the day; the meaning is at the time of midday.
"Having licked her own body, she sustains herself; death by one's own hand is not fitting. For noble disciples do not bring about their own downfall.

"By means of the bliss of the path and its fruit" means she sustains herself by means of walking meditation that brings about the bliss of the path and its fruit, and is associated with the bliss of the fruit of stream-entry.
"In the shrine courtyard" means in the shrine courtyard which is a place for worshiping with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. "For the purpose of sitting" means...

For the purpose of seating the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. In the world of the Four Great Kings... [and so on]... he was reborn there as a yakkha by virtue of his long-accumulated attachment resulting from having frequently been reborn there in the past.

"Having shaken" means that, due to the powerful nature of affection for his son and the expansive force of the co-nascent joy, [he shook it] by means of the material phenomena (rūpadhamma) originated thereby.
Having stirred the entire body by means of pervasion. Therefore he said: "It remained in contact with the marrow.
"The father’s quality" means the quality of affection the father had for himself. Regarding the word "having caused to release," the particle *iti* here has the sense of "manner";

thus, it refers back to the very manner mentioned as "by way of sending assassins and so forth. "The method of detailed exposition" refers to the detailed account beginning with the winning over of Ajātasattu.
This is merely the method for the discourse that ought to be spoken. But why is the discourse not given here in an expanded manner? He says:
"But because it has already been handed down, everything is not stated.

"Of King Kosala" means of the Great King of Kosala. "A designation for the wise" is a synonym for the wise. "They know" means they understand. "By the Vedas" means that which functions or proceeds by means of knowledge (*veda*) as its instrument.
"Ettha" means on this day. The word "vā" has the sense of non-exclusivity; by it, certain types of mental misconduct, immorality, and so forth are included.
For instance, the cowherd’s uposatha was described in terms of a mind accompanied by covetousness, while the Nigaṇṭha’s uposatha was described in terms of the fault of lying and so on.
As it is said: "He passes the day with that mind accompanied by covetousness."
“Thus, at whatever time one should be exhorted to truthfulness, at that very time she exhorts one to false speech,” and so forth.
“In this context” means in the word *uposatha*. “Enumeration of meanings” (*atthuddhāra*) refers to the extraction of the various meanings to be expressed.
But is it not the case that words settle upon their mere literal sense, such that multiple meanings are not denoted by a single word?

This is indeed true when specific words are considered; however, this investigation—spoken of as the "extraction of the meaning of the word *uposatha*"—is stated by taking into account the commonality (*sāmañña*) of those meanings being expressible by the word *uposatha*.
This same method applies even to the extractions of meaning that appeared previously in passages such as "Thus have I heard" (*evam me sutam*).
And although it is certainly the case that [the term] also pertains to the recitation of the *Pātimokkha* and so forth...
The word *uposatha* is a general term (*sāmañña-rūpa*) because it does not denote a specific [subordinate] term;

however, it should be understood that this meaning is stated by not adopting such a general sense. It is called *uposatha* because it is entered into (*upecca*) and observed (*vasīyati*) or performed (*anuṭṭhīyati*) by those who are endowed with purity of virtue (*sīla-suddhi*).
Alternatively, it is so called because one approaches (*upecca*) through formal undertaking (*samādāna*) or through resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). It refers to the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*.
It is called *uposatha* because one must dwell [in it] for the sake of the noble abodes (*ariyavāsa*) and so forth; it is virtue (*sīla*).

It is called *uposatha* because one must approach and dwell [in it], or dwell in accordance with it, by means of fasting (*anasana*) and other such practices. *Upavāsa* refers to the undertaking [of the precepts].

Because of its status as a family of *uposatha*, even a noble elephant included within the group of nine female elephants is called *uposatha* by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*), regardless of any specific action [performed]; thus he said, "the *uposatha*."
In the passage beginning with "nāgarāja," it is a designation (*paññatti*). Furthermore, the occurrence of the term *uposatha* during the day is stated precisely in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding the phrase "For one who is pure, there is always the *phaggu*":

here, "of one who is pure" (*suddhassa*) means of one who is pure by virtue of being entirely free from the stains of the defilements (*kilesamala*). "Ve" is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*). Alternatively, "ve" has the meaning of "clever" (*byatta*). "Always the *phaggu*" (*sadā phaggū*) means at all times.

It is indeed the Phagguṇa constellation. For those who hold the view that for one performing a ritual bath at a sacred ford on the day of Uttaraphagguṇī in the month of Phagguṇa, there is the casting out of the year's defilements—the Blessed One spoke this in order to separate them from that [view].

"The Uposatha is always pure for one who is pure" means that for one who is pure by virtue of the aforementioned purity, the factors of the Uposatha and the undertaking of the vows [are likewise pure].
And even for one who has not formally undertaken it, the Uposatha is constant; the meaning is that it is indeed a dwelling in the Uposatha.
It is called "pannarasa" by way of fulfilling fifteen lunar days.
It is "kumudavatī" because there are many, or especially abundant, water-lilies (*kumuda*) therein; [it refers to] that *kumudavatī*. Of the four...
It is called *cātumāsī* because it is the completion of the months. Since that very term is stated in the text as *cātumāsinī*, he says:

"But here it is called *cātumāsinī*. Then, there is the fullness of the month due to the fullness of the month of Kattika; the fullness of the season due to the fullness of the rainy season (*vassāna-utu*);
and the fullness of the year due to the fullness of the year characterized by the month of Kattika.
“Mā” refers to the moon, because by its movement the day is measured. Here, “full” means full of all its digits (kalā) on this night;
for at that time the moon is seen completely full.
And here, the phrases “on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth” are stated in terms of the day, while “Komudī,” etc., are stated in terms of the night.
"Surrounded by royal ministers" means surrounded by ministers born into the royal family; or alternatively, surrounded by both kings devoted [to him] and ministers.
"The four defilements" refers to these four defilements: clouds, mist, smoke and dust, and Rāhu; this is the determination made in the Commentary.

“Pītivacanaṃ” means speech originated by rapture (pīti). For that speech which, independent of a recipient, issues forth suddenly from the mouth by its own essence solely through the power of sublime rapture—this is what is intended here by the term “udāna.
Therefore he said: “That speech of rapture which cannot be contained within the heart,” and so forth.
“Dosehi itā gatā apagatā” means that the letter *ta* in *dosiṇā* is changed to *na*, as in the example: “One who has conquered the defilements (*kilesa*) is a Victor (*jina*), one who has won.
The term *anīya* should be understood in the sense of the agent; thus he says “it delights the mind,” i.e., “delightful,” just as in the expression “doctrines that lead out (*niyyānika* dhammā”).
Because of its moonlight, the night possesses a beautiful form; thus he says “free from the aforementioned defects,” and so forth.

In this context, "clouds and so forth" refers to the aforementioned defects; its beauty is to be understood through the very absence of those defects, as well as through the excellence of the season (*utu*).

It is "fit to be a characteristic" (*lakkhaṇaṃ bhavituṃ yuttā*): it is fit to serve as the defining mark for the day, month, season, and year—such as "the day of this night," "the month of this night," "the season of this night," or "the year of this night"—thus it is "characterizable" (*lakkhaññā*), meaning it is worthy of being characterized (*lakkhaṇīyā*).

Because it was stated, “so that our mind might become serene by attending upon him,” it follows that in the phrase “a recluse or a brahmin,” it is the ultimate recluse (*paramattha-samaṇa*) and the ultimate brahmin (*paramattha-brāhmaṇa*) that are intended, not one who is a recluse merely by way of renunciation, nor one who is a brahmin merely by birth.
Thus he said: “A recluse because of having stilled evil; a brahmin because of having banished evil. Although the plural number should have been used...

The singular number, or the use of the plural when the singular should be used, is a modification of the grammatical number (*vacanabyataya*). In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, the modification is shown using the singular alone.
For the word "oneself" (*attan*) and for those worthy of respect (*garuṭṭhāniya*), the use of the plural even when referring to a single entity is conventional (*nirūḷha*).

"By the whole" means by the entire expression beginning with "Truly delightful" (*ramaṇīyā vatā*). "The action that is the sign of illumination" (*obhāsanimittakamma*) means the action that has become the sign of illumination.

The meaning is "making a sign well-known. Regarding the word *ca* (and) in the phrase "and Devadatta": the particle *ca* is used here for the purpose of applying [the case] to oneself (*attūpanayane*).

By this, it conveys the following sense: just as King Ajātasattu committed a great offense by killing his own father, who was a noble disciple and an attendant of the Teacher, so too does he commit a great offense by providing support to Devadatta, who causes great harm to the Blessed One.
"Behind him" (tassa piṭṭhichāyāya) means by leaning against Jīvaka’s back; the meaning is: having made him the front and leaning against him.
"For the purpose of cutting off distraction" (vikkhepapacchedanatthaṃ) means for the purpose of severing the distraction that would arise regarding his own forthcoming discourse;
the intended sense is "for the purpose of its non-arising. Therefore he said, "For in that [discourse]," and so forth.

151. “*So kira*,” etc., is the method as it appears in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*). This same method applies to the subsequent etymological analysis of the word *makkhali*. “*Upasaṅkamantī*” means they approached.

“*Tadeva pabbajjaṃ aggahesī*” means that he took up that very form of renunciation (*pabbajjā*) after having performed it. It is called a “Saṅgha” because it is a collection of those who have gone forth;
it is a Saṅgha merely by virtue of being a group of those who have gone forth, not by virtue of possessing a liberating view or the commonality of perfectly purified virtue.
The intended meaning is "being a collection. "He has one" means that he possesses a retinue belonging to him who is recognized as a Teacher.

"That very same" refers precisely to what is designated as a group of those gone forth (*pabbajita*). Some, however, say: "He is a *saṅghin* by virtue of being a group of those gone forth, and a *gaṇin* by virtue of being a group of householders";
but that is merely their own opinion, because in the world the word *saṅgha* is conventionally established only for a group [of renunciants]. "By way of teaching conduct" means...

[He is so called] by way of training in ascetic practices such as nakedness and the practice of living in the open air. "Manifest" means he is made known through his status as a member of the Saṅgha and so forth.
Having said "one of few desires," in order to show the state of having few desires found therein, it is said: "Due to his fewness of desires, he does not even wear a cloth.
For in him, that kind of fewness of desires characterized by concealing one's existing virtues—which is found in those belonging to the [orthodox] Dispensation—is not present.
“Yaso” means a reputation or fame. Because it is recognized as such that “by this one crosses the flood of saṃsāra,” it is called a *tittha* (ford);
thus he said, “a *titthakara* is one who creates a doctrine. “Respected by the good” means respected as “good,” not respected by those who are good;
thus he said, “This one is good,” and so forth. “These vows of mine have been well-practiced for such a length of time.”
One who knows that many nights have passed since his going forth is called *rattaññū* (one who knows the nights).

Since those nights of his have become long-standing, he is one who has gone forth for a long time (*cirapabbajita*). In this context, by mentioning his state of having gone forth for a long time, he shows his wisdom and virtue;
by mentioning his knowledge of the nights, he shows his clear comprehension therein. *Addhānaṃ* means a long period of time.
When asked, "How many [reigns] was he? he said, "Two or three royal successions," meaning the sequence of the reigns of two or three kings.

Having said "advanced in years" (*addhagata*), he stated "having reached the final stage of life" (*pacchimavayaṃ anuppatto*) to show that the mention of "age" (*vaya*) refers to the concluding stage of life.
"Both" refers to the pair of phrases: "advanced in years" and "having reached the final stage of life."
He says, "Having previously gone with his father into the presence of the Teacher... desiring to hear," referring to the fact that he had heard the teaching before.

By the phrase "by seeing," it does not mean mere sight; rather, having seen him and engaged in conversation and discussion with him, he then heard their doctrine of non-action and became dissatisfied with them. By the phrase "talk of virtues," it means talk of non-existent virtues.
Therefore he said, "Being even more dissatisfied. If he was dissatisfied, why did he remain silent?
To this he replied, "Though being dissatisfied," and so forth. 152.
*Gosālāyaṃ* means in a village of that name. Some say it is a stall where cattle stand during the rainy season.

153. *Paṭikiṭṭhataraṃ* means more inferior. *Tantāvūtāni* means woven by stretching out on a loom. By the phrase beginning with “cold when it is cold,” he shows the state of being even more inferior than that which is already inferior through six modes.

154. *Vaccaṃ katvāpi*: by the word *api*, he includes this meaning: “even after eating food, or even if smeared by some impurity. *Vālikathūpaṃ katvā* means having made a stupa out of sand according to the prescribed manner. 156. *Palibuddhanakilesa*:
a defilement such as lust, etc., whose function is to obstruct one within saṃsāra, and whose objects are fields, lands, children, wives, and so forth.
Commentary on the Discourse concerning Jīvaka Komārabhacca: 157.
It was said, “Alas, this is a misfortune for me,” because it does not proceed according to one’s intention.
Jīvaka’s silence is like the crushing of my purpose; therefore, by questioning him and making him speak, my purpose must be fulfilled.
Showing that this was the king’s intention in this matter, he said, “Was it regarding the elephant?
and so forth. “Why silent? means: for what reason are you silent? What is that reason by which you remain silent? This is what is meant by the words, “For what reason are you silent?
Granted that the entire conduct of the Tathāgata is unique and of a wondrous, marvelous nature, never shared by others; nevertheless...

The descent into the womb, the birth, the great renunciation, the perfect enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the Twin Miracle, and the descent from the deva-world are exceedingly well-known in the world with its devas; they cannot be denied by anyone, and therefore these alone have been selected here.

"In the sense of describing how something has come to be" (*itthambhūtākhyānatthe*) means in the sense of stating that it has become or arisen in such a manner, in this way. [This refers to] the accusative case (*upayogavacana*).
Regarding the word "abhuggato" (exalted): here, *abhi* is a prefix (*upasagga*) indicating the sense of "having become such" (*itthambhūtākhyāna*).

Because of its connection with that [prefix], the accusative case in "taṃ kho pana bhagavantaṃ" (that Blessed One) is used in the sense of the genitive; thus he says, "The meaning is 'of that Blessed One'.
"Endowed with excellent qualities" (*kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgato*) means joined with excellent qualities; it depends on them because they are its object.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Regarding the word "best" (*seṭṭha*), the same method applies here as well.

It is called *kitti* because it is to be praised; it is called *sadda* because it is that which is sounded. Thus he said, "The sound of fame (*kittisadda*) is simply fame itself. Sound proceeding by way of praise is the cry of eulogy (*thutighosa*).
Because it proceeds with reference to qualities not shared by others, it has risen up, having overwhelmed and overspread the world including the devas.
"Thus, the Blessed One": he who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and shattered all defilements, awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
the god beyond gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahma beyond Brahmas;
the Lord of the World, whose fame and renown are spread everywhere in the world with its gods because of such qualities as blessedness—he is the Blessed One. "The Blessed One."
And this is the proclamation of the Teacher’s name. Therefore, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati said:
“‘Bhagavā’—this name was not given by his mother,” and so forth. But what follows is the proclamation of his qualities.
Just as one engaged in meditation (kammaṭṭhānika) applies the word *iti* to each of the nine attributes beginning with “Arahan,” [so too] the qualities of the Buddha [are proclaimed].
