To show that they are likewise recollected even by one who merely summarizes the qualities of the Buddha, he said: "Thus indeed is the Arahant, thus indeed is the Perfectly Enlightened One...
[and so on] ...thus indeed is the Blessed One. Here, the word *iti* has the sense of making something immediate and present, as in expressions such as "this is not so, this is untrue";
the word *pi* has the sense of inclusion, and by it, the great abundance of those qualities is indicated.
It has been illuminated. And showing that those [qualities] should be summarized by a wise person only after bringing them to mind, he said:

"It is meant: 'by this and that reason. For when one summarizes after investigating in this way, the listener who is being summarized gains an exceedingly great confidence in the Blessed One. "Because of being far away" means because of being very distant.
"Of enemies" means of the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*). "Of spokes" means of the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra.

"Because they have been destroyed" means because they have been shattered. "Of requisites, etc. refers both to the requisites such as robes and to the special forms of honor. "From that" means from the *Visuddhimagga*.
And just as [the details] are found in the *Visuddhimagga*, so too their full exposition should be understood from its commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*).

Because Jīvaka had frequently heard of the Buddha’s qualities in the presence of the Teacher, and because he had seen the Truths, he was free from doubt and had attained self-confidence regarding the Teacher’s dispensation;
therefore, the text says, “But Jīvaka,” and so forth. “Of five colors” means of five kinds, such as the small [flowers] and others.
It was continuously filled because of his state of having performed meritorious deeds. For, due to an obstruction caused by karma...
The king’s body was mangled by the arrows. 158.
Having said “supreme,” it is shown that not only the state of being excellent is the reason here, but rather the quality of making little noise is also a reason;
thus, the passage beginning with “horse-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, and carriages” was spoken. Among elephant-vehicles, only those that are without rut were used.

She had them dressed like female elephants as she took hold of them. For the purpose of dispelling the king’s suspicion, they were made to sit there in the guise of women because of their habit of moving about nearby.
To show the king that he was inaccessible to others, they were made to assume the appearance of men and were provided with weapons in their hands.
"She announced" means she made it known. "That very thing" refers either to the going or the not-going.
159. *Mahañca* is a nominative singular form used in the sense of the instrumental; thus he said, "and by the great. *Mahaccā* means "by the great";
it is stated with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*), meaning "by the great one. Therefore he said, "by the majesty of the king.
"The lordship and glory of two great provinces" refers to the sovereignty over the provinces of Aṅga and Magadha. *Āsattakhaggāni* ("with swords girt")—
Those who have swords fastened over their shoulders by way of being suspended therefrom.

"Mahāmattā" refers to those great officials, powerful royal persons, who possess great pride (*matta*) by virtue of their lineage, wealth, sovereignty, and so forth. "Like young *vidyādhara*s" means like the sons of *vidyādhara*s.
"Sons of *raṭṭhiya*s" means sons of *bhoja*s. "Elephant-herds" means multitudes of elephants. "Mutual collision" means by way of being uninterrupted.
They are mutually connected by way of their occurrence.
Mental trepidation is "fear" in the sense of being itself afraid; it is so called because it fears in that manner.

Knowledge is "fear" in the sense of investigating fear, because it regards as fearful an object that is actually to be feared when it appears as fearful, thinking, "This is to be feared. For this very reason, it was said:
"But as for the knowledge of the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*), does it fear or not fear? It does not fear.
For that is merely an investigation [into the fact] that 'past formations have ceased, present ones are ceasing, and future ones will cease.
It is "terror" (*bhaya*) because one fears this object. It is "terror" because by means of it one fears evil. It is "terrifying" (*bhayānaka*).
The form of fear (*bhāyanākāra*). "Fear" (*bhaya*) refers to the fear of knowledge (*ñāṇabhaya*). "Agitation" (*saṃvega*) is the knowledge accompanied by moral dread (*sahottappa-ñāṇa*).

"Terror" (*santāsa*) is being utterly terrified. In the sense of being something to be feared it is "fear" (*bhaya*); in its terrifying nature it is "dreadful" (*bherava*); thus it is "fear-and-dread" (*bhayabherava*), the object of fear.
Therefore he said, "it comes. "They praise the timid": the wise praise the timid person because of their fear of evil and their shrinking away from it. For indeed...
In this context, *sūra* means one who is bold and shameless in committing evil; such a person they do not praise. Therefore he said: “For the virtuous do not commit evil out of fear.
Here, “out of fear” (*bhayā*) means from the dread of evil; the meaning is: because of moral dread (*ottappa*).
“Trembling of the body” (*sarīracalana*) refers to the shaking of the body due to the influence of fear. “Some” (*eke*) refers to those dwelling in the Uttaravihāra. “In Rājagaha,” and so forth.
This is the explanation of their intention. Granted, one who is equal in age is called a "companion" (*vayassa*), as this is a conventional usage;
yet any friend whatsoever is a companion. Therefore, the expression "companion" (*vayassa*) means the expression "friend.
"You did not deceive" means you did not mislead. "He would perish" means he would be afflicted by mental distress.
Commentary on the Question on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life (Sāmaññaphala-pucchā-vaṇṇanā) 160.

"The Blessed One’s splendor" means the majesty of a Buddha. It pervaded the king's body just as it did when the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa was approaching the Blessed One and had entered the middle of the forest grove. "Some" refers to those residing at the Uttaravihāra monastery. 161.
Regarding the phrase "where [he was]," he explains that the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative, saying: "He went to where the Blessed One was."
Then, in order to show that the state of silence had completely pervaded that community of monks without exception, it was said, "silent, silent";

thus he said: "From whichever [side]... the meaning is 'only'. Because of the crookedness of the hand, lack of restraint and an act of lack of clear comprehension should be understood as *hatthakukkucca*.
The word *vā* has the sense of an unstated alternative; by it, something other than that [is included].

It should be understood that the state of non-restraint has been eliminated. In this context, however, since lack of restraint of the eye is the very first [of the senses] and is difficult to ward off, the phrase "adorned with every ornament" and so forth was spoken to demonstrate its absence.

Since mental tranquility is obtained through the attainment of physical and verbal tranquility, the latter is also obtained by inference; thus he said, "and by means of mental [tranquility]. "Tranquility" (upasama) means...
"Restraint" means the perfection of conduct (*ācārasampatti*). "In five turnings" means in the five turnings of the person.

"In five ways" means by the five modes mentioned beginning with "He is the same toward the desirable and the undesirable," and by the fivefold accomplishment of noble psychic power (*ariyiddhi*). "In the characteristic of being the same" means in the state of being the same (*tādibhāva*).
162. "I have no burden in answering questions" is a demonstration of the Teacher’s unimpeded range of knowledge in all respects.
When they do not say, "Whenever you wish," but rather say, "Having heard, we shall know," it is because they are established in partial knowledge (*padesañāṇa*).
The connection is that the Buddhas, however, offer the invitation of the Omniscient One (*sabbaññu-pavāraṇa*). [This applies to] "yakkhas, lords of men, devas, recluses, brahmins, and wanderers."
This is for the purpose of showing which individuals these sutta passages—beginning with "Ask, friend, whenever you wish"—were addressed to as they were asked.
"Ask, friend, whenever you wish" was an invitation made to the yakkha Āḷavaka;
the remaining [passages] were for Narinda and the others. *Manasicchasi* means "you desire in your mind. *Pucchavho*, what...
"Ask whatever you desire in your minds" means: ask Bāvari’s doubt with your minds. Furthermore, the intention is:
"Ask whatever doubt you all have—whatever it may be—with your minds, in another way, and exactly as you wish. "Sādhurūpā" means those of a virtuous nature.
"Dhamma" refers to the traditional lineage-dhamma. "Vuddha" means one who has attained growth through virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
"Garunti" means "indeed. "Esa bhāro" (this burden) refers to this burden known as the cutting off of doubt; the intention is that "the burden has arrived and must necessarily be carried.
"Ñatvā sayanti" (having known, they lie down) means having known by themselves, without instruction from another.
"Suciratenā" refers to a brahmin of such a name. "Taggha" means "certainly. "Yathāpi kusalo tathā" means "just as one who is skilled [would do]."
"Just as one who is skilled in all phenomena and all-knowing understands and explains them, so shall I declare it to you.

As for whether the king will act upon it or not—whether he who sent you here to ask will have his question answered by the king through you or not—I shall nevertheless declare it to you; 'I shall declare' means 'I will explain.'"
163. Because it must be learned in the sense of being a craft (*sippa*), and because it is the cause of one's livelihood, the craft itself is the "sphere of craft" (*sippāyatana*).

*Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "what are those? Having first pointed out the crafts in general by saying "various spheres of craft," the subsequent explanation—which describes individuals who subsist by various specific crafts—is an elaboration (*papañca*) based on a discourse concerning persons.

In order to avoid prolixity. Otherwise, having first shown the fields of craft as intended, if one were then to show those who subsist by each of those crafts, it would result in excessive elaboration.
Therefore he said, "elephant-riders," and so forth.
They ride elephants and cause others to ride them, thus they are "elephant-riders" (*hatthārohā*). By means of which applications a man becomes fit for riding an elephant...
When that application is being carried out for the elephant, there is the seizing of all of these as well. Therefore he said, "All of them," and so forth.
In that context, "elephant trainers" (*hatthācariyā*) refers to those who instruct the elephants and the elephant riders. "Elephant physicians" (*hatthivejjā*) refers to elephant doctors.

"Elephant groomers" (*hatthimeṇḍā*) refers to those who protect the feet of the elephants. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [those such as] the providers of barley fodder for the elephants are included.
He gathers them together. Regarding the terms *assārohā* (horsemen) and *rathikā* (charioteers), the same principle applies here. Those engaged with chariots are *rathikā*.
Those called *ratharakkhā* (chariot-protectors) are the guards of the chariot’s axle-pins (*āṇi*). They grasp the bow or cause it to be grasped, thus they are *dhanuggahā* (archers);
these include both the marksmen and those who teach the craft of archery. Therefore he said: “The archers are the teachers of archery. They desired battle with the *cela*, that is, with the banner.
“They go,” thus he said, “those who go at the front holding the victory banner in battle.
They are called *calakas* because they move (*calanti*) or cause to stir (*uccālentī*) the soldiers stationed there or otherwise, by means of forming battle arrays (*byūha*).
Like hawks and other birds, through their boldness as great warriors, they repeatedly cut apart the mass of the enemy army and pounce upon it.

"Alms-givers" (*piṇḍadāyaka*) means those who go leaping up [to give]. In the second interpretation, the meaning should be understood as: "alms-givers" are those who, amidst the crowd of people, give alms while going as if they were leaping up.

"Exalted, exalted" (*uggatuggata*) means exceedingly exalted or lofty by way of strength, speed, prowess, and so forth. "Rushing forward" (*pakkhandanti*) means not being held back by one's own heroic and brave nature against the enemy army.
The meaning is "entering. They are called "great nāgas" because they possess the perfection of steadfastness, speed, strength, prowess, and so forth, like great nāgas.
"Exclusively brave" means those who are brave when alone; by virtue of their own bravery, they fight while remaining solitary.
"With quivers" means equipped with arrows. "A shield for protection against arrows" refers to a shield bound with leather, or a shield made of leather.
"House-slave soldiers" refers to soldiers born within the household.
"Āḷāra" means a kitchen; those appointed there are "āḷārikas," namely, cooks.
"Pūvikas" are makers of cakes—those who live by preparing various kinds of cakes and selling them. By way of scratching the hair and nails, etc. [the text continues].
They are called *kappakas* because they fashion and arrange the methods of adornment for people.
They are called *nhāpakas* because they bathe [people] by means of the methods of removing dirt and producing a beautiful complexion with powders, ointments, and so forth.

That enumeration which proceeds according to the method beginning with "nine" and so on is called *acchiddaka* (unbroken) because there is no gap (*chidda*) in between; those who live by depending upon that enumeration are the *acchiddaka-pāṭhakas*.
Hand-gesture (*hatthamuddā*) is the communication of one’s intention by means of the hand;
here, the word "hand" (*hattha*) should be understood as referring to its parts, namely the fingers—as in such expressions as, "I shall not put my whole hand into my mouth while eating.

Therefore, counting by means of the contraction of the fingers and so forth is "counting by hand-gesture. Regarding the phrase "painters and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), potters, masons, scribes, and others are included.
The inclusion of the *vilīva*-maker and others should be understood. "In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"Visible here and now" (*sandiṭṭhika*) means that because it pertains to the present life rather than the future, it is to be seen by oneself, to be experienced by oneself, and is directly evident to one's own self;

this is the meaning of "pertaining to the present life. "Happy" (*sukhita*) means having attained happiness. "Above" (*upari*) refers to the world of the devas, for that is higher than the human world. Of karma...
Because it is produced by what has been done, its fruit is like a flame of fire; and since that [flame] goes upwards to the world of the gods, he says:
"It is *uddhaggikā* because it has an upward-pointing top (*agga*). It is worthy of heaven (*saggaṃ arahati*);

the meaning is that it is worthy of the heaven which is its own fruit, for it is capable of being produced there. It has a pleasant ripening (*sukhavipākā*) means it is the ripening of a desirable result.
"Suṭṭhu agge" means exceedingly excellent and sublime. It is called "dakkiṇā" because by it one sees (dakkhanti) or increases (vaḍḍhanti);
thus he said, "dakkiṇaṃ dānaṃ," meaning merit consisting of relinquishment.

Considering that the path is "sāmañña" because it is the state of a recluse (samaṇa) who has stilled (samita) evil, and because this king [gave] to those who have gone forth—such as slaves, farmers, and so on—

Thinking that the attainment of greetings and other honors from the world is a visible fruit of recluseship (*sandṛṣṭikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ*), and investigating whether there might be some ascetic or brahmin who knows such a matter, he questioned Pūraṇa and others;
being dissatisfied with their discourse, he also asked the Blessed One about that same matter. Therefore it is said: "What follows [is stated] above..."
"But he asks with reference to the simile of the slave and the farmer.
"The dark side" refers to the faction of defilement associated with speculative views (diṭṭhigata) that arises from the meaning as asked.
"The light side" refers to the faction of purification (vodānapakkha) which is the opposite of that and appears in the subsequent sutta. "The clamor of recluses" means the ostentation of recluses.

The mutual contradiction among those various doctrines of the ascetics (*samaṇavāda*). "Ascetic quarreling" (*samaṇabhaṇḍana*) refers to the reviling of each respective doctrine by means of that very contradiction, saying:
"This is the fault of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view; this is the fault of those who hold such a view.
By performing the king's burden through his own skill in teaching—this is the intended meaning.
164. “Of those who are like wise men”: of those who merely appear to be wise, just as raw fruit appears like ripe fruit.

165. *Ekaṃ idāhaṃ* means “for one day. Here, the word *idha* is a mere particle; the meaning is simply “for one day, for one occasion. *Saritabbayuttaṃ* means “suitable for recollection,” that is, appropriate for being remembered.
166. "Of one who acts with his own hand" means of one who acts by means of his own hand.

Here, even the offenses of forfeiture (nissaggiya), the minor rules (thāvara), and so forth, are included under the category of acting with one's own hand. "Hands, etc. refers to the hands, feet, ears, nose, and so on.
Regarding "cooking, burning, or injuring," it says "of one who presses with a staff"; in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the meaning is "or of one who threatens."
[In other contexts] this was stated [separately], but here, since rebuking and censuring are included within punishment itself, it is simply said:
"of one who oppresses with punishment. "Causing grief for oneself" means causing for oneself the cause of another's grief, or producing grief [in another].
"By others" means by those who carry out his word. "Himself also being agitated" means through the application of harming another.
“Even one who trembles”: the phrase “one who causes to kill” applies both to the sense of the direct agent (*suddhakattuattha*) and the causal agent (*hetukattuattha*);
thus he says, “of one who kills and of one who causes to kill. “By way of cause” means by way of causing [another] to act.
A house-joint is a joint of a house that stands connected on both the inside and the outside. “Without leaving anything behind” means entirely, without remainder.
*Lopa* means cutting off. One who is engaged in solitary dwelling (*ekāgāra*) is a *vilopa*, and thus an *ekāgārika*. Killing on a path in every way is *paripantha*.
Evil is not performed because it was previously unrestrained and impossible to produce;
therefore, there is no evil. If this is so, how is it that beings engage in evil? He says: "But beings have the perception, 'We are committing evil.'"
"…they exist. It occurs to him thus: "For these beings, acts such as violence do not touch the self, because of its permanence and its changelessness;
the body, however, is insentient, like a piece of wood or a log, and even when it is destroyed, no evil whatsoever accrues.
*Khuranemīhi*: with wheels made of sharpened hooves.
With the intention that the southern direction along the Ganges is an unsuitable location while the northern direction is a suitable location, he said "the southern [bank]" and so forth;
thus he stated, "On the southern bank the people are harsh," and so on. "A great sacrifice" (mahāyāga) means a great sacrifice similar to the Mahāvijita sacrifice.
"Or by the observance of the Uposatha" means by means of the Uposatha rite. For the word *dama* refers to restraint of the sense faculties.

And here, the term *uposatha* is intended to mean the observance of the precepts (*sīla*). Some, however, explain the meaning as follows: “The phrase ‘by the uposatha-act’ is a qualification of the taming of the sense faculties;
therefore, the sense is ‘by the taming of the sense faculties which constitutes the uposatha-act. By “restraint of virtue” (*sīlasaṃyama*) is meant bodily and verbal restraint.
By “speaking truth” (*saccavajja*) is meant truthful speech; it is mentioned separately because it is regarded in the world as a particularly weighty merit.
For just as false speech is weighty among unwholesome qualities, so is truthful speech among wholesome qualities. Therefore the Blessed One said:

"Of one who has transgressed a single quality," and so forth. "Occurrence" (pavatti) means the arising within the continuum of that which is called "the agent," by way of being the condition for the production of its fruit.
"In every way" means in all the modes described by the phrase "of one who acts," etc. [The author] rejects the very notion of action (kiriya).
The intention is that he did not explain to the King a fruit of recluseship that was visible here and now.
This restriction is for the purpose of excluding the denial of *vipāka* (ripening). For whoever denies action (*kamma*) has, in effect, also denied its ripening;
as he will say later: "By one who rejects action," and so forth.
It is called *vijita* (conquered) because it is specifically conquered by way of being invincible to rival kings; it is the territory where his authority prevails.
Because the dismissal with the words, "Do not dwell in my conquered realm," constitutes an offense against one who has gone forth—being a form of harassment and expulsion—it is stated:
"He should be dismissed" means "he should be harassed. *Uggaṇhanaṃ* (grasping) is the apprehension and discernment of the meaning spoken by him, [thinking], "It is so indeed."
“Bending down” (*nikujjana*) is the mental holding back by way of bringing that [person] to a state of inferiority. Rejecting both of these, he said:
“not favoring, not bending down. Therefore he said: “not grasping by way of essence,” and so forth.
*Commentary on the Discourse of Makkhali Gosāla*
168. "By both" means by the statement that negates the causal condition (*hetu-paccaya*). "Condition for defilement" (*saṃkilesa-paccaya*) is the cause of being defiled, of being stained.
"Condition for purification" (*visuddhi-paccaya*) is the cause of purification, of cleansing, from defilement.
"One's own action" (*attakāra*) is the deed to be done by a particular being themselves, the effort to be accomplished by oneself. "The action of another" (*parakāra*)...
A purpose that succeeds through the assistance of another. Therefore he said, “by which,” and so forth. “Mahāsatta” refers to a Great Bodhisattva in his final existence;
it should be understood that the Pacceka-bodhisattva is also included herein.

“Human good fortune” means the state of being fortunate among humans. “In this way” means by the manner already described. By the rejection of the doctrine of action (kamma-vāda) and the doctrine of efficacy (kiriyā-vāda)...
“Monks, there is action that is dark with dark result,” and so forth—by such a method, one strikes a blow at the Wheel of the Conqueror (jinacakra) as it proceeds.

“There is no personal effort” (natthi purisakāro) means that because of the absence of the aforementioned self-effort and effort by others, there is no such thing as an individual personal effort for sentient beings.

Therefore he said, “By which,” and so forth. “There is no power” (natthi balaṃ) refers to [the power] of sentient beings that brings about success in this life, the next world, or the attainment of Nibbāna.
There is no such thing as "power" (*bala*) in itself. Therefore he said, "In whom," and so forth. This is merely an illustration;
for even that which is defiled (*saṃkilesika*) is likewise rejected as power. If energy (*vīriya*) and the rest are synonyms for human effort (*purisakāra*), why are they mentioned separately?

To this he said, "This [is accomplished] by our energy," and so forth. But from the perspective of the meaning of the words, it is in the sense of being abundant (*ussanna*) in respect of each respective activity.
It is *bala* (power). It is *viriya* (energy) in the sense of bringing about the state of being brave and heroic.

That same [energy], by virtue of its firmness and because it must be exercised by one who bears the human yoke, is called *purisathāma* (human strength). It should be understood as being called *purisaparakkama* (human exertion) because it proceeds toward ascending to ever-higher stages.

It is called *satta* (clinging) because of its attachment to form and so forth, due to its state of being stuck and fastened. It is called *pāṇa* (breathing) because of its proceeding by way of inhalation and exhalation.
Regarding "living beings" (pāṇā): since he explains them by classifying them according to the single-facultied (ekindriya) and other categories, he says "the single-facultied," and so forth.
Because they come into being within egg-shells and such, they are called "beings" (bhūtā); thus he says "egg-shells... he speaks.

Because they sustain life as if supporting breath, and because they grow, they are "souls" (jīvā). Therefore he says "rice and barley," and so forth. They have no mastery over defilement or purification.
*Avasā*: They have no strength or energy, thus they are "powerless" (*abalā*) and "lacking vigor" (*avīriyā*).

"Fixed" (*niyatā*): like threads spun from an uncut [spindle] or gems that cannot be broken, there is a "fixedness" (*niyāma*) due to their proceeding in a determined manner by way of destiny, birth, bondage, and liberation. "Going here and there" (*tattha tattha gamanaṃ*):
the approaching of the six classes of beings to their respective destinies; their coming together through conjunction. "Only its own nature" (*sabhāvoyeva*):...

Just as the sharpness of a thorn, the roundness of wood-apple fruits, and the variegated forms of animals and birds are so, even so, the transformation of the entire world in such and such ways without causes or conditions is simply its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), not something produced by artifice (*akittima*).
Therefore he said, "By which... and so forth. The six classes of birth (*chaḷābhijātiyo*) will be explained in detail later. "And happiness..."
By saying, "and they experience suffering," he indicates that one does not know the plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure in its entirety;
thus he says, "he shows that there is no other plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
"Of the principal births" means of those births that are preeminent among humans, animals, and so forth, such as the khattiyas and brāhmaṇas, or lions and tigers.
“Sixty hundred” means six thousand. The phrase “and five hundred actions” is explained as “and five hundred types of karma.
By the words “the same method applies,” he extends this very point by indicating that [the opponent] merely demonstrates a useless view based on mere reasoning alone.
And here, by the phrase “by mere reasoning,” because logicians are unrestrained—
Regarding "conjecture" (*parikappa*): thinking that whatever they have conjectured is essential, they adhere to it as such and grasp at speculative views.
Therefore, he shows that wise people should not engage in critical investigation regarding the basis of their views.
"Some" refers to the residents of the Uttaravihāra monastery. For they [hold that] "the five faculties" are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body...
They say: "These five faculties are designated as 'five actions'. The doctrine that "action" is [only] bodily action is a doctrine because of its coarse nature;
it is the doctrine that "complete action" refers to this. The doctrine that "mental action is half-action" because of its non-coarseness—this is the construction.
Regarding "the sixty-two ways of practice": when one ought to say "sixty-two ways of practice," not knowing the conventional language (sabhāvanirutti), one says "dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā."
He speaks. He conceives it in one [aeon], in one *mahākappa*, and even therein, in one incalculable aeon known as the period of expansion (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*).

They kill sheep, thus they are called *orabbhikā* (sheep-slayers). In the same way, *sūkarikā* (pig-slayers) and others are to be understood. Hunters (*luddā*) refers to any others who are deer-hunters or fowlers.
Because they are intent upon evil deeds, he says they are "of dark birth" (*kaṇhābhijātī*). "Monks" refers to those in the Buddha’s teaching.
The monks. It is said that he spoke with the intention: "They enjoy [the requisites] according to their own whims and lusts," meaning they "eat by putting thorns into the four requisites.
Why is that? Because his misconception was that "they partake of the most excellent requisites";
therefore, even while using requisites obtained through legitimate means, they do so because of their contrary adherence to the Ājīvaka doctrine.
Others say: "They are said to eat after having thrown [food] upon thorns. Some who have gone forth are those who are especially devoted to the practice of self-mortification;
for they are like those living on thorns, and thus they are called "thorn-dwellers" (*kaṇṭakavuttika*).

Because of their adherence to vows such as standing while eating and the prohibition against bathing, they are exceedingly white; thus they are called "the disciples of the naked ascetics" (*acelaka-sāvaka*).
He speaks of the disciples of the Ājīvakas. It is said that because their minds are purified by the Ājīvaka doctrine, they are even whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas.
For Nanda and others have reached the pinnacle of such Ājīvaka practice;
therefore, his view is that they are "whiter and of a more supreme, pure birth" than both the Nigaṇṭhas and the disciples of the Ājīvakas.
“Purisabhūmiyo” (the stages of manhood) is a designation for the person who exerts effort. One should understand that those same stages apply to women as well.

“A bhikkhu and a pannaka,” etc., is their very own canonical text (*pāḷi*). Therein, a *pannaka* is one who wanders about for alms, or one who has entered upon the practice of their [the Buddhas'] way.
A *jina* is one who is worn out, having inferior constituents due to old age, or [one who is so called] because of his own practice.
He remained having conquered his adversaries. It is said that, being in such a state, he did not speak even the Dhamma to anyone; therefore it is said, "he said nothing.
Others also say that even when insults were made regarding his lips, face, and so forth, he said nothing because of his forbearance. Regarding "one who does not obtain":
this refers to the possession of the causes for non-obtainment as described in the passage beginning, "He does not accept from the mouth of a jar," and so on.
Because he had not obtained [any food] and was overcome by the weakness of hunger, he became intent on lying down; thus one says of him, "the ascetic who has fallen from his ground.

"Hundreds of livelihoods" means hundreds of ways of life that constitute the livelihood of beings. By the mention of "cattle," the species of sheep is included; by the mention of "wild animals," the entire species of wild animals such as the *ruru* deer, the *gavaya*, and so forth, is included.
"Many gods" refers to those belonging to the realm of the Four Great Kings, up to the Brahmakāyika gods, and so on.
There are many gods according to their internal divisions. Among them, the specific divisions of the Cātumahārājika gods are to be illustrated by means of the Mahāsamaya Sutta.
Humans are also infinite; humans are of infinite variety according to the distinctions of continent, country, clan, lineage, livelihood, and so forth.
*Pisācā* are the same as *pesācā*; they are the very large ones among the *aparapeta*s and others. One refers to the Chaddanta Lake and the Mandākinī by the names Kuvāḷiya and Mucalinda.
"Pavuṭā" means a bamboo joint. Even a wise person... [as before] ...does not go upward; why?
Because the time for the wandering of beings is fixed. One "ripens" an unripened cause for wandering by means of virtue and so forth, so that it may very quickly attain purification.
Having encountered and encountered a ripened karma, one brings about its state of full ripeness in due course.
"Brings about its exhaustion" (byantiṃ karoti) means it makes an end of it.

"A ball of thread" (suttaguḷa) means a coil of thread. With the simile, "It runs away even as it is being unwound," he shows that the saṃsāra of sentient beings is exhausted by gradual stages and does not increase, because its form is limited.
Commentary on the Doctrine of Ajita Kesakambala.
171. By the term "deyyadhamma" (an object worthy of being given), "giving" (*dāna*) is meant; thus he says, "he speaks of the absence of fruit for what has been given.
But how can one reject the actual substance that has been given, such as food and so forth? This same principle applies here to the terms "sacrificed" (*yiṭṭha*) and "offered" (*huta*).
A "great sacrifice" (*mahāyāga*) is a great gift common to all. "Hospitality" (*pāhunakasakkāra*) is the honor that ought to be performed toward a guest.
They bear fruit as the fruit of benefit (*ānisaṃsaphala*) and the fruit of outflow (*nissandaphala*). "Result" (*vipāka*) refers to the fruit of similarity (*sadisaphala*).
"For one standing in the next world, this world does not exist": for one standing in the next world, this world—which is to be obtained through karma—does not exist.
"For one standing in this world, the next world does not exist": for one standing in this world, the next world—which is to be obtained through karma—does not exist.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "All are cut off right there, right then.
These beings, wherever they abide—in whatever existence, womb, and so forth—are cut off right there; they perish by way of non-arising and non-destruction.
"By way of the absence of fruit" means by way of the absence of fruit for both proper and improper conduct toward one's mother and father.
When he says, “There is no mother, there is no father,” it is not because a mother and father do not exist, nor because of the absence of the honor or dishonor currently being rendered toward them,

for they are directly perceived in the world. Rather, it was said, “There are no spontaneously born beings,” in order to show that the arising of these beings is merely like that of a bubble, having no prior transition from one state to another.
He said, "He claims that there are no beings who pass away and are reborn.
A true ascetic, knowing things as they really are, ought to be restrained by not speaking anything to anyone; otherwise, it would be mere boasting.
For what can one person do for another? And in that case, he would have no support at all for his own attainment.
"In each and every instance, it is because of its being cut off" is why he said: "Those who proclaim this...

[and so on]... It is "composed of the four great elements" (*cātumahābhūtiko*) because it is connected with the four great elements. Just as a vessel produced from clay is called "made of clay," so too, because this is produced from the four great elements, he said: "consisting of the four great elements" (*catumahābhūtamayo*).
"The internal earth element" refers to the earth element contained within the continuum of a sentient being. "The external earth element" refers to the great external earth.
"It approaches" means that a portion of the earth from the external body comes forth and, having attained an internal state, becomes established as a sentient being;
it now returns to that very same external body, like the earth contained in a jar or similar object.
It approaches entirely and, being without distinction, attains a state of oneness with it. This same principle applies to water and the other elements as well;

here, just as water taken from the great ocean by Pajjunna returns again to the great ocean in the form of rainwater, or as the fire known as Indra and Agni taken from the rays of the sun returns again to the solar rays, [so too does it return] from the mass of the great wind.
The intention of the proponent of this wrong view is that [the faculties] enter and approach that very same mass of wind, like a great wind that has subsided.
They say that the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, leap into space because there is no objective field (*visaya*) for them;

for by mentioning the subject (*visayin*), the objects themselves are necessarily included. "Phrases of merit and demerit" refers to categories of virtues and faults. "The body itself is the phrases" means...
It is intended [to refer to the body] because it must be attained through various actions by means of that body. "Dabbā" means those who are deluded;
thus, they are "dattū," meaning deluded persons. By those "dattūs," that is, by foolish people. Those for whom there is the conviction that "the other world exists" are the "atthikā";
their doctrine is "atthikavādo," and that is the "atthikavādaṃ."
It denies action because of its state of being a proponent of non-action (*akiriyavāda*). It denies fruition because it rejects rebirth in the future in every respect.
It denies both because, by denying the cause altogether, the fruit is also rejected.
"Both" refers to both action and fruition. For he [the nihilist] holds that "beings become defiled without cause and without condition."

By saying "and they are purified," one indeed precludes both [defilement and purification], because it asserts that, unlike karma, fruition lacks the status of being a condition for defilement and purification.
Fruition is precluded because there would be no fruition in the absence of karma.
Karma is precluded because it would result in being purposeless in the absence of fruition. "In its own nature" means by way of its essential form.

“Both refuters” means that although they appear individually in the Canon as proponents of their respective views, each is indeed a holder of three types of views because they refute both [causality and kamma]. For “both refuters” is the statement of the reason (*hetu*), while “those who propound causelessness, etc.
is the formal proposition (*paṭiññā*). For one who is a nihilist and an annihilationist by way of refuting the result of kamma (*vipāka*)...

Thus, in terms of its meaning, by rejecting [the efficacy of] action he holds the view of non-doing (*akiriyadiṭṭhi*), and by rejecting both [action and non-action] he holds the view of causelessness (*ahetukadiṭṭhi*).
The same method applies to the other two [views] as well.
"They recite" means they learn and chant that text which illustrates those views. "They investigate" means [they investigate] its meaning.
They deliberate. The phrase beginning with “Of them” is a demonstration of the manner of investigation. “In that object” means:

in the object of the view that proceeds according to the formula “no evil is done by one who acts,” which [view] arises because of the absence of the fruits of karma as they have been imagined. “Wrong mindfulness settles” means:
through the conceptualization of that mode [of thought] regarding a matter acquired through hearsay in the form of “no evil is done by one who acts,” and so forth.

When [the object] has been grasped by means of "acceptance through contemplation" (*nijjhānakkhanti*)— having become familiar for a long time so that it appears to the mind as if it were actually present with its own form—
and when one repeatedly pursues and cultivates it in that very same way, there arises "wrong mindfulness" (*micchāsati*).
This wrong mindfulness is undertaken by wrong thought (*micchāvitakka*), propped up by wrong effort (*micchāvāyāma*), and perceives what lacks that nature as having "that nature."

The craving associated with that attainment, having acquired its name, comes to rest. "The mind becomes one-pointed" means that by obtaining its respective conditions such as applied thought (*vitakka*), it abandons distraction through its stability upon that object and becomes one-pointed, as if fixed.
By the term "mind," wrong concentration itself is expressed; for that too, through specific conditions, gains the power of cultivation.
In such a situation, it should be understood that one performs duties appropriate for composure, as in the case of warding off wild beasts and so forth.
"The impulsions impel" means that when several series of preliminary impulsions have occurred in that manner, seven impulsions impel in the very last series of impulsions.
In the first impulse they are with difficulty curable; likewise in the second and subsequent ones.
This is merely the perception of the intrinsic nature of phenomena; however, at that moment, it is not possible for anyone to provide a remedy for them.

"Therein" means among those three wrong views. "Someone enters upon one view" means that for one whose adherence (*abhinivesa*) and repeated practice (*āsevanā*) proceed toward only one [of the views], he enters upon that single view alone. But for one who [has them] in two or even all three...

When adherence and cultivation proceed, one falls into two or even three [of these views]. By this, that state of being possessed of all views—which was previously explained by way of the exclusion of both—is established as belonging to the prior stage.

However, that which constitutes the entry into the fixed course of falsehood (micchattaniyāma) is, due to its accomplishment through the convergence of its own respective conditions, like various specific attainments with distinct objects brought together into a single whole.

This shows that they are uninterrupted until their arising [is ended]. By the words "even when one has entered" and so forth, he shows that all three views possess equal strength and yield equal results.
Therefore, even if these three arise in a single person, they are indeed uninterrupted;
once the result of one has been given, the others act as its supporting forces. "This is called a 'stump of the round' (vaṭṭakhāṇu)"—this...
This statement is of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*), not of definitive meaning (*nītattha*). For it is said in the *Papañcasūdani*:
"But is this fixed to only one single existence, or to another as well? It is fixed to only one;
however, by way of habituation, one continues to find pleasure in that very same view even in another existence. Indeed, this unwholesome state is weak and feeble.
It is not as strong or very powerful as the wholesome [path]. Therefore, it is said: "fixed in that very same individual existence (*attabhāva*).
Otherwise, just like the fixedness in rightness (*sammattaniyāma*), the fixedness in wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*) would also be ultimate; however, it is not ultimate.
If this is so, how is the explanation of the "stump of the round" (*vaṭṭakhāṇu*) to be understood? To this he says: "But by way of repetition," and so forth. Therefore, just as "once... [is said].
It is said, "Even one who has submerged is indeed submerged," thus showing the stump of the round of existence (*vaṭṭakhāṇu*).

For when this person has fallen into such-and-such a view depending on certain conditions, it cannot be said that he will never again lift his head from it by depending on conditions contrary to those;
therefore it is said, "For generally, for one of such a kind, there is no emergence from existence."

Therefore, because the condition for the very state of being a seed of saṃsāra is thus established as an "infallible" (apaṇṇaka) one, [it is said]: "Desiring prosperity" means desiring one's own growth through qualities by way of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal.
Commentary on the Doctrine of Pakudha Kaccāyana: 174.
"Unmade" means not made or not produced by any cause, whether equal or unequal. What is the method of making? [It is] the manner of production.

"Those for whom there are none" means they are "those by whom no conditions have been made. By these two phrases, he shows that in the world there is nothing whatsoever—whether a cause or a condition—by which their non-arising could be brought about.
"Not even fashioned by psychic power" means they were not fashioned even by the psychic power of anyone, such as a deity who has attained mastery over the mind or a lord (Issara), etc.
"Unfashioned" means unfashioned by anyone. "The meaning is exactly as stated" refers to the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta.
The meaning is exactly as stated. "Barren" (*vañjhā*) means fruitless, like barren cattle, barren palm trees, and so forth; the sense is that they do not produce anything for anyone.

By this, he rejects the idea that the earth-element and the other elements possess the capacity to produce visible form and the rest. For his view is that visible forms, sounds, and so on, exist independently of the earth-element and the others.
"Fixed like a mountain peak" (*kūṭaṭṭhā*) means standing firm like a mountain peak. Just as a mountain peak...
The intention is that these [factors] are not produced by anyone, nor do they produce anything for anyone; such is the meaning of "joy" (pīti).
As for what is said, "the sprout and so forth arise from the seed," that which emerges from it exists already; it does not emerge as something non-existent.

Otherwise, there would be the perception of one thing arising even from something else entirely—this is the intention. "Because of its stability" means because of its stability through the absence of any modification.
"They do not move" means they do not undergo change. For it is because of the absence of change that those seven bodies possess the stability of a pillar fixed in its base.
And "immovability" is simply their remaining established in their own nature. Therefore he said, "they do not transform.

Precisely because they are of a nature not subject to transformation, they do not obstruct one another; for if there were the necessity of undergoing change, there would also be the quality of obstructing.
It might be thought that because [the earth] is to be assisted, it is therefore an assister; thus, in order to show the absence of such a thing, the text says "there is no," and so forth.

Because it is a part of the body, the earth itself is called the "earth-body. Since bodies in which a living being (*jīva*) is the seventh are eternal and thus devoid of modification, they cannot be killed nor can they be caused to be killed;
therefore, there is neither a killer nor one who causes killing. For this very reason, he said: "of the seven..."
“...only these bodies,” and so forth. If there is no killer at all, how can there be the striking of a weapon? To this he says:

“Just as in the case of a heap of beans,” and so forth. It is merely a matter of perception; however, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), there is no such thing as killing or slaughtering because the bodies are incapable of being disturbed—this is the intended meaning.
Commentary on the Doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta: 177.

"Four watches" (*catuyāma*) means four parts; "four-watch" (*cātuyāma*) is the same as "four-part," for here the word *yāma* has the sense of "part," just as in the expression "the first watch of the night.
Since that part here is characterized by restraint, he says: "restrained by the fourfold restraint" (*cātuyāmasaṃvuta*).
“Restrained by the fourfold restraint. “One who has rejected all cold water” means one who has rejected the use of all cold water.
“Endowed with the warding off of all evil” means possessed of every kind of characteristic of restraint (*saṃvara*).
“Shaken off evil” means one whose evil has been shaken off by every kind of warding off of evil characterized by wearing away (*nijjara*). “Touched” [refers] to the eight types of karma...

"Having reached the peak": having attained that [state] by means of the complete warding off of evil, characterized by the exhaustion of karma through the attainment of liberation (*mokkha*), he stands there.
"One whose mind has reached the pinnacle" (*koṭippattacitta*) means one whose mind has reached the supreme noble limit (*uttamamariyāda*) precisely through the attainment of liberation.

"Self-controlled" (*yatatta*) means one whose mind is restrained because there is nothing further to be restrained regarding the faculties such as the body. "Well-established in mind" (*suppatiṭṭhitacitta*) means completely and thoroughly...
One whose mind is firmly established. "Conformity with the Teaching" (sāsanānuloma) means being endowed with the warding off of evil. Therefore he said, "one who has shaken off evil," and so forth.
"Because of impure acquisitions" (asuddhaladdhitāya) means because of such impure acquisitions as: "The soul exists; and it may be eternal, or it may be impermanent," and so on.

"All" refers to all forms of reflective acceptance (nijjhānakkhanti) regarding objects such as the classification of karma and its nature. "Views indeed" (diṭṭhiye vā) means that they have arisen as precisely wrong views.
Commentary on the Doctrine of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta (179–181).
The method is the same as that stated for the Eel-Wriggler (*amarāvikkhepa*) because it consists of evasive answers, and because the doctrine of evasion is presented here in exactly the same way.
Commentary on the First Fruit of the Homeless Life (*sandiṭṭhika-sāmaññaphala*).
183. *Yathā te rucceyya*: "In whatever way it pleases you"—this refers to the matter I am now asking about, in accordance with what is agreeable to your mind.
*Antojāta*: born from the womb of a domestic slave. *Dhanakkīta*: purchased for money. *Karamarānīta*: brought as a prisoner of war.
*Sāmañ*: by oneself (as a slave). *Dāsabyaṃ*: the state of being a slave. Even though someone is a slave, if they are lazy and do not perform work...
One who does not act is not called a "worker"; thus he said, "one who is indeed diligent and habitually performs work.
"At the very beginning" means even before, that is, earlier than the time of approaching the place nearest [to the master]. "Afterwards" means after the master has lain down.
"While he has not risen from his bed" means while he has not risen from his sleeping place at the time when the night is turning to dawn. "Starting from the time of the early morning" means...
From the time of dawn following the end of the night, until the master goes to sleep at night—until his falling asleep at the hour of dusk.
"What is to be done" (*kiṃ kāraṃ*) means: what duty is there to be performed; having asked by way of the state of "what-is-to-be-done-ness," the meaning is the service that ought to be rendered.
Like a deva who possesses excellence such as sovereignty and a retinue, like a deva of exertion (*padhānadeva*). “*So vatassāhan*” means “*so vatassaṃ ahan*”;
“*so rājā viya aham pi bhaveyyan*” means “I too would be like that king; how could I perform meritorious deeds?
If I were to perform sublime meritorious deeds”—this is the construction. In the reading “*so vatassa’ssan*,” it means “that king would be, and I would be.”
"Vata, if one were to perform meritorious deeds"—this is the construction (*yojanā*). Therefore he said, "This is the very meaning.
In the employment of the term "supreme person" (*uttamapurisa*), the word "I" (*ahaṃ*) is indeed employed even when not explicitly used.

"I shall not be able to give for as long as life lasts"—even while making an effort for the sake of giving for the duration of one's life, [one realizes] that one cannot give even a hundredth part of what the king gives on a single day.
“I shall not be able [to fulfill my duties]. Therefore, I will go forth”—thus he made an effort toward the going-forth;

such is the construction of the sentence. Regarding the phrase “restrained in body,” the meaning here is: “having restrained the evil states that arise through the door of the body and ought to be restrained by the body, he should dwell”;
thus he said, “having become covered by the body,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “with food and clothing as the utmost”:
"Regarding the phrase *ghāsacchādanaparamatāya*: it means being established in the state of excellence (*paramatā*) by way of austerity (*sallekha*) in the search for food and clothing;

or, because food and clothing alone are his supreme limit (*parama*) and ultimate peak (*parā koṭi*), he does not seek or long for any other kind of material thing beyond those—thus he is "one for whom food and clothing are supreme" (*ghāsacchādanaparamo*).
The state of being such is *ghāsacchādanaparamatā*; [the compound ends] with that term, *ghāsacchādanaparamatāya*."
"Of those whose bodies are secluded" means those who abide in solitude, away from the company of crowds.

"Delighting in renunciation" means delighting in meditative absorption (jhāna). Because they have attained the highest, most excellent purification through that very delight in absorption, they are "those who have attained supreme purification.
Through the absolute disappearance of the acquisitions of defilements, kamma-formations, and material substrata, they are "without acquisitions" (nirupadhi).

"Those who have reached the unconditioned" (*visaṅkhāragata*) means those who have attained Nibbāna. Herein, it should be understood that the first seclusion can be attained both together with and apart from the other two seclusions;
likewise for the second. However, the third must be attained together with the other two, and not apart from them.
"Crowd" (*gaṇa*) refers to a gathering of people; "association with a crowd" (*gaṇasaṅgaṇikā*) is the act of congregating therein; having abandoned that, one is alone.
He dwells and moves about alone by way of person, due to being without companions. "The gathering of defilements in the mind" refers to mental defilement-congregation;

having abandoned that, he dwells alone due to being without companions by way of defilements. Because the Path lasts for only a single moment of consciousness, and because the states such as change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) have merely the object as their domain, there is no particularly intense contact with the bliss of Nibbāna by way of those [states];
rather, it occurs by way of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
“Extraordinary,” he said, “by entering either the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) or the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). For cessation is the conclusion of fruition.
“Having brought forward” means having led [them] into a state of presence. The elliptical sense of the phrase is: “I shall accomplish my purpose with robes and so forth.
“Beneficial” means bringing about assistance by way of removing all illness. [The phrase] “from future harm” refers to what is yet to come.
Guarding by way of preservation is protection and defense (*rakkhā-gutti*). Protection by way of warding off the present is prevention and defense (*āvaraṇa-gutti*).
Commentary on the Second Fruit of the Homeless Life (*Sāmaññaphala*) 186.
"He plows" means he performs the act of plowing. Regarding the term *gahapatika*, the word *ka* here has no meaning; thus he says: "in a single house alone..."

"An elder," by this he rejects the status of being an elder among many clans. "He does what is to be done" means he accomplishes it. "He increases it" means he increases it by accomplishing it further and further.
Thus, the point that it is difficult to go forth even after having abandoned so little should be illustrated by the *Laṭukikopama Sutta*.
Therefore he said: "Just as if, Udāyi, a man were poor..."
“He was a man without wealth or grain; he had a single hut that was dilapidated and in ruins, inhabited by crows and not at all beautiful”—this is the detailed account.
If it were difficult to go forth even after abandoning a small amount of wealth, why was the mention of "wealth" not included in the section on the slave?

To this he says: “But in the case of the slave,” and so forth. And just as the wealth of a slave is not truly his own wealth because of its state of dependence on another, [so too is the wealth of one who has gone forth].
Thus, it should be understood that even in the "slave section," the inclusion of the circle of kinsmen was not made.

189. Regarding the commentary on the more excellent fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*): "By such similes" means by means of similes similar to those of the aforementioned slave and farmer, in order to illuminate the fruit of recluseship.
The Blessed One is capable of teaching for an entire day and night, or even longer, because of his infinite eloquence and his mode of teaching through diverse methods.
"Even so" (*tathāpi*) means: even though the teaching possesses a state of diversity through various methods that are progressively superior;
this word has the same meaning [as *sādhuka*], because it is formed by adding the letter *ka* to the word *sādhu*, and thus it is the same as the word *sādhuka*.
When speaking of the meaning (*attha*), the word "well" (*sādhu*) was uttered by way of extracting the meaning.

In "entreaty" (*āyācanā*), it means in a direct request; the sense is "longing. In "acceptance" (*sampaṭicchana*), it means in receiving. In "encouragement" (*sampahaṃsanā*), it means gladdening or satisfying by way of existing virtues;
the sense is "causing elation. "One who delights in the Dhamma" (*dhammaruci*) means one who desires merit. "Possessing discernment" (*paññāṇavā*) means wise.
“He does not deceive, being one who does not cause harm”—this is the meaning. “In this case too” means even in this [discourse on] the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).

This is the word *sādhu*. “In strengthening” means in careful performance. “In commanding” means in causing to command. For when it is said, “Listen well, attend carefully,” the word *sādhu* indicates that the act of listening and attending is a careful performance; likewise, the act of commanding them is also indicated by it.
The sense of commanding should be understood here as being like the sense of requesting. "Even in the beautiful" means even in the sense of the beautiful.
Now, in order to show the specific distinction manifested by the three meanings of the word *sādhuka* as previously stated, it was said: "In the sense of strengthening," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "attend to it" (*manasi karohi*), here mental attention (*manasikāra*) does not have the characteristic of directing the object [to the mind], but rather it is preceded by the mental attention that directs [the mind] along the path and directs it through the impulsion (*javana*).
Showing that its characteristic is fixing [the mind] upon the object, he says, "One should attend," and so forth.

It is the warding off of distraction of the ear-faculty by way of directing one toward listening, because it has the nature of precluding other activities; thus, the meaning is "one should lend the ear.

It is the warding off of distraction of the mind-faculty by precluding thoughts of other things. It is the warding off of grasping the phonemes incorrectly by virtue of the specific qualification "thoroughly" (*sādhuka*).
The same method applies to the warding off of the grasping of the eight inversions regarding the latter [the Dhamma].

In the phrase "in retention, investigation, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes comparison, analysis, and the like, as well as the thorough penetration of views. Regarding the term *sabyañjana*:

here, that which makes manifest (*byañjayati*) the intended meaning is "expression" (*byañjana*), namely, the natural linguistic formulation. That which is together with expression is "possessed of expression" (*sabyañjana*), meaning it is endowed with expression.

Meaning (*attha*). "Possessing meaning" (*sāttha*) means that it has meaning because it is desirable, approachable, and to be pursued; this refers to the fourfold pure virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) and so forth.

"Together with that meaning" is *sāttha*, meaning it is endowed with meaning. Regarding the phrases "profound in doctrine" (*dhammagambhīra*) and so on: "doctrine" (*dhamma*) refers to the textual tradition (*tanti*).
"Teaching" (*desanā*) refers to the teaching of that textual tradition as it has been determined by the mind. "Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the [meaning] of the textual tradition...
Meaning (*attha*): "Penetration" (*paṭivedha*) refers to the realization, in accordance with reality, of both the scripture (*tanti*) and the meaning of the scripture.
Because these teachings on the Dhamma—like the great ocean to those with fish-hooks—are difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom and provide no foothold, they are "profound.
Therefore it was said: "Because this Dhamma... [and so forth] ...attend carefully to it."
And here, the profundity of the Dhamma’s meaning should be understood from the difficulty of its penetration;

the profundity of the teaching from the difficulty of the knowledge of teaching; and the profundity [of the Dhamma] from the impossibility of producing penetration and the difficulty of the arising of such knowledge. "Teaching" (desanā) means reciting; its "explanation" (niddisana) is...
He said, "I shall speak in detail," because here the term *bhāsana* (speaking) is intended in its primary sense.
For *bhāsana* is clear exposition; therefore he said, "I shall teach... [etc. ...an elucidation in detail.
The phrase beginning with "Therefore he said" was spoken in order to support the aforementioned meaning with a scriptural passage (*suttapada*). "Like the cry of a myna bird" (*sāḷikāyiva nigghoso*).
It is sweet like the warbling of a *sāḷika* bird, pleasant to the ear, and lovely. "Paṭibhāna" means sound. "Udīrayi" means it is uttered or spoken.

When this was said—"Thus, having conceived zeal"—that is, when it was said, "Listen well, attend closely, I shall speak," he became one who had conceived zeal, thinking, "The Blessed One will not teach by way of summary alone; he will also speak in detail," and thus being glad and joyful.
190. By the word "here" (*idha*), the locus being described is intended as the place of the Tathāgata’s arising.
He says: "It is a particle used in the sense of location. The word *svāyam* takes the word *idha* in its general sense alone, not the specific sense of *idha* as it might be further qualified.

For he will later say: "In some cases, it is merely for the purpose of completing the meter. It is said "with reference to the world" because it is expressed in grammatical apposition with the word *loka*.
However, in the case of the other two words, [the meaning is derived] merely through the proximity of the other words.
It should be understood that these terms are stated in relation to this or that specific context. Here, "the world" (*loka*) refers to the field of birth;
even within that, it is specifically this *cakkavāḷa* (world-system) that is intended by the term "world. A "recluse" (*samaṇa*) is a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
A "second recluse" is a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*). For this has been said: "And who, monks, is a recluse? Here, monks, a monk [who has abandoned] the three fetters..."
“...through the complete destruction [of the first three fetters], one becomes a stream-enterer,” and so forth. “And who, monks, is the second ascetic?
Here, monks, a monk, through the complete destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion... and so forth.
“A place” means a certain location. “While remaining right here” means while remaining in this very Indasāla Cave.
It is merely for the purpose of filling out the meter (*padapūraṇamatta*), because it is impossible to indicate an occasion [for its use] and because it does not convey any other meaning.

The construction is: "The words beginning with *arahanti* have been explained in detail. Since the detailed exposition in terms of meaning occurs only by way of the words, the mention of "words" (*sadda*) is used.
For it is said in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā* and other works: "For eight further reasons, the Blessed One is a *Tathāgata*," and so forth.
The terms beginning with *arahant* have been explained in detail by others in the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā*;

therefore, that meaning should also be understood according to the method stated therein. Having stated, "But here the world of beings (*sattaloka*) is intended," because the Tathāgata is included within the category of beings, [the author] now shows in which category of beings and in which location he arises, saying: "In the world of beings..."
And it was said, “Even as he is arising,” and so forth. Regarding such statements as “The Tathāgata does not arise in the world of the gods,” that which is to be said will be explained later.
“Attained to excellence” means having become excellent by way of lineage, wealth, sovereignty, and so on.
“Brahmins and householders” refers both to brahmins such as Brahmāyu and Pokkharasāti, and to householders such as Anāthapiṇḍika.
Among the four alternatives stated beginning with “of Sujātā,” the first alternative is stated by way of showing a practice that is closer to the state of Buddhahood.
For one who stands in a practice that is closer is said to “arise” because arising is certain;

how much more so for one who stands at the very summit of the practice! The second [alternative] is stated by way of showing a practice that is near, starting from the renunciation that brings about the state of Buddhahood.
The third [quality] is shown by way of demonstrating the practice for attaining Buddhahood, beginning from the time the quality that produces a Buddha is fulfilled.
For there is no such thing as the "accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment" for Great Beings (mahāsatta) starting from their birth or rebirth.
The fourth begins from the commencement of the qualities that produce a Buddha; it starts from the moment they attain the state of certainty regarding enlightenment (bodhi).
For indeed, it is possible for the wise to say, "A Buddha arises," because arising is an absolute certainty.

However, just as one says, "The rivers flow," by taking the uninterruptedness of the act of flowing as the basis for the present usage, so too—in the four alternative formulations—it is said, "He is called 'arising,'" by taking the uninterruptedness of the act of proceeding toward the state of arising as the basis. [This refers to] the state of having arisen first of all.
Among the four alternative explanations, the very first mentioned is the state of existence (atthibhāva) consisting in the Tathāgata’s having arisen.
Therefore he said: "‘He has arisen’—this indeed is the meaning here.
"That Blessed One" refers to the one whose qualities have been extolled by the passage beginning with "the Tathāgata, the Arahant," and so forth; that is the Blessed One. "'This world'"—

This was not said merely with reference to the presence of the great multitude; rather, it was stated as "together with the devas" and so forth in order to show that [the scope] is exhaustive and inclusive.
Therefore, he says: "He now points out what is to be said. "Because they have been born" means because they have arisen through their respective kamma and defilements.
The inclusion of the five classes of sense-sphere devas is by way of the method of elimination (*pārisesanaya*).
Because the others are included by way of other terms. As for "sadevaka" (with its devas), the analysis is by way of a part, while the meaning of the compound is the whole.
The inclusion of the six classes of sense-sphere devas (*kāmāvacara-deva*) is according to the principle of proximity; for he was born there and dwells there.
The inclusion of the Brahmakāyika and other Brahmā-world devas follows this same method. Regarding the inclusion of "adversaries... ascetics and brahmins," [the same applies].

This is merely an illustration regarding those who have no adversaries; for it is included by way of the expression "together with recluses and brahmins" because there are recluses and brahmins who have not stilled [the defilements] and have not cast out evil.

Granted, through the qualifiers such as "together with the devas," the word *loka* is understood to have "beings" as its object, since these [qualifiers] share a common grammatical connection (*tulyayoga*);
however, this compound occurs even in cases of non-common connection (*atulyayoga*), as in the examples "having hair" (*salomako*) and "having wings" (*sapakkhako*).
Because it is seen that [the term] "is obtained" (*labbhati*) is subject to ambiguity, he said, "By the word 'progeny' (*pajā*), the world of beings (*sattaloka*) is meant.

Sentient beings who are formless (*arūpin*), dwelling in their own imperturbable state (*āneñjavihāra*), "shine forth" (*dibbanti*); thus they receive this etymological derivation as "deities" (*deva*).

He said, "By the inclusion of 'together with the deities' (*sadevaka*), the world of the formless realm (*arūpāvacaraloka*) is included. Therefore he said, "of those who have reached the sphere of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*)."
"Into the company of the devas. By the mention of "together with Māra," the six realms of the sense-sphere devas (kāmāvacara) are included, because they specifically fall under the sway of Māra.
The world of the form-brahmas (rūpī brahmaloka) is included because the formless-brahma world (arūpī brahmaloka) is mentioned separately.

"By way of the four assemblies" refers to the four assemblies consisting of kshatriyas and so forth; as for the other four assemblies, they are included by the mention of "together with Māra" and the rest.
“Already included” means: the remainder of the world of all beings, consisting of the various classes such as nāgas, garuḷas, and so forth.

Having thus far taken the world part by part and demonstrated the application [of the term], he now says “But here also,” etc., in order to demonstrate the application by taking the world not part by part, but according to its various specific distinctions. In that context, “by way of the highest limit” means:
By knowing the highest state: for among the five destinies (*gati*), those included within the destiny of the gods (*devagati*) alone are the best;

even there, the formless beings (*arūpin*) are exceedingly superior due to such distinctions as having their defilements and suffering far removed, possessing peaceful, sublime, and imperturbable abodes, and having extremely long lifespans.
"The Brahmā of great power," and so forth, refers to the Great Brahmā in the ten-thousandfold world system.
He speaks by way of this. For it is said: "By way of the highest limit. "Unsurpassed" (anuttara) means the most excellent, the nine supramundane states (lokuttara).

"Sequence of the modes of existence" (bhāvānukkama) refers to the sequence of the phrases beginning with "together with the world of devas" (sadevaka), according to their modes of existence and according to the inclinations of others.

"In three ways" means by way of the three aspects consisting of being accompanied by devas, Māras, and Brahmas. "In three places" refers to [the phrases] beginning with "together with the world of devas."
"In three places. "In that and that manner" means by way of those various modes such as being "together with devas" and so forth.
The construction is: "The ancient teachers said, 'The triple world itself is exhausted.
Regarding "by direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*): this is a designation formed by the elision of the letter *ya*; its meaning here is "having directly known," as he says: "by direct knowledge."

"Having known through superior knowledge. The rejection of inference and so forth means the rejection of inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), logical necessity (*atthāpatti*), and the like, because [for the Buddha] there is but a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have direct perception (*paccakkha*) regarding all things due to the unimpeded range of their knowledge in every respect.

"Supreme bliss of seclusion" refers to the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*); by means of that, whether it be mixed with stability (*ṭhiti*), or mixed with the cognitive process (*vīthi*), or mixed with fortitude (*dhiti*).

[ka] “Sometimes there is a teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One” – the inclusion of the word *pi* (also/even) is for the purpose of excluding [the other possibility]. For when the Blessed One is teaching the Dhamma,
at whatever moment the assembly utters a cry of approval (*sādhukāra*) or reviews the Dhamma as it has been heard,
he delimits that moment by means of a prior resolution and enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), according to that very delimitation.
Having emerged from meditative attainment, he teaches the Dhamma starting from the point where he stood [upon emerging].

He teaches either briefly for one who gains knowledge through a condensed exposition (*ugghaṭitaññū*), or extensively for one who gains knowledge through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*), or for one who is guided by instruction (*neyya*).

Because the excellence of the Dhamma consists in its quality of leading out (*niyyānikatā*), and its quality of leading out exists solely through its being entirely blameless (*anavajja*), he says: "having made it entirely blameless."
"Teaching" (desanā) refers to the act of instructing and awakening [the listener] through methods such as commands directed toward those present;
this should be understood by way of the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma). Thus he said: "First, regarding teaching, even of a four-line verse," and so forth.

Since the introduction (nidāna) and the conclusion (nigamana) also follow the Teacher’s own method of teaching, they are included therein; thus he said: "The beginning is the introduction; 'This is said' is the end."

"Instruction" (sāsana) refers to the teaching that disciplines (vinayana) the person to be instructed according to their offense and other factors, by means of "discipline through the removal of the cause" (tadaṅgavinaya) and so forth;
this should be understood as the Dhamma of practice. Therefore, he said, "Virtue, concentration, and insight," and so on.
Regarding "of wholesome states" (kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ), this refers to blameless states: virtue, serenity, and insight, as well as the views associated with virtue.

It is the "initial state" because it is the root cause of the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*). Just as the Noble Path is the "middle way" by virtue of being free from the two extremes, it is also called the "middle" because it occupies the midpoint between the commencement and the accomplishment of right practice. As it is said: "There is, monks...
this is what is called the middle. The fruit is called the "conclusion" in the sense of having a residue remaining (*saupādisesa*); [and] Nibbāna...

"Conclusion" (*pariyosāna*) refers to the state of being without remainder (*anupādisesa*). Now, in order to show through scripture that both of these constitute the conclusion of the Dispensation (*sāsana*), he said, "For this purpose, this...
and so forth. Here, what is intended by "beginning, middle, and conclusion" is the teaching (*desanā*), because of the statement beginning with "together with the phrasing" (*sabyañjana*).
Within each respective meaning, there is a continuous string of words with established limits, arranged in the form of verses (*gāthā*).
The Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*), established by way of the discourses (*sutta*), is what is here called "teaching" (*desanā*).
Its specific meaning, however, consists primarily of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth; thus he said: "For when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma... he shows...
In that context, by the mention of "virtue," virtue together with its requisites is included; likewise, by the mention of the "path" (*magga*), [the path] together with its requisites is included.

"Maggā" (paths) means that, by way of both [the path and its fruit], the term "pariyatti" (mastery/learning) exhausts the meaning without remainder. "Tenā" (by that) refers to the demonstration of virtue and so forth.
For here, it is intended that the state of being "good in the beginning" and so on applies to the teaching by way of its purpose (*atthavasena*). "Kathikasaṇṭhiti" means the stability of the speaker;
that is, his firm establishment through the act of speaking.
He does not teach what is meaningful, because that teaching lacks the purpose of leading to liberation (*niyyāna*).

"Connected with a single consonant, etc. means it is connected with a consonant of only one kind or two kinds among the various types of consonants such as the lax (*sithila*), etc., like the Tamil language.
Because they must be pronounced without touching the lips due to the openness of the vocal organs (*vivaṭakaraṇatā*), all [the consonants] are labials (*oṭṭha*).
Or like the Kirāta language, because it is suitable for answering everything [in every respect], it has all its consonants clearly articulated, like the Savara language [or the Yavana language].
Or, because it possesses all the nasalized sounds (anusvāra) in every respect, it has all its consonants suppressed (niggahita), like the languages of the Mlecchas such as the Persians.
All these, however, are called "incomplete in their phonemes" because they function only by means of a portion of the phonemes.
Having done so, they are called "without consonants" (*abyañjana*).
A syllable to be pronounced with relaxed points of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and modes of formation (*karaṇa*)—such as the first and third letters in each of the five groups of consonants—is "relaxed.
A syllable to be pronounced with those [points and modes] not relaxed—the second and fourth letters in each group—is [the opposite].

"Protracted" (*dhanita*) is exemplified by such [terms] as these. "Long" (*dīgha*) has a duration of two *mātrās*. "Short" (*rassa*) has a duration of one *mātrā*, and that same [short vowel] is "light" (*lahuka*).

A light [vowel] followed by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), as well as a long [vowel], is "heavy" (*garuka*). The "visarga" (*niggahita*) is to be pronounced by suppressing the points of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the modes of formation (*karaṇa*).
That which is to be pronounced in connection with what follows is "conjoined" (*sambandha*). Likewise, that which is not so connected is "separated" (*vavatthita*).
It should be pronounced having abandoned the points of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the modes of formation (*karaṇa*); thus it is "liberated.
"In ten ways" means that this is the complete classification of the mind that produces syllables through the cognition of phonemes (*byañjana*), according to the manner of being relaxed and so forth.
For all syllables are mind-originated, and they are called "phonemes" (*byañjana*) because they manifest (*byañjanato*) the intended meaning.
“Without smearing” means without defiling, without destroying, or without omitting; such is the meaning.
When the Blessed One teaches a single verse or a single sentence in order to make a certain matter known, he teaches that very matter through that teaching with complete words and phrases;
thus it is said: “He teaches the Dhamma having made the phrasing entirely complete. Here, the word *kevala* [is used].
