It is called "a term for the whole" because it expresses everything without remainder, and not because it expresses a mixture of things and so forth.
"Complete" means full in every respect; however, since that [meaning] is neither deficient nor excessive in any way, it is described as "a term that is neither deficient nor excessive.
In this context, its non-deficiency should be understood from the fact that it establishes the very purpose for which it was taught, whereas its opposite does not establish that purpose.
Non-excess. "Entire" means possessing all parts. "Complete" means completely complete in every respect; therefore he said, "there is not even a single portion that is incomplete.
The teaching is impure because it is defiled by craving.
"Indifferent to worldly bait" means having a mind unattached to the requisites such as robes and so forth. "By the radiation of welfare..."
By the bringing about of welfare. Through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*) acting as the instrument, one becomes soft-hearted.

"Established in the nature of uplifting" means by a mind fixed in the mode of lifting [beings] out from all defilements and from the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*); the meaning is: by an intention of compassion (*kāruṇya*).
A "vow" (*vata*) is so called in the sense of something to be undertaken, thinking: "From now on, I shall give; and I shall give in this manner. Because it is prescribed by the wise...
"Brahmacariya" (the holy life) is giving, because it conducts itself as the supreme or as Brahmā.
It is "well-practiced" by means of restraining stinginess, greed, and so forth. "Iddhi" is divine power. "Juti" is radiance or majesty.
"Balavīriyūpapatti" is being endowed with such great strength and energy. "Puñña" is the fruit of merit. "Veyyāvacca" is service; this is the holy life.
Having considered that "conduct" (*cariyā*) is the best; this same method applies to the rest as well.

Therefore—because the entire teaching, which comprises the three trainings (*sikkhattaya*), is intended here by the term "holy life" (*brahmacariya*)—he demonstrates the meaning by connecting all the words in grammatical apposition with this term "holy life."
“He teaches the Dhamma... reveals it”—thus the meaning should be understood here.
(191) “The perfection of the aforementioned kind”: this refers to the perfection of qualities such as being excellent in the beginning, and so forth.

Right practice in the Dispensation is possible only for one who has cast pride far away, not for one whose nature is prideful; thus he said, “because of having humbled pride. “Because of its abundance”: [refers to the abundance of the teaching].
Because of their abundance. Intoxications based on wealth, health, and so forth are easy to abandon because their signs are unstable; intoxications based on lineage and learning are not like that.
Therefore, even for those who have gone forth from the families of Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas, the inflation of pride supported by birth and learning is difficult to abandon;
thus he said, "For the most part... they exercise pride. "By way of being of another caste" means by way of being of low birth.
"They are unable to establish themselves" means they are unable to guard their virtue having made it thoroughly pure.

For by means of virtue one establishes oneself in the Dispensation (*sāsana*); or, "to establish themselves" means to establish themselves in the supramundane foundation through the penetration of truth.

That indeed is, in the primary sense, what is called "establishment in the Dispensation," and it is generally possessed by those who are well-born and endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*).
Thus they are, not ill-born.
"Pure" means entirely pure due to the total absence of defilements, because it demonstrates the absolute abandonment of lust and the other [defilements].

"He acquires faith" means he believes by way of the faith of ordinary people (*pothujjanika-saddhā*). For those of a wise nature, the acquisition of the excellence of the Dhamma is preceded by [such] faith.

Faith is accomplishment because of one’s state of confidence in the Dhamma as the standard. One acquires faith [thinking]: "Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, he whose Dhamma is so well-expounded. "Husband and wife" means the master of the house and his wife.
Granted that when "husband and wife" is said, it is understood as referring to only two people by way of the master of the house and the mistress of the house.
But as for a man who has many wives, what need is there to say more? The word "two" is used in order to show that even cohabitation with a single one is crowded.

In the sense of being "possessive" (sakiñcana) through lust and so forth, and in the sense of being "obstructed" (sapalibodha) through fields, lands, and so forth, the two explanations—that it is the path for the arrival of the dust of lust and so on, and that it is the place of their arising—are identical in meaning; only the phrasing differs.
“Not clinging. By the sense of “not sticking,” that is, by the sense of not adhering and being unbound.

Having thus shown the confinement and the open space of household life and the life of renunciation respectively by way of their being the basis for the occurrence of unwholesome and wholesome states, he now says “Moreover,” etc., in order to show that same quality of confinement and open space in relation to them by way of their being the basis for the occurrence of wholesome states alone.
"A summary exposition" (*saṅkhepakathā*) means a concise commentary on the meaning without extracting each word individually. "Even for a single day" means for even a duration of one day.
"Having made it unbroken" means having made it free from breach by not committing even a minor offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Untainted by the stain of defilements" means having made it undefiled by the defilement of craving and so forth. In the sense of being purified...
Because it is stainless, it is like a conch shell that has been polished; thus he said, "having the appearance of a polished conch shell" (*dhota-saṅkha-sappaṭibhāgaṃ*).
By the use of the word "inhabiting" (*ajjhāvasatā*), the accusative case is used in the sense of a locative for the word "house" (*agāra*); thus he said, "in the midst of the house" (*agāramajjhe*).
Garments dyed with an astringent decoction are called *kāsāya*; thus he said, "due to being yellowed by the taste of astringent decoction. "Having put on" means having dressed oneself.

And having put on [the robe]. "House-dwelling" (*agāravāsa*) is "house" (*agāra*) with the elision of the final member; that which brings about the increase of that house, or what is beneficial to the house.

192. "Mass of wealth" (*bhogakkhandha*) means a collection of wealth. "In the sense of binding" (*ābandhanaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of a limited binding through affection, such as "son," "grandson," and so forth.
They are called "relatives" (*ñātī*) because they are known as "these are ours. By way of grandfather, father’s son, and so forth...
In the sense of turning back, it is a "turning" (parivaṭṭa). 193.
"Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" means that the doors of body and speech are closed by the restraint of the Pātimokkha;
and because one who has become such as that is said to be "endowed" with that restraint, it is therefore stated: "possessed of the restraint of the Pātimokkha."
“Endowed with proper conduct and resort,” and so forth, is the demonstration of the conditions for that very possession of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
“In even trifling matters” means in regard to minor offenses committed unintentionally, as well as in regard to unwholesome states of mind that arise impulsively.

“One who sees danger” means one whose nature is to perceive danger. “Having properly undertaken [them]” means having undertaken them with care, by way of non-transgression throughout one’s entire life.
"Having undertaken": each respective training precept (*sikkhāpada*), meaning each respective section of the training. "In this": in this passage, "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
"In brief" means a concise commentary. The detailed exposition has been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*;
therefore, it should be understood there according to the method explained in that commentary.

“By the very mention of conduct and resort” means by the expression “one who is perfect in conduct and resort. Therefore he said: “even though wholesome bodily and verbal actions have already been included.

Considering that a redundant statement indicates another meaning, [the word] “wholesome” was stated in order to show the door of origination for that virtue of purity of livelihood... [omission] ...as blameless, through the complete abandonment of improper search.

The meaning is as follows: Because, after showing that virtue (*sīla*) consists of wholesome bodily and verbal action in the passage, "And what, carpenter, are wholesome virtues? Wholesome bodily action and wholesome verbal action," the teaching in the *Muṇḍika-sutta* proceeds thus:
"Carpenter, I say that even livelihood-purification is included within virtue.
Therefore, [the Blessed One says]: "Endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action..."
Showing that this teaching—“one of purified livelihood”—is comprised within a single category and thus entirely converges and accords with it, he said:
“Or it is stated thus by way of the Muṇḍika-sutta. “I speak in regard to virtue” means: I speak of “virtue,” or the meaning is:
I speak of what is included and contained within virtue. “For the purpose of encompassing” means for the purpose of grasping.

"By threefold virtue" means by virtue that is threefold, namely: minor virtue, intermediate virtue, and major virtue. Regarding the faculties, it refers to those with the mind as the sixth, not those with the body as the fifth.
"By threefold contentment" means by contentment in three modes: according to what is obtained, according to one's strength, and according to what is appropriate.
This concludes the commentary on minor, intermediate, and major virtue.

194–211. Regarding the phrase "In regard to virtue" (*sīlasmiṃ*), he says that this is the locative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*), meaning "there is one kind of virtue. "This alone is the meaning" refers precisely to the meaning of the singular (accusative) case ending. This is from the *Brahmajāla* [Sutta], specifically in the commentary on the *Brahmajāla*. 212.

Self-reproach, reproach by others, fear of punishment, and so forth, are rooted in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). "From the non-restraint of virtue" (*sīlassāsaṃvarato*) means from the failure to restrain oneself through virtue;
the meaning is "due to the absence of restraint of virtue. "Would arise" (*bhaveyya*) means it would occur. "As prescribed by the rules" (*yathāvidhānavihitena*)...

"By that which has been accomplished according to the rule. Because there arises a sublime bodily pleasure for one whose body is touched by refined material forms produced by the mental happiness arising from such signs as non-remorse, it is said: "He experiences non-remorse... [and so on]... he feels it.
Commentary on the Discussion of Restraint of the Faculties (Indriyasaṃvara-kathā-vaṇṇanā)
213. Because the commonality [of the term] depends upon the specific application of its function, it is not abandoned by those [specifics];

thus he says: "The word 'eye' (cakkhu) in some instances refers to the Buddha-eye. For a word denoting a particular meaning (*visesa-sadda*) clarifies that very meaning which exists in the referent by way of excluding other particulars, not one that does not exist.
This same principle applies to the remaining terms as well. It is not shared with others.

The "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakkhu*) is the vision belonging only to Buddhas; it consists of the knowledge of the underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties in others (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*).
The "all-around eye" (*samantacakkhu*) is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), in the sense of seeing everything completely.

"Wisdom of the three lower noble paths" (*ariyamaggattayapaññā*) refers to the wisdom in the three lower noble paths. "Here" (*idha*) refers to this passage: "By the eye, visible forms. This is the word "eye" (*cakkhu*).
“Serenity” … [and so on] … it occurs because that which depends can be spoken of by means of its support, as in the expression: “The beds are making a loud noise.
“Unmixed” means unmixed with the suffering of the defilements. Therefore he said: “Pure.

For when restraint of the sense faculties is thoroughly purified, the pursuit of higher consciousness—through the disappearance of evil states that have become predominant—is indeed placed within one’s grasp.
He said: "One experiences the bliss of higher consciousness.
Commentary on the Discourse on Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension (214):
One who knows thoroughly, or who knows clearly and specifically, is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*); the state of one who clearly comprehends is "clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*).
Thus there is knowledge of occurrence. Its analysis is the “Exposition of Clear Comprehension” (Sampajaññabhājanīya);
it is within that Exposition of Clear Comprehension [that this occurs]. Regarding advancing, he says it is “advanced,” for “‘Advanced’ is said to be going.
Likewise, regarding retreating, he says it is “retreated,” for “‘Retreated’ is turning back. And “turning back” means merely the act of returning. Having turned back...
Going, however, is simply going. "Bringing forward" means moving the body forward by way of going.

By saying "even in standing," etc., he shows that "approaching" (*abhikkama*) is the movement of the body forward when it is devoid of the act of going while in standing, sitting, or lying down, whereas "retreating" (*paṭikkama*) is the drawing back of the body toward the rear.
"Of the seat" refers to a seat such as a stool and the like. "Facing the front part" means facing the front portion, such as the footstool and so forth.

“Crawling about” (*saṃsaranto*) means crawling forward. “Crawling back” (*paccāsaṃsaranto*) means crawling backward. By the phrase “the same method applies,” he demonstrates that for one who is lying down, there is crawling forward and crawling backward toward the front.

“Full awareness” (*sampajānaṃ*) is right understanding; one who has the habit of performing the duties to be done by oneself through that [understanding] is “one who acts with full awareness” (*sampajānakārī*).
He said: "One who performs all duties with clear comprehension. It has already been stated previously that the word *sampajāna* is a synonym for *sampajañña*.
"One who performs clear comprehension" means that one indeed generates non-delusion regarding the "going forth" (*abhikkanta*) and so on.

Alternatively, one is a "performer of clear comprehension" (*sampajānakārī*) because he possesses the performance (*kāra*) of clear comprehension. He conducts himself together with the purpose known as spiritual progress (*dhammavuddhi*).
"Meaningful" refers to [the four postures] beginning with "when going forward. Full awareness of what is meaningful is *sātthakasampajañña*.
Full awareness of what is suitable—that is, what is beneficial to oneself—is *sappāyasampajañña*.

Regarding "going forward" and so forth, full awareness regarding one's range of activity (*gocara*), namely the alms-round, as well as other activities that do not abandon the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) which constitutes one's range, is *gocarasampajañña*.
Non-delusion regarding such acts as stepping forward and so forth is itself clear comprehension; this is "clear comprehension through non-delusion" (*asammoha-sampajañña*).

"Having discerned" means having weighed, having investigated, and having reflected—this is the meaning. By the mention of "seeing the Saṅgha," going for the purpose of the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, and so on, is included.
Regarding the phrase "seeing the foul and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa* meditations and others should be understood.
In order to explain the meaning stated in brief, it was said: "Even upon seeing a cetiya or the Bodhi tree," and so forth.
"He attains arahantship" is the description of the highest attainment; for even the arising of serenity and insight is indeed the growth of a bhikkhu.
"Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri.
"But in that case" refers to the object grasped by means of purposeful clear comprehension (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).
Regarding the statement, "The 'purpose' (*attha*) is growth through the Dhamma," someone might suspect that what is intended by "purposeful" is merely what is suitable (*sappāya*);
therefore, in order to dispel that doubt, the passage beginning with "First, the visiting of a shrine" is commenced. "Like paintings and statues" means like images fashioned in painting.
Or like various statues produced by the application of machinery.
Non-observation is the unwise apprehension of an object due to equanimity associated with ignorance—that which was said in such passages as:
"Upon seeing a form with the eye, equanimity arises in the fool, the deluded worldling. There is danger to life through being crushed by elephants and so forth.
Seeing dissimilar forms and so forth constitutes an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariyantarāya*).
From the very day of their going forth, it has been the established practice for monks to engage in conversation that conforms [to the rules];

however, conversation that does not conform is called its "second" [type]. Thus he said, "Two kinds of talk had never been spoken before. The word "thus" refers to the passage beginning with "But if... and so forth.
He refers to all the modes already mentioned, not to what is being said here, such as "the unattractiveness of the female sex for a man.

Because it is the basis for the occurrence of the practice of yoga, the object of meditation is called a "meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna*); thus he says, "the range known as the meditation subject.
"Having mastered" means having done so in such a way that the learning-sign (*uggahanimitta*) arises.
"Having learned" means by way of accomplishing proficiency in learning.
"Carries" means he sets the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in motion; the meaning is that he applies himself to it until his return from the alms round.
"Does not bring back" means he does not withdraw the meditation subject from the time of engaging with food until the time of approaching the daytime resting place. "Body-care" refers to...
“Cleansing the face and so forth” refers to the maintenance of the body. “Two or three times on the meditation seat” means two or three sitting sessions, or two or three warmings of the seat.
Therefore he said, “causing warmth to be taken up.

“By way of the meditation subject itself” means by way of the meditation subject alone, not abandoning the meditation subject; thus it refers to the meditation subject that will be explained later, beginning with the words, “Even a bowl is insentient.”
This shows that it is not to be avoided or abandoned. "In that very way" means exactly three times.

Because a *sārīrika-cetiya* (relic shrine) is considered more venerable than a *paribhoga-cetiya* (use-enjoyment shrine), the phrase "having paid homage to the cetiya" is stated by way of the prior action.
For thus it is said in the Commentary: "The branches of the Bodhi tree that obstruct the cetiya must be removed. It is precisely by way of recollecting the Buddha’s qualities...
Regarding "prostrating at the foot of the Bodhi tree," he said: "having displayed an act of homage as if in the very presence of the Blessed Buddha.

"In the vicinity of the village" means in the area surrounding the village. "For the purpose of winning over people" means for the purpose of winning over people through the support of the Dhamma, thinking, "If I do not speak, who else will speak to them?
Therefore, because "a discourse on the Dhamma must indeed be delivered..."
The commentators say, "It is so," because there is no such thing as a discourse on the Dhamma that is divorced from a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Therefore, "by way of the meditation subject" means that, without abandoning the meditation subject he himself is maintaining, he should deliver a discourse on the Dhamma that is consistent with it.
Regarding the phrase "having uttered words of thanksgiving," here too the phrase "by way of the meditation subject" should be brought forward and connected.

“By the mere limit of what is obtained” means without making a distinction such as “familiar” or “unfamiliar,” but simply by the measure of what has been acquired; the meaning is: by the mere act of coming together. “In fear” refers to fear of foreign armies and the like.

He says “the fire born of kamma” with reference to the digestive heat. The meditation subject does not enter the cognitive path because, due to the body being exhausted by the distress of hunger, there is an absence of concentration.
“In the remaining places” means in those places not occupied by the rice gruel. “One after another” (poṅkhānupoṅkha).

This is a demonstration of the non-interruption of the establishment of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna); just as there is no interruption in a succession of arrows proceeding one after another, so it is with this as well.
He has laid down his burden regarding the application to development (bhāvanā). By not fulfilling the performance of duties, he breaks all the observances (vatta).
"One who is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from lust for the body, not free from lust for forms;
who, having eaten as much as he desires until his belly is full, dwells devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness;

and who leads the holy life with the aspiration for some order of devas"—thus is one whose mind is bound by the five kinds of mental obstructions mentioned. "Having practiced" means having engaged in [the holy life].

"By way of the practice of going and returning" means: that which possesses the going and returning—that is, the act of going for alms and returning from it—accompanied by meditation, is "that which involves going and returning";
it is this very thing that constitutes the practice (*vatta*), and it is by way of that.

"Those who desire their own welfare" means those who wish for their own benefit and happiness; the meaning is that they possess the desire for the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*). For the Dhamma is indeed benefit, and happiness has that as its cause. Now...
Or, because it is indistinguishable from the wise and because it is comprised within the personal existence (attabhāva), there is a phenomenon called "self" (atta);
those who desire or long for that are "self-desirers" (attakāmā).
An "ox-load" (usabha) consists of twenty *yaṭṭhi*s. "By that perception" means by that perception of stone, thinking, "I have come this far."
The intention is that they know. "This same method" means that the very same method stated for standing—beginning with "this monk"—applies to sitting as well.
By the fear of missing their meal for those coming from behind, one cultivates proper attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
"Pounding" means pounding the heads of rice in a place where grain is being processed.
“I shall honor the Great Struggle (Mahāpadhāna). I shall honor, according to my ability, that very practice of difficult austerities performed by the Lord of the World for our sake over six years.
For the worship of practice is the worship of the Teacher, not the worship of material things.

The phrase “only standing and walking” is stated with reference to the postures one must maintain; it is not intended as a prohibition against sitting, which is necessarily required at times such as during meals.
Having descended onto the street, one should first observe the streets without looking here and there; thus he said, "having observed the streets.
To show that which is referred to by the expression "graceful in his approach," he said, "and therein," and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "having established the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment," whatever is to be said will be explained later.

"He will come. "Endowed with the eight factors" means having made it endowed with the eight factors stated in the passage beginning, "only for the maintenance of this body," and so forth. "Neither for amusement," etc., is the demonstration of prohibitions.
"He realizes pratyekabodhi, provided he is possessed of the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya)"—this is the connection. Thus in all cases.

The same applies to those beyond this. Therein, for *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment), the perfection of the decisive support (*upanissaya-sampadā*) consists of two incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*) and one hundred thousand eons, along with the accumulation of the corresponding merit and knowledge.
For the supreme disciples (*aggasāvaka*) of *sāvakabodhi* (disciple enlightenment), it is one incalculable eon and one hundred thousand eons;
for the great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*), it is one hundred thousand eons, along with the accumulation of the corresponding merit and knowledge. For others...
It is wholesome merit conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) produced by way of reliance upon the process of world-evolution (*vivaṭṭa*) throughout past births.
As for "Bāhiya Dārucīriya": he was called "Bāhiya" because he was born and raised in the territory of Bāhiya, and he was called "Dārucīriya" because of his wearing of bark garments (*dārucīra*).
Indeed, that venerable one [was instructed]: "Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: 'In the seen, there is only the seen...'"

‘In the seen there will be merely the seen; in the heard, the merely heard; in the sensed, the merely sensed; in the cognized, there will be merely the cognized. Thus, Bāhiya, should you train yourself.

When, Bāhiya, for you there is merely the seen in the seen, merely the heard in the heard, merely the sensed in the sensed, and merely the cognized in the cognized, then, Bāhiya, you will not be [defined] by that.
When, Bāhiya, you are not [defined] by that, then, Bāhiya, you will not be with that. Then, Bāhiya, you will not be hereafter.”
"Not there. "Since you, Bāhiya, are not there, therefore, Bāhiya, you are neither here, nor yonder, nor between the two.
This itself is the end of suffering. By this much teaching alone, he realized arhatship.
In this way, the sūtra passages illustrating the great wisdom and other qualities of the Elder Sāriputta and others are to be understood in detail.
"That non-confusion is precisely this" should be understood by means of the very mode that is now being stated.

By the phrase "the self goes forward," he shows the confusion regarding going forward on the part of the blind worldling due to the grasping of a view; but by the phrase "I go forward," he shows it due to the grasping of conceit.
Since both of these do not exist without craving, [he shows it] also by way of the grasping of craving.

Confusion is indeed shown [to be absent]. Having stated, "Thus, not being confused," he spoke the words beginning with "I advance" in order to show that analysis of the compact by means of which that non-confusion occurs.
In this context, because the fire element accompanied by the air element is the condition for lifting up—for the fire element has the nature of lifting up—in the act of lifting up...

The air element follows that [fire element]; therefore, showing that between these two there is an excess of functional capacity while the others are deficient, he said: "In lifting one foot... [and so on]... they are powerful.
For the air element, which follows the fire element, is the condition for the drawing back and the stretching forward, since the air element moves transversely.
The activity in the acts of drawing forward (*atiharaṇa*) and drawing back (*vītiharaṇa*) is preeminent. The fire element possesses a state of conformity with that [activity];

therefore, he said, "likewise in the acts of drawing forward and drawing back," showing that here, by virtue of their functional capacity, these two [elements] are predominant while the others are subordinate.

Although there is a distinction between the conforming and the conformed-to, the inclusion of the word "likewise" refers merely to the fact that they both possess the nature of the fire element and the air element.
In this context, "lifting up" (uddharaṇa) is the raising of the foot from the place where it has been stepped upon.

"Bringing forward" (atiharaṇa) is carrying it forward beyond the place where it stood; or, for the purpose of avoiding stumps and the like, or for the purpose of avoiding contact with the foot already planted, it is the carrying [of the foot] sideways.
"Bringing back" (vītiharaṇa) is the drawing back as long as the foot remains planted; after that, it is "bringing forward."
"Carrying away" (paraṃ haraṇaṃ) means "taking away" (vītiharaṇaṃ); this is the distinction between them.
Because the water element (āpodhātu), which follows along with the earth element (pathavīdhātu), is the condition for emission. For the water element has the intrinsic nature of being heavy.
In the act of emission, the earth element follows along with that [water element]; therefore, here, by virtue of the functional capacity of these two—
Showing that [the water element] is predominant while the others are subordinate, he says: "In the act of relinquishing... they are powerful.

For, since the earth element accompanying the water element is the condition for its placement—because its function is especially prominent not only in providing a foundation but also in establishing something upon it—the earth element is said to be accompanied by the water element; likewise in the action of striking.
Since the cessation [of the body] is accomplished by means of the earth element, even there the earth element possesses the quality of being accompanied by the water element;
therefore it is said, "likewise in the placing down and the cessation.
"Therein" means in that forward movement, or in those aforementioned parts such as lifting up and so forth. In "lifting up":
At the moment of lifting. "Material and immaterial phenomena" refers to material phenomena occurring in the mode of being lifted, and the immaterial phenomena that originate them.
They do not reach the destination because they exist for only a single moment.
"Right there, right there" means wherever they have arisen, right there; for there is no movement of phenomena from one location to another. "Joint..."
It should be understood that the passage beginning with “pabbā” refers to the stages such as extraction (*uddharaṇa*), and is spoken by way of a similar continuity (*sabhāga-santati*).
For the moment of occurrence (*pavattikkhaṇa*) of even material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) is exceedingly swift;

it is swifter than the meeting of the edges of the hooves of the horses of those who delight in racing, when they are running head-on toward one another with their heads above and feet below. Just as:

Just as the breaking of sesame seeds being crushed is indicated by the sound *paṭapaṭā*, so too it is said "cracking like *paṭapaṭā*" for the purpose of showing the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), for those that have arisen necessarily break up.
The phrase "together with form" (*saddhiṃ rūpena*) refers to the material phenomena that cease simultaneously with the cessation of each respective consciousness.
This has been stated regarding that which arises at the moment of arising of the seventeenth consciousness from that point.

Otherwise, if material and immaterial phenomena were simultaneous, there would be a contradiction with such statements as, "Material form is heavy in its transformation and slow in its cessation," and likewise:
"Monks, I do not see even a single phenomenon that changes so rapidly."

"Even as this mind [is]," and so on according to the initial text. For consciousness and mental factors, having the nature of possessing an object (*sārammaṇa*), arise only while manifesting the object that serves as their objective condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) according to their respective capacities; thus, their cessation occurs immediately after the accomplishment of that manifestation of their own nature.
Material phenomena (*rūpa-dhammā*), however, are without an object and are to be manifested; thus, for them, there is the accomplishment of the state of being manifested.
The statement "it occurs with sixteen types of consciousness" implies that their momentary existence is intended;

for the three aggregates, it is due to their being conditioned merely by the conjunction of a swift consciousness and its object, while consciousness itself turns swiftly due to being conditioned merely by the conjunction with the object.

Material phenomena turn slowly because they are conditioned by the gross primary elements. Furthermore, the knowledge of things as they truly are regarding the various elements belongs to the Tathāgata alone.

Furthermore, since only material phenomena (rūpadhamma) are stated to be the pre-arisen condition (purejātapaccaya), and the post-arisen condition (pacchājātapaccaya) is likewise [restricted to material phenomena], it would be illogical for material and immaterial phenomena to exist simultaneously.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood according to the method already explained:
"One consciousness arises, another consciousness ceases. That which was the previously arisen consciousness is "another"; [it is not the same as the subsequent one].

Furthermore, as that [preceding consciousness] ceases, it ceases precisely by serving as the condition for another—such as the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*)—and thus another consciousness arises having obtained such conditions.
If this were so, would there not be an interval between them? No, he says: "uninterrupted succession" (*avīci-manuppabandho*).
Just as no gap or interval (*vīci*) is found, such that those who do not see the distinction might think, "This is that very same thing," so too is there a continuous succession from one to the next.
The mental continuum and the material continuum proceed like the flow of water in a river.
"Looking forward" (*ālokita*) refers to looking straight ahead; thus it is said, "gazing in front.

Since looking toward whichever direction one is walking, standing, or sitting is "looking forward," therefore, looking toward the intermediate directions following that [primary direction] is also included.
He said, "Looking around (vilokita) means looking toward the intermediate directions. He stated, "Or rather, by this term [looking forward],
all of those are indeed included," because there might be the possibility of "looking down" (olokita) when performing tasks such as sweeping or plastering,
"looking up" (ullokita) in cases such as removing the ceiling, or "looking back" (apalokita) when avoiding dangers approaching from behind.
“Kāyasakkhin” means one who has realized [the truth] with the body; the meaning is one who acts through direct personal experience.

For that venerable one, at the time of insight (vipassanā), having generated the effort, “I shall thoroughly restrain that very lack of restraint of the sense faculties by which I fell into such adverse states as dissatisfaction with the Teaching,” he possessed powerful moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa). And because he had performed his duties therein...
Having reached the highest perfection in the restraint of the sense faculties, for that very reason the Teacher placed him in the foremost position, saying:
"Monks, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who guard the doors of their sense faculties, Nanda is the foremost.
The connection [of the text] should be understood by bringing forward the words "looking ahead and looking aside," as well as "usefulness" and "appropriateness. Therefore...
He restates the very point already mentioned—that the state of clear comprehension of the range of movement consists precisely in not abandoning the meditation subject—as a supporting reason:

"Looking forward and looking aside should be done by means of one's own meditation subject alone; no other method apart from meditation subjects such as the aggregates (khandha) and so forth should be sought.
This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, even designations such as "looking forward" are merely specific modes of occurrence belonging to the mere phenomenon (dhamma) itself.
Therefore, in order to show that the thorough understanding of it as it truly is constitutes "clear comprehension through non-delusion," the passage beginning with “abbhantare” (within) was stated.
“By way of the diffusion of the air-element produced by mental activity” means by way of the occurrence of the mode of motion belonging to the air-element originated by functional consciousness.
“Sinks downwards” means it goes down. “Leaps upwards” means it jumps up.
It proceeds as if rising upward.

"Accomplishing the function of the factors" means acting as that which brings about the performance of the functions of the primary factors; this is the meaning. The statement, "Even in the first impulsion...
there is none," refers to the absence of lust and other such states regarding [the perception of] "woman" or "man" within the cognitive process of the five sense-doors.

This has been stated. For in that case, through improper adverting and determining, mere greed arises toward a desirable object such as a woman’s form, and mere aversion toward an undesirable one; however, at the mind-door, there occurs passion and so forth [thinking] "woman" or "man.
The root of that is the five-door javana, or else all that has been mentioned, beginning with the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Thus, the "full understanding of the root" (*mūlapariññā*) is stated with reference to the root of the mental-door impulsion (*manodvāra-javana*).
However, its "guest-like" and "temporary" nature is stated specifically of the five-door impulsion (*pañcadvāra-javana*) by way of its unprecedented occurrence and its brief duration.
The phrase "having broken and fallen in succession from below and above" refers to the successive attainment of dissolution (*bhaṅga*) by the lower and upper [moments].
The connection is that the impulsion (javana) is not appropriate for that [moment]. A guest is one who has arrived.
"Tāvataka" means those things whose duration is limited to such a short time, namely, the period defined by arising and passing away.

This is non-delusive clear comprehension (asammoha-sampajañña). "In a gathering" means in a collection. Regarding the word "therein": when looking forward and looking around are being discerned by way of the five aggregates, who is it—distinct from them—that looks forward, and who looks around? Who is that single entity?

“Strong-dependence condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*)”: this is stated figuratively according to the method of the discourses (*suttanta-naya*). “Conascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*)” is merely an illustration, since other conditions—such as mutuality (*aññamañña*), association (*sampayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*)—are also applicable here.

“At the time of stroking” means at the time suitable for stroking; the same applies to “stretching. They say that the *maṇisappa* is a particular species of snake. “Lolling” means shaking or performing a playful movement. “Of a hot nature” means one whose body is full of feverish heat.
[The term] arising through wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*) is used because it brings about harm by defiling one’s virtue (*sīla*).
“Unsuitable. By the passage beginning with “The robe, too, is insentient,” he shows that the body, like the robe, is insentient;

thus, by demonstrating the emptiness of a self in the body, he elucidates the very meaning stated in the passage beginning with “within,” thereby showing the reason for contentment with whatever comes.
Therefore, he says “Therefore,” and so forth.
“Struck by four or five knots” means one whose four or five knots have been struck, or likewise, one who has been struck by four or five knots.

The eightfold purpose should be understood as the eightfold specific utility stated according to the method beginning with “for the maintenance of this body,” following the doctrine of the Elder Mahāsīva. In this alternative, [it is understood] by the passage beginning with “not for sport.”
However, it should be understood that this was stated by way of showing a portion of the negation, as it has come down in the teaching with the words "by means of the method.
Just as water, which supports the earth, is maintained by the wind that supports it, so too does the consumed food remain in its receptacle solely by means of the air element;
thus he said, "it remains by means of the air element alone. "Carries forward" means it carries it up to the mouth.
“Vītiharatī” means that it carries [the food] while mixing it within the belly. Or, “atiharati” means that it carries it while passing it through the gateway of the mouth.
“Vītiharatī” means that it carries it while moving what has entered the belly; “parivatteti” means that it moves it back and forth.
And herein, the holding, turning over, crushing, and drying up of the nutriment are the air-element itself, accompanied by the earth-element.
It performs its function; it is not only [the other elements], for these are also described as functions of the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*).
"And it maintains moisture" means that it maintains moisture in such a way that there is no desiccation by other factors such as the air element (*vāyodhātu*).
"The fire element" refers to the fire element known as the digestive heat (*gahaṇī*); for it fully digests the food that has been ingested. "It becomes straight" refers to the food.

It is the path for entering [the mouth] and so forth. "Directs" (ābhujati) means that one turns the mind toward [the object] by way of seeking it out, and by way of experiencing its swallowing, its state of being digested or undigested, and so on;
the meaning is that one cognizes it. Indeed, the application (*payoga*) which serves as the condition for each respective cognition is called "right application" (*sammāpayoga*).
For whatever application brings about the seeking and so forth, that same [application] also brings about the cognition of that object.

It is so called because it is inseparable from that [mental application]. Alternatively, it is said thus because all activity of consciousness is preceded by mental application (*ābhoga*), as one applies the mind and directs attention based on right effort and right practice.
"By way of going" means by way of going toward the village for alms (*gocara-gāma*) by means of wandering for alms. "By way of seeking" means in the village for alms...
"From wandering for the sake of alms" means from roaming about. "From consumption" means from the eating of food. "From the seat" means from the seat of bile and so forth.

It is called a "seat" (*āsaya*) because even though it occurs in one place together, it remains, stays, and functions there—being established as the fruit of kamma and existing without mutual confusion by way of its own boundaries;
thus, it refers to the bile and other humors that reside upon the stomach (*āmāśaya*).
For this syllable *ā* has the sense of a boundary (*mariyāda*). "Store" (*nidhāna*) means that which is called the stomach (*āmāsaya*), because food, having been consumed, remains stored there;
[the term refers to] from that store. "From the unripened" (*aparipakkato*) means from that which has not yet been ripened by the kamma-born heat known as the digestive fire (*gahaṇī*).
"From the ripened" (*paripakkato*) means from the state of the food being fully digested after it has been consumed. "From the fruit" (*phalato*) means from the resulting outcome (*nipphatti*).
"From trickling" means from trickling here and there. "From smearing" means from smearing completely.
This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Sweat breaks out from the body" means that sweat breaks out from the body due to the fever produced by the suppression of natural urges.

And other diseases such as earaches, fistulas, and so forth. "In an improper place" means in a place occupied by humans or non-humans that is unsuitable, such as a field or a shrine dedicated to a deity;
for when non-humans are angry, or even humans, they may bring about the end of one's life.
It does not belong to oneself because it has been relinquished, nor to another because it has not been assigned to anyone, and because it is loathsome. "From the water-pot" means:
"From a water vessel such as a bamboo tube": *taṃ* refers to the discarded water.

"Postures of long journeys" (*addhānairiyāpathā*) are those postures that persist for a longer duration over a long period of time. "Intermediate postures" (*majjhimā*) are those occurring by way of going for alms and so forth.
"Miscellaneous postures" (*cuṇṇiyairiyāpathā*) are those occurring within the monastery or elsewhere, by way of turning here and there and so on.

They say: "In the phrase ‘gone’ (*gata*), it means ‘in going’ (*gamane*). Some maintain that since the forward and backward movement of the body was already mentioned by the previous inclusion of "approaching" (*abhikkama*) and "receding" (*paṭikkama*), here only "going" (*gamana*) itself is intended.
This is because, according to the doctrine of the Elder Mahāsīva, in each successive posture (*iriyāpatha*), the material and immaterial phenomena occurring therein [are included].
Since being "actively aware" (*sampajañña*) is included therein by way of seeing cessation, it should be understood as the practice of insight (*vipassanā*) through clear comprehension.
Therefore it was said: "This burden of non-delusion intended in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta was stated by the Elder Mahāsīva.
However, in this *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*, all four kinds of clear comprehension are obtained.
Since this teaching is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the specific fruits of the ascetic life (*sāmaññaphala*),

the phrase "only for one associated with mindfulness" is stated to show that mindfulness is predominant by way of its function— just as clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) was shown to be predominant by way of its function—
and not merely to show the simple presence of mindfulness. For the occurrence of knowledge never takes place devoid of mindfulness.
“There is. By the words “for this is the detailed exposition of this term,” he clarifies that mindfulness and knowledge are indeed equal in their function.
“These terms” refers to the terms beginning with “he acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning.
“Expounded” means they have been analyzed separately; by this, he clarifies that here, as with clear comprehension, mindfulness itself is the primary factor.
But the Majjhimabhāṇakas say: One bhikkhu goes along thinking of one thing, reflecting on another;
another goes along without having relinquished his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Likewise, one stands... [and so on]... sits... [and so on]...
lies down thinking of one thing, reflecting on another; another lies down without having relinquished his meditation subject.

However, since it does not become clear by that much alone, they demonstrate it by means of walking meditation (*caṅkama*). For a bhikkhu who, having descended onto the walking path, stands at one end and examines it thus:
"The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the eastern end of the walking path ceased right there without reaching the western end; and those that occurred at the western end..."
Those material and immaterial phenomena occurring while walking have ceased right there without reaching the eastern end of the walkway;
those occurring in the middle of the walkway have ceased right there without reaching either end; those occurring on the walkway have ceased right there without reaching the standing place;
those occurring at the standing place have ceased right there without reaching the sitting place; and those occurring while sitting [have ceased] without reaching the lying down place.
“Having not reached [it], they cease right here”—while examining in this way, as he is examining, he descends into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
When arising, he arises having taken up the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). This bhikkhu is called one who acts with clear comprehension regarding going and so forth.
In this way, too, the meditation subject does not become obscure while he sleeps; therefore, a bhikkhu should [practice] as long as he is able.
Having walked, stood, sat, and lain down in this manner, he lies down having thus discerned:
"The body is insentient; the bed is insentient. The body does not know, 'I am lying on the bed'; the bed does not know, 'The body is lying on me.
The insentient body is lying on the insentient bed. While discerning in this way, he causes the mind to sink into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Waking up, he wakes up having taken hold of his meditation subject; this is what is meant by "one who acts with clear comprehension while sleeping.

Because it is composed of that [meditation subject] through the production of bodily and other activities, and because it arises from the activity of adverting, every impulsion—indeed, all that proceeds through the six doors—is called a "proceeding consisting of activity. Perceiving that "when that exists, there is waking," he comprehends it.

One is called "practicing with clear comprehension while awake" (jāgarite sampajānakārī). Furthermore, one is also called "practicing with clear comprehension while awake" if one divides the day and night into six periods and remains awake during five of those periods.

It is also said that one who teaches the Dhamma under the heading of the "bases of liberation" (vimuttāyatana), and who speaks appropriate discourse based on the ten topics of talk while abandoning the thirty-two kinds of base conversation, is likewise [practicing with clear comprehension].

"One who acts with full awareness" (sampajānakārī) means: even when one directs attention toward whichever object among the thirty-eight is pleasing to the mind, and even when one has attained the second jhāna, one is said to be "acting with full awareness" in silence.
For the second jhāna, being devoid of verbal formations, is specifically called "silence.
Thus, in the manner described, the meaning is that [full awareness] occurs in four ways in all seven instances.
215. Showing that contentment by virtue of which a bhikkhu is called "contented" because it exists within him, [the author] says:
"endowed with contentment regarding this or that requisite. This refers to being satisfied with any requisite whatsoever, such as robes and so forth.
The meaning is "endowed with. Alternatively, the "other" is called inferior because it is different from the sublime;
likewise, the sublime is the "other" because it is different from the inferior. For the state of being "the other" is established through mutual dependence.

Thus, that non-greed which, by means of an inferior or a sublime requisite such as robes and so forth, finds contentment, is "contentment with whatever requisites are available" (*itarītarapaccayasantosa*) as it functions in that manner.
Endowed with that. Contentment according to what is obtained—meaning contentment in accordance with one's own gains—is *yathālābhasantosa*.

The same method applies to the other two [types of contentment] as well. Alternatively, "gain" (*lābha*) means that which is obtained; whatever gain there is is "according to gain" (*yathālābha*), and contentment by means of that is "contentment according to gain.
"Strength" (*bala*) refers to bodily strength. "Suitability" (*sāruppa*) refers to being appropriate for those who are naturally weak and so forth.
The non-longing for anything other than what has been obtained may indeed be a manifestation of fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*);
therefore, in order to show the true nature of contentment (*santosassa sarūpaṃ*) as distinct from that, he said, "Even when obtaining [something], he does not take it.

"Having exchanged that" means: because heavy robes do not bring comfort but rather cause physical exhaustion for those who are naturally weak and so forth—it is for this purpose, and not out of excessive desire (*atricchatā*) and the like.
Having exchanged that [robe]. He said, "Even one who makes use of light robes is indeed content," because using light robes does not contradict contentment.

He said, "Even while wearing those...," because even after receiving a costly robe or many robes, discarding them and taking up others according to what is appropriate does not contradict contentment, as it remains established in the proper manner.

“He is indeed content. In this way, the intended meaning of the inclusion of the word “api” (even/also) should be understood in the descriptions of the remaining requisites according to their strength and suitability.
“Muttaharītaka” means either a myrobalan fruit (*harītaka*) treated with cow urine, or one discarded due to its rotten state. By the Buddha and others...
"Praised" means commended by the Perfectly Enlightened One and others through such statements as, "The going forth is dependent upon medicine of putrid urine.
By enjoining the bhikkhus to fewness of wishes and contentment, he himself becomes supremely contented, owing to his being endowed with the highest,
most excellent degree of contentment.
They maintain and nourish the body, thus they are "body-maintainers. Likewise, "belly-maintainers" should be understood.

And since the state of being a belly-maintainer is intended by way of assisting the maintenance of the physical frame through the act of swallowing, the state of being a body-maintainer should be seen by way of assisting the body externally.

"Requisites" (*parikkhāra*) refers to the taking up of requisites. "A rug that remains in place" (*tatraṭṭhaka-paccattharaṇaṃ*) means a rug that stays right there without being formally resolved upon by oneself.
In this context, the "newness" and so forth of the rugs and other items should be understood according to the sequence already stated, not because they possess an inherent, fixed status as such.
Why? Because they do not maintain that state [permanently], due to their perishable nature.
“Great elephants” means they are like great elephants. If others as well possess the nature of fewness of wishes and so forth, why is this teaching intended specifically for them?
He says “But the Blessed One,” and so on, to answer that it is not so. That by which there is the maintenance of the body is “conducive to the maintenance of the body.
Therefore he said: “merely by maintaining the body.”

Because he dwells happily in the four directions, these four directions are his dwelling-places of happiness; thus he is "four-directional" (*catuddiso*), and being four-directional, he is "all-pervading" (*cātuddiso*).
He does not resist beings or conditioned phenomena with fear in any of those directions, nor is he himself resisted by them;
thus he is "non-resistant" (*appaṭigho*). Being content with "this or that" means with various superior and inferior requisites.
One who is content with what is one's own, with what is peaceful, and with what is equal; who lies down having relinquished [them];

and who, by means of patience through endurance and the Vinaya and so forth, endures and overcomes those "parissayas"—which are called *parissaya* because lions, tigers, and the like, as well as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth, lie in wait for and overwhelm both body and mind—one is "fearless" (*achambhī*) due to the absence of fear that causes rigidity.

“One should wander alone”: having become solitary, one would be able to wander. “Like the horn of a rhinoceros” means that, by virtue of that very state of dwelling alone, one is similar to the horn of the khagga deer.
A bird might be considered wingless if it has not yet developed the impact of wind [from flight]; therefore, it is stated with the qualification “a winged bird.”
216. Regarding the phrase "it becomes subject to censure":

this refers to the mode of criticism that [one might say], "For such-and-such a bhikkhu, there is in the forest merely a dwelling place like that of wild animals or forest-rangers, but there is no right practice whatsoever suited to forest-dwelling."
It becomes subject to censure either on account of misconduct with forest-dwelling animals or with people of a similar class who roam the woods.
Because it resembles a dark spot (*kāḷaka*), it is a "dark" offense; this refers to a grave fault (*thullavajja*). Because it resembles a mole (*tilaka*), it is a "mole-like" offense;

this refers to a minor fault (*aṇumattavajja*). "Secluded" means secluded from people. Therefore he said, "empty. That [seclusion] should be understood precisely by the absence of the sound and noise of people.
"Because sound is a thorn to meditative absorption (jhāna)," he said; thus the meaning is "little sound, little noise. "This very thing" refers to the state of being noiseless.
A *vihāra* is an entire residence demarcated by a wall. An *aḍḍhayoga* is a long palace; some also say it is a palace shaped like a garuḷa.
A *pāsāda* is a square palace. A *hammiya* is a palace with a flat roof. An *aṭṭa* is for [defending against] rival kings.
A *paṭibāhana-yogga* is a superior dwelling consisting of four or five stories. A *māḷa* is a superior dwelling comprised of a single upper chamber (*kūṭa*) and possessing many corners.
According to another method: a *vihāra* is a long-faced palace; an *aḍḍhayoga* is a lodging with a roof covering only one side.
It is said that in such a case, the wall on one side is higher while the other side is lower, and for that reason, it is called "covered on one side."
It exists. A *pāsāda* (palace) is a long quadrangular palace. A *hammiya* is a flat-roofed building provided with a courtyard (*candika-aṅgaṇa*).
A *guhā* (cave) is a natural mountain cave. A *leṇa* (shelter) is a rock-ledge enclosed by a door. The rest is exactly as previously described.
A *maṇḍapa* is a bower of branches.
“Vihāra-senāsana” means a lodging that serves as a dwelling place. “Mañca-pīṭha-senāsana” refers both to beds and chairs themselves, as well as the lodging associated with beds and chairs.
“Santhata-senāsana” is so called because it is to be spread out with rugs and the like.
“Sayanāsanā” is a lodging that consists merely of a space for lying down and sitting, due to the absence of any further preparation. By the phrase “a secluded lodging,” [the following is indicated:]
It is indeed included by the mention of "lodgings" because it is a general designation.
If this is so, why was "the forest," and so forth, stated? To this he says, "But this... and so on.
The phrase "as it has come down with reference to bhikkhunīs" is said with regard to how it appears in the Vinaya; however, even in the Abhidhamma, "the forest... [is stated].

"Having gone out beyond the threshold post, all this is 'forest'"—this has already been stated. For therein, that which is not included within the vicinity of a village is called "forest" in the literal sense;
thus it was so spoken. What is stated in the *Dhutanga-niddesa* is appropriate;
therefore, the intention is that it should be understood according to the method explained there. "At the foot of a tree" means near a tree. For this has been said:
“To the extent that at midday the shadow spreads all around, and leaves fall in a windless place—to that extent is it the ‘foot of a tree’ (rukkhamūla).
Since the word *sela* is used without distinction as a synonym for mountain, it is said: “a mountain (*pabbata*) is a *sela*”;

this does not refer only to that which consists of stone, for a mountain is of three kinds, including those made of earth and so forth. [The word] “opening” refers to the opening between two mountains.
For those standing very close to one another, it is like a gap such as a window-cavity, or [a space] on a single mountain.

"Like a thicket" (*umaṅga*) means like a dense jungle (*sudugga*). "A place not frequented by people" means a place that should not be traversed by people according to their ordinary course of movement.
By the word "etcetera," [it includes]: "A forest retreat" (*vanapattha*); this is a designation for dwellings situated in a forest formation. "Forest retreat" (*vanapattha*)...
This scriptural remainder includes the following: “‘Bhīsanaka’ (frightful) is a designation for this; ‘vanapattha’ (forest retreat) is a designation for that which causes the hair to stand on end;
‘vanapattha’ is a designation for that which is remote; ‘vanapattha’ is a designation for that which is not frequented by humans;
‘vanapattha’ is a designation for lodgings that are difficult to access. “Acchanna” (covered) means covered by anything whatsoever, even by a tree branch.
It was not covered. “Having driven out” means having expelled. “Resembling a mountain cave and a rock shelter” means resembling both a mountain cave (*pabbhāra*) and a rock shelter (*leṇa*).
Regarding “seeking almsfood,” by eliding the latter member of the compound, he says: “returned from seeking almsfood.
In the word *pallaṅka*, the prefix *pari-* has the sense of “on all sides”; therefore, [he sat cross-legged] with both the left thigh and the right thigh...
Having placed both feet evenly and joined them together, one sits; this is called *pallaṅka*.
It is said that *pallaṅka* is a sitting posture where the thighs are bound together on all sides. Regarding the term *ābhujitvā*:
it means having bent and folded both feet in such a way that the sitting is performed by means of the *pallaṅka* posture. Furthermore, those two...
Regarding the making of the connection between the feet, he says "having bound [them].

Since the placing of the lower body straight is already indicated by the word "sitting," he says "having placed the upper body straight" to show that here the word *kāya* refers to the upper part of the body. That...
However, in order to show the straightening [of the mind] according to its nature and its purpose, the words beginning with "eighteen" were spoken. "Do not bend" means they do not incline.
"Does not fall away" means it does not disappear; it does not overstep the proper course.
For that very reason, through the attainment of successive excellence, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) reaches growth, expansion, and abundance. Regarding the term *parimukha*: here—

The word *pari* has the same meaning as the word *abhi*; thus he says, "facing the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ*), which means having turned away from external, manifold objects and having placed the meditation subject itself before one.

Or, showing that the word *pari* has the sense of proximity, he says, "or having placed it near the mouth. And here, just as in such passages as "he resorts to a secluded lodging," etc., [the meaning is similar].
A dwelling place suitable for meditation has been shown; likewise, by the phrase "sits down," a mode of conduct that belongs to neither the side of sloth nor agitation is shown.
By the phrase "having folded his legs crosswise," the firmness of the sitting posture is shown;
by the phrase "having established mindfulness before him," the means of grasping the object is shown. *Pari* has the sense of grasping, as in such words as *pariṇāyikā* (a guide).
"Door" has the sense of an outlet, as in such passages as "the door of the void liberation. The sense of an outlet (niyyāna) indeed means emerging from the opposite [of defilements].

Therefore, "having made the outlet well-grasped" means having established mindfulness that is in every way free from confusion and has abandoned confusion—that is to say, having established supreme mindfulness and circumspection.
217. It is called *abhijjhā* because one covets (*abhijjhāyati*), hankers after (*gijjhati*), and longs for (*abhikaṅkhati*) by means of it;

thus, *abhijjhā* is greed. "In the sense of breaking" means in the sense of disintegrating; the meaning is "in the sense of disintegrating moment by moment. "By way of suppression" (*vikkhambhanavasena*):
here, suppression is non-arising and non-occurrence, not the thorough abandoning of opposites. And the phrase "because of being abandoned" refers to a state similar to what has been abandoned.

This was said with a hidden intention (*sandhāya*), because [the state of] jhāna has not yet been attained. Nevertheless, this mind is not free from covetousness by its very nature (*sabhāvato*) like eye-consciousness;
rather, it is so through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Therefore he said, "not similar to eye-consciousness. The same method applies here:
just as this mind is free from covetousness because it has been thoroughly cultivated by meditation, so too is it free from ill-will (*abyāpanna*).
The meaning is: free from sloth and torpor (thinamiddha), unagitated, and free from doubt. "The former natural state" refers to the state of being pure and bright.

It is said that "sloth is a sickness of the mind" and "torpor is a sickness of the mental factors," because sloth has been defined in the Abhidhamma by such passages as "that which is the unfitness of the mind," and torpor by "that which is the unfitness of the body."

It should be understood that the specific conditionality of the unwholesome states (*akalyatā*) and so forth of consciousness and mental factors— which, like the lightness of mind and body, are mutually inseparable—
toward their respective particular results according to karma, is their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Regarding the phrase "perceiving light" (*ālokasaññī*),
he says [the following] to show that this letter *ī* expresses the sense of existence as qualified by the sense of excellence (*atisaya*).

“Possessed of [these qualities] even at night…” and so forth—this refers to both mindfulness (*sati*) and clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). Having transcended and abandoned by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
“How is this?”—such a state of deliberation is doubt (*vicikicchā*). One who has that is a “doubter” (*kathaṅkathī*);

one who is not a doubter is “undoubting” (*akathaṅkathī*), meaning free from doubt. Regarding the phrase “by way of the distinction of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth,” here the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) includes—
The inclusion of the conditions for abandoning (*paccayapahāna*) and the abandoner (*pahāyaka*), etc., should also be understood;

for these too must be explained in detail. 218. "Of those" refers to wealth taken on account of a debt. "Remainder" (*pariyanta*) means the balance remaining to be paid. One obtains powerful gladness (*balavapāmojja*) thinking, "I am freed from the obstacle of debt. One attains joy (*somanassa*) thinking, "There is [wealth] for the sake of livelihood. 219.
"By the arising of a dissimilar feeling" means by the arising of a painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*). For a painful feeling is [the opposite] of a pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*).

They are "dissimilar" because they are opposed to the continuity of wholesome kamma-result (kusalavipāka). "Cutting off the four postures" means cutting off the occurrence of all four types of bodily posture;
for just as one who is afflicted by disease is incapable of standing or walking, so too is he incapable of sitting and the other postures.
"Afflicts" means oppresses. Disease (vyādhi) is a disorder or an abnormal state of the humors such as wind (vāta) and the rest.
He said: "Afflicted by the suffering arising from that. Regarding the state of illness as being painful feeling:

one is "sick" (*ābādhika*) in the sense of being afflicted by the primary disease at the outset; one is "afflicted" (*dukkhita*) in the sense of being tormented by the secondary disease, meaning suffering has arisen repeatedly.
"Sick" (*gilāna*) means one whose body is utterly exhausted through the depletion of the elements. "A little strength" (*appamattakaṃ balaṃ*) refers to a mere measure of strength.

"Both of those" refers to gladness (*pāmojja*) and joy (*somanassa*). In that regard, one may find gladness [thinking], "I am freed from disease," and one may attain joy [thinking], "There is strength in my body.
As for the remainder: "For when he adverts [to the thought], 'I am freed from bondage,' both of those arise. Therefore it was said."
And so forth. "In the manner already stated" means in the manner stated for the first and second sections. "In all sections" refers to the remaining sections, the third and so on. 221–222.

"Not dependent on oneself" means not subject to one's own will (*na attāyatta*). "Dependent on another" means subject to another. [The word] *bhuja* [is used here] because of the state of being independent of another.
One who must be sought for his own duties as if he were [free] is *bhujissa* (a free man). He said "belonging to oneself" (*sava-so*) to mean "one's own property.
Because there is no water, they cross the water (*kaṃ*) there; thus it is called a *kantāra*. He said "a long road without water" to explain this.
223. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that demonstration. "This" (*ayam*) refers to the similarity (*sadisatā*) now being described, by which the state of being a simile for debt and so forth occurs.
And since sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the rest serve as the objects of comparison, this relationship between the simile and the object compared should be understood as "similarity.
"Whoever is lustful through sensual desire for someone" means that a person who, by way of sensual desire, becomes impassioned toward another person who serves as the basis for sensual passion.
"He grasps that basis" means he grasps that basis of craving, thinking, "This is mine."
“Upaddavetha” means “you cause harm.
“Of the festival” (nakkhattassa) means of the great celebration. “Released” (mutto) means released from bondage.

“One who is ignorant of the disciplinary procedure” (vinaye apakataññū) refers to one who is unskilled in the sequence of the Vinaya; for such a person does not know what is permissible and what is impermissible as it truly is. Therefore, he said, “In some matter,” and so forth.
"He goes" means he goes little by little. But while going, because of that very state of being suspicious and apprehensive, he stops here and there.
In such a wilderness, thinking "Who knows what will happen?", he even turns back;
therefore, the places not gone over are more numerous than the places already gone over. This is a matter to be accepted through faith (*saddhā*).
He is unable to believe, thinking, "This is exactly so. As for "exists" or "does not exist," it means "Does it exist, or does it not exist?
"Crawling about" (*āsappana*) refers to the initial crawling of one who has entered the forest. "Crawling around" (*parisappana*) means crawling all around or crawling repeatedly.
By both terms, he speaks of wandering about right there. Therefore, he said, "without fathoming."
“Trembling” means the state of being terrified that has arisen due to the perception of a forest; the meaning is that they are afraid.
224. Herein, this “similarity” should be understood according to the method already stated:
for to the same extent that sensual desire and the rest are like a debt and so forth, to that same extent their abandonment is like freedom from debt and so forth, being their non-existence.

"Having made": [referring to] the six things, which are these six factors: the apprehension of the sign of foulness, devotion to the development of foulness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, friendship with the virtuous, and suitable talk. "Having developed": having increased.
We shall explain this in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* by way of the manifestation of the non-arising of what has not yet arisen and the abandoning of what has already arisen, and so forth.
It is specified because it has come down in the Pāḷi. This same method applies to the state of abandoning ill-will (*byāpāda*) and so forth.
"In another's object" means in another person who has become the objective support (*ārammaṇa*).
"One who causes harm" means one who brings about misfortune for oneself and for others. "Six things" refers to the grasping of the sign of loving-kindness (*mettā-nimitta*), and so on.

These six things are: devotion to the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*), the sense of being the owner of one’s own kamma (*kammassakatā*), abundance of reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhānabahulatā*), association with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamittatā*), and appropriate discourse (*sappāyakathā*).

"In that very place" means in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna [Sutta] itself. The "prescription of conduct" (*ācārapaṇṇatti*) refers to the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) formulated with reference to conduct (*cārittasīla*).
A man who, because he has been cast into prison, does not experience the joy of the festival night, [thinks]: "On the day of the festival, I am in prison..."
When it is said, “the man has entered,” this refers to one who has been treated in that way on the very day of the lunar mansion (nakkhatta) for the purpose of not experiencing that [pleasure].
“Causing great harm” means causing great disadvantage by way of the loss of benefits pertaining to the present life and so forth.
“The six things” refers to: not grasping at the signs of overeating, changing one’s posture, and attending to the perception of light.
These six things are: dwelling in the open air, having virtuous friends, and engaging in beneficial conversation.

Regarding "restlessness and worry cause great harm": they are said to cause great harm because, by making one dependent on others, they produce great misfortune according to the method already explained.
"The purpose is the six things" refers to: being well-versed in the scriptures, being inquisitive, knowing the rules of the Vinaya, and associating with the elders.
These six things are: having virtuous friends and appropriate conversation.
"Powerful" means powerful by virtue of the strength capable of crushing adversaries. "Equipped with weapons" means equipped with weapons such as a strung bow and so forth.
"With a retinue" refers to being accompanied by brave and heroic attendants. "Him"—that is, the person previously described—by virtue of his power and his being equipped with weapons.
And because he is accompanied by a retinue, the thieves would flee upon seeing him from afar.
"One who acts for harm" means one who creates obstacles to right practice; thus, as stated in the aforementioned method, they act for harm.

"Six qualities" refers to these six qualities: being learned, inquisitiveness, knowledge of what is established in the Vinaya, abundance of resolute conviction, having virtuous friends, and appropriate discourse.
Just as much learning and so forth lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse, so too here joy leads to the abandoning of doubt;

thus, much learning and the other factors are included here as well. Just as having good friends and appropriate talk are [the conditions] for the five [hindrances], therefore one should understand that they consist in cultivating what is suitable for each respective case.
By way of being the cause for the non-practice of right practice...
Since doubt nourishes only wrong practice, its abandonment is the means for shaking off misconduct;
thus he said, "having crossed the wilderness of misconduct," and so forth. 225.
*Pāmojja* (gladness) is fresh joy; it is a state of satisfaction in some way or another, hence he said, "gladness arises."
"An appearance of satisfaction arises. "Of one who is satisfied" means: of one who is satisfied by way of the rapture (*pīti*) that has reached the state of pervasion.
Rapture arises characterized by pervading the entire body, shaking it through its own expansive nature and the arising of sublime material forms originating from oneself.
"Accompanied by rapture" is [expressed as] *pīti* by the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*); what, then, is that? It is the mind (*mano*).
"Pītimano" means one whose mind has joy; thus it is "of that one with a joyful mind. Showing merely the sense of this, he said, "of a consciousness associated with joy.
Here, "body" (kāya) is intended as the immaterial aggregate (nāma-kalāpa), not just the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling; therefore he said, "the mental body (nāmakāya) becomes tranquil.
Here, the "tranquility" is intended in the sense of the two types of tranquility (passaddhi) characterized by joy. "Free from distress" (vigatadaratha).
Having abandoned the distress of defilements such as restlessness, he experiences mental happiness by means of the aforementioned preliminary development;
and because his body is touched by the sublime matter originated by that [mental happiness], he also experiences bodily happiness.
Thus it is said: "He experiences both bodily and mental happiness. By this [phrase], "he experiences happiness,"...
By what has been said. Because it has emerged from the side of defilement and belongs to the category of the first jhāna, it is [characterized] by the happiness of renunciation.
"Of one who is happy" means of one who possesses happiness.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the first jhāna.
226. By the phrase “the mind becomes concentrated,” the concentration of the mind is described both by way of access (upacāra) and by way of absorption (appanā).

This being so, one might ask: what is the purpose of the teaching beginning with “he, quite secluded from sensual pleasures”? To this he says: “He, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [as stated]... it is said.
Therein, “for the purpose of showing further distinctions” means for the purpose of showing the further distinctions to be attained, such as the first jhāna and those above it.
For indeed, without the attainment of access concentration (upacārasamādhi), it is not possible to attain the distinctions such as the first jhāna.

It should be understood that even in the attainment of the second jhāna and those following, a sequence of causes beginning with the arising of gladness (pāmojja) must be accepted, just as the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi) is required for the attainment of the second path and those following.
Regarding the phrase "by means of that concentration" (tassa samādhinā): "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated."
Thus, regarding that concentration which has been described by way of its general characteristics as having the characteristic of absorption (*appanā*):
"For the purpose of showing its divisions" means for the purpose of showing the divisions of the second jhāna and so forth, as well as the divisions of the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and so forth.

"Kara" is said to be the source of flowers because it is produced within the womb; the body born from the *kara* is the "body born of *kara*" (*karaja-kāya*), which is the support for that [concentration].
