It is a collection of material form consisting of the four continuities. Granted that the mental body (nāmakāya) also receives such assistance from the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion;
nevertheless, because of the statement beginning with “it moistens,” it is the material body (rūpakāya) that is intended here. Thus he says, “this body born of karma.
“Moistens” means it performs the act of moistening. And that [moistening] is performed upon the body born of karma by means of the rapture and pleasure consisting of jhāna.
“Temetī” and so forth are said because it brings about a state of moisture and removes dryness everywhere.
This moistening should be understood, in terms of its meaning, as the suffusion of the body by superior material forms arising from the aforementioned joy and happiness.
The same method applies to the terms “parisandetī” and so on. That which has all [these qualities] is “sabbavā. Of that...
“Entirely” (*sabbāvato*). In the case of a relationship between a part and a whole, the genitive case is used for the whole; thus, the word *sabba* refers to the whole.

Therefore, it is said: “possessing all parts. There is nothing that is not pervaded, because wherever there is kamma-born matter, there the mind-born matter completely permeates it. Hence he says: “the continuity of what is clung-to,” and so forth.
227. "Skilled" (*kusala*): His skill should be understood as the capacity for kneading and forming a lump of bath-powder;
thus he said, "capable," and so forth. The word *kaṃsa* occurs in reference to gold in such passages as "in a large bronze bowl" (*mahatiyā kaṃsapātiyā*).
In such passages as "just as a bronze vessel is struck," it refers to bell-metal (*kittimaloha*). In some instances, it is used merely as a designation, as in "King Upakaṃsa."
“...the son of Mahākaṃsa,” and so forth [as found in the commentary on the Ghaṭapaṇḍita Jātaka, 4.10, which is identical in meaning].
Here, however, regarding the phrase “any kind of metal,” he says: “in a vessel made from any metal whatsoever.
“Followed by moisture” means entered or approached by way of the moisture of water. “Overcome by moisture” means by the moisture of water...
“Pervaded” (*parito gatā*) means touched on all sides; thus, it is touched inside and out by the moisture.
By this, he expresses the state of being completely saturated with water. “And not dripping” (*na ca paggharaṇī*) indicates that even though it is soaked, it remains thick and solid.
Therefore, he says: “not drop by drop,” and so forth.
Commentary on the Second Jhāna (229).
It is called *ubbhida* because it breaks forth through various water-channels; that which has such breaking-forth water is *ubbhidodaka*.
"Breaking-forth water" (*ubbhinnaudaka*) refers to water that wells up like a well dug on a riverbank. "Rising water" (*uggacchanakaudaka*)...
"Water rising by means of a stream" refers to water that wells up. Why, then, is only a spring-fed lake (*ubbhidodaka*) mentioned here as a pond and not the other types?
He says: "Because the water rises from below," and so forth. "By the falling of streams and water bubbles" means by the falling of streams and by water bubbles;
the words "and by masses of foam" should also be supplied. "Merely still" means perfectly motionless due to the absence of agitation.
The intended meaning is "only very easily. "The rest" refers to the passage beginning with "he moistens," and so forth.
231. Regarding the commentary on the discussion of the third jhāna:
"Uppalāni" means "lotus groves. "Among white, red, and blue" refers to the lotuses; that is, among white lotuses, red lotuses, and blue lotuses.
The meaning is as follows: whatever is a blue lotus (*uppala*) is indeed a blue lotus, because of the inclusion of the general term.

Regarding the word *satapatta*, here the word *sata* is a synonym for "many," as in the expression *satagghī* ("worth a hundred") and so forth; by this, the inclusion of even those with many hundreds of petals is established.
Furthermore, in the world it is said that the red lotus is the *paduma* and the white one is the *puṇḍarīka*. [This applies] from the tip down to the root.
The mention of "not emerging from the water" is for the purpose of showing the occurrence of being drenched by water and so forth.
Here, the physical body made of kamma is like the blue lotuses and others, while the bliss of the third jhāna is like the water.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Fourth Jhāna:

233. Since the phrase "with a pure mind" refers to the consciousness of the fourth jhāna, and that consciousness is stainless and immaculate due to the departure of defilements such as lust, he therefore said: "It is 'pure' in the sense of being free from defilement.

Furthermore, since it is precisely through the specific condition of purification (*pārisuddhi*) that there is a specific mode of occurrence characterized by brightness—just as gold becomes bright through polishing—he said...
Just as there is luminosity, therefore he said: "It should be understood as 'purified' in the sense of being luminous. "This" refers to the word "white.
"For the purpose of showing the pervasion of the heat-element" means for the purpose of demonstrating the pervading of the warm temperature.
The intention is that the pervasion of the temperature is not particularly distinct [at other times]; therefore he said: "At that moment... it becomes powerful. "The physical body is like a cloth."
The body born of the kamma of the yogi should be regarded as like a garment, because it is to be suffused by the bliss of the fourth jhāna, which is similar to the spreading of heat.
The fourth jhāna should be regarded as like a person’s body, because it serves as the basis for the bliss that takes the place of the spreading of heat.
Therefore he said, “Therefore,” and so forth. And here, the phrase “with a pure mind” refers to the mind...
It should be understood that the bliss of jhāna is spoken of by way of its grasping; hence he said, “The bliss of the fourth jhāna is like the pervading of the weather.
But is it not the case that there is no bliss at all in the fourth jhāna? True, there is none.
However, because equanimity here has the characteristic of being pleasant and the nature of peace, it is intended as “bliss. Therefore, it is stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*: “But equanimity...”
“Being heated, it is spoken of as ‘pleasure’ alone.
One should not understand [the phrase] “not an attainer of formless-jhāna” as being invariably concomitant; therefore he said, “for not,” and so forth. Therein, “by way of fourteen modes” means:
by way of the forward order of the kasiṇas, the reverse order of the kasiṇas, the forward and reverse order of the kasiṇas, the forward order of the jhānas, and the reverse order of the jhānas.
By way of these fourteen modes: by way of the direct and reverse order of the jhānas; by way of skipping jhānas; by way of skipping kasiṇas; by way of skipping both jhānas and kasiṇas;
by way of shifting factors (aṅga); by way of shifting objects (ārammaṇa); by way of shifting both factors and objects; by way of defining the factors; and by way of defining the objects.
Although mastery over adverting and so forth exists within the jhānas, this specific mastery is for the purpose of producing the supernormal powers (abhiññā).
Showing that [this] must be desired exclusively, he said: "For... [pe] ... it does not exist. This method is not accomplished without the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*);
therefore, their inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) should be understood here as well. If this is so, why are the formless meditations (*ārūpyajhāna*) not mentioned in the Pāḷi?
Specifically, because all direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) have the fourth meditation of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) as their basis, they are included therein.
Having done so, they were taught by her; however, the immaterial-sphere jhānas are not included here because they are of no use in this context. Therefore he said:
"The immaterial-sphere jhānas should be brought in and explained.
*Commentary on the Discussion of Insight-Knowledge* (Vipassanāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā)
234. It should be stated in such passages as, "When the mind is thus concentrated," and so forth. That which knows the knowable is *ñāṇa* (knowledge);
furthermore, because it sees that knowable by making it directly present (*paccakkha*), it is *dassana* (vision). Thus, knowledge itself is vision, which is *ñāṇadassana*.
This term *ñāṇadassana* is established elsewhere in the Dispensation (*sāsana*) for specific types of knowledge; all of that [is included] here by way of enumerating the meanings.
He said, “‘Knowledge and vision’ is also called path-knowledge,” and so forth.

Because insight-knowledge knows the conditioned phenomena of the three planes as impermanent and so on, and from the stage of contemplation of dissolution onwards, it sees them directly, he therefore said:
“But here... ‘knowledge and vision’ is what is meant.”
"He brings forth" means that, according to the method already stated, he directs [the mind] toward insight when that eightfold-constituted consciousness has arisen through the sequence of insight;
therefore it is said: "insight... makes [it so]. For its state of being directed toward that [insight] is precisely what constitutes its quality of inclining toward it and so forth.
This has indeed been stated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. It is called "an accumulation of rice and gruel" because it is built up by means of rice and gruel.
“Subject to impermanence” means having an unstable nature due to its liability to break up. “For the sake of removing bad odors” means for the removal of foul smells from the body.

“Subject to rubbing” means having a nature that requires being rubbed; for by means of rubbing, there occurs the disappearance of the sweat, feces, bile, phlegm, and other disturbances of the bodily elements, as well as heaviness and foul odors in the body.
Since vigorous massage is for the purpose of increasing the strength of the arms and so forth in wrestlers and others, [the text specifies] “by means of light massage.”
It has been said. "Subject to being rubbed" means its essential nature is that of being rubbable.
"It breaks up and is scattered" means it breaks up by way of impermanence, and having broken up, it becomes something that fails to accomplish any purpose and is dispersed.
"Possessing form" (rūpī) means possessing form (rūpa) by way of the temperature and nutriment that serve as its own conditions; this is the intended meaning here.
He said: "The origin is stated by six terms. For this vowel *ī* occurs in the sense of conjunction (*saṃsagge*).
Since the production of shape also occurs through the arising of such-and-such matter, it is said that the origin is also stated by the terms "smearing" and "rubbing.

Thus, the contemplation of the phenomena of origination and dissolution in the body as appropriate has been shown by means of nine terms. And it is "dependent" because it is dependent upon the sixth base (the mind).

[It is so called] because it is bound up with insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*), because it does not function without that [knowledge], and because it takes as its object those material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) designated as "body. 235.
It is "beautiful" (*subha*) because it shines forth clearly; he says "beautiful" because the gem is auspicious even by virtue of its excellence of radiance.
"Beautiful. Even the primary distinction of the Kuruvinda species of gem is rooted in the purity of its source;
thus he said, "arisen from a pure mine. The perfection of the preparatory work is achieved through the removal of defects;
thus he said, "well-prepared, with stones and grit removed. Its translucence is due to the smoothness of its surface, not because of its mass.
He said, "It is clear, with a smooth luster"; therefore he said, "it is translucent.
By "washing, piercing, and so forth" is meant washing on four stones and piercing with a thread for the purpose of removing black specks and the like.
The word "and so forth" includes heating, smoothing, and other such processes. "Perfection of color" refers to the perfection of the thread's color. The physical body is like a gem.
Because it is to be reviewed. Because it remains having entered into insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) like a thread woven through [cloth].
Like a man with sight, a bhikkhu who has attained insight sees correctly. "Having those as their object" means having material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) as their object.
By the inclusion of the mind and mental factors with contact as the fifth, the phenomena grasped are also included within the arising of the insight-consciousness.

Thus it should be understood. For in this way, because they fall within the scope of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), the statement that "insight-knowledge is like a thread strung through [them]" is not contradicted.

But are these manifested to knowledge, or rather to the person? To knowledge. And because they are manifested to that [knowledge], they are said to be manifested to the person. And "to knowledge" means to the knowledge of reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa*).

The knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) should be mentioned after the mundane superknowledges (lokīyābhiññā) and before the sixth superknowledge, immediately following the knowledge of the path (maggañāṇa).
Even though this is so— meaning, even though this is the sequence of knowledges— even so,

there is no room for it [to be inserted] in between when the five mundane superknowledges have been discussed, as in the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta* and other such texts, where the sixth superknowledge [is mentioned directly].
Regarding the phrase "should be told": there is no opportunity for that insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), which has the characteristic of non-penetration, to intervene between those [attainments].
Therefore, because there is no occasion for it there, the insight-knowledge is shown here specifically immediately after the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
And as for the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "yasmā ca" (and because): it has the sense of conjunction; thus, it indicates that not only is that [previous reason] so, but this is also a reason.
This explains that the vision of insight-knowledge occurs right here [in this very life]. Regarding the statement, "one sees even a terrifying form with the divine eye," it should also be said:
"having fashioned a terrifying form by means of the knowledge of supernormal powers (iddhividhañāṇa), one sees it with the eye.
Even so, fear and terror arise in one who has attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) but has not fully understood the basis [of phenomena].
As in the case of the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt at Uccāvālika, there is a distinct fruit of recluseship that is directly visible. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“When one discerns, again and again, The arising and passing away of the aggregates, One finds rapture and gladness— That is the deathless for one who knows,” and so forth.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of the Mind-made Power (Manomayiddhiñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 236–7.

"Produced by mind" means produced by the mind of direct knowledge (abhiññā). "By limbs such as hands and feet" refers to the major limbs (aṅga), and "by minor parts such as knees and shanks" refers to the minor limbs (paccanga).
"By way of shape" means merely by way of a shape resembling a lotus petal and so forth, not by way of the sensitive matter (pasāda-rūpa) or the primary elements capable of receiving physical impact.

"In all aspects" means in all aspects such as color, shape, specific parts, and so forth. "By that possessor of psychic power" means precisely for the purpose of demonstrating similarity—namely, for the purpose of demonstrating similarity in shape, in color, and in specific parts.
"Standing among his own kind" means he does not take on a form of a different species through the psychic power of a nāga.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of the Supernormal Powers, etc. (239). Just as well-prepared clay and so forth serve as a basis for the work of a potter, so too does the knowledge of the supernormal powers serve as a basis for the act of transformation.
(241). "Easily" means without difficulty, without exertion.
243. Since even a dull-witted infant lying on its back is called "young" (*dahara*), the term "youth" (*yuvā*) is stated for the purpose of distinguishing him from such.
Since even some youths may be lacking in desire and unadorned by nature, the phrase "of an ornamental disposition" (*maṇḍanajātiko*) and so forth is stated for the purpose of further distinction;
thus he says, "even though he is a youth," and so on. "Black sesame-sized spots" refers to *kāḷatilakāni*, which are either black or dark-brown specks.
"Spots" (*tilakāni*) are drops the size of sesame seeds. "Vaṅga" refers to a deformity. "Youthful pimples" (*yobbanapīḷakā*) and so forth are pimples that defile the face.

"Facial blemish" (*mukhadoso*) refers to a defect located on the face; this is a term used figuratively (*lakkhaṇavacana*), because it is intended to include even the absence of defects when they are clearly visible on the face.

Alternatively, just as a defect on the face is called a "facial blemish," so too the absence of defects on the face is called a "facial blemish" by means of the elision of the initial syllable (*saralopa*). Thus, both "facial blemish" and "absence of facial blemish" are termed *mukhadoso*.
And here the meaning should be understood according to the method of single remainder (*ekasesanaya*) as "the fault of the mouth.
For it is in this way that the statement, "The sixteenfold consciousness of others becomes manifest," is justified.
245. "By the simile for the knowledge of past lives" means by the simile shown for the knowledge of past lives. The action performed on that day...
The mention of "that very day" was made in order to show that [the deeds] are generally manifest even to an ordinary being.
By the mention of the three villages visited on that day, it should be understood that through the great resolves (mahābhinīhāra),
the deeds performed by others who have attained the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa) in the three realms of existence are likewise generally manifest.
247. "Moving from one to another" means moving here and there according to various functions.
The physical body of the bhikkhu should be regarded as being like the aforementioned palace, because for one established therein, the vision of what is to be seen is accomplished.
For one with eyes, the attainment of the divine eye occurs; as it is said: "The arising of the fleshly eye is the path to the divine eye."
This should be understood in this way: the bhikkhu who has attained the divine eye is like a man with sight, because he sees what is to be seen.
"Entering" means entering this house of the personal existence (*attabhāva*); the meaning is, being reborn. "Departing from the house" means having gone out from this house of the personal existence;
the meaning is, passing away. Or rather, the meaning here should be understood in this manner.
"Beings wandering from one state to another" refers to beings who are revolving repeatedly in *saṃsāra*.
However, by the phrase "beings reborn here and there," he speaks of those beings who have been born and raised within that particular existence (*bhava*).

Now, since this is a discourse on the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), why is there an inclusion of the fourfold existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*) here by saying "in the three existences"?
To the question "Which?", he said: "And this," and so forth. Therein, "this" refers to the statement: "of the beings reborn in the three realms of existence.
The phrase "merely for the sake of ease of teaching" means solely for the sake of making the teaching easy to understand;

it is not because the divine eye is absent in beings reborn in the four-aggregate realm of existence (the formless realm). For it has not been said, "excluding the formless realm," or "in two realms of existence."
Or, when it is so stated, the teaching becomes easy to understand.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse on the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa). 248.
"The basis for insight" means that which serves as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for insight. And insight is threefold, according to the distinction between the individuals who possess it.

For the insight of the Great Bodhisattvas and the Pacceka-bodhisattvas is developed through knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya-ñāṇa*) and becomes self-originated knowledge (*sayambhu-ñāṇa*);
for others, however, it is developed through knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*) and is said to arise from the instruction of others.

This [insight] is described in many ways, such as: "Having emerged from one or another of the remaining fine-material and immaterial jhānas, excepting the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," and so forth; and in the analysis of the four elements by way of the formless [meditations].
These have been explained in many ways through various methods in the *Visuddhimagga* by means of one or another of the aforementioned approaches for discerning the elements (*dhātu*).
However, for the Great Bodhisattvas, because it proceeds through twenty-four quadrillion methods,
this [knowledge] constitutes the embryo of preliminary knowledge— the foundation for the noble path-knowledge that is the support of omniscience— and thus possesses manifold methods.
As one grasps [the objects], there arises the insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) that is fully matured, proceeding, supremely profound, exceedingly subtle, and not shared by others;
this is what is called "the Great Vajira-knowledge" (*mahāvajirañāṇa*) in the commentaries.

And by means of its function as a basis for the twenty-four hundred thousand millionfold divisions according to the analysis of their occurrence, the number [of attainments] reached is likewise twenty-four hundred thousand million.
The meditative attainments (samāpatti) employed by the Teacher on a daily basis are what are being referred to here;
this practice of insight (vipassanā) of the Buddhas has been shown in brief in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*, titled *Paramatthamañjūsā*. Those who desire it should take that [work] as their source;
however, in this context, the insight intended is that of the disciples (sāvaka).
"Knowledge for the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya*): because it exhausts and utterly cuts off the taints, it is the "destruction of the taints," which is the Noble Path.
Knowledge regarding that [path] is "knowledge of the destruction of the taints. For the sake of that, he said: "for the purpose of producing knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
Alternatively, the "destruction of the taints" is Nibbāna, wherein the taints are exhausted; "destruction" (*khayo*) is the Path, because it exhausts unwholesome states.

However, since the destruction of evil does not exist without the destruction of the taints (*āsava*), it is said that by the mention of "destruction" in the phrase "knowledge of destruction," the destruction of the taints is intended; thus he says, "knowledge of destruction," and so forth.

Considering one who has stilled evil to be a *samaṇa*, he says, "One becomes a *samaṇa* through the destruction of the taints"; herein, the fruit [of the path] is indicated. Regarding the increase of the taints...

Increasing formations, one is very far indeed from the state of non-formations; thus, regarding the phrase "far from the destruction of the taints" (*ārā so āsavakkhayā*), he says, "In this context, the term 'destruction of the taints' is a designation for non-formations," meaning that "nibbāna is what is spoken of here as the destruction of the taints.
The construction is: "destruction" (*bhaṅgo*) refers to the momentary cessation of the taints, which is expressed by the phrase "the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khayo*).
“This is suffering”: this shows that the noble truth of suffering was then grasped by the bhikkhu through direct perception.
“So much is suffering”: this shows that it was grasped by him with its limits clearly defined. “There is nothing more than this”: this shows that it was grasped by him without remainder.
Therefore he said, “The entire truth of suffering,” and so forth. “By penetration of its specific characteristic” means...
It is called "penetration by non-delusion" because of the penetration through non-delusion regarding the characteristic known as intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

It functions in such a way that once that knowledge has occurred, there is no longer any delusion in the subsequent discernment of the true nature, characteristics, and so forth, of the truth of suffering;
thus he said, "he understands it as it really is. That from which suffering arises is the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudaya*).

He said "craving" (taṇhā) [and] "of that" (tassa ca), and so forth. "Having reached which state" means having approached that Nibbāna which, in the sense of being an object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), serves as the cause for the Path.
And the word "having reached" (patvā) is stated by treating the attainment of that person who possesses both [the Path and its fruit] as if it were the attainment of those two themselves.
Alternatively, "having reached" (patvā) refers to the cause of reaching. "Non-occurrence" (appavatti) means the cause for non-occurrence, or those two...
It is called "non-occurrence" (*appavatti*) because nothing occurs therein; it is *nibbāna*. "Of that" refers to the cessation of suffering.
"Leading to the wholesome" means that by way of realization, it is truly wholesome.
"By way of defilements" means by way of the defilements known as the taints (*āsava*). Since the taints are a synonym for the truth of suffering, because they are included within that [truth].
The other truths also possess their own respective modes of exposition regarding their origin and so forth; therefore, it is said, "by way of a mode" (*pariyāyato*).

The construction is: "showing [this], [he speaks of] the truths. And here, only the taints (*āsava*) are taken up, because the discourse has commenced with the words, "for the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.

For indeed, by means of the liberation from the taints as its primary heading—as in the passage, "the mind is liberated even from the taint of sensual desire"—there is liberation from all defilements.
It has been stated: "He understands as it really is, 'This is suffering,'" and so forth; thus, the mixed path is explained here.

Therefore, it is said that "he spoke of the path that has reached its culmination together with insight. By the phrase "of one who knows and sees," the clear realizations (abhisamaya) of full understanding, realization, and development are expressed.
By the phrase "he is liberated," the clear realization of abandonment is expressed; hence he says, "By this, he shows the moment of the path."

“Of one who knows and sees”: this is a statement of the cause (*hetu-niddesa*). The construction is: “By reason of knowing and by reason of seeing, the mind is liberated even from the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*).
For even among phenomena that are simultaneous, the relationship of condition and conditioned can be obtained in the sense of co-nascence (*sahajāta*).

And here, by the inclusion of the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), both the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*)—just like craving for existence (*bhavarāga*)—is likewise encompassed; thus, there is also the inclusion of the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*).
The inclusion is to be seen by means of the phrases beginning with "Birth is destroyed. "Of that" refers to the knowledge of reviewing. "Ground" means the sphere of occurrence.
Expounding the intention behind the objection raised in the passage beginning with "But what of it?", he says: "Not yet, for him... and so forth.
Therein, the intention is that "birth of the past has not yet been destroyed for him by the cultivation of the Path. He states the reason for this:
“Because it has already been exhausted previously. The construction is: “His future birth is not [merely] exhausted.
He objects by way of a figurative interpretation, grasping the commonality of the state of being “future,” saying: “Because there is no effort regarding the future.

However, what is intended here is a specific kind of future [birth], and regarding its exhaustion, effort is indeed possible; therefore he says: “But as for that of the Path,” and so forth. “In the one-, four-, and five-aggregate existences.”

The inclusion of the three states of existence is for the purpose of showing, according to the method already stated, that birth has been exhausted without remainder. "That" refers to the aforementioned birth.
"He" refers to the bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted.
He says that "dwelling in the holy life" (brahmacariyavāsa), by way of the highest description, is precisely the production of the holy life of the Path.

“Parivuttha” means: while right view is active by way of accomplishing the tasks such as full understanding (*pariññā*) regarding the four truths, the activity of right intention and the others is likewise in accordance with the realization of full understanding regarding the truth of suffering;
furthermore, their activity regarding the other truths—such as the realization of abandonment (*pahāna*)—is indeed evident. Therefore it is said: “In the four truths, by means of the four paths...”

“By way of full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development. Regarding the paths of the cessation of suffering and the path itself, full understanding, realization, and development are for the sole purpose of abandoning the origin;
thus he said, “the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path have been abandoned.
“Itthattāya” means: these modes are *itthaṃ*; the state of being that is *itthattaṃ*; the meaning is “for the sake of that,” so it is said. And those...
The factors beginning with full understanding (*pariññā*), which constitute the functions of the Noble Path, are intended here; thus he says, "Thus, because of the state of having sixteen functions.
For these [functions] become manifest and present to one who reviews the Path through the power of the Path.

Furthermore, among full understanding and the others, abandonment (*pahāna*) alone is primary, since the others exist for its sake; thus he says, "or because of the state of the destruction of defilements. This is by way of reviewing the defilements that have been abandoned.

Or rather, it is stated thus. In the second interpretation, regarding the phrase *itthattāya*, he says "from this state of being" (*itthabhāvato*), because it is an accusative of attainment used in the sense of the ablative.
"The other" refers to the future. However, these five aggregates, designated as the final existence (*carimaka-kattabhāva*), remain once they have been fully understood (*pariññāta*);
by this, he shows their lack of a foundation (*appatiṭṭha*). For a foundation is rooted in non-understanding (*apariññā*). As it is said: "In the case of physical nutriment..."
“Monks, in regard to this nutriment, there is lust, there is delight, there is craving; therein consciousness is established and has grown,” and so forth.
For this very reason he said, “like trees whose roots have been cut,” and so on. 249.
“On the mountain peak” means on the summit of a mountain. For that [place] is for the most part narrow and constricted.
In the Pāli text, it is said: “in a mountain cleft. Alternatively, a region encompassed by a mountain is a “mountain cleft.
“Untroubled” means not turbid at the wrong time; and since this lack of turbidity occurs due to the absence of mud, he says “free from mud.
“Sippiya” means a shell. “Sambuka” means a bivalve shell. [This applies] whether the cows are standing or sitting. “While they were present” means...
When the others are available, even those that are standing or sitting are called "moving" by way of their common mode of movement.
It refers specifically to what is standing, and never to what is moving. "The pair" means both the oyster shells and the schools of fish.
The phrase "standing" implies that they are also moving. And the phrase "the other pair" refers to the same pair previously mentioned, namely the oyster shells and so forth.
It says: "For he practices that. Or rather, what is the use of this "practicing together"? Here, it should be understood as taking [the state] according to what is obtained.
For by way of pebbles and gravel, they are said to "stand"; likewise, by way of oysters and shoals of fish, even though they "stand," the construction should be made as "they move" (*carantaṃ pīti*).
Of those ten knowledges. "Therein" means in that analysis of objects, or among those knowledges.
Insight-knowledge has a sevenfold object by way of distinction of plane, distinction of time, and distinction of continuity.
The phrase "only the sense-sphere of visible form" is said because that knowledge proceeds by taking only the sense-sphere of visible form as its object when the mind-made body is being manifested.
It is stated [as such], because there is no absence of odors, bases, and so forth therein. Indeed, there is no aggregate of material form that is devoid of odor, base, and the rest.
Created matter (*nimmitarūpa*) is exclusively fully accomplished (*pariniṭṭhanna*); therefore, he said, "having a limited, present, and external object.

Although the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) has Nibbāna as its object, it is classified as having an immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇa*) by way of the category of the immeasurable (*appamāṇattika*).
Because it has an external object by way of the internal triad, and an indeterminable object by way of the past triad, he said, "immeasurable, external, and indeterminable object.
He said, "by the pinnacle of Arahantship," because Arahantship is the supreme limb of the Blessed One’s teaching, just as the roof-peak is the supreme part of a gabled house.
He brought the teaching to its conclusion—that which reveals the essence of the doctrines of the heretical teachers.
He brought his teaching to completion— a teaching that destroys various kinds of wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy and flattery,
adorned with the threefold morality, illuminating the practice of supreme austerity, embellished with superhuman qualities such as meditative absorption and direct knowledge,
and graced by the fourteen great fruits of recluseship, which are not shared by others.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Declaration of Upāsaka-hood by Ajātasattu:
250. "Beginning, middle, and end" means the beginning, the middle, and the end. "Carefully" means with reverence. It was undertaken by the compilers of the Dhamma.
He said, "It is seen in the sense of destruction," because the meaning is "passed away" or "vanished. For instance, it is said: "The first watch has passed."
This has been stated above. "More excellent" (*abhikkantataro*) means exceedingly desirable and delightful; such a one is beautiful and auspicious, hence it is said, "it is seen in what is beautiful.
"Who? (*ko*) means which one among the gods, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so forth. "Me" (*me*) means my. "Feet" (*pādāni*) means the feet.
"By means of psychic power" (*iddhiyā*) means by means of this kind of divine majesty. "By means of glory" (*yasasā*) means by means of such [glory].
"Accompanied by a retinue and attendants. "Shining and radiant": [this means] with a complexion that is exceedingly lovely, desirable, and beautiful.
"By complexion" means by the color of the skin, the luster of the body.
"Illuminating all directions" means shining upon the ten directions like the moon and like the sun, creating a single radiance and a single light; such is the meaning of the verse.
*Abhirūpa* means having a sublime form or a perfected form.
In expressions such as "thief, thief! or "snake, snake!", it is a reduplication used for fear; in "pierce, pierce! or "strike, strike!", it is used for anger;
in "well done, well done!", it is used for praise; and in "go, go! or "reap, reap!", it is used for haste.

In expressions such as “Come, come,” it signifies curiosity; in “Thinking ‘Buddha, Buddha,’” it signifies wonder; in “Come forward, venerable sirs, come forward, venerable sirs,” it signifies laughter;
in “Where is my only son, where is my only son,” it signifies sorrow;

and in “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! it signifies confidence. The particle *ca* has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*avuttasamuccaya*), by which [it includes] censure, disrespect, and so forth.

The inclusion [of these terms] should be understood. Therein, in expressions such as "wicked, wicked," it should be seen as censure; in expressions such as "handsome, handsome," it should be seen as disrespect.
Showing that this is not stated twice by way of repetition (*āmeḍita*), but rather by way of two distinct meanings, he says: "Then..."
He spoke the words beginning with “or,” and this was stated in the neuter gender in reference to the word “excellent” (*abhikkanta*).
However, that speech of the Blessed One was so stated because it is considered the teaching of the Dhamma. Alternatively, this is merely a demonstration of the meaning;
therefore, one should understand that here there is a transformation of gender and case-ending according to the sense. The same applies to the second phrase as well.
This is the method (*naya*). "By the destruction of faults" means by the dispelling of defilements such as lust (*rāga*).

"By the attainment of virtues" means by the accomplishment of virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*). Since those virtues which the teaching brings about must be shown, and among them the primary ones should be indicated, it is said:
"by generating faith (*saddhā*) and by generating wisdom (*paññā*). For mundane virtues have faith as their foremost, while [supramundane virtues] have wisdom as their foremost.

It is supramundane. It is "meaningful" because of its accomplishment of the eightfold purpose beginning with virtue. It is "well-phrased" because of its accomplishment of the intrinsic nature and etymological derivation.
It is "clear in expression" because of the employment of easily understood words. It is "profound in meaning" because its meaning is difficult to discern due to its subtle and delicate nature.
It is "pleasant to the ear" because of the employment of words that are smooth, soft, and sweet. It is "heart-stirring" because its meaning is vast, pure, and lovely.
It is free from self-exaltation through the dispelling of pride and arrogance; it is free from disparaging others through the crushing of stubbornness and provocation;

it is cool with compassion through its operation with the intention of welfare and by allaying the fever of passion and other defilements in others; it is bright with wisdom through the dispelling of the darkness of the afflictions;
it is delightful to the senses through its sweetness like the song of the cuckoo; and it is perfectly pure through its lack of contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

Because it is capable of withstanding scrutiny; because it is pleasant to hear precisely due to its aesthetic appeal; and because it is beneficial when investigated due to its capacity to withstand scrutiny and because it proceeds from an inclination toward what is wholesome.
By the phrase "and so forth," the word "etc. includes: the turning back of the wheel of saṃsāra and the setting in motion of the wheel of the True Dhamma;
the destruction of false doctrines and the establishment of right doctrine; and the uprooting of the roots of unwholesomeness and the planting of the roots of wholesomeness.

The inclusion of such [phrases] as "by closing the door to the states of misery," "by opening the door to the path to heaven," "by the pacification of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*)," and "by the uprooting of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*)" should be understood.
"Placed face downwards" means placed face downwards by someone; "naturally facing downwards" means [facing downwards] by its very nature.

"Born. "He should uncover" means he should open it. Without saying, "Take my hand and go facing east or facing north," and so forth, but rather taking the hand and making [the path] free from doubt, he should show it, saying, "This is the way; go thus.
"The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight" means the fourteenth day of the dark half of the month. "Upside down" means that which has no support for what is placed upon it.

One should turn the vessel upright by way of causing it to assume its supporting state. Because ignorance faces [the truth], it is "turned away from the True Dhamma" (*saddhamma-vimukha*) due to being produced with its mouth facing downward;

and because it is placed face-down, it has "fallen into the non-True Dhamma" (*asaddhamme patita*). Thus, these two phrases should be applied according to their respective meanings, not according to their numerical order.
Granted, sensual desire and the other hindrances are concealers by virtue of their nature as *nīvaraṇa* (hindrances).
But wrong view is especially a concealer, because it causes beings to adhere to what is false; thus he said, “concealed by the thicket of wrong view.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, I declare that wrong view is the supreme fault.

This is because the entire path leading to the states of misery is a "bad path" (kummagga), in the sense that it is a contemptible path. Wrong view and the others are so called because they are the direct opposites of right view and the rest.

The eight states of wrongness are the wrong paths. For it is precisely with reference to their being the opposites of both [the right path and its fruit] that it was said: "by one who reveals the path to heaven and liberation.
A lamp dependent on ghee and so forth is not as bright as one dependent on oil; hence the mention of an "oil-lamp.
"By these modes" means by these various types of similes to be illustrated, such as those of turning upside-down back upright, uncovering what is hidden, and so forth.
Or rather, by these aforementioned various modes of explaining wrong livelihood, such as hypocrisy, flattery, and so forth, as well as the manifold mental diversions and the like.
Therefore he said: “The Dhamma has been proclaimed in many ways.
“An act of faith” means the honor that should be performed by those who have faith. “Refuge” means a resort; therefore he said: “the ultimate resort.”
The state of being a refuge arises through the prevention of what is harmful and the accomplishment of what is beneficial; thus he said, "Protector from evil (agha) and provider of welfare.
Regarding "from evil" (aghasmā), they say it means "from suffering," but the meaning "from evil" is more appropriate;
furthermore, this is the genitive case used in the sense of the ablative. And here, this word *gama* is not transitive with two objects like the word *nī* and others.
Therefore, just as one says, "He leads the goat to the village," it is not possible to say, "I go to the Blessed One for refuge";
rather, one should say, "I go [to what is] refuge. Here, the word *iti* is indicated as being elided.
Its meaning is this: showing that "going" means adhering to or knowing with that same intention, he says, "By this..."
He said, beginning with "with the intention," and so forth. Therein, in the phrases "I resort to" and so on, each subsequent term is an explanation of the meaning of each preceding one:
"resorting" (*bhajana*) is approaching with the intention of seeking refuge; "serving" (*sevana*) is remaining in his presence;
"honoring" (*payirupāsana*) is attending upon him by performing duties and services. Thus, in every respect, it is precisely the state of having no other refuge that is meant.
He illuminates [the meaning]. To the question, "How is the meaning 'I understand' obtained for the word 'I go'?", he says, "For those who...

and so forth. By the two phrases "those who have attained the path" and "those who have realized cessation," only those established in the fruit (phalaṭṭhā) are shown, not those established in the path (maggaṭṭhā).
Showing this, he says, "And for those practicing according to the instruction," and so forth. But is it not the case that even a noble worldling (kalyāṇaputhujjana) [is included]?

Is it said that "he practices according to the instruction"? Although it is so said, in the ultimate sense (*nippariyāyena*), only those established on the path (*maggaṭṭha*) should be described in that way, and not the other, because the latter lacks entry into the fixed course of rightness (*niyāmokkama*).
For it is they alone who have been stated [in the scriptures] as "sustaining one from falling into the states of misery" (*apāyesu apatamāne dhāreti*).
Indeed, through the entry into the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāmokkama*), there arises the possibility of being exempted from the states of misery. It is thus declared.
Here, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*) or the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*);

by this, it includes the Sutta passage: "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost among them," or [it is included] by the word "in detail" (*vitthāra*).
And here, the Noble Path is [foremost] because of its nature as a means of deliverance (*niyyānikatā*), while Nibbāna is [foremost] because it is the cause for the accomplishment of that purpose.
Both are indeed called "Dhamma" in the non-figurative sense. For it is by obtaining Nibbāna as its object-condition that the Noble Path achieves its purpose.

Nevertheless, because the Noble Fruits possess the function of pacifying and abandoning the defilements already eradicated by the Path—due to their being conducive to deliverance—as stated in such passages as, "By that faith which has not yet been stilled," and so forth; [they are also called Dhamma].
And because it culminates in deliverance (*niyyāna*), the status of being the Dhamma is indeed obtained for the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*) by this method of explanation:
"because it is the cause for the attainment of the Dhamma that leads to deliverance. Showing that this matter is actually established in the text, he says "not only," and so forth.
“Lust for sensual pleasures and lust for existence”—all such classifications of lust are called *rāgavirāga* (the fading away of lust) because by means of this [path], lust is made to fade away;

thus the path is described. Because craving—which is reckoned as *ejā* (agitation)—and sorrow, which is characterized by inward brooding, have been completely exhausted at the time of its arising, the fruit is described as *aneja* (unagitated) and *asoka* (sorrowless). It is called *appaṭikūla* (not repulsive) because it demonstrates non-opposition.

The meaning is that it is not contradicted by anything, or that it is desired and sublime (*paṇīta*). It is "familiar" (*paguṇa*) because it has proceeded in a familiar form, or because it manifests distinguished qualities (*pakaṭṭhaguṇa*).
As it is said: "Perceiving harm, O Brahmā, I did not speak what is familiar, the sublime Dhamma among men.
The construction is: "all the aggregates of Dhamma have been told."

“By way of view and virtue”: by the view described thus, “Whatever noble view is emancipating and leads the one who acts upon it to the complete destruction of suffering—one dwells having attained conformity with such a view”;
and by those virtues which are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, and unadhered-to.
And by the state of being unified of those virtues spoken of as "conducive to concentration," [he] dwells having attained commonality of virtue with such [beings];
the meaning is: through the commonality of both view and virtue. "Unified" (saṃhata) means joined together; the meaning is "harmonized.
For noble persons, even when standing far apart anywhere, are unified by the harmony of their own qualities.
Thus. And "eight seers of the Dhamma among persons": by way of the pairs of persons, these four become eight;
they are "seers of the Dhamma" because of their direct vision of the Noble Dhamma. "Three goings for refuge":
by virtue of going with the thought "I take refuge," and by virtue of going three times, there are three goings for refuge. "He declared": he made known what was in his heart by means of speech.
The commentary on the discourse on going for refuge states: "In order to achieve proficiency regarding the goings for refuge, the refuge... [etc. ...should be understood;

for proficiency therein arises from the analysis of the refuge, its objects, its classifications, its fruits, its defilements, and its divisions, as well as from the analysis of the one who goes for refuge. Thus it was said.
Because it is impossible [to practice] without going for refuge itself. But why is purification (*vodāna*) not included here?

Is it not the case that the analysis of purification also brings about skillfulness in that regard? True, this is so; however, it is not included because it is already indicated by implication through the mention of defilement (*saṃkilesa*).
For those causes of their defilement, such as ignorance (*aññāṇa*) and so forth, when they have not arisen in any way whatsoever—
"Purification comes about through non-arising and through the abandoning of what has arisen. This term should be understood by way of the word *sara* having the sense of "to harm" (*hiṃsa*).

Having stated, "It is a refuge (*saraṇa*) because it harms (*saratīti*)," he then spoke the words beginning with "of those who have gone for refuge" (*saraṇagatānaṃ*) in order to resolve the inquiry as to whom, how, and whose harming it is.
In that context, "fear" (*bhaya*) refers to the fear of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-bhaya*). "Terror" (*santāsa*)...
“Mental terror” is mentioned because mental suffering is included therein. “Suffering” refers to bodily suffering.
“The affliction of miserable destinies” refers to all suffering comprised within the miserable destinies; all of this will be clarified later in the discussion on the fruits.
“This” refers to the word “refuge.”
Having thus shown the meaning of the word *saraṇa* (refuge) without distinction, the phrase beginning with "Alternatively" (*atha vā*) is now stated to show it with distinction.
"By causing [beings] to proceed toward their welfare" means by directing them toward the goal through such instructions as, "Monks, dwell endowed with virtue" (*sampannasīlā bhikkhave viharathā*).

And "by turning [them] away from what is harmful" means through such statements as, "The result of the destruction of life is indeed evil, and its future consequence is evil. (*Pāṇātipātassa kho pāpako vipāko, pāpakaṃ abhisamparāyan*) etc.

By means of seeing the danger and so forth, and by turning away from what is harmful. "It destroys fear" means that it eliminates, by preventing its occurrence, the calamity caused by the non-occurrence or occurrence of what is beneficial or harmful respectively.
The Dhamma known as the Path destroys the fear of beings by delivering them from the wilderness of existence (*bhava-kantāra*); the other [Dhamma] does so by providing consolation.
This is how the construction should be understood. "Of those who act" refers to [those acting] by way of giving and by way of worship.
And regarding "the honors that have been brought forth": the construction is that [the Dhamma] destroys the fear of beings by causing them to obtain abundant fruit;
the intention is that it possesses the state of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). "By this method as well" means by this reason stated through analysis.
Therein, [the faith] proceeds thus: "The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha is practicing rightly."
Confidence in the Triple Gem is *tappasāda*. That very Triple Gem is "heavy" (*garu*) to him;
thus it is *taggaru*. The state of being so is *taggarutā*. Confidence in it and reverence for it constitute *tappasādataggarutā*;
by means of these two, he is one whose defilements have been destroyed because of the shaking off of wrong views, doubt, delusion, lack of faith, and so forth. That very Triple Gem...
"Ultimate resort, supreme goal, protection, refuge"—thus, the arising of consciousness that occurs in the mode of being intent upon those [qualities] as its ultimate resort is "going for refuge.
It is called "going for refuge" because one goes by means of this.

"One who possesses that" means one endowed with that aforementioned arising of consciousness. "Thus he approaches" means he associates with, serves, and attends upon; or else, he thus knows and awakens.
The meaning should be understood in this way. Here, by the mention of "serenity" (*pasāda*), he refers to mundane going for refuge, for that is characterized primarily by serenity.

By the mention of "reverence" (*garutā*), he refers to the supramundane [going for refuge]. For the Noble Ones regard the Three Jewels with reverence—as if they were a stone parasol—due to their direct knowledge of their qualities.
Therefore, through serenity toward them, one is free from defilements by way of suppression; and through reverence toward them...
"By way of complete eradication" is to be connected [to the phrase "lack of reverence"] because of the cutting off of the causes that produce lack of reverence.

Furthermore, "having that as one's ultimate resort" means having that as one's destination; thus, it should be understood that by this term, all four kinds of going for refuge that will be explained are included.
Alternatively, "clarity and respect" are expressed without distinction; by the mention of "clarity," both verified clarity (*aveccappasāda*) and other forms of clarity are included.
Thus, by both [the taking up of the burden and the laying down of the burden], both forms of going for refuge should be connected.

The construction is: "It succeeds at the moment of the Path. By the phrase "having Nibbāna as its object," he shows that, in actual meaning, the attainment of the Four Truths itself is the supramundane going for refuge.
For therein, the Dhamma of Nibbāna is [realized] by way of the clear comprehension of realization (*sacchikiriyā-abhisamaya*).
The nature of the Path, while being penetrated precisely through the clear realization of cultivation (*bhāvanābhisamaya*), accomplishes the purpose of going for refuge.

However, the qualities of the Buddha that fall within the range of disciples [are accomplished] through the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*); likewise are the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha. Therefore it was said:
"In terms of function, it is accomplished in the entire Triple Gem. And when it is being accomplished, it is accomplished simultaneously; it is not mundane (*lokiya*).
The intended meaning is that it has been penetrated through a penetration of non-delusion in successive order.

As for those who say, "Going for refuge does not proceed by having Nibbāna as its object; rather, because the Path has been attained, it is simply 'attained' [in relation to it], just as certain types of mundane knowledge, such as the three Vedas, are attained," for them, going for refuge would be merely mundane.
It might be argued that it is not supramundane; however, that is incorrect because both types [of going for refuge] are intended.
"That" refers to the mundane going for refuge. The acquisition of faith consists of such [thoughts] as "The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened.
"Rooted in faith" means that right view—preceded by the aforementioned faith—is directed toward the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma’s perfect nature, and the Saṅgha’s perfect practice.
Because it is seen by means of right method through the very process of mundane awakening.

By the statement, “Right view has faith as its root,” he shows that wisdom characterized as previously described, which is supported by faith, constitutes mundane going for refuge; therefore he says, “It is called the straightening of view.
This is because view itself is made straight by its own conditions, or else it is view that is made straight.
By this, "rectification of view" (*diṭṭhijukamma*) is meant; it is the arising of consciousness proceeding in such a manner.
And by doing so, this statement—"the arising of consciousness proceeding in the mode of having that as its ultimate resort"—is justified.

Furthermore, the mention of "right view preceded by faith" should be understood as indicating that the arising of consciousness has that [faith] as its primary focus. By the phrase "acquisition of faith," [the text refers to] mothers and so forth...
It shows that going for refuge dissociated from knowledge is like that of children and others who have been encouraged [to do so];
by the phrase "possessing right view," it shows going for refuge associated with knowledge. This is mundane going for refuge.
"Surrendering of self" (attasanniyyātana) means that by this [right view], one surrenders, relinquishes, and abandons oneself; it is the rectification of view as previously described. That—
One for whom the Triple Gem is the supreme goal and the refuge is "one who has that as his supreme goal" (*tapparāyaṇo*), whether referring to a person or a state of consciousness.
The state of being such is "having that as one's supreme goal" (*tapparāyaṇatā*), which is precisely the rectification of view (*diṭṭhijukamma*) as previously described.

With the intention of "going for refuge," one enters into the status of a student (*sissa*) or a resident pupil (*antevāsika*); thus, it is "entering into the status of a student. It is by means of the very intention of going for refuge...
*Paṇipāta* means "that by which one prostrates. In all instances, the meaning should be understood precisely through the rectification of views (*diṭṭhi-ujukamma*) as previously described.
*Attapariccajana* (self-surrender) means the relinquishing of one's own personal existence (*attabhāva*) for the sake of crossing over the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. The restriction "only of the Buddhas and so forth" applies even to self-dedication (*attasanniyyātana*) and the others therein.
In this regard, it should be stated: for in this way, the exclusion of anything other than that is accomplished.
Having thus shown the surrendering of oneself and so forth by one manner, the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apica*) is now commenced in order to show them by other ways as well;
by that, the surrendering of oneself and so forth is indeed established through alternative methods as well, because of the meaning.
He shows that they are "undivided. Regarding the phrase "of Āḷavaka and the others," by the word "others" (ādi), the inclusion of Sātāgira, Hemavata, and so forth is to be understood.

Now, one might ask: since these individuals such as Āḷavaka had already gone for refuge by means of the Path itself, how can it be said that their going for refuge was "having that as their ultimate resort" (*tapparāyaṇa*)?

[The answer is: Even in the case of those who went for refuge by means of the Path, [it is so because] they said: "I shall wander... [and so forth]... because of its excellence" (*sudhammatā*). "They... [and so forth].

"We shall wander from village to village, from mountain to mountain... [and so on]... because of its excellence," it was said thus because they proclaimed their state of being intent upon that [practice].
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by way of relatives... and so on," here it means by way of relatives, by way of fear, by way of teachers, and by way of those worthy of offerings.
Each [term] should be applied individually. In that context, "by way of kinship" means by way of the state of being a relative; the same applies to the remaining cases.

"By bowing down to those worthy of offerings" means by bowing down caused by their worthiness as objects of offerings. "By the others" refers to the three types of bowing that proceed from the state of kinship and so forth.
The passage beginning with "Therefore" is stated to show in detail the meaning that was briefly expressed by the words "by the others," and so on.
"Vandati" (he pays homage) is a statement defining the characteristic of prostration (*paṇipāta*). "Of such a kind" refers to that which pertains to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*);

for the intention is that one who desires instruction leading to the future life (*samparāyika*) or to liberation (*niyyānika*) performs prostration only toward those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
"The classification of going for refuge" (*saraṇagamanappabheda*) means the analysis of going for refuge.
The Noble Path itself is the supramundane going for refuge; thus it is said: "The four fruits of recluseship are fruition-results.
"The destruction of all suffering" means the non-arising and cessation of the entire suffering of saṃsāra.
"This" refers to the vision of the Noble Truths as stated thus: "One sees the Four Noble Truths with right wisdom."
“By way of not approaching what is constantly tormented,” etc., means by way of not grasping at it as “permanent. “There is no possibility” (*aṭṭhāna*) is a negation of the cause.
“There is no occasion” (*anavakāsa*) is a negation of the condition. By both [terms], he negates the very reason. “That” (*yaṃ*) refers to the reason.

“One endowed with right view” (*diṭṭhisampanna*) is a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) possessed of the path-view. “Any formation” (*kañci saṅkhāraṃ*) refers to those belonging to the four planes of existence.
“Even a single conditioned formation among conditioned phenomena”—to "approach it as permanent" means one would grasp it as "permanent. "To approach it as pleasant":
this is said with reference to grasping it as pleasant by way of the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*), such as: "The self is exclusively happy and healthy after death.
However, with a mind dissociated from views, the noble disciple [approaches it] for the sake of allaying the fever of distress.
Just as a refined brahmin who is terrified of a rutting elephant approaches a dung heap with a sense of pleasure toward some formation (*saṅkhāra*), so it is here.
In the section concerning the self, instead of saying "some formation" (*saṅkhāra*) for the purpose of including the designations of the kasiṇas and so forth, it is said "some phenomenon" (*dhamma*).
In these sections as well, the delimitation should be understood either by way of the four planes or by way of the three planes. Whatever...
For whatever an ordinary person grasps by way of attachment, from that very thing the noble disciple disentangles his grasp.
Regarding the terms "mother" and so forth: it is the biological mother, the biological father, and an Arahant who is a human being and has exhausted the taints (khīṇāsava) who is intended.
But could a noble disciple ever deprive another of life? That too is impossible, because of the state of being an ordinary person [which he has transcended].
However, this was said for the purpose of showing the great gravity of the offense and for the purpose of demonstrating the fruit for a noble disciple.
"With a corrupt mind" means with a mind defiled by a murderous intent. "Should shed blood" means that he should shed even as much blood as could be drunk by a small fly from a living body.
"Should cause a schism in the Saṅgha" refers to one who shares the same communal recitation.

He would split the Saṅgha standing within a common boundary by means of these five causes mentioned: by formal act (*kamma*), by recitation (*uddesa*), by discussion (*vohāra*), by proclamation (*anussāvana*), and by the taking of voting tickets (*salākaggāha*). He would take another teacher—another founder of a sect—as "this is my teacher";
the meaning is that such a thing is impossible. They will not go to a state of misery (*apāyabhūmi*).
The meaning is that those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha will not go to the states of misery because of that, but will rather fill the hosts of devas.
"By ten grounds" means by ten reasons. "They surpass" means they overcome.
"Also by way of the Velāma Sutta and others" refers here to eighty-four thousand golden, silver, and bronze bowls, each measuring one-quarter of a *karīsa* of rice.
In due order, [he gave] eighty-four thousand elephants filled with silver, gold, and bullion, adorned with every ornament;
eighty-four thousand horses; eighty-four thousand chariots; eighty-four thousand milch cows;
eighty-four thousand maidens; eighty-four thousand couches; and eighty-four thousand...

Compared to the great *velāma* almsgiving that proceeded continuously for seven years and seven months by way of relinquishing thousands of millions of garments and immeasurable varieties of food such as hard and soft edibles,
a gift given to a single stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) bears far greater fruit;
and compared to a gift given to a hundred stream-enterers, a gift given to a single once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*) bears even greater fruit.

Then, for one who is a non-returner, then for one who is an arahant, then for a paccekabuddha, then for a perfectly enlightened Buddha, then for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha—the gift given to them has greater fruit;
then the construction of a monastery dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters; and then the going for refuge—this is the meaning he was illustrating as having even greater fruit.

By way of the Velāma Sutta. For this has been said: "Householder, compared to the gift, the great gift, which the brahmin Velāma gave, he who would feed even one person endowed with right view would have a much more abundant fruit," and so forth.
By the word "etc. in the phrase "the Velāma Sutta, etc.," the inclusion of the Agga-ppasāda Sutta and others is to be understood.
Ignorance (*aññāṇa*) is the non-knowing of the qualities of the Triple Gem; it is delusion regarding them.

Doubt (*vicikicchā*) is uncertainty, such as thinking, "Is he a Buddha or is he not? Wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*) is a perverted grasp resulting from the conceptualization of his qualities as being non-qualities.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), disrespect and lack of reverence are included. "Not of great radiance" means not brilliant, that is, impure.
The meaning is "not purified. "Not of great expansion" means it is not sublime. "With fault" means it is defiled by way of craving, views, and so forth;
like the worldly going for refuge or the undertaking of training, it lasts only as long as life itself without having a fixed time limit taken.
Therefore, because it is destroyed by the breaking up of the aggregates, he said: "It is blameless at the time of death. "That" refers to the blameless one.

The classification of the going for refuge. Although it is blameless, it does not yield a desirable fruit; therefore, he says "fruitless. Why? Because it is without karmic ripening (*avipāka*). For that [going for refuge] is not unwholesome (*akusala*). "What is a lay follower (*upāsaka*)?
is a question concerning its specific nature; what is meant is: "What is the characteristic of a lay follower? "Why? is a question concerning the cause.
This shows by what basis for application (*pavatti-nimitta*) the term *upāsaka* is established for that person; therefore he asks, "Why is he called an *upāsaka*?
The basis for application is the ground upon which a word functions regarding its referent (*abhidheyya*), and it is the cause for the existence of that meaning within the thing itself.
"What is his virtue? means: of what kind is the virtue of this lay follower (*upāsaka*), and by what extent of virtue is he said to be "perfected in virtue" (*sīla-sampanna*)?

The meaning is "it occurs. What is livelihood? What is his right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*)? Furthermore, since that arises through the avoidance of wrong livelihood (*micchā-ājīva*), that too is analyzed.
What is failure? What is the failure of his virtue (*sīla*) or of his livelihood? For there is either an injunction or a prohibition regarding what immediately precedes it.
The same method applies here to "success" (*sampatti*).

"Whoever" (*yo ko ci*) means anyone among the kṣatriyas and so forth; this shows that the reason for [the efficacy of] going for refuge is precisely that, and not distinctions such as birth and so on.

"From attending" (*upāsanato*) means from attending upon [the Triple Gem] by means of that very going for refuge, through the performance of it with care, and through the application of reverence, respect, and esteem.

"Abstentions" (*veramaṇiyo*): "enmity" (*vera*) refers to misconduct such as killing living beings; because they ward off (*maṇanato*), strike down (*hananato*), and destroy (*vināsanato*) that, they are "abstentions. These are the five abstinences, because that virtue has abstinence as its primary characteristic; for this very reason, it is said: "he is refrained."
"Wrong trading" means trade that is not right, improper trade, and unbecoming trade. "Having abandoned" means having relinquished by simply not engaging in it.
"In accordance with the Dhamma" means not departing from the Dhamma; by this, he rejects any other livelihood that is contrary to the Dhamma.
"Justly" means without injustice; by this, having avoided bodily misconduct and so forth, [he lives] by bodily good conduct and the like.

He shows his livelihood. "Trade in weapons" means the sale of weaponry, whether one has made them oneself, had them made, or acquired them already finished. "Trade in living beings" means the sale of human beings.
"Trade in meat" means the sale of meat obtained by raising deer, pigs, and so forth, like butchers and the like. "Trade in intoxicants" refers to any kind of intoxicant whatsoever.
The sale of poison consists of either compounding poison or taking it up and then selling it.
Among these, the trade in weapons is declared improper because it is a cause for the obstruction of others; the trade in living beings because it renders them non-independent;
the trade in meat because it is a cause for killing; and the trade in intoxicants because they are a basis for negligence.
"Of that very same" refers to both the virtue (sīla) characterized by the five abstinences and the livelihood (ājīva) characterized by the five wrong modes of trade.
"Failure" means breach or corruption. "By which" means by which practice. "Outcaste" refers to an outcaste among lay followers (upāsaka). "Dirt" refers to the dirt of a lay follower.
"Lowest" refers to the lowest among lay followers. [This applies] regarding the Buddha and others, as well as regarding karma and the fruits of karma.
Lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) is the opposite of faith; it is wrong resolve. One who possesses such lack of faith as described is "faithless" (*assaddha*).
One who, by way of the aforementioned failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) and failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*), is devoid of virtue is "immoral" (*dussīla*).

[One who is deluded] by means of the auspiciousness seen, heard, sensed, or known—which is reckoned as the "superstitious excitement" imagined by foolish people, such as: "By this view and so forth, this particular thing is an auspicious omen."
One who is possessed of [the view of] omens and auspicious signs: he believes in omens alone, such as the various types of omens consisting of what has been seen and so forth.
He does not believe in "action," meaning he does not accept the principle that one is the owner of one's own karma (*kammassakata*).

And "outside of this" means outside of this teaching of the Omniscient Buddha, in the systems of outsiders (*bāhiraka*). "He seeks out a worthy recipient for offerings" means he perceives one who has entered upon a wrong path as being worthy of offerings.
He seeks out [those worthy of offerings]. He performs prior service means that he first of all performs wholesome deeds such as giving and honoring.
Here, by treating the seeking of those worthy of offerings and the performance of prior service as one, five factors are to be understood.
Success is to be understood as the opposite of what was stated regarding failure. However, this is the distinction: for all four assemblies...

In the sense of producing delight, a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is itself a jewel; thus, he is a "lay-follower-jewel" (*upāsakaratana*). Because of the fragrance of his virtues, beauty, fame, and reputation, a lay follower is himself a lotus;
thus, he is a "lay-follower-lotus" (*upāsakapaduma*). Likewise, he is a "lay-follower-white-lotus" (*upāsakapuṇḍarīka*).

The word "in the beginning" (*ādimhi*) has the sense of "at the start. "At the limit" (*koṭiyaṃ*) means at the ultimate boundary. "By way of the dwelling" (*vihāraggena*) means by way of the section consisting of the private chamber; "in this... [text continues].
The meaning is: "by way of each respective place of residence," as in the passage beginning, "For those dwelling in the womb, this very fruit of the jackfruit tree reaches [maturity].
Alternatively, *ajjatagga* or *ajjadagga* has the same meaning as *ajja* (today).
By the phrase "endowed with life" (*pāṇehi upetaṃ*), he shows that going for refuge extends until the end of one's life, saying: "As long as my life..."
Having spoken such words as “it proceeds,” he spoke the passage beginning with “For I...
to clarify the intention that had arisen in the king’s mind—that he would protect the going for refuge by honoring those three objects even at the cost of his life.
For the phrase “endowed with life” means that as long as his life-breaths endure, he remains endowed with the refuge; and in taking it, he does so not merely with words.
The meaning here should be understood as follows: it is not by a single arising of the thought alone, but rather it is approached for as long as life lasts through the relinquishing of living beings.
"Transgression" (*accaya*) refers to the overstepping that occurs after crushing the good boundary; thus he said, "an offense" (*aparādha*). It transgresses (*acceti*).
Or, it is called *accaya* because one transgresses by means of it; it is the unwholesome state that causes transgression to proceed.
It is called *aparādha* because one offends by means of it; for it proceeds by overcoming the person who offends. Therefore, he said: "proceeding by transgressing and overcoming.
*Carati* means he conducts himself or acts. *Dhammeneva* means not departing from the Dhamma.
"By means of practice. "May he accept" means "may he receive by way of consent"; thus he said, "May he forgive. 251.
Because he is worthy of being sought as a refuge by the world including the devas, he is "noble" (*ariya*);

thus he said, "In the Vinaya of the Noble One, in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One. While establishing the discourse with reference to the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), [he said] "This indeed is growth," etc.

Although the sentence was begun by way of a reference to the Dhamma (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*), nevertheless, the construction is as follows: "he undertakes restraint," speaking the teaching by way of a reference to the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*). 253.
He is "wounded" by the destruction of his own roots of merit (*kusalamūla*) that were about to ripen within this very selfhood (*attabhāva*).
It is impaired by the very impairment of those [faculties]. By both [of these], he speaks of nothing but the fault of that person’s karma.

It is called a "foundation" (patiṭṭhā) because one enters the fixed course of rightness (sammattaniyāma) by means of it; it is the perfection of its supporting condition (upanissaya). Because this [person] has broken and destroyed that foundation through a fault of action, he is "one whose foundation is broken" (bhinnapatiṭṭha);
thus he said, "In such a way," and so forth. "The eye regarding phenomena" (dhammesu cakkhu) refers to the eye regarding the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths.
It is called "eye" (*cakkhu*) in the sense of seeing. "In other places" means in other sections of the Suttas.
"He will be released" means that after being boiled for sixty thousand years, he will be released from the *lohakumbhī* hell.
If he is to be boiled in hell in his very next existence, what benefit does the King derive from hearing this Sutta?
He said, "It is of great benefit," and so forth. That benefit, however, is stated by way of obtaining sleep;

it consists of the removal of bodily and mental suffering at that time, the performance of great honor toward the Three Jewels, and the attainment of an especially eminent faith characteristic of ordinary worldlings—such as these are its benefits pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*).
As for the benefits pertaining to future lives (*samparāyika*), they should be understood as being truly immeasurable throughout subsequent existences.
Here it is asked: If the Eye of Dhamma were to arise for the king on that very seat due to the absence of any obstacle to his karma, how could he later become a Paccekabuddha and attain Parinibbāna?
Conversely, if he is to become a Paccekabuddha and attain Parinibbāna, how could the Eye of Dhamma have arisen then?
Are not these two—the support for Sāvaka-bodhi and the support for Pacceka-bodhi—mutually exclusive?
"Of different bases"? This is not a contradiction, because from this point onward he will gather the requisites for individual enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*).

For even those beings who are destined to awaken to the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*) will, in the absence of the conditions for that [disciple-enlightenment], awaken to individual enlightenment at a later time, due to the possibility of having previously made the necessary resolution (*abhinīhāra*). However, others say: "This [resolve] is for individual enlightenment alone..."

One who has made the aspiration. For even those who have made the aspiration, if they have not yet reached certainty (*niyati*) therein because that knowledge has not reached its full maturity, the Blessed One said, “If, monks, this king...,” and so forth, [meaning] that they will attain the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*) in the presence of the Teacher.
Furthermore, liberation from the immediate offenses (*ānantariya*) belongs only to Great Bodhisattvas, not to other types of bodhisattvas.

For it should be understood thus: although Devadatta was destined for Pacceka-bodhi, due to his long-standing malice toward the Lord of the World, he committed even more grave *ānantariya* (immediate) offenses;

therefore, by way of this obstruction of karma, this King—who is now unable to achieve the realization of the vision—will, according to the destiny of Pacceka-bodhi, become a Pacceka-buddha and attain final Nibbāna in the future.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the *Sāmaññaphala-sutta*.
3. The Commentary on the *Ambaṭṭha-sutta*:
The Description of the Journey.
254. *Apubbapadavaṇṇanā* (Commentary on the Unprecedented Phrase):

This refers to the commentary—that is, the analysis of the meaning—of a phrase not previously taken up in the preceding commentary on the meaning. For it is said: "Having abandoned the meaning that has come again and again.
