*Janapadino* means those possessing a country, or rather, the princes who are the lords of the country; they are called *Kosalā* by way of their lineage. If there is only one country, how [is it plural]?
He says "plural" because it is "by way of conventional usage" (*rūḷhisaddena*). For etymologists (*akkharacintaka*) desire such genders and numbers in such instances as if they were appropriate;
this is the convention here, just as elsewhere in expressions such as "he dwells among the Kurus" and "he dwells among the Aṅgas.
Even when used as an adjective for that [word], the singular number alone is used for both the word *janapada* (country) and the word *jāti* (class). But as for the "ancients" (*porāṇā*):
The word *pana* indicates a specific sense; by virtue of its referring to a manifold object, it illuminates the specific distinction that will be stated as "this is a plural number.
For that region consists of many divisions, measuring three hundred *yojanas*.
"Having abandoned even the ploughs" means having relinquished even the ploughs by way of abandoning work; this is merely an illustration. It is not only farmers [who do so].
Then other people as well, having abandoned their respective duties, gathered there.
"That region" (*padeso*) is stated by way of the commonality of the term *padesa*, or else through a change in the grammatical number; the meaning is "those regions.
It is called "Kosala" because they are indeed skillful (*kusala*); thus, they are termed "Kosala."
*Cārikā* means walking (*caraṇa*), or *cāra* (movement) is the same as *cārikā*.
Here, this refers specifically to traveling on the path, not merely moving about in small steps; thus he said, "while going on a journey.
To show that by way of classification, he said, "And this kind of journey," and so forth. In that context, "even far" means even not very far. "Going hastily" means going quickly.
Having briefly mentioned the account of the meeting with Mahākassapa and others, and having related in detail the story of the novice Tiṣya who dwelt in the forest,

[the Buddha] began the discourse on the wandering through the countryside with the words, "The Blessed One," and so forth. Desiring to go together only with those possessing the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā),
he said, "Proclaim the possession of the six supernormal powers."

They say that although full ordination (*upasampadā*) is accomplished by means of a formal act of the Sangha (*saṅghakamma*), it is said, "I shall give you the inheritance of the Buddha," because it is accomplished solely through the Teacher’s command.
Others, however, say that he said, "I shall give it," because he was permitting the full ordination of one who was not yet twenty years of age.
"Having ordained him" means having ordained him with the General of the Dhamma as preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
Even a place extending nine hundred yojanas is included within the Middle Country; beyond that is not intended here, because [the Buddha] did not travel further on account of his rapid journeying.
"On all sides" means in every direction, on the four sides of each place he had visited.

"For another reason as well" refers to another cause besides the fact that the monks' trees of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) were still tender, namely, the ripening of the wisdom of those to be trained (*veneyya*) within the Middle Mandala.
He descends to the middle circle. The phrase “or with seven,” etc., should be construed according to the sequence stated in the passage beginning “or for one month,” etc.
“For the sake of bodily comfort” means for the sake of the comfort of the body whose elements have become aggravated due to residing fixedly in one place alone;
it is for the sake of seeking an occasion for the arising of a discourse, as in the *Agniskandhopama-sūtra*.
One who desires the occasion for the arising of a teaching (aṭṭhuppatti) should do so, as in the case of the teachings such as the Maghadeva Jātaka.

For the purpose of enacting a training rule (sikkhāpada), as in the enactment of the rule against drinking intoxicants. For the purpose of awakening those beings capable of being awakened, such as Aṅgulimāla and others.
A journey undertaken with reference to a specific person or a few individuals is a "fixed journey" (nibaddhacārikā); any other is an "unfixed journey" (anibaddhacārikā).
"In the ten-thousandfold world-system" means in the ten thousand world-spheres that constitute the field of birth.
For it is said that the Blessed One, having extended his Buddha-knowledge in order to perceive beings therein whose faculties have reached maturity, spreads out a net of knowledge.
"Has entered within the net of omniscient knowledge" means he has come within the range of that knowledge. The Blessed One...
It is said that after entering the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) and emerging from it, he resolves his mind, thinking:
"May those beings who are capable and whose knowledge is ripe, and who are to be disciplined by me today, appear before my knowledge," and then he applies his attention.
Simultaneously with his application of attention, one, two, or many individuals who are then ready for discipline come into the range of his knowledge.

This, in this context, is the power of the Buddha. Furthermore, he observes their underlying predisposition (*upanissaya*), past conduct, past causes, and their present practice as they come into his range of perception;
therefore, he says, "Then the Blessed One," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having engaged in debate and counter-debate":
[it refers to] my speaking the words beginning with "Is it thus for you, Ambaṭṭha? and [Ambaṭṭha’s reply], "And those who, Master Gotama... and so on.

Having replied with such words as “shavelings, wretched ascetics,” he will speak various kinds of unseemly speech—unfit words for one of a virtuous nature—by uttering insults against the outcastes three times.
*Nibbisevanaṃ* means free from irritation; the meaning is that it is devoid of agitation caused by pride and arrogance.
*Avasaritabbaṃ* means "should be approached. *Icchānaṅgale*: this indicates the Blessed One’s alms-resort village at that time;

it is used in the locative case in the sense of proximity. *“In the grove of Icchānaṅgala”*: this indicates the place of residence; it is used in the locative case in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
Explaining both of these, he said: “Dependent upon Icchānaṅgala,” and so forth. [Of] the Dhamma-King...
The Blessed One’s practice is entirely devoted to the suppression of unrighteousness (adhamma), and that occurs by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom;
to demonstrate this, it is said: "the camp of the aggregate of virtue," and so forth.
"In whatever way he pleases" means by whichever dwelling among the divine abodes (dibbavihāra) and so on is pleasing to himself.
Commentary on the Story of Pokkharasāti (255).
*Manta* refers to the collection of mantras such as the *Irubbeda* and others. He sat reclining upon a lotus (*pokkhara*), which is why he is called *Pokkharasāti*.
*Sāti* denotes a shape; because he was born from a part of the lotus that possessed its characteristic shape, he is also called *Pokkharasāti*.
"Resembling a white lotus" means having the color of a white lotus. "Well-rounded" means well-circled in the places appropriate for being circular.
"Very pure" means free from black moles, freckles, and the like.
What kind of past application did this brahmin have, such that the Blessed One approached that place in order to favor him?
He said, "But this," and so forth. Because he was born within the interior of a lotus, he is thus born from moisture (*saṃsedaja*).
"It does not bloom" means it does not open. "A silver image" refers to a figure made of silver.
Demonstrating that the prefix *adhi-* here indicates the sense of sovereignty and the prefix *ā-* indicates the sense of a limit, [the author] says: "He dwells there."
He said, “Having overcome,” and so forth. Because it is joined with those [prefixes], it is called *ukkaṭṭha*; thus he said, “by way of the prefix (*upasagga*),” and so on.
“By which boundary” means by which state. “The site of the city”: thinking, “This is the moment;
let not this auspicious hour pass,” they placed torches at night while guarding against the break of dawn, and while the torches were burning—
They took the site for the city; therefore, because they were situated among torches (*ukkāsu*), they are called *Ukkaṭṭhā*.

The grammatical derivation of the word should be understood through the application of the *mūlavibhuja* rule and others—meaning they were established while the torches were shining—or according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*), they are called *Ukkaṭṭhā* because they remained while the torches were being held.
Others, however, say it was due to the excellence of the ground and the excellence of the requisites.
"And because of its association with superior qualities due to the excellence of its human inhabitants, that city received the name 'Ukkaṭṭhā' (Superior).
*Tassa* refers to the word "Ukkaṭṭha" expressed in the accusative case. *Anupayogattā* means because it is not employed as a qualifying attribute.
*Sesapadesu* refers to the phrases beginning with "sattussadaṃ" (abounding in seven things). For in the preceding [case], there was non-employment according to the rule. *Tattha* means therein.

Regarding the rule stated by the phrase "by way of prefixes" (*upasaggavasena*) and so forth: by the statement "it should be sought from the science of grammar" (*saddasatthato pariyesitabbaṃ*), he shows that this application of words follows the characteristics of linguistic science (*saddalakkhaṇa*).

Grammarians maintain that when the verbal root *vas* (to dwell) is preceded by such prefixes as *upa*, *anu*, *adhi*, and *ati*, it takes only the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) for the location of the action.

“Excessiveness” (ussadatā) here means abundance; to demonstrate that abundance, the words beginning with “bahujanaṃ” were spoken. “To be nourished” (posāvaniyaṃ) means that which is to be taken up and sustained. “Having enclosed” (āvijjhitvā) means having surrounded it. Or, it is called “rājabhoggaṃ” because it is to be enjoyed by the king as if it were his own.
It is “a portion belonging to the king” (rañño dāyabhūtaṃ) in the sense of being suitable for the royal lineage, having been obtained from the king as an inheritance.
Therefore he said, “the meaning is ‘heritage’” (dāyajjaṃ). Because it is to be enjoyed through the king’s authority...
He said, "There is no such thing as a gift being superior to the gain of a meal," thus stating, "Having raised the royal umbrella, one should eat under the designation of a king.
By the phrase "all that may be cut or broken," he refers to all forms of punishment, such as corporal punishment, fines, and so forth.
"At river fords, mountains, and so on" means at river fords, the foot of mountains, village gates, forest entrances, and the like. "A royal gift" (rājadāya).
Since the fact that it was given by the king is already established by this [statement], he asks: "What is the purpose of the words ‘given by King Pasenadi of Kosala’?
He replies: "For the purpose of indicating the donor-king," and so forth. "Relinquished and abandoned" means having abandoned it through the exercise of open-handed generosity;
for in this way, it becomes a gift of the best, a supreme gift.
By saying "he perceived," he shows the meaning of perceiving through the mode of hearing; thus he said, "At the ear-door... he knew.
Because every sentence has the function of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and thus contains an implicit restriction, he said, "The particle [kho] is used merely for the purpose of completing the meter.
Furthermore, by the phrase "in the sense of restriction," he demonstrates that the word *kho* is employed here to restrict the intended meaning alone.
Regarding the word "assosi": when the particle *kho* is included, it becomes as if filled and adorned, and thereby the preceding and following words become well-connected (*siliṭṭha*).
He says, "merely for the sake of the smoothness of the expression through the completion of the metrical foot," because the word *matta* has the sense of excluding further qualification;
thus, it indicates that this [particle] does not express any additional meaning.
It has been shown; however, by the word *eva*, its absolute certainty is indicated through the elegance of the phrasing.
"Because evil has been stilled" means because evil has been stilled absolutely, without remainder, and together with its latent tendencies (*savāsana*).

For in this way, the Blessed One’s stilling of evil is distinguished from the stilling of evil by outsiders, those in the state of fading away (*virāga*), and those who are trainees (*sekha*) or non-trainees (*asekha*). Therefore he said, "For it has been stated," and so forth. This is because particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings.
Here, "tradition" (anussava) is intended as the source; thus he said, "The word *khalu* is a particle used in the sense of tradition. "Mere address" means mere words of affectionate speech.
For these are expressions of endearment such as "Sir," "Friend," or "Beloved of the Gods" (*Devānaṃ Piya*).

Regarding the phrase "by way of clan" (*gottavasena*): here, that which protects one is a "clan" (*gotra*). For the term "Gotama" refers both to the speech currently in use and to the intellect [that identifies it].
It is called a *gotta* (clan) because it protects (*tāyati*) and guards (*rakkhati*) by means of its status as a unique domain.
For just as cognition cannot function without an object that serves as its referent, so too expression cannot exist without that which is expressed;
therefore, that object designated as "clan" is said to protect and guard those [expressions]. But what is it? It is that which belongs to that particular family and is not shared with other lineages.
It should be understood as the common form of asceticism (sāmañña-rūpa), which has been perfected by the Primordial Person and is shared by those belonging to his lineage.
In this context, by the term “ascetic” (samaṇa), the Blessed One’s state of being highly esteemed by similar persons is shown through the praise of his having stilled evil.
By the term “Gotama,” his descent from a noble family is indicated to worldly people.
It is an illumination of a high lineage because it reveals a noble and exalted khattiya clan that has risen higher and higher.
For from the Great King Mahāsammata, the very first of all khattiyas, down to the present, the Śākya royal family remains unadulterated and most preeminent.
"By any loss" means by any kind of decline, such as the loss of relatives, the loss of wealth, and so forth. "Unconquered" means not overwhelmed. For thus is that family...
There was no loss whatsoever for the Lord of the World at his birth; rather, there was only increase.
And upon his Great Renunciation, he became even more renowned and famous in the world for his supreme prosperity.
Thus, the statement "he went forth from the Sakyan clan" is said to illustrate that the Blessed One went forth out of faith, [leaving behind] a vast circle of kinsmen and a great...
Because the state of having gone forth is accomplished by abandoning the mass of enjoyments (*bhogakkhandha*). "Sundara" means auspicious (*bhaddaka*).
And its auspiciousness should be understood as being the bringing of welfare and happiness to the one who sees it; thus he said, "bringing welfare and bringing happiness.

In that context, "bringing welfare" means bringing the welfare connected with the ultimate goal, pertaining to both the present life and the future life. "Bringing happiness" means bringing the three kinds of happiness as previously described.

“Of such a kind” means of that sort. However, showing that by whatever qualities the Blessed One is endowed, he is in every way worthy of inspiring faith and confidence in the world of the fourfold measure because of his true nature as it really is, he said, “of such a kind,” and so forth.
Therein, by the phrase “as it really is … [omission] … arahant,” [he shows this] for those who take the Dhamma as their measure and those who take austerity as their measure.

This shows that [seeing the Blessed One] brings about confidence in beings. It should be understood that by the demonstration of this very fact, the quality of bringing about confidence in others is also shown by implication, because of its invariable concomitance with it.
Regarding the statement "even mere seeing is good," the story of the Kosiya bird should be told here.
*Commentary on the Ambaṭṭha-Māṇava Sutta*

256. "He turns over the mantras" means he recites the Vedas; the sense is that he masters them. "He bears the mantras in mind" means he places in his heart the mantras exactly as they have been studied, keeping them from being forgotten by means of lip-movements and so forth, but not by way of explaining their meaning.

Regarding the phrase *sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ*: here, because it "carves," "breaks," and "shows" the meaning and the word by way of the relationship between the signified and the signifier, it is called *nikhaṇḍu*;
this very term, with the substitution of the letter *gha* for the letter *kha*, is here [referred to as] *nighaṇḍu*.
It is called *keṭubha*. It "drives" (*kiṭayati*), that is, it causes one to understand or makes known the classification of grammatical functions such as verbal roots and so forth;

or, because it "fills" (*gamanto*) by exhausting [the subject] without remainder, it is *keṭubha*. "Exhibiting synonyms" means illuminating words used as alternatives; the meaning is that it reveals many alternative expressions for each single meaning.
And this is merely an illustration, since it also functions by way of revealing how many different meanings can be expressed by a single word.
Because that treatise (gantha) has come into existence. It is called *kiriyākappa* because by means of it, an action characterized by vocal expression and so forth is fashioned (*kappīyati*).

Furthermore, since it possesses many alternative formulations (*vikappa*) due to its divisions such as phonemes, words, their connections, and word-meanings, it is called the "alternative formulation of the *kiriyākappa*" (*kiriyākappavikappa*).
And this was said with reference to the root treatise on the *kiriyākappa*, for it consists of one hundred thousand [verses] and comprises works such as the *Nayacariyā*.

The *akkharappabhedā* (divisions of phonemes) are the rules of phonetics (*sikkhā*) and grammar (*nirutti*), so called because phonemes are analyzed through them by way of the divisions of places of articulation (*ṭhāna*), modes of formation (*karaṇa*), and so forth, as well as by way of the divisions of etymological derivation (*nibbacana*).
"Of these" refers to the Vedas.
One who recites those very Vedas word-by-word is a *padaka*. One who explains and expounds various words and their meanings is a *byākaraṇika*.
*Etena* means "by this," namely, grammar (*saddasattha*). It is called *lokāyata* because by means of it the world does not strive (*yatati*) nor exert itself (*īhati*) for its welfare in the future;
for, relying on that treatise, beings do not even give rise to the thought of performing meritorious deeds.
*Vaya* means "decay" (*vayati*); it refers to those treatises which, at their beginning, middle, and end, are in no way exhausted or expanded.
The meaning is that it "sustains" (sandhāreti) and "fills" (pūreti). Showing that two negations revert to the original positive state, he says, "there is no diminution" (avayo na hoti);
then, in order to demonstrate what that diminution is, it is said: "diminution means... [etc. ...he is not able.

The meaning of the word *anuññāto* should be understood as a passive construction (*kamma-sādhana*), whereas the meaning of the word *paṭiññāto* should be understood as an active construction (*kartṛ-sādhana*).
Demonstrating this, he said: "By the teacher," and so forth. *Ācariyaka* refers to that which has been handed down through the succession of teachers.
It is difficult to depart after having freed oneself from what is heavy—that is, from the burden of the teacher—because harm may arise, such as censure, reproach, and attack.

(257) Regarding the word "abhuggato" (*emerged*), because of its connection with the prefix *abhi*, the accusative case is used specifically in the sense of expressing a state of being so characterized.
258. "Characteristics" (*lakkhaṇāni*) refers to the mantra-words that illuminate the characteristics.
"They disappear" means that not only the mantras for characteristics, but other [mantras] as well, gradually disappear due to the absence of the power of knowledge among brahmins.
For they say: "The hundredfold *addhariya*, the thousand-fold *sākhā*, the *vattaka*, the *sāmā*, and so forth. ... [regarding] the aspiration ... "great."
Here, the word "great" (*mahanta*) should be applied respectively to each term, beginning with "one whose aspiration is great" and "one whose undertaking is great.

His greatness of aspiration and so forth should be understood through such works as the *Buddhavaṃsa*, the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, and their commentaries. "Accomplishments" (*niṭṭhā*) means results or attainments.
"In the various states of existence" (*bhavabhedeti*) means in specific types of existence. "Pervasive state" (*visaṭabhāvo*) refers to the quality of being spread out and established here and there.
"By way of commonality of genus" means by virtue of the state of being identical through the mere fact of possessing the nature of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).
For while the characteristics of Buddhas are perfectly clear, well-defined, and complete, those of wheel-turning monarchs (*cakkavatti*) are not so;
therefore it was said: "One does not become a Buddha by those [characteristics] alone. [The same applies to] beauty of form, long life, freedom from illness, and so forth for brahmins and others.

"Beloved and pleasing" refers to these four wonderful qualities. "By means of the four bases of sympathy"—namely, generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality—"by causing delight" means by generating joy. One who causes the wheel—the wheel-treasure—to turn and proceed is a *cakkavattī*.
He himself proceeds by means of the wheels of prosperity, and by them he causes the other world of sentient beings to proceed.

He is called a *cakkavattī* because he causes [the wheel] to turn and proceed. He is a *cakkavattī* because the turning (*vatta*)—that is, the proceeding (*vattana*)—of the wheels of postures and of the welfare of others belongs to him, or because it occurs therein.

Alternatively, he is a *cakkavattī* because he turns the unobstructed wheel known as his command. Or, he is a *cakkavattī* because he brings under his own control the wheel—that is, the assembly—known as the circle of kshatriyas and so forth.
[He is a *cakkavattī*] by means of the Dhamma known as the conduct of a *cakkavattī*.

Or, he is "righteous" (*dhammika*) because the duty known as the conduct of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-vatta*) exists within him. Because he does not deviate from the Dhamma, he is the Dhamma;

and since he is a king in the sense of being one who delights (*rañjana*), he is a "Dhamma-king" (*dhammarāja*). Since it is said, "He is a king, a wheel-turner," the term "ruler of the four quarters" (*cāturanta*) clarifies his sovereignty over the four continents;
thus he says, "of that [earth] bounded by the four oceans," and so forth. In that context, the phrase "adorned with the four continents" means:
The inclusion of the term "fourfold" (*catubbidhā*) by way of specifying the categories should be understood as being for the purpose of including the various protective charms (*paritta-dīpa*).
In the phrase "anger and so forth" (*kopādī*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes lust, delusion, conceit, pride, and the like. "Victorious" (*vijitāvī*) means one who has conquered.
By virtue of being unshakable by anything, he has attained stability in the realm; or else, because of his state of firm devotion, the realm has attained stability.
"Attained here" means having attained the status of being stationary in the countryside (*janapada-thāvariya-patta*).
The quality of being a "jewel" (*ratana*) for the Wheel should also be understood through its state of being honored (*cittīkata-bhāva*) and so forth. This same method applies to the others as well.

Alternatively, because the state of being honored and so forth serves as a cause for delight (*rati-nimitta*), it is not mentioned separately since it is subsumed under the sense of "producing delight. However, by these...
In order to demonstrate each specific benefit that a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) enjoys by means of the [seven] jewels, the passage beginning with “But among these...
was stated. He conquers what is unconquered because of the nature of the outflow of karma conducive to great majesty.
Having mounted the elephant-jewel and the horse-jewel, he traverses his realm at will, and through their power, even within a single morning—
This is because, after traveling across the earth bounded by the ocean, he returns specifically to the royal capital.

He protects the conquered realm through the counselor-treasure (*pariṇāyakaratana*), because that treasure provides the necessary arrangements for whatever duties must be performed here and there. "By the remaining [treasures]" refers to the jewel-treasure (*maṇiratana*), the woman-treasure (*itthiratana*), and the householder-treasure (*gahapatiratana*).
Among these, by means of the jewel-treasure, one experiences happiness through the dispelling of darkness over an area measuring a league (*yojana*) and the resulting sight of light, and so forth.

By means of the Woman-Treasure (*itthiratana*), through the manifestation of a physical perfection that surpasses that of humans; by means of the Householder-Treasure (*gahapatiratana*), through the acquisition of whatever wealth one desires, such as gems, gold, and silver.

By means of the last—the Counsellor-Treasure (*pariṇāyakaratana*)—there is the application of the power of resolve, because of the accomplishment of the state of having a wheel of command unobstructed by anyone.
For he is skilled in all royal duties and possesses an unfailing application; therefore, it is said: "the application of the power of counsel. As for the Elephant and Horse Treasures...

Because the perfection of majesty (*pabhāvasampatti*) is also established through the possession of a treasury (*kosasampatti*) due to great power (*mahānubhāvatā*), it is said: “The elephant... [etc. ...the application.
For a treasury—namely, when there is the perfection of effort—is the complete fruit of the application of the threefold power (*sattiyoga*):
*dugga*, *teja*, *kusumora*, *parakkama*, *pabbatomukha*, and *amosapaharaṇa*. This is the connection. “By the remaining ones” means by the remaining five jewels.
"By the power of karma produced by the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adosa-kusalamūla*):

through the influence of karma generated by means of co-nascence and other conditions by way of the wholesome root termed non-hatred, they come to be because of their nature as exceedingly gentle jewels.

The middle [jewels] are the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, and the householder-treasure. By the power of karma [produced] by non-greed (*alobha*)... [as above] ...they come to be because of the great wealth and the causes for obtaining such great wealth."

And because it is caused by the perfection of relinquishment (*pariccāgasampadā*). "The last" refers to the Jewel of the Counsellor (*pariṇāyakaratanam*). For that [Jewel] arises through non-delusion (*amoha*)...
[and so on] ...by the power of karma, since the duties of a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*) must be guided by one of great wisdom (*mahāpañña*) alone.
What is called "instruction" (*upadesa*) is a discourse proceeding by way of a detailed investigation of the seven jewels.
They are "brave" (*sūra*) because they destroy their adversaries through recourse to refuge; hence he says, "of a fearless nature.
He is "Vīra" (the Hero) because he stands having conquered the asuras; he is Sakka, the lord of the gods.

Because his body is like that of a divine youth (*devaputta*) due to his being a member of the host, it is said, "of heroic form" (*vīraṅgarūpa*), meaning possessing a body similar to that of a divine youth. "Some" refers to the teacher of the *Sārasamāsa*. "Nature" (*sabhāva*) means a meaning that constitutes its inherent nature.

"Vīrakāraṇaṃ" means the cause of heroic state. "As if having bodies made of energy" means they resemble embodied energy; the sense is that if energy were to have a physical form, they would be like it.

Anticipating the objection—"But surely there is no opposing army for a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti) such that his sons might crush it; then why is he called 'the crusher of enemy armies'?"—he says:
“*Sacca* and so forth” means that whether or not there is an opposing army, he shows that they possess such great majesty (*mahānubhāva*).
“By the Dhamma” means by his own accumulated merit (*puñña-dhamma*).
Thus impelled by that, all the kings on earth go out to meet him, say, “Welcome to you, Great King,” and so forth, and hand over their own kingdoms to the Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*).

Therefore it was said: “He, having... [pe] ... dwells as lord. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, in order to show the excellence of his application—which consists in the fulfillment of the duties of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) and serves as the condition for that aforementioned Dhamma to ripen over a longer period—it was stated:
“By means of the Dhamma of the five precepts, beginning with ‘no living being is to be killed’... For in this way, [he rules] “without the rod...”
The statement, "by one who is weaponless," is thus more thoroughly established.

Because the evil states such as lust (*rāga*), when arising, remain having covered and enveloped the continuum of a being (*sattasantāna*) and obstructing the occurrence of the wholesome, they are therefore called "coverings" (*chadana*) and "obscuring" (*chada*).
"Having uncovered" means having removed. The state of being worthy of worship is expressed by the term "Arahant" (*arahati*).
"Arahant" means worthy of worship. Because he is the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), he is therefore an Arahant.

The state of having "uncovered the covering" (*vivaṭṭacchadatā*), which serves as the cause for Buddhahood, is mentioned because the state of being a Buddha is preceded by the abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*).

"The Arahant by virtue of the absence of the round [of existence]" (*vaṭṭābhāvena*) is a demonstration of inferring the cause from the fruit. "The Perfectly Enlightened One by virtue of the absence of the covering" (*chadanābhāvena*)...
This is a demonstration of the inference of the effect from the cause. Two causes were stated: "the turning away [from saṃsāra] and the cutting off [of the defilements].
By the second intrepidity—that which was stated as "for you who claim to have destroyed the taints," and so forth.

"The establishment of the former" means the establishment of the meaning of the preceding word. By the first—that which was stated as "for you who claim to be a perfectly enlightened Buddha," and so forth.
By the intrepidity thus described. "The second accomplishment" means the accomplishment of the meaning of the second phrase;
that is to say, the accomplishment of the Buddha’s purpose. "By the third and fourth" refers to the third and fourth forms of intrepidity stated respectively as:
"Those things which are obstructive... and "That for the sake of which you [teach]... "The third accomplishment" is the accomplishment of the state of having the veil removed.
Indeed, by way of teaching the obstructive and emancipating states exactly as they are, the Teacher’s state of having removed the veil [of ignorance] became manifest to the world.

The first phrase, "the eye of Dhamma," establishes the Blessed One’s *dhammacakkhu* (eye of Dhamma), because it demonstrates the destruction of the spokes of the defilements—the enemies—and of the wheel of *saṃsāra*. The second phrase establishes the *buddhacakkhu* (eye of a Buddha).

This is because that [quality] exists only in the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). The third term, "all-seeing" (*samantacakkhu*), establishes this by illustrating the abandonment of all defilements (*kilesa*) together with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*).

For, having stated "Perfectly Enlightened One," the expression "one who has rolled up the veil" (*vivaṭṭacchada*) elucidates the abandonment of all defilements which brings about the state of Buddhahood.
In the explanation of the characteristic "heroic nature" (*sūrabhāva*), it refers to the clarity of knowledge (*visadañāṇatā*).
259. Thus, *evaṃ* here is a particle used for accepting a statement. And in this context, "accepting a statement" refers to the acceptance of the words spoken by Pokkharasāti, which proceeded thus:
"In that way we shall know that venerable Gotama; you are a receiver of mantras.
Regarding the phrase "He too, by that... and so forth: therein—

"By that" means by that aforementioned exhortation. "A non-ground for the vehicle" means a place where there is no ground for a vehicle. "Those who practice daytime meditation" means those devoted to the practice of meditating during the day.
(260) Although the Ambaṭṭha family was previously unknown, it became known at that time; thus he said, "It is said that at that time," and so forth. "Without haste" means without being hurried.
261. "Just as [the Blessed One] inquired about their well-being, etc. means that just as the Blessed One—inquiring about their well-being with the words, "Is it bearable for you, young men?

Is it sustainable? and so forth—first initiated a joyful conversation with those young men by being the first to speak, in imitation of that, those young men likewise shared in the joy with the Blessed One.
The construction is: *ahesuṃ* (they were). To illustrate that state of being equally flowing with a simile, it is said: "like cool water," and so forth.
Therein, *sammoditaṃ* means blended together. *Ekībhāvaṃ* means the commonality through the act of mutual greeting.
*Khamanīyaṃ* [refers to] this body-machine, consisting of four wheels and nine doors, which by its very nature is full of suffering...
"Do you think it would be possible to endure what is difficult to bear?"—thus they ask. "Is it sustainable? means:
Is it possible to sustain one's life through the continuity of long-term maintenance, which depends on the requisites such as food?

"Are you free from illness? means: Are you free from afflictions such as diseases of the head? "Are you free from distress? means: Are you free from the hardships of a miserable livelihood? [And] "Are you at ease in your exertion" means: because of the ease with which you undertake various duties...
The meaning should be understood by applying the word *kacci* (I hope) to each instance: "Is there lightness? because of its association with corresponding strength;
"Is there strength? because of the presence of dwelling in happiness; and "Is there well-being? because of the presence of dwelling in comfort.

Joy that has reached the stage of strength is simply *pīti* (rapture). Fresh joy is *pāmojja* (gladness). It is called *sammodanika* because it generates or produces gladness (*sammodana*); that very same thing is also *sammodanīya* (conducive to gladness).
The phrase "suitable for greeting" (*sammodanīya*) is stated here to show the meaning [of the root] as "that which is fit to be greeted" (*sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato*).
Because it is a state to be remembered and a state to be recollected, although it should be called "saraṇīya," it is stated with a long vowel as "sāraṇīya.
By the phrase "because it is pleasant when being heard," he refers to its sweetness upon first reaching the senses; by the phrase "because it is pleasant when being recollected,"...
“Delightfulness in crushing”: by the phrase “purity of phrasing,” he expresses the eloquence of speech in that discourse through its possession of natural expression;
by “purity of meaning,” he expresses the state of the meaning being free from defilement. “By numerous methods” means by numerous reasons.
“I will cause him to be put to shame” means I will make him feel humiliated. “Having hung it around his neck” means having fastened the garment upon both shoulders.
"Having hung [it] around his neck. "Grasping the hem of the robe" means grasping the end of the corner of the lower garment (*sāṭaka*) with one hand.
"Having ascended the walking-path" means having begun to walk up and down. "Balance of the elements" (*dhātusamatā*) means the state of equilibrium among the elements such as taste (*rasa*);
the meaning is health (*arogatā*). "Leading to a state of misconduct" means that which is to be remembered by way of misconduct.
“‘Indeed, this is improper conduct’—this is what must be remembered.
(262) The phrase beginning with “As if desiring to seize the pinnacle of existence” is stated to show that he undertakes a difficult task because it is impossible [to accomplish].
For this—that is, the disparagement of the Blessed One—is impossible even for the world together with its devas; therefore, he said:
“He exerts himself inappropriately”: this fool will only further increase his pride, thinking, “If I say nothing, he does not even dare to speak with me”;
however, when he speaks, if his birth and clan are revealed through the course of conversation, his pride will be subdued.
Therefore, the Blessed One said, “Is it thus for you? and so forth. Thus it was said: “Then the Blessed One,” etc.

They are *ācariyas* because they train others in proper conduct (*ācāra*) and right behavior (*samācāra*). Furthermore, they are *pācariyas* because they are preeminent among those *ācariyas*, just as one speaks of a "great-grandfather" (*papitāmaha*);
thus he said, "by their teachers and by their preceptors.
Commentary on the First Charge of Arrogance.
263. "In three postures" means while standing, walking, or sitting. "Slandering by way of talk" refers to taking up a position of opposition through speech.
For one who lies down together with a teacher, such talk is not proper conduct;
here, "slandering by way of talk" refers to speaking in a manner that treats oneself as equal to the others.

Furthermore, that which was spoken by the Teacher while conversing with Ambaṭṭha—intended to reveal his state of improper conduct—is not included in the formal recitation (saṅgīti), but has been handed down through oral tradition.
Showing this as the connection to the subsequent text, he said, "Then it is said," and so forth.
In the terms *muṇḍakā* and *samaṇakā*, the suffix *-ka* expresses contempt; therefore, he said, "scorning. Of the ibha...
The term *ibbha* is formed by eliding the latter member of the compound; those who deserve (*arahanti*) that *ibha* are called *ibbhā*. What is meant?

Just as an *ibha*—being a mount for an elephant—is subject to the control of another and not to its own will, so too these *suddas*, being subservient to the brahmins, are subject to the control of others and not to their own;
therefore, because their mode of application is similar to that of an *ibha*, they are called *ibbhā*.
Because they live as householders with families and are masters of their homes, he calls them "householders" (*gahapatika*). "Black ones" (*kaṇha*) means those of black birth;
for his intention is that only the twice-born (*dija*) are of pure birth, not others, which is why he says "the dark ones" (*kāḷaka*).
"Emerged from the mouth" means that the ancestors of the brahmins emerged from the mouth of Brahmā; this is [the meaning] regarding them.
The intended meaning is "the first arising. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

However, the statement "recluses from the back of the foot" is an exceedingly unconsidered remark, even more so than the statement "emerged from the mouth," because the state of being a recluse is possible for one belonging to any of the four castes.
"Without specifying" means without making a distinction; the sense is "without designation."
"He speaks by way of human conceit" means that, relying on human conceit, exalting himself and disparaging others, he says "shavelings," and so forth.
"I make known" means that by explaining the measure of one's birth and clan as it truly is, he makes that measure known.
"It has a purpose" means it possesses a purpose, according to the principle of the "staff-bearer" (daṇḍika-nyāya).

Regarding the phrase “But for whatever purpose,” they say it is stated by way of the feminine gender; however, that is not appropriate because later it will be stated, “by way of the masculine gender.
Alternatively, in the expression “for whatever purpose” (*yāya atthāya*), the dative case is used in the sense of the object (*tadattha*) by way of the masculine gender;
the meaning is “for the sake of which purpose. The connection is: “having shown this to him,” namely, to Ambaṭṭha. “To others” (*aññesaṃ*)...
"Of others who are of good character": of those who have approached the presence of those worthy of reverence. "Conduct": the behavior that ought to be practiced by them.
"Untrained": untrained in conduct; for that very reason, he was of little learning.
Indeed, much learning should be sought only insofar as it serves the purpose of tranquility; because of the absence of that, Ambaṭṭha was of little learning and untrained.
"It is understood as 'unbound' (avusita)"; therefore he said, "Of this," and so forth. 264.
"Displeased" means being unwilling due to a mind overcome by anger. "For the purpose of crushing pride" means for the purpose of humbling pride.
"Having made it vomit up" means having caused that which was moistened by the intake of oil to be ejected. "Lineage after lineage" means by that ancient lineage spoken of by him.
Now, having raised up and extracted that respective lineage (gotta) designated as blameless from its state of being blameworthy—the same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

In this context, "lineage" (gotta) should be understood by way of the primordial ancestors, while "defilement of the clan" (kulāpadosa) is to be understood by way of the famous persons who arose in their descendants, such as "Ādicca" and "Māghadeva.
This is because the contemptibility of the root of the lineage is explained through the fact that it does not constitute a basis for being considered superhuman (amānava).
“It is said: ‘Having cut down the banner of conceit at its root. *Ghaṭṭento* means insulting.
That in which the underlying tendencies of conceit and anger are mutually entrenched is called “fierce”;
thus he says, “‘Fierce’ means possessed of anger based on conceit. *Kharā* means harsh in mind and speech. *Lahukā* means tender. *Bhassā* means...
"Some say 'violent ones' (sāhasikā), others say 'aggressive ones' (sārambhakā). Being equal, the meaning is 'those who exist';

thus he said, 'The word "santa" is a synonym for the preceding word. "They do not honor" means they do not perform acts of respect. "Acts of veneration" (apacitikamma) refers to the act of prostration;
"not in accordance" means not suitable for one's own birth.
Commentary on the Second Type of Unrighteousness (Dutiya-aihibhavādavaṇṇanā) 265.
Granted that in the Sakyan royal family, only he who is the most eminent among all and capable receives the consecration;
yet, once consecrated, some become disillusioned with it, thinking, "This thing called kingship involves many duties and much toil."
He hands over the kingdom to his immediate successor in age, and sometimes that person in turn to another; it is with reference to such cases that he says, "The Sakyas are consecrated kings.
"Knowing their family lineage" means they know it by way of oral tradition, handed down in succession starting from Kaṇhāyana.
For those who take pride in their lineage generally describe the high and low status of other families in various ways.
They know their own family lineage, and Ambaṭṭha did likewise; for when he was questioned later by the Blessed One, he spoke truthfully out of fear of Vajirapāṇi.
The commentary on the third reproach regarding being an outcaste.
266. "Clods from the field" means clods raised by the plough in the course of tilling the field.
The small bird known as the *laṭukikā* is referred to in the commentary on the *Laṭukikopama Sutta* as the "cātaka bird.
"To seize through anger" means to provoke or to harbor resentment; this is the meaning. "Us, who are like swans, cranes, and peacocks..."

By the words "he does," he shows that the statement beginning with "No swan indeed... was spoken by the Blessed One at that very time, even though it had not yet been included in the formal recitation (saṅgīti).
He says, "thinking 'now he has become conceited,'" with the intention that the statements beginning with "Is it thus for you?
and "He has surely lived in vain" were spoken by the ascetic Gotama out of pride.
267. Regarding the commentary on the "Discourse on the Son of a Slave Woman":
He says "he humbles" (*nimmadetī*) because this is a grammatical explanation formed by changing the vowel *a* to *ā*.
Granted, a clan name (*gotta*) is indeed received from the father, not from the mother; for among the Brahmins, marriage with a woman of the same clan is not desired.
As for the name of the clan (*gottanāma*), however, because it is established by birth and not artificial, and because birth pertains to both [parents], it is therefore said:
"maternal and paternal" means "belonging to the mother and father. "Name and clan" (*nāmagotta*) refers to the clan-name, not an artificial name or a name based on qualities.
In this context, referring to that conventional designation which is well-established as "Kaṇhāyana," he says: "by way of designation... (*paṇṇattivasena*).
They call it that. Furthermore, that [name] has come down from the time of Kaṇha onwards by way of family lineage; it is not merely conventional (*nirūḷha*) for this [individual] alone.
Therefore it is said: "Gotra (clan) by way of tradition. The meaning of the word *gotra*, however, has already been stated above.
Regarding the phrase "recalling," here not only mere recollection is intended, but rather [recollection] by way of investigating the purity of the family.
He said, "Of one who purifies his lineage to its very root. He said, "The son of a noble lady" (ayyaputta), meaning "the son of a noble woman" (ayyikāputta), which means "the son of a master.
He said, "The son of a house-slave," because Ambaṭṭha was born as a slave within the household of King Okkāka.

And herein, since Ambaṭṭha was stiff with pride on account of his birth, and his pride would not be subdued unless his birth were revealed as it truly is, [the Buddha spoke thus]. Regarding the subduing of pride:
And later on, he will have faith in the Triple Gem; thus, although the words "slave" are indeed harsh speech, they do not constitute [a fault] because of the gentleness of the mind.
In this regard, the *Abhayasutta* serves as an illustration. Furthermore, some beings become softened by harsh speech, just as iron and other metals are softened by fire;
therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to make Ambaṭṭha free from his haughty pride, [spoke thus].
“Noble sons, you are Sakyas; you are the son of a slave-girl of the Sakyas,” he said.
“They establish” means they designate; therefore he says, “Okkāka,” and so forth. Light radiates from his teeth because of their exceedingly brilliant nature.
“Of the first-kappa beings” means of those born at the beginning of the first kappa. The word *kira* indicates hearsay or tradition.
By this, he indicates any disagreement regarding the succession of kings that might arise when it is being recounted.
"Of Mahāsammatassa" means of him who was so designated as "Mahāsammatassa" because the great multitude, having deliberated, established him [with the words], "This one is our king.
With reference to whom they say:
“Born of the Solar Dynasty, a mine of perfectly pure virtues,
you are a king of great majesty named Mahāsammata.
You are the eye of the world, radiant with the rays of your qualities.”
Dispelling the darkness, he shone forth like a second sun.
By him, who seeks the welfare of the world, the boundaries established in the world are fixed such that people are unable to transgress them.
"That which they call 'Manu' is the first-born Great Hero, the protector of the world's boundaries, possessed of glory and splendor.
And this refers to the succession of his sons and grandsons.
His son was Mahāteja, a lord of the earth named Roja;
his son was Vararoja, preeminent within the circle of kings.
His biological son was Kalyāṇa, possessed of auspicious qualities.
The king had a son named Varakalyāṇa.
His son was the great hero Mandhātā, the foremost among those who enjoy sensual pleasures,
who was honored by Mahinda with half the kingdom.
His son was Mahāteja, named Varamandhātu;
his son was the highly renowned one known by the name Uposatha.
His son was Mahāteja, named Vara; his son was Mahāvara.
To her was born Upavara, a king of great power.
His son was Makhādeva, a lord of the earth equal to a god;
his lineage of sons numbered eighty-four thousand.
"The last of them was a king known as Okkāka,
of great fame and great majesty, not insignificant within the circle of kings.
The phrase "the beginning of them" refers to those in the lineage of Maghadeva, ending with Kaḷārajanaka.
After many hundreds of thousands of kings, there was a king named Okkāka;
after many hundreds of thousands of kings descended from him in succession, there was another king named Okkāka;
and after many hundreds of thousands of kings descended from him in succession, there was yet another king named Okkāka—it is with reference to this that it was said.
“There were three Okkāka lineages. Among them, [it was] of the third Okkāka,” and so forth.

“He gave a boon hastily” means that, having attained joy through seeing his son, he gave a boon hastily, without reflection, out of delight, saying, “Take whatever you wish. She desired to transfer the kingdom.
“Jantukumāra’s mother, setting aside that boon of mine, wishes to divert this kingdom [to him].
“He would not be able” means he would not be capable.
“Having gone forth” means having departed from the household life and having departed from sensual pleasures. By the word “and” (*ca*) in the phrase “eight cubits,” it is understood as “and below.”
This draws [the following] into context: "By them" means by the deer and pigs, and by the frogs and mice. "Those" refers to the lions, tigers, and so forth, as well as the snakes and cats.
"With the rest" means with their respective younger siblings.

Regarding the term "vaḍḍhamānānaṃ," the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (anādara). As for leprosy (*kuṭṭharoga*), it is said that "having considered that this disease is contagious," because, like smallpox (*sāsa*) and measles (*masūrī*), it is for the most part of a contagious nature.
Regarding the phrase "deer, pigs, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes forest-dwelling animals such as boars and the like.
The connection is with the words "while he was seated there. By declaring his lineage through the proclamation of his Kṣatriya status, he made known his own status as a member of the warrior caste.
"Build a city" means the intention is: "build a city provided with provisions."
"Seizing by the hair" means binding the hair with a fillet. "Seizing by the garment" means the manner of wearing a cloth as an undergarment.
"For the sake of releasing himself from reproach" means for the purpose of removing the slander that should have been directed against himself by both the Teacher and Ambaṭṭha.
"In this statement" refers to what was spoken by himself, beginning with: "There are these four castes, Master Gotama."
And regarding the statement "in the discourse on birth" spoken by the venerable Gotama— referring to this very subject under discussion—
it is said "in the speech of the three Vedas" because he must respond according to the method prescribed in the Vedas;
and it is also said "or in this speech concerning the son of a slave-girl."

270. *Dhamma* here means a cause, as in such expressions as "analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*). That which is together with the *dhamma* is *sahadhamma*; that which is *sahadhamma* is thus called *sahadhammika*.

Therefore, he says "with a reason" (*sahetuka*). 271. "Therefore, because of what was admitted at that time. He had come thinking, "I will make him answer the question by intimidating him," just as occurred in the assembly with Saccaka.
Regarding the statement, "The Blessed One sees and Ambaṭṭha sees," in order to show the reason why others do not see, [he asks]: "If..."

The words beginning with "Hī" have been stated. "Having summoned" means having brought [him] by the power of mantras. "Of him" refers to Ambaṭṭha. "In the clash of debate" means in the clash of speech. 272. "Seeking protection":
seeking the Blessed One alone as his "protection," thinking, "This very ascetic Gotama is my protector from this fear.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "He protects" means [he protects one] from the fear that has arisen.
He protects; therefore, it is said, "he guards. By this, he expresses that the word *tāṇa* (protection) has the agent as its grammatical derivation (*kattusādhana*).

That which is resorted to for concealment by one who is afflicted by fear as it arises is a *leṇa* (refuge); it is a place of shelter. By this, he expresses that the word *leṇa* has the locus as its grammatical derivation (*adhikaraṇasādhana*).
By the word "he remembers" (*sarati*), he expresses that the word *saraṇa* (recollection/refuge) has the agent as its grammatical derivation.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Ambaṭṭha Lineage: 274.
“To the south of the Ganges” means to the southern direction of the river Ganges.
“The weapon does not turn” means that when one wishes to hurl an arrow, a spear, or the like at another, the hand does not turn; [the weapon] remains in the hand.
But since there was no exchange of weapons when [the body] had not yet been exchanged, he said, "The weapon is not exchanged.

It is said that, loathing that lowly birth, thinking, "How indeed have I been born in the womb of a slave-girl of the Disā clan?", he went forth, saying, "Come now, I shall purify this birth by whatever means possible";
therefore he said, "Now I shall fulfill my heart's desire," and so forth.

His intention was that from the moment he had obtained the king’s daughter by intimidating the king with the power of his *vijjā*, she would become one whose birth was purified for him. *Ambaṭṭha* refers to a spell;
the meaning is a charm (*manta*) so named because it places an ointment (*abbhaṅga*) upon the bodies of beings. Since this [spell] exists in him, he is called *Ambaṭṭha*.
The seer Kaṇha was known as Ambaṭṭha; because this youth was born of his lineage, he is designated as "Ambaṭṭha.
The meaning is that [he knew] the most excellent mantras and Vedic spells. By the power of those mantras, the king’s arms became paralyzed;
because of that paralysis of his arms, the king became afraid, apprehensive, and terrified, thinking, "Who knows? What will happen?"
Because he was thus [afraid], it is said: "He stood trembling with fear.
They spoke these words beginning with "May there be safety, O Venerable One," thinking, "This is a seer of great power.
"Undriyissati" means it will be scattered; therefore, he said, "it will break apart. "Mante parivattite" refers to the *bāhukkhambhaka* charm.
When the mantras known as *paṭippassambhaka-vidyā* were recast as "Let the arrow descend," such mantras are exclusively pacifying spells, just like those of the *kusumāraka-vidyās*.
His making [the boy] a freed slave was for the purpose of clearing his daughter of reproach;
and for the purpose of establishing her in a corresponding high station of authority, [he bestowed upon her] the magnificent...
And he established him in his proper place.
[This was] said for the purpose of consolation, out of compassion, not for the purpose of displaying noble birth; therefore he said: "Then..."
“‘The Blessed One,’ and so forth. ‘Among the brahmins’ means in the vicinity of the brahmins;
with reference to the seats and other things obtainable from them, it is said ‘in the midst of the brahmins. ‘To be done out of mere faith’ (saddhaṃ) means it should be performed out of faith alone;

the meaning is that it should be done by one who does not expect anything in return for the sake of one who has passed away to the next world. Therefore he says: ‘at a meal prepared in honor of the dead.’”

By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "Maṅgalādibhatta," one includes [rites such as] festivals and propitiation of deities. "Yaññabhatta" refers to offerings made under the impression that they are meritorious or for similar reasons.
"Pāhunakānaṃ" means guests. He has not attained the status of a *khattiya* because he lacks birth on both sides;
therefore, it says: "The meaning is 'impure.'"
276. Regarding the phrase "having made into a woman": here, since the term *karaṇa* (making) refers to the general category of action, he says, "having sought out a woman.
Even if one takes a Brahmin girl as a woman to be the wife of a Kṣatriya prince, the Kṣatriyas are still superior and the Brahmins are inferior;
such is the construction. Or, regarding the phrase "or by a man having made [him] a man," the same method applies here as well. In the context (*pakaraṇe*).
When the cause is corrupted and disturbed by passion and the like, he therefore said "in faults" (*dose*). It is called *bhassa* because it is scattered—that is, thrown away—due to its uselessness;

it means ashes. "In that which is produced" (*janitasmiṃ*) means produced by karma and defilements. Or, "in that which generates" (*janetasmiṃ*) means among humans; thus he said "those who rely on their lineage" (*gottapaṭisārino*). "Having combined" (*saṃsanditvā*) means having joined together, that is, having made them non-contradictory.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge and Conduct (Vijjācaraṇakathā): 278.
“This is permissible” means that this—such as Vedic recitation (*ajjhena*) and so forth—is allowed to be performed. “Bound to talk about birth” means bound to discourse based upon birth (*jāti*).

"Bound": Just as for a brahmin there is the study, teaching, sacrificing, and officiating at sacrifices, so too those [conceits] that proceed by way of self-exaltation and disparagement of others are bound to pride and the like;
whereas those bound by marriage—by way of the three types of kinship—are those that proceed thus: "Are you worthy of me, or are you not worthy of me?"
“In which”: in which perfection of true knowledge and conduct (*vidyā-caraṇa-sampad*). “We shall cling”: we thought, “we shall become attached and included within.

Since, in the ultimate sense, it is ignorance and misconduct themselves that are grasped under the name “true knowledge and conduct,” when true knowledge and conduct are analyzed in their ultimate sense, he is said to have been cast far away from them; thus he said, “he has thrown him far away.”
"Starting from its origination" means beginning from the point of its arising, such as "from its full attainment" and so forth. 279.
"Threefold morality" refers to the threefold morality divided into the minor and so on. "By way of morality alone" means by way of the synonym for morality (*sīlapariyāyena*).
"This or that" means there exists this or that morality characterized by the prohibitions and observances, such as non-violence and so forth; in each respective case.
"Would cling": it would cling to that very mere morality established in the various systems of the brahmins, [thinking] "this is conduct.

The eight attainments are presented as "conduct"; they are presented—that is, demonstrated—because by the very exposition of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, the state of being expounded is attained for the formless jhānas as well.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Four Gateways to the Lower Realms (Catuapāyamukhakathāvaṇṇanā) 280. "Failing to reach" means being unable to reach [the goal] after having begun. "Unable to endure" means being unable even to begin.
"Requisites" (khāri) refers to the necessary equipment. To demonstrate these by way of classification, it is said: "The fire-drill," and so forth. Therein, "fire-drill" (araṇī) means...
A fire-drill consists of two pieces of fire-wood (araṇī). A ladle is made of *sujāti* wood. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he includes a tripod, a water-pot, and so forth.
"Filled with a *khārī*" means full of *khārīs*. Now, for a fully ordained monk (*upasampanna*), even any non-ordained person belonging to the Dispensation is in fact a servant;
why then mention one who has gone forth as an outsider? In this regard, what is the distinction?
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “kāmañca” was stated. “By the method already described” means by the method stated thus:
“by way of making things allowable... [and] by way of performing the duties. He is an attendant because of the distinguished nature of his status as one who has received full ordination (upasampadā).
By undertaking and practicing the thousands of restraints and disciplines of various kinds mentioned in the passage beginning with “nine thousand million,” he has become superior.
For "attainment" (sampadā) is called "full ordination" (upasampadā) because it is the foremost attainment. "One superior in virtue" means one who is preeminent in virtues.
"But this [ascetic]" refers to the ascetic possessing the characteristics already described.
Those called "ascetics" (tāpasa) are proponents of karma and proponents of action; they are not a bulwark for the Dispensation, which is why one should not go forth among them.

The accuser raises the objection: "Since it was permitted that those who have come [to the Saṅgha] may receive the going-forth even without the probationary period (titthiyaparivāsa) for former sectarians, why then...
The Teacher addresses this objection with the words beginning "Because... To explain in detail the meaning stated briefly as "it will sink back," he says "For in this case...
and so forth. The phrase "the simile of the razor's edge" means by way of the very top of the razor's edge.
"Having stepped upon it, like one going forth"—"others" refers to other bhikkhus. "Fire-hall" means a hall for the fire-sacrifice (*aggihutta*).
"With various kinds of wood" means with various types of fuel-wood such as *palāsa* branches and so forth.
"This" refers to what was stated in the passage beginning, "having built a house with four doors. "Of him" refers to this fourth person.
"Entrance to the practice" means merely the entrance to the practice of hypocrisy. For he remains there, deluding the world with various kinds of hypocrisy;
therefore it was said: "By this entrance, he practices in such a manner.
Standing near people in threshing floors and other such places, [he collects] rice, mung beans, sesame, beans, and so forth, according to the manner of alms-gathering.
"Gathering" (*uñchana*) means picking up scattered grains; those whose practice and livelihood consist of that are "those who live by gleaning" (*uñchācariyā*).
They are called "fire-cookers" (*aggipakkikā*) because they live by food cooked with fire; those who are not fire-cookers are "non-fire-cookers" (*anaggipakkikā*).
For those who live by gleaning go to threshing floors and take the grain known as *khalagga*—that which is being given by people—but these do not take that, and thus they are "non-fire-cookers."
They were born with such names. "Asāmapākā" means those who do not cook for themselves. They subsist by means of *asmamuṭṭhi*, that is, stones held in the fist; thus they are called *asmamuṭṭhika*.
"Dantavakkalika" refers to those who subsist by means of *dantavakkala*—the bark of trees stripped off with the teeth—and thus they are called *dantavakkalika*.
"Pavattaphalabhojina" refers to those who eat fruit that has fallen from trees and other sources; thus they are called *pavattaphalabhojina*. Because of being ripe through age...

*Paṇḍupalāsa* means a withered leaf; that which is similar to this is *paṇḍupalāsa*. They are called *paṇḍupalāsikas* because they subsist by means of it—those who feed on flowers, fruits, and leaves that have fallen of their own accord.

Now, in order to show these eight types [of forest-dwellers] according to their specific characteristics, the passage beginning with "Therein" (*tattha*) was stated. "Having gathered together" (*saṅkaḍḍhitvā*) means having brought together in one place the grain obtained through wandering for alms.

“Seeking” (*pariyeṭṭhi*) means suffering: going from one person’s house to another’s house, seeking [food] is suffering by way of a miserable mode of livelihood. “The grasping of a stone is suffering for a renunciant”:

or else, they eat [the fruit] having plucked it out with their very teeth. “By these four alone”: by these very four types of ascetic renunciation mentioned in the passage beginning with “taking up a basket of salt,” and so forth.

282. One who is fixed upon ruin or destruction is *āpāyika*. Being unable to fulfill that state, one is thereby incomplete or not fulfilling it; this word is used in the instrumental case. Therefore he said: "even by one who is *āpāyika* and not fulfilling [the state].
Commentary on the Practice of the Former Seers (Pubbakaisibhāvānuyoga):
283. It is given (*dīyati*), thus it is a gift (*datti*); a gift itself is a "gift-thing" (*dattika*). He said "given" (*dinna*) in this sense. If there were the presence of a brahmin...
"It should not be given to the king; why was his approaching [the Buddha] not rejected?"—to this he said, "Because... and so forth.

"In the science of agriculture" (*khettavijjā*) means in the treatise on political ethics (*nītisattha*). "Offered" (*payāta*) means with faith or as a regular provision; therefore he said, "brought forward and given.
Why did the Blessed One say, "He eats the gift of King Pasenadi of Kosala," and so on, regarding the brahmin?
To show the reason why he spoke those words of Mamma, it was said: "But this is the reason," and so forth. 284. *Rathūpatthare*:

on the surface spread over the chariot. *Pākaṭamantanaṃ*: a disclosure that has become manifest. For since that is known by the *suddas* and others, it is not a secret counsel (*rahassamantana*). *Bhaṇati*: does he speak? [The question implies] "Does he indeed speak? 285. *Pavattāro*:
those who cause them to proceed by way of oral tradition; because they are the ones who set those counsels in motion, therefore...
He said: "Those who cause it to proceed. In the sense that they are to be spoken in secret, excluding the *sudras*, they are indeed *mantras*;

because they are the cause for the practice of their respective purposes, they are "words" (*pada*); or, because they are not to be shared with those not yet initiated, they are what is to be spoken in secrecy as the means for attaining beneficial action.
"Recited" (*sajjhāyita*) means recited by way of chanting; furthermore, [this refers to] the acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and other [accents].
It is said, "by way of the perfection of the sārās," because it is desired precisely by way of accomplishing the *sārās*.
"Stated for others" means stated for others by virtue of being the oral tradition (*pāvacana*). "Well-arranged" means collected and piled one upon another.

"Compiled" means compiled according to the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and so forth; therein too, each according to the *mantras*, *brahmans*, and so forth, and according to the *adhyāyas*, *anuvākas*, and so forth.
"Of them" means of the authors of the mantras. "Having observed with the divine eye" means:

having observed, by means of the knowledge of the recollection of past lives—which is similar to the divine eye in the sense that it directly sees the ownership of karma and so forth for beings through the supernormal power of the divine eye, and which pertains to past eons—the procedure for the mastery of the mantras of the brahmins; and "having compared it with the current scripture."
Having made it non-contradictory with whatever teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Kassapa was dependent upon the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
For the meaning dependent upon the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*) was not directly evident to them.

"But others and others" means those who arose later and later than Aṭṭhaka and the rest, during the time of King Okkāka and so forth. "Having inserted" means into the sections of the mantras composed by Aṭṭhaka and the others.
Having inserted words concerning the defilements (kilesa) here and there among the various phrases.

"They made them contradictory" means that they made them opposed by illustrating the meaning of defilement according to the method found in such discourses as the *Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta*. "In this place" refers to the context of the statement, "I study those mantras.
"Without taking a formal admission" means without having taken a formal admission in the manner of asking, "What do you think of that? etc.
286. "Free from the stench of raw flesh" (*nirāmagandhā*) means being devoid of the foul odor of the impurities of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"Free from the scent of women" (*anitthigandhā*) means being devoid of the scent of women because they cannot endure even the mere fragrance of women.

And here, by the term "free from the stench of raw flesh," he demonstrates that those ancient Brahmins had suppressed their defilements; and by the phrase "free from the scent of women, living the holy life" (*brahmacārino*), [he shows they were celibate].
By this [phrase], their dwelling alone is indicated; by “wearing dust and dirt,” the absence of devotion to adornment and decoration;
by “they dwelt in forest regions at the foot of mountains,” the secluded life having abandoned the vicinity of humans;

by “they dwelt subsisting on forest roots and fruits,” the rejection of refined food such as fine rice, meat, and boiled rice; and by the words beginning with “when,” the rejection of vehicles and carriages.
By the words beginning with “in all directions,” he rejects the idea of protection and defense.

And speaking thus, he shows that even the conduct of those brahmins—which belongs to the side of the right practice when considered in relation to the noble discipline—is actually a wrong practice when compared to the conduct of Ambaṭṭha and his teacher, which belongs to the side of the wrong practice. How, then, could their practice be associated with the practice of effacement?
With the words “Thus it was heard,” etc., the Blessed One shows that he rebukes and restrains Ambaṭṭha by means of intimidation.

“By means of veṭhakas” means by means of veṭhaka-bands. “Around the city” means all around the city. The intended meaning is that the place at the base of the rampart is called the *katasudhākamma* (the plastered foundation).
Commentary on the Showing of the Two Characteristics.
287. “He is not able”: because their modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*), being contracted, cannot be clearly discerned in their entirety.
“He sought” means he performed a search by means of knowledge. “He brought together” means that, while reflecting with knowledge, he properly brought them together and collected them.
Regarding the word “doubts” (*kaṅkhati*), its meaning is “he desires”; thus he said, “‘Oh, may I see!’—he arouses such an aspiration.”

“Kicchati” means he is weary. Having previously stated that the word “kaṅkhati” has the sense of wishing, he now says, “or by doubt, weak uncertainty is expressed,” showing it as having the sense of doubt through another alternative interpretation. “By three things” means by three kinds of doubtful states.
“The state of turbidity” is the condition of being clouded, which serves as the cause for lack of confidence.
Because the Blessed One’s sheath-covered private organ—the unique, uncommon possession of all Buddhas, not shared by others—is like a perfectly pure circle of gold;
because of its own beautiful shape and configuration, it possesses the supreme loveliness of the noble limbs of a well-bred scent-elephant;

it has the playful grace of the whorls of filaments in a blooming golden lotus; and it bears the splendor of the full orb of the moon distinguished against the expanse of a water-laden forest suffused with the radiance of twilight.

He shines forth, having surpassed [all others] by his own glory; because he is unsullied by external or internal stains, because of his long-standing mastery over the duties of the holy life (*brahmacariya*), and because of the perfection of his well-proportioned form, even though he possesses only a loincloth, he is as if unclothed.
Therefore it is said: "Of the Blessed One," and so forth. "Abundance" (*pahūtabhāva*) means vastness.
For his doubt concerned only this; as for qualities such as his slender, delicate, and tender nature, he did not even consider them.
288. "The occasion for feeling shame" means the ground for being ashamed. "Reflection" means a reflected image. To the question "How? Of what kind?", he says:
"By supernormal power," and so forth. "A mere reflection-form" refers to the Blessed One’s reflected form. And that, moreover, [arose] from the Buddha’s own mental continuum.
Because it is devoid [of consciousness], it is a mere form—a mere magical image consisting of the color, shape, and limbs of the Blessed One’s body.
Yet, when showing that mere form, the Blessed One displays it by acting in such a way that his own Buddha-form is not seen.
"Having led out" means having brought forth. "You are skillful" means you are clever and proficient in answering questions.
“By acting thus” means by making it like a needle for stiffening (kathina). “In this case” refers to the large tongue. It should be understood that its softness is made manifest;
and because it is impossible to make what is not soft dense and subtle, its length and thinness are also indicated. 291.
By the phrase “by one who acts for the benefit [of others],” he clarifies, by way of contrast, the state of acting for the benefit [of others]. Not...
"Aññatra" means "not in another happy destination. "Upanetvā upanetvā" means having repeatedly brought forward each respective fault;
hence he said, "having attributed the state of being a thorough slave and so forth. "Pātesi" means he caused him to fall by way of causing him to roll down.
*Pokkharasātibuddhūpasaṅkamanavaṇṇanā* (The Commentary on the Approach to the Buddha by Pokkharasāti)

293–6. *Āgamā* means “has he come? *Nu* is a mere particle. *Idha* means “here,” that is, “in your presence. *Adhivāsetu* means “may he consent”; since that consent is an acceptance by way of the mind, he says “may he accept.

297. *Yāvadatthaṃ* means “as much as is needed”; the meaning is that the meal was prepared for him to that extent. *Oṇittaṃ* means made clean by the removal of food; therefore he says, “having washed both hands and the bowl.”
298. "Gradual discourse" (*anupubbī-kathā*) means a discourse that ought to be delivered in a gradual sequence; thus he says, "a discourse in successive order.
But what is that? He replies, "the discourse on giving and so forth," beginning with, "After giving comes virtue," and so on.

For this reason, the discourse on giving (*dāna-kathā*) is placed first, because it is common to all people, including the ordinary folk, because it is easy to practice, and because it serves as the means for establishing oneself in virtue.

It should be explained as follows: For a person whose nature is generosity, because of their state of non-attachment toward possessed objects, they undertake the precepts with ease and become well-established therein.

Having spoken of benefiting others through the purity of both giver and recipient by means of virtue, and having spoken of the cessation of harming others; and having spoken of the phenomenon of action (*kiriyadhamma*), one speaks of the phenomenon of non-action (*akiriyadhamma*).

Having spoken of the cause for the attainment of wealth, the discourse on virtue (*sīla*) should be taught immediately after the discourse on giving (*dāna*), because it is the cause for the attainment of existence (*bhava*).
Furthermore, this should be done to show that if that giving and virtue are dependent on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), this attainment of existence is their fruit.

And by means of these bases of meritorious action consisting of giving and virtue—which are distinguished by various degrees such as superior and more superior—one [attains] among the Cātumahārājika gods and so forth.

Immediately following that, the discourse on heaven (*saggakathā*) is given for the purpose of showing that immeasurable celestial enjoyments, distinguished by degrees such as "excellent" and "more excellent," are to be obtained.
This heaven, however, is defiled by lust and other passions;

therefore, to show that the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is entirely undefiled, the discourse on the Path must be taught after the discourse on heaven. And when teaching the Path, one must demonstrate the means for its attainment.

Even those included within the heavenly realms, let alone all others—sensual pleasures (kāma) indeed have many disadvantages; they are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change: this is the disadvantage of sensual pleasures.
They are base, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and not conducive to welfare: this is their degradation and lowliness.
All states of existence (bhava) are the basis for defilements (kilesa): therein lies the corruption. [That which is] entirely free from all corruption...
The meaning should be understood as follows: "Nibbāna" refers to the fact that the benefit (*ānisaṃsa*) in renunciation (*nekkhamma*) must also be explained;

this is what is meant by "awakening" (*bodhi*). Furthermore, in the phrase "the path," the word "iti" indicates the sense of "beginning," thereby including such [teachings] as "the danger in sensual pleasures" (*kāmānaṃ ādīnavo*);
thus it should be understood that this is how the commentary on the meaning has been composed. Why was it said, "for the purpose of showing the manner of its arising"? Is it not [already implied]?
Regarding the objection that "knowledge of the path (maggañāṇa) has the unconditioned dhamma as its object, not conditioned dhammas," [the author] says "for therein," and so forth.
Therein, "penetrating" means penetrating by way of penetration through non-delusion; therefore he says, "by way of function.
[This concludes] the commentary on the discourse concerning the declaration of the lay follower status by Pokkharasāti.
299. And here, regarding the passage beginning with "one who has seen the Dhamma" (*diṭṭhadhammo*), there is another kind of "seeing" apart from the seeing of knowledge (*ñāṇadassana*);

to exclude that, the term "one who has attained the Dhamma" (*pattadhammo*) is stated.
