Furthermore, since there exists another kind of "attainment" apart from the attainment of knowledge, the term "one who has realized the Dhamma" (*viditadhammo*) is stated in order to show its specific distinction.
Moreover, this state of having realized the Dhamma [is not limited to] even a single part...
The term "one who has plunged into the Dhamma" (*pariyogāḷhadhammo*) is stated in order to show that its state of being known is exhaustive.

By this, it illuminates his very full awakening to the Truths (*saccābhisambodha*). For path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*), by accomplishing the tasks of full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth through a single simultaneous realization (*ekābhisamaya*), is said to have "plunged all around" into the Dhamma of the Four Truths exhaustively;
therefore, he says: "One by whom the Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen is 'one who has seen the Dhamma' (*diṭṭhadhammo*)."
"Crossed over doubt": doubt, which resembles a perilous wilderness and has sixteen or eight bases, has been crossed over and transcended.
"Free from wavering" regarding occurrence and so forth: wavering, which occurs in the form "Is it thus?
Is it not thus?", has been removed and utterly cut off. "Attained intrepidity": [freedom] from those evil states that cause timidity.

Because [the obstacles] have been abandoned and because he is well-established in the qualities of virtue and so forth which are their opposites, he has attained and reached *vesārajja*, the state of being confident and proficient.
Considering that this attainment of confidence (*vesārajjappatti*) is a state of being well-established, he says, "in the Teacher’s Dispensation.
Because he has seen it for himself through direct experience and has realized it, he does not rely on another; he does not... [of him].
That which must be understood by oneself is "not dependent on another" (*aparappaccaya*). Whatever remains to be said here that has not yet been stated will follow later.
The rest is easily understood. This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta.
4. Commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta 300.
They are called *Aṅgas* because they possess limbs (*aṅga*) that are preeminent in their beauty; thus he said, “The Aṅgas are so named because of the beauty of their limbs,” and so forth.
Here too, they are intended, not only in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. “They will not allow [him] to come” means...
The intention is that, by demonstrating the disadvantage in coming, they will not allow [him] to come, nor will they grant permission.

Because it is interspersed with blue *asoka*, *kaṇikāra*, *koviḷāra*, *kunda*, and royal tree (*rājarukkha*) blossoms, that campaka grove should be regarded as "adorned with flowers of five colors, such as blue and so forth.
This is not because the campaka trees themselves possess those five colors, such as blue and so forth.
They say: “The Blessed One dwells in the Campaka grove, fragrant with the scent of flowers.
By this it is shown that it was not only at the time of the measuring out [of the city] that Campaka trees were abundant in that city, but rather that they became so at a later time.
For it was due to the abundance of Campaka trees at the time of the measuring out that the city received the name “Campā. “Sovereignty” (issaratta) means the state of being a lord (adhipati).
"One who has an army" is *senika*; *senika* itself becomes *seniya*. And since "possession" here is qualified by multiplicity, it is said:
"because of being endowed with a great army.
301–2. *Saṃhatā* means assembled; where one should say *saṅghino*, the singular form *saṅghī* is used in the sense of plurality.
Because [the term] refers to brahmins and householders, he said, "of these.
The men who carry the goods for kings, royal ministers, and so forth, are *khatā*; they are called *khattā* because they protect (*tāyana*) them.

For wherever and for whomever he is sent, he avoids their faults and explains the matter asked about according to what is appropriate and fitting; therefore he said, "one capable of answering questions when asked."
One who possesses great authority (*mattā*) by virtue of his lineage, position, and so forth, is a *mahāmatta* (high official).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Qualities of Soṇadaṇḍa (303):
A distinguished kingdom is a *virajja*; a *virajja* itself is a *verajja*, just as "vekaṭa" is the same as "vesaya"; it means manifold.
"Various kingdoms" means different kingdoms; everything beginning with "born there" should be understood according to the method already stated.
"A supreme brahmin" refers to one who is more exalted or eminent by virtue of his noble lineage, wealth, and knowledge.
"Not gathering together" means that because he is not oppressed by the desire for gain, he will remain as if not gathered in a crowd.
“It makes known, it causes to go, it indicates, thus it is a ‘factor’ (*aṅga*). It says ‘by this cause as well’ to mean ‘it is the reason.
When only ‘well-born on both sides’ is stated, one might understand being well-born by means of any two parts whatsoever.

Furthermore, since the word ‘well-born’—as in such phrases as ‘well-born and beautiful to behold’—is a synonym for excellence of physical proportions, he uses the phrase ‘from the mother’s side’ to clarify that the state of being well-born is intended here specifically in terms of birth.”
And it is said, “from the father as well. The designation “mother” and “father” is seen in the world even with respect to non-biological children;

however, to show that here it is intended specifically with respect to biological children, it is said, “one of pure lineage” (*saṃsuddhagahaṇiko*). One “takes” (*gaṇhāti*) or “bears” (*dhāreti*) the embryo, thus it is the “womb” (*gahaṇī*);
this refers to the region of the mother’s belly known as the seat of the embryo. By way of digesting the food as it has been consumed...
The *gahaṇī* is the kamma-born fire element because it receives and does not discard [nutriments].
"Father and mother" are the parents; the parents of those parents are the grandfathers (*pitāmahā*). Their pair or dyad is the "grandfather-dyad" (*pitāmahayuga*).
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "as far as the seventh grandfather-dyad," that is, the seventh pair of grandfathers. For it is thus...
By the mention of the "grandfather" (pitāmaha), the maternal grandfather is also included; therefore, he is not mentioned separately in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

Here, the word *yuga* should be understood according to the rule of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*) as "the father and the father—[these] are the *yugas*. For in this way, the dual compound (*dvanda*) is effectively captured in each instance.
Thus it was said: "Beyond that, all preceding ancestors are also included by the mention of the grandfather."
In this context, it should be understood that the mention of "a man" (*purisa*) is made by way of a formal description of the highest limit (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*).

For it is in this way that the Pāli expression "on account of his mother" (*mātito*) is justified. "Not thrown away" (*akkhitta*) means one who has not been cast off. "Not discarded" (*anavakkhitta*) means one who has not been thrown away or abandoned in matters such as offerings of faith or *thālipāka* rice-porridge.
To show that the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*) is used here in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), [the text] says: "by what reason," and so forth.

It has been stated. And here, by the phrase “from both sides... through ten generations of ancestors,” the absence of defects in the Brahmin’s lineage is shown, because of the description of his being of pure descent on both maternal and paternal sides.
By the term “uncensured” (*akkhitto*), the absence of transgression in ritual action is indicated; for it is through transgression in ritual action that beings incur reproach.
By the term “unreproached” (*anupakkuṭṭho*), the absence of improper association is indicated. Improper association also...
For it is by depending on these that beings receive abuse.
"Lord" (issara) means one whose nature is to rule through the power of karma conducive to sovereignty;

however, since his lordship becomes manifest through the condition of the attainment of wealth, he says, "The wealthy man is the lord," speaking thus in the sense of being a synonym for opulence. Great wealth...
“Possessing great wealth” means having both land-based and aerial [treasures]. “Of him” means of this or that [person]. They say:
“We shall describe the reasons for not approaching, both through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
“Of superior form” means of distinguished form, one with an excellent body. “Worthy of being seen” means *dassanīya*; thus he said, “suitable for seeing.”
It brings forth confidence, thus it is "gracious" (*pāsādika*); hence he said, "because it generates confidence in the mind.
"Of the complexion" means of the complexion-element (*vaṇṇa-dhātu*). "Body" refers to the collection of parts—hands, feet, neck, head, and so forth—distinguished by their arrangement;

and since that is understood by way of its configuration (*saṇṭhāna*), it is stated: "by the supreme excellence of the bloom of complexion... and by the attainment [of beauty]. Among all complexions...
"Of supreme golden hue" means "endowed with the most excellent golden color.
For it is indeed Buddhas and Universal Monarchs who possess such a golden complexion. "Brahmavacchasī" means having the radiance of a supreme body; the sense is that he has the luster of gold.
It is with reference to this very meaning that [it is said]: "With a body exactly like the body of Mahābrahmā..."
It is said, “endowed [with these]”, but not with the quality of having limbs as straight as a Brahma’s.

“One who has no small space for being seen” means that because of his perfection of height and girth, and because of the fullness of his limbs, the space for seeing him is not small; thus he says, “all of them,” and so forth.

He is “virtuous” (sīlavā) because he possesses virtue (sīla) characterized by restraint and non-restraint. Furthermore, that virtue of his is “grown” and “increased” due to its long-standing familiarity.
"An elder in virtue" (*vuddhasīlī*) means one who is always endowed with virtue through right application.
They say all this refers only to the five precepts, because beyond those there is no further virtue in that context, and because they [the interlocutors] do not know it.

Due to the perfection of the places and modes of articulation (*ṭhānakaraṇa*), and due to the perfection of training (*sikkhā*), there is no deficiency anywhere; thus the words are complete and well-rounded (*parimaṇḍala*).

"Parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā" means that its syllables (*akkharāni*) are the "phrasing" (*byañjanāni*). Alternatively, a "word" (*pada*) is so called because meaning is reached (*pajjati*) through it; thus, it refers to nouns and the like.
A "phrase" (*byañjana*) is so called because it makes manifest (*byañjeti*) the intended meaning; thus, it refers to a sentence. It is "parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā" due to the completeness of those two.
Or, speech itself is the "instrument of speech" (*vākkaraṇa*) because it is the means for making the meaning known; thus, it is the sound of utterance.
By virtue of the perfection of qualities belonging to that brahmin, or to the meaning expressed by him; *pūre* means in the state of being full.
In the first sense, the locative case is used for the substratum (*ādhāra*); in the second, for the object (*visaya*).
By the phrase "by way of delicacy," he expresses the soft and smooth nature of that speech. It is unobstructed by bile, phlegm, and so forth. All is directly perceived (*sanditṭha*).
“Partial exposition” is speaking by way of showing only a portion, as if [the whole were being shown]. “Dilated” means speaking slowly, after a long delay.

Alternatively, the reading is “doubtful, dilated, etc.”; therein, “doubtful” means that which generates doubt. By the word “etc.,” one includes [qualities such as] being difficult to enunciate (*dukkhalita*) or being dragged out (*anukaḍḍhita*).
By the phrase “having made the beginning, middle, and end clear,” they state the completeness of the meaning of that speech.
The words beginning with “*jiṇṇo*” (old) are easy to understand, and their meanings have already been explained above.

However, in the second method, “*jiṇṇo*” does not mean old merely by way of age (*vayomatta*), but rather old by way of the antiquity of his lineage (*kulaparivaṭṭena*). Thus he said, “*jiṇṇo* means ancient,” and so forth;
by this, he expresses that the brahmin’s status has been successively elevated through his family line. By way of increase in birth, [he is] “*vayoanuppatto*” (one who has reached [advanced] years).
Because [the term] will be explained later, and because he possesses an excellence that is superior even to the increase of virtues, it is said:
“*Vuddho* means one who is endowed with the increase of virtues such as moral conduct (*sīla*) and behavior (*ācāra*).

Likewise, because his great age will be explained later, the word “*mahallako*” (venerable) is applied to denote greatness in worldly prosperity (*vibhava*). “*Maggapaṭipanno*” means having entered the path of practice of the brahmins, because he proceeds without deviating from it.
"Antimavayanti" means they reach the final stage of life.
Commentary on the Qualities of the Buddha (304):
Even for those of such great majesty, to be held in a pair with me is not fitting for one like me.
Regarding the phrase "But from where [could there be] an exaltation?", he said, "Indeed, this is not fitting for me," and so forth, demonstrating that such a claim is not appropriate for a brahmin.
"Similar" means similar in some respect; for no qualities whatsoever can be found in others that are identical in every way to the qualities of the Buddhas.
"The others" refers to those qualities that are not similar to his own qualities. "This" refers to this collection of matters.
*Gopadakaṃ* means water standing in a cow’s footprint.
*Saṭṭhi-kula-sata-sahassaṃ* means one hundred thousand and sixty thousand families; that is, it has come down through the succession of the royal lineage of the Great King Suddhodana.
*Tesupi* means even among those four treasures. *Gahita-gahitaṃ* means taken, taken [again and again].
The place was filled with wealth and returned to its original state. "Immeasurable indeed" means it was truly unlimited, being impossible for anyone to delimit it by saying, "It is this much.
"Therein" means on the couch. "He assumed the lion’s posture" means just as Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, does in terms of length, width, and height...
And just as one cannot grasp the limits of the Blessed One’s physical body, so too, while performing a supernormal feat of form, he lay down in the lion’s posture.
Because it is far removed from defilements (kilesa) in the sense of being utterly pure, he said, "noble, supreme, and perfectly pure. In the sense of being blameless...
It is wholesome, but not by way of having a pleasant ripening. In some places eighty-four thousand beings, in others even immeasurable gods and humans;

because in twenty-four locations incalculable and immeasurable gods and humans drank the nectar of the Path and its Fruits—even by a measure of hundreds of thousands of millions they are indeed many—therefore, it is [called a *saṅgaha*] by way of training them in the unsurpassed conduct.

The Blessed One is the teacher of many. "Those" refers to the defilements abandoned by the Blessed One other than sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). "Keḷanā" means fondling (*keḷāyanā*), or seeking after (*dhanāyanā*).

Regarding "one who has no evil as foremost" (*apāpapurekkhāro*): it is said that he places what is not evil before him; or alternatively, it is said that he does not place evil before him—this is the meaning intended to be shown.
To illustrate this, it is stated: "In the nine supramundane states which are not evil," and so forth. Therein, "not evil" (*apāpe*) means the opposites of evil.
And [it refers to] those who are free from evil. Because they have been born into the noble birth by means of the Blessed Buddha—the supreme Brahmā—through his teaching of the Dhamma;
or because they are beneficial (*hitā*) to the Blessed One, that Brahmā, through honoring him and so forth, and through practicing according to his instructions;
or because they know the supreme (*brahma*), noble path, they are called *brahmaññā*—the people known as noble disciples.

Therefore he said, “Sāriputta,” and so forth. To show that the meaning of the phrase “of the brahmin folk” (*brahmaññāya pajāya*) should also be understood by way of the natural brahmin caste, he said, “Furthermore,” and so on. Regarding the terms *tiroraṭṭhā* and *tirojanapadā*:

here, a kingdom (*raṭṭha*) is so called because it is ruled (*rajja*); kings (*rājāno*) are so called because they rule (*rājanti*) by means of it; and those who constitute a portion of that [kingdom] are...
"A region," however, is a country (*janapada*); it is so called because people (*jana*) go there and attain a happy livelihood. Or, the connection is: "having observed the fault in the question.

"Incapacity" means one's own incapacity. The Blessed One provides the answer having understood their *upanissaya*-perfection, the ripening of their knowledge, and the disposition of their minds; this is the intended meaning.
By the phrase “Come, welcome,” he shows affectionate speech preceded by pleasant conversation;
by “gentle,” softness of speech; by “cordial,” skill in returning greetings;
by “not frowning,” a countenance that is serene in every respect; by “open-faced,” ease of address; and by “speaking first,” [he shows...]
By this, he clarifies the Blessed One’s disposition toward welfare, since it creates an opportunity for assistance through the Dhamma.

Regarding the phrase "yattha kira," the particle *kira* has the sense of indicating a lack of approval; by this, he shows that in the place where the Blessed One resided, the absence of danger for humans was not due to the power of the deities, but rather due to the power of the Buddha. Therefore, he says "apica" and so forth.

Since the term "to be instructed" (*anusāsitabbo*) refers to the entire assembly of people to be trained, in order to show specifically the Noble Saṅgha who had been produced [thereby], he says "sayaṃ... [and so on].
The phrase beginning with "or" was stated because it is understood as either an affirmation or a negation of what immediately precedes it.
By the words "or just like him," the alternative already expressed by "or himself" and so forth is reiterated. The inclusion of "or of the first word itself" is the adoption of another alternative.
"Of many founders of sects" refers to Pūraṇa and others—many such founders of sects; and this genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).
“By reason” means by reason characterized by the application of such qualities as fewness of wishes and contentment.
“Newcomers who are new” means newcomers who have recently arrived. “I master” means I know how to delimit or I am able; therefore he says, “I know.
“Even for an eon, if not speaking another [word]”—this is a statement of hypothetical assumption (*abhūta-parikappa*), because there is no one who speaks in that manner.
305. The word *alaṃ* can also mean "worthiness" (or "arahantship"), as in such passages as "it is indeed enough to become disenchanted. Therefore, he said: "‘Alameva’ means ‘it is indeed appropriate.
Because it is to be carried in a bag (*puṭa*) and eaten—that is, consumed—it is called *puṭosaṃ*, meaning provisions for a journey. [The phrase] "by a man with a bag" refers to this.
[End of] the commentary on the reflections of Soṇadaṇḍa.
307. "Belonging to both sides" means belonging to both factions by way of wrong view and right view.
"Cunning" means deceitful. 309.
"Affliction" means mental suffering.
"311-3. *Sujanti homadabbiṃ paggaṇhantesūti*: among those who take up the sacrificial ladle for the purpose of offering;
the meaning is "among the *irubbijja* priests. *Paṭhamo vā*: among those assembled there, he is either the foremost in the act of sacrificing.

*Dutiyo vā*: or the one immediately following him. He says "of the *suja*" (*sujāya*) because this word *suja* is used in the instrumental case. Because it is the primary [vessel] for the *aggihutta* sacrifice..."
Regarding the sacrifice, because it is said that what is given at a sacrifice is given through the mouth of the *sujā*, he says, "given by the *sujā*.

"The Ancients" refers to the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*). "By way of distinction" means by way of the distinction of knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇa*), not merely by the knowledge and conduct desired by the brahmins.
"Of the supreme brahmin" means of the most excellent brahmin by virtue of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*anuttaradakkhiṇeyya*). "The brahminical system" (*brāhmaṇasamaya*)...
The Brahmin’s tenet. Do not break it; do not destroy it. 316.

"Equal and equal" means being equal precisely because one is equal. Since equality is also spoken of by way of comparison with something inferior, he says "except for partial similarity," and so forth, in order to exclude that.
"The elucidation of the family lineage and so forth" means the elucidation of the family and other such matters. Furthermore...
“Siyā” means: moreover, if such a reflection should occur to you—namely, that “complexion establishes the state of being a brahmin”—the same principle applies to the birth from the mantras as well.
[One might think: “Virtue alone will establish the state of being a brahmin. Why so? He says: “For in that case,” and so forth. Complexion and the rest are merely delusions;
for the idea that complexion and birth from the mantras are factors of the state of being a brahmin is nothing more than a delusion.
Because of the absence of unexamined conceit. 317.
Commentary on the Discussion of Virtue and Wisdom:
"The question was asked by the brahmin" refers to the two factors beginning with "he is virtuous," and so forth.
"In this matter" means in this meaning that has been answered exactly as the question was asked. "Of him" refers to Soṇadaṇḍa.
"Pure in virtue" means completely pure and unstained by the attainment of virtue.
How could there be wisdom in one who is immoral? Because of his lack of concentration. How could there be virtue in one who is dull and mute? That is, in one who is dull and mute, lacking in wisdom.
Whence [comes] virtue? From not knowing the classification of virtue and the means for purifying virtue.
"Paññāṇa" is superior, exalted knowledge; it is called "paññāṇa" in order to exclude ordinary knowledge.
Thus, because it knows by way of various modes, it is wisdom (paññā); therefore he said, "Paññāṇa is simply wisdom."
“Washed by virtue” means washed and purified by virtue, which has concentration as its proximate cause, through the purification of all defilements and stains;
therefore he said, “But how? and so forth. In that context, “it washes” means it is purified.

“Like the Elder Mahāsaṭṭhivassa” means like the Great Elder of sixty years. “Even the mere discernment of feelings” (vedanāpariggaha): here, the discernment of feelings refers to [the observation] of whatever has arisen.
Having examined feeling according to its intrinsic nature and its essence, one applies the three characteristics—thinking, "This feeling depends upon contact;
that contact is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change"—and thus develops insight.
For one who is thus practicing insight, it is possible to endure that feeling with ease, thinking, "It is feeling itself that feels. To "suppress feeling" means...
Without following after the arisen painful feeling, but rather initiating insight (vipassanā), one should dispel it by means of insight that has entered its proper course.
"By falling like a jackal" means by lying on the ground on one's chest like a hyena.
"Having washed morality with wisdom" means having thoroughly purified morality at its beginning, middle, and end through wisdom by establishing it in a state of being unbroken and so forth.
318. “Why did he say so?”—with this, he asks for the reason behind the subsequent instruction.

“Modesty” (*lajjā*) refers to the public recognition by the assembly that [he] answered the question asked by the ascetic Gotama through the manifestation of the virtues and faults of his moral conduct and birth.

“No more than this” (*ettakaparamā*) means that the five precepts have this as their highest limit; and the discernment (*paññā*) that clarifies the three Vedas is [to be understood] from its characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), and so forth.
There is no discerning knowledge [that can distinguish between them]; rather, it shows that in this matter we are merely those for whom speech is supreme.
Thus he said: "For us, the mere statement 'virtue and wisdom' is supreme. As for the phrase "But this is the distinction," this refers to the presentation [of the teaching] in the *Sīlaniddesa*;
therefore he said, "It is presented simply as 'virtue' (*sīla*). However, in the *Sāmaññaphala*, it is presented simply as "the fruit of recluseship" (*sāmaññaphala*).

In the exposition of wisdom (*paññā-niddesa*), however, having taken the wisdom of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna-paññā*) as the basis, the presentation of wisdom is made specifically by way of the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*);
therefore, he says, "the first absorption and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse concerning the lay follower Soṇadaṇḍa’s declaration of his status as a lay follower.
"321-2. *Natta* means 'the son of a son. There was no lack of respect [for the Blessed One], nor did he say, 'But as for me,' and so forth, out of disrespect toward the Blessed One;
rather, it was out of fear of the loss of his own gain.
For he, having somehow or other produced esteem for himself among the great multitude and deluded others with hypocrisy, was seeking to acquire gain."
He reflects; therefore he spoke thus. By that, he said: "By this indeed," and so forth.
"In accordance with that moment" means: according to the way his inclination was proceeding at that time; such is the meaning.
Because at that time there was an absence of the ripening of such knowledge as was based on turning away (vivaṭṭa), it was based solely on worldly prosperity (abbhuydana).

Thus, it is said that "the meaning has been shown" by the phrase "having demonstrated the welfare pertaining to the present life and the future life," which means having made it manifest through direct experience.
"Wholesome states" refers to wholesome states belonging to the three planes;

it is also appropriate to say "belonging to the four planes," for which reason he says, "or those conducive to the impression for the sake of Nibbāna in the future. "Therein" refers to the wholesome states.

"In the manner in which he was exhorted": "having incited the brahmin" means having properly encouraged him further and further, having caused him to attain a state of sharp and keen intensity regarding the performance of meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, since this in fact constitutes the generation of enthusiasm for that [task], he said, "having made him zealous.
Thus, both the zeal for the performance of meritorious deeds and such possession of virtuous qualities are necessarily pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*).

"Accomplishing the purpose" means that, having thus encouraged him with zeal and having gladdened him by pointing out other existing virtues, he brought him to a state of perfect joy and satisfaction. [The interlocutor asks:
"If the Blessed One rained down the rain of the Dharma-jewel, why then does he not attain distinction? To this, he says:
“Now as for the brahmin,” and so forth. If this is so, why did the Blessed One rain down such a shower of the jewel of the Dhamma upon him?
He said, “But it was for him alone,” and so forth. For the teaching of the Blessed One is never without purpose.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) of the commentary on the *Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta*.
5. Commentary on the Kūṭadanta Sutta 323.
"In the two previous suttas" refers to the Ambaṭṭha and Soṇadaṇḍa suttas.

"In the same manner as stated" means that whatever has been included here that is similar to what appeared there is explained in the very same manner; the meaning is that it should be understood according to the method already stated there.
He said, "The *ambalaṭṭhikā* is similar to what was stated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* commentary as 'the young mango tree,
the mango stone,'" because it was stated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* commentary:
"Having prepared a sacrificial enclosure, for the sake of a great sacrifice, [one prepares] sacrificial requisites both with consciousness and without consciousness."
Regarding the statement in the Pāḷi, “A great sacrifice has been prepared,” this refers to the act of making those [animals] ready;
thus he said, “‘Prepared’ means made ready. Regarding “a hundred young bulls,” this refers to a hundred strong young bulls who have reached the state of youth;
since they are merely calves and not yet trained oxen or draft animals, he said, “a hundred calves. “These” refers to the bulls and so forth.
"Ending with the bull" (*urabbhapariyosānā*). "Many" (*anekesaṃ*) means of many births. Their multiplicity by way of number is delimited by the mention of seven hundred [beings].

"Of beasts and birds" (*migapakkhīnaṃ*) refers both to wild animals such as the buffalo, the ruru deer, the *sasa* hare, the *kuruṅga* antelope, and the *gokaṇṇa* deer, as well as to birds such as the peacock, the *kapiñjala* partridge, the francolin, the pigeon, and so forth.
(328) They are called "various" (*vidhā*) because they prevent and prohibit that defilement which belongs to merit designated as sacrifice (*yañña*).
It is the dispelling of remorse. For that very reason, because they establish that flow of merit without interrupting it, they are called "establishments" (*ṭhapanā*).
Furthermore, because they function during the three periods—the beginning, middle, and end—of the sacrifice, it is said that "the sacrifice is established";
thus he says, "the meaning is 'establishment' (*tiṭṭhapanā*). They surround and construct, thus they are "requisites" (*parikkhārā*).
"Retinue" has been stated. "The sixteen requisites" means "the sixteen attendants.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Sacrifice of King Mahāvijita (336):
"Former conduct" refers to the practice of merit consisting of the accumulations for enlightenment, which arose in one's own previous births.
For thus, by means of a following treasure, a stationary treasure has been illustrated for him.
"Wealth" (*aḍḍhatā*) means the possession of riches; since that is spoken of in relation to various [levels], he said: "Whoever is wealthy through some personal wealth.
Likewise, in order to show that even "great wealth" reaches its ultimate limit, he said: "By great, immeasurable number..."
It is said, "endowed with wealth. Because they are to be enjoyed and consumed, sensual pleasures (kāmā) are specifically called "possessions" (bhoga);
thus he says, "by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure. "By way of morsels" means by way of mere fragments, without making distinctions such as vessels, ornaments, and so forth.

“Māsaka, etc.”—by the word “etc.,” items such as bowls (*thālaka*) and so forth are included. “Vessels, etc.”—by the word “etc.,” items such as clothing, bedding, and dwellings (*vasatha*) are included.
Gold, silver, gems, pearls, beryl, diamonds, and coral are called the “seven treasures” (*sattaratanāni*).

Rice, paddy, and so forth are “grain” (*pubbaṇṇa*), because they are considered to have the six fruits at their head. By way of contrast to that, mung beans, black gram, and so forth [are called “after-harvest”].
"Other food. "Daily," etc., means by way of the procedure for consuming, giving, and increasing [the supply] day after day;
it refers to the rotation of wealth and grain.
A "storehouse" (koṭṭha) is said to be the place where grain is stored; a house that serves as such a storehouse is a "granary" (koṭṭhāgāra); thus he said.

“With grain... and with respect. Having thus shown that the inner core is the “sheath” (*kosa*) and the place where the grain is stored is the “storehouse” (*koṭṭhāgāra*), the passage beginning with “or else” (*atha vā*) is now stated to show it in another way.
In this regard, just as a covering is called a “sheath” because it preserves the sharpness of a sword, so too [it is called a sheath] because it preserves the king’s sharpness.
Regarding the "fourfold army," he said, "The treasury is fourfold: elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Because the mention of the "storehouse" (vatthakoṭṭhāgāra) already includes all places where goods are stored, it is stated that "the storehouse is threefold.
Saying, "This is so much," and so forth, the King—already knowing the matter himself—had the treasurer speak [these words] for the purpose of ensuring silence among the assembly.
He said, "In this way, there will be no disturbance to my established order.

(337–8) The brahmin thought: "For the sake of ensuring the country remains free from calamity and for the sake of allowing the sacrifice to proceed for a long time," and therefore he said, "This king," and so forth.
Because they ruin the welfare and happiness of beings and bring about harm and suffering, they are indeed thieves.
"Thorns" refers to those thorny robbers. Just as "village-destroyers" are those who kill villagers, so too "road-robbers" are those who plunder and harass travelers on the road.
"One who acts unrighteously" (*adhammakārī*) means one whose nature is to perform what is contrary to the Dhamma and improper;
a Kshatriya is so called because he protects his own realm, country, and so forth from harm, which is the duty of a Kshatriya (*khattadhamma*).
The meaning is that they have the habit of not performing [their duties]. Because they are like stakes (*khīla*), they are called "stake-like spies" (*dassukhīla*).

For just as a stake in a field obstructs the easy progress of plowing and so forth, and—by means of its root-spread—obstructs the growth of the crops, even so do spies, within the kingdom, obstruct the easy administration of royal commands and, through the proliferation of their roots, obstruct the prosperity of the districts.
Therefore it was said: “The *dassu* (eye) itself, because it is like a stake, is the ‘stake of the eye’ (*dassukhīla*).

For the word *vadha* also has the sense of harming; thus it was said: “by killing or by beating. By the phrase “by means of binding with leather straps, etc.,” the word “etc. includes binding with ropes, binding with chains, and so forth.
“By loss” means by the loss of wealth; hence he said: “Seize a hundred,” and so on. “Shaving the head into five tufts” (*pañcasikhamuṇḍakaraṇa*)...
"Making [the head] like a crow's wing. "Sprinkling with cow dung" means sprinkling the head with water mixed with dung.
"Binding with a cudgel" means binding with a leather thong. By the word "etcetera," one includes such acts as shaving the head with a razor and crushing it with a handful of ashes.
"I shall remove" (*ūhanissāmi*) means I shall lift up or take away. "They strive" refers to what they did there previously.
Through familiarity, they are able to exert effort. "Anuppadetū" means to give again and again; thus he said, "when what was given is not sufficient," and so forth.
The making of witnesses and the depositing of documents are for one who wishes to take back [the debt] either with or without interest;
however, since that is not the case here, he said, "without making witnesses," and so forth; thus he said, "by way of cutting off the root. From the perspective of its nature...
"Pābhata" means that by which one brings, gathers, and prepares goods; it is the capital for merchandise.
"Devasika-bhatta" is food to be given day by day. "Māsika-ādiparibbaya" is the monthly or other allowance to be given as wages according to the phrases "every month," "every uposatha," and so forth.
This is [given] in accordance with each respective family, in accordance with the work, and in accordance with the person's courage.
The word *anurūpa* (suitable) should be applied individually [to each term]. "Senāpaccādi-ṭhānantaraṃ" means a position such as that of a general and so forth.

Because of being devoted to one's own duty and because of the absence of calamity regarding wealth and grain, he is a "rāsika," meaning one who causes [wealth] to be gathered. "Khemena ṭhitā" means existing without calamity; therefore he says "abhayā," which has the sense of being free from fear from any quarter whatsoever.
Commentary on the Four Requisites (Catuparikkhāravaṇṇanā) 339.
They follow and conform to each respective task; thus they are "followers" (*anuyantā*). Followers themselves are "attendants" (*ānuyantā*), just as "power itself" is called "majesty" (*ānubhāvo*).
"Of him" means of the king. "They" refers to the attendant nobles and others. They will not be "satisfied in mind."
“We build this here outside. A *gāma* is a place where there is an extensive arrival of inhabitants;
a *nigama* is one where great wealth has increased—the meaning is a large town. The word *janapada* has the meaning already explained above.

Through the six natural qualities, there is the increase of the king’s welfare and happiness, as well as that of his followers and so forth; thus it is said: “Whatever authorization you have, may that be for my long-term welfare and happiness.”

They are called *amaccas* because they are together (*amā*) with the king in his duties; they are those who bring the affairs of state to completion. Furthermore, because they are dear to the king and are his constant companions, he says, "dear friends" (*piyasahāyakā*).

They are called *pārisajjas* because they exist within the king’s assembly (*parisā*); as to who these are, he says, "the rest, those who carry out commands" (*sesā āṇattikarā*), meaning that all others besides the aforementioned dependent nobles (*ānuyantakhattiya*) and so forth are those who execute the king’s orders.
Even if there were material goods worthy of being given, it would not be possible to give such things in the absence of both majesty and a retinue;
furthermore, in old age, even for kings who possess these two qualities, both of them surely decline. Therefore he said: "In old age... it is not possible.
"By consent" means by granting permission. "Partisans" means those on one's own side who constitute the constituent parts of the sacrifice. "They provide" means—

“Requisites” (*parikkhārā*) means “provisions” (*sambhārā*). Since these constitute the constituent parts of that sacrifice, like its attendants, it is said: “they become attendants” (*parivārā bhavanti*).
340. Commentary on the Eight Requisites: “By fame” (*yasasā*) means by power;
thus he says, “by the capacity for issuing commands. “He has faith” means: “The giver [has faith] in the gift...”

“He experiences the fruit”—thus he gains conviction. “A hero in giving” means a hero of generosity who, having not formed even the slightest attachment to the object to be given, is one who gives with total relinquishment.
This meaning should be understood through the sharp and clear nature of the knowledge of the ownership of kamma;
therefore he said, “Not by mere faith alone,” and so forth. For one to whom the ownership of kamma appears as if directly perceived before the eyes—
Thus it was said. "Whatever gift he gives" means whatever object worthy of being given (*deyyadhamma*) he bestows upon another.
"Being its master" means that, having thoroughly overcome the greed directed toward that object, he gives while acting as its sovereign because it cannot overcome him.

Having stated, "Neither a slave nor a friend," the passage beginning with "For he who... is intended to demonstrate both of those points through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya* and *vyatireka*).

It has been said: One gives as a slave because one has entered into the state of servitude to craving through giving. One gives as a friend because one does not relinquish one's affection for that [recipient].
One gives as a master because, having liberated oneself from the slavery of craving therein and having overcome it, one proceeds [to give];
for this [giving] proceeds in a manner similar to the enjoyment of a master.
“Ascetics” (samana) are those who have calmed their evil; “brahmins” (brāhmaṇa) are those who have banished their evil—this is according to the highest description.
However, the intention here is that those who are ascetics by mere ordination and brahmins by mere birth are included only by the mention of the "miserable" (kapaṇa) and so forth.

"Wretched" (duggata) means those who have entered upon a difficult livelihood and a hard way of life; thus he said, "poor people. "Travelers" (addhika) are those going on a long journey. "Beggars" (vaṇibbaka) are...
By way of praising the virtues of the donors and by way of praising the fruit of kamma, [the Buddha spoke of] beggars such as those who practice naked asceticism;
thus he said, "A desirable gift was given," and so forth. "The measure of a *pasata*" is stated with reference to grains of rice and the like;

"the measure of a *sarāva*" is with reference to gruel, cooked rice, and so forth. An "opāna" is called a public watering place at rivers, ponds, and the like, because one must descend into it to drink.

“Becoming like a well” means being like a well; thus he said, “become like a well,” and so forth. He states that the word *jāta* expresses no difference in meaning from the word *suta* (heard), just as in the expression “born from a sheath” (*kosajāta*).
The King’s capacity to contemplate past and other objects is by way of inference and by way of determining what ought to be done.

It should be understood that this is not because the Buddhas possess direct perception (*paccakkha-dassitā*) regarding those matters as they do; rather, it was said, "in the past," and so forth, to demonstrate this.
Now, let it be granted that being wealthy and so on are requisites for sacrifice, since it cannot be accomplished without them;

but how can being well-born and handsome be so? To address this, he said, "By these, indeed," and so forth. And here, some [hold that] just as being wealthy and so on [are requisites] for sacrifice...
They say that the inclusion of the word *kira* is intended to show that the factors [of sacrifice] are one-sided, whereas noble birth and physical beauty are not;

they do so thinking that the statement beginning with "this one is ill-born" is inconclusive. However, this is without substance, for since this undertaking of sacrifice is common to all, there might be such a reflection in some individuals;
therefore, [the word *kira* is used] to show that there is no room even for that [reflection].
Because it was stated thus. Furthermore, the word *kira* should be understood as indicating the manner in which the brahmin thought at that time.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*evam-ādīni*), by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the following [statements] should be understood: "This man is ugly, poor, of little influence, faithless, of little learning, ignorant of what is beneficial, and not wise."
Commentary on the Four Requisites, etc., 341.

By the mention of the domestic priest himself taking up the ladle in the phrase "while lifting the sacrificial ladle," it is shown that one should desire to be engaged in giving with one's own hand and with due respect.
Regarding the phrase "thus for one of evil birth," the meaning here should also be understood according to the method explained below.
342. "Of three states" means in the three stages consisting of the beginning, middle, and end of giving;
that is the meaning. "They waver" means they shake; they do not remain in their former state. In the sense of the instrumental case (karaṇatthe) refers to the meaning of the third grammatical case.
This genitive form is used for the agent in relation to the word *karaṇīya*. Having stated, "Remorse should not be felt," [he says:]...
To show the means for not doing [that which is unwholesome], it is said: "But the prior volition must be made firm and established.
In this context, "firm" means strong and unshakable by anything. "Must be established" means it must be made well-established.
For by acting in this way, just as that gift succeeds in accordance with one's intention at present, so too will it result in abundant fruit in the future.
He said: "For it shows that giving is thus of great fruit," because it is unsullied by remorse.

*Muñcacetanā* is the volition of relinquishment. Its state of being unshakable means its loftiness due to the force of prior mental formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*), characterized by a state of having let go;
whereas the state of being unshakable for the volition of recollection is [the thought]: "Oh, a gift was given by me—how excellent!"
"Very well"—this is to be understood by way of his careful reflection.

"For one who does not do so" means for one who, according to the method already stated, does not make the volition of relinquishing (*muñcacetanā*) and the volition of subsequent recollection (*paccāsamanussaraṇacetanā*) steady, and thereby gives rise to remorse.
Because a gift has been made to a distinguished field of merit, even when excellent wealth is obtained, the mind—
Nor does it bend. To explain how this is so, he says: "As in the case of the merchant householder who was reborn in the Mahāroruva hell.

It is said that when he saw the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī standing at the door of his house for alms, he commanded his wife, "Give alms-food to this ascetic," and then departed to attend upon the king. The merchant’s wife...
Being of a wise nature, she thought: "In all this time, I have never even heard the words 'give this to him';
yet he was, I believe, a Paccekabuddha. Therefore, rather than giving [anything] as before, I shall give him excellent almsfood.
Having approached and paid homage to the Paccekabuddha with the fivefold prostration, she took his bowl and went inside her residence.
Having had him seated on a prepared seat, she prepared a meal of pure rice grains, along with appropriate hard foods, sauces, and soups.

Having adorned it with various perfumes and presented it into the hands of the Paccekabuddha, she paid homage to him. The Paccekabuddha [thought], "I shall provide for other Paccekabuddhas as well..."
Thinking, "I shall do so," he departed after offering words of appreciation without even consuming [the food].
Then the merchant, returning from his attendance upon the king, saw the Paccekabuddha and asked: "I said, 'Give almsfood to you,' and then departed;
have you received the almsfood? "Yes, merchant, it has been received. "Let me see," he said, and lifting up his neck, he looked.
Then the fragrance of his alms-food arose and filled his nostrils.
Unable to restrain his mind, thinking, "Oh, what a great loss of wealth has occurred for me! he later became remorseful.

The manner in which this remorse arose is already recorded in the Pāli text beginning with the words, "It would have been better... Furthermore, this brother [gave] one little son [to the other] for the sake of the inheritance...
Because he deprived [the monk] of life, he was reborn in the Mahāroruva hell.
However, by the gift of almsfood, he was reborn seven times in a happy destination, in the heavenly world, and seven times he was reborn in a family of wealthy merchants;
yet his mind did not incline toward magnificent wealth. Therefore it is said: "Nor does his mind incline toward magnificent wealth."
343. It is called an *ākāra* (mode) because it produces a fruit that is commensurate with itself, having limits and boundaries;
thus he says, "by ten *ākāras* means by ten causes. Regarding the phrase "from the recipient":
when [the result] arises as something more powerful, it arises from the recipient; however, the other [result] arises from the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*) and also from the retinue of people.
It would indeed arise. "Fit to arise" means worthy of arising.

For those very same persons who commit the destruction of life, what is intended here by "sacrifice" (yajana) is giving (dāna), not the offering into the fire; thus he said, "For those sacrificing, let there be giving.
"Let him relinquish" means let him relinquish by way of open-handed generosity. "Internal" means within oneself; the meaning is: in one's own continuum.
344. The sixteen requisites mentioned below were stated by making them the basis for the sacrifice;
however, here, because the expression of thanksgiving (*anumodanā*) is commenced by way of showing [the fruit] and so forth, it is said, "by way of sixteen aspects.

Having shown [the fruit], and having shown the result as if before one's eyes through the power of his own teaching, the repetition (*āmeḍita-vacana*) is used because he spoke of it many times. "That meaning" (*tam-atthaṃ*)...
The connection between the fruit of action and the fruit of giving is as previously stated. "Having encouraged" means:

not merely having heard it, but having caused him to take up that matter with due care—just as the king himself would properly undertake it, reflecting upon it in his mind and grasping it well—and thus having made him adopt it respectfully.
The reason for the repetition has already been explained below.
“By the removal of remorse”: this is merely an illustration, for greed, hatred, delusion, envy, stinginess, pride, and so forth are also defilements of the mind intent on giving;
by their removal as well, that mind is said to be “encouraged,” because it attains a state of sharpness and clarity.
Or rather, because remorse is the most immediate [obstacle], only its removal is mentioned; for even when the act of giving has already occurred, [remorse may still arise].
"From its occurrence": *sampahaṃsanā* (encouragement) is the act of bringing about a state of satisfaction and joy through qualities that truly exist;
thus he said, "It is beautiful for you... having made praise, he spoke. "According to the Dhamma" means according to truth. For truth is called *dhamma* because it does not deviate from the Dhamma;
it is called *sama* (even/equanimous) because of its nature of peaceful conduct; and it is called *kāraṇa* (reason) because of its state of being appropriate.
345. At that sacrifice, there was not even the cutting of trees or grass, let alone the taking of life.

In order to strengthen the absence of killing living beings and to show that [the sacrifice] was entirely corrupted by perverted grasping, the text states, after first saying "not even cows were slain," etc., "nor were trees cut down," and so forth; hence he said, "But what of the cows? and so on. "For the sake of sacrificial grass" (*barihasatthāya*).
For the purpose of delimitation. "In the manner of a forest-garland" means according to the fashion of garlands woven from forest flowers.
"Or spreading on the ground" means they spread it there, surrounding the altar-ground (vedibhūmi). "Slaves born within the house, etc.

refers to those who are slaves by birth, purchased with wealth, captured as prisoners of war, or inherited. "Even beforehand" means prior to the time of performing the labor for wages. Having taken [it].
“They do so” means they do so by taking [the materials] day after day. “Threatened” means threatened with thunder. “By means of endearing conduct alone” means by means of agreeable speech alone.
Regarding the phrase “and with molasses,” the word *ca* (and) here has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*avutta-samuccaya*);
by it, there is the inclusion of various kinds of superior and inferior foods and edibles, as well as robes, garlands, perfumes, ointments, vehicles, couches, and so forth.
The inclusion is to be understood; therefore he said, "only with excellent things mixed with ghee, oil, and so forth," and so on.

346. *Saṃ* means wealth (*dhana*); one who possesses that is a *sapati*, i.e., a wealthy person. Because it brings welfare pertaining to both the present life and the future life, it is *hita* (beneficial) to him;
thus it is *sāpateyya*, which is simply wealth. Therefore he said, "taking much *sāpateyya*" means taking a great deal.
“Having taken wealth. Regarding “by way of a village portion”: it means by way of a portion to be taken from the village through a formal assignment (*saṅkittana*).
“Having drunk rice-gruel”: by means of the term “rice-gruel,” he refers to the morning meal. “To the east of the sacrificial enclosure (*yaññavāṭa*):
the meaning is that it is in the eastern direction, not too far from the King’s hall of giving; for having eaten the morning meal there, [he departed].
They reached the *sāla* tree in the evening as if their forms were untiring; the same method applies to such passages as “to the south of the sacrificial enclosure,” and so forth.
348. “With avoidance” means with an avoidance of disrespect by treating the Blessed One with reverence. This is the commentary on the perpetual giving and the customary sacrifices.
349. "Rising up again and again" means having performed the effort of exertion in giving with thorough care.

"Having very few requisites" means possessing extremely limited materials. "Samārambhā" refers to those things by which a sacrifice is undertaken; it denotes the harassment of living beings occurring through the act of gathering the necessary materials.
"Being of little concern," however, means being exceedingly free from duties. [The term] "vipāka" signifies that which is characterized by fruition in an eminent degree...

"More fruitful" (*mahapphalatara*) means that its fruit is exceedingly great and equal to [the donor]. "More beneficial" (*mahānisaṃsatara*) means that its outflowing fruit (*nissandaphala*) and so forth is exceedingly great and designated as "arising" (*udaya*).
"Constant gifts" (*dhuvadāna*) refers to gifts that should be given by making them constant, firm, and uninterrupted.
"Family sacrifices" (*anukulayañña*) refers to gifts that should be given according to the family and the lineage; thus he said, "ours," and so forth.
“Nibaddhadānāni” means gifts that have been established and fixed, which are carried on by way of tradition.
“Dantamayasalākā” refers to ivory sticks made from elephant tusks, upon which the names of the donors are engraved. “Rañño” refers to King Setavāhana.
By the word “ādi,” [the following] is included: “Why do you pounce and seize me like a hawk seizing a piece of meat? and so forth.
Inclusion: There are three factors on the part of the giver, consisting in the perfection of prior intention, the intention at the moment of relinquishing, and subsequent intention;
and there are three factors on the part of the recipient, consisting in the practice of being free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion.
Thus, regarding a gift endowed with these six factors, by way of the successive arising of intentions, it is like a great river and like a mighty flood flowing from here.
And having flowed forth and overflowed, it proceeds as merit alone; this is the "overflowing of merit" (*puññābhisanda*).
There is no end to the task, because the donor continues to engage in activity day after day; therefore he said, "by one," and so forth.
There is an end to the task, because the dwelling as it was undertaken must be completed within a certain period of time.
Therefore he said, “a leaf-hut,” and so forth. “By way of the Suttanta” means according to the method of the Suttanta canon.
“Nine benefits” refers to the nine advantages beginning with the warding off of cold and ending with delighting in seclusion (*paṭisallānārāma*).
These are stated by way of heedfulness (*appamattatā*), because for one who gives a dwelling, all requisites are indeed given. [One should go] for alms in two or three villages.

Having wandered about and returned empty-handed, even when one enters a monastery well-supplied with shade and water, bathes, lies down for a moment in the lodging, and then sits up after rising, strength seems to have been restored to the body as if it had been replenished.
Furthermore, while wandering outside, the element of beauty (*vaṇṇadhātu*) in the body is exhausted by the wind and heat; but upon entering the lodging and closing the door—

For one who lies down for a moment after closing [the door], the dissimilar continuity (*visabhāga-santati*) subsides, the similar continuity (*sabhāga-santati*) becomes established, and it is as if the element of beauty (*vaṇṇa-dhātu*) has been brought in and placed there.
Furthermore, for one wandering outside, a thorn pierces the foot, a stump strikes him, and dangers such as reptiles as well as the fear of thieves arise; whereas, having entered a shelter...
For one who lies down after closing the door, all those dangers cease; for one reciting the scriptures, the bliss of the joy of the Dhamma arises;
and for one attending to the meditation subject, the bliss of tranquility arises due to the absence of external distraction.
Furthermore, for one wandering outside, perspiration breaks out on the body and the eyes twitch at the moment of entering the dwelling.

Beds, chairs, and so forth do not appear; however, for one who has sat there for even a moment, the clarity of the eyes becomes as if it had been taken out and put back in again, and doors, windows, beds, chairs, and so forth become visible.
Furthermore, seeing him dwelling in this residence, people attend to him with due care by means of the four requisites. Therefore it was said: "By one giving a residence..."
“Every kind of requisite that has arisen is indeed given. Therefore, all these aforementioned benefits should be understood.
For this reason it was said: “And these are stated by way of heedfulness.
“Cold” refers to coldness arising either through the disturbance of the internal elements or through the change of the external season.
"Hot" refers to the heat of fire; its occurrence should be understood as arising from forest fires and the like (*vanadāhādīsu*).
"Wards off" means he repels it; that is, he acts in such a way that no affliction of body or mind arises through those two [extremes].
For when the body is afflicted by cold or heat, a monk whose mind is distracted [cannot practice] with wise attention (*yoniso*).
He is unable to go forth. "Wild beasts" refers to fierce animals such as lions, tigers, and the like.
For even when one has entered a forest dwelling that is well-guarded and sits with the door closed, those dangers do not exist for him.
"Reptiles" refers to any long-bodied creatures that crawl or move, such as snakes and the like. "Gnats" is merely an illustration; gadflies and other such insects are also included among these.
(See *Sāratthappakāsinī*, Cūḷavagga 3.295) "Inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) is to be understood here.
"In the cold" (*sisire*) means by way of the cold season and by way of the occurrence of cold sensations such as those arising from a seven-day rainstorm.
"Rainfalls" (*vuṭṭhiyo*): the construction is that he repels the rainfalls whenever they arise.
"Terrible wind and heat": the wind—distinguished as dusty and dustless—is terrible because it occurs by uprooting and breaking trees, shrubs, and so forth;
and the heat of the sun is terrible because it arises during the seasons of summer and the feverish heat. "Is struck back" means it is warded off.

"For the sake of a shelter" means for the purpose of delighting in seclusion by turning the mind away from various objects. "For the sake of comfort" means due to the absence of the aforementioned dangers.
"For the sake of dwelling in comfort" (*phāsuvihāratthaṃ*). "To meditate" (*jhāyituṃ*) means to contemplate after having fixed the mind upon any one of the thirty-eight meditation objects.
"To see with insight" (*vipassituṃ*) means to comprehend conditioned phenomena as impermanent and so forth.
"Dwelling" (*vihāre*) means in a shelter. "Should cause to be made" (*kāraye*) means he should have it built. "Delightful" (*ramme*) means pleasant for living. "He should dwell there" (*vāsayettha*).
Having designated those who are "learned," one should cause the learned, virtuous, and noble-minded to dwell in these monasteries;

and while providing them with residence, one should give food, drink, clothing, and lodgings to those who are upright and endowed with noble aspirations, so that those learned ones do not suffer from a lack of requisites, [and likewise provide for] those who understand the nature of actions and their fruits.
With a mind purified by faith in the qualities of the Triple Gem.
Now, in order to show how householders and those who have gone forth benefit one another, he spoke the verse beginning with “They to him.
Therein, “they” refers to the learned ones; “to him” refers to the lay follower (*upāsaka*). “Teaching the Dhamma” means teaching that which dispels the entire suffering of the round of existence.
They teach the true Dhamma. Regarding the phrase "having understood that Dhamma here":

that lay follower, having understood the true Dhamma in this Dispensation through right practice, becomes free from taints (anāsava) by attaining the supreme path and attains final Nibbāna; he becomes cool through the subsiding of the eleven fires.

There are thirteen [factors] beginning with the warding off of cold and ending with the culmination of insight: the obtaining of food and so forth, hearing the Dhamma, the awakening to the Dhamma, and final Nibbāna. Thus, there are seventeen.
351. "One's own property" means belonging to oneself. This refers to one who is unable to restrain greed, which is difficult to abandon.
The construction is: "in the presence of the Saṅgha or the Gaṇa. "Therein" means in the refuge as it was taken.
The intention is that for one of a wise nature, there is no need to perform [the act] again and again. "[The merit consisting in the renunciation of life]"—if you...
"I shall kill you only if you break the refuge as it was taken"— even if someone were to deprive one of life with a sharp weapon,

this statement was made on account of the refuge that had been taken with even greater firmness, thinking: "I do not say 'not Buddha' of the Buddha, nor 'not Dhamma' of the Dhamma, nor 'not Saṅgha' of the Saṅgha."
352. One who has gone for refuge should perform the worship of the Triple Gem with body, speech, and mind in a diligent manner, and therein defilement must be abandoned.
However, the training precepts (sikkhāpada) are merely a matter of undertaking and merely a matter of abstaining from what has been attained;
thus, it should be understood that compared to going for refuge, the virtue (sīla) is less established and involves less effort. This applies to all.

Its great fruitfulness and great benefit are to be understood from its laying aside of the rod through the giving of life to living beings and so forth, and from its being the foundation for all mundane and supramundane qualities.

Furthermore, according to the method that will be explained, the term "enmity" (*vera*) refers to unwholesome states such as the destruction of life because they are causes of enmity; it crushes that [enmity].
“While I am standing right here, how have you come?”—driving him away as if rebuking him is *veramaṇī*.

Or, because one abstains from evil states by means of this, it should be called *viramaṇī*; however, by way of linguistic derivation (*niruttinaya*), the letter *i* is changed to *e*, and thus it is called *veramaṇī*.
[This applies] to one who has not undertaken the precepts, from the attainment [of the path], and from the objects that ought to be transgressed as they present themselves.
Abstention through attainment is *virati* by way of attainment. Abstention arisen by way of undertaking is abstention through undertaking. A "bridge" (*setu*) is said to be the Noble Path;
abstention that destroys evil states by means of their total eradication, having become included within that [Path], is "abstention through the destruction of the bridge" (*setughāta-virati*).

Now, in order to show these three kinds of abstention according to their specific nature, the passage beginning with "Therein" (*tattha*) was stated. "He avoids" (*pariharati*) means by way of non-transgression.
He avoids [them]. In the phrase "I do not kill," the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*); by this, there is an inclusion of such [vows] as "I do not take what is not given," and so forth.
Alternatively, it is by means of the word *vā*. Therefore, he says: "for one who is undertaking the training rules.
"Associated with the Path" means associated with the Path beginning with right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*). Now, regarding the objects (*ārammaṇa*) of those abstinences (*virati*):
The phrase beginning with “Therein” is stated in order to show the classification. “The first two” refers to the abstinences consisting of the undertaking of what has been attained.
“The latter” refers to the abstinence consisting in the destruction of the bridge. All of them are broken because they were undertaken together as one.

That very same [abstinence] is broken because it was undertaken separately. And this is stated with reference to householders; there is no such thing as a breaking [of the precepts] for those who have completely severed their opposites.
Because its nature is unshakable, he said, "even in another existence. "Established by nature" (yonisiddha) means established by birth, just as height is established for humans and animals;

it is established by way of natural law (dhammatā), like the virtue of the Bodhisatta’s mother when the Bodhisatta has entered her womb, or by the power of the Noble Path through the natural law of the Path (maggadhammatā).
It is established; it is established by the very nature of things (*dhammatā*). Correcting one's views is indeed a heavy burden of suffering;
therefore, the intention is that going for refuge is of greater significance than the undertaking of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), and not of lesser significance.
"Even for one who takes them in whatever way" means even for one who undertakes them without showing respect or reverence. "Even for one who takes them properly" means...
Even for one who undertakes the precepts with reverence, no double or triple effort need be made.
Because it grants fearlessness, virtue has the nature of a gift (*dāna*); or rather, it is a gift because it bestows (*dayati*) and protects (*rakkhati*) the entire multitude of beings;

thus it is virtue (*sīla*). They are called "foremost" (*aggaññāni*) because they are known as the foremost. They are called "ancient" (*rattaññāni*) because they have been known for a long time. "Of the Noble Ones" (*ariyānaṃ*)...

They are called "lineages" (*vaṃsa*) because they are known as the lineages of the virtuous (*sādhūnaṃ vaṃsā*). Regarding the phrase "ancient" (*porāṇāni*) and so forth: these belong to those of the past, thus they are "ancient.
They are "unmixed" (*asaṅkiṇṇāni*) because they have not been mixed, scattered, or discarded by anyone in any way whatsoever by the virtuous.
And this method [of their preservation] has been as it was in the past, so it is now and will be in the future; thus he said: "Unmixed in the past... and so on.

"They have been suspected, and they will not be suspected. For that very reason, minor forms of injury were not prohibited. Indeed, wise ascetics and brahmins never sanction evil states such as violence.
"He gives fearlessness to immeasurable beings" means that because he has laid down the rod toward all living beings, he grants the absence of fear to the entire aggregate of sentient beings.

Indeed, no one has fear from a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*). "Without enmity" (*avera*) means the absence of enmity (*verābhāva*). "Without affliction" (*abyāpajjha*) means the state of being free from suffering (*niddukkhatā*).

Now, while the five precepts (*pañcasīla*) are for all times, they are not exclusively a sphere of liberation; however, going for refuge (*saraṇagamana*) is caused by the arising of a Buddha and is exclusively a sphere of liberation. In that case, how [can it be said that] the five precepts [are superior] to going for refuge?
He said, "Even though," and so forth, to show that it has great fruit. "The eldest" means the most excellent.
By the phrase "by being established in the going for refuge itself," he indicates that this virtue is conditioned by the going for refuge.
"Just such as this" means that, having become the very opposite of such defilement. "By the qualities mentioned above"—here [is the reference].
The qualities mentioned below are: taking refuge, perfection of virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, and so forth.
The construction is: "one does not weary while producing the first jhāna. "Those" refers to the first jhāna and the others.
Since the term "first jhāna" is used here as a designation for the highest grade, he says "for one *kappa*," meaning for one great *kappa*. However, the inferior first jhāna—
And for the middle asaṅkhyeyya-kappa, he grants a third part, as well as half a kappa, as its lifespan.

The meaning in such passages as “the second [asaṅkhyeyya] lasts eight kappas,” etc., should be understood according to this same method; and it should be taken strictly in terms of great kappas (mahākappa).
Or rather, it is because only the superior jhānas are intended here, since the purpose of the teaching is to show that they yield more abundant fruit.
Therefore, it was said: "The first jhāna lasts for one eon," and so forth. "That very same" refers to the fourth jhāna itself.
If this is so, how can there be formless attainments? To this he says: "the base of infinite space," and so forth.

It is precisely by way of the destruction of the opposites such as the perception of permanence—occurring while still in the preliminary stages—that the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhammā) function.
"Insight, when correctly comprehending, brings about no small measure of rapture and mental joy for the one who sees clearly; thus it was said: 'Insight...
[omitted] ...due to its absence. Therefore the Blessed One said:
'From whatever point he comprehends The rise and fall of the aggregates;'"
"One who understands that attains rapture and gladness; that is the Deathless.

Since this teaching proceeds by way of one who generates these types of knowledge in this specific sequence, therefore, [the phrase] "generating while established in insight-knowledge" refers to each preceding stage as the basis for each subsequent one.

This was said by making it a firm foundation. Regarding "the creation of a form identical [to oneself]," he said, "one's own... [is] of great fruit," because the power of mind-made psychic potency (*manomayiddhi*) has a function not shared with others.
"The capacity to display transformations" means that transformation (*vikubbana*) is the assuming of various forms such as elephants, horses, and so forth;
it refers to the state of being capable of displaying such transformations. "Every desired place" refers to [places] in previous births.
"Icchiticchito" means a desired portion of the aggregates (*khandha*). "Samāpento" means bringing to a conclusion.
Regarding the commentary on the discourse concerning the announcement of the lay follower status by Kūṭadanta (354–8):
"All those living beings" refers to all sentient beings mentioned in the passage beginning with "seven hundred bulls. "State of agitation" (*ākulabhāvo*)...
Because he had heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, he established compassion toward living beings;
as he stood there, a state of mental agitation arose in him, [the thought]: "How is it that I have had so many living beings bound for the sake of execution?
"Having heard" means having heard that they were "released from bondage. Through the departure of sensual desire, there is a state of pliancy of mind, a state of healthiness of mind.
Through the disappearance of ill will, there is pliancy of mind and non-hardness of mind by way of loving-kindness;
through the abandoning of restlessness and remorse, there is unobstructedness of mind due to the disappearance of distraction, meaning the mind is not shut off by them;

through the disappearance of sloth and torpor, there is exaltation of mind and non-languor of mind by way of uplifting; and through the disappearance of doubt, there is inclination toward right practice.
And because there is a state of serene mind, it is said: “‘With a ready mind,’ etc.; this was spoken with reference to the suppression of the hindrances through the power of the gradual discourse.
Whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Kūṭadantasutta*.
6. Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta:
Commentary on the Episode of the Brahmin Messenger 359.
Regarding the phrase "by repeatedly attaining a state of expansion": it is said that previously, by way of sons and daughters, there were two pairs.
As the sixteen Licchavi princes, along with their retinues, grew up over time,
the city was enclosed three times by a distance of one *gāvuta* each, because the original site was insufficient to accommodate the dwellings,
monasteries, parks, lotus ponds, and other facilities; thus, it came to be called Visālā (the Expansive) due to its repeated enlargement.
The name “Vesālī” indeed arose; therefore it is said: “in the city that received the name Vesālī because of its repeated becoming vast.
“Self-born” means grown spontaneously, not planted.
“Precisely by its greatness” refers to the greatness of the trees and shrubs, as well as the extent of the space they occupy; thus he said: “joined as one with the Himālaya.”
"Having offered. "By way of a gabled hall" means by the arrangement of a gabled hall with a *haṃsavaṭṭaka* roof-covering.
Those born in the Kosala country, or those whose existence or residence is in that kingdom, are the *Kosalakas*. In the same way, the *Māgadhakas* are to be understood.
That which, if not performed, makes a person greatly destitute, is worthy of being done; thus it is "that which ought to be done" (*karaṇīya*), and by means of that which ought to be done...
Therefore he said, "by means of the action that must necessarily be done. That is called a duty (*kicca*) because it must be performed when the conditions have come together.

(360) Regarding the various perceptions (*nānattasaññā*) that are appropriate for Buddhas to arise: by way of those [perceptions], there is a movement toward various objects. This is a negation of that which is possible.

"Having turned back" (*paṭikkamma*) means having desisted and not giving rise to the mind in that manner. "Withdrawn" (*sallīna*) means [withdrawn] through the attainment of meditative absorption (*jhānasamāpatti*).
He clung to a single object. 361.
Regarding the description of the Licchavi Oṭṭhaddha:
"Because of his half-lip" means that, it is said, because his upper lip was small, it was slit horizontally and half of it was removed.
His four tusks appear as if they were [separate] lips, and his two fangs do not cover them; therefore, people refer to him as "Oṭṭhaddha" (Lip-Lower).
It is said that this lay follower was faithful, confident, a donor, a master of giving, devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha;
thus he said, "Before the meal," and so forth.
362. "One who is devotedly engaged in the Dispensation" means one who is intent upon meditation.

Although the Blessed One’s conduct was like that of a lion in all respects, when his assembly was large, there was a distinction in the teaching of the Dhamma as it proceeded in accordance with their inclinations;
thus it is said: "He will teach the Dhamma with great enthusiasm."
Having said "trustworthy," the passage beginning with "for this one" was spoken in order to clarify his state of trustworthiness.

It cannot be said that the Elder’s state of indolence, which had been exhausted for a hundred years, was "not abandoned"; rather, it is said "it is as if slightly unabandoned" by way of a trace of residual habituation (*vāsanā*).
For the defilements of disciples are not abandoned along with their residual habits.
363. It has been said that the manifestation of miracles by the Buddhas occurs in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained; thus it is said, "Then the Blessed One," and so forth.
For this very reason, it is stated, "He departed having signaled his intention.
Indeed, at the moment of departing from the Fragrant Chamber, the six-colored rays of the Buddha issued forth in an especially brilliant manner, interlacing one with another and shimmering intensely.
364. "After that" (*tato paraṃ*) means immediately following the day mentioned as "yesterday" (*hiyyo*); it is "after" because it is further away, being more prior due to its exceeding priority.
Thus, among these two, the state of being "prior" and "more prior" is established according to their respective order.
Even so, whatever is proximate to what was called "more prior" herein is "prior," and whatever is further away is "after."

Because each preceding state is established in dependence upon its respective predecessor—just as the state of "this shore" (orapāra) depends upon the state of "the further shore" (pāra)—it is said, "starting from that," and so forth. "Starting from the initial day" means starting from that first day.

"The limit" (agga) means the first. However, since here the "limit" (koṭi) refers to the ultimate past, it is said, "making the ultimate limit. This is due to the connection with the relative pronoun *yam*.

Furthermore, although this is a present-tense usage in the form “I dwell” (*viharāmi*), the meaning should be understood as referring specifically to the past; therefore he said, “it means ‘I have dwelt’ (*vihāsiṃ*).
In the first alternative, the direct connection of the word “I dwell” with the phrase “from which time forward” (*yadagge*) is shown;
however, in the second alternative, it is also connected with the phrase “for three years.”
"Pleasant by nature" means having a desirable essence. "Sweet by nature" means having a sweet essence.
For anything that is delightful is called "sweet," as if it were actually sweet. "Connected with sensual desire" means connected with the desire that takes them as its object;
the meaning is "desirable. Therefore he said, "fitted for the gratification of sensual desire," meaning they are suited for the gratification of sensual desire.
The meaning is "suitable. Regarding "the configuration of the body" (*sarīrasaṇṭhāne*), this refers to the bodily image; here, the locative case denotes the basis.

Therefore, "by means of sound" means by means of the sound produced depending upon that [image] and arising from it. "By means of what is sweet" means by what is desirable. "By this much alone" refers merely to the statement of the preliminary work for the divine ear-knowledge (*dibbasotañāṇa*).
[One might ask: "If he does not speak even of what he knows himself, what is the point of his resolve in the Teaching?"
