Becoming angry and binding a grudge, he fell away from his meditative absorptions and higher knowledges at the very moment of his anger. He thought:
“Why indeed did he not tell me that preparatory work? Thus he reflected, thinking in a way that was based on improper attention (*ayoniso*).
“In due order” means that, following the method set forth in the *Pāṭhika-sutta*, he continued to think and speak only about those various things which were inappropriate.
And acting thus, gradually failing to find a footing in the Dispensation due to his resentment toward the Blessed One, he returned to the state of a householder.
[End of] the commentary on concentration developed one-sidedly (366–371).
Regarding the word *ekaṃsāya*: it is the dative case used in the sense of "for that purpose"; therefore, the meaning is "for the sake of one-sidedness. The word *aṃsa*—

And here there is a sense of "portion" (koṭṭhāsa), which should be understood according to the context as referring to the seeing of divine forms and the hearing of divine sounds; thus he said, "for one portion," and so forth.

"In an intermediate direction" means in the fourfold intermediate directions, distinguished as southeast and so on. "For both portions" means for the purpose of seeing divine forms and for the purpose of hearing divine sounds.
"Developed" means it has been developed in such a way that the knowledge of the divine eye and the knowledge of the divine ear are attained.
Regarding this, there is no need to speak of them succeeding through separate preparatory exercises;

for even when they succeed together, the accomplishment of their functions occurs only sequentially, since the simultaneous accomplishment of their functions is impossible. Even in the Pāli, this is stated solely for the purpose of showing that a single person is capable of both.
It is said, “for the seeing of divine forms and for the hearing of divine sounds,” not because the accomplishment of both functions occurs simultaneously.

By the phrase “because concentration is cultivated in one aspect,” it is shown that Sunakkhatta did not hear the existing divine sound because he had performed the preliminary work solely for the sake of the knowledge of the divine eye. *Apaṇṇakaṃ* means...
“Blameless” (anavajja) means that which is not subject to reproach, or it means blameless.
372. Concentration itself is “development of concentration” (samādhibhāvanā) in the sense of being something to be developed.

Even though Mahāli thought that “the knowledge of the divine ear is the best,” he nevertheless included the knowledge of the divine eye along with it and asked, “Surely these, venerable sir...,” and so forth.
"It means 'concentrations developed in both ways,'" it is said. These developments of concentration are external because they do not lead to liberation;
for they are accomplished even by those outside this [teaching]. They are not internal because they have not been proclaimed by the Blessed One as his own uniquely exalted realization.
"For the sake of which" means for the purpose of which. "Those" refers to those noble fruit-states (ariyaphala-dhamma), for they are what must be realized.
Commentary on the Four Noble Fruits (Catuariyaphalavaṇṇanā) 373.

Therefore, because of being bound within the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*), the phrase “has entered the stream of the path” (*maggasotaṃ āpanno*) is stated with reference to one who stands at the fruit (*phalaṭṭha*).

For it is one standing at the path (*maggaṭṭha*) who enters the stream of the path. For this very reason, he says “stream-enterer” (*sotāpanna*) and “for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.”

And [it is said]: "for one who has entered upon the path. "Subject to non-falling" means having the nature of not arising again. "By the fixed order of the Dhamma" means by the fixed order of the Dhamma of the Path.
Or, it is "fixed" (niyata) in the sense of being subject to non-arising from the seventh existence downwards at the very least. "The further going" (parāgati) means the supreme destination.
"Tenuity" (tanutta) refers to the slowness and sparseness of its occurrence; thus he says "by tenuity," and so forth. "Of the lower fetters" (heṭṭhābhāgiyānaṃ).

“Beneficial” means being conducive by way of being a condition for the lower portion, which is sensual existence (*kāmabhava*). “Spontaneously born” (*opapātiko*) is one who is born spontaneously (*upapātiko*), meaning one who is skilled (*sādhukārī*) in the act of arising (*upapatane*).
“Liberation” (*vimutti*) is that by which one is liberated; thus he says, “the mind itself is liberation,” and “mental liberation” (*cetovimutti*) is a designation for all defilements...
[etc. ... In such passages as “Develop the mind and wisdom,” concentration is included under the heading of “mind.”
The same method applies here to the term *paññāvimutti* (liberation by wisdom); therefore he said, "Wisdom itself is liberation by wisdom.

*Sāmaṃ* means by oneself, that is, independently of another (*aparappaccayena*). Regarding *abhiññā*, it is a designation with the elision of the letter *ya*; thus he said, "having directly known" (*abhijānitvā*).
Commentary on the Noble Eightfold Path.
374–5. It is called *paṭipadā* because by means of it the noble disciple proceeds toward Nibbāna and the noble fruit;
and since that [practice] constitutes his preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), the term “preliminary-stage practice” (*pubbabhāgapaṭipadā*) here refers to the Noble Path.

Regarding the word *aṭṭhaṅgika*, one should understand its grammatical derivation not as a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (possessive compound), but rather as “that which has eight factors” (*aṭṭhaṅgāni assa santīti aṭṭhaṅgiko*).
Right view has the characteristic of right seeing, because its nature is to see the four noble truths directly, correctly, and without error, just as they are.
Right intention has the characteristic of right application, because its nature is to direct the mind toward Nibbāna as its object.

Right speech has the nature of abstaining from its opposite, for speech endowed with the four factors wins over people; thus, by abandoning divisive and false speech, it is characterized by such restraint.
It has the characteristic of right grasping because it possesses the function of grasping objects that are present and associated.
Just as a work such as making a robe initiates one task to be done, or the work termed volition—which produces various actions—initiates activities such as the moving of hands and feet;
so too, by abandoning wrong action, which initiates blameworthy activities to be done...
Right action has the function of originating what is blameless; and since it proceeds only while originating its associated states, right action is characterized by right origination.

Right livelihood is characterized by right purification through the abandoning of wrong livelihood, which is a defilement of the body, speech, and the continuity of the aggregates. From the side of indolence...
Right effort has the characteristic of right exertion, its nature being to uphold the associated mental states without allowing them to fall away.
Right mindfulness has the characteristic of right establishment, its nature being to establish [the mind] correctly.
Right concentration has the characteristic of right composure, its nature being to compose the mind correctly by destroying distraction.

"One's own adverse defilements" refers to ignorance and so forth, which are to be abandoned by vision (*diṭṭhekaṭṭha*). "Sees" means he reveals them through the penetration of their function, and thus penetrates them;
therefore it says, "because of the non-obscuration of that... because of non-delusion.
For it is precisely by means of that factor known as right view that the reviewing occurs therein; thus, "in that very way" means together with one's own adverse defilements—this is the sense.
"By way of function": because the function that is to be performed by the preceding knowledges of suffering and so forth is here brought to a preeminent completion;
or because this very knowledge performs the function of illuminating suffering and the rest. It receives four names because it accomplishes the functions to be performed regarding the four truths.
It receives three names because it accomplishes the function of abandoning sensual intention and the rest.
In the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*, it is stated: "The volition of abstention and all associated mental states are training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
Therefore, with reference to the primary factors—the volitions of abstention—it is said: "They are both abstentions and volitions.

Alternatively, they should be understood as abstentions at the time of refraining from false speech and so forth, and as volitions at the time of uttering well-spoken words and so forth. At the moment of the Path (*magga-khaṇa*), [they are both].

Furthermore, because abstinences (virati) are not themselves factors of the path (magganga) among volitions (cetanā), just as a single knowledge cannot possess the nature of the various knowledges such as the knowledge of suffering, and just as a single abstinence cannot possess the status of being the various abstinences from false speech and so forth, a single volition lacks the inherent nature to accomplish the three functions of right speech and so on;

thus, the status of right speech and the rest is not established. Moreover, even if that were established, the state of having three factors would not be established. "By way of the right efforts and the foundations of mindfulness" [is said].
By way of the cultivation of the four right endeavors and the four foundations of mindfulness.
Even in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path, it is indeed right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*).

Although right concentration is analyzed into four jhānas by way of the factors that assist concentration—namely, applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth, which perform the functions of directing, smoothing, gladdening, and intensifying—it nevertheless possesses, like effort (*vāyāma*), the fourfold function of effort, such as the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states.
Just as in the case of mindfulness, a single concentration does not accomplish the fourfold task of abandoning the perception of beauty and so forth regarding the body and other objects—
which are actually ugly, painful, impermanent, and non-self— nor does it accomplish the task of the fourfold jhāna-concentration; thus,
the first-jhāna concentration in the prior stage is indeed the first-jhāna concentration at the moment of the Path, and likewise for the fourth-jhāna concentration in the prior stage.
The meaning is that the concentration of the fourth jhāna itself is [the path] even at the moment of the Path (*maggakkhaṇe*). "Therefore" means:
because it dispels the darkness of ignorance through its lamp-like nature of wisdom (*paññā*), and because it slays the thieves of the defilements through its sword-like nature of wisdom.

"Because of its great assistance" refers to this mass of defilements which has never before been eradicated throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) by means of this [concentration].

The Noble Path is its eradicator. And herein, this right view is highly beneficial because it acts as the precursor through its occurrence by way of full understanding, clear realization, and so forth;
therefore, it is called "highly beneficial" (*bahukāra*).
Having stated that it is "highly beneficial," in order to clarify that state of being highly beneficial by means of a simile, [the text says]: "Just as..."
"‘Hī’ and so forth were said. ‘This’ [scale] is a counterfeit because it is made of copper, bronze, or other such materials. This one is clever due to its evenness and great substance.

‘In this way’ means: just as for a money-changer, once he has seen with his eye, the hand is of great utility as an instrument for discerning the various types of kahāpaṇa coins, so too for a practitioner of yoga, after observing with wisdom, [the faculty of mind is of great utility] for discerning the various phenomena."
Another factor that is very helpful is this: applied thought (*vitakka*), because by applying thought one realizes that [object].
Therefore, the intention is that right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) is very helpful for right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*). In the second simile, "just as" means:
just as a carpenter, having repeatedly turned over the building materials provided by another, cuts them with an axe and brings them to the work of house construction, so too...

The construction is as follows: the practitioner of yoga, having applied initial application (vitakka) by way of its characteristics and so forth, and having delimited the given phenomena according to their true nature, brings them forward for the work of the clear realization of full understanding (pariññā-abhisamaya).

Since initial application is an aid to verbal expression, it is also an aid to right speech (sammāvācā), which effects the cessation of faulty verbal expression and the engagement in faultless verbal expression; thus it is said, "This [initial application]," and so forth.
Speech is the regulator of verbal expression and is an aid to the action of the body which regulates physical activity.

"Immediately after those two" means immediately after the pair of right speech and right action, which serve as the cause for fulfilling the two types of good conduct while abandoning the two types of misconduct.
"This energy" refers to the fourfold energy of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*). The evenness of the faculties (*indriyasamatā*) and so forth [are the conditions] for concentration (*samādhi*).

These are qualities that are beneficial. By way of their opposite, those that are harmful should be understood. "Destinies" (*gatiyo*) refers to accomplishments, or to the essential nature of functions and so forth.
"Having investigated" means having scrutinized. This concludes the commentary on the two cases concerning those who have gone forth.
Having asked the reason for the connection with the words, “Why was it begun?”, the passage beginning with “It is said that this... was stated in order to clarify that;
by this, he shows that the subsequent teaching proceeds by way of a connection based on the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*).

“By that” means because of having acquired such a disposition. “His” refers to the Licchavi king. “In the teaching” refers to the teaching as it was taught—subtle, delicate, and associated with emptiness (*suññatā*).
“He does not resolve” means he does not believe or has no confidence.
“Speaking on the ‘thread-dharma’” means speaking on the dharma merely as a thread within the Dispensation for those for whose sake the dharma is taught, even though they lack penetration of the Path.
“Of such a one” refers to one who, because of being a Perfectly Enlightened One, possesses a clearly manifest Dhamma-body due to teaching the Dhamma without error.
"Is this appropriate for the Teacher?"— he asks whether this grasping at views such as annihilationism,
expressed by the phrase "that is the soul," is indeed appropriate for a clansman whose mind has become concentrated through the attainment of the first jhāna and so forth. However,
because [the view] has not yet been fully cleared away merely by the attainment of jhāna due to the persistence of the underlying disposition (*laddhi*), it is said that "it is appropriate for them."
"Having rejected the doctrine" means that even for one who has attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*), that grasping at [a self] is "entirely improper";

thus, having rejected that doctrine of annihilationism or eternalism, they became "satisfied in mind. Because one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is free from delusion and has crossed over doubt, they heard my words with the conviction that had arisen:
"Therefore, it is not proper for him to speak in such a manner."
"Attamanā ahesuṃ" means they were joyful. That Licchavi king also became joyful, just like them, because he had likewise reached a firm conviction.
Whatever remains unexplained here in terms of meaning is indeed easy to understand. This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) on the commentary to the *Mahālisutta*.
7. Commentary on the Jāliya Sutta:
The Story of the Two Renunciants (378).
Having stated, "In the monastery built by the merchant Ghosita," [the question arises]: who was this merchant Ghosita, and how did he [come to build it]?
In order to show, in brief, everything starting from the origin of how the monastery was built and how the Blessed One dwelt there, the passage beginning with “It is said that formerly...
was spoken. “From there” means from the province of Allakappa. “On that day” means on the day they entered that village.
“A large quantity of milk-rice” means a greater amount of thick rice porridge. “When it was not yet ready” means...
"Having gone outside the house. "He bellowed" means he cried out. He was named Ghosaka-devaputta precisely because of the excellence of his voice.

"By way of distinction" means by way of the distinction of wisdom (*paññā-veyyattiya*). He became known as the merchant Ghosita because of that very excellence of his voice; he received the name Ghosita on account of that perfection of sound.

"For the purpose of refreshing the body" means that their bodies were exhausted from subsisting on fruits and roots in the Himalayas, [and thus they sought relief] by partaking of salt and sour liquids.
For the purpose of warming him and for the purpose of nourishing him. "Thirsty" means parched with thirst. "Exhausted" means with bodies worn out.
It is said that having reached that banyan tree and seen its magnificent beauty, they thought, "Surely there is a deity of great power dwelling here;
it would be well if this deity would dispel our fatigue from the journey," and thus—
It is said: "Therein, those dwelling... sat down. "He" refers to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika.
"Of the laborers" means of the slaves, messengers, and workmen who perform service for wages. "Ordinary food and wages" means the food and wages that are normally to be given;
even though they were not working at that time because it was the Uposatha day, [it was given] according to the rate for a working day.
The meaning is: "only that which is to be given as food and wages. *Kañci* means even a single hired servant.
*Upārambho* is the attacking or harassing of another by means of their speech;
the meaning is a provocation by way of perceiving faults. Therefore he said: "having become desirous of launching a dispute with the intention of attacking. They speak [thus] by way of censuring.
It is called a "doctrine" (*vāda*) because one speaks by means of it; that is, a fault. The meaning is: "desiring to attribute that [fault], desiring to establish it.

Regarding the statement "that which is the soul is the body": here, taking up the doctrine that "one regards form as self," they say that whatever thing is designated as the soul is precisely what is designated as the body. Having made form and the self non-dual, [they speak thus].
Or they speak of a "being" with reference to a self imagined by outsiders, by way of viewing [it as such].

"It breaks up" means it perishes through the process of ceasing at its arising and passing away. This is because [the proponent] admits the non-difference of the soul from the body and shows the breaking up of the body;
for here, just as in the case of one who possesses parts, the soul—though not seen—is [inferred] from the body.
The distinction has been stated; thus, because there is no otherness from that which has not seen the distinction, it can be understood that the body is also undivided.
Since that distinction is established by direct perception, and because there is no body existing apart from the primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), he said:
"It becomes a doctrine of annihilationism (ucchedavāda)."

“‘The soul is one thing, the body another’—taking this to mean that the entity designated as the ‘soul’ is one thing and the entity designated as the ‘body’ is another, they speak by adopting a doctrine that proceeds according to the method beginning with ‘one regards the self as possessing form,’ and so forth.
Since the disintegration of form is observed, yet its absence is seen in the case of the self, it follows that the self must be eternal; thus he says: ‘For you... [it] results in...’”
379–380. Considering that this [question] is like imagining the height or shortness of the son of a barren woman, the Teacher set it aside as a question to be put aside (*ṭhapanīya*).
Having closed his eyes to that matter, he began the teaching of the Dhamma to them with the words, "Therefore, friends, listen," and so forth;
thus he said, "Then the Blessed One," and so on. "Of that very" refers to the Middle Way (*majjhimā paṭipadā*).
"Of one who has gone forth out of faith" means of one who has entered the homeless life with the thought, "In this way I shall escape from this suffering of the round of existence," and who,
having fulfilled the virtue appropriate thereto, possesses a mind concentrated through the first jhāna.
"This is the course" refers to that which is based on the defilement of views, such as "the soul is the same as the body," which illustrates the growth of the cycle of defilements.
The meaning is: "to speak words. "He is not free from doubt" means he has not crossed over doubt regarding phenomena;
the meaning is that he continues to move back and forth, shifting and wavering, here and there.
"'I know this very thing'" refers to that by which the bhikkhu, having attained and dwelling in the first jhāna, [knows] this together with its associated states.
"I know it as 'mind,' yet I do not speak thus"— that is, unlike those who hold wrong views,
who proclaim their own false grasp by taking that class of phenomena together with its basis non-differently, saying "the soul is the same as the body," or by taking both as different,
saying "the soul is one thing and the body another," I do not speak in such a way.

Because that Dhamma has been thoroughly understood, he said, "Then indeed," and so forth. Since outsiders for the most part produce only the meditative absorptions (jhāna) based on the kasiṇas, he said, "while developing the preliminary work (parikamma) of the kasiṇa.

Because the attainment of jhāna occurs through the power of meditation, and because meditation takes place by way of perceiving the earth-kasiṇa and so on, it is therefore described under the heading of "perception" (saññā). Thus:
He said: "It has arisen through the power of perception (*saññā*). Therefore he said: "One perceives the earth-kasina," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "it is not fitting for him," this was spoken with the intention that since the Blessed One stated in various places, "And yet, I do not say so," it should not be asserted by one who is a *kevalin* (an absolute one), a supreme person; thus it is said: "while conceiving..."
"...so they say. The remainder is easy to understand throughout.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Jāliya Sutta*. 8.
The Commentary on the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta*.
381. The commentary on the story of Acelaka Kassapa:
In whatever kingdom that city was located, and in whatever city within that kingdom the Blessed One resided at that time, that city also had this very name;
therefore, it is called Uruññāya, meaning "in the district of Uruññā," specifically in the place known as Uruññā.
"In the city" is the meaning. "Delightful" means charming due to its beautiful landscape, its excellence of shade and water, and its seclusion from people.
"Named" refers to a clan-name (*gotta-nāma*). "Austerity" (*tapas*) is that which burns, torments, and exhausts the body;
one who possesses this is an ascetic (*tapassin*), and he is addressed as such. Because he is thus constituted, he relies upon austerity, or rather, austerity relies upon him.

Therefore he says, "one who depends on heat. One who lives or conducts himself with what is coarse or harsh—unpleasant because it lacks the conduct esteemed by the virtuous—is a "coarse-liver" (*lūkhājīvī*);
[the text refers to] that coarse-liver. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "urinating, etc.," the actions such as hand-washing mentioned later in the text are included.
"He ridicules" means he reviles with derision. "He censures" means...
He reviles preceded by contempt; therefore it says, “he despises and ridicules. Regarding the phrase “in accordance with the Dhamma”:

here, *dhamma* means cause (*hetu*), as in such passages as “knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma” (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*); thus it says, “the corresponding cause of the cause.
And here, “cause” is intended in the sense of the meaning of a word that has arisen in such a way, because it is the state of being the cause for its occurrence.
For the application of words is dependent upon the application of meanings. And "imitation" (anukāraṇa) refers to that very [word] being spoken by others in such a manner.
"By others" means by those other beings who were referred to as "those who. "By the reason stated" means:
if you have not spoken in the same way as they spoke, then, being possessed of a reason by virtue of the reason stated by them, your doctrine [is refuted] beyond that.
Regarding this, there would not be even the slightest reproach or ground for censure by the wise;
the construction is: "Why would such a thing not occur? With the words "This is what is meant," etc., he shows that very point in brief.
382. Now, with reference to the doctrine of analysis (*vibhajjavāda*), the Blessed One said in brief: "They do not speak according to my teaching."
Having stated that, in order to demonstrate it by way of analysis, he said, "In this case, Kassapa," and so forth. Showing that analysis, he said, "Here, a certain person," and so on.

For the Blessed One censures useless bodily mortification—which does not lead to peace—with such words as, "Devotion to self-mortification is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial. However, [he praises] that which is purposeful...
He praises [the practice] conducive to peace, saying, “One becomes a forest-dweller, one becomes a wearer of rag-robes,” and so forth. “By way of little merit” means by way of demerit.
“Having fulfilled the three types of misconduct” means that, because of the presence of wrong view, one rejects the fruit of kamma;
having placed wrong view foremost by saying, “There is no giving,” and so forth, one thus fulfills the three types of misconduct.
"By way of deception" means by way of wrong livelihood, out of a desire to be esteemed for qualities one does not possess, while standing in hypocrisy.
"These two" refers to two types of persons who commit misconduct when it is said, "one with little merit" and "one with merit.
However, in the second method regarding the phrase "referring to these two," when it is said, "one with little merit" and "one with merit," they refer to those who practice good conduct.

The [remaining] points should be applied starting from the beginning. For these two types of persons are proponents of the efficacy of kamma. Thus, the application in the third and fourth methods should be understood according to the very same method stated for the first and second methods.
"Engaged in the conduct of outsiders" means engaged in the conduct of sectarians, not in the conduct of liberation. "Having made oneself comfortable" means by unrighteous means.

Having comforted oneself with pleasure, he therefore said, "having fulfilled misconduct. By means of the three conceits, such as "Now there is no one equal to me," he spoke of the fulfillment of misconduct.
"By way of wrong view" means by way of the wrong view that occurs in the form, "There is no fault in sensual pleasures.
"Paribbājikāya" refers to a female ascetic who has entered the life of renunciation.
“Daharāya” means to one who is young. “Mudukāya” means to one who is delicate. “Lomasāya” means to one who has fine, thin, and sparse body hair due to the presence of such hair.
“Kāmesu” means regarding sensual objects (vatthukāma). “Pātabyataṃ” means that which is to be consumed; or alternatively, “pātabyataṃ” refers to the state of being something to be consumed.
“Āpajjanto” means approaching. For this word “pā-” has the sense of consumption, and the suffix “tabba-” functions as an agentive derivation.
The meaning is: "they enjoy it according to their pleasure. For even *kilesakāma* (the desire of defilement), when it is relished, is included within *vatthukāma* (the desire for objects).

"This" refers to the analysis of the aforementioned categories of meaning, because it has been analyzed in that manner in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) according to the tradition of the non-Buddhist sects (*titthiya*). "In this Dispensation" means even in this teaching of the Buddha.

Having falsely claimed, "I possess" what is not actually present in oneself, namely *arahatta* (Arahatship)—this constitutes bordering chatter (*sāmantajappana*) and the use of requisites (*paccayapaṭisevana*).
"Dependent on deportment" refers to these three bases for hypocrisy (*kuhanavatthu*). "One such as that" means one who lives a coarse life by way of undertaking the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
The intention is: "I shall find happiness difficult to obtain through rebirth in the miserable states.
(383) "From such-and-such a place" means from such-and-such an existence (*bhava*). "Come" means come here by way of rebirth. "The place to go now" means...
The place of rebirth in the future. "Again, rebirth" means the third rebirth after the immediately preceding existence in the future;

"again, rebirth" means repeated arising. For what reason? One who does not know things as they truly are might censure anything at all through the influence of desire and aversion; but since I know things as they truly are, for what reason would I censure any of that?
The intention is that there is no such reason; therefore he said, "It is indeed to be censured," and so forth.
"That matter" refers to the censuring of what is to be censured and the praising of what is to be praised.
No one says, "This is not good," because it serves as the means for accomplishing welfare both pertaining to this visible world and to the future world.
Because of the auspiciousness of its occurrence. "Fivefold enmity" refers to the fivefold enmity beginning with the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*).
For that is called "enmity" (*vera*) because it acts as an adversary to the fivefold virtue (*sīla*) and because it is a cause of enmity for living beings.

Precisely for that reason, no one says of it, "This is good. Likewise, because it does not accomplish aims pertaining to this present life and so forth, [it is opposed] to the state of goodness of living beings.

And [it is so] because of its being a fault. "It should not be restrained" means it should not be prevented from grasping at form; for their intention is that the acquisition of the eye is for the purpose of seeing what is worth seeing.
To the extent that non-restraint in the five doors is good for them, to that same extent restraint therein is not good; thus he said: "Furthermore, as for those few... restraint in the five doors."
Alternatively, those "certain recluses and brahmins" who say "it is good" refer to the heterodox teachers (titthiyas) who say "it is good" regarding the practice of self-mortification and so forth;

we do not say that such things are "good. However, as for that which they say is "not good"—namely, the use of blameless requisites and the right practice consisting of being properly clad and properly robed—we say that this is indeed "good."
When they say, “It is not good,” we say, “It is good”—thus the meaning here should be understood.

Having thus shown the tetrad based on the opponent’s position (*paravāda*), he says “In this way,” etc., demonstrating that the very same [tetrad] is now presented as being based on one’s own position (*sakavāda*).
For whatever is similar to something by anyone, it is indeed similar to that [thing] as well; likewise...
"Unequal" means unequal. "The state of being equal and unequal" refers merely to the condition of being equal and unequal.
For in our own doctrine (sakavāda), the abandonment of all phenomena that ought to be abandoned is seen in their entirety, whereas it is not so in the doctrine of others (paravāda).

Likewise, in our own doctrine alone, the full ordination (upasampadā) of those phenomena that ought to be conferred is complete, and not so in the doctrine of others. Therefore it was said: "He said this," and so forth.
Commentary on the Discussion on Causing to Investigate (Samanuyuñjāpanakathāvaṇṇanā) 385.

"Asking about the tenet" means asking about the tenet by saying: "Does the ascetic Gotama live having abandoned all things subject to defilement without exception, or do other teachers of schools? First, state your own tenet on this matter. This is the reason.

"Questioning" means: when it is said, "The ascetic Gotama conducts himself having abandoned the phenomena of defilement without remainder," one questions the reason, asking, "For what reason do you cause others to grasp this meaning? "Questioning both" means:

after stating the reason, "This indeed is the reason here," and while the meaning thus affirmed is being established, one questions the reason through both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Inquiring after two examples of similes—both similar and dissimilar—in order to establish [the point], and inquiring after both while the cause is endowed with the three characteristics and the meaning as promised has been proven, he concludes by speaking correctly and without subsequent hesitation;

this is called "reiterating" (samanubhāsati). "Having brought together" (upasaṃharitvā) means having led [the conclusion] forward. The phrase beginning with "What to you? is a demonstration of the manner of bringing it together.
"In the second phrase" means in this phrase: "by the Saṅgha, or to the Saṅgha.

"That meaning" refers to the purpose consisting of practicing after having abandoned, without remainder, those states that are to be abandoned, and practicing after having undertaken, without remainder, those states that are to be undertaken.
"Having joined" means having joined [the explanation] with the terms beginning with "unwholesome" (akusala).
In the sense of being produced through heedlessness, they are both unwholesome (*akusala*) and are reckoned as such; thus they are so designated.
Therein, by the first term he speaks of those that are exclusively unwholesome, and by the second term, those associated with them and those belonging to their faction.
Therefore he said, "or having been set aside by making a division," meaning they are determined by way of belonging to the faction of the unwholesome.

Because it has the sense of being blameworthy (*sāvajja*), the sense of being faulty (*sadosa*), and is a synonym for what is censurable (*gārayha*), he said: “‘Blameworthy’ means ‘faulty. The Noble Ones (*ariya*) are indeed faultless;
however, these [states] are not faultless in any respect, and thus they are incapable of, or unable to, become Noble Ones in the sense of being faultless.

(386–392) Regarding the word *yaṃ*, this is a nominative singular used in the sense of a causal instrument; therefore he said: “by which the wise person. Or else, regarding *yaṃ vā pana*: “that which...”
"But whatever [little]"—this is a statement expressing lack of esteem; thus he said, "whether it be this or that, however slight. The "teachers of groups" refers to Pūraṇa and others.
Since the Saṅgha originates from the Teacher, the excellence of the Teacher is also manifested through the excellence of the Saṅgha;
therefore he said, "because even in the praise of the Saṅgha, the praise of the Teacher alone is established. Furthermore, that praise is rooted in serene confidence (*pasāda*).
In order to demonstrate that by way of confidence (*pasāda*), it is said: “Even while having confidence,” and so forth.

In this context, it should be understood that just as praise is accumulated through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of the word “even” (*pi*), so too is lack of confidence (*appasāda*) in the disciples due to a transgression of the Teacher, and lack of confidence in the Teacher due to a transgression of the disciples, thereby accumulated.
“Perfection of the body” (*sarīrasampatti*) means perfection of form (*rūpasampatti*), that is, the fulfillment of the physical body (*rūpakāya*).

The meaning is as follows. There are those who speak [of] the measure of form (*rūpa*) and the measure of sound and phenomena (*dhamma*). Again, "there are those who speak" should be connected specifically by way of the measure of phenomena.
Having brought forward the phrase "whatever praise belongs to the Saṅgha," the connection is made.
In that context, the fact that praise belongs only to the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha, and the absence of it in others, is thereby illuminated.
In order to present that [abstinence] by way of its exposition as abstinence through renunciation and restraint, it was said: “This is the intended meaning,” and so forth.
Therein, “abstinence by the destruction of the bridge” (setughātavirati) refers to the abstinence of the Noble Path.

“By means of mere insight” (vipassanāmattavasena) means by way of various modes of seeing such as “impermanent” or “suffering,” but not preceded by the discernment of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-vavatthāna) and the grasping of conditions.

By means of the contemplation of formations after having applied the three characteristics. "The others" refers to abandonment by cutting off (*samuccheda*), subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*).
"The rest" refers to all other restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) besides the five precepts; the perfectly pure restraint of patience (*khantisamvara*) described by the words "he is patient," etc.;
and that which is called "they are covered by wisdom," namely, the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*) consisting in the cutting off of the defilements.

He spoke with reference to this pentad of restraints: (1) restraint of knowledge; (2) pure restraint of the faculties, which functions by way of closing the doors of the six sense-faculties, headed by the mind;
and (3) restraint of energy, known as right exertion (*sammappadhāna*), described by the passage beginning, "for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states," and so forth.
Furthermore, there are these five recitations of the Pātimokkha, and so on.

Having shown the great abundance of virtue within the Dispensation, the aforementioned restraint of virtue is mentioned again for the purpose of showing that others abide in only a single portion of it.
393. *Sīhanāda* means the best roar, the roar of fearlessness, the roar that cannot be countered by anyone. "This..."

"My teaching as it has been stated is unerring; its state of being unerring is to be known by one's own independent realization through practicing this path"—this is for the purpose of awakening to its state of being unerring.

Regarding the phrases "There is, Kassapa," and so forth, that path which the ascetic Gotama speaks of when practicing at the appropriate and fitting time is "real" (bhūta) because of its actual existence, and it is "beneficial" (hita) because it leads exclusively to welfare.

He says that it is the goal (*attha*) because it is not devoid of the Dhamma, the Dhamma because it is not devoid of the goal, and the Vinaya because it leads to discipline and the disciplining of others;
thus he will know it for himself through his own direct experience:

"Kassapa, there exists a path that has been proclaimed by me after realizing it myself through direct higher knowledge—a path that constitutes the escape from the entire suffering of saṃsāra—and there is also the preliminary practice which serves as the means for its attainment."

This is the application here. By this, he shows that the discourse proceeding in the manner beginning with “The ascetic Gotama [teaches] these things,” which cannot be shaken by anyone, is the lion’s roar according to reality (*yathābhūta-sīhanāda*).
Just as in passages such as “One sees this thus as it really is with correct wisdom,” the path and the practice are treated as one.

Having done so, he shows [this] by saying, “This very one. This statement is for the purpose of negating the multiplicity of the path, for the purpose of showing its commonality to all noble ones, and for the purpose of showing its renown within the Dispensation. Therefore he said:
“Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path,” and “This alone is the path; there is no other for the purification of vision.”
“The one who sees the end of birth knows the single path,
the way that leads to welfare, out of compassion;
by this path, those of old have crossed over.”
“And those who have crossed and those who are crossing the flood.
In all these passages from the Suttas and the Abhidhamma, this one path alone is evident, well-known, and has come down [in the tradition].
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the practice of asceticism (*tapopakkama*).

394. Because it must be undertaken and initiated through austerity itself, it is called "the undertaking of austerity" (*tapopakkama*); thus he says, "from the undertaking of austerity" (*tapārambhā*).

And since the undertaking here is simply the performance [of the act], he says, "the meaning is 'austerities' (*tapokamma*). "Designated as the work of recluses" means they are known as the works that ought to be performed by recluses.
"Naked" (*niccola*) means one who has cast off clothing; one who has entirely and completely rejected clothing. He is "naked" by virtue of having undertaken the vow of nakedness.
“Standing, he voids excrement,” and so forth, is merely an illustration, for even such conduct as rinsing the mouth after vomiting was neglected by him.
He scrapes his hand with his tongue because he does not wash it with water. The same method applies to the second alternative as well.
When it is said, “Come, venerable sir,” the procedure consisting of approaching is called *ehibhadanta*; one who practices that is an *ehibhadantika*.
"Ehibhaddantika" means one who says "Come, good sir"; its opposite is "na ehibhaddantika.

This is with the intention that one should not act as a mere servant to another's word by saying, "One who is called a recluse must do whatever he is told. "Puretaraṃ" means prior to his own approaching of that place.
It is said that he [approached] with the intention: "A bhikkhu may indeed accept almsfood according to his own wish."
He does not accept it. He does not accept what has been prepared specifically for him, thinking, "Because of me as its cause, many small living beings have been brought to destruction.
He does not consent to an invitation, thinking, "In this way, their word will have been fulfilled.
Because he perceives even in pots and such things as being sentient beings, the author says, "a collector of water-pots," and so forth.

"An obstacle to food" (*kabaḷantarāyo*) means it is an obstacle to a morsel of food. "Collective alms" (*saṅkitti*) refers to that by which people gather together and praise [the meal] according to their village associations and so forth; likewise, it is a collection of rice and other grains gathered together. "People" (*manussā*) refers to people who perform services.
"Only the drinking of *surā*" means the drinking of *surā* that has reached the characteristic of being an intoxicant;

and here, by the mention of *surā*, *meraya* (distilled liquor) is also included. One who begs from only a single house is an "one-house-beggar" (*ekāgārika*). One who subsists on only a single mouthful of food is an "one-mouthful-eater" (*ekālopika*). It is given.
It is called *datti* because it is given; it is a small alms-bowl that receives only two or three mouthfuls, hence it is called a "small bowl" (*khuddakapāti*).
That which exists for one day by way of not eating is "one-day" (*ekāhika*), referring to food. That "one-day" [food] is, in substance, a fast of one day;
thus he says "intervening for one day. The same method applies to "two-day" (*dvīhika*) and so forth. One day...

Not eating for one day and then eating on the first day is the "one-day turn"; in terms of its actual meaning, it is simply the one-day practice. Not eating for two days and then eating on the second day is the "two-day turn.

The same method applies to the remaining two as well. However, the most rigorous practitioner who subsists on meals taken in rotation does not eat for two days and eats only on the first day. The same method applies to the remaining two as well.
395. *Kuṇḍaka* refers to very fine rice husks. 396.
*Sāṇa* garments are those produced from *sāṇa* fibers and *vāka* fibers. *Masāṇa* is a mixture of *sāṇa* and *masāṇa*, not made of *bhaṅga*.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in "eraka grass, etc.," there is an inclusion of *akkama*, *kacika*, *kadalī*, *vāka*, and so forth. For [garments] are indeed made from eraka and the others.
Tattered and worn-out robes deserve to be called "poor.
It is precisely by way of wrong effort that the practice of squatting is undertaken; thus he said, "devoted to the energy of squatting.
Alternatively, *thaṇḍila* refers to level, natural ground—as in such expressions as "he appeared on level ground" (*patthaṇḍile pāturahosi*)—and therefore, *thaṇḍilaseyya* means...
It is said that he lies on his natural ground, which is free from any covering. "The seat obtained" means the seat as it was found for sitting.
"Without disturbing" means not moving elsewhere; therefore he says, "one who is habituated to sit right there.
For he is called "undisturbed" because he does not discard it, does not abandon it, and does not move away from it. "Vikaṭa" refers to excrement by way of its source.
"Having considered it to be ugly.
And herein, the phrases of conduct beginning with "he is naked" and ending with "he does not drink rice-gruel water" constitute a single section.
The phrases beginning with "or he visits a single house" constitute various sections, or belong to different times. Likewise, the phrases beginning with "or he eats greens," and so forth.
And there are such passages as, “He wears hempen garments,” and so forth. Thus, the particle *vā* (or) and the particle *pi* (also/even) are employed here.
The particle *pi* should also be understood as having the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*). However, this was not done in the preceding cases.
Having stated, “He is naked,” the statement “He wears hempen garments, and so forth” follows; and having stated, “He wears dust and dirt,” the practice of “immersion in water” [is mentioned].
Thus, there is established no contradiction with the statement "devotedly engaged. Alternatively, what need is there for such consideration of non-contradiction here?

For the doctrine of the sectarians is like the talk of a madman. Or rather, it should be understood that having begun with the words "he is naked," the passage beginning with "he wears hempen garments" was spoken by way of illustrating all forms of self-mortification in connection with that topic.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Futility of Undertaking Austerities (Tapopakkamaniratthakathāvaṇṇanā) 397.

Without the perfections of virtue and so forth: without these supramundane perfections—namely, the perfection of virtue, the perfection of concentration, and the perfection of wisdom—neither the state of a recluse nor the state of a brahmin can ever come to be; and since that is the case, [the discourse follows].
Therefore, the construction is: "showing the fruitlessness of those ascetic practices.

The phrase "free from hatred and enmity" is stated because hatred is the direct opposite of loving-kindness (*mettā*). Alternatively, by the mention of "hatred," all defiled states that are opposed to the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) are included;
and by the mention of "enmity," sentient beings who act as adversaries are included. For to the extent that it is free from hatred, [it is loving-kindness].
“Free from enmity for that very reason.

(398) It is called *pakati* because it speaks (*kāyati*) or goes (*gameti*) by way of being manifest; it is a worldly conventional expression. Therefore he said: “This is indeed a natural state (*pakati*), thus this is a discourse on the natural state (*pakatikathā*).
Regarding the word *mattā*: the term *mattā* has the sense of “little,” as in such expressions as “the small amount of the sacrifice of happiness” (*mattā sukhapariccāgā*).
Having brought [the word] forward, he says "by this measure" (*pamāṇavācako*), meaning "by this very small measure.

But because the sequence of practice (*paṭipattikkamo*) that has reached its culmination must be abandoned by means of that measure, he says "by the sequence of practice" (*paṭipattikkamena*). "In all cases" (*sabbattha*) means in all sections. "If you were to speak otherwise" (*aññathā vadatha*) means:
if the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*) or the state of a brahmin (*brahmañña*) were to exist through such things as nakedness (*acelakabhāva*) and so forth.

"A recluse is easy to recognize; a brahmin is easy to recognize. However, because you describe the state of a recluse and the state of a brahmin in a manner entirely different from this, therefore "a recluse is difficult to recognize;
a brahmin is difficult to recognize. Thus he said, "It was with reference to this that I spoke.
Having rejected that doctrine of primordial nature (*pakativāda*), [he did so] by first keeping in mind that which constitutes the natural state of being a recluse and a brahmin.
Therefore, he said, "It is difficult," and so forth; and with reference to that very point, the Blessed One also said, "This is indeed the nature of things," and so forth.

Here, however, having rejected and withdrawn that doctrine of inherent nature (*pakativāda*) which pertains to ordinary recluses and brahmins, and thereby revealing and clarifying that it is by their very own nature and in the ultimate sense alone that the state of being difficult to know belongs to the recluse and the brahmin.
"In that case too" means according to the same method stated in the discourse on the ascetics and brahmins.
Regarding the praise of the perfection of virtue, concentration, and wisdom:
"A wise man" means one endowed with wisdom established through the perfection of causes; how did he learn it? Because his knowledge was fully matured.
With the clarity of wisdom shining within him like a lamp inside a jar, he grasped the meaning taught by the Blessed One here and there, and he reflected upon that teaching as well.
"Tassa ca" means: "and of him who is a naked ascetic (acelaka), even one who dwells devoted to the practice of bathing in water. I ask about those attainments (*sampatti*) by which—
The intended meaning is that he is a *samaṇa*. Regarding the phrase "by the perfection of virtue" (*sīlasampadāya*), the word "iti" has the sense of "beginning";

by it, the two phrases "by the perfection of mind" (*cittasampadāya*) and "by the perfection of wisdom" (*paññāsampadāya*) are included. For *arahantship* is comprised within the three aggregates beginning with the virtue of one beyond training (*asekha*).
Therefore, he said: "It was stated with reference specifically to the fruit of *arahantship*," and so forth. In this context, "this" refers to this statement.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Lion’s Roar:
402. He roars the unsurpassed lion’s roar of a Buddha because it is not shared by others and because its object is a meaning not shared by others.
It is supremely pure because of its extreme and absolute purity. "Supreme" (*parama*) means exalted; therefore he said:

"Supreme": this refers specifically to virtue (*sīla*) because it is mundane virtue. Just as the Blessed One’s supramundane virtue is unique and not shared by others because it destroys its opposites along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*), so too his mundane virtue has arisen in a manner that is commensurate with that [supramundane virtue].
Therefore, "equal with the equal" means "equally equal"; thus he said, "by virtue equal to my virtue, I am equal."
“‘That which is higher virtue’ (adhisīla)” refers to the Buddha’s virtue, spoken of by combining both the mundane and supramundane types together.
Therefore he said, “In regard to virtue as well. Thus, “this” means this very object of virtue. “First” because it occurs first.

“It heats” (tapati) means it causes suffering; the sense is that it dispels [defilements]. “It loathes” (jigucchati) means it despises [them] and sets them aside as base. Because it is free from taints...

The noble ones (ariya) are far removed from the defilements (kilesa). This is connected by supplying the phrase "asceticism and disgust" (tapojigucchā), which refers to energy (vīriya) associated with the paths and fruits (maggaphala).

It is called "supreme" (paramā) because it is the most excellent state of all. Just as the state of one who is young is "youth" (yobbana), so too the state of one who feels disgust is "disgust" (jeguccha).
The severing and the subsiding of the defilements are the liberation through severance (samucchedavimutti) and the liberation through subsidence (paṭipassaddhivimutti).

Nirvana is liberation as escape. Alternatively, because right speech and so forth are included under the heading of higher virtue (*adhisīla*), right effort under the heading of higher disgust (*adhijeguccha*),
and right view under the heading of higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*), the headings of what has not been mentioned include—

by way of inclusion of the unmentioned— the right intention, mindfulness, and concentration comprised within the paths and fruits, which constitute the liberations of eradication (*samuccheda*) and tranquility (*paṭipassaddhi*).
[These] are to be seen. But liberation as escape is nibbāna alone.
403. Any place secluded from people is intended here by the term "empty hut.
Since there can be no sound without one who roars therein, he said, "sitting all alone. "In the eight assemblies" refers to the assembly of khattiyas, [and so forth].

In these eight assemblies: the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā.
"Confidences" (*vesārajjāni*) means states of fearlessness; they are the state of being undaunted by anything, characterized by the perfection of knowledge and abandonment.

The meaning is as follows: "The place of the bull" (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*) means the best place, the supreme place; such is the meaning. Alternatively, the "bulls" (*āsabhā*) are the previous Buddhas, and it is their place;

such is the meaning. Furthermore, "belonging to the bull" (*usabhassa idaṃ*) is *āsabhaṃ*; it is *āsabhaṃ* because it is like [the place] of the bull. For just as that which is reckoned as the "leader" (*nisabha*)—*The input text was cut off here.*
Just as a bull, by means of his own bull-like strength, presses down upon the earth with all four feet and stands in an immovable position,
so too the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, presses down upon the earth of the eight assemblies with the four feet of self-confidence and stands in an immovable state,
unshakable by any adversary in the world including the devas. Thus...
Remaining [in that state], he claims, approaches, does not renounce, and attributes to himself that "bull-like position" (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*).
Therefore it is said: "He claims the bull-like position.
He "roars the lion’s roar" (*sīhanādaṃ nadati*); just as the king of beasts roars because of his endurance of dangers from forest buffaloes, rutting elephants, and the like—
And because he slays, he is called a "lion. Likewise, the Tathāgata is called a "lion" because he endures the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) and because he slays the doctrines of others.

The "lion's roar" is the roar of the lion spoken of in this way. In that regard, just as a lion, endowed with lion-like strength, confident in every respect and free from timidity, lets out a lion's roar; so too does the Tathāgata.
In the same way, the Tathāgata-Siṃha, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, is confident and free from trepidation among the eight assemblies;
he roars the lion’s roar, rich in various manifestations, according to the method beginning with "Such is form.
"Having formulated a question" means having composed it according to the power of his own knowledge regarding the matter he wishes to know.
“At that very moment” means he answers with spontaneous eloquence at the very instant of being questioned. He satisfies the mind because he answers in accordance with their inclinations.
And they consider it worth hearing because it is obtained through the ninth moment, excluding the eight forbidden moments.
Thus, having conceived reverence and respect, [they think]: “Whatever our Teacher speaks, we shall hear that.”
They think that it should be heard and received with great enthusiasm.

With profound clarity, through the increase of serene confidence and the removal of defilements, their minds become ready and supple. "An act of faith" (*pasannakāra*) means the honor to be performed by those who have faith;

the meaning is "worship consisting of both the Dhamma and material gifts. In this context, showing the worship of material gifts, he says "exquisite things," and so forth. [Then follows] the worship of the Dhamma.
But this is shown by the phrase "for suchness" (*tathattāya*).

"For the state of being thus" (*tathābhāvāya*) means for that state of being according to the way in which the Dhamma was taught for the purpose of escaping the suffering of saṃsāra; therefore he said, "for the purpose of fulfilling the practice in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammānudhammapaṭipattipūraṇatthāya*).
And that practice in accordance with the Dhamma is the sequence in which one should practice, provided that those practicing possess the internal factors.
To show the sequence for the fulfillment of that single [lion’s roar], it was said, “some in the refuges,” and so forth.
“Standing in this place” means standing in this passage of the Pāḷi which illuminates the fulfillment of the function of the lion’s roar: “And those who have entered the path succeed.
“Should be combined” means they should be compiled. One lion’s roar is not shared with others.
It is called "the irreversible, the best roar, the roar of the fearless. This same method applies to the remaining [roars] as well.
Regarding the phrase "of the first ten," this refers to the first ten lion-roars starting from the beginning up to "there is no one equal to me in liberation";
here, the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*), which is why he says "of each one. The phrases beginning with "and he roars amidst the assemblies" follow.
The Blessed One, roaring a lion’s roar among the assembly, saying, “I see a certain ascetic reborn in hell,” roars with confidence as far as the phrase,
“those who have entered the path attain [their goal]”— this is the application of the meaning as it occurs.
The same applies to the remaining nine cases as well.
“*Evaṃ*,” and so forth, is the presentation of those [qualities] as previously stated, taken collectively.
“Those ten” refers to the ten lion-roars beginning with “he roars amidst the assemblies. “Of the previous ten” means of the ten previously mentioned.
“By way of retinue” means that when each is joined individually by way of its retinue, there are one hundred lion-roars. “And the previous ten” refers to them when not so joined.

“Ten former ones”: thus there are one hundred lion-roars plus ten. “The doctrine of those who speak thus”: the doctrine of the sectarians (tīrthikas) who maintain such views and whose discourse proceeds in that manner.

“Having refuted”: having rejected it by demonstrating the absence of such a state [of purity]. This refers to what the Blessed One stated in the Udumbarikasutta, beginning with “Here, Nigrodha, an ascetic,” regarding the classification of defilements and the classification of complete purity.
To show that he uttered a lion’s roar in the presence of the wanderer Nigrodha and his assembly, it was said:
"Now, displaying the lion’s roar previously uttered in an assembly," and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the probation for those of other sects (*titthiya*).
404. This refers to the statement: "While I was dwelling at Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagaha... [he] asked me this question.
Granted that when Nigrodha asked the question and the Blessed One gave the answer, the Blessed One was not actually dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain at that moment;
however, taking into account that he was dwelling in the vicinity of Rājagaha, it is said: "At Rājagaha, on Vulture Peak Mountain..."
Regarding the statement "while dwelling," his dwelling on Vulture Peak was uninterrupted at that time; therefore, he said, "That which the Blessed One," and so forth.
*Yoge* means in the method, that is to say, in the means for escaping suffering. 405. The construction is:
"the probation (*parivāsa*) which one who stands on the stage of a novice (*sāmaṇera*) undergoes. Because [he was] on the stage of a novice...
One must remain [in the status of a probationer] while staying; one does not become a householder. Therefore, one receives the going-forth (pabbajjā) even without having completed the probation.

Regarding the phrase "he desires the going-forth, he desires the full admission" (upasampadā), the mention of "going-forth" here is merely for the sake of euphony in speech, just as the mention of "two nights" in the expression "sleeping together for two or three nights. By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "entering villages, etc.,"...

Frequenting prostitutes, widows, courtesans, eunuchs, and bhikkhunīs; being clever and untiring in various tasks for one's fellow celibates; having an intense desire for recitations, inquiries, and so forth;
being displeased at the disparagement of the teacher from whose sect one has come here, and likewise displeased at the praise of the Triple Gem—both of these, respectively, [constitute] praise.
And the inclusion of these [terms]—praise and blame, and being glad at heart—should be understood; therefore he said, "by fulfilling the eight duties.
"Having rubbed and ground" means having rubbed and ground like gold by way of testing one's underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*).
"Sitting in the midst of the assembly" refers to the Elder of the Saṅgha sitting in the midst of those monks sufficient in number for the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*).
Having sat down for the sake of favoring him, [the Blessed One said]: "Withdrawn" means secluded.
Since for one such as this, diligence in the purification of virtue is established even without being explicitly stated, he says: "not abandoning mindfulness regarding the meditation subject.

"With mind directed" means with the mind directed toward Nibbāna—leaning toward it, tending toward it, and inclining toward it. Even those born into noble families must likewise be endowed with proper conduct.

Thinking that they were desirous of going forth for the attainment of Arahatship, he included them in the same category as those [others] and said, "Noble sons" means "noble sons by virtue of their conduct.
Therefore he said, "In the right way" means "by means of the cause itself, by means of the reason itself.

For here, the phrase "in the right way" is used with reference to the going-forth according to the instruction, preceded by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), in the manner beginning with, "I am immersed in birth," and so forth.

“By way of cause” means by way of the method. “Having reached” means having attained or arrived at. “Having accomplished” means having brought to completion the virtues, concentration, and wisdom of one beyond training (*asekha*);
the meaning is “having fulfilled them.
“To bring to a conclusion” means to bring to a final end by way of a conclusion. “He dwelt having reached the consummation of the holy life... [and so on]...”
For it is with this very pinnacle of Arahantship that the teaching is brought to its conclusion. Concluding that section, however, the compilers of the Dhamma stated: "Now there was a certain one...
[as far as] ...it came to pass. Whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of meaning is indeed easy to understand.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta*.
9. Commentary on the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta;
Commentary on the Background of the Wanderer Poṭṭhapāda. 406.
Regarding the phrase "at Sāvatthī," he says, "in dependence upon Sāvatthī," using the locative case in the sense of proximity. [It was] of Prince Jeta...
"In Vaneta" means in the grove planted by the prince named Jeta. It is called an "ārāma" (monastery/garden) because renunciants delight there due to its comfort for dwelling and other such qualities;
it is a *vihāra* (dwelling). He was born with a tumor on his feet, thus he is Poṭṭhapāda.

Because he had entered the wandering life while still covered by the shadow of a cloth, he is a "Channa-paribbājaka" (a cloth-covered wanderer). A "brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla" is a brahmin who has attained great worth through the possession of great wealth. "Samaya" means...
"Sāmañña-niddesa" means "that which brings together various [doctrines]"; the meaning is that they speak from their own perspective (*pakārato*).
"They speak" (*pavadanti*) means they speak of a doctrine according to the specific system each has individually grasped; this is the meaning.

By the word "and so forth" (*pabhutayo*), [the text] includes Todeyya, Jāṇussoṇi, Soṇadaṇḍa, and others; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes Channa the wanderer and others. Here, "Tindukācīra... [refers to...]
"Atthi" refers to the Tindukācīra Monastery. Likewise, "ekasālaka" means a place where there is a single hall; thus, it is "in that Tindukācīra Ekasālaka.

Because it reveals the meaning of all that is knowable in its manifold aspects without exception, and because of the successive arising [of knowledge], the Blessed One’s knowledge is as if spread out over that place;
hence it is said, "having spread out the knowledge of omniscience," since that knowledge possesses the nature of a net.
It has already been stated below that those to be converted (veneyya) are included therein.
When attention is directed for the purpose of encompassing sentient beings who are to be converted, they first appear to him precisely as beings to be converted;
then, the accomplishment of their task by means of going for refuge and so forth is investigated. Thus it is said: “Investigating, ‘What indeed will happen? [The word] *nirodha*...
The cessation of perception (*saññānirodha*). "Emergence from cessation" means the arising of perception upon emerging from that cessation.
"In harmony with the knowledge of all Buddhas" means in accordance with how they have explained, and will explain, both the cessation and the emergence from cessation.
"Hatthisāriputta" means the son of Hatthisārin. [He spoke of] "Mount Yugandhara..."
“Having surrounded [it],” this is a hypothetical expression meaning, “if such a thing exists, as if it were that.
“Cloud-colored” means the color of a red cloud; the sense is that it resembles a cloud suffused with the radiance of twilight.

“Priceless” (paccaggha) means brand new, having received its designation from the very beginning, because it has not been used by anyone else, or likewise because of the Teacher’s resolve regarding that bowl.
It is always called "priceless" (*paccaggha*); or rather, because it possesses the characteristics of a superior jewel such as stone and so forth, that bowl is called "priceless.
(407) The intention is that [he did this] according to his own inclination and his aspiration for the endurance of the True Dharma, not because he was urged by another.
“Seeing that it was indeed too early” is a statement of fact; it is not for the purpose of showing that the time for the alms-round had not yet arrived.

For at that time, the Blessed One had already departed from the monastery early in the morning with the thought, “I shall favor Poṭṭhapāda with a teaching on the Dhamma pertaining to the stage of latent tendencies. The phrase “What if I... indicates doubt elsewhere, but here—
It is like an illustration of doubt. Why? He says, "Of the Buddhas," and so forth.

There is no such thing as doubt, because it has been eradicated right at the foot of the Bodhi tree. "The preliminary stage of reflection" means precisely the reflection that precedes the intended task.
That mental activity—such as "we shall do" or "we shall not do"—is what pertains to the Buddhas.
It is "possible" (labbhati) because it occurs by way of investigation, and not by way of doubt. Therefore he said:

since this is possible even for Buddhas, for that very reason the Blessed One said, "What if I were to... Alternatively, this particle (*nipāta*) is used in the sense of a supposition (*parikappana*).
For the meaning being expressed by the verbal form "he might approach" (*upasaṅkameyya*) is indeed illuminated by the particle "what if" (*yannūna*).
The construction is: "What if I were now to approach? As for the phrase "yadi pana," he says that this has the same meaning as the former, stating:

"the meaning is 'if, however, I [should go],' etc. 408. Just as the word *unnatappāya* (high-sounding) means a loud noise (*unnāda*), so too a sound that proceeds higher and higher by way of its vastness is called *unnāda*.
Having combined both of these together in the Pāḷi as "unnādiniyā" (resounding), he then shows them separately by saying "uccāsaddamahāsaddāyā" (with a high-pitched and loud noise).
Explaining that meaning, he said, "shouting loudly," and so forth. "Of her" refers to the assembly.

"By way of moving upward" means by way of proceeding higher and higher due to its great height. "By way of spreading in all directions" means by way of extending across all quarters through its vastness and continuous succession of beings.
Now, regarding the loud and great noise of the assembly of wanderers...

Showing the cause and the manner of its occurrence, he said, "For of those... and so forth. "Delight in sensual pleasures" (kāmassāda) means the gratification derived from the strands of sensual pleasure. "Delight in existence" (bhavassāda) refers to the gratification found in the realms of sense-sphere existence and so on.
409. "He established" means he placed [the mind] correctly by way of restraint; and here, "establishing" refers to [restraint] from frivolous talk.
He said, "He trained them," and so forth, because there was a training in conduct by way of causing the abandonment of mutual disrespect, as well as the concealment of the aforementioned fault.
"Quiet" means noiseless; the intention is the absence of loud or great noise.
"They did not neglect" means they did not act with disrespect.
410. “No āgate ānando”: when the Blessed One has arrived, there is no joy or rapture for us. “Piyasamudācārā” means those who speak with affection.

Having stated, “He went out to meet him,” [the author] says “for the Blessed One,” and so forth, in order to show that it was not only he, but rather that most other renunciants as well generally paid homage to the Blessed One. In this regard:

He states the reason: "Because of being born into a high family. By this, he shows that even those who have no faith in the Teaching might still pay honor to the Blessed One out of respect for his noble lineage.
Regarding the phrase "What kind of talk was there in the meantime?": it asks what kind of talk occurred within the aforementioned interval.
"Interrupted" means having been commenced but not brought to completion. When he says, "What talk was interrupted?"...
In terms of its meaning, he acknowledges that it is the conclusion of that [teaching]. As for the phrase "What more could there be?", this is a challenge made without distinction;
thus, since the conclusion of every such discourse has been promised, yet that remains outside the scope of others who are not omniscient, he said:
"Having brought it to its limit, I offer the invitation of an omniscient one."
Commentary on the Discussion of the Cessation of Perception (Abhisaññānirodhakathāvaṇṇanā) 411. *Sukāraṇaṃ* means a beautiful cause, one that brings about welfare and benefit.

*Nānātitthiyā* refers to those engaged in various sects (*nānātitthesu*) and various views (*nānāladdhīsu*); they are called "those of various sects" (*nānātitthiyā*), having changed the letter *k* to *y*. *Kutūhalaṃ ettha*... [text continues]
"It exists" is the marvel; that very hall is the "marvel-hall," which is why he said, "from the place where the marvel arises.
Regarding "the cessation of perception," this teaching is given by way of the headword "perception"; therefore, all phenomena accompanied by perception are included therein.
However, since consciousness is the primary factor there, he said, "in the cessation of consciousness. This is because their absolute cessation was not intended by him.
And because it is not their object, he said, "in the momentary cessation. Granted, that [cessation] is also not an object for them;
however, since the discussion of cessation being spoken of actually pertains to that very state, it was stated thus. Regarding the cry of praise: "Oh, the power of the Buddha!
He shows, as if it were a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand, a cause concealed by other existences, and such disciples as these in their undertaking of restraint..."
“...he establishes [it]”—thus the sound of praise spreads as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).
“Performing a simulated action” means performing an application that is merely a semblance (*paṭibhāga*) by way of delusion (*paḷāsa*).

“At a time in another existence” means taking some fabricated (*abhūtaparikappita*) object that has arisen somewhere as one’s own occasion (*samaya*), at the time of emerging in various places. “Any precept whatsoever” means...
They prescribe various rules as sections of training, establishing such reasons as: "One must remain mute; for this much time, one must sit in exactly one place," and so forth.
"Discourse on cessation" refers to the discourse on the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"Among them" refers to the ascetics, recluses, and brahmins who had assembled in the Hall of Wonders. "Some" means certain individuals. "The former" refers to...
"One who speaks thus: 'without cause, without condition'—this is how it should be construed: 'one who arises here [in this world].

'Attainment' refers to the attainment that brings about the state of non-perception (*asañña*). 'In cessation' means in the cessation of perception (*saññānirodhe*). 'Not seeing a cause' refers to the cause by which there is the total cessation and non-arising of perception in the realm of non-perception, and the cause by which, having passed away from there, there is the arising of that same perception here in the five-aggregate realm."
Not seeing that [state] because it is not an object of perception.
"Him" refers to the first speaker. "Having refuted" means having rejected it by saying, "Indeed, sir, this will not be so.

"The state of being non-percipient" refers to the condition of being devoid of perception due to the presence of a functional (kiriya) consciousness at the moment of falling into a swoon. He will explain [this further].
For it says, "having become unconscious. One who torments oneself (*attantapa*) is so called by means of scorching the defilements through suppression.

A "terrible ascetic" (*ghoratapo*) is one whose austerity is formidable due to its difficulty of performance. One who has "withered away his faculties" (*parimāritindriya*) is one whose eye and other faculties have been completely withered by bringing them to a state of non-indulgence.

"Broken" (*bhagga*) means one whose inclination toward the wholesome (*kusalajjhāsaya*) has been shattered. He spoke thus: "In this way, perception, O sir, is indeed the self of a person," and so forth.
He spoke of the cessation of perception (*saññā-nirodha*). By this method, the application [of the text] should be understood as appropriate for the two subsequent instances.
"The practice of *āthabbaṇa*" refers to the practice prescribed in the *Āthabbaṇa-veda* by which practitioners of *āthabbaṇa* induce unconsciousness.
"Having employed the *āthabbaṇa*" means having employed the recitation of mantras preceded by the offering of fire as it appears in the *Āthabbaṇa-veda*.
By showing the decapitation and so forth, he speaks of the cessation of perception (*saññā-nirodha*). "Of him" means of that person for whom the decapitation and so forth were displayed.

"Of the female spirits" (*yakkhadāsīnam*) means of the female deities (*devadāsīnam*), who are also called "those brought by the deities. "Sleep induced by intoxication" (*madaniddam*) refers to sleep caused by the sign of liquor-intoxication.
"Offering to the deities" (*devatūpahāram*) refers to the worship of the deities through dancing, singing, and so forth. "Drinking of liquor" (*surāpātim*) refers to drinking [liquor] to fullness.
"Suram" means liquor. "Divā" means after midday, that is, when the sun has risen high.
"Like the talk of the deaf and mute" means that the talk of these who fancy themselves wise is like the talk of blind children.
"The four cessations" means they describe four cessations that are mutually incompatible. And it is not by way of various intrinsic natures that are mutually contradictory...
It must exist, moreover, as a single intrinsic nature; therefore he said, "And by this," and so forth.
"By another indeed" means it must exist in a mode other than the modes described by these [preceding statements].

The repeated expression, "This is cessation, this is cessation," is for the purpose of showing that the Teacher, through his skill in teaching, will clarify cessation in its manifold aspects and forms.
Regarding the phrase *aho nūna*: here, *aho* is a particle used for what is wonderful (*acchariya*), and *nūna* is a particle used for recollection (*anussaraṇa*). Therefore, the intended meaning is:
"Oh, surely the Blessed One, because his teaching is not shared by others, would speak even of cessation as something wonderful (*aho acchariyaṃ*), having made it so.
The same method applies to the phrase "Oh, surely the Sugata. And it is precisely because of this manifestation of wonder that—
The word is repeated twice; furthermore, the term *aho* here also carries the sense of wonder. Since it is grasped by him precisely through the mode of recollection (*anussaraṇa*), it is said:
"‘Aho nūna’ is used in the sense of recollection. Because these phenomena subject to cessation are manifold due to their divisions into time, person, and so forth, the plural form is used;
and because of its connection with the word *kusala*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative.
