It should be seen. "Because of having practiced mastery" means because of having practiced mastery over the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"He knows its intrinsic nature" means he knows the intrinsic nature of cessation as it truly is.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Arising and Cessation of Causeless Perception.

412. "They slipped right in the middle of the house" means that men wishing to go out from the house did not descend the path, but instead met with a slip on the very level, open courtyard of the house itself; such is the meaning here.

There is no purpose in making a distinction here between a "specific cause" (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*) and a "common condition" (*sādhāraṇa-paccaya*), for this is merely a conventional designation (*saññā*).
Because the censure serves to refute the notion that there is no causal relationship, it is said:

"It is indeed called a cause. In the Canon it is stated, "They arise and they cease"; therein, the word "cease" is used for the purpose of showing that "perceptions arise with a cause and with conditions, but once arisen, they only cease; they do not remain."
This is not for the purpose of showing that cessation has both a cause and a condition. For arising has a cause, but cessation does not.
If cessation were also to have a cause, it would likewise have to undergo cessation, just as sprouts and the like do;
yet there is no cessation of that [cessation]. Therefore, the meaning of the text should be understood according to the method already stated. And this is the principle:

This is stated by way of momentary cessation. However, that which is the absolute non-arising and cessation according to the previously delimited time should be understood as "with cause" (sahetuka), because it cannot exist without such a practice. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"With the training, one perception ceases. And for that very reason, it is also stated here: "to illustrate the arising and cessation of perception together with its cause."
Regarding the phrase *sikkhā ekā*: here, *sikkhā* is in the instrumental case used as a nominative;

the word *eka* is a synonym for "some" (or "a certain"), as in such passages as "some thus assert," or "but some [say] of a being who is mindful," and it does not denote a numerical count. Thus he says:
"A single perception arises through training" means "a certain perception is born from training. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
413. *Tattha* means in that aforementioned higher teaching. Because they are included by way of right view and right intention, they have come down [in this context].

Since they are included—that is, subsumed—within the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) both by their intrinsic nature and by their function, the third training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*) has come down by way of right view and right intention.
For it has been said: "And as for that which, friend Visākha, is right view..."
"And whatever is right intention— these states are included within the aggregate of wisdom. Although, according to the method stated here,
all three trainings are indeed presented, nevertheless, the cessation of perception and feeling is shown specifically through the training in higher consciousness,
while the other two are brought in as its requisites.
"Lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcakāmaguṇika-rāga*) is the lust that arises with reference to the five categories of sensual objects.
"Sensual desire not yet arisen" (*asamuppanna-kāmacāra*) refers to any occurrence of sensual desire or any arising of greed that has not yet arisen by way of its present manifestation.

The former should be understood as greed having the strands of sensual pleasure as its object, because it is delimited by way of its specific object; the latter, however, comprises various types such as attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna-nikanti*) and lust for existence (*bhava-rāga*).

All modes of greed are also [included] because they proceed toward sense-pleasures in the sense of being desirable. For all phenomena belonging to the three planes are called "sense-pleasures" (kāmā) in the sense of being desirable.

Since both of these are designated by the name "perception of sense-pleasures" (kāmasaññā) according to the principle of association, both are indicated by extracting the term "perception of sense-pleasures."

The passage beginning with “Tattha” (therein) and so forth shows the distinction between passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇika-rāga*) and passion for unarisen conduct (*asamuppanna-kāmacāra*).
Granted, passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure is indeed eradicated by the Path even when it has not yet arisen;

however, even when that [specific passion] is eradicated, not all passion reaches eradication. Therefore, by the mention of passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure, [the text does not exclude] the other.

Since there is a grasping for all lust, the term "perception of sensual desire" (*kāmasaññā*) was employed in the Canon by way of a method that applies to both [types of lust] in order to include them both.
Having shown both of these according to their essential nature and their specific distinctions,
it is stated— because it encompasses everything— that "one who has not yet given rise to sensual conduct is suitable for this stage."

“Similarity” (sadisatta) refers to their being identical by way of having the same nature as the perception of sensual desire and so forth; by this, he shows that the term “preceding” (*purima*) used in the text is stated by way of establishing such similarity.
For here, those [perceptions] yet to come are said to “cease” because non-arising is intended;
therefore, he says, “it does not arise even though it has not arisen.”
Because they are born from seclusion from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), they are to be described together with the joy and bliss of the first jhāna, which are "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*);

thus, they are called "born of seclusion" because they consist of that portion [of the jhāna]. Because they are subtle due to their refinement over the various perceptions (*nānattasaññā*) and perceptions of resistance (*paṭighasaññā*), they are "subtle perceptions" (*sukhumasaññā*).
They have become such by way of their subtlety; in their ultimate sense, they possess an unerring intrinsic nature. This is the jhāna, along with the states associated with it.

The subtlety accomplished through development is known by way of the suppression of the hindrances; thus it is said: "It is subtle by way of the abandoning of the gross factors such as sensual desire.
"By way of its reality" means by way of its actual existence. "In all instances" means in all sections.
Just like the attainment and the resolution, the emergence is also included within the jhāna, just as it is with [the inclusion of] states.
Since the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*) among mental states does not involve advertence (*āvajjana*) or reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā*), it is said:
"One trains while entering, resolving upon, and emerging from the first jhāna," and not "while adverting or reflecting.
"That" refers to the first jhāna. "By that" is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a cause; thus, it means "by means of the first jhāna acting as a cause."

The meaning is as follows. Herein, the state of being the cause (*hetubhāva*) for the arising of the aforementioned perception by means of the jhāna consists in its being a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so forth, and in its serving as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya*) for the cessation of sensual perceptions; and this is according to the method of the Suttanta. It has been commented upon accordingly:
"because it cannot exist without such a mode of practice. By this method refers to that which [was explained] by way of the perception that is the opposite of the first jhāna.
“The training: one perception arises; the training: one perception ceases”—this is the meaning stated here according to this method.
“In all instances” means in all sections.
However, since here the arising and cessation of those respective perceptions are being discussed by way of attainment (*samāpatti*), [they are treated] by way of factors (*aṅga*).

Thus it was said; therefore he said, "But because... and so forth. "Comprehension by way of factors" (*aṅgato sammasana*) is a term for the characteristic of insight into phenomena according to their sequence (*anupadadhammavipassanā*).
For one practicing insight into phenomena according to their sequence, having attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), performs comprehension by way of factors;
yet perception (*saññā*) is not any factor of that absorption. And it has been said: "This perception is perception... and so on.

"Thus, the comprehension by way of factors has been set forth. "By way of factors" (*aṅgato*) means "by way of constituent parts" (*avayavato*); what is meant is "by way of each successive phenomenon" (*anupadadhammato*).
"That very same" refers to the base of nothingness itself.

Regarding the phrase "from which" (*yato kho*), he says "that which is called" (*yo nāmā*) because it is an ablative used in the sense of a nominative; as in the case of the word "at the beginning" (*ādimhi*).

“From the beginning” is said because the suffix *-to* can also be obtained from other case endings. *Sakasaññā* means a perception belonging to oneself (*sakasmiṃ attanā*) regarding what has been attained;
one who possesses that is *sakasaññī*. Therefore he says: “possessing the perception of one’s own first jhāna.
And here, the term *sakasaññī* refers to the pre-eminent perception of jhāna which serves as the basis for the cessation to be described below.
The vowel *ī* should be understood as indicating existence; for this very reason it says, "He touches the peak of perception by way of gradual succession," and so forth.

Therefore, it should be understood that in each respective case, by the mention of mastery over one's own perception, the state of complete proficiency through long practice in those various meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) is illustrated.

“Of the mundane” (*lokiyānaṃ*) is a genitive used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*), or it expresses the sense of ownership (*sāmi-atthe*). For in whatever respect that [attainment] is the best among them, in that same respect it is also the best for them.
The qualification “of the mundane” is because it is not the best among the supramundane attainments (*lokuttara-samāpatti*).
The qualification “of the functional and non-functional attainments” (*kicca-kāraka-samāpattīnaṃ*) is because it is not the best among the non-functional attainments (*akicca-kāraka-samāpatti*).
And its state of performing no function is understood from the statement that it lacks the function of clear perception (*paṭusaññā*).

For just as perception is there, so too are contact and the other [mental factors]. Indeed, to the extent that they exist there in a form impossible for natural insight-observers to comprehend—due to their having reached a state of extreme subtlety with only residual formations remaining—to that same extent, although they are capable of performing their functions clearly, [they do not do so].
"They do not exist. This matter has been explained in detail in the *Paramatthamañjūsā*, the commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*, within the discussion on the formless attainments (*ārūpyakathā*);
therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated there.

However, some hold that "just as each successive lower attainment fulfills the function of a basis for each successive higher one, the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-samāpatti*) does not [do so]."

Some say, "Because it accomplishes the function of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) for anyone, it is called 'one that performs what is not its duty' (akiccakārikā), whereas the other is called 'one that performs its duty' (kiccakārikā).
That is incorrect, because that [other] also accomplishes the function of resolution through such things as the taming of the insight-consciousness.
Therefore, only the former meaning is correct.
"Pakappeti" means he prepares (saṃvidahati). For one entering jhāna indeed prepares the bliss of jhāna within himself.
"Abhisaṅkharoti" means he exerts; the meaning is that he accumulates. For the sense of accumulation is the sense of origination (samudaya).
Since volition reaches its peak through the influence of craving (nikanti), [the author], showing the cause by way of a metaphorical designation of the effect, says:

It is said: “One who forms an attachment conditions [a perception] by name. Now, these perceptions of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-saññā*) which are currently being experienced by me would cease;
for it is possible to condition volition for the sake of the higher jhānas precisely through the transcendence of those. “Other” means other than the perceptions of the base of nothingness.
They are “gross” because of their more substantial nature. If one asks, “Which ones? he says: “the life-continuum perceptions” (*bhavaṅga-saññā*).
For indeed, after emerging from the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), there would be volitional formations (cetanābhisaṅkharaṇa) for the sake of the higher jhānas;

and this emergence occurs by way of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Since there is an intermittent occurrence of the life-continuum until the attainment of the higher jhāna, he said, "perceptions of the life-continuum (bhavaṅgasaññā) might arise."
“Intending” means one who is entering the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for one or two mental moments.

One does not intend in that way as in the lower jhānas; for it is by intending through prior application (*pubbābhoga*) that one prepares for a jhāna, and thus here it is said, “he intends. This is because [one thinks], “I shall produce this jhāna, I shall attain it.”
The mental formation [expressed by] “I enter upon [it]” occurs only for one who has attachment (*sālaya*) toward that state, not for one who is without attachment (*anālaya*);

therefore, the meaning is that even when practicing a meditative absorption (*jhāna*) lasting only a single moment of consciousness, one is forming a volitional construction because of the non-abandonment of craving (*nikanti*) for it.
Furthermore, because there is no such prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*) toward it as there is in the case of the lower absorptions, [the above applies].
Therefore, it is said: "he does not form [volitional formations]. The passage beginning with "Of this bhikkhu" is an exposition of the very meaning already stated.
With the words "And this meaning," etc., he illustrates that same meaning by means of a simile.
"In the rear part" means in the rear part of the father's house. "From there" means from the son's house. "Only the house obtained" refers to that from which...
"Alms have been obtained by him from this very house"—that is, from his own son's house.

It is "like a sitting hall" because the attainment of the base of nothingness must be approached as the place corresponding to the father's house and the son's house, since one must approach the attainments of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and cessation in those respective places.
"Without giving attention to the father's house" means that even though he has entered it and transcended it, he does not direct his mind toward the father's house.
Just as in the case of pointing out the son’s house, even though one must enter the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for one or two mental moments, one does not attend to it;
rather, one attends solely to the attainment of cessation that follows.

Thus, the relationship between the simile and the subject illustrated should be understood through both the commonality of non-attention and the commonality of attention, since even by means of pointing out, it is precisely attention that is being manifested.
For without attention (*manasikāra*), the act of describing is not possible.

"Those perceptions of jhāna" refers to those perceptions of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception that have occurred during one or two mental moments. "They cease" means they cease only partially;
however, due to the force of previous formative volitions (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*), there is no further arising of them. And just as it is with the perceptions of jhāna, so it is here.

Thus, he stated that for the other perceptions, rapture (*pīti*) arises, saying: "And other gross life-continuum perceptions (*bhavaṅga-saññā*) do not arise," the intention being "at the time as delimited.
A monk who has practiced in this way is a monk established in Arahantship or in the fruit of Non-returning while standing at the pinnacle of perception as described;
he is endowed with two fruits [of stream-entry and once-returning], and [he has abandoned] three formations.

By way of these—namely, subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*), the sixteenfold course of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*), and the ninefold course of concentration (*samādhicariyā*)—he has entered upon the practice of accomplishing cessation.
Regarding the word "touches" (*phusati*): here, "touching" means finding (*vindana*) or obtaining (*paṭiladdhi*); thus it is said, "he finds, he obtains.
In terms of its actual meaning, however, it is simply the total non-occurrence of mind and mental factors for the duration of time as previously delimited.
The prefix *abhi* is merely a particle and is devoid of meaning; therefore, the sense is simply "perception" (*saññā*).

Since the term for attainment (*samāpatti*) ought to have been stated immediately after the term for cessation (*nirodha*), the word "clearly comprehending" (*sampajañña*) is placed between those two;
thus he says, "stated by making it immediate to the term for cessation. Consequently, he says, "anupaṭi... [etc. ...the meaning. In that case as well, it is likewise.
The construction is: "This is the specific meaning even in the sequential arrangement of the terms. "Of one who is fully aware" (*sampajānantassa*) means:
of one who, having entered and emerged from each respective attainment, understands (*pajānantassa*) the conditioned phenomena therein by way of comprehension (*sammasana*).

"At the end" (*ante*) means at the conclusion of the practice leading to cessation as previously described. In the second alternative, "of one who is fully aware" means "one who acts with full awareness" (*sampajānakārī*).

This is the purpose; therefore, by means of that, the wisdom that accomplishes the goal—along with the wisdom of all wonders—from the very beginning for the bhikkhu entering the attainment of cessation, has been shown according to its function. That is why he said, "of the wise bhikkhu.
"In every aspect" refers to: the specific nature of the attainment, the one who enters it, the place of entry, and the cause.
"In every way, such as 'the manner of entering' and so forth. "Therein" means in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"Should be understood from where it is already stated" means it should be taken from the very place where it has been explained; the intention is that we do not state it here again for fear of redundancy.

In the phrase "Thus indeed, I [speak]," the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) has the sense of "manner," considering it as a demonstration of the manner in which it was learned. But in the phrase "Thus, Poṭṭhapāda," it has the sense of "acceptance"; therefore he says, "acknowledging, 'It has been well learned by you.'"
415. "The summit of perception" (*saññāgga*) means that perception is the highest (*agga*) therein; it refers to the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*).

Having considered that the summit of perception exists and is found even among the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), he said "many also" (*bahūnipi*), showing a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*) from the word "various" (*puthū*) in the canonical text.
By the word "as" (*yathā*), a specific mode—the manner of the instrument—is intended, not a general mode; thus he said: "by which... (*yena*).

"By which *kasiṇa*? means "by the earth-*kasiṇa* acting as the instrument. First, the status of being an instrument is appropriate for *jhāna*, because it is the most effective means for touching the cessation of perception (*saññānirodha*).
How [is it appropriate] for the *kasiṇas*? That status is indeed appropriate for them as well;
for to the same extent that *jhāna* possesses the quality of being the most effective means for touching cessation, to that same extent do the *kasiṇas* as well.
Because of its inseparable connection with that. Even though there are many causes, the action indeed occurs, just as one says, "He goes by means of a horse, a vehicle, and a torch.

"At once" means simultaneously. "The cessation of the preceding perception" refers to the cessation of the preceding perceptions such as the perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*), and not to the cessation of perception known as the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"One peak of perception" means one perception that is a peak, that is, the best; this is in relation to the lower perception.
Because it is the highest state. It is called "the peak of perception" (*saññāgga*) because it is both perception and the peak;
it does not mean the peak among perceptions. "Twice" means two times. "In the remaining kasiṇas": only the kasiṇas are mentioned here because the discussion of cessation is the primary subject.
For that very reason, it should be understood that by the mention of "jhāna" here, only the kasiṇa-jhānas are intended. "By the first jhāna..."

By the phrase "by means of [the kasiṇa] as an instrument," he speaks without referring to the object, just as in the expression "by whichever kasiṇa," where it is stated without referring to the jhāna.
With the words "Thus," etc., he concludes by summarizing the very meaning already stated.
"All" means all the jhānas entered upon on a single occasion. "Summarizing" means by way of the characteristic of perceiving, because there is no difference in their essential nature.
"Having gathered together in one place. "Again and again" means repeatedly. 416.
In the first method, the perceptions and knowledges are shown according to the individual who is increasing insight, which has the jhānas as its proximate cause.
In the second method, however, because one is connecting [insight] with the path after having brought insight to its peak, there is the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*).
Therefore, perceptions and knowledges were shown by way of the insight path.
However, because the first method is coarse due to its mundane nature, and the second method is mixed, both of these were disregarded;
instead, perceptions and knowledges were shown by way of the path and fruit solely to demonstrate that which is produced as supramundane—extremely subtle, beautiful, and stable.
In the third method. These three methods are shown by way of purifying the path.
To clarify that "this, however, is the essence here," the doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva is cited.
Having asked about cessation and having that explained, one asks about the arising of the knowledge of perception immediately thereafter; this is, in meaning, emergence from cessation.
He asks: "Emergence from cessation" may refer either to the arising of the fruit of Arahantship or to the arising of the fruit of Non-returning.
In that context, perception (*saññā*) is primary, and immediately following it is the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).
Determining both of these, the Elder said, "What are these bhikkhus saying? and so forth. Therein, "What are these bhikkhus saying? refers to that moment.
In the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, having reached this point, he speaks with reference to those monks who, according to the aforementioned sequence, explain the three methods.
Just as, when the knowledge of the path and its fruit have arisen on the course of the path, the reviewing knowledges of the path and fruit necessarily arise; [so too here].
Thus, it is said that "the knowledge of subsequent reviewing" refers to the knowledge of reviewing the fruit within the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*).

The phrase "this is the fruit of Arahatship" is a demonstration of the mode of occurrence of this reviewing knowledge. "Conditioned by the perception associated with the concentration of the fruit" means conditioned by the perception accompanied by the concentration of the fruit.
The particle *kira* has the sense of recollection; it belongs to the class of recollecting the Dhamma as it was attained.
For this is reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇā*). And here, by way of concentration (*samādhi*), the entire fruit of arhatship is included according to the principle of concomitance;

for in its absence, reflective contemplation is impossible. Thus he said, "with this as condition" (*idappaccayā*). *Commentary on the Discussion of the Selfhood of Perception* (*Saññāattakathāvaṇṇanā*)

417. Through the smoothness of the teaching, knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*) becomes like one who has been bathed, owing to the cleansing of the impurities of passion, malice, and so forth;

through its subtlety, it becomes like one anointed and smeared with fine unguents; and through being struck by the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*), it becomes like one adorned with earrings and other ornaments.
And for the knowledge that cultivates that [teaching], there is such a state, which results in the person possessing it attaining such a state.
He said, "The entry into his dwelling during the discourse on cessation is like entering a royal bedchamber," in the passage beginning with "even though it was placed upon a fine and subtle...
and ending with "...was set forth. "Therein" means in that discourse on cessation. "Not finding happiness" means not obtaining it due to dull-wittedness.
"Like a place of excrement" because of its being defiled by impurities. "His own tenet" means his own view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*). "Having obtained consent" means...
"Having obtained permission" means having caused [the opponent] to grant permission by saying, "Such is my self," and thus having established one's own tenet.
"But which? means: among the three types of theories of self—namely, the coarse, the mind-made, and the formless—which one?
"Maintaining" means maintaining by way of refuting [the opponent's view]; the intended meaning is that he conceals it.
Because the proponent of self (attavādī), grasping the continuity of the fourfold stream of material form as a unity, believes "the self is gross" due to its material nature;
and by imagining it to be supported by food and drink, he conceives of it as "eternal.

Furthermore, its distinctness from consciousness is established through its very material nature, which the proponents of the Vedas describe in two ways: as "consisting of food" and "consisting of drink."
They speak thus; therefore, the wanderer said with reference to that, "It is indeed gross.

In this regard, if the self were possessed of form (rūpī) yet non-percipient (asaññī)—because perception (saññā) is of an immaterial nature and because material phenomena (rūpadhammā) have the inherent characteristic of not being percipient—and if, while being possessed of form, it were eternal according to your view, then [perception], because it arises again and again in various places...

"It breaks apart" means it is impermanent because of the existence of disintegration; likewise, because of the absence of perception in the sense that "perception is one thing, the self is another," it is insentient.
Thus, it follows that it is neither the doer of karma nor the enjoyer of its fruit. Therefore, he said: "For it is coarse for you," and so forth.
"Paccāgacchato" means of one who returns; the meaning is "of one who knows. "And perception is other..."

"Why was it said: 'other perceptions arise and other perceptions cease'? Is it not the case that cessation is preceded by arising, and that there is no such thing as what has arisen and yet does not cease?
With reference to this objection, he says: "Of the four aggregates," and so forth.
(418–420) "Mind-made" (*manomaya*) means made of mind by way of the mind of meditative absorption (*jhāna*). For that which is independent of external conditions—

It is called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because it is produced by the mind alone. This refers to the body produced in the realm of form (*rūpaloka*), which those who propound the Vedas describe in two ways as "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) and "consisting of consciousness" (*viññāṇamaya*). "In that case too" means even in this position that "the self is mind-made.
"When the fault has been pointed out" means when the fault has been stated by such words as, "there will be another perception," and so forth. "In this case too" refers to the previous argument.
The refutation of this [view] should be understood according to the same method already stated. However, there is this distinction:

if the self were mind-made, possessing all its major and minor limbs and with no faculties lacking, then, this being the case, one would have to say as before, "Form might be the self, but it is not percipient.
Therefore he said: "For if it were mind-made for you," and so forth. But why did this wanderer first [propound] a coarse self?
Having asserted that doctrine and then abandoned it, he again asserts a mind-made self; and having abandoned that as well, he asserts a formless self.

Granted that the reason for this has already been stated above, nevertheless, in order to show that these so-called sectarians possess unsettled minds and are as fickle as a stake driven into a heap of chaff, [the text says] "just as..."
"...is called 'one who is insane,'" and so forth. Therein, "by perception" means by natural perception (*pakatisaññā*).
He desires its arising and cessation because he sees the rise and fall of perception as it occurs in continuous succession.

Nevertheless, taking the conventional designation (*samaññā*) that occurs as "perception, perception" and grasping it as "self," and imagining its non-interruption, he conceives of eternalism; therefore he said, "the self..."
"But he conceives [the self] as eternal.

"In the same way" means that just as in the two doctrines—"the self possesses form" and "the self is mind-made"—there is the distinctness of the perception from the self, so too there is the unavoidable consequence of the fault of insentience;
in the same way, there is a fault in this doctrine as well. Therefore he said:
“Showing its fault in the same way”: by means of wrong adherence, which is to say, the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*). “Because it is overcome”:
because it is overwhelmed by the state cultivated since beginningless time, and because the range of knowledge has been obstructed. “Not knowing that diversity”:
the fool, deceived by the density of continuity (*santatighana*) and the density of the collection (*samūhaghana*), [perceives] that which proceeds as a continuous stream.
One adheres to and expresses [the view] by way of a false grasp, clinging to the collection of phenomena as "self" and "permanent.
The resolution of the compact is the knowing of that which is designated as a unity according to its true nature after having analyzed it;
this does not exist at all for the sectarians, and thus, because of the absence of such ripened knowledge, even when this is being stated, this wanderer [does not understand].
He did not know it. Therefore it was said: "Even while being told by the Blessed One, he did not understand that diversity.

This so-called perception arises with various objects at various moments and passes away; yet, even while seeing the arising and ceasing of perception, one might still imagine a self consisting of perception, a self that is perception itself, and—due to the absence of the aforementioned thorough analysis of its density—regard it as permanent.
He conceives by means of the conceiving of views. And for one who has become thus, the nature of the Dhamma—which is subtle, delicate, supreme, and profound—is simply not known;
hence it is said, “It is indeed difficult to know,” and so forth.
Among view and the rest, the seeing and the dogmatic adherence that “this is exactly so” is view. That which constitutes its preliminary stage—
“Acceptance by way of reflection that ‘this is so’ is *khanti* (patience/endurance). Likewise, approval is *ruci* (liking).

The passage beginning with “otherwise” (*aññathā*) is the detailed exposition of those views and so forth. In this context, “otherwise” means: whereas in the Noble Discipline there is a vision by way of the Middle Way, avoiding the two extremes, it is precisely otherwise than that.
“Something else indeed” (*aññadeva*) refers to that which, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramatthato*),...

The aggregates, sense bases, and so forth exist, as do their impermanence and other characteristics; yet you accept and prefer a self—which is something entirely different from those and does not exist in the ultimate sense—along with its eternalism and other attributes.
"Application" (āyoga) means the practice, the engagement, or the devotion [to such views]; thus he said, "being devotedly engaged.
"In the practice" (paṭipattiyā) refers to the practice of a wandering ascetic, such as the contemplation of the ultimate self and so forth. This is difficult to discern.

Regarding the nature of things (*dhammatā*), you [might think] that because the distinction between "this is the ultimate truth" (*paramattha*) and "this is conventional truth" (*sammuti*) is difficult to discern, [one is confused].
Having thought, "If this is difficult to understand, let it be for now; however, I shall ask the Blessed One about this matter," he acted accordingly.
To show how he did so, the passage beginning with "Then the wanderer... was spoken. Or, another [explanation] is that he is restrained (*saññata*).
The meaning is: let there be a self that has a nature other than the nature of perception (*saññā*). "His" (*assa*) means of the self (*attano*).

It is called "the world" (*loka*) because merit and demerit, as well as their ripening, are seen (*lokīyati*) or perceived therein; thus, it refers to the self. That [self] is intended by him to be the doer and the experiencer.
"A speculative view" (*diṭṭhigata*) refers to a speculative view proceeding according to such methods as "the self and the world are eternal," and so forth.
This adherence to views is not based on matters pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and so forth, because it does not lead to them.

For only that which brings about such results can be said to be "based" upon them, as is the case with the equipment of merit and knowledge (*puññañāṇasambhāra*). By this very fact, it should be understood that its lack of basis in the Dhamma is also described.
"Of the beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyassa*): [the compound] *ādibrahmacariyaṃ* means the beginning of the holy life; that very thing...

It pertains to the fundamental holy life (*ādibrahmacariyaka*), as in the expression “the discipline itself is that which leads to discipline” (*vinayo eva venayiko*). Therefore, he said, “of that which is comprised of the three trainings,” and so forth.

The fact that adherence to wrong views does not lead to disenchantment with, detachment from, cessation of, or peace within the round of saṃsāra should be understood because it is included within the round and because it binds one to the round.
Likewise, it should be seen as not leading to direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.

"For the purpose of higher knowledge" (*abhijānanāya*) means for the purpose of knowing through the mastery of full understanding of the known (*ñāta-pariññā*). "For the purpose of awakening" (*sambujjhanatthāya*):

they say this means for the purpose of awakening through the mastery of full understanding by investigation and abandonment (*tīraṇa-pahāna-pariññā*). "For the purpose of higher knowledge" (*abhijānanāya*): it means for the purpose of knowing by means of the wisdom of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-paññā*);

since that indeed constitutes the making manifest of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he says "for the purpose of making [it] manifest" (*paccakkhakiriyāya*). "For the purpose of awakening" (*sambujjhanatthāya*):...
For the sake of penetration by means of the clear realization through full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*).
Although craving (*taṇhā*) is indeed of the nature of suffering, it is stated "setting aside craving" because it is grasped separately as the origin (*samudaya*) [of suffering].
From its production—that is, from its arising—even though craving produces suffering, it does so when accompanied by other conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*).
He says "with conditions" (sappaccayā) to show that they do not arise alone. "The non-occurrence of both" means the cause for the non-occurrence of both;
it is "non-occurrence" because suffering and its origin do not occur therein, or because they have been reached in this state.
One goes to, that is, attains, the cessation of suffering which is Nibbāna, and the path leading to that end is thus the "path leading to the cessation of suffering."
The manifestation of the path means the arising of the supreme path. The realization of the fruit means the attainment of the fruit of one beyond training (asekkha).
The mode refers to that sign of going. 421. "Piercing" (*sannitodaka*) is the act of piercing or pricking by way of restraining from all sides;
and since "by speech" (*vācāya*) is used as an instrumental case in the sense of an agent, he says "by the goad of speech. "Filled with dung" (*sajjhabbharita*) means filled excessively on all sides.
"Akaṃsu" means that about three hundred wanderers, like three hundred leather-workers, pricked [him] with verbal goads.
"Sabhāvato" means existing by way of ultimate nature (*paramattha-sabhāva*), not unperceivable like primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth.
"Tacchaṃ" means true. "Tathaṃ" means non-erroneous. "Lokuttara-dhammesu" is the locative case denoting the object; [it refers to] those supramundane states.

Having made it its object. "Stable by nature" means having a firmly established nature; the sense is that which produces that [stability]. "The fixed order of supramundane states" means determined by the fixed order that leads to the attainment of supramundane states;
thus he said, "For of the Buddhas," and so forth. "Of such a kind" refers to the manner described by the phrase "the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhitatā), etc.
*Commentary on the Episodes of Citta, Hatthi-sāriputta, and Poṭṭhapāda*
"422. Regarding 'subtle matters' (sukhumesu atthantaresu): this refers to phenomena such as the aggregates (khandha) and bases (āyatana), which are the domain of subtle knowledge.
'Skilled' (kusalo): he was proficient due to having cultivated familiarity with the Buddha’s teaching in the past.
Because he had previously spoken of the benefits of the householder's life and thereby incited a virtuous monk to disrobe by speaking in that manner, he himself has now become virtuous."
Having done so, he fell away six times. For the fruit must correspond to the action.
"Spoken by a Great Disciple" means spoken for the purpose of disparaging the Great Disciple, the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita.
"Unable to establish himself" means unable to find a firm footing in the Teaching.
423. "Due to the absence of the eye of wisdom" means due to the lack of the eye of wisdom capable of discerning well-spoken and ill-spoken words, as well as the even and the uneven.
Regarding the phrase "one who possesses the eye," the words beginning with "well-spoken" are stated to show what kind of eye makes a person "one who possesses the eye.
"Single-sided" means exclusive; the intention is that they are determined by their quality of leading to Nibbāna.

"Established" means determined. The intention is that they are not of a single aspect, nor are they absolute; they are not definitively fixed as leading to Nibbāna because they are included within the round of existence (vaṭṭa).
This is the commentary on the "one-sided dhammas."
425. Having asked the reason, "For what purpose was it begun?", the purpose is answered as:
"To demonstrate its lack of leading to liberation. For when the fruit is established, the cause is thereby established. Regarding the phrase "for the goal that has been made known":
"goal" (niṭṭhā) refers to liberation, because one goes to the end of the suffering of saṃsāra by means of it; thus it is said that liberation is the goal. Indeed, the path to the goal—

Here, by the elision of the latter member of the compound, it is called "niṭṭhā. For it is the state of not leading out and the state of leading out that is being spoken of, not the final goal (niṭṭhā) itself.
Alternatively, *niyyāna* means going forth, emerging, or escape; the meaning is the subsiding of the suffering of saṃsāra.
That which leads out is *niyyānika*; that which does not lead out is *aniyyānika*. The state of being such is *aniyyānikabhāva*.

The phrase "for the purpose of showing that" should be supplied [to the sentence]. He says "thus" because he takes up the mere commonality of the verbal expression "nibbāna, nibbāna," but not because the designation "nibbāna" is actually applicable within their system from the perspective of ultimate truth;

therefore it is said, "And that is not conducive to liberation," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by way of being a worldly monument, etc.," here the word "etc. includes [the following]: "another..."
"Release is the awakening to another person as distinct from oneself;

release is the abiding of the self in its own nature, free from qualities such as intelligence and the like; release is the non-occurrence [of rebirth] through the non-neglect of the cessation of bodily activity, destinies, births, and bonds;
release is co-residence with that other radiant person; release is proximity [to him]."
The inclusion of such [views] as "liberation is through association" should be understood. Regarding the phrase "as it has been described":

it does not lead out by way of the specific mode in which it was described; for it does not lead out by that mode in which it was proclaimed by them—that is, the manner in which "the final goal is to be reached"—because that [goal] is not to be attained [by those means].
It is rejected by the wise because "this is not the final goal, nor is it the path, since it does not transcend the round of existence."
It is rejected by the Buddhas and other wise ones. "It turns back" is a statement of the reason for that rejection;
therefore, the goal and the path prescribed by them does not lead out, but rather, it turns back, causing the person who possesses it to wander only within saṃsāra.
"Knowing through striving" means knowing by direct perception (*paccakkha*), because that is the primary authority for knowledge, whereas the other [type of knowing] is bound up with doubt;
thus it is said, "knowing and seeing. By this, he distinguishes knowing by means of seeing. This is what is meant:
you possess the vision of knowledge directly perceived in a world of absolute happiness. Or alternatively, they know that world.
He asks whether [the world] is an object of inference; they see it as an object of direct perception (*paccakkha*). This is the meaning here:
"Is the world known to you through direct perception, or rather through inference?
Since an object that has become directly perceived in the world is manifest by way of being within the range of the sense faculties, it is therefore said, "previously seen," and so forth.
“Seen before” means having been seen; the meaning is that they were previously grasped by means of knowledge consisting of seeing and its concomitants.
By taking it in this way, the expression “the shape of the body and so forth” is justified.

Regarding the phrase “it was made without a basis,” he says “it was made *appāṭihīrakaṃ*,” explaining that the nasal vowel has been elided in the grammatical description. Thus, it is “made *appāṭihīraṃ*.”

Thus they explain it here. It is called *paṭihāriya* because it removes opposing views; that very thing is the miracle (*pāṭihāriya*), namely, speech that is without superior. Here, the term *pāṭihīraka* is used as a synonym for *pāṭihāriya*.
That which is not a miracle is "non-miraculous" (*appāṭihīraka*) because it has a superior when countered by others; hence he says, "devoid of removal. For that which has a superior—
Because speech is countered and turned back by that superior [state], it is therefore called "not leading out" (*aniyyānika*), owing to the absence of a path for emergence that counters [suffering].
426. *Vilāsa* means playfulness (*līḷā*).

*Ākappa* refers to specific modes of appearance such as the arrangement of hair, the wearing of garments, and so forth; or it is the contrivance of dress. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of demeanor (*bhāva*) and other qualities should be understood. Furthermore, "demeanor" (*bhāva*) should be understood as cleverness or grace.
**Commentary on the Attainment of the Three Selfhoods (Attapaṭilābha)** 428.
That wherein the conceit "I am" is established is the *attā* (self); thus he says, "The attainment of selfhood (*attapaṭilābha*) means the attainment of personal existence (*attabhāva*).

He indicates the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), because it is grosser than the other two forms of personal existence. He indicates the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) by means of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).

Because, having been produced, they are apprehended through their material form. "Defiled phenomena" refers to the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness, since in their absence no defilement whatsoever can occur.
"Purifying phenomena" refers to serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), because by means of these, the complete purification of the mind is accomplished.
429. However, as long as opposing states are not completely eradicated, the fulfillment or abundance of blameless states can never occur;
it occurs only when they have been eradicated. This is why the wisdom of the path and the wisdom of the fruit are mentioned.
For once these are fulfilled, they remain fulfilled, because they are by nature incapable of decline. "Fresh joy" refers to that which has just arisen.

Pīti that has not yet been cultivated is weak. "Strong satisfaction" (balavatutṭhi) refers to pīti that is more stable because it has been cultivated through repeated arising and serves as a condition for attaining further distinctions.
Regarding the passage beginning with "What we have said," this is the summary of the meaning:
the conventional expression which is the culmination of the abandoning and increase of defiled and purified states, consisting in the fulfillment and expansion of wisdom.
"In this very life, he will dwell having accomplished [the goal] through his own knowledge, independent of others," so we said.
In that regard, in that monastery, for that monk who follows my instruction, there will arise rapture (pīti) born of joy as a sign of dwelling in the manner just described;
and there will also be the two-fold tranquility (passaddhi) which serves as its condition.

Rightly established mindfulness and exalted knowledge, as well as that state of being thus constituted—due to its peacefulness and excellence—it deserves to be called an "unsurpassed" and "incomparable" abiding in happiness, not shared by others.
When the first jhāna is merely attained, rapture is weak and belongs to the side of gladness; when it is well-developed...
However, when that [joy] has become familiar, it is called "rapture" (pīti) because it is superior, powerful in nature, and its function is fulfilled; thus it is said:
"In the first jhāna, all six factors beginning with gladness (pāmojja) are found. By the phrase "a blissful abiding" (sukho vihāro), concentration (samādhi) is included.
Others say that "bliss" (sukha) itself is included; according to their view, because of its peaceful blissfulness, equanimity (upekkhā) is intended as "bliss" in the fourth jhāna.
Therefore he says, “Likewise in the fourth,” and so forth. “Joy ceases” means that joy, characterized as weak rapture (*pīti*), ceases and diminishes among the six mental states.
Due to the absence of the agitation caused by applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*), rapture is always powerful in the second jhāna;
it is not, as in the first jhāna, sometimes weak. Pure insight (*suddha-vipassanā*) is precisely the jhāna that serves as its basis.

Without explaining the path above, only the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā) was explained. The meaning is that after explaining the jhānas as the basis for insight—since insight was explained together with the four paths—the four paths preceded by insight were then explained.
When it is said that the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) belonging to the fourth jhāna was explained, [it refers to] those beginning with the first jhāna.
Without mentioning the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) in general, only that which consists of the fourth jhāna is described as the attainment of fruition.
"Making *pāmojja* a synonym for *pīti*" means that because the two types of *pīti* do not arise simultaneously in a single moment of consciousness, *pāmojja* is treated as a synonym for *pīti*.
Because joy (*pīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) have not been abandoned, it is called "a blissful abiding" (*sukho ca vihāro*), referring to an especially exalted state of blissful dwelling.
And because it has been grasped, it is called the "fruition attainment of the second jhāna.

Although joy and bliss are indeed obtained in the first jhāna as well, they are not peaceful and sublime due to the agitation caused by applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*); and it is these peaceful and sublime states that are intended here.

432–437. "The meaning of manifestation" (*vibhāvanattha*) means the meaning of making clear, the meaning of determining according to its specific form; therefore he said, "This is that," and so forth.
"Coarse" refers to the gross acquisition of a self. "With resistance" means that which is subject to refutation by the words of another, being defeasible and surpassable.
"Empty" means false and unreal. "That very same" refers to that very acquisition of a self.
"At that time it exists" means it is found existing at that present moment. He pointed it out merely as the "acquisition of a self," but did not describe its specific nature.

Having extracted it, he showed it. Here, "phenomena such as form" refers specifically to the aggregates of form, feeling, and so forth; these alone are the phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) in this world.
"The acquisition of a self," however, is a designation (*paññatti*) based upon those five aggregates beginning with form; therefore, he said, "This is a mere name.
"By way of the designation of a name" means by way of its being a mere designation that has become a name.

438. "And having spoken thus" means: having stated the point that "the acquisition of a self is a mere designation based upon form and so forth," by means of the passage beginning with "At whatever time, O mind... and so on. "For the purpose of training by way of questioning" means:
for the purpose of training by making known that meaning after questioning the other person according to the divisions of time, in the manner in which others might ask.
"At that time it was real" means that, because of the existence of clinging at that past time, it could be said to have been truly real and present;
however, a future or current acquisition of self (*attapaṭilābha*) is not [real] at that time, because its corresponding clinging did not exist then.
Those past phenomena which, at the past time, [belonged] to the past acquisition of self...
The material form and other aggregates that have become the objects of clinging do not exist now because they have ceased; for that very reason, they have entered into the reckoning of "were.

Therefore, because it is obtained at that very same time, that acquisition of a self (attapaṭilābha) which has those [aggregates] as its basis was, in that very past time, real, actual, and as if existing. Of the future and the present... of both the future and the present.

Because the material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) that serve as the basis for appropriation (*upādāna*) were non-existent at that past time, the acquisition of a self (*attapaṭilābha*)—which is dependent upon them—in the future and the present was, at that past time, vain, empty, false, and non-existent;
this is the meaning. "Merely a name" means merely a conventional designation (*samaññāmatta*). One "claims the acquisition of a self" because it is not found in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).

“‘The same method applies’ means: those future phenomena which do not exist now, but will be reckoned as ‘they will be,’ therefore that acquisition of a self of mine will also be real at that very time.
But because past and present phenomena are non-existent then, at that time the past is vain and the present is vain.”
"Those phenomena which are present exist right now; therefore, this acquisition of a self (attapaṭilābha) that I have is real at this time.
But because past and future phenomena do not exist now, at that time [of their non-existence], the past is vain and the future is vain.
Thus he refers to this meaning: that one merely acknowledges the acquisition of a self as being a mere name in substance.

439–443. *Saṃsandituṃ* means to bring together. "At whatever time there is milk" means at whatever time, depending upon a particular kind of clinging designated as the primary elements and derived matter (*bhūta-upādāya*), there comes to be the designation "milk.
It does not [persist]... [etc. ... because it goes; for the designation "milk" ceases to be clung to when there is the designation "curd" and so forth.
For a single worldly convention has a fixed basis; therefore he said: "Those..."
“By depending on the Dhamma,” and so forth. In that context: it is called *saṅkhā* because one enumerates (*saṅkhāyati*) by means of it; thus, it is a designation (*paññatti*).

It is called *nirutti* because they speak (*vadanti*) having extracted [the meaning] by means of it. It is called *nāma* because one inclines (*namanti*) toward it. It is called *vohāra* because one expresses oneself (*voharanti*) by means of it;
this too is simply a designation. This method applies everywhere. Thus, by the phrase “at whatever time,” etc., the method stated regarding milk is extended by analogy to curd and the other products.

"Merely by way of approval" means that, just as one approves of the conventional designations handed down through tradition in the world regarding specific types of primary and derived matter— such as "this is milk" or "this is curd"— without rejecting them, so too,
based on the collection of aggregates such as form distinguished by their specific conditions, there are the [terms] "the gross acquisition of a self" and "the mind-made acquisition of a self."
And the phrases “formless acquisition of self” and so forth are merely ways of assenting [to such views] in various ways;
the meaning is that there is no other entity apart from clinging distinct from those [terms]. “Merely verbal expressions” means they are merely means for grasping the linguistic terminology.
For, after the word “being” or “contact” has been grasped, the comprehension of its meaning occurs precisely by way of grasping the designation (paññatti) that follows upon it.
“Merely a path of speech” is a synonym for that very thing. “Merely a conventional expression” means merely expressed in such and such ways.
“Merely a designation by name” is a synonym for that same thing; it means merely the conceptualizing of various names.
“All this” means that everything—whether called “the acquisition of a self,” “a being,” or “a person”—is all merely a conventional expression from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).
Because it is not apprehended, he said: "Since, in the ultimate sense (paramattha), there is no such thing as a 'being' (satta)," and so forth.
If this is so, why is it spoken of even by the Buddhas? To this he said: "But for the Buddhas there are two kinds of discourse," and so forth.

Discourse concerning conventional designation (sammuti) and worldly usage is "discourse on convention" (sammutikathā). Discourse concerning the ultimate sense—the phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma)—is "discourse on the ultimate sense" (paramatthakathā).
The discourse on impermanence and so forth is called "ultimate-discourse" (*paramatthakathā*) because it is a discourse based upon the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*).
For it is the ultimate phenomenon (*paramatthadhamma*) that is described as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," not the conventional phenomenon (*sammutidhamma*).
As for the reason why the Buddhas' discourse proceeds in these two ways, the cause is stated therein with the words "In that regard, which... and so forth. Because:

The penetration of the truths occurs through the discourse on the ultimate meaning (*paramattha-kathā*), and the teaching reaches its culmination in the discourse on the Noble Truths (*ariyasacca-kathā*).
Therefore, even when the Blessed One speaks a conventional discourse (*sammuti-kathā*) according to the individuals to be trained, he is in fact speaking only the discourse on the ultimate meaning;
thus it is said: "To him, the Blessed One, from the very beginning... [speaks]"; hence he says "in that way" (*tathā*), and so forth. Consequently, in some instances...

Discourse on ultimate truth is preceded by discourse on conventional truth according to the inclination of the person, while in some cases discourse on conventional truth is preceded by discourse on ultimate truth.
Thus, he shows that the Teacher, who is skilled in training those to be trained, proceeds with his teaching in various ways according to the inclinations of those to be trained.
Yet in all instances, the Blessed One does not abandon the nature of reality (*dhammatā*) regarding conventional truth.

One conforms [to conventional usage], and while not abandoning conventional designation (*sammuti*), one clarifies the true nature of phenomena (*dhammatā*); therein there is neither dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*) nor over-extension (*atidhāvana*).
For this has been said: "One should not adhere to local dialects, nor should one overstep common parlance.
Furthermore, speaking after first employing conventional designation is generally the established practice of the Buddhas for the sake of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

Showing that together with its cause, he said, “But by nature...,” and so forth. [An objection: Since what is called conventional designation (*sammuti*) is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), it is unreal;
how then do the Buddhas speak of it? To this he replied, “Even when speaking a conventional discourse,” and so forth. “It is indeed true” means it is exactly as it is.
“It is indeed its own-nature” means that by way of being a conventional designation, it has that very nature; therefore he said, “it is not a falsehood.”
But as for the ultimate reality (*paramattha*), there is nothing at all to be said regarding its being a truth (*sacca*) and so forth.
Now, what is the distinction between these conventional (*sammuti*) and ultimate realities?

That which, when broken or when its parts are analytically separated by the intellect, no longer retains that designation—such as the various categories of "pot," "cloth," and so on—is the conventional; the ultimate is the opposite of that. Not...
For this method is applicable to those things whose intrinsic nature consists of hard contact and so forth.
Even so, since conventional designations (*sammuti*) are also of the nature of truth according to the stated method, he said, "He proclaimed two truths," and so on.
Now, demonstrating the truth-nature of these two by means of a reason, he spoke the verse beginning with "Conventional speech is truth. Therein:
Conventional speech is true because it is non-deceptive. Regarding this, he states the reason: "because it is the cause for worldly convention.
For the convention established by the world is the cause for the non-deceptiveness of conventional speech. Ultimate reality (*paramattha*) is the supreme, highest meaning;
it is the actual nature of phenomena as they truly are. Speech concerning that is true by way of its non-deceptiveness regarding things as they really are.
And because it causes [the truth] to proceed. Regarding this, he states the reason: "It is the characteristic of the reality of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ bhūtalakkhaṇaṃ*).

This is said by taking into account that it is the characteristic, the domain, and the means of making known that which is the real, non-erroneous intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena that possess an intrinsic nature.
Even though the Tathāgata stands having perfectly awakened to the ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*), he does so only by employing worldly convention (*lokasamaññā*).
He said: "Who here has any distinction from the worldly masses? [The answer is: "That by which the Tathāgata expresses himself is without misapprehension," and so forth.
Because the worldly masses have not abandoned misapprehension (*parāmāsa*), they express themselves while misapprehending with such thoughts as "this is mine.
But the Tathāgata, having completely abandoned misapprehension, does not misapprehend; for, apart from worldly conventions (*lokasamaññā*), there is no worldly object.
It is difficult for anyone in the world to understand [this directly]; therefore, he expresses it by means of those [conventional terms].

And by expressing it in this way, through the elegance of his own teaching, he establishes those beings who are to be trained in the ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*). "Having turned back from the teaching" means having turned away from and separated from the discourse that proceeded below;
he turns the teaching toward the "non-grasping" (*aparāmāsa*) by describing the abandonment of the grasping of craving, conceit, and views, culminating in the summit of Arahantship.
It was completed. Whatever herein has not been analyzed according to its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Poṭṭhapādasutta*. 10.
Commentary on the *Subhasutta*.
Commentary on the Story of the Young Brahmin Subha 444.
In the phrase “not long after his final Nibbāna,” the proximity to the Teacher’s state of final Nibbāna is shown by the negation of a long period having elapsed;
since the specific limit of time was not shown, it is stated as follows to demonstrate that limit: “after his final Nibbāna...”
It is said, "in a mere month. Therein, by the inclusion of the word *matta* ("mere"), it indicates that the time was not complete [i.e., less than a month].

He whose residence is a village known as Tudi is Todeyya. Since he, like Soṇadaṇḍa, presides over Campā, and like Kūṭadanta, over Khāṇumata, it is therefore said, "by his lordship," meaning by way of his sovereignty.

"Accumulate" means to store up. Because wealth diminishes even when expended little by little, yet increases even when accumulated little by little, the wise person—being of discerning nature—should dwell the household life by causing only income to arise without incurring any expenditure; thus he points out the practice taught by greed.
Having been trained only in non-giving, he was reborn in that very same house as a dog due to being overcome by greed;
for one who is a slave to greed, a miserable rebirth is to be expected. He loved him exceedingly because of their former acquaintance.
He entered for alms desiring to favor the youth Subha. "You will be reborn in hell," [he said], because it is impossible to ward off karma for which the opportunity has already been created.
Referring to the cultivation of the conduct of a brahmin, and likewise extolling his father, he said, "He was reborn in the Brahma-world.
He asked about that occurrence: "I have heard this from you—that my father was reborn as a dog;
is this true? He spoke in that same way as had previously been said regarding the dog.
Having spoken thus: "For the sake of non-deception" means for the sake of making it true;
that is to say, for the sake of his own word not being deceptive—that the brahmin Toḍeyya had been reborn as a dog—and for the purpose of demonstrating the state of its non-deceptiveness.
"He showed everything" means that by the power of the Buddha, that dog led him [to the place] and showed it all; it was not through the power of remembering past lives (*jātissara*).
But as for his laughing upon seeing the Blessed One, it was due to the latent tendencies (vāsanā) established through his previous births. Having asked fourteen questions, he said:
"For, Master Gotama, some humans are seen who are short-lived, and others are seen who are long-lived. Some are seen who are afflicted with many illnesses, and others are seen who have few illnesses.
Some are seen who are ugly, and others are seen who are beautiful. Some are seen who have little influence..."
“Some are seen to be of great influence; some are seen to be of little wealth, while others are seen to be of great wealth.
Some are seen to be from low-born families, while others are seen to be from high-born families. Some are seen to be lacking in wisdom, while others are seen to be possessed of wisdom.
Having asked these fourteen questions, he reportedly received the name “Subha” because of the excellence of his limbs.
445. By the words, “I have one doubt,” he shows that the question being asked below was already prepared by him beforehand.
“Dissimilar feeling” (*visabhāgavedanā*) refers to painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).

For it is called “dissimilar feeling” because it is the opposite of the pleasant feeling that arises in a personal existence produced by wholesome karma (*kusalakamma*). [The phrase] “pressing upon the body” (*kāyaṃ gāḷhā*)...

Because it afflicts and oppresses after having arisen, it is called "affliction" (*ābādha*). "Having arisen in one part" means that even though it has arisen in only one part of the body, it seizes it as if binding it with an iron band, because it causes the body to become unable to turn over;
by this, he shows that a powerful disease is what is meant by "affliction. "Making life difficult" means bringing about an unhappy existence; by this, he indicates that which is weak and slight.
This shows that "disease" means affliction (*ātaṅka*). "Rising up" (*uṭṭhāna*) refers to rising from lying down or sitting;
by this, he speaks of the body’s turning over here and there in whatever manner [necessary]. "Heavy" (*garuka*) means burdensome and difficult to accomplish.
Regarding the phrase "there is no strength in the body," here too the word "only for one who is ill" (*gilānasseva*) should be brought forward and connected. From the four [factors] below...
Having asked by means of the [previous] words whether there was an absence of lack of comfort in dwelling, he now asks whether there is the presence of comfort in dwelling;

therefore, it should be understood that a superior degree of comfort in dwelling is being asked about. For even when a word expressing a sense of superiority is absent, the sense of superiority can still be obtained, just as in the expression:
"A gift should be given to one who is beautiful."
447. “Depending on the time and the occasion”: here, “time” (*kāla*) refers to the appropriate and opportune moment for approaching [the Teacher].

“Occasion” (*samaya*) refers to the convergence of conditions for that very act; in terms of its meaning, it consists of both the physical strength of the body suited to that task and the absence of obstacles related to those conditions.
“Depending” (*upādāya*) means grasping or discerning them by means of knowledge; this is what is shown by the statement beginning with “depending on the time,” and so forth.
"Pharissati" means it will increase. 448.
"Cetiyaraṭṭhe" means in the country of Ceti; for the word was spoken by adding the letter *ya* [to form *cetiyaraṭṭhe*].
And they say that there is another, entirely separate country apart from the country of Ceti. "Connected with death" refers to what is called death for such [beings].
"By way of illness indeed it occurs": this refers to the specific illness by which he was born;

it is a question concerning its nature, a question concerning its cause, a question concerning the mental anguish caused by death, the universality of that anguish throughout the world, and likewise the incurability of death—it is with such points as these that he spoke a friendly discourse connected with death, as shown by the passage beginning, "O Ānanda."
It has been said. The intended meaning is: "not like Māra, who seeks out faults; nor like the student Uttara, whose intention was to test [the Buddha].

Regarding the phrase "in those states" (*yesu dhammesu*), it refers to the means of liberation, the factors leading to deliverance (*niyyāna-dhamma*). "They endure" (*dharanti*) means they remain or persist. 449.
Because the application of words is directed toward the meaning, the three Piṭakas—characterized as a continuum of words—are [connected] with those things which constitute their meaning.
It is said that they are "comprised within the aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue (sīla) and so forth," and thus it is stated: "having comprised the three Piṭakas by means of the three aggregates.
It is spoken "in brief" because it is stated concisely through the inclusion of the phrase "of the three aggregates" both by way of their commonality and by way of their specific enumeration.
The question, "Of which three? is a question for the purpose of revealing what is not yet seen; it is not a question arising from a desire to have something explained.
It is said: "Having thought, 'I shall ask in detail,' he said, 'Of which three? However, in the absence of a desire to speak, this might be the Elder's way of speaking.
[End of] the commentary on the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).

450–453. Regarding the phrase *sīlakkhandhassa*: here, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*) or the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*). Therefore, it should be understood that by this [phrase], the entire passage ending with “he established him in the noble aggregate of concentration...
[and so on]... in liberation” is indicated. Thus he says, “when these have been shown,” the intention being that they were shown by way of a summary (*uddesa*).
“In the very manner spoken by the Blessed One” refers to [the discourses] such as the *Sāmaññaphala-sutta*.
By the very method taught by the Blessed One, he demonstrates that this sutta is spoken by the Teacher and is the word of the Conqueror (*jinavacana*).

In the Dispensation, it is not virtue alone that is the essence; for in the Blessed One’s Dispensation, whose essence is the Noble Path, the virtue as it has been shown here is not itself the essence, because it stands in the place of the outer bark of a great tree that possesses an essence. If this is so, why is it included here?
He said: “For this is merely a basis. For one who desires to attain the higher human states such as jhāna and so forth, it is merely a foundation;
for without being established therein, those [higher states] are impossible. Alternatively, it is not that virtue alone is the essence;
although in this Teaching even this supramundane virtue—namely, the virtue of the path and the virtue of the fruit—is indeed the essence, nevertheless...

The meaning here should be understood as follows: it is not only the aggregate of virtue that is the essence, but rather the aggregate of concentration and the aggregate of wisdom are also the essence.
Only the former is the essence; therefore he says, "Beyond this," and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the aggregate of concentration.
454. But why did the Elder, when questioned here about the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*), answer with the restraint of the faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) and so forth?
Is it not the case that, this being so, he would be answering one thing while being asked another—like one who, being asked about a mango, answers about a *labuja* fruit?
To show that such an objection finds no place here, [the text says]: "And how, young man, does a bhikkhu... [the aggregate of] concentration? etc.

He began [the exposition] with the intention of showing this. Therefore, it is shown here that even the restraint of the faculties and so forth are included within the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*), by virtue of their being conducive to concentration.

Only the fine-material jhānas (*rūpajjhāna*) are mentioned here, not the immaterial jhānas (*arūpajjhāna*), because the occasion for teaching the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) follows immediately after the teaching of the fourth fine-material jhāna. [The text] is based upon the fourth fine-material jhāna.
For even the mundane higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) are accompanied by their respective adjuncts.

Since mundane higher knowledges, when being accomplished, do not succeed without the fourteenfold taming of the mind within the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), therefore, when the higher knowledges are taught, the immaterial jhānas are also necessarily taught because they are inseparable from them;
thus he said, "but they should be explained by bringing them forward. In the manner already stated...
The meaning is that, having been taught, they must be elucidated by the commentators.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, the phrase "by means of the fourth jhāna," and so forth, was stated to show that the formless (arūpa) jhānas are also included by the expression "having attained and dwelling in the fourth jhāna.
For the fourth jhāna, which proceeds by way of the cultivation of dispassion toward the fine-material (rūpa), is called a "formless jhāna."
471–480. Regarding the phrase "not by mere one-pointedness of mind" (*na cittekaggatāmattakena eva*), the meaning should be understood according to the method explained below.
Because mundane concentration (*lokīya samādhi-kkhandha*) is intended here, it is said: "In the mind... [etc. ...there is not.

Furthermore, the word *ariya* here is used in its pure sense, not in its supramundane (*lokuttara*) sense. Likewise, in the preceding section as well, it refers to mundane direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*).

It can be said that once Arahantship has been attained, there is nothing further to be done for the sake of which one leads the holy life under the Blessed One, because that purpose has been accomplished.
Furthermore, mundane direct knowledges (*lokīyābhiññā*) are also included here. The rest is easy to understand.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) of the commentary on the Subha Sutta.
11. Commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta;
Commentary on the Account of the Householder’s Son Kevaṭṭa. 481.
“In the Mango Grove of the Cloth-Merchant”: this refers to the grove rich in mango trees belonging to the merchant Seṭṭhi. It is said that the merchant [presented] it to the Blessed One...

Having constructed a fitting fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) for the Buddha and provided for the Saṅgha of monks dwellings for night and day, huts, pavilions, and so forth, he enclosed it with a wall and equipped it with gate-towers; then he offered it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
Because of its previous designation, however, it is called "Pāvārika’s Mango Grove," and [the Buddha stayed] in that Pāvārika Mango Grove.
“Kevaṭṭa”: this is his name; some say it is because he was protected by fishermen (*kevaṭṭa*), or because he was raised in their presence.

Regarding the phrase “the son of a householder” (*gahapatiputta*): although at that time he stood in the position of a householder, because his father had recently passed away, he was still addressed by his former title as “the son of a householder”; therefore, he said, “householder.”

"Mahāsāla. Because of his great wealth (*mahāvibhava*), he is "mahāsāra"; the meaning is "householder" (*gahapati*), having changed the letter *ra* to *la*, as in such expressions as "I am a mahāsāla, a sukhumāla," and so forth.
"Endowed with faith" (*saddhāsampanna*) means possessed of faith by way of the faith of an ordinary person (*pothujjanikā*).
"Prosperous" (*samiddha*) means truly successful; the meaning is that he has attained abundance through success (*iddhi*) and the perfection of wealth. "Come..."
“Bhikkhu, from time to time—every half-month, every month, or every year—you should perform a miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya) for the sake of inspiring confidence in people.
Thus, the command given to a single bhikkhu is what is meant by his being “appointed to that position”; therefore he said, “let him be appointed to a specific office.
“By way of the qualities of superhuman beings” means by way of the qualities of attainment belonging to superhuman beings such as the Buddhas and others.
This is an ablative used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*), for it selects the miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) from among those [three].
"Superior to human nature" means above the ordinary human nature. "A burning lamp" means a lamp that is blazing.

"I shall not burn you" means I shall not cause you to fall away from the perfection of virtue; therefore he says, "the breaking of morality," and so forth. "Having increased his confidence" means having expanded his state of trust in the Blessed One, making it manifest and evident.
Commentary on the Miracle of Psychic Power (Iddhipāṭihāriya) 483–4.
“Danger” (ādīnava) means fault (dosa). “Gandhārī” refers to two types of Gandhārī magic: Cūḷagandhārī and Mahāgandhārī.
Therein, Cūḷagandhārī is the science of knowing the place of rebirth for beings who have died within three years.
Mahāgandhārī knows that as well; moreover, she accomplishes most of the functions of the supernormal powers (iddhividha) by means of a portion of the knowledge of supernormal powers.

It is said that a person who masters her science, having recited the mantra at a suitable place and time, manifests himself in many forms, displays elephants and other such things, becomes beautiful to behold, and even creates a pillar of fire.
He causes water to solidify and displays himself even in the sky; all this should be regarded as being like a magician’s trick (*indajāla*).
*Aṭṭo* means one who is pained or afflicted; therefore he says "oppressed.
This concludes the commentary on the miracle of mind-reading (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*).
485. Granted that the term “mental factor” (*cetasika*) is a common designation for those things connected with the mind, associated with consciousness;
yet, when the general category is grasped, the specific instance of consciousness is also included, and a general indication settles upon its particulars.
