Thus, clarifying the intention behind the inclusion of the term “mental factor,” he said: “It is intended as joy and grief. By the inclusion of “joy,”...
And herein, by the mention of [mental] joy, greed and the like, as well as faith and the like, are shown; by the mention of grief, hatred and the like are shown;
while applied thought and sustained thought are shown in their own form. The meaning of "thus your mind" is that your mind functions in this manner.
To the question "In what manner does it function?", he says: "either joyful," and so forth. This phrase "thus your mind" refers to this.
However, this is merely a demonstration of the state of being joyful and so forth;
it is not a demonstration of each specific thing by which one is made joyful or dejected. "The second" refers to the phrase, "In this way too your mind [is].

Here, the word *iti* has the sense of illustration (*nidassana*), as in such passages as, "Kaccāna, 'it exists'—this is one extreme," and so on. Therefore, he says: "Contemplating this and that meaning."
The word *pi* has the sense of including what has already been stated. It is called a *cintāmaṇi* because by means of it one thinks—that is, knows—the thought of another.

It is said that the person who accomplishes this lore, having recited the mantra at a suitable place and time, infers and declares the mental disposition of the one whose mind he wishes to know, by way of discerning their specific perceptions regarding what has been seen, heard, and so forth.
Some [say this]. Others say: "By means of causing speech to issue forth and by way of observing the syllables therein.
Regarding the commentary on the miracle of instruction (anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya):
"Causing to proceed" means being those who cause it to proceed; the sense is "by way of causing it to proceed. For the word "thus" (evaṃ) refers to that which has been instructed.
By way of injunction and by way of prohibition, there is an examination of the mode of occurrence;
and that occurs by way of showing the modes of occurrence of right thoughts and wrong thoughts, for the purpose of clarifying therein the benefit and the disadvantage.
"Perception of impermanence itself, not perception of permanence" is the meaning. For it is for the purpose of excluding the opposite [that this is stated].
The inclusion of the word *eva* (only/just). Here too, the meaning and purpose of including the word *evaṃ* (thus) should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
The same principle applies to the inclusion of the word *idaṃ* (this).

The mention of "lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcakāmaguṇikarāga*) should be regarded as merely an illustration, because the abandoning of other forms of lust, hatred (*dosa*), and so forth is intended, and because the abandonment of those [sensual pleasures] serves as the means for casting off other forms of lust, hatred, and the rest.
Thus it has been said, just as [the application of] putrid flesh is a means for discharging corrupted blood.
The restriction "only the supramundane dhamma" should be understood as intended to exclude blameworthy dhammas because of their being opposites;

for other blameless dhammas, which constitute the means and benefits for its attainment, do not possess the quality of being "immediate" (ānantariya). This shows that the supernormal power (iddhividha) is a miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya).

Because, by means of the manifestation of psychic power (*iddhidassana*), one removes the opposites of faith and so forth within the mental continuum of others. The meaning should be understood in this same manner for the remaining two phrases as well.
"Constant teaching of the Dhamma" (*satataṃ dhammadesanā*) means the teaching of the Dhamma that is to be taught at all times.

In the phrase "by the miracle of psychic power" (*iddhipāṭihāriyena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment; the meaning is "together with the miracle of psychic power. [In] "by the miracle of mind-reading" (*ādesanāpāṭihāriyena*)...
The same principle applies here as well. The construction is: "It was the habit of the General of the Dhamma.

By the phrase "having known the movement of the mind," he demonstrates the miracle of mind-reading (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*). By the phrase "he taught the Dhamma," he demonstrates the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*).
This is stated because the miracle of instruction—namely, "the constant teaching of the Dhamma by the Buddhas"—is particularly predominant in that case. [These] are accompanied by censure...
Because they are subject to being censured by those who are worthy of respect; because they are tainted with hatred, as they are not the means for the total eradication of hatred;
and because, precisely due to being tainted with hatred, they do not endure for long—that is, they do not persist over a long period of time.

From the fact that they do not endure for long, it is inferred through their result that they do not lead to liberation (*niyyanti*). For it is because they do not lead to liberation that they are not enduring. This is the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*).
It is beyond reproach because it originates from purity and is supported by purity. For that very reason, it is faultless;

for in it, there is no possibility of faults such as contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Precisely because it is faultless, it stands the test of time, being incapable of being struck down by the winds of opposing doctrines or the winds of the defilements.
Therefore—due to the reasons stated above—it is, by that [faultlessness], beyond reproach and so forth.
And both "without reproach," etc., and [the following] are mentioned respectively as the causes for the states of being censurable and praiseworthy in both cases. 487.
Regarding the commentary on the section on the cessation of the primary elements (*bhūtanirodhesaka*):
"For the purpose of showing the lack of leading-out (*aniyyānikabhāva*)" means that because the monk seeking the great elements [failed] in the first two...
Although one who has attained mastery in the miracles is skilled, they did not realize Nibbāna—which is defined as the complete cessation of the great primary elements;
therefore, because those [other paths] do not bring about deliverance, they are "not leading out. This is for the purpose of showing their lack of leading-out quality.
But the third [path] leads to deliverance with absolute certainty for the one who practices it; this is for the purpose of showing its quality of leading out.
Having thus shown the primary purpose of this teaching, the passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apica*) is commenced in order to show the incidental purpose as well.
“Seeking the great elements” (*mahābhūte pariyesanto*) means seeking the great elements by way of their cessation without remainder;
the meaning is that he investigates their complete cessation. “Having investigated” (*vicaritvā*) means having investigated while being impelled by the nature of things (*dhammatā*).

It is said that this wandering of that bhikkhu was established by the very nature of things (*dhammatāsiddha*), just as the great earthquake and other phenomena occurred at the time of a Buddha’s birth.

"For the purpose of manifesting his greatness" means for the purpose of illustrating the majesty and great power of the Buddhas, which is not shared by anyone else in the world including the devas. And this is the reason for all [of them].
He shows this reason as well, namely: "In the teaching of the Buddhas, such a single bhikkhu alone manifests such power at that time.
*Kattha* (where) is the locative case used in the sense of a sign; therefore, *kattha* means "in what place" acting as the cause.

*Kiṃ āgamma* (having approached what) means having attained what object serving as a condition; hence he says, "Of what [state] having been attained? *Tetī* refers to the great elements (*mahābhūtā*). *Appavattivasena* (by way of non-occurrence).

By way of non-arising. "In every aspect" means by way of all modes: from the perspective of the meaning of the words, characteristics, and so forth; from the perspective of the groups, collections, and analyses of the aggregates; from the perspective of diversity, unity, analysis, and non-analysis;

from the perspective of similarity, dissimilarity, internal, and external inclusion; and from the perspective of the classification of conditions, the gathering of conditions, the analysis of conditions, the grouping of constituent parts, the brief summary of constituent parts, the detailed exposition of constituent parts, the single characteristic, the brief summary of characteristics, and the detailed exposition of characteristics—in short, by every mode.
488. They "divine" (*dibbanti*) here in the sense that they move about endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, play, and shine;
thus it is a "divine world" (*devaloka*). That which leads one to go to or approach that [world] is the "path of the gods" (*devayāniya*).
"Exercising mastery" (*vasaṃ vattento*): here, "mastery" (*vasavattana*) means going to whatever place one desires. The four Great Kings are the lords of these [beings].
Those deities of the Cātumahārājika realm who have attained the paths and fruits would know that matter only partially;
however, considering that this question pertains to the domain of a Buddha, they said, "We do not know. Therefore, he said, "In the domain of a Buddha," and so forth.
Here, "overwhelming" means pressing hard; thus he said, "He asks again and again. "More excellent" refers to the perfection of form (*rūpasampatti*).
And by virtue of qualities such as wisdom and eloquence, they surpass us and are more desirable to others. "More excellent" means more sublime;
therefore, he said "more supreme.
(491–3) It is like the Devayāniya [path] because it is intended specifically as the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhañāṇa*). Or, "the path leading to the gods... and so forth.
"All this is merely a name for the knowledge of supernormal powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa)"—this was stated according to the conventional usage found here and there in the Pāḷi and the commentaries. 494.

"A sign prior to his arrival" means a sign arising before the arrival of Brahmā. "He appeared" (pāturahosi) means he became manifest; it means he became visible (pākaṭo). It means he became clear (pakāso).

"By way of a portion" (padesena) means by way of a single part; the meaning is: by way of what is clung to (upādinnaka), and that which is included within the continuum of a sentient being. "Even in the case of what is not clung to" (anupādinnakepi) means even in the case of those things not bound to the faculties.
"Without partiality" (nippadesato) means without remainder. "Of one confused about the question" (pucchāmūḷhassa) means of one who does not know how to ask.
"Having shown the fault in the question" (pucchāya dosaṃ dassetvā) means having revealed the fault in the manner in which the question was asked by him. Because...

"Answering" (vissajjana) means that it must be answered in accordance with the question and in conformity with the nature of the question; for the Tathāgatas do not answer by overlooking the question, but rather provide an answer corresponding to it.
Furthermore, because the answer shares the same nature as the meaning [of the question], those who ask may become confused if they do not understand that meaning.
Therefore, it is the custom of the Buddhas to instruct through questioning; thus he said, "having instructed by means of a question," and so forth.

498. "Without support" (appatiṭṭhā) means "without condition" (appaccayā), that is to say, with the cause completely cut off. "Only what is clung-to" (upādinnaṃ yeva) means precisely that which is bound to the sense faculties.

Because the designation "long" applies to a continuity of matter established as a stream directed toward a single direction, and based on that, the designation "short" applies to what is smaller than that;
and both of these are specifically grasped by way of the apprehension of matter.
Therefore he said: “‘Long and short’ refers to derived matter (upādārūpa) by way of its configuration (saṇṭhāna). The designation “atom” (aṇu) is applied to a minute collection of material phenomena;
based on that, the designations “large” and “gross” are applied to what is greater than that. These two as well are grasped specifically through the gateway of the perception of matter;
hence he said, “By this also,” and so forth. And here, by the word “also” (pi), [it is implied] “by way of configuration.”
Regarding the statement, "derived matter has been explained," they say that this summarizes the point that only color (vaṇṇa) was discussed there.
"Beautiful" (subha) means lovely; the meaning is "desirable. "Ugly" (asubha) means unlovely; it is said to mean "undesirable. For this very reason, he says:
"Thus, the desirable and undesirable object has been described. Long, short, fine, coarse, beautiful, and ugly.
In these three instances, only derived matter (upādārūpa) is included, because the primary elements (bhūtarūpa) have already been taken separately.
"Name" (nāma) refers to the four aggregates beginning with feeling; it is called "name" because it bends (namana) toward the object and because it performs naming (nāmakaraṇa).

As for what was previously stated as "long," "short," and so forth, that is here included under "matter" (rūpa) in the sense of being subject to transformation (ruppanaṭṭha); thus he says, "divided into long and so forth."
"And form. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "long and so forth," the inclusion of water and the other [great elements] should be understood.

Alternatively, since designations such as "long" and so on do not have only the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) as their foundation, but rather also have the primary materiality (*bhūtarūpa*) as their foundation—since shape is apprehended even by way of contact—therefore, by the mention of "long, short," and so on, primary materiality itself is indeed included; thus, it is simply called "form divided into long and so forth."
It has been said. "Depending on what" means having attained what; for the sake of attaining what.
"It ceases" is said with reference to non-arising cessation (*anuppāda-nirodha*), not momentary cessation (*khaṇa-nirodha*); thus he says, "This does not proceed without remainder. 499.
"To be known" means to be specifically known, to be directly perceived by the supreme knowledge of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga-ñāṇa*).
The meaning is "it is to be known"; therefore he said, "This is the name of Nibbāna. It is called *nidassana* because it is demonstrated; that which is cognizable by the eye.
That which is not a demonstration (*anidassana*) means it is not cognizable by the eye—this is what they say. Alternatively, *nidassana* means a simile;
since this [Nibbāna] has no such thing, it is *anidassana*. For Nibbāna is eternal, unique, and of an absolutely peaceful and sublime nature.

"A similar illustration can be found elsewhere. That which, having not existed, comes to be, and having existed, passes away, is conditioned (*saṅkhata*), possessing the two ends of arising and passing away, and thus has an end.
But for the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) Nibbāna, which is eternal, neither of those two ends exists;
for that very reason, it lacks even "aging," which is defined as the departure from a new state. Therefore, he said: "The end of arising... [etc. ...infinite."

Having stated, "It is called *tittha*," in order to show its etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) therein, it is said: "They descend (*papanti*) into this, thus it is a *papa*. For here, they descend into the drinking-place (*pānatittha*).
The letter *bha* has been substituted according to the rules of philology (*niruttinaya*). Or, in the sense of being purified, it is *sabbatopabha*;
the meaning is that it shines forth on all sides because it is unstained by anything. By means of which [path], Nibbāna is attained.
It is stated that here, the non-arising and cessation intended refers only to those things included within the continuity [of existence]:
"The class of phenomena that has been acquired ceases and becomes non-proceeding.
Regarding the phrase "by the cessation of consciousness," it is in reference to that word which was spoken; "consciousness" means *viññāṇa*.

"Because it is to be analyzed, it is here that this [process] comes to an end": in this Nibbāna, this name-and-form (nāmarūpa) ceases by way of non-arising through the cessation of final consciousness (carimakaviññāṇa), that is, in the Nibbāna-element without residue (anupādisesā nibbānadhātu). Therefore he said:
"It goes to a state of non-designation (apaṇṇattikabhāva), like the flame of an extinguished lamp. For "final consciousness" refers here to the death-consciousness (cuticitta) of an Arahant.

By the passage beginning with “Of the volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa) as well,” he speaks of *nirvāṇa* without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*) by way of *nirvāṇa* with residue (*saupādisesa-nibbāna*), because what is intended is the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) without remainder; therefore he says, “It ceases by way of non-arising.

In the phrase “by the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimaggañāṇa*),” the word is used in the sense of the agent or the instrument. “By cessation (*nirodhena*)”: [this refers to the cessation of suffering].
But [it is used] in the sense of a cause. "In this" means in this Nibbāna. Whatever else here has not been analyzed according to its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Kevaṭṭa Sutta*.
12. Commentary on the *Lohicca Sutta*.

**Commentary on the Account of the Brahmin Lohicca (501).** *Sālavatikā* is the name of that village according to its feminine gender; some say it is so called because of the presence of a village headman (*gāmaṇika*). *Lohicca* is the name derived from the clan of that brahmin, based on an ancestor named Lohita in his family line.

(502) Regarding the term “view-position” (*diṭṭhigata*), he said, “it refers merely to a subjective opinion, and not to either annihilationism or eternalism,” because he intended only a mere tendency of thought.
For there is no mode of view whatsoever that is free from the grasping at annihilationism or eternalism.
By the words “he indeed speaks,” he shows the public notoriety of that particular tenet in the world. Regarding the phrase “another who is other than oneself”:

just as the one to be instructed is “other” in relation to the instructor, so too the instructor is “other” in relation to the one to be instructed; thus it is said, “‘Another, another,’ meaning whoever is another,” and so forth. This is in reference to the word *kiṃ* (what/who).
And here, the expression “he will do” refers to the future tense; or rather, it is for the purpose of showing that even in the future, there is nothing for him to do by means of that [action].

“A wholesome state” (kusalaṃ dhammaṃ) means a blameless state, a state free from defilements, a state of liberation—this is the meaning. What is the purpose of wandering about having surrounded oneself with those [followers], thinking, “I shall preach the Dhamma to others”?

"Even for one who possesses the wisdom of [knowing] dispositions, that [result] does not occur without [the appropriate cause]; therefore, he says: '...one must dwell having attained it for oneself...
etc. Thus he said: 'In this same way, I declare this evil state of greed.
(504) "He" refers to the brahmin Lohicca.
508. "For the sake of facility in conversation" means for the sake of ease in conversation; the sense is that it is easy both to speak and to hear the conversation.
In the phrase "perhaps it might be so," the repetition (*āmeḍita*) should be understood as being due to joy. For that [speech] is called the "Buddha’s thunder.
Indeed, in such instances, the Blessed One especially experiences joy and gladness. Therefore he said: "This..."
“Such is the intended meaning here,” and so forth.
Regarding the commentary on the interrogation of the Brahmin Lohicca:
*samudayasañjāti* means the arising of life. Since the prefix *anu-* combined with the word *kampī* has the sense of desiring, [it is said] “he desires.”
"Meaning" has been stated. Or, one who is compassionate and benevolent through preeminent welfare is "one who is compassionate and seeks welfare.
"It comes to pass" means it is accomplished through the gain of repeated practice; it becomes powerful, which is to say it is firmly grasped; hence he said, "it becomes fixed.
One who holds wrong view is reborn in hell.
510–11. The second rebirth: The phrase beginning with “Is not King Pasenadi of Kosala... establishes the second rebirth through a logical argument (*sādhanayutti*).
For the Blessed One demonstrates the cause by way of a simile. The construction is: “And those who... and these sons of noble family who are ripening divine wombs.
This refers to those who, being unable [to attain the goal] due to the perfection of their supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) and the ripening of their knowledge...
Or [it is so] by way of their non-existence. As for those who read "they ripen" (*paripaccanti*), there is no purpose for the alteration of the expression to "in a divine womb" (*dibbe gabbhe*).

And the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the second alternative. And they are "compassionate toward what is harmful" (*ahitānukampitā*) by way of the beings associated with that state.
They are "divine" (*dibbā*) because they exist in heaven (*divi*). They "womb" (*gabbhenti*) because they cause the continuity of the stream of existence to persist through the process of ripening.
“Wombs. This is an illustrative expression for “the six divine worlds,” for even the Brahma-world possesses the nature of a divine womb because it is caused by divine abodes.
And by taking it this way, the statement “cultivating meditation” is also justified.

They are called *bhavā* (abodes) because beings dwell therein, endowed with happiness according to their desire; they are celestial mansions (*vimānāni*). Because they bring about the state of a deva...

"Divine. In the same manner as previously stated, [this refers to] the womb. "Generosity and so forth" refers to specific merits conducive to rebirth in the heavenly worlds (*devaloka*). "Divine existences" (*dibbā bhavā*) refers to the existences by way of rebirth included within the heavenly worlds;
for the "kamma-existence" (*kammabhava*) that brings about those [rebirths] was already taken up previously.
This concludes the commentary on the three types of exhortation.
513. "By one who is unspecified" means by one who is indeed unspecified, such that [the teacher] does not designate him, saying, "You hold such a view;
you are such a doer of harm to beings. "Pride" refers to the pride of being wise, thinking, "I know this; I see this. "Having shattered" means having dispelled it;

the sense is "having caused it to be abandoned. "The three types of teachers" refers to: (1) a teacher who has not accomplished his own welfare and does not provide instruction to his disciples;... [and so on].
"One who has not accomplished his own welfare and does not accept correction," and "one who has accomplished his own welfare but does not accept correction"—these are the three kinds of teachers.

As for the fourth, the Perfectly Enlightened One, he is not subject to censure; thus, thinking, "I shall speak only when asked by him," [the Buddha] first showed the three teachers who are subject to censure, and afterwards the fourth teacher. Now, in this context:
The fourth teacher is solitary, without a second, and not shared with others; nevertheless,

because he possesses those superhuman qualities by virtue of which he is called a "body made of Dhamma," the Blessed One said, "This teacher too, Lohicca, is a teacher," thereby showing that although he is a composite of those qualities, one should regard those individual qualities as standing in the place of the Teacher.
"Aññā" is a designation formed by the elision of the letter *ya*, as in "sayaṃ abhiññā" and similar expressions. Regarding "aññāya," it is a dative case used in the sense of purpose;
thus he says, "for the sake of thorough understanding. Because they remain having professed discipleship, they carry out his instruction only partially;
therefore he says, "without carrying out his instruction continuously. "They proceed by skipping over" means according to their own desire.
The meaning is "they act. Regarding "she who retreats": she departs due to lack of delight and lack of reverence; therefore he said, "one who does not desire," and so forth.
"By one" means by a single woman. "One might desire" means a single man might desire union with her who does not desire it.
This demonstration of the connection between woman and man by way of retreating and so on is [given] by way of the concern for the household life regarding that Teacher.
He shows that this is the practice among disciples. "Not even wishing to see [him]" because of an extreme state of detachment.
"By greed" means by the greed for gain and honor arising from the influence of a retinue. "Accomplish him therein" means, having established him in that Dhamma of practice, bring him to fulfillment.
"Make him straight" means by removing crookedness of body and so forth.

515. "He is worthy of such exhortation" means that he is worthy of exhortation in the manner described—that is, by way of directing his disciples toward the state of being free from worldly concerns—but not as in the first case, with words such as "Such is your state of greed," nor as in the second case, with words such as "First, establish yourself therein.
Why? Because the third [type of person] has already accomplished his own welfare.
516. Regarding the commentary on “not deserving of censure”:
here, what is called “deserving of censure” consists of either a transgression by the Teacher, a transgression by the disciples, or a transgression by both;
since none of this exists in this Teacher, he is therefore “not deserving of censure.”
To demonstrate this point, the passage beginning with “For this [person]” was spoken.

(517) “By a view held by me”: by means of falsely imputing non-existent faults upon the Teacher—who is entirely blameless, correctly practicing, and who demonstrates to others exactly how to practice correctly—one holds a wicked view leading to hell that has been wrongly grasped.
"Narakapapāta" means the great precipice known as hell; it is called a "precipice" (*papāta*) because beings fall into it.
"Saggamaggathala" refers to the level ground of meritorious deeds that serves as the path leading to heaven. The remainder is easily understood.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Lohicca Sutta*.
13. Commentary on the Tevijjasutta 518.
Regarding the word *uttarena*: here, after a word denoting direction ending in the fifth case (ablative), the suffix *-ena* is intended to express proximity.
Therefore, showing that the word *uttarena* indicates the sense of proximity, [the commentator] said, "in the vicinity, on the northern side."—The Grammarians.
However, when used in conjunction with the word *ena*, they require the dative case (*upayogavacana*) for the term expressing the limit (*avadhi*).
Since the meaning here is intended solely in the sense of possession (*sāmiva*), it is stated here using the genitive case (*sāmivacana*). 519.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "family conduct, etc.," one includes such perfections as mastery of mantras (*mantajjhena*) and physical beauty. [The phrase] "for the purpose of reciting mantras" (*mantasajjhāyakaraṇatthaṃ*)...
For the purpose of reciting the *Atharvaveda* mantras, he said: "having prevented the entry of many others.
520. Regarding the commentary on the discussion of the path and non-path:
"Jaṅghacāra" refers to the walking back and forth of one who is pacing. For that is for the purpose of dispelling fatigue in the legs.
“Wandering” (*cāro*) is spoken of in that way. Therefore he said, “of those who are walking back and forth (*anucaṅkamantānaṃ*) and wandering about (*anuvicarantānaṃ*).

By the word “therefore” (*tena*), it is because both walking back and forth and wandering about are applicable [to them]. For those companions are of a similar disposition toward one another. “Path” (*maggo*):
it is called a path because by means of it one seeks (*maggati*) or approaches the desired place; thus it is a straight path. Anything other than that is a non-path (*amagga*).
In that which is both the path and the non-path. "The way" (*paṭipadā*) refers to the preliminary practice for the path leading to the Brahma-world.
"Leads out" (*niyyāti*) means it is "leading out" (*niyyānika*); since it is described as "leading out," he says "while leading out.
Because its quality of being leading out is established by way of the person who is led out, therefore, by way of the person's practicing wisely while "leading out," he says "while leading out."

The path is called “leading out. It “makes” [one reach] in the sense that it causes [the result] to arise within one’s own continuum; for it is precisely while causing it to arise that one is said to “practice” therein.

Because it moves or proceeds together [with others], it is “companionship” (*sahabya*), meaning that which functions together. Its state is “companionship-ness” (*sahabyatā*); thus he said “for the sake of co-existence,” and so forth.
And “co-existence” (*sahabhāva*) should be understood as being in the same world (*salokatā*) or proximity (*samīpatā*); therefore he said, “in one place.”
“For the sake of manifestation. “Our own teacher’s doctrine” means the very doctrine spoken by one’s own teacher, Pokkharasāti.
Having praised it, having upheld it, and having commended and extolled it, saying, “This alone is the straight path;
this is the direct way,” [he spoke]. Bhāradvāja also—“our own” means the young Brahmin Bhāradvāja [spoke] his own [teacher’s doctrine], that of his own teacher Tārukkha.
The construction is: "Having praised and upheld the teacher’s doctrine as it has been stated, he wanders [in this way].
"Stated by him" means stated in the Pāḷi by him, whether in such a manner or otherwise, due to his state of dogmatic adherence.
521–2. "Not leading out" (aniyyānikā) means indeed lacking proof; for, having shown the faults in each other's doctrines, they fail to demonstrate the unerring meaning.
They are indeed devoid of a superior [position]. *Viggaha* (conflict) is the initial grasping of a contradiction between two opposing views;
that very same thing, arising repeatedly through the process of disputing, is called *vivāda* (dispute). Thus it is said: "Conflict arises first, and subsequently there is dispute.

Although this conflict and dispute are described as being of two kinds, they both constitute opposition (*virodha*). Or, "the discourse of teachers with diverse opinions" refers to those of various inclinations.
Because of the existence of various doctrines among teachers; that is, taking it as "a diverse doctrine" or "a doctrine of many kinds.
523. "Even of one" means even of one among you two. "In one" means in either of the two positions, namely our own doctrine or the opponent's doctrine.
"There is no doubt" means there is no doubt or perplexity such as, "Is this the path, or is it not the path? regarding the state of being the direct way.
However, there is doubt. Therefore he said, “It is said that this...,” and so forth. But if the Blessed One were to perceive a path everywhere, then why would he ask, “In what do you disagree?

(524) “That by which one seeks—that is, approaches—the desired place directly is the path; it is the ‘straight path. That which is other than this is called ‘not a path’”—this is the intended meaning. “All those” means all those paths taught by various teachers.
Those mentioned in the Pāli as "the *addhariya* brahmins" and so forth: *addhara* is a specific type of sacrifice;
because they are employed for that purpose, the *yajus* formulas are called "*addhariya*. Those who recite these are *addhariya*, i.e., those who know the *Yajurveda*.
Furthermore, those who recite the mantras composed by Tittiri are *Tittiriya*, likewise knowers of the *Yajurveda*. These are the branches of the *Yajurveda*.
This is, namely, the *tittira*. By "chant" (*chanda*) is specifically meant the Sāmaveda; those who sing that with melody are called *chandokas*, i.e., followers of the Sāmaveda.
They are also read as "*chandogas*," which has the same meaning. Because there are many melodies (*iriyā*) therein, it is the *bahvṛca*;
that is the Ṛgveda. Those who study that are *bahvṛca-dhyās*.
Regarding the word “many,” this is the application of the simile: just as those various paths lead exclusively to the entry of that village or town,
so too the various paths pointed out by the brahmins lead exclusively to the attainment of the Brahmā-world and to companionship with Brahmā.
527–529. The letter *va* is merely a phonetic junction (*āgama-sandhi-matta*); thus, the letter *va* is devoid of meaning.
The sense is that by means of this phonetic addition, a mere junction between two words has been made. "A blind procession" (*andha-paveṇī*) means a line of blind people.

The phrase "fifty or sixty blind men" is an illustration of the suitability of that blind procession for wandering around a large thicket of trees. For in this way, they [wander] along the path for a very long time...
“They think, ‘Let us go. Thus they perceive it. “Merely a name” means that because there is no actual object, it is a mere name;
yet, although that speech is perceived by them as having substance, because it lacks substance due to being a mere name, it is indeed base—thus he says, “merely base.
(530) “From which” (*yataḥ*) is an ablative used in the sense of a locative; and since a general statement must rest upon a particular instance, he says:
"At what time": "they entreat" means they long for. It is a praise in that manner because the rising [of the sun and moon] is of great benefit to the world.
For this is the conviction of the brahmins: "By the entreaty of the brahmins, the moon and sun go forth and bring light to the world. But what is to be said here?
Regarding this companionship with Brahmā, which is not directly perceived—
Regarding the teaching on the path for those possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*), what more need be said?

The intention is that they are unable to teach the path even to the companionship of the moon and sun, which are directly perceived. The phrase "where" (*yattha*) refers back to the meaning already stated by the phrase "but here" (*idha pana*).
This concludes the commentary on the discourse using the simile of the Aciravatī River.

542. *Samabharitā* means completely full. For that very reason, it is *kākapeyyā* (drinkable by crows). *Pāra* is the further shore; *apāra* is this shore. *Ehi* means "come. 544. Regarding the five precepts...
[they] should be understood [as such] because the duties of a brahmin, such as the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), are included within them.

*Tabbiparītā* means those things opposed to the five precepts and so forth, namely the five types of enmity (*verā*) and the like. By saying "furthermore" (*punapi*) and then stating "another [point]" (*aparampi*), [the author indicates] that this applies to the other [set of qualities] as well.
[This is] for the purpose of including [them] by way of the simile of the river.

(546) "In the sense of being desirable" means by way of the state of being desirable. "In the sense of binding" means by way of that very state of being desirable, which serves as a binding for the minds of beings.
And although this word *guṇa* is seen to be employed in other senses as well, [here it is used in its primary sense].

However, since those other meanings are impossible here, the extraction of the meaning (atthuddhāra) beginning with "I allow" is commenced to show that only the sense of "binding" (bandhanaṭṭha) is appropriate by way of elimination (pārisesañāya).

"This very same" refers to the sense of binding alone. For when the state of being desirable is predicated of form and so forth, the sense of a "chapter" (paṭalaṭṭha) is not applicable, because such desirability is not intended [in that context].
The same applies to the senses of "heap" (rāsaṭṭha) and "benefit" (ānisaṃsaṭṭha).
Even so, because the sense of being desirable is not intended here, the sense of "bondage" is taken by way of elimination.
For to the same extent that these [objects] are desirable, to that same extent they possess the nature of bondage.

Furthermore, the sense of "constituent part" (koṭṭhāsa) is indeed applicable to them, since they are desirable as constituent parts cognizable by the eye-consciousness and so forth. Moreover, the word *guṇa* is seen in the sense of a "constituent part" in such expressions as "the double portion must be increased. It is also used in the sense of "possession" (sampadā)—
"Incalculable are the names of the Great Seer according to his qualities;
even from a thousand names, one name should be selected according to its quality.
In such passages as these, that [name] is not applicable here, and thus it is not mentioned.
"Cognizable by the eye" means they are to be known by eye-consciousness; since that knowing is itself seeing, he says "they are to be seen.
By this same method, he extends the application to "to be heard by ear-consciousness," and so forth. Even that which is sought after is called "desirable," but that is not intended here;
thus he says, "whether they have been sought or not. [The phrase] "having become desirable objects" refers to those things that constitute desirable objects.

They have become objects of pleasure. "Desirable" means they are to be craved. They are called "agreeable" because they satisfy the mind by way of being desirable. "Of a pleasant nature" means having a pleasant essence. The construction is:
"Overcome by greed," that is, by *lobha*, they partake of the five strands of sensual pleasure.

"In the manner of infatuation" means in the manner of delusion (*moha*). "Adhering closely" means having seized upon and clung to, thereby becoming dejected; hence he said, "plunged. "Reached the final consummation" means...

They have reached completion by way of swallowing and finishing [the food]. They do not see the danger (*ādīnava*)—the fault—in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, both in the present and in the future.
"Escape" (*nissaraṇa*) means that by means of this, one goes forth from or departs away from the defilement caused by the signs of enjoying food, clothing, and so forth;

it is the wisdom of reflecting thoroughly (*yoniso paccavekkhitvā*) upon those enjoyments. Because of the absence of that [thorough reflection], it is called "wisdom lacking escape" (*anissaraṇapaññā*).
Showing this meaning, he said, "In this regard, it is as follows," and so forth.
(548–9) They obstruct (*āvaranti*): they prevent the arising of wholesome states from the very beginning. They hinder (*nivārenti*): they ward them off without remainder.
They enshroud (*onandhanti*): they cover them as if immersing them. They completely envelop (*pariyonandhanti*): they cover them in every way. [This refers to] the obstructions and so forth.

"By way of" means by way of the meanings such as "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth. For these [factors] are said to reach states of being progressively more firm and so on, with each subsequent one being stronger than each preceding one due to the power of repeated practice (*āsevana-bala*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Correlation (*saṃsandana-kathā-vaṇṇanā*).
550. When there is the possession of a woman, a man’s possession of the five strands of sensual pleasure is indeed complete; thus it is said:

“With possessions” means “with possessions consisting of the possession of a woman. And the phrase “without possessions through the possession of a woman” is a demonstration that among the Brahmins learned in the Three Vedas, the possessions they actually exhibit are not even the most gross form of non-possession.
What common ground could there be with Brahmā for such threefold-knowledge possessing brahmins? For Brahmā is entirely without possessions. The intention is:

he is free from enmity toward one who possesses a mind of enmity; how, then, could there be any application of enmity toward him? "By what is reckoned as a mental ailment" means by that which is designated as a malady of mental arising;
thereby, his state of being a malady for the entire aggregate of form is expressed. "By affliction" (byāpajjhena).
"By suffering. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "restlessness, remorse, etc.," those defiled states associated with them are included.

Since, when doubt—which is the cause for non-practice—is present, the mind never comes under the control of a person, whereas when it has been abandoned, there may be such control, he said: "Because of the absence of doubt, one brings the mind under control."
"Cittagatikā" means those who are subject to the mind; therefore it is said, "they proceed under the sway of the mind.

"Not such as that" means he is not one subject to the mind like the brahmins; rather, because he has mastery over meditative absorption (jhāna) and direct knowledge (abhiññā), he makes the mind proceed under his own control, and thus he is called "Vasavattī" (the Master).
"On the path to the Brahmā-world" means on the path leading to the Brahmā-world, which is either to be entered upon or to be pointed out; they point out that path.
The intention [is as follows]. "Having approached" means having approached by way of practicing wrongly, thinking "this is the path" when it is actually not a path;

or else, having acknowledged it as such. "As if having entered a mire" means as if they had entered a great mire many fathoms deep, while perceiving it to be level ground because it was dry for a finger’s breadth or half a finger’s breadth at its surface.
"Entering" means entering the path to the states of loss (apāya) with the perception that it is the path to the Brahma-world.
They plunge in; from that very act, having become submerged, they fall into despair. "In this way" means by the method described as "level ground," and so forth.
"Having become submerged" means having sunk down. "They seem to cross by means of a dry crossing" means they seem to cross by means of a dry river.
"Therefore" means because those possessing the threefold knowledge, having approached what is not a path thinking it is a path, become submerged; therefore. Just as...
Thus, just as they entered the mud with the perception that it was "level ground," so too here in this very existence (*attabhāva*), they do not obtain ease or satisfaction;
that is to say, they do not obtain the bliss of *jhāna* or the satisfaction of insight (*vipassanā*). What need is there to mention the bliss of the Path or the satisfaction of Nibbāna?
This is the intended meaning. "A lamp for the Path" means what is regarded as a lamp for the Path. "A desert" (*iriṇa*)...
This is a designation for forest-dwellings; thus he said, "a great wilderness without a village.

Even for deer, ruru-deer, and other such animals, there are trees that cannot be used [for shelter], as they are impossible even to turn around because of their great thorns. The ruin or destruction of kinsmen is "kinsman-ruin" (*ñātibyasana*).
In this way, the ruins of wealth and virtue are to be understood. Disease itself afflicts and oppresses, hence it is "disease-ruin" (*rogabyasana*). Thus...
The calamity of views (diṭṭhibyasanam) should also be observed.
554. "Born and raised" means having been born, he was raised. They are not entirely evident because of a lack of familiarity.
"Long departed" means having departed for a long time. "Slowness" (dandhāyitattam) is dullness in responding; it is a slow mode of proceeding.
However, because such delay occurs by way of doubt, he said, "due to the state of being delayed through uncertainty" (*kaṅkhāvasena cirāyitatta*).

"Being distressed" (*vitthāyitatta*) means being agitated (*sārajjitatta*). In the commentary, however, with the intention that "being distressed" means a state of paralysis (*chambhitatta*), it is stated as "the grasping of a stiffened condition."

555. In the phrase "u-lumpatu," since the prefix *u-* is joined with the word *lumpa*, the latter has the sense of "lifting up" (*uddharaṇa*). Thus, he explains that the word "ullumpatu" means "let him lift up. For through the influence of prefixes, verbal roots come to express specific meanings, as in the case of "uddharatu" (let him lift up).
556. One who possesses strength in an eminent degree is called "strong" (*balavā*); thus he says "endowed with strength" (*balasampanna*). [Regarding] the conch...

One who blows [a conch] is a "conch-blower"; having blown it, he is one from whom sound proceeds. Only absorption (*appanā*) is suitable, because it is the complete liberation of the mind from its opposites.
What is called "limited action" (*pamāṇakata-kamma*) is that of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), because it does not suppress the defilements that produce limits.

For indeed, that [kamma] which constitutes the preliminary stage for the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) cannot be increased by transcending its limits through the methods of specific, non-specific, or directional pervasion (*disāpharaṇa*).
However, conversely to what was stated, that which is called "immeasurable" (*appamāṇakata*) kamma belongs to the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpāvacara*);
thus he said, "For that," and so forth. In that context, within the immaterial sphere, neither pervasion by way of the specific/non-specific nor pervasion by way of directions is possible.
Some, however, say that it is obtained by way of its arrival; that is incorrect.
For the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are not the outflow of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), but rather the outflow of the meditation subjects (*kasiṇa*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the formless attainment which has been well-developed and brought to mastery is what is called "made measureless" (*appamāṇakata*). Or else, [it is so called] because of its preeminence through the cultivation of the divine abodes.
Others say that what is produced by a conditioned continuum, as well as the immaterial-sphere jhāna attained after emerging from an attainment of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra)—
that may, by this method, be called "immeasurable" in terms of its measure of pervasion.
This should be investigated and accepted.
"Regarding 'kamma of the fine-material and immaterial spheres'": this refers to when there is kamma of the fine-material sphere and kamma of the immaterial sphere.

"It does not lag behind nor does it remain" means that even though sense-sphere kamma has been performed and accumulated, as long as the attained sublime jhāna has not been lost, [that sense-sphere kamma] is overwhelmed and obstructed by it;
thus, while remaining behind, it lacks the capacity to provide rebirth-linking.
"It does not remain" means it cannot be caught, obstructed, or restrained. "To stand" means to be able to stand firm.
"Having struck back" means having counter-attacked. "Having exhausted" means having spent its power.

Regarding the "exhaustion of kamma," this refers to the prevention of that [kamma] from producing its result and the production of one's own result; thus he said, "having warded off its result," and so forth.

"Thus abiding in loving-kindness and the rest" means: by way of those divine abodes (brahmavihāra) beginning with loving-kindness that have been mentioned, one is "abiding in loving-kindness and the rest.

559. "In the *Aggañña Sutta*... they obtained": according to the method presented in the *Aggañña Sutta*, they obtained and attained both full ordination (*upasampadā*) and Arahantship. The remainder is easy to understand.
This concludes the elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the *Tevijja Sutta*.
Thus ends the *Līnatthappakāsanā*, the elucidation of the meaning of the *Sīlakkhandhavagga*,
which is adorned with thirteen suttas.
The commentary on the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* is finished.
